Japan’s annual inflation holds at 1.9% in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:41:38 UTC
16:41:38 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Japan’s annual consumer inflation remained unchanged at 1.9% in August, staying at its highest level in seven months, official data showed Friday.
The consumer price index stood at 102.2, based on 2025 prices, according to the country’s Statistics Bureau.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile fresh food prices, eased to 1.7% from 1.8% in July, falling short of market expectations of 1.8%.
The reading remained below the Bank of Japan’s 2% inflation target for the eighth consecutive month.
The index excluding both fresh food and energy, closely monitored to assess underlying price pressures, rose 1.9% annually.
Among major components, food prices increased 3.1% year on year in August, slowing from a 3.5% rise in July.
Prices rose 4.9% for furniture and household utensils, 3% for medical care, 2.3% for transportation and communication, and 2.2% for culture and recreation.
Electricity prices fell 2.4% from a year earlier, compared with a 0.1% decline in July, while education costs decreased 3.8%.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices edged up 0.1% in August.

Rare Christian amulet holding bible scrap, ancient stone seal unearthed at Turkish site - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:41:15 UTC
16:41:15 KST

A rare early Christian gold amulet and a roughly 3,500-year-old stone seal bearing a hieroglyphic inscription were discovered during excavations by Turkish archaeologists, Turkish outlet Turkey Today reported in late July.
According to Turkey Today, researchers from Bilkent University, the University of Chicago, and Bilecik Seyh Edebali University found the artifacts during the third excavation season at the Turkmen Karahoyuk archaeological site.
The Christian amulet, which is believed to date back to the fourth or fifth century CE, according to Turkiye Today, was found within a small copper container.
Inside the amulet, archaeologists found a thin sheet of gold that is reportedly thought to carry a passage from the bible.
“Inside a copper box, we found an extremely thin gold sheet, only 0.1 millimeters thick, most likely carrying a passage from the Bible,” Turkey Today cited Michele Ruzgar Massa of Bilkent University as saying.
Amulet likely was a protective charm
Massa explained that the amulet likely belonged to a small child, and that “we can think of it as something like a nazar boncugu, a traditional evil-eye charm.”
Such amulets are rare, noted Massa, adding that a similar artifact was discovered in Germany.
The stone seal, which was also discovered at the site, bore hieroglyphic Luwian inscriptions, reported Turkey Today.
Luwian, also known as Luvian or Luish, is an ancient Anatolian language used during the Bronze and Iron Ages.
The inscription includes a personal name and an official title, which, Massa explained, indicates that it belonged to an individual who held a lower-ranking position in an organized state bureaucratic system.
The name on the seal is “Kurunti-ziti,” according to Turkey Today, related to the Hittite stag god and a guardian deity of the countryside, Kurunta.
Further, the discovery suggests that Turkmen Karahoyuk had functioned as a major administrative center at the time.
Two additional copper seals and a clay seal impression bearing a different name were also unearthed at the site.

Iran reconstructing nuclear test-linked Taleghan 2 site after IDF strikes, satellite imagery shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:40:51 UTC
16:40:51 KST

New satellite imagery from Vantor Technologies appeared to show the Iranian regime rapidly attempting to reconstruct the Taleghan 2 facility in the Parchin military complex, the Institute for Science and International Security stated on Thursday.
The facility is located approximately 30 kilometers southeast of Tehran. It was initially destroyed in Israeli strikes in October 2024, before being partially rebuilt starting in May 2025. Israel again struck it in March 2026 during Operation Roaring Lion, and it has been heavily damaged since.
The satellite imagery appears to show the regime having erected a tarp above the hardened buried facility, which has been tied to nuclear bomb testing as part of Iran's AMAD program.
The tarp seems to be an attempt to hide reconstruction activity from satellite view or aerial reconnaissance, the institute assessed.
This assessment was boosted by significant activity being seen throughout the construction site, including various construction vehicles, such as dump trucks, bulldozers, concrete pump trucks, concrete mixers, and cranes being seen at the site in the latest satellite imagery.
The "repair and rehabilitation work began in June," the institute stated.
The first step Iran took in its reconstruction project was to repair and place concrete caps over penetration holes caused by bunker-buster heavy bombs dropped on the facility, the institute said.
Iran reinforces nuke test facility with 'concrete apron' during reconstruction project
Iran also appears to have built a new "concrete apron reinforcement on the right side of the facility," the institute said, adding that it will "provide additional blast protection from an aerial attack."
"Significant questions remain as to Iran's plans for the facility; not least is why Iran keeps rebuilding it," the institute stated.
"What is clear is that Iran remains committed to rebuilding this facility, a deeply concerning development considering the long history of nuclear weapons research and development activities that occurred there," it warned.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:40:39 UTC

Saudi Arabia has conveyed through the Sultanate of Oman a new proposal to the Houthis in Yemen, including a two-week ceasefire and the opening of direct talks between Riyadh and the Houthi leadership.
According to the Lebanese newspaper Al Akhbar, which is affiliated with Hezbollah, the aim is first to discuss the Houthis' humanitarian demands and then attempt to reach a comprehensive agreement by the end of the ceasefire period.
According to sources who spoke with the Lebanese newspaper, the proposal was formulated after a series of contacts Saudi Arabia held in recent days with the United States, Egypt, Pakistan, and the Sultanate of Oman.
The sources claimed that Riyadh sought to convey a message to the Houthis that it was interested in using the period of calm to "discuss addressing all humanitarian demands," and afterward "reach a comprehensive agreement at the end of the truce."
Oman, which has played a central mediating role between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in recent years, was asked to deliver the proposal to Sanaa.
Houthis escalate, seize areas around Red Sea coast
The report comes amid a sharp escalation in fighting in Yemen and rising tensions between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia. In recent weeks, Houthi forces have seized strategic areas along the Red Sea coast, while also carrying out attacks with missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles against targets inside Saudi Arabia.
Riyadh has accused the Houthis of attacking civilian and economic facilities in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan, and Najran, as well as threatening commercial shipping in the Red Sea. In an official statement issued by Saudi Arabia last week, it was claimed that 73 civilians, including women and children, were injured in one of the waves of attacks.
US secretly holds talks with Houthis
At the same time as the Saudi contacts, secret talks were held over the weekend in Oman between US representatives and senior Houthi officials.
According to a Reuters report, the meeting took place at the US Embassy in Muscat with the assistance of the Omani government. The Houthis told the Americans that they intended to continue honoring the ceasefire reached with Washington in 2025 and that they did not intend to attack US vessels.
The Saudi move reflects an attempt to shift from a military channel to a diplomatic one as the fighting takes an increasing toll and also threatens regional trade and energy routes. According to Al Akhbar, Sanaa has not yet provided a final response to the proposal, and the Houthis continue to demand a comprehensive settlement that includes an end to the war, the lifting of the blockade, and addressing humanitarian demands. At this stage, Saudi Arabia has also not officially confirmed the details of the proposal published by the Lebanese newspaper.

Lockheed Martin reveals new secret missile, fast tracks production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:40:39 UTC
16:40:39 KST

Lockheed Martin unveiled on Thursday details of a next-generation air-to-air missile developed to counter threats from China and a new agreement with the Defense Department to boost production as the Pentagon rebuilds munitions stockpiles.
The war on Iran depleted US and allied missile stocks, spurring a push to rapidly acquire less expensive long-range precision-strike weapons.
The missile, known as the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile (JATM), has been developed in secrecy for years as the US military's answer to increasingly capable long-range air threats from China. Lockheed said the weapon offers greater range and effectiveness than existing air-to-air missiles — an advantage against Chinese fighter jets like the J-20.
 
The AIM-260 will be used on stealth fighters like the F-22 Raptor and F-35.
"JATM is one of our nation's most important air dominance capabilities, but because of the classified nature of the program, it's also a story we haven't been able to tell," Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control, said in a statement. "We're proud to finally talk about the extraordinary work behind this missile and how we're working with the U.S. government to rapidly scale production."
The first images of the weapon emerged in May and Australia has announced it will buy roughly $521 million worth of JATM missiles. The quantity and unit price were not disclosed.
 
The framework agreement lays the groundwork for a multiyear procurement contract aimed at strengthening the defense industrial base for the program. Lockheed said it would fund investments needed to boost output under the deal.

Port CEO calls for action after dry summer costs millions of euros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:38:32 UTC
16:38:32 KST

The dry summer has cost businesses in the North Sea Port millions of euros, CEO Cas König has said. At the height of the crisis, one of the two sea locks in Terneuzen was completely closed, while the other could only be used for four hours at high tide. At one point, some companies also opted to transport their cargo by lorry rather than by ship.
This had an immediate impact on the entire maritime supply chain in Ghent and Terneuzen, both of which are downstream of the locks. Ships found it more difficult to enter or leave the port and were forced to remain moored for longer. They had to wait for the lock; then, as soon as the lock reopened, there was a rush for pilots, tugs and mooring crews.
At the deepest point, the draught, the permitted depth of a vessel below the water line, was approximately 25cm lower than in normal conditions. That meant ships had to carry lighter loads or wait longer. Due to the persistent drought, some companies switched to lorries to transport their goods.
We cannot wait and see how things go next year. We must take action
The restrictions were not only necessary for shipping. According to König, an excessively low water level can also pose risks to quays, bridges and other infrastructure.
The impact can quickly mount for businesses. “If the whole supply chain grinds to a halt, you have to be careful that their production process doesn’t come to a standstill as well,” König said. Waiting ships incur fees if they have to remain moored for longer than anticipated.
“We don’t know exactly what the financial impact is for businesses, but it certainly runs into millions,” says König.
The port’s management expects such situations to occur more frequently and wants to accelerate its climate adaptation efforts, with the relevant authorities and businesses, by implementing technical and organisational measures to tackle both drought and extreme rainfall.
The port is home to major industrial employers and production sites that depend on the smooth flow of goods in and out via the canal. Problems with water levels and draught directly affect the economic strength of Ghent’s industry.
“The situation cannot remain as it is,” says König. “We cannot wait and see how things go next year. We must take action.”

Malaysia: Jailed ex-leader Najib allowed house arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:38:00 UTC
16:38:00 KST

Malaysia: Jailed ex-leader Najib allowed house arrest
September 18, 2026
Malaysia's graft-convicted former Prime Minister Najib Razak was granted royal clemency and will be allowed to sit out the remainder of a six-year jail term in house arrest, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's legal department said on Friday.
King Sultan Ibrahim "has granted a conditional pardon" to Najib, "allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest" until August 23, 2028," lawyers said.
The conditional pardon is subject to the payment of 50 million Malaysian ringgit ($12.3 million; €10.7 million).
Billions stolen from state funds
Najib, 73, is currently serving a six-year term in prison for his role in the 1MDB corruption scandal, named after 1Malaysia Development Berhad, a state investment fund he co-founded while serving as prime minister from 2009 to 2018.
In 2020, Najib was originally sentenced to 12 years in prison for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving $10.3 million funneled into his bank accounts. He began his sentence in 2022.
In a separate case, Najib was convicted in December 2025 of abuse of power and money laundering, accused of misappropriating nearly $569 million from 1MDB. He was fined $2.8 billion and sentenced to another 15 years in prison, which is to take effect after his existing sentence ends. He is currently appealing that conviction.
It was not specified on Friday whether the clemency applied to the first conviction affects the second case.
Royal clemency and the law
It is not the first time Najib has received a pardon. Under the previous king in 2024, Najib saw the sentence from his first conviction of 12 years cut in half, and fines reduced. At the time, he had sought unsuccessfully to secure house arrest.
Najib's legal team has not yet commented on Friday's decision, and it is not immediately clear when the former leader will be released into house arrest.
Investigators allege the 1MDB scandal involved at least $4.5 billion in state funds that were stolen and laundered by top executives and associates of Najib. Najib has always denied wrongdoing and has tried to frame himself as a scapegoat.
The embezzlement scandal sparked national outrage in Malaysia and led to the 2018 election defeat of Najib's party United Malays National Organization (UNMO), which had governed the country since independence from Britain in 1957.
The scion of a prominent political family, Najib was long seen as untouchable. He still holds political clout in Malaysia, and Friday's royal clemency could lead to questions over equal treatment under the law.

Kabir Adeniyi
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Nigeria’s authorities have launched investigations after 37 people suspected of illegal mining died while in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in the central state of Niger.
The victims were among suspected illegal miners arrested during enforcement operations in the M.I. Wushishi/Lukoto area of Niger State on Sept. 15 and 16, according to the NSCDC.
Niger State Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago confirmed that 37 detainees died while in NSCDC custody in the state capital, Minna, and declared three days of mourning.
The NSCDC, in a statement on Friday, said some of the detainees were found dead on Thursday following what its state command described as a suspected disease outbreak.
However, the corps' national headquarters said the cause of death had not been established and cautioned against attributing the fatalities to any particular disease before medical and laboratory examinations are completed.
The NSCDC has constituted an investigative team, led by its deputy commandant-general for intelligence and investigation, to examine the circumstances surrounding the deaths.
The investigation will examine the condition of the suspects when they were arrested, their period in custody, detention conditions and medical attention provided to them, as well as other circumstances surrounding the deaths, the corps said.
The bodies have been taken to Minna General Hospital for medical examinations and autopsies to establish the cause of death. Police in Niger State have also opened an investigation.
NSCDC sources told Anadolu that overcrowding and inadequate ventilation inside the detention facility were possible factors.
A survivor identified only as Dauda said over 70 detainees were held in a poorly ventilated cell and that those inside struggled to breathe.
The deaths have triggered public concern and protests in Minna, with reports of damage to vehicles and other property.
Illegal mining remains a major challenge in Niger State, which has deposits of gold and other minerals. Authorities have intensified enforcement against unlicensed mining, which officials and analysts have also linked to financing networks associated with armed criminal groups.

Iconic US talk show host Oprah Winfrey made her first ever visit to Finland this week as she delivered a keynote address at the Nordic Business Forum (NBF) on Thursday.
Although the forum promotes itself as "Europe's largest business and leadership event", Winfrey dispensed with the business jargon throughout her 90-minute speech, focusing instead on a more humanistic message.
Oprah Winfrey shot to fame during the 1980s, when her ground-breaking daytime TV programme The Oprah Winfrey Show revolutionised the talk show format by focusing on self-improvement as well as other more human-centred topics.
That focus was clearly evident during her speech at NBF too.
She told her sold-out audience that her long career as a talk show host taught her that everyone — from presidents to pop superstars to everyday people — are looking for one thing in life: validation.
"At the end of every conversation, I kept hearing the same thing: did you see me? Did you hear me? Did what I say get through?"
She added that there is however an inherent danger in this "disease to please".
"When you do things with the intention to please other people, guess what: they feel pleased and keep coming back for more and your frustration, anger, and resentment don’t matter," she said.
Her message certainly seemed to resonate with her Finnish audience, with one participant interviewed by Yle calling it "inspirational".
Fee not disclosed
Oprah Winfrey follows in the footsteps of many other high-profile Americans who have taken to the NBF podium in recent years, including former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Al Gore, actors George Clooney and Will Smith, as well as Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak.
Securing Winfrey's services was still seen as a significant achievement — although organisers remained tight-lipped about the fee she was paid. Yle inquired about the amount from NBF, but no response was received.

NBF tried in 2018 to recruit Winfrey as a speaker, with Helsingin Sanomat reporting at the time that the star's representatives requested a fee of 1.2 million dollars.

Mercedes G-Class Gets a Military Makeover in Rheinmetall’s New Timber Wolf and Silver Wolf
On September 17, Rheinmetall UK and Mercedes-Benz unveiled two new light tactical vehicles, Timber Wolf and Silver Wolf, at the DVD 2026 defense exhibition in Britain.
Both vehicles are built on the Mercedes-Benz G-Class W464 platform and join the manufacturer's Wolf Pack family, developed to meet the British Army's evolving tactical mobility requirements, Rheinmetall reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The unveiling of Timber Wolf and Silver Wolf is an exciting next step for Team Wolf and demonstrates that the Wolf Pack is about much more than individual vehicles," stated Rebecca Richards, Managing Director of Rheinmetall UK.
The Wolf Pack, which also includes Shadow Wolf and Caracal, is designed as a single fleet capable of multiple missions, spanning:
- command and general mobility;
- troop transport and logistics sustainment;
- ambulance and specialist roles.
Both Timber Wolf and Silver Wolf share a common base platform, with Mercedes-Benz supplying the vehicle foundation and Rheinmetall UK handling military integration and mission systems. The company noted that common chassis, systems and interfaces are intended to simplify training, maintenance and sustainment across the fleet.
Rheinmetall presented the Silver Wolf in a medical configuration, one of several roles the family is built to cover.
Olivier Reppert, CEO and Managing Director at Mercedes-Benz Cars UK, described the G-Class as a proven foundation.
"For more than 45 years, the Mercedes-Benz G-Class has proven its strength in the toughest conditions," he added, noting that the partnership pairs the carmaker's platform with Rheinmetall's defense expertise.
The Wolf Pack will be engineered, integrated and supported at Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land in Telford. Team Wolf is targeting up to 50% UK content, engaging 30 UK suppliers, including small and medium-sized enterprises, and supporting hundreds of British jobs, Rheinmetall reported.
The program is designed to provide support for more than 20 years, with a clear route for upgrades and capability growth throughout the fleet's service life.
Rheinmetall's push into British Army mobility comes as the company deepens its defense-industrial footprint across Europe and inside Ukraine itself.
In early August, Germany moved to procure a third batch of Puma infantry fighting vehicles worth roughly €5 billion ($5.75 billion), an order expected to generate about €2.5 billion ($2.88 billion) for the manufacturer.
The firm has also begun opening a localized repair hub in Ukraine to sustain Marder infantry fighting vehicles and Leopard main battle tanks operated by Ukrainian forces.

Trump administration moves to cut protections for endangered species
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:30:51 UTC
16:30:51 KST

Brett Hartl, the government affairs director at the Center for Biological Diversity, said the move "stabs at the very heart of the Endangered Species Act by giving federal approval to the killing of some of America’s most beloved wildlife."
The Trump administration has issued a sweeping new directive that could see the unintentional killing of protected wildlife no longer treated as unlawful.
A memo from Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) director Brian Nesvik distributed to FWS field offices earlier this week called for a reinterpretation of "take," a term relating to the pursuit, killing or capture of a species under the 1973 Endangered Species Act (ESA).
The definition would now be altered to "affirmative conduct intentionally directed against a particular animal or animals," effectively excluding incidental harm caused by economic activities from being considered "take."
"A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it, because the vessel's course was not set against the whale," the memo says, quoting former Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia in a 1995 case. "Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them".
The document, which was obtained and shared by the Center for Biological Diversity, comes after a previous rule change that rescinded the definition of "harm" under the ESA.
The Interior Department confirmed the memo’s authenticity to the AFP news agency.
"The memorandum accurately reflects the US Fish and Wildlife Service's guidance for implementing the Endangered Species Act following the final rule rescinding the regulatory definition of 'harm,'" the department said.
"Under the guidance, the ESA's prohibition on 'take' continues to prohibit conduct including harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting protected wildlife," it added.
The move has drawn strong criticism from environmental groups.
Brett Hartl, the government affairs director at the Center for Biological Diversity, said the move "stabs at the very heart of the Endangered Species Act by giving federal approval to the killing of some of America’s most beloved wildlife."
"The Trump administration is desperate to annihilate environmental protections, but this incredibly radical measure is both cruel and profoundly unlawful. Killing endangered wildlife is illegal, whether that’s your purpose or not," Hartl added in a press release.

16:30:24 KST

The European Parliament has called for stronger protection of the EU’s external borders and closer cooperation with Morocco after mass irregular crossings into the Spanish city of Ceuta, where 141 people died at sea during events on July 30 and 31.
Lawmakers adopted the resolution on Thursday by 339 votes to 225, with 16 abstentions. The text described Ceuta and Melilla as Spanish and European cities and called for their territorial integrity to be respected.
The resolution follows the Ceuta crisis and comes a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced plans for a new mechanism covering mass movements of migrants that authorities regard as engineered or weaponised.
Ceuta authorities and the Spanish government linked the initial mobilisation to a Spanish Supreme Court ruling concerning people who reach the territory by sea. The decision required legal procedures before such migrants were returned to Morocco. Social media posts subsequently presented the ruling as meaning that people who swam into Ceuta would be allowed to remain.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said criminal trafficking networks exploited and distorted the ruling to encourage people to travel to the border. Reporting found that messages giving routes, crossing advice and information about boats and swimming equipment spread through social media networks in several countries.
Questions were also raised over whether Morocco had deliberately allowed the movement as political pressure on Spain, including over Madrid’s closer relations with Algeria. Morocco claims Ceuta and Melilla, while Spain regards both as sovereign Spanish territory.
Sánchez later said Spanish intelligence agencies had found no evidence that the Moroccan government organised the crossings. He described cooperation with Rabat as necessary to resolving the crisis.
Sánchez separately accused accounts linked to Russia, Israel and international far-right networks of spreading or amplifying false information about the crisis. Israel rejected the accusation, while the Kremlin also denied Russian involvement.
The Parliament expressed sorrow over the 141 deaths and described the loss of life as preventable. At the same time, lawmakers condemned what the resolution called the instrumentalisation of irregular migration as a form of hybrid warfare against an EU member state.
MEPs called on Spain to strengthen its police and security presence in Ceuta and make full use of emergency assistance from the European Commission and operational support available through EU agencies.
The resolution also called for more funding for external border infrastructure and stronger Frontex capabilities.
MEPs criticised Spain’s large-scale regularisation policy, saying in the resolution that the measure acted as a pull factor and sent the wrong signal to prospective migrants and smuggling networks. Parliament asked the Commission to assess the effects of national regularisation programmes on movement between EU countries and the Schengen area.
The Parliament also urged Spain and Morocco to increase cooperation on returns and readmission. It said people without a right to remain in the EU should face prompt return procedures in accordance with EU and international law.
The EU’s Pact on Migration and Asylum has applied in full since June 12. The rules include procedures covering sudden migration pressures and cases in which third countries instrumentalise migrants, as well as provisions for faster asylum and return procedures in crisis situations.
The Parliament called on Morocco to meet its commitments on border security, migration and readmission. It also said relations between the EU and third countries should link access to EU funding and markets with cooperation on border management, migrant smuggling and returns.
Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a separate European Emergency Response Framework during her State of the Union address in Strasbourg on Wednesday.
“The events of this summer show that our tools need to evolve, especially for emergency situations,” von der Leyen said. She said the framework would apply under defined criteria and permit temporary flexibility in standard procedures.
Von der Leyen specifically referred to Ceuta while setting out the plan, telling Spain that “Ceuta’s border is a European border”. She also said the Commission intends to strengthen Frontex, accelerate returns and improve early-warning systems with countries outside the bloc.
The Commission has not yet presented the detailed legislative proposal for the emergency framework.

French PM vows to cut public spending by €54 billion to reduce deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:23:41 UTC
16:23:41 KST

French PM vows to cut public spending by €54 billion to reduce deficit
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Thursday that France will cut public spending by €54 billion next year to reduce the country's deficit. The announcement comes seven months ahead of the country's presidential election, and the government is wary of a new wave of demonstrations with a jump in global oil prices sparking concerns over the rising cost of living.
France's prime minister promised Thursday that the government will reduce the country's deficit next year by cutting public spending by €54 billion ($62 billion) in 2027.
But Sébastien Lecornu insisted his plans did not amount to austerity, as high fuel prices cause renewed social tensions just months before the presidential election.
Read moreFrench candidates race to claim the cost-of-living issue ahead of 2027 vote
In an interview with the Le Figaro business newspaper, he said the cuts will bring the public deficit down to 4.8 percent of gross domestic product excluding defence spending, and five percent including military spending.
The French government initially aimed to cut the deficit from 5.1 percent of GDP last year – one of the highest in the eurozone and above the three-percent limit set for EU members.
But the government acknowledged on Thursday that it will likely rise to 5.4 percent.
The 2027 budget takes "an assertive stance on cutting public spending in a country that relies too heavily on it", Lecornu told Le Figaro.
"It is a political risk, I am not unaware of that. But we are a long way from austerity!" the prime minister added.
The jump in global oil prices above $100 per barrel has led to record petrol and diesel costs in France, prompting calls to demonstrate against the high cost of living.
With a presidential election seven months away and France's economic situation worsening, the government is wary of a new wave of demonstrations like the so-called yellow vest movement that swept the country over fuel tax hikes.
Pensioners let off
Lecornu said retirees would only be asked to make a limited contribution to the cost-cutting effort.
"No pension will be reduced," he said.
"Then the debate on the pace of increases will be settled in parliament," he added.
French state pensions are normally increased in line with inflation.
Lecornu also excluded freezing the level of many benefits.
Public sector workers will not get cost-of-living adjustments.
The government will also let the income tax rate thresholds rise, bringing in more revenue from individuals.
But taxes on some companies will drop as the government is set to exclude them from an additional levy on larger businesses.
Worries about the French economy, which contracted in the first quarter and was stagnant in the second, have led to fresh concerns about the sustainability of France's public spending and debt.
Yields on government bonds have soared to levels not seen since the global financial crisis in 2008, raising the cost of financing the government's debt, which is at 117.5 percent of its GDP, to a level last seen in World War II.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

U.S. Army tests tethered drone on a light squad vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:23:09 UTC
16:23:09 KST

- The U.S. Army's Maneuver Battle Lab tested two tethered drone systems on an Infantry Squad Vehicle at Fort Benning from July 27 to Aug. 7, 2026.
- The drones stay powered through a physical tether, avoiding battery swaps, and the assessment will inform whether the Army adopts them as a formal program.
U.S. Soldiers and Army capability developers spent two weeks at Fort Benning testing drones that stay tethered to the ground, aiming to give small infantry units a way to see farther and keep radios working even when the terrain or enemy jamming gets in the way.
The Maneuver Battle Lab ran the assessment from July 27 to Aug. 7 at the post’s McKenna Field Landing Site, putting two commercial tethered unmanned aircraft systems, known as Te-UAS, through static tests, moving tests and emergency scenarios. The lab worked with the Army’s Air Robotics office, its Dismounted Requirements Branch, the Maneuver Future Capability Directorate and Product Lead Strategic Spectrum Warfare to design and run the trial.
A tethered drone stays connected to a ground vehicle or station by a physical cable that supplies continuous power and carries data both ways, so the aircraft never has to land for a battery swap and can theoretically stay airborne indefinitely. During the Fort Benning tests, the drones climbed to altitudes the Army considers operationally useful, and evaluators timed how fast they could go up and come back down. One test tracked a drone in “follow mode” as it stayed positioned above an Infantry Squad Vehicle-Utility moving through the training area, an Army light transport built by GM Defense to carry nine soldiers across terrain too rough for a Humvee or Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. Operators used the drones to bounce communications signals around terrain obstacles, work around signal jamming, and spot targets from a safer distance than they could on the ground.
“The Maneuver Battle Lab’s mission is experimentation,” said Tollie Strode Jr., government oversight lead for the assessment and unmanned systems team chief at the lab. “We take technology to the field, employ it in an operational context, look under the hood, kick the tires and report what we find to inform programmatic decisions.”
“This is a great opportunity for long-endurance mission sets,” said Capt. Sarah Runion, executive officer of the lab’s Live Experimentation Branch, who took part in the assessment. “Tethered UAS bring a lot of pros to the force: we don’t have to worry about battery life or anything like that, which you see on other drones. It can go through different levels of height, and it can follow you along on whatever platform you deem it on.”
Evaluators also looked at how easy the systems were to operate without extensive training. “In a matter of minutes, I was able to get [the drone] launched up in the air … and then it’s a quick, easy one-step button to bring it back down,” Runion said. “This has been a user-friendly experience.”
Mark Pagliaro, a contractor with Product Lead Strategic Spectrum Warfare, compared the setup to a mobile version of a fixed surveillance tower. “It’s similar to a very high tower,” Pagliaro said. “Having a sensor up that high in their [area of operations] is going to influence [the maneuver unit] and allow them to extend ranges and see targets farther.” He added that the simple launch process leaves operators free to focus on incoming camera feeds and data rather than piloting the aircraft.
The Maneuver Battle Lab is now compiling soldier feedback, technical performance data and details on the systems’ operational footprint into a final report for Army decision-makers. “When we develop a clear concept of operation and employment, it gives us credibility behind the numbers and information we provide to decision-makers,” Strode said. “It answers the ‘so what?’ and provides the essential analytical underpinning to determine if this technology should transition into a permanent Army program of record.”

Margit Sutrop: AI Leap requires technological courage and educational wisdom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:20:00 UTC
16:20:00 KST

Margit Sutrop: AI Leap requires technological courage and educational wisdom
As Estonia brings artificial intelligence into its schools through AI Leap, its success will depend not on how widely the technology is used, but on whether it strengthens learning while safeguarding teachers' role, educational values and the Estonian language and culture.
In mid-September, a working group at the University of Tartu Centere for Ethics published an analysis of the risks and value choices associated with the AI Leap (TI-Hüpe) education innovation program and an AI-based learning application. The analysis describes 12 risks related to the use of artificial intelligence in education and offers recommendations on how AI Leap, the state, schools, research institutions and technology providers can mitigate them.
The analysis was based on the premise that introducing an AI-based learning application in Estonian schools is not merely a technological innovation. It has implications for learning, teachers' work, educational equality, the Estonian language and culture, as well as our system of values. Ultimately, it is also tied to the question of what kind of people and society our education system shapes.
Risks not confined to technology
The 12 risk scenarios described in the report fall into three categories: pedagogical, societal and infrastructure and governance risks. This breakdown shows that the challenges associated with the use of artificial intelligence are not limited to technical performance and cybersecurity. Among other things, they concern the goals of learning and the reliability of assessment, the role of teachers, the sustainability of the Estonian language and culture, data protection and the reliability and sustainability of technological solutions.
The purpose of the risk analysis is not to sow fear or put the brakes on the use of artificial intelligence. On the contrary, risks need to be analyzed so that innovation can succeed. The risk scenarios described are possible developments that can be prevented if the various stakeholders recognize their responsibilities and make informed decisions. AI Leap is already working to mitigate some of the risks, while for others, agreement is still needed on who is responsible for implementing which measures. Responsibility is shared among AI Leap, schools and school operators, government agencies, research institutions and technology providers.
In addition to the risks, the Center for Ethics working group also mapped out the value choices involved to make clear what is at stake in the development and use of an AI-based learning application. One of the analysis's most important conclusions is that the greatest risks do not stem from the technology itself, but from how it is used and from the educational and policy choices that are made.
Will learning become deeper or merely faster?
A study conducted in Estonia in early 2024 showed that 90 percent of upper secondary school students had used AI in their studies, mostly free versions of commercial applications, to complete schoolwork more quickly. When a student uses artificial intelligence to quickly produce the required result, that does not necessarily mean learning has taken place. A student may submit a flawless text without being able to independently reconstruct its reasoning, justify its claims or apply the knowledge in a new situation. In this way, learning can imperceptibly be replaced by the appearance of learning. The AI Leap education program was created precisely to prevent this kind of development. However, AI Leap is not only a program to develop a learning application for students, but also to develop teachers' AI competencies. The need is clear: In a study conducted in fall 2024, 47 percent of teachers said they had not used AI tools in their work.
The Socratic learning application being developed for Estonian schools through a collaboration between OpenAI and Estonian researchers differs from a conventional chatbot. Its purpose is to use questions, hints and feedback to help students arrive at solutions themselves, organize their thinking and plan their own learning.
This is a noble goal. A Socratic learning application could make learning deeper, provide learners with more personalized support and make high-quality learning assistance more accessible. But no technology can, by itself, ensure that these possibilities are realized. At least as important is how the application is integrated into the learning process, what kinds of assignments it is used for, how much insight teachers have into students' learning processes and what support is provided to schools.
The use of artificial intelligence also requires changes to assessment. In the age of AI, academic integrity cannot be protected through prohibitions and monitoring alone. Assignments need to be designed in ways that make students' thinking processes visible, clear rules need to be established for permitted uses and young people need to be taught to disclose their use of artificial intelligence honestly, verify its responses and take responsibility for them.
The most fundamental question concerns the goals of education in Estonia. Education must prepare people to manage their personal lives, participate in society and succeed in working life. This requires competencies comprising knowledge, skills and values. An AI-based learning application can help develop some of these competencies. Developing critical thinking, communication and collaboration skills and a readiness to participate responsibly in society, however, remains the responsibility of schools.
AI must not become a parallel teacher
A second major set of questions concerns the learning relationship between teachers and students. Artificial intelligence can serve as an always-available, patient and personalized guide. For precisely this reason, students may also come to see it as having an authority that it was never deliberately given.
Artificial intelligence is not a teacher, a friend or a moral authority. It does not know the student as a person, nor does it bear responsibility for the student's development. In addition to imparting knowledge, a teacher's role is to inspire students, set boundaries, recognize sensitive situations and discuss values with students — all within a safe and trusting learning environment.
For this reason, teachers must retain their pedagogical leadership in the implementation of AI Leap. The learning application must support a teacher-led learning process rather than becoming an invisible, parallel pedagogical authority alongside it.
Teachers cannot be held responsible for the consequences of using a tool if they lack sufficient insight, decision-making authority and the necessary support. The current solution does not yet give teachers sufficient insight into students' learning processes. Teachers are being introduced to the possibilities offered by artificial intelligence and are being supported in experimenting with it and sharing their experiences. But they also need subject-specific instructional support, guidance on adapting assessment practices and time to develop shared rules.
The responsibilities of schools, school operators, the state, the AI Leap Foundation and technology partners must also be clearly defined. Schools remain responsible for the quality and safety of the learning environment and for protecting students' rights. That responsibility does not disappear simply because the introduction of the application is being coordinated by a foundation or the technological solution is provided by a private company.
AI is not value-neutral
One of the less visible but more profound risks is value drift. The responses generated by large language models are shaped by training data, developers' choices, safety filters, content policies and commercial objectives. The risk does not necessarily involve malicious influence. The impact on values can be gradual and difficult to detect, manifesting itself in the repeated selection of examples, the way problems are framed, patterns of argumentation and implicit assumptions.
This raises important questions: Whose values does artificial intelligence reflect? Are they compatible with Estonia's constitutional values and the fundamental values of its education system? How does the application respond in situations where there are legitimate conflicts of values within society and no single indisputable answer exists?
Aligning artificial intelligence with values does not mean programming a single moral doctrine into a machine and making it binding on everyone. In a democratic society, a plurality of values is inevitable and often necessary. Human rights and human dignity must, however, be protected, harm and discrimination must be prevented and significant value choices must be made transparently and democratically rather than through the default settings of a foreign technology company.
It is particularly important to prevent students from becoming alienated. Artificial intelligence can give the impression of being an empathetic and supportive conversational partner: It is always available, responds patiently and encourages the user. As a result, students may begin to prefer interacting with artificial intelligence even in situations where they need support — or constructive criticism — from a teacher or fellow students. This could reduce teachers' contact with students and their ability to recognize when students are struggling. Education must preserve space for discussion, collaboration, making mistakes and human connection.
Role of Estonian needs to be more than a user interface language
AI Leap is also a language and cultural policy choice. International large language models may not draw sufficiently on Estonia's national curriculum, high-quality Estonian-language learning materials, correct terminology or the local cultural context. As a result, Estonian could be reduced to merely the language of the user interface, while more complex concepts, examples, explanations and forms of argumentation are drawn predominantly from English-language data. In the longer term, this concerns the substantive autonomy of Estonia's education system and the continued viability of Estonian as a language of learning, thought and knowledge creation.
We cannot expect artificial intelligence to produce high-quality Estonian if its development cannot legally make use of high-quality Estonian-language learning materials, literature and professionally edited media content. Copyright-compliant solutions must therefore be found that allow the best content from Estonia's linguistic and cultural sphere to be used both in developing the learning application and in assessing its quality.
Assessing linguistic quality, factual accuracy, cultural appropriateness and alignment with values must be an ongoing process rather than a one-time exercise. This requires the sustained involvement of Estonian universities, researchers, teachers and subject-matter experts.
Risk analysis must become a tool of managing AI Leap
The success of AI Leap should not be measured solely by how many schools, teachers or students use the application. A large number of users may indicate that the application has been adopted quickly, but it does not tell us whether learning has actually become deeper and more meaningful. Creating a Socratic learning application alone is therefore not enough. Schools must teach students to use artificial intelligence in ways that support both learners and teachers. This also requires redesigning learning tasks and assessment. Alongside earning good grades, the goal must be to develop the competencies needed for life, independent thinking and learners' ability to manage their own learning.
In assessing the program's impact, we need to ask whether students' independent and critical thinking improves, whether educational disparities decrease or increase, how teachers' workloads and professional autonomy change, whether a relationship of trust between teachers and students is maintained and how the application affects the Estonian language and culture.
A risk analysis is not a document to be put on a shelf after publication. It should become a tool for managing AI Leap. Efforts to mitigate risks and the program's actual impact must be assessed regularly, with changes made as necessary to the application, its rules of use and the way the program as a whole is organized.
Estonia has set an example for other countries with its technological boldness. In education, that boldness must be accompanied by responsibility and a willingness to change how technology is used based on evidence. The true test of AI Leap is not how quickly the new application reaches schools or how widely it is used. We can call it a success when AI helps make learning deeper, supports teachers' professionalism and serves the goals of Estonian education without losing any of what makes education valuable in the first place.
The risk analysis and its main recommendations are available on the AI Leap website both in Estonian and English.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

U.S. Marines test new AI-driven automated security system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:18:16 UTC
16:18:16 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps' MA-DOSS system automatically detected and tracked a vehicle intrusion during a live-fire exercise at Twentynine Palms on Aug. 19, 2026.
- The AI-driven system needs only two Marines and 30 minutes to set up, replacing the heavier, fixed G-BOSS surveillance towers.
A new automated security system helped Marines detect and track a vehicle that strayed toward a live-fire range during a training exercise at Twentynine Palms, California, on Aug. 19, the U.S. Marine Corps said, marking one of the first real-world uses of a system built to replace hours of manual guard duty with radar and artificial intelligence.
The system, called the Mobile All-Domain Observation and Sensing System, or MA-DOSS, was operating in support of the installation’s Provost Marshal’s Office during Service Level Training Exercise 4-26. When a vehicle approached the edge of the exercise’s alert zone, MA-DOSS detected and classified it automatically, alerting two Marine operators inside a command post. The operators confirmed the intrusion on their monitors and passed the tracking data to range safety personnel, and the live-fire event continued without interruption.
MA-DOSS pairs radar and camera sensors with artificial intelligence and machine learning software built to spot and classify targets across air, land and littoral domains at once. The system processes that data on site rather than streaming continuous video over tactical networks, which the Marine Corps says keeps bandwidth demands low while still filtering out background clutter from genuine incursions. The underlying models continue learning from what they detect, a process the program office runs in coordination with the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office, with the goal of cutting down false alarms over time.
“[AI implementation] is going to help us not just learn what the enemy’s already thrown at us, but learn what new systems may come our way in different ways and how the enemy may employ them,” said Capt. Griffen Hedrick, MA-DOSS project officer for Program Manager Ground-Based Air Defense. “So it’s not just a giant library of what they’ve done before, but predictions of the future.”
The system is meant to replace the Ground-Based Operational Surveillance System, or G-BOSS, a network of trailer-mounted towers up to 107 feet tall that the Marine Corps has used for years to watch over installations and forward bases. Those towers provide steady surveillance but are heavy and fixed in place once erected. MA-DOSS, by contrast, needs only two Marines and about 30 minutes to set up, according to the Marine Corps.
Program Manager Ground-Based Air Defense fielded two MA-DOSS Medium prototypes now in use after working with the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit and drawing on funding from the Physical Security Enterprise Analysis Group, a path meant to move faster than the traditional acquisition process. MA-DOSS is not currently an official program of record, and the Marine Corps described the Twentynine Palms demonstration as evidence supporting the case for further investment rather than confirmation of a formal program.
“In traditional security setups, maintaining that level of persistent, multi-domain awareness forces Marines to spend endless hours fixed to surveillance monitors,” said Master Sgt. Daniel Sloniker, operations chief for the Twentynine Palms Provost Marshal’s Office. “By automating detection and cueing the cameras directly to the threat, MA-DOSS eliminated screen fatigue and served as a true force multiplier, freeing our trained military policemen from passive observation so they could focus on dynamic patrols and rapid tactical response.”

A 23-year-old Israeli man who had recently completed his military service died in a paragliding accident in Medellín, Colombia, after the glider he was riding in lost control and crashed into a cliff in a wooded area, according to local reports.
The accident occurred around noon local time Wednesday. The Colombian pilot operating the paraglider was seriously injured and taken to a hospital for treatment.
According to reports in Colombia, weather conditions are believed to have contributed to the crash. The paraglider apparently lost control before plunging into a forested area and striking a cliff.
Witnesses reported strong winds in the area shortly before the crash.
Firefighters and rescue crews were dispatched to the scene, where they recovered the Israeli traveler’s body. He was pronounced dead at the scene, while emergency personnel evacuated the injured pilot to a hospital.
Investigators from the Colombian Attorney General’s Office Technical Investigation Corps, known by its Spanish initials CTI, arrived at the crash site to conduct a forensic examination and collect evidence as authorities began investigating the circumstances of the accident.
Authorities also inspected the paragliding company involved in the flight and found that its documentation was valid and in compliance with legal requirements, according to the reports. The business was not ordered to close, though authorities said the investigation would continue to determine what caused the crash.
The Israeli was traveling in Colombia as part of the extended overseas trip commonly taken by young Israelis after completing their mandatory military service.
Following news of the accident, Rabbi Levi Vanunu, a Chabad emissary in Medellín, began working closely with the Israeli Embassy and Colombian authorities to expedite the necessary procedures for repatriating the man’s body to Israel for burial.
Israeli officials and the local Chabad representative were working to complete the bureaucratic arrangements as quickly as possible so his remains could be returned to his family in Israel.

Ireland has ruled itself out of next year's competition over the "appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza". This follows the announcement from Dutch broadcaster AvroTros, who are boycotting next year's show as it is no longer consistent with "trustworthiness, independence and humanity".
Ireland will boycott the Eurovision Song Contest for the second year in a row in protest at Israel's participation, according to Ireland's national broadcaster RTÉ.
RTÉ said in a statement: "RTÉ feels that Ireland's participation cannot be justified given the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk."
RTÉ added that they also remain "deeply concerned by the continued denial of independent access to international journalists to the territory". They also said they would not be broadcasting the competition, which will take place in Bulgaria in 2027 after singer Dara's victory for the country in May.
Ireland has won the competition seven times between 1970 and 1996, a joint record holder alongside Sweden.
Eurovision director Martin Green said he "regretted" RTÉ 's stance, but "fully respect their decision".
In 2026, RTÉ withdrew from the contest in Vienna, after the European Broadcasting Union confirmed that Israeli public broadcaster KAN would be allowed to take part.
Ireland's decision to boycott Eurovision 2027 follows that of Dutch broadcaster AvroTros, who announced last month that they would boycott next year's show as it was no longer consistent with "trustworthiness, independence and humanity". It said the competition can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict.
Both Ireland and the Netherlands were among the five countries who decided to opt out of the 2026 competition, along with Spain, Iceland and Slovenia.
It remains to be seen whether Spain, Iceland and Slovenia will follow suit.
Hamas launched an attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the last three years of Israeli bombardment. Organisations including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the United Nations have described Israel's actions as "genocide".
A report published in June by a UN independent commission found that "Israeli authorities and security forces have deliberately targeted Palestinian children, resulting in genocide and atrocity crimes in the Gaza Strip and war crimes in the West Bank."
A previous report last September found that Israel had committed genocide and claimed that these acts were incited by senior Israeli officials, including prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Israel has repeatedly labelled the accusations as “defamatory” and “distorted”.
Eurovision 2027 contest will take place in Burgas, Bulgaria, with the Grand Final being held at the Arena Burgas on 15 May.

French prosecutors and regulators step up scrutiny on smart glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:15:00 UTC
16:15:00 KST

French prosecutors and regulators step up scrutiny on smart glasses
PARIS – Paris prosecutors have opened a criminal probe into suspected sexual harassment involving smart glasses, while French data protection authorities have received complaints from businesses, as countries around the world grapple with the devices’ social impact.
There are several smart glasses available, but US tech giant Meta’s glasses made in collaboration with EssilorLuxottica are the market leader, with a roughly 76 per cent share globally.
Meta’s AI-enabled glasses, which have a small embedded camera allowing the wearer to record discreetly, have been a global hit, selling 7 million units in 2025. Essilor’s latest sales figures point to “exponential growth” in 2026.
But their success has led to growing international scrutiny from prosecutors, regulators, rights groups and companies over issues including sexual harassment, corporate wrongdoing and illicit surveillance.
Some cinemas in Britain have banned smart glasses, and a German consumer advocacy group has filed a criminal complaint against Meta and other companies involved in selling the devices in Germany, citing privacy laws.
The Paris prosecutor’s office told Reuters it had recently opened at least one criminal probe following sexual harassment complaints related to a social media trend of using smart glasses to film women on the street, without their consent, and posting the videos online. The prosecutors did not specify the brand of devices used.
It declined to give more details, but said its cybercrime unit tested the devices two weeks ago to gain a better understanding of the potential crimes that smart glasses could be used to commit.
A Meta spokesperson said the company had “built privacy into our AI glasses from the ground up”, adding that “we will keep strengthening our protections as our glasses become even more capable”. EssilorLuxottica declined to comment.
CNIL, France’s data protection authority, said it had received under 10 complaints around smart glasses being used in the workplace. It did not disclose which brands. It also said it was being increasingly contacted by businesses wanting to know whether they could ban smart glasses at work.
Australia said on Sept 17 it is considering barring the use of camera-equipped smart glasses in government workplaces due to privacy and security concerns, in what it said could be the first ban of its kind.
Smart glasses pose “real challenges” in terms of informing people that they are being filmed and getting consent when needed, said CNIL’s head of economic affairs Nacera Bekhat.
AI-enabled wearable devices are regulated by the European Union’s AI Act and the General Data Protection Regulation, or GDPR, which set rules on how people’s personal data can be used.
Though French law provides privacy protections – including penalties of up to a year in prison or a €45,000 (S$66,000) fine – for recording the image of a person in a private place without their consent, enforcement can be difficult, particularly when content is quickly disseminated online, CNIL and other legal sources said.
A small light in the devices’ frames indicates that filming is taking place, but rights groups said that shifts the responsibility of avoiding being filmed onto the individual.
“Seeing a light come on doesn’t mean that you consent to being filmed, nor to have your image distributed to thousands of people afterwards,” said Ines Legendre, legal expert at internet safety organisation e-Enfance.
Women are the primary target of abuse done using smart glasses, rights groups say.
Ines Girard, who runs projects relating to technology-facilitated gender-based violence at feminist organisation Hubertine Auclert, said the tech industry should do more to prevent abuse.
“We can’t respond to a surveillance technology by telling the people being surveilled that they should be more vigilant,” she said.
“This places an additional burden on these individuals, particularly women, gender minorities and people already exposed to violence, online abuse and scrutiny in public spaces.” REUTERS

Japan raises interest rates to 31-year high to curb impact of rising prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:14:13 UTC
16:14:13 KST

Japan’s central bank has increased interest rates to a fresh 31-year high as it attempts to combat high global inflation linked to the war in Iran.
The Bank of Japan voted to raise its target interest rate from 1% to 1.25%, the highest level since 1995.
The move meant the BoJ joined the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank in tightening monetary policy this month, as central banks attempt to curb the impact of rising prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The Bank of England on Thursday voted to leave UK interest rates on hold at 3.75% but warned they could soon rise amid the fallout from the Iran war.
The BoJ has been raising rates since 2024, when it lifted its base rate out of negative territory. It has been under pressure to raise borrowing costs as the yen weakened steadily against the dollar this year, to levels that prompted policymakers to intervene to stabilise the currency. The Japanese currency weakened about 0.7% against the dollar on Friday.
The vote to raise rates was not unanimous – with two board members dissenting to the increase.
“The tone of the statement, along with two dissenters for the decision to raise rates, leaves lingering doubts that Japan’s central bank will be cautious in tightening monetary policy further,” Fred Neumann, the chief Asia economist at HSBC, said.
“While back-to-back hikes appear unlikely, investors will look for clues as to whether officials are prepared to raise interest rates again in December.”
The drop in the yen helped the Nikkei stock market index to rise nearly 2%, while the Japanese two-year government bond yields, which are most sensitive to monetary policy expectations, fell four basis points to 1.82%.
European stock futures slipped 0.35%, indicating a lower open.
Prashant Newnaha, a senior rates strategist at TD Securities, said the BOJ reiterated its concerns that underlying inflation could deviate upwards from its 2% target, but “we don’t see a smoking gun supporting a back-to-back hike in October”.
He said: “We stick with our call for rate hikes roughly every quarter with the next 25 basis points hike in December.”
Hopes of alternative ways for oil supply from the Middle East to reach markets pushed Brent crude futures down as much as 1.5% to $103.29 a barrel even as concerns about strikes between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis lingered.

MSI-DS debuts a new gun mount made for the drone fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:11:57 UTC
16:11:57 KST

- MSI-Defence Systems unveiled the TERRAHAWK RAPTOR remote weapon station at DVD 2026, calling it its lightest counter-drone gun mount yet.
- The 7.62mm or 12.7mm system can add a 40mm grenade launcher and uses AI-enabled tracking to counter both drones and ground targets.
British manufacturer MSI-Defence Systems unveiled a new remote weapon station called TERRAHAWK RAPTOR at the DVD 2026 exhibition in Millbrook, calling it the lightest gun mount in its counter-drone product line.
RAPTOR is a remote weapon station, a gun turret a soldier can aim and fire from inside a vehicle rather than exposing themselves on top of it. The system comes fitted with a 7.62mm or 12.7mm machine gun, with an option to add a 40mm automatic grenade launcher, and MSI-DS built it specifically for countering drones rather than the ground-suppression role most remote weapon stations were originally designed for. Its compact size is meant to let it mount on tactical ground vehicles and uncrewed ground vehicles alike, using an open standard called Generic Vehicle Architecture that lets different vehicle systems share data without custom wiring for each installation.
The weapon station carries a multispectral sensor suite paired with an AI-enabled fire control system, which MSI-DS says can track, classify and engage both drones and ground targets while filtering out visual clutter that might otherwise confuse the system. RAPTOR is built to plug into multiple command-and-control systems, letting it operate as part of a larger, layered air defense network rather than only as a standalone gun.
“Conventionally speaking, RWS have been designed and deployed primarily for ground suppressive fire,” said David Codling, Business Development Director at MSI Defence Systems. “RAPTOR is different; we have designed and built an RWS optimised for the C-UAS fight in addition to class leading ground suppression and point fire.”
MSI-DS said it built RAPTOR in response to demand for specialist counter-drone systems roughly doubling across the UK, US and European markets. “The proliferation of explosive FPV and reconnaissance drones has necessitated armed forces to either retrofit legacy armoured vehicles or introduce new tactical units into the formation with lighter RWS,” said John Meldrum, Managing Director at MSI Defence Systems. “TERRAHAWK RAPTOR was designed to meet this need, and transform vehicle platforms into highly effective mobile air defence units capable of rapid response against swarming threats.”
RAPTOR extends a product family MSI-DS has built over more than 40 years of gunfire and remote weapon system work, spanning its Seahawk naval systems and its Terrahawk land line, which the company says is now used by more than 40 armed forces. An earlier Terrahawk variant, the Paladin, has already seen combat, with footage released in November 2025 showing Ukraine’s 156th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment operating the system against drone threats.
MSI-DS said future development will expand the RAPTOR architecture into a small modular launcher capable of firing interceptors, rockets and small missiles alongside its gun options.

Russia, China veto US resolution about Iran sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:09:31 UTC
16:09:31 KST

The meeting was held under France’s rotating presidency of the Security Council. The draft resolution received 11 votes in favor among the council’s 15 members, but failed to pass after Russia and China voted against it, while Pakistan and Somalia abstained.
China’s representative to the Security Council, Fu Cong, opposed the draft and called for “responsible action” by the council on issues related to Iran’s nuclear program. He also described US attacks on Iran as the “root of the current crisis” and said sanctions would contribute to escalating tensions.
Fu also referred to the expiration of Resolution 2231 on October 18, 2025, stressing that the Security Council’s consideration of Iran’s nuclear issue had come to an end. Beijing also opposed turning the Security Council into a platform for advancing unilateral objectives and called on all parties to play a constructive role in preserving the credibility of multilateralism and creating conditions for a political resolution to the Iranian nuclear issue.
Russia’s representative to the Security Council, Vasily Nebenzia, also described the 1737 Committee as “illegitimate,” stressing that the snapback mechanism had not been activated and that previous UN Security Council resolutions against Iran had not been reinstated.
Referring to the expiration of Resolution 2231 on October 18, 2025, Nebenzia reiterated Moscow’s position that the resolution had expired and was no longer on the council’s agenda. He said the meeting on the issue lacked legal and procedural grounds and rejected attempts to establish legitimacy by invoking the snapback mechanism.
Nebenzia also said Russia voted against extending the mandate of the panel of experts because it considers the 1737 Committee illegitimate. According to him, neither the snapback mechanism nor the reinstatement of the old resolutions 1737 and 1929 against Iran had taken place.
The Russian envoy added that Moscow had warned the sponsors of the draft resolution ahead of the vote about the consequences of such a move, but said the United States had chosen a path of political confrontation by insisting on extending the panel’s mandate. He described the move as part of what he called the Western countries’ “escalatory steps” over Iran’s nuclear issue.
Pakistan’s representative, who abstained from the vote, stressed the importance of diplomatic tools and the role of the International Atomic Energy Agency in addressing Iran’s compliance.
The UN Security Council’s 1737 Committee was established in 2006, before the implementation of the nuclear deal known as the JCPOA, following the adoption of Resolution 1737 against Iran. The committee was tasked with responsibilities related to implementing sanctions and restrictions imposed on Iran.
Following efforts by three European countries to activate the snapback mechanism, Russia and China repeatedly stressed, citing Iran’s commitments under the JCPOA, that they would oppose the restoration of the mechanism and the 1737 Committee. The two countries used their veto power on Thursday to block the US-drafted resolution.

Hanwha, General Atomics test runway-free drone in South Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:06:21 UTC
16:06:21 KST

- Hanwha Aerospace and General Atomics flew the Mojave STOL drone from a South Korean Army airfield to a tank maneuver route and back at a Pocheon exhibition.
- The companies are developing a production version called the Gray Eagle STOL, targeting first flight in 2027 and deliveries in 2028.
Hanwha Aerospace and General Atomics Aeronautical Systems flew the Mojave short-takeoff-and-landing (STOL) drone from a South Korean Army airfield, landed it on a tank maneuver route, and flew it back again during a demonstration at the 2026 Defense Drone Technology Exhibition in Pocheon.
The maneuver was meant to show the aircraft can operate from short, unimproved sites rather than depend on a conventional runway. Mojave uses a 450-horsepower turboprop engine paired with high-lift wing systems to shorten its takeoff and landing distances, and the companies say the design supports surveillance and reconnaissance, ground attack, logistics runs and communications relay missions.
Hanwha Aerospace said in a statement that it plans to build research, development and production infrastructure for the aircraft in South Korea, with a goal of sourcing more than 70 percent of the components domestically once the program reaches mass production.
“The successful demonstration marks another step forward in our collaboration with GA-ASI and our efforts to advance next-generation unmanned capabilities in Korea,” Hanwha Aerospace said.
Mojave is General Atomics’ short-takeoff variant of its MQ-1C Gray Eagle drone, built around the same avionics and flight control systems but fitted with enlarged wings and a rugged undercarriage for rough-field operations. The company unveiled the concept in December 2021 and has since put it through a series of unusual tests: a 2023 demonstration on a dirt strip near El Mirage, California, where it took off in as little as 586 ft (179 m) and landed in 335 ft (102 m); a launch and recovery from the deck of the Royal Navy carrier HMS Prince of Wales that same November; and live-fire tests in 2024 in which the aircraft destroyed stationary targets. In November 2024, Hanwha and General Atomics launched and recovered Mojave from the South Korean Navy’s amphibious ship ROKS Dokdo off the coast of Pohang, the first time the aircraft had operated from a Korean warship.
That partnership became a formal program in October 2025, when the two companies signed an agreement at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference to jointly develop a production version of the aircraft, renamed the Gray Eagle STOL. Hanwha is investing more than 750 billion won, roughly $517 million, in Korean development and production facilities for the airframe and its engines. Under the deal, Hanwha will supply engines, landing gear, fuel systems, avionics and mission equipment, while General Atomics handles final systems integration and continues building its other Gray Eagle models in San Diego. The companies are targeting a first flight in early 2027 and initial deliveries in 2028, with South Korea’s Ministry of National Defense and the U.S. Department of War identified as the program’s first likely customers.
The production aircraft is expected to carry a payload of roughly 1.6 tons, including up to 16 Hellfire missiles, and to fly at speeds around 140 knots (161 mph) with an endurance of about 25 hours, according to General Atomics.
