China Focus: Along the Long March route, remembrance endures amid change
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:05:38 CST
16:05:38 KST

NANNING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Every so often, Jiang Shilin leaves his home in a village in south China and walks about 10 minutes up a mountain path to visit a grave.
The 82-year-old has made the journey for as long as he can remember. Sometimes he carries a sickle to clear away the weeds. Other times, he brings a brush and paint to retrace the fading characters on the gravestone.
Seven people are buried there. Jiang never knew them. He does not even know their names.
But he knows how they died.
REMEMBRANCE
More than 90 years ago, the hills around Caiwan Village in Quanzhou County, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, became a battlefield. The seven were soldiers of the Red Army, the armed forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC).
They were taking part in the Long March, a 1934-1936 military maneuver that helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the CPC. Red Army soldiers braved raging rivers, snow-covered mountains and vast grasslands, with some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers -- a trek later described by American journalist Harrison Salisbury as "a great human epic."
In the winter of 1934 during the Long March, the Red Army fought its way across the Xiangjiang River in Guangxi and broke through the Kuomintang troops' blockade, but suffered tens of thousands of casualties in the battle.
For families such as Jiang's, however, memories of the Red Army were shaped not only by the fighting, but also by their encounters with the soldiers.
Jiang grew up hearing stories of those days from his father.
"My father told us that when the Red Army came to the village, the soldiers helped villagers carry water and do chores. The villagers, in turn, showed them the way, cooked sweet potatoes for them and brought them water," Jiang said.
Not long after the Red Army moved on, Jiang's grandfather, Jiang Zhongtai, and Jiang's father found the bodies of seven soldiers while collecting firewood on a nearby hill. They buried the bodies where they found them and marked the site with three small bricks.
Before Jiang Zhongtai died, he left his son with a request: Don't forget the grave.
For over nine decades, the family has kept that promise.
As a boy, Jiang would follow his father up the hill before festivals. He once asked why they returned year after year to honor men whose names they did not even know.
"My father said the Red Army fought for ordinary people," Jiang recalled. "We may not know who these men were, but we must not forget them."
Traces of the Battle of the Xiangjiang River can still be found along the river and in the surrounding hills. Old ferry crossings remain, along with graves of fallen Red Army soldiers. Some bear names. Others do not.
Jiang's family is not alone in caring for them. In nearby Xing'an County, generations of Li Guida's family have tended the graves of 12 Red Army soldiers.
Li, an ethnic Yao villager, said his grandfather once guided Red Army troops through the area. After the fighting, he joined other villagers in recovering and burying fallen soldiers under the cover of darkness.
"My grandfather used to say that the Red Army helped farmers have enough to eat, so we should always remember what they did for us," Li said.
Similar memories of the ties between Red Army soldiers and local residents have been passed down elsewhere along the route of the Long March. In Rucheng, central China's Hunan Province, three female soldiers are remembered for sharing their only quilt with a villager who had given them shelter. Before leaving, they cut the quilt in two and left half behind.
CHANGE
In Quanzhou, Guanyang and Xing'an counties, where the Battle of the Xiangjiang River was fought, rugged terrain and poor transport links long constrained local development. Today, roads wind through mountains that Red Army soldiers once crossed on foot, connecting once-isolated villages with the outside world.
Economic development accelerated in the decades after China launched its reform and opening-up drive in the late 1970s. By 2020, more than 100 impoverished villages across the three counties had been lifted out of poverty following years of targeted poverty alleviation efforts.
This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March and the start of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The plan calls for developing county economies with distinctive local strengths and fostering counties that excel in agriculture, industry or tourism.
Today, the three counties are developing specialty agriculture, rural tourism and traditional industries as part of their rural revitalization efforts.
Citrus farming, for example, has become an important source of income in Xing'an, where more than 40,000 farming households benefit from citrus exports. The citrus industry there generates over 1.1 billion yuan (163 million U.S. dollars) in annual output.
Near the Xiangjiang River, Guilin Jolly Cool Fruit Agricultural Products Co., Ltd. ships locally grown mandarins to markets in Central and Southeast Asia. Some local farming households now earn 50,000 to 60,000 yuan a year from growing the fruit and working at the company's factory.
"Our goal is not simply to sell the fruit, but to make sure more local people benefit from the industry," said Sun Kai, a sales manager at the company.
The area's wartime history has also become a resource for tourism and local development.
Not far from a memorial hall dedicated to the Battle of the Xiangjiang River in Quanzhou County, entrepreneur You Wei runs a study tour center that receives about 40,000 students a year. Through activities such as learning battlefield first aid, making stretchers and transporting supplies, students gain a better understanding of what happened there more than nine decades ago.
"The hardships endured by the Red Army on the Long March helped pave the way for the better lives we have today," You said. "We hope young people can also learn from their courage and draw strength from it when facing challenges of their own."
The changes are visible within Jiang's own family.
His father attended night school after the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, while the family's thatched home was eventually replaced by the two-story house where Jiang lives today. One of his granddaughters now works at a company in design and cost estimation; another is in high school and hopes to study in Beijing and pursue a career in technology.
Jiang himself has traveled across much of China and visited Vietnam, Singapore and Malaysia. Yet one journey has remained unchanged.
Around traditional festivals, Jiang still walks up the familiar mountain path, bringing offerings such as liquor, candies, biscuits, zongzi (sticky rice dumplings), and mooncakes. When fruit from the family's trees ripens, he brings plums, loquats or peaches.
These days, his children and grandchildren sometimes make the walk with him. At the grave, they bow three times.
"Thank you," Jiang silently told them. "You gave us the life we have today." ■

Column: BRICS and the evolving global financial system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:05:36 CST
16:05:36 KST

by Maya Majueran
The 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi highlighted a transformation that once seemed largely theoretical but is becoming increasingly tangible: the emergence of a more diversified global financial architecture.
For BRICS and much of the Global South, the objective is not necessarily to replace one dominant currency or financial center with another. It is to create more choices -- more currencies for trade, more payment channels, more sources of development finance, and greater protection from external financial shocks.
These are not luxury demands. They are fundamental elements of financial sovereignty and economic resilience.
Nor should the Global South's search for alternatives automatically be interpreted as hostility toward the dollar or aggression against the existing financial system. Wanting more choices does not mean wanting to destroy what already exists. It means becoming less vulnerable to any single part of it.
What is taking shape in the BRICS framework is arguably more pragmatic and potentially more consequential: a financial architecture built around choice rather than replacement.
Greater use of national currencies, interoperable cross-border payment systems, diversified development finance, and stronger alternative institutions do not require dismantling the existing financial system. They create additional pathways alongside it.
The most practical driver of this transformation is the growing push to settle more intra-BRICS trade in national currencies.
The logic is straightforward. If two countries trade extensively with each other, not every transaction necessarily needs to pass through a third currency. Direct settlement can, where sufficient liquidity and financial infrastructure exist, reduce conversion costs, diversify currency exposure, and provide additional channels for trade when traditional payment systems face disruption.
The significance lies in accumulation. One local-currency transaction will not change global finance. Millions of them might.
Financial multipolarity therefore does not require the dramatic creation of a single BRICS currency. It can emerge gradually as countries trade more frequently in national currencies, connect payment networks, and develop alternative settlement mechanisms.
The new financial architecture may not be declared into existence. It may simply be built, transaction by transaction. This is where BRICS Pay becomes significant. It is being developed as a cross-border payment framework intended to improve interoperability among national payment systems and provide businesses and consumers with additional ways to settle transactions.
Payment networks must communicate. Currencies must be exchangeable efficiently. Settlement mechanisms must function reliably. Regulatory systems must be compatible enough for transactions to move securely across borders.
Financial multipolarity may ultimately be built not through political spectacle, but through financial plumbing -- the payment networks, settlement systems, currencies, and institutions that quietly give countries more choices.
If BRICS Pay represents the payment infrastructure of financial multipolarity, the New Development Bank (NDB) represents its institutional dimension.
Created by the BRICS countries, the NDB provides an additional source of financing for infrastructure and sustainable development beyond traditional multilateral institutions.
Its founding governance structure is particularly significant. The NDB's original five BRICS members began with equal shareholding and voting power, in contrast to the weighted voting structures of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, where influence reflects shareholding and remains concentrated among major advanced economies.
But the NDB's significance lies not simply in lending money. It is also about how development finance can be structured.
Its growing emphasis on local-currency financing speaks directly to one of the Global South's most persistent vulnerabilities: earning in one currency while owing in another.
A government or business may operate a perfectly viable project and generate revenues domestically. But if its debt is denominated in dollars, a sharp appreciation of the dollar can make that debt substantially more expensive to service in local-currency terms.
U.S. monetary policy provides a clear example. When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates in response to domestic American economic conditions, the consequences can extend far beyond U.S. borders through a stronger dollar, tighter global financial conditions, capital movements, and higher debt-servicing costs for developing economies.
The Federal Reserve is understandably mandated to manage the U.S. economy. But developing countries also have a legitimate interest in reducing their vulnerability to monetary decisions over which they have no control.
With tens of billions of dollars approved for infrastructure and sustainable development, the NDB demonstrates such institutions can finance transport, clean energy, water systems and other productive investments.
Progress toward financial multipolarity may come through technical agreements: payment systems becoming more interoperable, national currencies being used more frequently in trade, alternative sources of development finance expanding, and emerging economies gaining a stronger voice in global financial governance.
Every transaction settled through an additional currency, every payment network successfully connected, and every development project financed through an alternative institution adds another pathway to the global financial system.
For the Global South, that is ultimately what financial sovereignty means: not replacing one dependency with another, but having enough credible choices that dependence itself begins to diminish.
Editor's note: Maya Majueran serves as the director of the Belt and Road Initiative Sri Lanka, an independent and pioneering organization with strong expertise in Belt and Road Initiative advice and support.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

Estonia considers delaying Rail Baltica completion to 2034
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:05:00 UTC
16:05:00 KST

Estonia’s government is considering delaying completion of its section of the Rail Baltica railway project until 2034 to make better use of European Union funding.
The issue is being considered as part of negotiations over Estonia’s 2027 state budget. The government is weighing whether to complete the Estonian section by 2030 or spread construction over a longer period, Estonian public broadcaster ERR reported.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Estonia is technically capable of completing its section by 2030, but doing so could require significantly more domestic funding.
“That could mean that we would have to invest more of our own taxpayers’ money in the project,” Michal said.
By slowing construction on some sections, Estonia could make greater use of EU funding, he said.
The EU’s current funding period runs through 2034. Michal said the project would nevertheless have to be completed by then.
The three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – are currently coordinating a common position on the project. The Estonian government is expected to clarify its plans next week.
“Next Thursday, we will set out exactly what position we have taken. It will be a common position of all three Baltic states,” Michal said.
Estonia has made the most progress of the three Baltic countries in building its section of the railway, according to the prime minister. The country now faces a choice between completing construction more quickly at a higher cost or extending the timeline to make greater use of EU funding.
“We are the most advanced and can complete our section by 2030,” Michal said. “But if we build faster, we will spend more of our own money. If we build somewhat more slowly, we will be able to use significantly more EU funds.”

RAF test autonomy projects against US Air Force architecture
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:00:36 BST
16:00:36 KST

The RAF Rapid Capabilities Office is assessing whether its autonomy projects are compatible with the US Air Force’s Autonomy Government Reference Architecture, with Britain’s PYRAMID open avionics standard already shown to work with the American framework.
The work was confirmed in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what steps had been taken to ensure the RAF Rapid Capabilities Office was aligned with the USAF Autonomy Government Reference Architecture, known as A-GRA.
Defence Minister Louise Sandher-Jones said: “Work is being conducted to assess the compatibility of relevant projects/activities in the RAF Rapid Capabilities Office with the USAF Autonomy Government Reference Architecture (A-GRA).”
She added: “For example, the UK’s PYRAMID Technical Standard open avionics system reference architecture developed by the Ministry of Defence has been shown to be compatible with the A-GRA.”
A-GRA is a US government-owned modular architecture intended to provide common interfaces between autonomous mission software and the aircraft or other platforms carrying it. The approach is designed to make autonomy software less dependent on a particular airframe and allow different compliant systems to be integrated more readily.
That has become increasingly important as the United States develops Collaborative Combat Aircraft and other uncrewed systems expected to operate alongside crewed combat aircraft. Rather than treating the autonomy package, mission software and aircraft as a single tightly integrated product, the architecture is intended to establish common technical boundaries between them. In principle, that makes it easier to update software, introduce new suppliers and move autonomy capabilities between compatible platforms.
The British PYRAMID standard follows a similar open-architecture philosophy. Developed for military avionics, it is intended to provide common interfaces that allow aircraft mission systems and individual applications to be introduced or replaced without redesigning an entire avionics architecture around them.
The work comes as both countries put greater emphasis on autonomous aircraft, collaborative systems and software-defined combat air capabilities, where the ability to integrate different sensors, mission applications and autonomy packages quickly is increasingly important.
Compatibility between the two architectures could also make future UK-US experimentation easier by reducing the amount of bespoke integration required when British and American systems are brought together.

Slowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UK | Simon Jenkins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:00:11 UTC
16:00:11 KST

Monday must have been a historical first. Never before have three of the four “nations” of the United Kingdom jointly demanded freedom to vote for its dissolution. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have lost confidence in England. They declared in Cardiff that the unionist government at Westminster is “coming to an end”.
There was no such Celtic alliance against the Normans, Edward I or Cromwell. Celtic MPs have never formed a voting coalition in parliament. The Victorian Liberal party advanced “home rule for all”, but that was not independence and it got nowhere. Ireland rebelled, but it did so alone. When this eventually succeeded, Britain said good riddance, kept hold of Belfast and continued to centralise power in London.
So this is serious stuff. Yet London politics this week treated the declaration as on a par with the Oxfordshire village of Piddington voting to go it alone to ward off the possibility of asylum seekers being housed nearby.
The UK’s only serious geographical devolution came in 1999. It was half-hearted, mostly decentralising the running of the welfare state. But it surged the vote for Scottish and Welsh separatism and fed rather than abated the cause of independence. We can only imagine if ruling parties in Bavaria or Provence or Sicily had opted for independence from Germany, France or Italy – or if California said it had enough of Donald Trump’s US. The result would be political eruption.
What does the Cardiff “memorandum of understanding” actually mean? The answer is not much in detail. There was advocacy of policy collaboration, as on childcare and economic growth. There were hints of moves towards further devolution, of the sort promised by Andy Burnham. But there was no suggestion of a new Celtic state, a British Celtica. The talks seemed to concentrate on self-determination, which Burnham had described as “off limits”, at least in the case of Scotland. Yet this was a man who declared self-determination for the Falklands would be defended even at the cost of tens of millions of pounds a year.
The reality is that these three nations of the union have markedly different relations with England. Northern Ireland’s bipartisan government, a legacy of civil war and the Good Friday agreement, is clearly dysfunctional. As Donald Trump remarked last week, it really should advance toward Irish union.
As interfaith relations slowly improve, a possible majority in favour of reunion also becomes more plausible. Support for union in Northern Ireland is now around one-third, with a majority among the young. Self-determination is not in Burnham’s gift but is written into Northern Ireland’s constitution. Observers accept that it must and will happen one day.
Wales may also have a majority of its under-35s in favour of independence. But only a bare Welsh majority voted for even mild devolution in 1997 and support for independence hovers at 32%. The poor performance of the Welsh health and education services makes self-government ever more alarming, and the generosity of the London Exchequer ever more essential. Perhaps the novelty of the new Plaid Cymru government can transform things, but Welsh independence is at best a distant fantasy.
This leaves Scotland. Here independence is an active issue. The population of 5.5 million puts the country in the 5-10 million band of Europe’s medium-sized states, such as Denmark, Norway, Finland, Austria and Switzerland. “Small is beautiful” appears to suit Europe’s distinctive welfare economies and keeps them ahead of their larger neighbours.
Scottish unionists keep pointing to Scotland’s £25bn fiscal deficit, financed by London’s Treasury and sustaining the country’s struggling health service. But independence is a dynamic not static state. In 1922 Ireland was among the poorest countries in Europe, far behind Scotland. Its economic self-sufficiency seemed hopeless, and for some 30 years it was indeed in desperate straits. Yet by the 1990s Irish membership of the EU and the adoption of a fierce fiscal autonomy had utterly transformed it into the celebrated “Celtic Tiger”. From limping behind Scotland and other poorer European regions, Dublin raced ahead. It has become one of Europe’s richest nations per capita, albeit partly thanks to its status as a base for corporate tax avoidance.
Ireland’s burst of economic vitality in the late 20th century could never have taken place had it remained an adjunct of Britain. Income per head is now ahead of Scotland’s, having once lagged far behind. It grew between 2012 and 2022 by 9% on average, against Scotland’s 1%. Whether Ireland is richer than Denmark is much debated, but the performance of an autonomous Ireland cannot be gainsaid. It is a lighthouse for the macro-economics of smallness.
There is every reason why Scotland could feel held back by longstanding English dominance. Its economy, like the rest of Britain’s, has always been down the queue from London and the south-east. It has long felt cheated of its maritime oil and gas reserves. Trade has been crippled by Brexit. Unionists argue that the Barnett formula subsidy of £50bn a year is fair compensation. But Ireland’s experience suggests that dependence on foreign subsidy is a curse, not a blessing. The most glaring comparative statistic is that health outcomes in both Ireland and Denmark are now well ahead of Scotland’s. The scale of Glasgow’s drug deaths are a horror story.
British loyalist though I may be, if I were a Scot I would have no hesitation. This is a real nation, and has been throughout history. Scotland has a personality and a culture recognised worldwide. Its capital, Edinburgh, is among Europe’s finest cities. Its “Silicon Glen” should be leading Europe’s AI revolution. Tourism is an obvious attraction. That the country should stumble behind its Nordic neighbours is absurd.
Scotland would have a tough transition to self-reliance, as did Ireland. But experience everywhere suggests that small autonomous democracies fare well, witness other relative newcomers such as Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia and the Baltics. Their governments can concentrate on their own priorities and promote their own virtues.
An independent Scotland would be bespoke. It could retain its royal figurehead and Commonwealth membership. It could even honour a “united kingdom” and the king could stay in Balmoral. Relations with other states, EU and non-EU, would be complicated, as they are at borders across the continent. That is for diplomacy to resolve. The issue is self-determination, not convenience.
Burnham is the first British prime minister to appear sincere in decentralising political power. How far he understands its significance is moot. His beloved “metro mayors” are accountable regionally, not representatives of truly local loyalties. They appear as his agents, enacting his policies and enforcing his planning quotas on subordinate councils. He has shown he will stamp the Piddingtons of England into the ground.
That is why Burnham should welcome any Scottish desire for “independence”. It would be the most exciting constitutional reform of the UK in centuries and one that, on current figures, would save the Treasury around £25bn a year – the cost of the Scottish fiscal deficit. It would also release the Tartan Tiger.
- 
  Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

Rachel Griffiths to return to Aussie stages for first time in 25 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Rachel Griffiths returns to Australian stage after 25 years for Clarice Beckett play
Rachel Griffiths will return to the Australian stage for the first time in 25 years in a new play about artist Clarice Beckett.
Next year, the Total Control and Muriel's Wedding actor will star as the artist, considered a visionary of Australian modernism, in the play Clarice at Melbourne Theatre Company (MTC).
It's Griffiths's first stage role since 2012, when she made her Broadway debut in the play Other Desert Cities. At home, her last stage role was in the modern classic Proof at MTC in 2002.
"When Other Desert Cities finished, I swore I'd never do theatre again," Griffiths says.
For the play's six-month run, Griffith juggled her emotionally charged role with raising her three kids.
Now they are mostly grown, she feels ready to return to the stage, to tell the kind of distinctly Australian story that motivated her to move home after 20 years in the US.
"This is a snapshot of 30s Melbourne and how hard it was for women artists of the time to practice and be collected," she says.
Still, she admits to finding making theatre exhausting, which has kept her away from the stage.
"I haven't come across something I've wanted to bleed for until now," she says.
"The pull for me is the times we live in. There's a desperate desire to connect in a world where we are increasingly alone on our own screens.
"This will be a chance to collectively share something very tender, ephemeral and human — something only theatre can do."
But it's not a case of Griffiths being convinced to return to theatre. It was the actor who brought Clarice — by actor-turned-writer-director Trudy Hellier (Round the Twist) — to MTC's artistic director Anne-Louise Sarks.
Originally pitched as a movie, Griffiths had a sense the story could be "sublime" for a theatre audience that could be "perhaps more abstract and ephemeral than a film".
For Sarks, it was a no-brainer.
"[I love] telling stories about who we are and our history and shining a light particularly on brilliant women and stories audiences may know but not as deeply as they could," she says.
Clarice is one of 11 plays in MTC's 2027 season, which also includes a new Indigenous-led adaptation of sci-fi classic The War of the Worlds and a play exploring how then-prime minister Bob Hawke's reaction to a "rebel" cricket tour to South Africa was one of the catalysts for greater sanctions against the apartheid regime.
An overlooked artist
Beckett all but disappeared from Australian art history after her death in 1935, at the age of 48.
For decades, almost 2,000 of her works were stored — and neglected — in an open-sided farm shed near Benalla in rural Victoria before they were uncovered by curator and art historian Rosalind Hollinrake in 1970. Only 359 were salvageable.
In recent years, Beckett has been celebrated with retrospectives in Geelong in 2023 and Adelaide in 2021. A touring exhibition of Beckett works collected by the National Gallery of Australia opens in Goulburn on September 25.
She's an artist Griffiths has long been interested in. In 2022, she hosted an episode of ABC TV's Great Southern Landscapes where she tried to find the exact spot from which the artist painted Melbourne's Luna Park.
Beckett painted Luna Park when it was closed due to the Spanish flu pandemic.
The painting gained greater resonance for Griffiths over the course of the COVID-19 pandemic.
"It's magnificent," she says. "I walked past it every day during our lockdowns."
One of the starting points for bringing Beckett's story to the stage was the spate of interactive digital exhibitions coming to Australia, featuring artworks by the likes of Frida Kahlo, Claude Monet and Vincent van Gogh.
"They offered an insight into art through accessible and immersive experiences," Griffiths says.
"At the end of them though, I didn't really come out understanding the process of the artists.
"With Clarice, we have a chance to do both."
It's also an opportunity to challenge the idea "dying infamous or unrecognised is a tragedy", she says.
Instead, she thinks there's much we can learn from the artist about how to connect with the world around us.
"Clarice died unknown but she got to sit and observe nature every day she practised her craft," Griffiths says. "Her life was lived on her terms."
Griffiths is also interested in Hollinrake's role ensuring Beckett's place in the canon.
"It speaks to the theme of women hunting history to make sure great women are not forgotten," she says.
New Australian writing
MTC's 2027 season features six new Australian works, including Clarice; the cricket play, titled Rebels; and a new play by Andrew Bovell (Lantana) about the loved ones of people with substance use disorders.
Phar Lap: The Electro-Swing Musical, which premiered at Hayes Theatre in Sydney in 2025, also transfers to MTC as part of a national tour.
The focus on new Australian work is deliberate.
"I wanted to continue the mission to put new work at the centre of everything we do," Sarks says.
Kate Mulvany (My Brilliant Career) has drawn upon her experience of severe scoliosis (a sideways curvature of the spine) and related chronic pain to adapt William Shakespeare's Richard III as a one-woman show.
"To play multiple characters or tell a whole story alone on stage, you have to employ very clever, quite virtuosic theatre-making techniques," Sarks says.
"The audience is almost constantly aware they are in a theatre being told a story … It couldn't be television. It's capital-T theatre."
Two new Australian works are by Indigenous writers: road-trip comedy Dirty Diamonds by Abbie-lee Lewis, a co-production with Belvoir in Sydney, starring Lila McGuire and Ruby Henaway; and a new War of the Worlds by Claire G Coleman.
Researching the story while she was living in London before the pandemic, Sarks learned English writer HG Wells was partly inspired by the Black War between settlers and Indigenous people in Tasmania, which ran from 1824 to 1831.
Sarks recalls thinking: "This is a story about us and we need to own that."
Reading Coleman's speculative fiction novel Terra Nullius, which draws on Australia's colonial history, Sarks decided she might be the right person to make a new Australian version of The War of the Worlds.
After its Melbourne season, Coleman's The War of the Worlds is expected to tour regional Victoria.
"It's incredibly exciting to be able to champion First Nations work in the way that we are, and to place these stories front and centre in the season," Sarks says.
It's also a kind of course correction, the artistic director boasting the company has presented and collaborated on more work by Indigenous artists since she joined in 2021 than the 70 years prior.
"The increase is enormous, but it's vital if we want to talk about understanding who we are and our history," Sarks says.
"[We] learn and benefit so much from the artistry and the making practices of these brilliant artists."
Unexpected dangers
Dirty Diamonds and Phar Lap aren't the only shows that will see MTC collaborate with other companies in 2027.
Stereophonic by David Adjmi is a co-production with Belvoir and Queensland Theatre Company (QTC), while John Proctor is the Villain by Kimberly Belflower is a co-production with Sydney Theatre Company (STC).
Both are buzzy American plays making their Australian debuts.
"It's wonderful for us to be able to hold up the quality of our new work next to these international works and for audiences to be able to see and appreciate both," Sarks says.
The artistic director praises how companies working together increases how many people get to see a show, which becomes "richer, deeper and stronger over time" and keeps cast and crew employed for sustained periods.
"It is something companies are needing to do more," Sarks says. "It has really helped us stay large in our season, because we really want to be able to make a very ambitious big offer for audiences."
But Sarks is frank about the potential consequences of that increased collaboration.
"The danger is that over time there will be fewer shows," she says.
"I want us to be cautious as an industry and sure that we are still providing opportunities for artists — and that's why new work development is still at the core of everything we do."
It's a mission that has been successful this year, with the three Australian shows that opened the season — the return of the My Brilliant Career musical, Jean Tong's Do Not Pass Go, and Dennis McIntosh's West Gate, about the 1970 bridge disaster — selling out in their final weeks.
"They're works we created and developed here and audiences were hungry for them," Sarks says.
"That gives me so much hope for the future of Australian storytelling and theatre."

15:57:51 KST

Nearly half of German voters believe Chancellor Friedrich Merz will no longer be in office by the end of the year, according to a YouGov poll published on Thursday, as his Christian Democratic Union faces two closely watched state elections on Sunday.
The representative survey found that 48 percent of respondents did not expect Merz to remain chancellor through December, while 31 percent expected him to stay in office and 21 percent were undecided.
The poll surveyed 1,611 people, according to German media reports.
The findings come as the CDU faces difficult races in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, following a major setback in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month.
CDU faces pressure in eastern states
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU is polling at around 6 percent, close to the 5 percent threshold required to enter the state parliament.
The latest projection by ZDF put the SPD at 37 percent and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) at 36 percent.
The CDU also faces a challenging contest in Berlin, where recent polling has put it around 20 percent, with the Left Party narrowly ahead. Local issues, particularly housing and rents, are major campaign concerns in the capital.
The pressure follows the CDU's poor showing in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won 43.8 percent of the vote and the CDU took 17.2 percent.
Merz has rejected speculation that he could leave office early. He said on Tuesday that he was elected for a four-year term and remained determined to lead Germany through what he described as a difficult period.
What could happen if Merz faces party pressure?
Poor results in Sunday's elections could intensify internal debate within the CDU over Merz's leadership, although the elections themselves would not trigger a national vote.
Senior CDU figures are expected to meet on Monday, followed by a meeting of lawmakers from the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the CSU, two days later.
If Merz were to step down as CDU leader or chancellor, Germany's Bundestag could elect a new chancellor without holding a nationwide election.
The state contests therefore carry implications beyond the regional governments being elected, as Merz's coalition faces questions over its support and the CDU seeks to respond to the AfD's growing electoral strength in eastern Germany.
Recent national polling has put the AfD ahead of the CDU/CSU bloc.

“Possible casualties” – Sārts warns of escalation of Russia’s hybrid war in Europe

15:57:20 KST

As Russia intensifies its hybrid war in Europe, more serious attacks could be expected, according to Jānis Sārts, Director of the NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence.
The expert said on X that reports of planned Russian attacks against European countries have once again appeared in foreign media in recent days.
The reports refer to hybrid attacks, something Latvian officials have also warned about. Sārts, however, believes that “hybrid attacks” is not the best description of what is happening.
In his view, the growing number of such reports most likely indicates that new intelligence has become available.
“As the hybrid war in Europe is already underway, this signals Russia’s decision to intensify it –
more serious attacks, possible casualties and less caution in carrying out attacks,”
he said.
According to Sārts, intelligence and security services apparently believe that efforts in recent months to deter Russia from such an escalation have been unsuccessful. Therefore, Europe must be prepared for such a development, he stressed.
Sārts said that if a larger attack takes place, the key factor determining what happens next will be how strong the collective response is and how painful it proves for Russia.
As previously reported, the number of Russian hybrid attacks against NATO member states has increased significantly, a senior Alliance official revealed in September.
More than 200 such incidents were recorded last year alone,
the official said, adding that this figure does not include routine cyberattacks. NATO headquarters itself faces thousands of cyberattacks every month.
The official said Russia is seeking to undermine political and practical support for Ukraine while preparing for possible further escalation. This includes spying on critical infrastructure and logistics chains, as well as pre-positioning malware in key industrial control systems.
NATO is particularly concerned about changes in the nature of the attacks, the official said, explaining that their “number is increasing, their severity is increasing, and the appetite for risk is increasing”.
NATO is seeking to strengthen deterrence through military measures and better protection of critical infrastructure.
The Alliance also plans to establish a critical energy infrastructure network to exchange security information with operators and support joint emergency exercises, counter-drone measures and cyber defence.
In particularly serious cases, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander could ask member states to use offensive cyber capabilities, the official said.
Latvia’s Constitution Protection Bureau (SAB) told LETA in August that Russia currently does not pose a direct military threat to Latvia, although a number of indicators point to potential longer-term plans.
National Armed Forces (NBS) Commander Kaspars Pudāns has also said that Latvia currently faces no direct military threat. At the same time, the NBS is preparing for possible hybrid provocations by Russia.

Unknown

06:55:57 UTC
15:55:57 KST

Former Malaysian leader Najib Razak, jailed for his role in the country’s 1MDB corruption scandal, has been granted house arrest subject to paying a $12 million fine, officials said on Friday.
Najib, 73, was jailed for his role in one of the largest-ever global plunders of a sovereign wealth fund, the now-defunct 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
Malaysian King Sultan Ibrahim “has granted a conditional pardon... allowing him (Najib) to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until 23 August 2028,” lawyers from Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s office said.
The conditional pardon was “subject to the payment of a fine of 50 million Malaysian ringgit ($12.3 million),” Legal Affairs Division officials said in a statement.
Najib “must comply with all set conditions. If he fails to comply with any of these terms, the conditional pardon will be automatically revoked, and he must immediately serve the remainder of his sentence in prison,” the statement said.
A Malaysian judge late last year rejected an original request to allow Najib to serve the rest of his time at home.
Najib was sentenced to 12 years’ imprisonment in July 2020 in a first trial over vast sums of money siphoned from a former 1MDB subsidiary called SRC International Sdn Bhd.
But a pardons board later halved the term, and his fine was reduced to 50 million ringgit.
His sentence in this case is scheduled to be completed by August 2028.
Abused his positions
Days after Najib’s December bid for house arrest was turned down, the former prime minister was again sentenced to another 15 years behind bars in a separate trial, also linked to the 1MDB graft scandal.
Najib was also fined 11.4 billion ringgit for his role in the corruption scandal, which took place more than a decade ago.
He is currently appealing the 15-year sentence, which is set to begin only after the six-year sentence is completed.
The son of one of Malaysia’s founding fathers, Najib was groomed for leadership from a young age but fell from power spectacularly as public anger mounted over the corruption scandal.
Investigations under successive governments have ensnared him and his wife, Rosmah Mansor, in graft allegations since his loss in the 2018 elections.
Prosecutors said Najib abused his positions as prime minister, finance minister and 1MDB advisory board chairman to move vast sums from the fund into his personal accounts.
According to investigators, proceeds from the fund were used to bankroll high-end real estate, a luxury yacht and valuable artworks, including a Monet and a Van Gogh.

The museum’s project has received several international architecture and design honours. In Lithuania, the project was named the country’s best recreational architecture work in a competition organised by the Lithuanian Architects Association. It was also named Lithuania’s most successful tourism project of 2025 in the Tourism Successes awards.
Construction of the museum began in 2018, and it opened in September 2025.
The project was initiated and established by YouthAid Foundation, a philanthropic organisation registered in Switzerland.

It is the first parliamentary election since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, and the vote - which will determine the make-up of the 450-seat lower house of parliament, the State Duma - is widely expected to see the ruling pro-Putin United Russia party retain its dominance in what is a tightly controlled political system.

Voting is taking place at a time when opinion polls show some Russians have become more anxious about how the conflict affects them. The economy is also under strain and the authorities are expected to use the vote to gauge the depth of society's war weariness as fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian drone strikes roil some parts of the country and businesses grapple with high interest rates, a labour crunch and Western sanctions.

Philippines: Authorities must ensure right to protest as fresh anti-corruption demonstrations planned

Ahead of planned demonstrations marking one year since mass anti-corruption protests took place in the Philippines on 21 September 2025, Ritz Lee Santos III, Executive Director of Amnesty International Philippines, said:
“As people prepare to take to the streets once more to demand accountability for corruption, Philippine authorities must ensure the right to peaceful assembly is protected and refrain from using excessive force. The authorities must not repeat the mistakes of last year’s violent response to peaceful protest.
“One year on, protesters arrested during the 2025 demonstrations continue to face charges, while authorities have failed to thoroughly, independently and impartially investigate allegations of police violence.
“Charges against those who exercised their right to peaceful assembly should be immediately dropped. Any use of force by police must be strictly necessary, proportionate and in line with international human rights standards.
“Instead of arresting activists and criminalizing dissent, the authorities must address the reason people are returning to the streets: they must act decisively and transparently on the country’s corruption scandal. Filipinos should not have to choose between demanding accountability and protecting themselves from state violence.”
Background
One year after mass protests erupted in the Philippines over allegations of corruption in flood-control projects, demonstrators are once again expected to take to the streets on 21 September. The date coincides with the commemoration of the declaration of Martial Law in 1972, which has long served as a focal point for public mobilization and calls for accountability.
In the aftermath of 2025 anti-corruption protests, Amnesty International documented physical abuse by state forces, including violations that may amount to torture and other ill-treatment. The demonstrations were sparked by a nationwide corruption scandal involving flood-control infrastructure projects. Investigations into government officials, senior politicians and contractors implicated remain ongoing.
Lawyers’ groups in the Philippines have informed Amnesty International that over 100 people continue to face a range of criminal charges, one year after the 2025 protests.
While some cases have been filed against government officials, senior politicians and contractors in the country’s flood-control scandal, broader efforts to establish transparency and accountability have remained piecemeal and elusive.
A Senate inquiry into allegedly corrupt flood-control projects has yet to release a draft report of its findings, reportedly owing to a lack of signatures from senators. Some findings were later disclosed by Senator Panfilo Lacson, and documents were reportedly turned over to the Office of the Ombudsman. In addition, the Independent Commission for Infrastructure, established to examine flood-control and other infrastructure projects, concluded its six-month mandate without publishing its full report.

Finland considers sending prisoners abroad to ease overcrowding
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:52:48 EEST
15:52:48 KST

Finland is examining whether prisoners sentenced by Finnish courts should serve their terms abroad as authorities seek more space in an overcrowded prison system.
The Ministry of Justice published a study on Thursday examining the legal conditions for renting prison places from another country. Finland is following Sweden’s arrangement with Estonia, which began receiving prisoners from Sweden in August.
Justice Minister Leena Meri said the option requires further examination because transferring prisoners abroad raises constitutional questions over Finland’s responsibility for enforcing sentences imposed by its courts.
“I consider it important that, because of overcrowding in our prisons, we examine what such a model would require in practice from the perspective of our legislation,” Meri said at a press conference in Helsinki.
No country has been selected and Finland has not started formal negotiations with another government.
Meri said Estonia does not, according to her information, want further prison rental agreements at present.
Finland has about 3,900 prisoners, according to figures from the Prison and Probation Service cited by the ministry. Around 950 are foreign nationals.
The number of foreign prisoners has risen by 76 per cent over the past decade. Their increase accounted for about four-fifths of the overall rise in Finland’s prison population during the same period.
Among foreign prisoners serving sentences, drug offences account for 49 per cent of principal offences, sexual offences for 21 per cent and homicides for 10 per cent, according to the ministry.
The ten largest foreign-nationality groups in Finnish prisons last year came from Estonia, Iraq, Sweden, Lithuania, Romania, Albania, Latvia, Gambia, Nigeria and Somalia.
Finland is studying Sweden’s agreement with Estonia as one possible model. Under that arrangement, Sweden rents space at Tartu prison.
Finland is also monitoring Denmark’s prison agreement with Kosovo as authorities consider the legal and operational issues surrounding transfers abroad.
The government is pursuing domestic capacity at the same time. Meri said Finland plans to add about 500 prison places. Modular units in Helsinki, Hämeenlinna and Kylmäkoski are expected to enter service next year, while Turku prison is due to receive another wing by 2028.
Authorities also plan to increase transfers of foreign prisoners to their home countries and pursue removals of foreign nationals convicted of crimes.
A government-funded study due by the end of 2026 is examining how prisoners who have received deportation decisions should be transferred from Finland to their home countries.

Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian trains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:52:46 UTC
15:52:46 KST

Russia is increasingly targeting Ukrainian passenger trains with drones, thereby threatening the railway network – infrastructure that is vital to the country’s economy, military logistics, and civilian transport – reports Politico.
Since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, Russian strikes have damaged more than 500 locomotives, with over 60% of that damage occurring in the last eight months alone. Ukrainian Railways is losing between 37 and 40 locomotives per month. The Russian Ministry of Defence has acknowledged targeting trains, describing the tactic as part of a strategy to destroy the Ukrainian logistics network used for transporting weaponry.
Ukrainian officials have noted that the campaign has broader objectives. Russia is reportedly seeking to isolate communities near the front lines, sow panic and fear among a local population already facing exhaustion, and paralyze the economy.
Russia began targeting passenger trains last autumn after acquiring network antennas. The technology allows drones to relay signals to one another or connect to ground-based transmitters in Belarus or Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories; this enables operators to control them in real-time—despite electronic jamming—and strike moving targets, such as trains. Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, Chairman of the Board of the Ukrainian state railway operator JSC Ukrzaliznytsia, stated that last autumn, Russian forces struck a train near Lozova in the Kharkiv region, killing six people. Evacuation protocols have been implemented since then; while most people are saved, the country continues to lose locomotives.
Russia primarily uses jet-powered drones to target trains,
a threat Ukraine is unable to fully counter. While the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence develops solutions to combat these drones, JSC Ukrzaliznytsia is creating an integrated transport model to move passengers by bus when trains are halted or hit. Although most attacks occur within 200 kilometers of the contact line with the Russian border or Russian army positions—thereby disproportionately affecting eastern and southern Ukraine—Moscow has expanded both the geographical scope of its operations and its choice of targets.
Pertsovskyi noted that the Russians are now using antennas and transmitters in Belarus to launch strikes on western Ukraine as well. This expansion of the geographical scope was clearly evident last weekend, when a Russian drone struck a train at a station near the Polish border—a station that had recently been departed by European security advisors and former national leaders, including former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson. Although the diplomats were already in Poland at the time of the strike, JSC Ukrzaliznytsia indicated that the actual target was very likely the diplomatic train, which had left the station slightly earlier than scheduled. Pertsovskyi stated that the recent strikes near the Polish border demonstrate a Russian intent to increase the risk for foreign guests, partners, diplomats, politicians, and journalists. The Russians want people to be afraid to travel to Ukraine, as they are infuriated by the fact that, despite efforts to enforce total isolation, Ukraine remains open and connected to the rest of the world.
Yuliia Chykolba, Director of the Ukrainian Information Resilience Center, was traveling by train from Kyiv to Chełm, Poland, on the day of the strike. She said she arrived at her destination seven hours behind schedule, having been forced to evacuate twice due to the drone threat. The evacuation process was reportedly very organized: staff instructed passengers to leave the carriages and move as far away from the train as possible. Passengers then saw drones approaching—the very same ones that later struck the train near the border. Due to the delay, Chykolba missed his flight and arrived in the Netherlands 12 hours later than originally planned.
Ukraine is in critical need of funds to repair or replace locomotives.
Each new locomotive costs around five million euros. Pertsovskyi stated that repairing locomotives is the top priority, requiring spare parts, materials, and personnel to ensure continuous repair operations. He emphasized that while Ukraine has reliable partners providing financial assistance, the rate at which trains are being destroyed far outpaces the available funding. Money is not the only issue; JSC Ukrzaliznytsia operates on a 1,520-millimeter gauge network, whereas the standard gauge in Europe is 1,435 millimeters, limiting the amount of rolling stock partners can quickly transfer to Ukraine. Similar equipment is used only in the Baltic states and Finland. Lithuania has also pledged to send locomotives to Ukraine as part of a winter aid package. Pertsovskyi reported that Ukraine is also cooperating with other partners.
Meanwhile, JSC Ukrzaliznytsia is preparing for various scenarios. Pertsovskyi noted that various operational plans have been developed to balance safety, but a complete suspension of operations is not being considered. Just as Ukraine has no intention of surrendering, its railway system does not plan to come to a complete halt.

Organized crime and drug-related deaths rise Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:51:00 UTC
15:51:00 KST

Organized crime and drug-related deaths rise Germany
September 18, 2026
"We are experiencing a flood of cocaine in Germany," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, from the Christian Democrats (CDU), said earlier this week as a new police report was presented. "We are experiencing a record number of drug-related deaths. We are seeing children being exploited as criminals."
Standing alongside Dobrindt, Holger Münch, the president of the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), and Hendrik Streeck, the German government's drug and addiction commissioner, presented findings described as alarming.
Last year, 10 tons of cocaine were seized, two thirds of that amount in German ports. And 2,150 people lost their lives because of drug use, 13 more than in 2024.
Profits generated from drugs by international organized crime networks are often invested in real estate to conceal their origin. Münch said that 195 cases of money laundering, amounting to almost €1.4 billion (ca. $1.6 billion) had been investigated in 2025.
"They [the criminals] use their considerable financial clout to bribe and to exert influence," he said. "And they launder the money and funnel it into the legal economic system."
He added that the most widely used drug was cocaine and that it posed a threat to the state, the economy and society as a whole.
'There is blood on every gram of cocaine consumed for pleasure'
"It is not only the state that is being damaged," said Streeck. "Above all, it is people who are being damaged."
About 83% of the drug-related deaths concerned men, whose average age was 41.
"They are all customers of a market that deals in deadly substances and is driven by violence, environmental destruction, extortion and exploitation," said Streeck, who trained as a doctor.
He insisted that there should be zero tolerance for those who profited from addiction and zero indifference to those suffering from it. His focus is on preventative measures, which include a public awareness campaign about the impact on health and the environment.
He explained that in some countries, rainforests were being cleared to make way for cocaine production. Streek pointed out that toxic substances used for processing the drug, such as kerosene or battery acid, ended up in the soil and water. Farmers and their families were blackmailed. He lamented the fact that cocaine had become more popular in Germany.
"There is blood on every gram of cocaine consumed for pleasure," the drug and addiction commissioner stated.
Digitalization of drugs trade
Streeck added that the situation had changed significantly in recent years and the market had gone digital.
"Dealers are no longer on the street corner; they're on the phone. For example, people can order so-called 'cocaine taxis' [cars that deliver drugs to any location] via QR code," he said.
"What is particularly alarming is that criminal groups are recruiting minors through social media or gaming platforms," he added. "Organized criminals look for recruits in the places where young people spend their free time."
Münch noted that this development posed a particular challenge for German and international law enforcement agencies. He said that, more and more, the cliched image of organized crime — discretion, isolation and closed structures — was a thing of the past. The fact that people can purchase criminal services on the dark web represents a paradigm shift, according to Münch: "It's not just a question of who commits a crime, but of who ordered it, who financed it, who is profiting from it?"
Moreover, there is a suspicion on the part of investigators that state actors are increasingly involved in opaque crime activities, launching attacks as "hybrid threats."
Münch said that "money laundering, corruption and violence can contribute to social destabilization."
In 2025, there were about 600 investigations into cases of organized crime in Germany, which has been the average for the past five years. The German police considers one of its major successes to be the shutdown of the Archetyp Market, an online drug marketplace on the darknet. Its administrator was arrested in June 2025. He had overseen the sale of cocaine, heroin, cannabis and other drugs, amounting to 250 million. When the platform was shut down there were 3,200 registered sellers and 612,000 customer accounts according to the police.
This article was translated from German.

A KLM flight en route to Curaçao was forced to return to Amsterdam on Thursday evening after a passenger’s powerbank caught fire.
Flight KL735 was five and a half hours into its trip when the electronic device started emitting smoke.
Crew members were able to extinguish the fire and no one was injured, a KLM spokesperson said.

Airlines have special rules for powerbanks to reduce the fire risk. Passengers may only bring two on board, with a capacity of 100 Wh or less. KLM bans travellers from storing powerbanks in the overhead bins and from charging them on board.

‘Outrageous lies’: How Israeli voters are shrugging off Western sanctions
New sanctions highlight Israel’s isolation, yet analysts say they won’t sway voters before October’s elections.
Israeli politicians reacted to sanctions by states including the United Kingdom, France, and Canada on the country’s illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank with self-righteous anger. But what is the latest example of Israel’s international isolation brought on by its treatment of the Palestinian people has not been influential in swaying the electorate in the run-up to October’s elections, analysts tell Al Jazeera.
Responding to the UK Foreign Minister Ed Miliband’s accusation that Israelis were ethnically cleansing the occupied West Bank, Israel’s Gideon Saar accused his counterpart of spreading “outrageous lies” and attempting to interfere in the election through foreign pressure.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog also condemned the measures, branding them a “gross interference in the democratic elections” of Israel.
But, in reality, the majority of Jewish Israelis have supported their country’s genocidal war in Gaza and the occupation of the West Bank.
A poll from August, published as the death toll for Palestinians killed in the West Bank had already reached 76 this year, showed that more than half of Jewish Israelis supported retaining the illegal settlements as part of any future agreement on a Palestinian state, while nearly 40 percent supported annexing the territory in defiance of international law.
“People just don’t care that settlements are illegal,” Israeli political analyst Ori Goldberg said.
”Ed Miliband expressed a number of laudable sentiments when announcing the measures,” Goldberg said, referencing the UK foreign secretary’s references to his own Jewish heritage when announcing the cessation of trade with Israel’s illegal outposts. “But we’re at the stage where Israelis aren’t even interested in the truth so much as they are the sentiment.”
Little political impact
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu goes into the elections at serious risk of losing, with many polls predicting that a coalition of parties opposed to him could win the majority in Israel’s parliament.
But it will not be issues like the settlement-related sanctions that will lose him votes, analysts said.
Public backing for the “government and opposition blocs are pretty hardened, and nobody is going to switch from one side to the other over sanctions arising from [the settlements],” Michael Koplow, chief policy officer at the Israeli Policy Forum, said. He added that the sanctions were unlikely to weigh as heavily with the electorate as “this government’s record and the related feelings people have about Netanyahu”.
“When people were asked what would determine their vote, security came first,” Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani said.
“I think there are several mechanisms operating simultaneously,” he added.
First, he said, is the normalisation of the settlements. In Israeli public discourse, the occupied West Bank is increasingly referred to by the biblical name “Judea and Samaria” – a shift he said was becoming institutionalised.
“Second, external sanctions don’t necessarily translate into domestic political costs,” Shenhav-Shahrabani said. “And perhaps most importantly, politically foreign pressure can be absorbed into an existing Israeli narrative [of anti-Semitism] rather than [changing how the issue itself is understood].”
No criticism of the voters
None of Israel’s most prominent politicians has criticised the government for its support of the settlements in defiance of international condemnation. Yair Lapid, a former prime minister and one of Netanyahu’s leading opponents, has, instead, focused his ire on the countries condemning Israel. “Imposing boycotts and sanctions on Israel is a grave mistake,” he said. “This is a wrong and dangerous policy, at the wrong time and for the wrong reasons.”
Another of Netanyahu’s principal rivals, Gadi Eisenkot – whose Yashar Party manifesto does not mention either the West Bank or Gaza – has declined to speak on the sanctions directly. Netanyahu has also yet to comment on the sanctions publicly, despite his Likud party having championed settlement expansion for decades.
“The sanctions haven’t particularly hurt Netanyahu, at least not as far as we can see in terms of direct influence on … polling,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, a pollster and public opinion researcher based in Tel Aviv.
Instead, the focus has been on other elements of an eventful electoral cycle, including the emergence of new challengers to Netanyahu on the right.
“We aren’t seeing any real backlash from the sanctions,” Scheindlin said. “Instead, it’s just getting filtered through what people already think of him – his critics dislike him even more, and his supporters basically say, ‘Well, the world hates us no matter what.'”

Mysterious Bolivian 'weird cat' recognized as new species, marking first discovered in over century
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:47:13 UTC
15:47:13 KST

Scientists have identified a new species of wild cat living in Bolivia’s cloud forests, the first new living feline species described in more than a century, according to research published Thursday in the journal Current Biology.
The small, spotted cat, named Leopardus tilcayo, lives in the Yungas forest on the eastern slopes of the Andes. The animal is smaller than an average domestic cat and bears dark, leopard-like rosettes across its light-brown coat, National Geographic reported.
Its path to scientific recognition began in 2016, when Bolivian biologist Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz received a call from the Senda Verde wildlife sanctuary about what staff described as an unusual cat.
A local man had reportedly found the animal as a kitten on a road near a forest and brought it home, initially believing it was a domestic cat. After about a year, its wild behavior convinced him to transfer it to the sanctuary.
Nogales-Ascarrunz, founder of the Bolivian Felids Research Program, initially believed the animal belonged to Leopardus tigrinus, one of a group commonly known as tiger cats. She photographed the animal extensively but did not immediately suspect that it represented a species unknown to science.
Several years later, while preparing a guide to Bolivia’s wild cats, she noticed that the animal’s markings differed substantially from those of tiger cats found in neighboring Brazil. In particular, its rosettes appeared considerably larger.
That observation ultimately led Nogales-Ascarrunz and an international team of researchers to investigate its genetics. The scientists compared complete genomes from 38 animals belonging to the Leopardus genus, according to National Geographic.
The analysis placed the Bolivian animal on a distinct branch of the feline family tree and indicated that its lineage separated from related tiger cats roughly 1.4 million years ago.
The name was chosen in recognition of the people of the region
Researchers proposed the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo in recognition of the name people in the region traditionally used for the cat.
Nogales-Ascarrunz told National Geographic that when researchers asked residents why they called the animal “tilcayo,” they said the name had simply been passed down through generations. Its precise linguistic origin remains unclear.
Scientists currently know that the species inhabits Bolivia’s Yungas, a humid forest ecosystem where the Andes descend toward the Amazon basin. Beyond that, much of its biology remains unknown.
Separating one widespread animal into several species can have immediate conservation implications.
If a population previously considered part of a species distributed over a vast territory is instead recognized as an independent species confined to a limited habitat, its conservation status may look dramatically different.
“If you think [the tiger cat] is a single thing from southern Brazil all the way to Costa Rica, you’re going to find it’s not endangered,” Eizirik told National Geographic. “But if we find that it’s not a single thing, but actually five things, each of them must be assessed separately.”
Scientists do not yet know how many L. tilcayo individuals remain in the wild, making it difficult to assess its conservation status.
The discovery also shows why small wild cats can remain scientifically obscure even when local communities have long known they exist. Unlike lions, tigers and other heavily studied members of the cat family, smaller felids are often elusive, nocturnal and difficult to distinguish from closely related species.
For Nogales-Ascarrunz, the importance of the discovery extends beyond taxonomy.
“Our world is extremely complex,” she told National Geographic. “Sometimes we think that most of it is known, that there's not a whole lot to discover, but in fact, it's the other way around.”
Even among mammals as familiar as cats, she said, species may still be waiting for science to recognize them.
“Even in the cats, there are things out there that are undescribed, things that people haven't found yet,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “So let's go out and find them and protect them.”

====================================================================================================

Israel can reject NAZA’s claims without ignoring Gaza’s suffering - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:47:02 UTC
15:47:02 KST

How many people in Israel, or even around the world, could name the winner of the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival last year? Probably almost no one.
Venice is one of the world’s most prestigious film festivals, but it is an industry event – a place where filmmakers, directors, and producers showcase their latest projects, generate buzz, and hope that distributors and critics take notice. Most of what happens there never reaches the wider public.
Then came NAZA, the documentary by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor that won the Special Jury Prize at Venice this weekend and almost immediately became the center of a political and public storm in Israel.
The film examines allegations surrounding Israeli military targeting in Gaza, including anonymous testimony from purported soldiers and intelligence officers claiming that the IDF permits “mass killing” with AI-powered tools.
And if the goal of the Israeli officials attacking the film was to prevent people from seeing it, they accomplished exactly the opposite. Culture and Sports Minister Miki Zohar’s announcement that he would seek to revoke the filmmakers’ citizenship only increased the world’s attention to the film. He can be sure that now viewer numbers will go up exponentially.
What Zohar fails to understand is that this is not the way to counter the false allegations raised in the movie. Like Zohar, and almost everyone else attacking the film, I have not seen it (it is not available yet in Israel), and so it is hard to start to dissect the details.
Nevertheless, we can argue about the general way the IDF fights – in my view, in one of the most humane ways in modern warfare – and against the perverse claims of genocide that have been leveled for the last three years against Israel.
In other words, you can hate the film, believe it is distorted, unfair, or even defamatory. You can challenge every allegation and even take the filmmakers to court and sue them for libel. But threatening to strip Israelis of their citizenship because they made a film critical of their country is something else entirely.
Not only does such a move not make Israel look stronger, but it creates the impression that we have something to hide and are afraid of criticism. It makes it seem like we fear to stand up for our truth and what we believe in.
Doing this undermines one of the basic values Israel has always insisted distinguishes it from its enemies: that as a vibrant democracy, we allow people to say things that the government – and many citizens – might find outrageous.
This is not how a side confident in its case should behave. Someone wants to make a movie accusing the IDF of war crimes? Then fight back. Explain why the claims are wrong.
Show how the combatant-civilian ratio is historically low when compared to any urban warfare conflict with remotely similar conditions. Produce a film showing your truth and the other side of what happened in Gaza. Make the case. But don’t try to silence the criticism. Confront it head-on.
But the political response was only one part of the problem. Then came the IDF’s response.
Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir ordered the establishment of a multidisciplinary, interorganizational team led by the head of the IDF Planning Directorate to develop ways to counter what the military described as false allegations against the IDF and its soldiers.
I read that announcement and had one question: Where has Zamir been for the last three years?
Did nobody in the IDF, the Prime Minister’s Office, or the Foreign Ministry read an American or European newspaper over the last three years? Did nobody watch CNN or the BBC? Did nobody see the way Israel and the IDF were being portrayed around the world?
Now, because of a movie, the IDF is creating a multidisciplinary team? This should have been done years ago. Israel needed a coordinated effort to collect facts, release information, quickly investigate accusations, and challenge false claims in real time.
A responsible country doesn’t wait for a movie to come out before realizing it has an information problem. It identifies the problem early on (the massive protests around the world should have helped them wake up) and builds the tools needed to confront it.
But even if Israel had handled the public diplomacy surrounding the war perfectly, NAZA would still raise a deeper and far more uncomfortable question – one that Israelis need to confront regardless of whether the movie itself is accurate, distorted, or something in between.
It is a question about Gaza itself.
A few months into the war, in a meeting with a senior executive at one of Israel’s leading television stations, I asked her a simple question: Why don’t we see on the evening news what is happening inside Gaza? She answered that we did, since almost every night there was footage from IDF operations there.
I explained that what I meant was not what the IDF was doing in Gaza but what was happening to Gaza.
To her credit, she paused before answering.
“We have limited time on the news,” she said. “We have hostages, dead soldiers, evacuees from the north and the south, and protests across the country. We can’t show everything.”
I was not arguing that Israeli television had some ideological obligation to generate sympathy for Gaza. My point was simpler: Israelis were forced into a war that they did not want and were now fighting in one of the most just wars in the nation’s history.
In addition, what was happening in Gaza was Hamas’s fault. They embedded themselves in civilian infrastructure since they wanted Israel to attack and kill as many civilians as possible. It was for this reason that Israel, for almost 20 years, held back from launching such an operation despite fighting a conflict almost every two years since the withdrawal from the Gaza Strip in 2005.
But none of that meant that Israelis should ignore the full scope of the war. We can believe that Israel was 100% justified in responding the way it did to October 7 and in fighting Hamas with the aim of its elimination, while also recognizing the consequences of that war.
To understand the conflict we are fighting, we also need to understand what it has done to the people living on the other side. War is terrible. That we know. It is why we tried for so long to avoid it. But understanding a war means looking not only at why it was fought and what our soldiers were asked to do, but also at what happened as a result.
Importance of recognising the suffering of the other side
Our sympathy will obviously be first and foremost for ourselves. That is the way it should be. But that does not mean we should ignore what is happening on the other side, including the pain and suffering there as well. That, too, is part of the story.
Recognizing that does not mean accepting the accusations against Israel. It does not mean agreeing with claims that Israel committed genocide or deliberately targeted civilians. I have repeatedly explained why I believe those accusations are baseless and false.
But rejecting those accusations does not require us to deny what happened in Gaza. It simply means recognizing what happened.
We can believe that the war was forced upon Israel by Hamas and that Hamas bears responsibility for the devastation because of the way it fights and embeds itself in civilian infrastructure. We can believe that after October 7, Israel could no longer tolerate a genocidal terrorist army on its border with a declared desire to carry out another massacre.
We can remain committed to the mission that has yet to be accomplished to ensure that Hamas no longer exists and at the same time, we can look at what happened in Gaza and acknowledge the tragedy.
Those two thoughts can coexist.
In many ways, that tension helps explain why NAZA has touched such a raw nerve. Whatever one thinks of the film itself, it forces Israelis to look directly at something that, as a society, we have largely managed not to look at for nearly three years.
Our own suffering has understandably dominated our consciousness since October 7. We suffered the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust, saw entire communities destroyed, people killed in the worst ways known to man, and hostages starved in complete darkness inside tunnels.
That trauma is real. But recognizing what subsequently happened to civilians in Gaza does not diminish it. It does not create some moral equivalence between October 7 and the war that followed. It simply requires us to look at the full picture.
Part of the reason that has been so difficult is leadership. Israeli political leaders do not speak publicly about Palestinian suffering during the war. Even acknowledging it is viewed as an admission of guilt rather than a recognition of the human consequences of war.
But leadership is only part of the explanation. There is another reason Israelis have struggled to look at Gaza: For much of the public, the war does not feel over.
All of the hostages, living and dead, have returned home, but Israeli soldiers remain deployed in Gaza, and Israeli strikes continue. Hamas has yet to disarm, and significant parts of President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan for Gaza remain unfinished. The objective of the war – Hamas’s destruction – has yet to be met.
As a result, the wound of October 7 therefore remains open, and when your own wound is still open, it is difficult to look at somebody else’s.
But eventually Israel will have to. Part of recovering from October 7 will mean confronting what was done to us: the failures that allowed the attack to happen, the trauma that followed, the lives that were lost, and the damage this war inflicted on Israeli society.
Recovery will also require something else: the confidence to look honestly at what happened on the other side without believing that doing so somehow weakens our own story.
What it means is understanding that a country can believe deeply in the justice of its cause and still recognize the consequences of the war it was forced to fight.
Israel is strong enough to do both.
