NAZA, the money trail, and what the film leaves out about October 7 - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:46:53 UTC
15:46:53 KST

When a film accuses Israel of calculated mass killing, wins the Venice Special Jury Prize, and receives a nearly 25-minute standing ovation, we should examine not only the screen, but who produced it, which investigations it relies on, and who funded the organizations behind them.
In other words: follow the money.
NAZA, directed by Israelis Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is listed by the Venice Biennale as a production of The Guardian and JW Films. The festival synopsis says the film reveals systems behind what it calls Israel’s “calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.”
The filmmakers state that many revelations were first published by The Guardian with +972 Magazine and Local Call.
The film relies on 24 anonymous Israeli military and intelligence personnel whose identities are concealed, faces obscured, and voices altered. Viewers cannot independently determine their positions, what they witnessed, or whether they were positioned to know the strategic decisions they describe.
The IDF categorically rejected the allegations, saying it could not verify the identities, roles, or relevant knowledge of the anonymous sources and disputing claims about how targeting decisions are made.
But the journalistic ecosystem behind the film also deserves scrutiny.
+972 Magazine is published by the nonprofit 972 Advancement of Citizen Journalism. The same nonprofit co-publishes the Hebrew-language Local Call (Sicha Mekomit), with Just Vision. Both publicly describe this partnership.
Now follow the financial trail.
According to +972’s donor disclosures, Local Call received Open Society Foundations grants every year from 2018 through 2024, totaling $562,900.
Open Society Foundations were founded by George Soros, who, according to the organization, has given them more than $32 billion of his personal fortune since 1984.
The documented chain is real, but must be described precisely: Soros founded and financed Open Society; Open Society granted hundreds of thousands of dollars to Local Call; and NAZA, according to its directors, draws partly on investigations published by Local Call, +972 Magazine, and The Guardian.
That does not prove Soros, Open Society Foundations, or another donor directly financed NAZA. I have seen no evidence of such a link. Nor does funding itself prove journalism false.
But funding and institutional context are not irrelevant.
Open Society has also taken clear public positions on the Israel-Hamas War. On November 1, 2023, it unequivocally condemned Hamas’s October 7 attack, calling its cruelty heartbreaking and inexcusable.
In the same statement, however, it said Israel’s campaign was becoming “increasingly indiscriminate” and argued that restrictions on electricity, water, fuel and food, together with bombing, were likely to be judged as collective punishment.
In December 2023, Open Society published a fact sheet saying it supports human-rights organizations documenting what it describes as Israeli abuses and advocating accountability, alongside policy and civil-society groups.
It reported providing $14.3 million in 2023 to groups working on Israel and Palestine, excluding an additional $3.3 million emergency commitment after October 7. The Foundations also say they do not support Hamas and their grantees are committed to nonviolence.
On May 20, 2024, Open Society welcomed the ICC prosecutor’s decision to seek arrest warrants for senior Israeli and Hamas leaders, calling it an important first step toward accountability.
These are Open Society’s own published positions. They do not establish that the Foundations dictated the editorial line of Local Call, +972, or NAZA, but they are relevant context when audiences assess reporting that later becomes the basis of a major international documentary.
Follow the testimony. Follow the credits. And follow the money.
Then ask what has been pushed to the margins: October 7, 2023.
Hamas and other armed groups invaded Israel, murdered about 1,200 people, and abducted around 250. Families were slaughtered in their homes. Young people at the Nova festival were hunted down.
A UN mission led by Pramila Patten later found reasonable grounds to believe rape and gang rape occurred during the October 7 attacks in several locations, and “clear and convincing information” that hostages were subjected to rape, sexualized torture, and other forms of sexual violence.
Yet the horror that began this war is pushed to the margins while Israel’s military response is placed under a microscope.
Civilian deaths in Gaza are tragic. Every innocent child who dies is a catastrophe, and Israel must investigate suspected violations.
But there is a fundamental moral and legal distinction between deliberately murdering civilians and attacking a military target while facing a foreseeable risk of civilian casualties. Assessing possible civilian harm before an attack is not, by itself, proof of an intention to murder civilians.
In my view, NAZA takes an extraordinarily complicated battlefield and compresses it into a devastatingly simple accusation: civilians died, therefore Israel intended to kill them.
That may be powerful propaganda. It is not a serious description of war.
Because these accusations come from Israelis, their international power is multiplied. The social-media takeaway will not be: “Anonymous Israeli sources make allegations disputed by the IDF.”
It will be: “The Israelis themselves admit it.”
Israel should respond with the truth
Israel’s answer should not be censorship. It should be truth – delivered faster, more intelligently, and more persuasively.
Israel must acknowledge Palestinian suffering without allowing October 7 to be erased, and investigate misconduct without accepting that killing civilians is state policy.
When films and investigations present themselves as fearless examinations of power, the public should apply the same scrutiny to them.
Examine the evidence. Examine the sources. Examine the producers.
And follow the money.
Because sometimes what is missing from the screen can be found in the credits – and in the financial reports.
The writer is the CEO of Radios 100FM, an Honorary Consul and vice dean of the Consular Diplomatic Corps, president of the Israel Radio Communications Association, and previously served as a monitor for Israel Army Radio and as a television correspondent for NBC News.

Another defense official sought to play down concerns, saying the Israel Air Force's advantage lies "not just in the machine, but mainly in the people."
Following the Saudi-US deal and the wider arms race in the Middle East, Israeli officials are already planning to approach negotiations with the US administration differently over future procurement deals.
Israel seeking to participate in production of classified weapons systems
Israeli officials will also seek participation in the development and production of classified weapons systems.
The IDF's focus is not limited to advanced fighter jets and the next generation of stealth aircraft. It also includes the development of space-based weapons and US participation in the development and production of interceptors for the Arrow 4 and Arrow 5 systems, which are intended to address future threats.
There are also advanced munitions that the United States has declined to sell to Israel. These include systems in the field of bunker-busting weapons, systems designed to operate underground deep inside rocky mountains, autonomous strike systems, and swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles.
Israel is currently struggling to finance a third F-15 squadron and additional F-35 squadrons.

German producer inflation accelerates to 4.6% in August, exceeding forecasts

Mücahithan Avcioglu
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Germany’s producer prices increased more than expected in August, driven by sharp rises in energy and intermediate goods costs, official data showed Friday.
Producer prices rose 4.6% in August from a year earlier, accelerating beyond the market forecast of 4.1%, according to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
On a monthly basis, prices increased 1.1%, also exceeding economists’ expectation of a 0.6% rise.
Energy prices climbed 8.3% year-on-year and 3.2% month-on-month, making them the main contributor to the annual increase.
Amid the conflict in Iran and the broader Middle East, prices for mineral oil products surged 40.5% from August 2025 and rose 4.9% from July.
Heating oil prices jumped 65.3% annually, while naphtha and motor fuel prices increased 44.4% and 37.7%, respectively.
Natural gas distribution prices rose 7.5% year-on-year, while electricity prices increased 1.7%. District heating prices, however, fell 0.5%.
Excluding energy, producer prices advanced 3.1% annually and 0.2% monthly.
Intermediate goods prices rose 6.1% from a year earlier, led by a 14.8% increase in metal prices. Precious metals and copper products both became 34.6% more expensive, while basic chemical prices climbed 11.2%.
Capital goods prices increased 2.4% annually, and durable consumer goods prices rose 2.1%.
In contrast, non-durable consumer goods prices fell 2% year-on-year as food prices declined 4.3%.
Butter prices plunged 40.5%, while pork and beef prices dropped 16.3% and 9.3%, respectively. Vegetable oil prices, however, increased 17.5%.

Kode9, Hyperdub founder and dubstep pioneer, to play Tallinn
British electronic music legend Kode9, founder of the Hyperdub label and a pioneer of dubstep, will perform at Paavli Kultuurivabrik in Tallinn in November.
Kode9, real name Steve Goodman, is a native of Glasgow and relocated to London for the music and DJing scene.
Goodman began DJing in the 1990s, moving from psychedelic jazz and funk to jungle and later garage and dubstep. In 2004, he founded Hyperdub, which has grown into one of the most important British electronic music labels, releasing music by Burial, DJ Rashad, Zomby and Fatima Al Qadiri.
As Kode9 he is regarded as one of the figures who shaped early dubstep. One of his key collaborators was the late MC and poet Stephen Samuel Gordon (1970-2014), aka The Spaceape, with whom Kode9 released the albums "Memories of the Future" (2006) and "Black Sun" (2011). He later released the solo albums "Nothing" (2015), "Astro-Darien" (2022) and "Escapology" (2023).
He had originally studied philosophy before turning to music, earning a doctorate from the University of Warwick. In 2009, MIT Press published his book "Sonic Warfare: Sound, Affect, and the Ecology of Fear," which examines the impact of sound on human behavior and emotions, and its use as a tool for exerting power and creating fear.
The Paavli Kultuurivabrik show is on Friday, November 13 and Kode9 will be joined by Polish drummer and composer Gary Gwadera, London artist Silvia Kastel, Bristol DJ Wash Electra, and Estonian artists Type1, Nikolajev and Susanna Raiend.

The increase was driven partly by a recovery among non-store retailers after declines in July, while department-store sales rebounded following earlier stock-availability problems.

On an annual basis, retail sales volumes increased 2.4% in August.
Sales volumes also rose 0.9% in the three months through August compared with the previous three-month period and climbed 2.4% from the same period last year.
Online spending values increased 2.5% month-on-month and 8.9% year-on-year in August.

In Yemen, war at home and in the region drives up prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18

15:45:23 KST

In Yemen, war at home and in the region drives up prices
Families in Sanaa brace for higher food and transport costs after first fuel price increase in four years.
Sanaa, Yemen – Ahmed Yahya, 28, fills his taxi with 10 litres of petrol as he begins his workday early in the morning.
“I feed my taxi with fuel first so that it can help feed my family,” Yahya, a taxi driver, said as he wiped the dust from his front window at a petrol station on the outskirts of Sanaa.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Migrant crossings to Europe by sea drop sharply amid heightened risks: IOM
- list 2 of 3Trump administration approves sale of F-35 jets to Saudi Arabia
- list 3 of 3US approves visas for top Iranian leaders to attend UN General Assembly
Up until earlier this week, Yahya used to pay 4,750 Yemeni riyals, the equivalent of roughly $8.90 in Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen. The price had remained unchanged for about four years in territory under the rebel group’s control – including the capital Sanaa.
But then, on Monday, the Houthis announced a roughly 10 percent increase in the price of petrol, up to 5,250 Yemeni Riyals ($9.80). After years of economic misery, Yahya described the price hike as another “painful surprise to an already devastated people”.
The Houthi-run Yemen Petroleum Company said the diesel and petrol price increase was the result of a “global increase in fuel prices”, and promised that it would be temporary. The increase in global oil prices this year comes off the back of the impact of the United States-Israel war on Iran. But, more recently, the Houthis’ own capture of Yemen’s southern Red Sea coast from government forces last week, and attacks on Saudi Arabia, have played a major role in increasing prices.
“When I heard the announcement of the new fuel price, I was shocked and frustrated. We’re hardly surviving, and this price increase will make survival even harder,” said Yahya, as he lamented another burden in a country where 18 million already face acute food insecurity – a lack of reliable access to enough food.
‘Rent or food?’
Yahya, a father of three, has been working as a taxi driver for five years. Although the job helps make ends meet, he feels financially insecure, especially with the ongoing changes in food and fuel prices.
“My family spend about 75,000 Yemeni riyals [$140] a month on food expenses such as flour, rice and cooking oil. With the fuel price rise, we will need at least 85,000 Yemeni riyals [$159] a month for the same food items,” said Yahya.
The resumption of fighting in Yemen in the past few months, after a four-year period of relative calm in the country’s war, has contributed to the price rises. But for Yahya, relatively safe in Sanaa, it’s the increased expenses that are the more troubling development.
“When prices rise, they affect what we eat, drink, and how we live,” he said. “Let me give you an example: I pay 25,000 Yemeni riyals [$47] in rent every month. With the increase in food prices, putting money aside to pay the rent has become more challenging. What is the priority? Rent or food?”
An April report by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said that Yemen’s internal conflict has led to significant macroeconomic vulnerabilities and a marked decrease in income per capita, leaving more than half of the population in urgent need of humanitarian assistance.
“It [the conflict] has caused widespread food insecurity, disease outbreaks, mass family displacement, and limited access to clean water,” the report said.
Risky and costly transportation
One of the links between the renewed fighting and the increase in prices is the longer distances needed to transport products across the country, as truckers avoid roads near the front lines.
“A truck carrying goods from the south to the north or vice versa now takes up to a week to reach its final destination. Before the renewed fighting, a similar journey would have taken three days or less,” explained Saleh Abdullah, a shopkeeper in Sanaa.
The increased transportation costs, including the higher fuel prices, are passed on to the consumer.
“This means no family is immune to this trouble,” Abdullah said. “Whether it is the flour, the baby milk, the fruits, the vegetables, or anything else, families will feel the pain of price increases.”
“Some customers become angry at us when we sell products at a higher price,” he added. “We didn’t impose prices. We just react and adapt to the changes in the country or the region.”
Ibrahim Abdu, an employee at the Nehm customs checkpoint in Sanaa governorate, said the number of trucks arriving in the capital has declined over the past few weeks.
“Fighting has cut off many roads, and merchants have avoided risking their products and drivers,” he told Al Jazeera.
‘A hunger multiplier’
Years of war have taken a heavy toll on Yemen’s economy, disrupted businesses, and pushed millions of people into poverty and food insecurity. Against this bleak backdrop, the country’s humanitarian tragedy has been worsening.
Ahmed Mohammed, a former humanitarian worker in Hodeidah, describes the fuel price rise as a “hunger multiplier” in war-torn Yemen.
“If a breadwinner struggles to buy a family three meals a day, he may be able to afford only two given the rising price of food commodities. This will deepen hunger among families,” said Mohammed.
He added: “War is ugly, and one of its ugliest aspects is seeing a family unable to afford a kilogramme of flour, sugar or rice.”
The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) warned this week that the violence threatens to trigger a humanitarian crisis as more people are displaced, pressuring communities with limited resources.
A multi-faceted impact
Wafiq Saleh, an economic researcher and executive director of the Taiz Centre for Yemeni-Gulf Studies, said the 10 percent hike in fuel prices in Houthi-controlled areas deals a blow to Yemeni consumers.
“Its impact will manifest as a major inflationary wave, placing a heavy burden on the most vulnerable and income-deprived segments of society,” Saleh told Al Jazeera.
While this price increase may appear modest in percentage terms, its effects extend far beyond the petrol station, rippling through various goods and services and creating new hardships, according to Saleh.
“Petroleum products serve as intermediate inputs for a wide range of goods and services. Consequently, a 10 percent rise in fuel prices does not merely increase people’s expenses by 10 percent; it triggers a cascading effect on prices,” he said.
“The most severely affected sectors include agriculture – which relies on diesel for crop irrigation – and the transport and services sectors, where rising costs immediately drive up passenger fares and food prices.”
He added that the increase would also affect water and electricity services, many of which rely on diesel-powered generators, further increasing the cost of basic services.
Small- and medium-sized enterprises are similarly affected.
“Small enterprises are operating on narrow profit margins, and they may be forced to either cease operations or pass the increased costs on to the final consumer,” Saleh said.

The suspects were arrested during an operation targeting illegal mining on Tuesday and Wednesday, the head of the NSCDC in Niger State, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, said in a statement. The region is known for small-scale gold mining.

However, survivor Dauda Shehu told The Associated Press news agency that 65 detainees were packed into a poorly ventilated cell, suggesting they may have suffocated.
“We were jam-packed and there was no ventilation for us to breathe well,” Shehu said. “All of a sudden, we realised that we could not breathe and we started scrambling to get fresh air.”
Speaking at the Minna General Hospital, where the bodies were sent for examination, Shehu said the detainees tried to get the attention of the security agency’s guards by banging on the cell door.
Investigators have urged relatives of the victims to come forward with any information that could help.
Niger State Governor Farmer Mohammed Umaru Bago has announced three days of mourning, calling the deaths “sad and tragic”.
Protests were reported to have broken out on Thursday evening, with police responding by firing tear gas. Local outlets reported that NSCDC commander Aniviye has been suspended.

Malaysia’s king allows ex-Premier Najib to serve remainder of jail term under house arrest

Faisal Mahmud
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Malaysia’s King Sultan Ibrahim on Friday granted former Prime Minister Najib Razak a conditional pardon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his prison sentence under house arrest until August 2028.
The decision was made at the 64th meeting of the Pardons Board for the Federal Territories of Kuala Lumpur, Labuan, and Putrajaya at Istana Negara, state news agency Bernama reported.
The pardon is conditional on Najib paying a fine of 50 million Malaysian ringgit ($12.3 million). He must also comply with conditions imposed under the order or the pardon could be revoked.
Najib, now 73, has been imprisoned at Kajang Prison since August 23, 2022, after Malaysia’s Federal Court upheld his conviction in a corruption case involving SRC International, a former unit of the state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
He was convicted in 2020 on seven charges of abuse of power, criminal breach of trust, and money laundering involving 42 million ringgit ($10.3 million) transferred from SRC International into his accounts, widely known as the 1MDB corruption scandal.
Najib was originally sentenced to 12 years in prison. In 2024, the Pardons Board under the previous king halved his prison term to six years, moving his scheduled release to August 23, 2028.

In the Arctic, the ice is moving – and so is the India-Russia agenda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:43:10 UTC
15:43:10 KST

In the Arctic, the ice is moving – and so is the India-Russia agenda
Russian-Asian rapprochement in the Arctic is currently unfolding along two distinct tracks: the first driven by logistics and operations, and the second focused on resources and investment.
Russia’s new Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor (TATC), whose key section is the Northern Sea Route (NSR) running along its Arctic coast, is intended domestically to connect major Russian ports – from St. Petersburg through Murmansk to Vladivostok – and link them to inland cities and towns via land, rail, sea and inland waterway networks.
On the international front, the larger TATC is aimed at linking the consumer markets of Europe and Asia via shorter, safer, more cost-effective, and alternative maritime routes. Similarly, on the resource and investment side, Russia remains keenly interested in developing Arctic and Siberian potential in critical minerals, energy resources, and infrastructure projects that require capital and technology.
The overall Russian approach in the Arctic remains focused on linking its energy and mineral projects in mainland Russia, the Arctic, Siberia, and the Far East to the TATC through multimodal transport connectivity.
The ice is moving
Last month marked a turning point for container transit along the NSR when Sea Legend Shipping launched its regular container service – the China-Europe Arctic Express – consisting of eight voyages, that are scheduled between August and early October 2026. The first shipment, which set sail from China’s Ningbo-Zhoushan port on August 15 via the Northern Sea Route, reached the Port of Teesport in the United Kingdom on September 9 – in just 25 days.
The goal is to deliver high-value and time-sensitive cargo including electronics, lithium batteries, electric vehicle components and photovoltaic modules to multiple European ports (Felixstowe, United Kingdom; Rotterdam, Netherlands; Hamburg, Germany and Gdynia, Poland). Sea Legend Shipping is making use of Russian ice breaking services, and is delivering good to its European clients in far less time than via traditional routes. So far it hasn't faced any kind of criticism or sanctions from Europe.
Similarly, South Korea’s PanStar Group has conducted its own pilot voyage along the NSR to European ports, carrying chemical products. South Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and Panstar reported on Monday that the containership Panstar Arco has completed the first leg of its demonstration voyage, reaching the UK and Rotterdam on September 12 and 13 respectively – successfully covering the route in 21 days. The vessel will then sail to Gdynia, Poland, where it is expected to load additional cargo before beginning the return trip. The vessel is currently scheduled to return to Busan on October 12.
While Seoul hopes this pilot test will position Busan as a leading Arctic shipping hub, currently there are no plans to move regular commercial traffic along the NSR until 2030.
India’s logic of engagement
Against this backdrop, India’s interest in the Russian Arctic is positioned quiet differently. It is primarily about integrating into the resource and investment aspect of the region. The economic viability of sending goods to Europe from India by transiting the entire NSR remains unfavorable for the foreseeable future, but it does offer a secure, strategic alternative maritime route to the traditional shipping lanes, given ongoing geopolitical challenges.
For India, in shipping terms, Russia’s proposed TATC offers greater potential if cargoes are picked up from, or delivered to, Vladivostok and then sent either to other points in Russia via the TATC’s multimodal transport network or to India through the Eastern Maritime Corridor (EMC), also known as the Chennai-Vladivostok Maritime Corridor.
Similarly, some segments or shipping connectivity between India and Eastern ports of Russia along the NSR can become viable options for enhancing point-to-point shipping connectivity between both the countries, if Russia becomes successful in integrating those with its energy and mineral development projects in the region.
New prospects for India-Russia partnership
The India-Russia partnership dates back to the 1971 Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation. Despite contemporary global geopolitical challenges, the underlying character of India-Russia bilateral cooperation has remained intact.
On bilateral trade and economic fronts, it in fact has grown exponentially. Despite western pressures, India’s oil imports for Russia have continued and it has emerged as a significant factor in supporting the Russian economy in challenging times. In 2022, India’s oil imports from Russia surged to $45.9 billion and crossed $79 billion last year.
Russia’s Pivot to the Arctic and its planned large-scale projects in terms of shipping, energy, and mineral development need Indian industrial attention to take these trade figures between the countries to new highs in the future.
Critical minerals
India’s projected demand for rare and critical metals is expected to increase four to tenfold by 2047. India is heavily dependent on imports of lithium, cobalt, nickel, and a number of other rare-earth elements. Furthermore, India’s net cumulative demand for minerals such as copper, graphite, silicon, and nickel is also expected to increase exponentially between 2025 and 2070. Russia’s resource base appears almost ideally complementary to such Indian needs.
The Pavlovskoye lead-zinc deposit in the Novaya Zemlya archipelago; the Tomtor deposits, which constitute one of the largest deposits of niobium and rare-earth elements in Yakutia; and the Angara-Yenisey cluster for the deep processing of non-ferrous and rare metals in Siberia are some of the potential projects that could fulfill India’s future mineral resource demands. Any significant progress in terms of joint investments and partnership could open new prospects for India-Russia economic partnership and reduce Indian reliance on traditional hegemons for these resources.
Energy imports to refined exports
India’s demand for oil is expected to be around 14 million barrels per day by 2050, while its gas consumption is also expected to rise to 103 billion cubic meters annually by 2030. Of this, around 65 billion cubic meters would be supplied by India’s LNG imports.
Crude continues to remain the key commodity in the India-Russia trade basket, and Russia’s vast LNG potential, mainly its Arctic projects, remains largely untapped by India. LNG imports require specialized vessels, and longer distances add to its transportation costs, which ultimately affect its final price. New investments in Russian Arctic LNG projects could offer a strategic diversification and long-term solutions for meeting India’s energy demands in any future geopolitical scenarios in West Asia if both sides are successful in factoring in pricing and transportation aspects.
India, on the other hand, possesses substantial refining capabilities in terms of crude and its related derivatives while Russia is currently facing difficulties in meeting its own demand for refined petroleum products. This is opening another avenue for greater cooperation between the two sides. India has recently scaled up deliveries of refined petroleum products to Russia to meet its domestic needs.
Shipping synergy
In March this year, New Delhi allocated approximately $8.4 billion to bolster shipbuilding, shipbreaking, and maintenance infrastructure under the ‘Make in India’ initiative. Concurrently, Russia’s growing demand for vessel construction and maintenance presents high-value opportunities for Indian shipbuilding and ship-repair enterprises. Synergizing these capabilities directly aligns with both nations’ strategic interests, offering a mutually beneficial avenue for bilateral maritime cooperation. Both Russia and India are placing significant emphasis on developing sustainable maritime operations for the future.
Both countries are pursuing major reforms to build greener ports and cleaner maritime infrastructure, promote alternative fuels, deploy hybrid and electric vessels, and launch green shipping corridors. They are also focusing on advanced technologies and AI to modernize ports and improve logistics and cargo handling – creating strong potential for high-value economic cooperation between India and Russia.
In its efforts to advance its artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, India has recently allocated about $1.25 billion to the IndiaAI mission. Similarly, India’s ‘Semicon India Programme’ aims to build a self-reliant semiconductor ecosystem in the country. Such initiatives create new avenues for collaboration in high-growth digital sectors between India and Russia.
A way forward
Russia’s Arctic pivot to the East is the sum of several parallel experiments at different stages of maturity. Container shipping along the NSR remains niche, seasonal, and dependent on who ultimately assumes the commercial risks. Russia’s Atomflot tariff depends on a vessel’s gross tonnage, ice class, distance, and the period of escort. Added to this are the higher costs of icebreaker escorts, high insurance premiums for Arctic voyages, and the need for crews trained to operate in Arctic conditions. Despite these challenges, countries like China and South Korea are already sending test consignments to Europe via the NSR and are competing for the benefits of first movers.
Russia’s total foreign trade turnover reached $697.3 billion in 2025, of which 73.4% was accounted for by Asia. India contributed approximately $63.6 billion, and remains Russia’s second-largest trading partner after China, significantly ahead of the UAE, Brazil, Iran, and South Africa.
India has highlighted its plans to send its first cargo via the NSR by 2027, but its broader comprehensive plans for the region are still at the nascent stage of development. Opening up of the Russian Arctic offers immense new untapped business potential for India and Russia, requiring a stronger government push and greater Indian industrial exposure.
This would not only help India and Russia to reach their bilateral trade target of $100 billion by 2030, but to surpass it in the future.

US, Poland Making Progress On Permanent American Army Base, Trump Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:40:30 UTC
15:40:30 KST

WASHINGTON -- US President Donald Trump says Washington and Warsaw are making "major progress" toward establishing a permanent US Army base in Poland, potentially expanding the American military presence on NATO's eastern flank.
"Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland," Trump said in a post on Truth Social on September 17. "If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance."
Nawrocki welcomed the announcement, saying Poland was ready to continue efforts to strengthen defense cooperation with Washington.
"I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base," Nawrocki said in a post on X.
The announcement came on the 87th anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Poland. Zbigniew Bogucki, head of the Polish president's chancellery, called the development "great news for Poland."
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said in August that Warsaw and Washington had already completed an initial stage of discussions on a possible permanent US military presence in Poland.
Polish and US officials held further talks in Warsaw on September 10 on strengthening the US military presence, with additional consultations and working groups planned.
The United States already has troops stationed in Poland, but they have largely been deployed on a rotational basis. Warsaw has reportedly been seeking a larger allied presence on NATO's eastern flank since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
US Force Posture Review
The discussions over a possible permanent base come as the Pentagon conducts a broader review of the US military presence in Europe.
The review has prompted concern among some lawmakers that diplomatic considerations could receive insufficient attention.
In a letter led by Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Senate Democrat on foreign policy, eight Democratic senators urged Secretary of State Marco Rubio to ensure that the State Department is fully involved in the review.
The lawmakers said decisions involving troop deployments, basing arrangements, status-of-forces agreements, and host-nation negotiations should be handled through an interagency process that takes both military and diplomatic considerations into account.
They also said US ambassadors and chiefs of mission in countries potentially affected by changes in troop deployments had not been adequately included in consultations.
The State Department has disputed the characterization that its officials have been excluded from the process.
A senior Western official familiar with the discussions told RFE/RL that the possible base in Poland is being considered as part of the broader US force-posture review. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the review could involve changes to the deployment of US forces elsewhere in Europe, including Germany.
Trump also spoke by phone with Chancellor Merz on September 17 about "next steps" toward ending the war in Ukraine, according to German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius.
Security Concerns
The discussions come as Poland faces heightened security concerns linked to Russia's war against Ukraine.
Polish authorities temporarily closed airports in Lublin and Rzeszow on September 17 as Russian strikes targeted parts of Ukraine, according to Polish officials.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has also warned that Russia could seek to conduct drone or missile attacks against NATO countries supporting Ukraine while presenting them as accidents. He said such incidents could be intended to test NATO's response and undermine allied unity. The assessment was based on intelligence from NATO, Ukraine, and the United States, according to Tusk.
Shaheen has separately warned of increased Russian use of hybrid tactics, including drones, cyberattacks, and sabotage.
"Hybrid warfare has been going on for some time, and we're seeing an increase now," Shaheen told RFE/RL.
The German government has also warned about the broader security situation in Europe.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz said recently the coming weeks and months could be a particularly important period for defending peace and freedom in Europe.
Poland's Military Role
Poland has sought a larger US military presence for years, arguing that its geographic position makes it an important part of NATO's eastern defenses.
In June, Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the US Defense Department was open to Poland's offer to host a permanent US military presence but that no final decision had been made.
He made the comments after meeting US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in Brussels, where Hegseth announced the review of US troop deployments in Europe.
The possible base would represent a change from the predominantly rotational US troop presence currently maintained in Poland.
The US and Poland have also expanded defense cooperation through infrastructure and military agreements, while Warsaw has increased its defense spending. Poland's Defense Ministry said the latest US-Polish talks are being conducted under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement signed in 2020.
For now, Trump has said the location of the proposed army base could be announced soon. No final location or timetable has been publicly announced.

Russians begin voting in controlled election as war drags on

- Moscow defended against over 350 Ukrainian drone attacks, highlighting the war's reach into Russian territory and increasing domestic impact.
- Opposition parties were barred or weakened; calls for anti-Kremlin voting contrasted with some urging a boycott, amid fears of a new military mobilisation.
AI generated
MOSCOW – Polling stations opened early on Sept 18 in Russia’s Far East, kicking off a three-day election that President Vladimir Putin’s party is all but guaranteed to win in the fifth year of war with Ukraine.
It will be Russia’s first parliamentary election since Moscow sent troops to Ukraine in February 2022.
The conflict has since killed hundreds of thousands.
Only parties that support Putin and the Kremlin’s dragging military campaign have been registered to run.
Moscow has also organised voting in occupied Ukraine.
While few in Russia doubt Putin’s United Russia party will sail to victory again, the vote is an opportunity for the Kremlin to gauge public support for the Ukraine war, the effects of which have hit home more than ever this year.
In a grim reminder of the fighting, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Sept 18 that Russia destroyed dozens of Ukrainian drones bound for the capital overnight.
“More than 350 UAVs flew towards the Moscow region between 8pm on Sept 17 and 7am on Sept 18,” he said on Telegram, adding that most were destroyed at an outer defensive perimeter and some 64 were shot down as they were approaching the sprawling city.
The vote to renew the 450 seats in the Duma, Russia’s Lower House of Parliament, will run until 1800 GMT on Sept 20.
Russia’s Kamchatka peninsula and Chukotka – on the Pacific – are the first of Russia’s 11 time zones to begin voting.
Putin has ruled Russia since New Year’s Eve 1999 and his United Russia party has dominated Russian politics since the early 2000s.
Moscow has banned criticism of its Ukraine campaign and the Russian elections, tightly controlled by the Kremlin, are bringing few surprises.
‘Emotionally important to Putin’
United Russia is only facing parties who back most of Putin’s policies and the war in Ukraine: the Communist Party, the nationalist LDPR, A Just Russia and New People.
Yabloko, which called for an end to fighting, was barred from running shortly before the vote.
One of its main figures, Lev Shlosberg, was imprisoned for criticising the war.
Apostol, a 20-year-old Muscovite, told AFP he “did not see the point” in voting for anyone but United Russia because they will “win anyway”.
Tatiana Stanovaya, a France-based Russian political expert, said Putin liked to “compare his political situation” to those in European countries.
“So he can always say, look, we had an election. I benefit from such significant support of Russians,” she told AFP.
“So for him it’s personally, emotionally, politically very important,” she said.
Ahead of the vote, the 73-year-old leader called on Russians to vote to show troops that “behind our fighters stand millions of people” and to demonstrate a “common answer to those who want to weaken Russia.”
The war has broken Moscow’s ties with the West, which has hit Russia with massive economic sanctions.
New mobilisation?
In the absence of a public debate and with protests banned, the vote will serve as a barometer for the Kremlin of public frustration with the conflict, which has no end in sight.
In 2026, the war hit ordinary Russians more than ever, with Ukrainian strikes reaching as far as the Urals and Siberia, and causing billions of rubles in damage – as well as civilian deaths deep inside Russia.
Putin’s political opponents have mostly been driven into exile and his main opponent Alexei Navalny – who once brought thousands to the streets during elections – died in an Arctic prison in 2024.
Russia’s exiled opposition called on anti-Kremlin Russians not to boycott the elections but to vote “against Putin’s party”, publishing recommendations of who to back in which region.
Navalny’s widow Yulia Navalnaya also called on anti-war Russians to vote at the same time – at noon on Sept 20.
Yabloko, however, disagreed, arguing that it was better not to vote.
“You are suggesting that we once again go, like sheep, dancing to their tune, and vote for those who have caused the deaths of people in Russia and Ukraine?” its chairman Nikolay Rybakov said at a party meeting in Saint Petersburg this week.
Some fear the post-election period in Russia will bring a new military mobilisation, similar to the one in 2022, when Putin called up 300,000 reservists.
That hugely unpopular move led to an exodus of draft-age men out of Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused the Kremlin of planning a fresh mobilisation campaign “this autumn”, a suggestion Putin has denied. AFP

Energy shock drives new round of rate rises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:39:23 UTC
15:39:23 KST

People look through the window an estate agents window in Uckfield, south of London, on September 16, 2026. (AFP Photo)
Higher energy costs are prompting central banks in major economies to raise interest rates or warn of further increases, adding to borrowing pressures for households and businesses.
The U.S. Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time in more than three years, Japan approved an increase to its highest level since 1995, and the Bank of England warned that persistent energy price pressures could require it to follow.
The decisions reflect concern that the disruption caused by the Iran war will spread beyond fuel prices into wages, business costs and inflation expectations.
The Fed raised its target range by a quarter percentage point to 3.75–4 percent on Sept. 16, with all 12 voting members backing the move.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said.
Warsh said the central bank could not control individual oil or food prices, but could act to prevent those increases from generating broader inflation.
He cited stronger hiring and business investment, while saying underlying inflation had shown no meaningful improvement over the summer.
Officials’ median projections pointed to another quarter-point increase by year-end and rates at the same level at the end of 2027.
The Bank of Japan voted 7–2 on Sept. 18 to raise its policy rate from 1 percent to 1.25 percent.
It said high oil prices and a weaker yen were increasing business costs, with companies passing more of those increases on to consumers. The bank signaled further rate rises, while saying financial conditions would remain supportive of economic activity after the increase.
Britain held its benchmark at 3.75 percent on Sept. 17, although three of the Bank of England’s nine policymakers favored a quarter-point rise.
Annual consumer inflation reached 3.1 percent in August. Based on energy prices earlier in the week, the bank expected it to rise to around 3.75 percent in the final quarter of 2026 and slightly above 4 percent in early 2027.
The bank said there was little evidence so far that higher energy costs were significantly changing wage and price-setting, but warned that the risk would increase the longer those costs stayed high.
The European Central Bank had already raised its deposit rate by a quarter point to 2.5 percent on Sept. 10, citing inflation pressures from the Middle East conflict.
Its latest forecasts put eurozone inflation at 3 percent this year and 2.5 percent in 2027, above its 2 percent target. The bank raised its growth forecast for 2026 to 0.9 percent, citing greater resilience than expected.
Separate Eurostat figures showed industrial production in the eurozone fell 0.1 percent in July from June and was unchanged from a year earlier.
For households, the pressure is already visible in housing finance.
The average U.S. 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 6.95 percent in the week to Sept. 17 from 6.76 percent a week earlier, according to Freddie Mac.
Mortgage rates are influenced by inflation expectations and longer-term bond yields. They had been climbing before the Fed’s latest decision.
For a borrower taking out a $400,000, 30-year loan, a 6.95 percent rate means roughly $255 more in monthly principal and interest payments than at the 5.98 percent average recorded in late February.
In Britain, quoted rates on two-year fixed mortgages were about 0.95 percentage points above their pre-conflict level, the Bank of England said.
Financial markets offered some relief on Sept. 17. Brent crude settled at $104.82 a barrel, down from nearly $110 earlier in the week, while the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield fell to 4.93 percent from 5.01 percent the previous day.
The Bank of England cautioned that even a resolution to the conflict would likely bring only a slow, gradual recovery in energy supplies.

Russia votes for new parliament in controlled elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:39:00 UTC
15:39:00 KST

Russia votes for new parliament in controlled elections
September 18, 2026
Russians began casting ballots on Friday to elect a new lower house of parliament, kicking off a three-day vote that President Vladimir Putin's party is all but guaranteed to win.
This is the first such election being held since Moscow sent troops to invade Ukraine in February 2022.
Parties that support Putin's war in Ukraine are the only ones registered to run, and the opposition is barred from taking part.
Despite expectations of Putin's easy win, the elections are widely being viewed as a referendum on the continuation of his military campaign — now in its fifth year.
The polls are taking place at a time when public sentiment is starting to shift against the war over rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages and rumors of another mobilization drive following the elections.
Meanwhile, Putin has called the vote a "collective contribution to Russia's victory against Ukraine.
Vote for control
More than 110 million Russians are eligible to vote for 450 members of the lower house of the Russian Parliament, known as the State Duma.
Putin's United Russia party currently controls over two-thirds of the seats and is expected to retain its dominance, allowing it to continue the military campaign despite ebbing public support.
The Kamchatka peninsula and Chukotka were the first of Russia's 11 time zones to begin voting on Friday.
Polls will remain open until 1800 GMT on Sunday.
Voting is being held for the first time in the Russia-occupied Ukrainian territories of Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, against Kyiv's wishes. The Black Sea peninsula of Crimea, annexed by Moscow in 2014, is participating for the second time.
While voters select their parliamentarians, members of regional parliaments will also be elected in eight regions.

North Korea warns of ‘more offensive’ response to US-led military drills

Faisal Mahmud
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
North Korea’s Kim Yo Jong on Friday warned of a stronger response to US-led multinational military exercises in the Asia-Pacific, saying Pyongyang would continue strengthening its nuclear deterrence.
Kim, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and a senior ruling Workers’ Party official, accused Washington of being the “main source” of worsening tensions on the Korean Peninsula and across the region, according to a statement carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
She singled out Pacific Vanguard 2026, a multinational naval exercise near Guam involving the US, South Korea, Japan, and other countries.
Kim called the exercise a threatening “war game” and accused Washington of seeking to expand its military influence through alliances in the Asia-Pacific.
She also criticized growing US-Japan-South Korea military cooperation, claiming North Korea was its primary target.
“The present situation ... stresses the need to break records in our responsive action, proportional or more offensive in its nature,” Kim said.
She added there would be “never ever change” in North Korea’s course of strengthening its nuclear deterrence and warned Pyongyang could “mobilize all means available” if its sovereignty or security were seriously threatened.
The warning came as South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said Friday that Seoul should make every effort to facilitate renewed dialogue between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and US President Donald Trump, according to Seoul-based Yonhap News Agency.
“The possibility cannot be ruled out,” Lee told a televised news conference, adding Seoul should do its “utmost” to help make such talks happen. Lee said renewed North Korea-US dialogue could become an important stepping stone toward restarting inter-Korean talks and promoting peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula.

Argentina posts first quarterly contraction since 2024
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18

Argentina’s economy shrank 0.6 percent in the second quarter from the previous three months, recording its first quarterly contraction since 2024 as spending and investment declined.
The decline was smaller than the 0.9 percent forecast by economists surveyed by Bloomberg. Gross domestic product grew 2 percent from a year earlier, according to official figures released on Sept. 17.
Household spending, government consumption and investment all fell from the first quarter. Higher exports and lower imports helped cushion the decline.
Unemployment rose to 7.9 percent in the second quarter. An August survey by AtlasIntel identified joblessness as Argentines’ leading economic concern.
President Javier Milei’s government has pursued tight fiscal policies to curb inflation and eliminate chronic budget deficits while opening the economy to more international trade. It has also allowed the peso to strengthen in inflation-adjusted terms.
Bloomberg Economics said the weak second-quarter figures offered limited guidance on the outlook.
Its analysts expect positive but modest growth in coming quarters, with strong performance in primary industries and limited signs of expansion across the wider economy.

Abraham Accords need 'constant push' six years on; Iran war has made Gulf alliance stronger, says Sen. Lankford in i24NEWS special interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:35:14 UTC
15:35:14 KST

- i24NEWS
- Analysis & Opinion
- Abraham Accords need 'constant push' six years on, says Sen. Lankford in i24NEWS special interview
Abraham Accords need 'constant push' six years on, says Sen. Lankford in i24NEWS special interview
Reflecting on the six years since the signing ceremony on the White House South Lawn, Lankford said the accords proved more durable than critics expected, including in the aftermath of October 7
The Abraham Accords will "never" advance on its own and requires a constant push from Congress and the White House. That is what Sen. James Lankford (R-OK), co-chair of the Senate Abraham Accords Caucus, told i24NEWS' Mike Wagenheim on American View.
Sen. Lankford spoke to i24NEWS to help mark the sixth anniversary of the Abraham Accords, which normalized relations between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain and Morocco, with Sudan and, more recently, Kazakhstan later joining.
Reflecting on the six years since the signing ceremony on the White House South Lawn, Lankford said the accords proved more durable than critics expected, including in the aftermath of October 7. "Everyone said the Abraham Accords won't hold, won't make a difference during that time period, and that has proved to be absolutely not true," Lankford said, adding that the growth in economic, humanitarian, and technology cooperation among signatory countries has made "a difference in the last six years."
Lankford also said he had expected the accords to expand well beyond economics. Already this week, news came out regarding a meeting between US Central Command (CENTCOM), the defense chiefs of Israel and many of their Gulf allies, evidence of a growing military partnership.
"When you start economic engagement, you start person-to-person engagement outside of government. Then you start developing that relationship back and forth. That then expands to government leaders," the senator said. "Government drags behind business leaders most of the time in most issues."
Host Mike Wagenheim asked Senator Lankford whether expectations of a domino effect, with one Middle Eastern country after the other normalizing relations with Israel, were too high, particularly with Saudi Arabia. In response, Lankford said yes, at least on timing.
The senator argued the bigger obstacle to expansion is that the US has not clearly defined what member states get in return for joining. "Nations that are already a member: Morocco, UAE, Bahrain. They've asked the question several times. What does America bring to the table?" he said. "America has not been able to define that yet. I think America still owes the rest of the region that."
On why the accords survived the Israel-Hamas war despite friction, Lankford pointed to relationships built before the agreements were signed. "It held together because people already knew each other. They had their phone numbers. They had already engaged... Once those relationships started, people wanted to be able to maintain those relationships long term, even when there's an enormous challenge like the war against Hamas."
He recalled 'real conversations' during the early Biden administration over whether they would continue trying to advance the cooperation. "Is this the Trump Accords or is this the Abraham Accords?" the Senator exclaimed, noting that there was "about six or eight months that there was a real dialog behind the scenes."
On the prospect of new countries joining, including Lebanon and Syria, which have both been floated as potential candidates, Senator Lankford said active talks are underway, though the timing remains uncertain. "There are active conversations with new members," he said, noting that some countries have said they want to see progress on a Palestinian state or other resolutions before joining. According to the senator, the central question remains who legitimately represents the Palestinians in any negotiation.
However, Senator Lankford also acknowledged what he called a shift in Israel's standing in Congress, from a largely nonpartisan issue a decade ago to one that now draws significant opposition from Democrats. "I've seen over 100 members of the House, for instance, vote against any kind of support for Israel," he said, calling the shift "very, very frustrating."
Nevertheless, while discussing Israel's upcoming elections and its future relationship with the US, Lankford said that whereas several regional governments are waiting for Israel's election results before committing to further negotiation, the US-Israel relationship "is not based around who's elected this week."
On the Iran war, Senator Lankford argued that the war actually strengthened rather than damaged US relationships with Gulf allies, demonstrating US commitment to allies like Bahrain and the UAE. "I think this has been a reminder of how close our relationship is with Bahrain and with the UAE, in particular," he stated, adding that both countries "have taken a tremendous amount from the Iranians" and have seen direct US intelligence, training, and missile-defense support in response.
Lankford was blunt when asked whether the accords have reached a point where they could sustain themselves without constant political attention from Washington, regardless of future administrations. "Never," he said. "It's always going to need a push."
The senator said the State Department is "easily distracted with a lot of issues globally," and that without sustained pressure from Congress and the White House, expansion of the accords risks becoming one of "a list of 100 other priorities, which means none of them are a priority."
Lankford believes America's overall role in the accords is primarily as a convener and, at times, an intermediary between countries that lack direct relationships with one another. "The United States has a role to be able to say if relationships are broken, how can we pull two people together," he said, adding that many of those diplomatic introductions happen "behind the scenes, out of the public eye," including conversations between Israeli officials and other regional leaders that remain largely unknown to the public.

Germany, France lead Europe’s civilian space spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:33:29 UTC
15:33:29 KST

(AFP Photo)
Germany and France lead Europe in civilian space spending, while the continent trails the United States in private investment and launches, according to a new OECD report.
Germany allocated about 2.5 billion euros to civilian space programs in 2025, followed by France with 2.4 billion euros and Italy with around 2 billion euros.
Italy has doubled its civilian space budget over the past 15 years. Relative to GDP, it now ranks second in Europe behind Luxembourg, overtaking France.
Defense is also driving investment. Germany plans to spend 35 billion euros on space-related defense capabilities by 2030.
Britain had Europe’s largest satellite fleet, with 757 in orbit as of June, compared with 104 for France, 80 for Italy and 65 for Germany. Private operators owned 98 percent of British satellites.
Europe attracted 12.8 percent of global private space investment in 2025, compared with 67 percent for the United States.
The United States attempted 181 orbital launches last year, China 92 and Europe eight.

Introduction: Japan joins the rate-hiking party, as Bank of England lurks
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
The global interest rate rising cycle has spun again today, after the Bank of Japan decided to raise interest rates to their highest level in 31 years.
The BoJ voted to raise its target interest rate by a quarter of one percentage point to 1.25%, the highest level since 1995. The vote was not unanimous – with two board members dissenting to the hike.
The move meant the BoJ has joined the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank in tightening monetary policy this month, as part of the global fight against inflation.
But the Bank of England is, so far, resisting joining the battle, having yesterday voted to leave UK interest rates on hold at 3.75%.
The BoJ has been in a rate-rising cycle since 2024, when it lifted its policy rate out of negative territory. It has been under pressure to raise borrowing costs as the yen weakened steadily against the dollar this year, to levels which prompted policymakers to intervene to stabilise the currency.
A hike today had been expected. So the news that two BoJ policymakers opposed the move has excited the markets.
Jim Reid, strategist at DeutscheBank, reports:
So although the central bank reiterated that it will continue raising rates if economic and inflation conditions evolve as projected, the market has reacted to the two high profile dissenters. The Yen is -0.72% lower at 157.10, having been at around 153.40 at the start of the week and the JGB curve has steepened, with 2yrs -2.2bps and 30yrs +3.2bps

Mothercare facing “highly uncertain” future as Middle Eastern partner plans store closures
Mothercare has warned it faces a “highly uncertain” future after its Middle East franchise partner revealed it was set to close most of its franchised stores across the region next year.
The troubled baby products group said it was a “heavy blow” for the firm and has now launched an urgent strategic review, adding that it has sufficient resources to trade for “a number of months”
Clive Whiley, chairman of Mothercare, told shareholders this morning:
“Whilst our recent financial performance has been resilient, this is a heavy blow to the Mothercare business and our stakeholders. We will continue to pursue discussions to restore critical mass and value for stakeholders, against this more difficult backdrop.”
Investors are taking fright, knocking Mothercare’s share down by 67% in early trading.
BoJ governor Ueda give press conference - the key quotes
Bank of Japan governor Kazuo Ueda is giving a press conference in Tokyo now, to explain today’s decision to hike interest rates.
Reuters has helpfully collated some of the important quotes
ON 50-BP OR BACK-TO-BACK RATE HIKES:
“That depends on how price conditions develop. There could be various possibilities. We shouldn’t rule anything out.“
“We’re at a phase where we need to look at various data carefully. But that doesn’t mean we can move slowly. We will analyse data carefully and take timely action as needed.“
“As for the pace of future rate hikes, we don’t have any pre-set idea in mind such as once every three months. We will determine at each policy meeting how best to ensure underlying inflation stabilises at 2%.“
RISK FACTORS:
“If the renewed rise in energy costs persists, that could add further pressure to wholesale inflation and then consumer inflation. That’s something we need to look out for.“
FINANCIAL CONDITIONS:
“Financial conditions are becoming less accommodative as we raise rates ... It’s important to avoid financial conditions from tightening too much, or to cause a big adjustment in asset prices, by raising rates too sharply.“
NEUTRAL RATE UNCERTAIN:
“It is hard to pinpoint where the neutral rate is, and therefore the terminal rate. It might be the case that as we adjust policy as appropriate, we will know where those rates sit ex-ante.“
ON INFLATION:
“Up till now, our short-term policy focus was to push up underlying inflation from levels below 2%. Now, underlying inflation is approaching 2%. If risks of underlying inflation overshooting 2% materialise, that could have a negative impact on Japan’s economy. It’s important to stabilise underlying inflation at 2%. Our policy phase has changed.“
Fuel sales dropped again, down 1.7% in August and 2.5% across the three month period, as motorists cut back on non-essential journeys following major increases in the price of petrol and diesel since the start of the Iran conflict in February.
That followed a jump in sales volumes in March, when motorists stocked up on fuel after the conflict in the Middle East broke out,
The oil price has dropped by 2% this morning, pushed down by hopes that supply disruptions from Saudi Arabia may not be as severe as feared.
Brent crude has dropped to $102.55 a barrel, following reports that Saudi authorities hope to bypass a damaged section of its 1,200-km East-West Pipeline and restore roughly half its capacity within days.
That pipe was damaged in an attack last week which drove oil up over the $100/barrel mark, as traders anticipated significant disruption to supplies.
A drop in the oil price would cheer households, businesses and central bankers alike!
Despite the inflationary squeeze on households, retail sales across Great Britain have risen over the summer.
The heatwave, a pick-up in web shopping, and the joys (and pain and disappointment!) of the men’s football World Cup, helped to lift spending over the three months to August, new data shows.
Retail sales volumes rose by 0.9% in the June-August quarter, the Office for National Statistics has reported this morning.
Non-store retailers’ sales volumes rose following a particularly strong June period – perhaps because people preferred to order goods online rather than braving the high street in the heatwave.
Retailers selling alcohol and beverages performed well across all three months to August, which they attributed to promotions, the hot weather, and the World Cup.
In August alone, retail sales volumes rose by 0.5%, reversing a 0.5% drop in July.
August’s rise is unexpected (economists had forecast a 0.2% fall), so this is the latest piece of economic data to beat expectations after last week’s jump in UK GDP.
ONS senior statistician Jon Gough said:
“Retail sales increased in the latest three months, with a particularly strong June for online outlets helping to boost their sales across the period. Food store sales also rose, with supermarkets doing well in July and August.
“Meanwhile, retailers selling alcohol and beverages performed well across all three months, which they attributed to promotions, the hot weather and the World Cup.”

Russia Opens Three-Day Election as Kremlin Tests War Support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:31:17 UTC
15:31:17 KST

Russia opened polling stations in its Far East early Friday, launching a three-day parliamentary election that is expected to hand President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party another sweeping victory.
The vote is Russia’s first parliamentary election since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. With meaningful opposition largely excluded, the election is less a contest for power than a Kremlin test of public support for Putin and his war.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Only parties broadly aligned with the Kremlin and its policies are allowed to compete. Moscow has also organized voting in occupied Ukrainian territories, a move condemned by Ukraine and Western governments.
The 450 seats in Russia’s State Duma, the lower house of parliament, are up for election. Voting will continue until Sunday evening, with Russia’s Pacific regions of Kamchatka and Chukotka among the first to cast ballots.
United Russia dominates Russian politics and is widely expected to retain control of the Duma. It faces four other parliamentary parties – the Communist Party, LDPR, A Just Russia and New People – all of which support most of Putin’s policies.
Anti-war parties and opposition figures have been pushed out of the political system. The liberal Yabloko party was barred from competing shortly before the election, while one of its prominent figures, Lev Shlosberg, has been imprisoned after criticizing the war.
Tusk: Intelligence Warns Russia Plans ‘Accidental’ Hybrid Strikes Against Ukraine’s Allies
The Kremlin is closely watching how the war affects public sentiment, particularly as Ukrainian strikes have reached areas far from the battlefield and Russia faces mounting economic and military costs.
Putin, who has ruled Russia since 1999, urged Russians to vote, saying participation would demonstrate that millions of people support Russian troops and oppose efforts to weaken the country.
Opposition sidelined
With protests and public criticism of the war heavily restricted, the election offers few avenues for Russians to openly challenge the Kremlin.
Much of Russia’s organized opposition has been driven into exile or imprisoned. Opposition leader Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic prison in 2024.
Russia’s exiled opposition has urged anti-Kremlin voters to participate and vote against United Russia. Navalny’s widow, Yulia Navalnaya, has called on anti-war Russians to coordinate their voting at noon Sunday.
Yabloko has taken a different position, arguing that participating would legitimize a political system it considers controlled by the Kremlin.
The election could also provide clues about public reaction to the possibility of further military mobilization.
Putin ordered a call-up of 300,000 reservists in September 2022, triggering widespread protests and an exodus of draft-age men from Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused the Kremlin of preparing another mobilization campaign this autumn. Putin has denied the claim.

Energy crunch and inflationary fears loom over EU finance talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Hello, this is Mared Gwyn holding the newsletter pen in Brussels. This morning: Eurozone finance ministers gather amid mounting economic pressures, and EU ambassadors make another push to break the Russia sanctions deadlock.
Economic jitters: Finance ministers from eurozone countries gather in Dublin, Ireland, today, against a fraught backdrop of mounting energy costs, rising inflation and weak growth.
Painful at the pump: Oil prices have surged rapidly in recent days, driven by a reduction in global supplies and exacerbated by recent attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which have been attributed to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
European leaders are rushing to mitigate the rising prices and their impact on the broader economy. French President Emmanuel Macron has ordered a "mobilisation" to tackle fuel prices, as my colleague Marta Pacheco explains.
Windfall tax on the table: Finance ministers could today respond to calls from some capitals for a windfall tax on energy companies.
Speaking to our correspondent Shona Murray in Dublin ahead of the meeting, Irish Finance Minister Simon Harris — mindful of the neutrality required while chairing the EU Council presidency — spoke plainly about the soaring profits being posted by energy companies as ordinary taxpayers struggle to fill their tanks.
“Energy companies are making extraordinarily large profits on the back of this energy crisis,” he said. “And they're not making those profits on the basis of being more enterprising or being innovative."
“This isn't about rewarding enterprise. They're making the profits because of the chaos that we're seeing in the energy markets as a result of the strait of Hormuz being closed.” Watch.
Not about Ukraine: Harris also disputed US President Donald Trump’s claims that petrol and diesel prices were skyrocketing due to Ukraine’s targeting of Russia’s refineries, which are part of the Kremlin’s war machine. “The reason there's a major energy crisis in the world right now is because the Strait of Hormuz is closed,” he said.
The volatility of the global bond market and signs of rising inflation are also of concern to eurozone ministers, our economy reporter Eleonora Vasques writes, with European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde set to join the discussions after the institution raised interest rates on 10 September.
All 27 EU finance ministers and central bank governors will also meet today and tomorrow for informal talks on the same issues, joined by finance ministers from Canada, the UK, Ukraine and Switzerland, as well as International Monetary Fund (IMF) director Kristalina Georgieva.
Yet another try: Meanwhile in Brussels, EU ambassadors will meet this morning to try, once again, to renew the individual sanctions against Russia, which are due to expire next week if no deal is struck in time, Jorge writes.
The chief obstacle remains that France wants to remove oligarch Alisher Usmanov from the blacklist in an attempt to secure the freedom of several French citizens detained in Azerbaijan. The demand has put Brussels in an unprecedented conundrum: never before have the EU sanctions been entangled with a prisoner release.
While some diplomats feel sympathy for Paris, others wonder why Azerbaijan cares so much about Usmanov. The vast majority, though, remains opposed to delisting the billionaire. “We need the regime to stand,” a diplomat said. “Couldn’t this really be solved in another way, without delisting heavy Russian oligarchs?”
Consultations intensify: France, as the bloc’s second-largest member state, carries considerable weight around the table and its veto is something that you can’t just shake off. Intense consultations have been going on between capitals to find a palatable solution for everyone. The Irish presidency of the EU Council and the External Action Service (EEAS) are also involved.
As of now, the contours of a unanimous agreement are still blurred. Also, let’s not forget that Slovakia also wants Usmanov out, though for different reasons.
Fresh support: Jorge also reports that the European Commission will disburse €3.3 billion for Ukraine to procure missiles and drones later today. Von der Leyen confirmed the move on Thursday after talks with President Zelenskyy over Ukraine’s budget deficit, which Brussels is still trying to pin down.
US drawdown: Meanwhile, the Pentagon is weighing a drastic withdrawal of as many as 25,000 troops from Europe, reducing the US’s military presence on the continent by about a third, NBC News reported overnight citing seven current and former US and Western officials.
While no final decision has been taken, according to the report, the recommendation is set to be laid out to Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as part of a six-month review of US military presence in Europe later today.
Analysis: Bruised by Trump, the EU and Canada find solace in each other’s arms
The blossoming EU-Canada alliance cannot be understood without the long shadow of Donald Trump, who has alienated both sides with his punitive tariffs, annexationist threats and scathing attacks.
The breakup has been painful, to say the least. After all, both the EU and Canada have long defined the United States as their closest ally, their main security provider, their trade partner of choice. But Trump's return to the White House abruptly overturned these long-held assumptions, forcing them to reckon with their place in a cruel, cold world.
Bruised and battered by the mercurial commander-in-chief, Brussels and Ottawa this week found solace in each other’s arms, my colleague Jorge Liboreiro writes in his post-Strasbourg analysis.

Russia seizes control of Nestlé subsidiaries
Swiss food giant Nestlé is losing control of part of its Russian business. Russian president Vladimir Putin has placed two Nestlé companies under Russian control.
A decree issued on Thursday stated that shares in Nestlé Russia and Nestlé Kuban would now be managed by the Russian firm LEV Management. The presidential order also applies to French supermarket chain Auchan.
Although Nestlé remains the owner of its subsidiaries, it cannot make decisions regarding these holdings for the time being.
+ Russian supermarket shelves ‘full of Nestlé products’
When asked by the AWP news agency, a Nestlé spokesperson was initially unable to provide any details on the exact consequences.
In August, the Russian company KS Logistika had called on Putin to place five Russian Nestlé subsidiaries under external administration. At the time, Nestlé stated that it had not been contacted by state authorities.
The company added that a withdrawal from Russia was not on the cards.
Nestlé generates around 2% of its group turnover in Russia. The company operates six production sites in Russia, where it manufactures, amongst other things, coffee, confectionery, baby food and pet food.
More
Swiss pharma exports to Russia continue despite war
Following Russia’s military invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Nestlé decided not to completely cease its operations in Russia, despite criticism. The group justified this at the time by stating that, as a food manufacturer, it wished to continue supplying the population with essential foodstuffs, even in conflict regions.
Danone and Carlsberg as role models
Russia has been using the instrument of temporary administration since 2023 to take control of foreign companies’ assets. Nestlé is by no means an isolated case.
For instance, the French food group Danone lost control of its Russian operations as early as 2023. Danone eventually sold them in 2024 for around 180 million euros and recorded a total loss of 1.2 billion euros.
The Danish brewing group Carlsberg faced a similar fate. Its Russian operations were also placed under Russian state administration in 2023. At the end of 2024, Carlsberg completed its withdrawal through a management buy-out worth 320 million dollars. The Dutch brewer Heineken, for its part, sold its Russian subsidiary for the symbolic price of one euro and recorded a total loss of 300 million euros.
