As Iran war grinds on, Trump to face sceptical world leaders at UN
WASHINGTON, Sept 18 - When President Donald Trump addressed the United Nations a year ago, he touted the US bombing of Iran’s nuclear sites just months earlier as "totally obliterating everything" and said he had brought peace between Israel and Iran.
Returning to the world body on Tuesday, Trump will face a deeply skeptical audience increasingly rattled by six months of war between US forces and an emboldened Iran, growing regional instability and a nuclear threat that has not disappeared despite his claims.
Though battered militarily and economically, Tehran has remained defiant, obstructing oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and in recent days gaining new leverage as its Houthi allies in Yemen tighten their grip on a Red Sea chokepoint, further spiking global energy prices.
The lightning advance by the Houthi militants has put Trump in an ever-tighter bind over the unpopular conflict, dealt a blow to US ally Saudi Arabia and exposed the limits of Washington’s ability to protect its regional partners.
Most European and Asian allies have spurned Trump's demands for assistance in a conflict he launched without consulting them and which has had damaging fallout for their economies.
And with US gasoline prices high and his approval ratings low, Trump could pay a price in November’s midterm elections when his Republican Party’s control of Congress is at risk.
“We are seeing what happens when a president launches a war of choice without anticipating the unintended consequences,” said Aaron David Miller, a former adviser on Middle East policy to Republican and Democratic administrations.
In Trump’s speech to the annual gathering of heads of state and government in New York, he is likely again to frame as a victory a military campaign he promised would be over in weeks.
The conflict has instead hardened into an uneasy stalemate that has failed to achieve Trump’s shifting goals while depleting the Pentagon's missile stockpiles.
Trump’s problems have only deepened since Houthi fighters overcame Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, sweeping down the Red Sea coast and seizing islands at the mouth of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping corridor that allows Iran to further threaten global oil supplies.
In response to Reuters' questions, a senior Trump administration official said the US is focused on security interests such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea "while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges."
DOUBTS ABOUT NUCLEAR CLAIMS
Iran took up only a small portion of Trump’s speech at last year's UN General Assembly.
He recounted how, three months before, he had sent B-2 bombers to drop 30,000-pound bombs that “demolished” Tehran’s uranium enrichment capacity. However, experts determined the strikes had only seriously set back the program.
“No other country on Earth could have done what we did,” Trump said.
The US president – who campaigned on a vow to avoid foreign military entanglements - also presented himself as a peacemaker, repeating claims to have ended conflicts around the world, including a 12-day war between Israel and Iran in 2025, and again insisted he should receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
Events since then stand in contrast to his remarks.
Trump joined Israel in striking Iran on February 28, citing what he said was an imminent nuclear threat to the US. Experts have disputed his claim that Iran was close to developing a nuclear weapon, which Tehran has always denied seeking.
But Trump underestimated Iran’s resilience, analysts say. Despite airstrikes that killed many of Iran’s top leaders, it has hit back at Gulf neighbors and the US bases they host.
At the same time, Iran has retained a stockpile of near-weapons-grade highly enriched uranium believed buried by the US strikes in June 2025.
White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said Trump alone had “possessed the courage” to confront Iran over its nuclear program, that he had achieved all his objectives and Iran's economy was being crippled by stepped-up sanctions and a US maritime blockade.
Trump, meanwhile, has rebuffed Saudi pleas for direct military intervention against the Houthis, who agreed to a ceasefire with the US last year.
This has dented confidence about US security guarantees among Gulf states, whose doubts had already been fed by Trump’s decision to go to war over their objections, analysts say. He plans to meet Gulf leaders on the UN sidelines next week, Axios reported.
TRUMP'S DILEMMA
The dilemma for Trump is that while the US can ill afford to have the Houthis close a second major shipping corridor, he is reluctant to undertake a dangerous new mission for a US military stretched by the fighting against Iran.
US officials met the Houthis last weekend in Oman, where the group said that while it was targeting Saudi shipping it had no intention of attacking American vessels, according to five people familiar with the matter.
“The US clearly has (military) capacity challenges but even so the cost of inaction here is likely to intensify tensions among Gulf allies,” said Jonathan Panikoff, a former deputy national intelligence officer on the Middle East.
The Houthis’ sudden re-emergence as a regional threat has further complicated Trump’s efforts to find a way out of the conflict.
With the war grinding on in a seventh month, the US is mired in a battle of attrition while Trump tries to intensify economic pressure on Tehran.
Trump, who has offered shifting timelines, told reporters on Wednesday that “hopefully we are towards the end.”
But analysts warn that the conflict is likely to drag on well past the midterm elections.
“Iran isn’t about to let him off the hook here while they have so much leverage to damage him in the midterms and make him a lame duck,” Brett Erickson, a geopolitical analyst and managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors, wrote on X. REUTERS

Australia to detain tourists who overstay visas amid immigration crackdown

Australia to detain tourists who overstay visas amid immigration crackdown
More than 77,000 visa overstayers face detention or departure as Australia cracks down on immigration violations.
Australia will begin detaining visa overstayers as part of a broader immigration crackdown, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced.
The Australian Border Force will expand its team by 100 compliance officers, who will work to detain or encourage the departure of roughly 77,000 people currently living in Australia without a valid visa, Burke said Thursday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3The US border runs straight through the World Cup
- list 2 of 3Trump plans largest mass visa cancellation in history: Who will it affect?
- list 3 of 3US says far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported to UK
He said the policy was designed to reintroduce consequences for overstaying.
“Before 2015, we had a routine process in Australia for overstayers where, when people had overstayed a visa, we would bring people into detention centres … and within a few weeks they would organise their own flight and leave,” Burke announced at the National Press Club.
To aid the operation, 250 new detention beds will be created, including the possible use of a former quarantine facility in Melbourne.
He rejected comparisons to the United States’ hardline Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency, saying, “This is not the sort of operation that some people have seen on TV happening in other countries.”
Burke also said the government would clamp down on “visa hopping”, a system that Canberra alleges is when foreigners who are already in Australia move from one type of temporary visa to another to extend their stay.
A new “No Further Stay” provision would prevent people arriving on tourist visas from lodging new applications once inside the country, while international students would be required to advance their qualifications when seeking a new study visa, closing off the option of jumping between courses at low-level institutions to extend their stay.
Burke said separate legislation would be needed to curb a significant caseload of people making what he called “disingenuous” asylum claims to prolong their time in the country.
Rights groups pushed back, and the Human Rights Law Centre warned the change could deter exploited undocumented workers from reporting abuse.
Australia’s governing Labor Party has denied that its tightened visa rules are a response to the growing popularity of the far-right One Nation Party, which has emerged as one of the country’s most popular parties in 2026.
Australia remains one of the world’s most popular tourist destinations, drawing millions of annual visitors with its beaches, wildlife and cities, while also relying heavily on international students and working-holiday visa holders as a major source of migration and economic activity.
The overstayer population has grown steadily, from about 64,000 in 2016 to more than 77,000 in 2026, even as net overseas migration has fallen.

Greenland and Antarctica have lost 12 trillion tonnes of ice since 1979
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:02:24 UTC
14:02:24 KST

Ice loss began accelerating in the 1990s, according to a major scientific study.
Greenland and Antarctica have lost 12.5 trillion tonnes of ice since 1979, raising global sea levels by around 3.2 centimetres, according to a major scientific study.
The researchers found that ice loss has accelerated in recent decades, particularly since the 1990s.
Most of the loss is linked to warmer ocean temperatures, which cause glaciers to discharge more ice into the sea.
Ice loss accelerated sharply during the 2010s
The study combines satellite observations covering more than four decades. It extends the record back to 1979 for Antarctica and 1972 for Greenland.
The data shows the ice sheets were relatively stable through the 1970s, 1980s and into the 1990s.
Ice loss then increased, with the strongest acceleration recorded during the 2010s.
“There is a clear trend that the ice sheets are losing more mass and it has been increasing from decade to decade,” says Inès Otosaka, an ice scientist at Northumbria University.
She says the changes were clearly linked to rising air and ocean temperatures.
Warmer oceans drive most of the ice loss
Around 84 per cent of the ice loss is linked to increased ice discharge into the oceans, the researchers found.
Surface processes account for the remaining 16 per cent. Warmer seawater can erode ice from below and around the edges of glaciers, increasing their flow towards the ocean.
In Greenland, the Jakobshavn glacier is retreating by up to 50 metres a day, Otosaka says.
Ice loss is raising sea levels
The ice loss has contributed around 3.2 centimetres to global sea level rise since 1979. Scientists say even small increases can have significant consequences for coastal areas.
For every centimetre of sea level rise, an estimated two to three million more people could face annual coastal flooding.
Ice loss slowed between 2020 and 2023, but researchers say this reflected short-term weather patterns rather than a change in the longer-term trend. They also warn that ice-sheet responses to climate change can take decades. This means ice loss could continue even if global warming were brought under control.
The study was published in the journal Scientific Data.

Premiumisation, industry recovery and AI: What’s trending in travel at ATM Dubai 2026?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:49 UTC
14:00:49 KST

At Arabian Travel Market in Dubai, much of the conversation on the sidelines was about the major disruptions so far this year, but there was also a big focus on recovery as new trends and products shape the industry’s future.
There’s no doubt about it, it’s been a tough year for the tourism industry – especially in the Middle East, where regional conflict and the knock-on effects have disrupted travel.
Despite a record-breaking year for global tourism in 2025, the geopolitical situation has impacted travel to the Middle East and Gulf in 2026, with visitor numbers, air capacity and hospitality bookings all taking a significant hit.
While much of the conversation on the sidelines at Arabian Travel Market (ATM) in Dubai centred on this year’s major disruptions, there were also signs of industry recovery.
Unveiled this week, the ATM Travel Trends Report 2026 revealed that international travel across the Middle East, North Africa and South Asia (MENASA) region is forecast to rebound by 17% in 2027, “more than twice the projected global growth rate of 8%”, according to Tourism Economics, which co-produced the report.
It's also expected that international visitor spending in the Middle East will increase by $116 billion (€100.58 billion), or 57%, between 2025 and 2030.
Speaking at ATM Dubai, Dave Goodger, Managing Director EMEA of Tourism Economics, was “optimistic” about the forecasts.
“Over the next five years we see travel expanding on a structural basis rather than just a cyclical rebound,” he said. “International travel has never mattered more. This year is disrupted by an uncertain economic and geopolitical backdrop, but consumers are treating travel as essential.”
As the industry looks towards recovery and the long-term, many trends are emerging that could shape the next era in tourism.
From the “premiumisation” of travel and rise of lesser-known destinations to the use of AI for trip discovery, we take a look at the report’s main findings and some of the other big talking points on the ground this week at ATM Dubai.
The ‘premiumisation’ of travel
Luxury remains an important part of the travel market, particularly in the Middle East and Gulf, where Goodger said nearly 80% of prospective visitors prioritise luxury when travelling. But “premiumisation” extends beyond traditional five-star hotels.
Travellers are increasingly willing to spend more on particular elements of a holiday that matter to them, from upgraded airline cabins to memorable activities.
“People want those luxury experiences, they want those premium experiences, but they will save money where they can,” Goodger said. The report also found that 35% of travellers were more interested in premium experiences than two years ago.
Value hunting and price-conscious travel
The search for value is happening alongside premiumisation rather than replacing it. In a separate interview with Euronews Travel, Goodger said greater price-consciousness was a “global challenge”, evident across Europe, North America, China and other Asian markets.
“People are price conscious, they’re looking for value, but they are looking for valuable experiences,” he said. That could mean spending less on accommodation to pay for the experiences that motivated the holiday in the first place.
“They’re not just saying… ‘I’m going to find the cheapest package holiday I can do’,” Goodger added. “They are saying, ‘I will downgrade on the hotel, but I still really want to do that experience that I’m doing while I’m there’.”
The rise of lesser-known destinations
Of the travellers surveyed, 56% are more interested in exploring new destinations than they were two years ago, rising to 68% among prospective visitors to MENASA.
While this creates opportunities for secondary cities and regions away from established tourism hotspots, it doesn’t mean that Paris, London and other tourism giants are losing their appeal.
Goodger said first-time international travellers still want to “stand in front of the Eiffel Tower” or “see Buckingham Palace”, while repeat visitors are increasingly venturing further afield.
“They’re the ones that are going to the new destinations, the new regions, the secondary destinations,” he told Euronews Travel.
Experience-first travel
Travellers are increasingly choosing an experience or passion first and building their trip around it.
Culture and authentic experiences are among the priorities highlighted by Tourism Economics, while travellers are showing greater interest in activities, food and sport.
“People are looking for experiences,” Goodger said at ATM. “They want new experiences. They want these cultural experiences.”
Overtourism and when people travel
Mass tourism is also beginning to influence travel decisions. Tourism Economics' research found that three in 10 travellers actively avoid destinations because of overcrowding concerns.
Goodger told Euronews Travel that overtourism remains particularly significant in Europe, although the shift away from crowded destinations is still “very subtle”.
One emerging trend is travelling outside the busiest months. “We are seeing a bit of a flattening of seasonality,” he said. “People are looking outside of peak season for travel, just so they can have that experience without the crowds.”
This could benefit destinations attempting to spread visitors more evenly across the year, as well as lesser-known places looking to attract travellers away from overcrowded hotspots.
Event tourism
Travellers are increasingly crossing borders specifically to attend events, adding further momentum to the rise of sports and music tourism. Three in 10 travellers surveyed said they were more interested in event-related travel than two years ago.
Goodger highlighted “sporting, cultural [and] religious events” as increasingly strong drivers of travel, particularly in the Middle East.
Business events are also important with association meeting attendance in the Middle East nearly doubling over the past decade.
AI for trip discovery
Perhaps the biggest change to how travellers discover and plan their next trip is the growing use of AI. Goodger said travellers interested in visiting the Middle East are particularly "tech-forward", with AI chatbots already playing a significant role in trip planning.
The report found that 28% of prospective visitors to the Middle East had used an AI chatbot to plan a trip, compared with 12% of travellers interested in other regions.
AI could also help bring lesser-known destinations into consideration as travellers move away from traditional keyword searches towards more conversational queries based on the type of holiday they want.
For destinations, Goodger said that means being visible in a rapidly changing discovery landscape. “It’s absolutely crucial for the destinations to be discoverable through those different platforms.”

The EU and Canada are getting closer than ever. And the world is watching
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:15 UTC
14:00:15 KST

The EU's move to make Canada an "associate member" is being watched worldwide as a new model to attract other democracies in its orbit, but it risks alienating candidate countries and further straining ties with Washington.
With Canada, the European Union has opened the door to a new way for the European project to affiliate with third countries that aren't even on its own continent. The rest of the world will be watching closely.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spearheaded the idea of an alliance of middle powers in his seminal speech in Davos earlier this year. A few months later, Canada might provide the blueprint for how the EU integrates third countries.
On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become "the first associate member of the European Union," proposing an unprecedented arrangement that still has to be fully defined.
Whichever framework Brussels and Ottawa manage to agree on will have consequences well beyond Europe, as there is international attention on whether the EU can create an attractive blueprint to pull other democracies into its orbit.
"A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies. An alliance not defined by what we oppose, but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability," Carney told the European Parliament on Thursday.
Unprecedented arrangement
The EU does not currently envisage an "associate membership." The idea was first floated by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as an innovative way to integrate Ukraine into the EU, but the proposal was rebuffed by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
So far, the Union has consisted solely of member states and candidate countries. Canada, meanwhile, has no intention of joining the bloc, as Carney has made clear, and its treaties would not permit it in any case, given that Canada is not a European country.
"The precise nomenclature is a question for Europe," the Canadian PM said, arguing that what mattered was the substance.
The EU treaties do allow some flexibility, as they state that "the Union may conclude with one or more third countries or international organisations agreements establishing an association involving reciprocal rights and obligations, common action and special procedure."
What exactly this associate status would entail is still not clear. Carney proposed deep cooperation across the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space and payments.
But while the details remain to be hashed out, what appears clear is that whatever deal Brussels and Ottawa reach will be a highly influential precedent for how the EU engages with other partners.
Trusted partners
The idea of making Canada an associate member of the EU was first made public via a WSJ report earlier this week.
"We are on the same page," Australian Trade Minister Don Farrell told the Sydney Morning Herald. "We will take great interest in what Carney does."
In an exclusive interview with Euronews, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said that Australia and New Zealand might follow Canada's path, as the EU seeks to deepen ties with like-minded countries.
MEP Tobias Cremer (Germany/S&D), the European Parliament's rapporteur for Canada, told reporters he was receiving an increasing number of media requests, not only from Canadian outlets but also from Australian, British and Japanese ones.
Meanwhile, the UK is reportedly feeling left out of Brussels' newfound love for Canada, as some in London believe the EU is more interested in closer relations with Canada than with the UK.
"We need to think of partnerships that go beyond EU membership," Austria's Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger wrote on X. "Let's make that a model for the future — one that Europe also offers to other partners: Norway, Iceland, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand."
In other words, the success of the special relationship with Canada might put the EU at the centre of a new international alliance, as democratic countries that have lost faith in the US as leader of the Western world realign.
International order
The newfound alignment between Brussels and Ottawa might be one step closer to the realisation of Carney's vision of an alliance of middle powers, meant to strengthen each other's sovereignty by weathering shifting geopolitical realities together.
"I want to be precise about what I am not proposing. I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival, only with better manners," he said.
"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law," Carney continued.
In Brussels, officials tend to point out that, while member states taken on their own might be middle powers, the EU as a whole is not, and might actually emerge as a leader of a democratic coalition to support the faltering rules-based international order.
"We are by definition a convening power of middle powers in the way we function. I think that makes us actually attractive to many other middle powers, because the EU, like no other global player, has in its DNA leveraging small and middle powers without trampling on their interests," Cremer said.
At the same time, as the EU pursues global ambitions to forge deeper ties with democracies on other continents, some fear it might lose sight of its most immediate neighbourhood.
Unsettled candidates
The acceleration of the EU-Canada partnership, and the entirely new format on offer, has fallen flat especially among countries that have been standing in line to join for decades, such as in the Western Balkans.
It is not the first time the EU has floated a new membership structure. Candidate countries have seen, in close succession, the growth plan, reverse enlargement, gradual integration and now a tiered form of membership.
There is also a risk that the move further strains transatlantic relations with the US, with President Donald Trump already threatening possible retaliation, which might put pressure on candidate countries to pick a side between the two blocs.
"I don't feel comfortable with the constant new ideas over membership and the lack of discussion concerning the acceptance of new members," Obrad Kesić, the head of Bosnia and Herzegovina's mission to the EU, told Euronews.
"Canada is a large country, it could have negative ramifications for small candidate countries if the discussion becomes too broad. It changes the contour of the debate," Kesić said. "Conceiving memberships as going beyond Europe opens up a new set of issues."

Analysis: Bruised by Trump, EU and Canada find solace in each other's arms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:13 UTC
14:00:13 KST

The blossoming partnership between the European Union and Canada cannot be understood apart from the behaviour of the US president, who has assailed both sides with his punitive tariffs and annexationist threats.
Taunted, scorned, belittled, pushed aside, ditched – it is fair to say that the European Union and Canada each know how the other feels.
For the past 20 months, the two have been relentlessly subjected to Donald Trump's threats, demands and commands. Their experiences have been nearly identical: punitive tariffs, annexationist attempts, regulatory intrusion, bitter recriminations, all amplified in scathing personal attacks splashed all over social media.
The breakup has been painful, to say the least. After all, both the EU and Canada have long defined the United States as their closest ally, their main security provider, their trade partner of choice. But Trump's return to the White House abruptly overturned these long-held assumptions, forcing them to reckon with their place in a cruel, cold world.
This week, they found solace in each other's arms. In back-to-back highly publicised speeches, the EU and Canada brought their courtship into a full-fledged, out-in-the-open romance.
Ursula von der Leyen made the first move during her State of the Union address, inviting Canada to make history by becoming the bloc's first-ever "associate member" – a brand new legal status devised to accommodate Ottawa.
"We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us," the European Commission president said, in a thinly veiled swipe at Trump.
"This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength," she went on. "We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible."
The announcement, which was not included in the embargoed speech sent in advance to the press, was met with thunderous applause inside the European Parliament. Smiling in the audience, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney got up to kiss von der Leyen on the cheek.
The following day, she took a seat as he addressed the same audience himself.
"Europe and Canada are stronger together," Carney declared to more applause. "Let us now deepen these roots, widen this canopy and grow a transatlantic forest under which our citizens can flourish as free people on free ground."
The grand statements sent Europe's Canada fever into overdrive. Lawmakers in Strasbourg lined up to take selfies with Carney. The leader of the Greens, Terry Reintke, donned a Canada jersey for his speech; Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez tweeted a European flag with a maple leaf next to the 12 stars, while French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the EU and Canada were "destined" to closer bonds.
Roberta Metsola, the European Parliament president, went further and name-checked Australia and New Zealand as next in line to be the bloc's "associate members".
"I don't doubt that it will include other countries, and others will come knocking at our door," Metsola told Euronews. "In such times of uncertainty, having friends matters."
The other side was no less enthusiastic: a poll conducted ahead of Carney's trip showed that 56% of Canadians think they have more in common with the EU, which is one ocean away, than with the US, with which they share an 8,891 km land border.
Beyond the love, anxiety
Brussels and Ottawa have framed their fascination as self-evident.
The two see themselves as equally committed to liberal democracy, the rule of law and open markets, making them, on paper, a perfectly compatible match.
In their speeches, von der Leyen and Carney spare no effort in listing the multiple areas of cooperation in which the EU and Canada can thrive together: trade, energy, critical raw materials, batteries, AI, quantum, finance, defence, space, the Arctic.
Carney touted a scheme to grant young people freedom of movement to "live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic", while von der Leyen spoke of a "common prosperity and economic security space".
It is not by coincidence that these are areas where cooperation with the US has become increasingly difficult, at times prohibitive, under Trump, with whom Carney is currently embroiled in a trade war that could wreck key sectors of the Canadian economy.
They did, however, disagree on semantics.
Von der Leyen went all in on the headline-making "associate member" title, despite lacking legal precedent and raising more questions than answers. It was not clear how, or if, the Commission chief had consulted with capitals before her pitch.
Carney, meanwhile, opted for "alliance for the future", a less charged term. For the premier, "associate membership" carries the connotation of ceding sovereignty to Brussels, something he stressed would not be the case under any circumstance.
"The precise nomenclature is a question for Europe," he said.
Beyond that hiccup, the two stayed very much on the same script, sometimes using the same words to lavish praise on each other.
But underneath the smiles, the hugs and the adulation lay a creeping anxiety about what the future holds.
The EU and Canada are today trapped between adversarial forces – Trump's "America first" agenda, China's unfair competition, Russia's aggression – that risk undoing their wealth and plunging them into a spiral of stagnation. They can only watch as the global norms they seek to uphold are weakened from within.
Their friendship is therefore as much about thriving as it is about surviving.
Trump, in particular, has proven a powerful push factor forcing them closer together. His penchant for disruption has made the blossoming partnership feel almost inevitable.
The US president was quick to take note of the love fest and threatened to impose "very serious tariffs" if the "associate membership" were perceived as a "hostile act".
Carney insisted the EU-Canada alliance was a "positive initiative" and "not a reaction to something else". But in his speech, he implicitly chided Trump when he said Canada was not a "fair-weather" ally that pursues "zero-sum deals".
Penny Naas, the director of the Brussels office at the German Marshall Fund, believes the newfound EU-Canada affinity is but a "natural outgrowth" of the past 20 months.
"The US is moving away from anchoring and leading its traditional alliance of democratic countries. This is clearly motivating the look for new partners in an uncertain world," Naas told Euronews.
"Trade status and regulatory alignment are no longer background conditions for prosperity. They are the terrain on which power is being contested directly," she added.
"Any EU-Canada architecture will be judged, and attacked, on those terms from the start."

Helen Goh’s recipe for blackcurrant and vanilla finger buns | The sweet spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:10 UTC
14:00:10 KST

Soft, feather-light and topped with a thick strip of icing: few things are as irresistible to me as an iced finger bun. Here, I’ve flavoured the fondant with blackcurrant jam, which lends a gentle tartness to balance the sweetness, though almost any good-quality jam will work. A simple tanzhong (a cooked flour-and-milk paste) gives the buns their wonderfully fluffy crumb and keeps them soft for longer. For a more indulgent version, split the buns along the top and fill with whipped cream and a spoonful of jam instead. They’re best assembled just before serving, and make a particularly lovely afternoon treat.
Blackcurrant and vanilla finger buns
Prep 10 min
 Prove 2 hr+
 Cook 1 hr 15 min
 Makes 12
For the dough
  270ml whole milk 
  7g dried instant yeast
  400g strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
  50g caster sugar
  1 large egg, lightly whisked
¾ tsp fine sea salt
  1 tsp vanilla paste
  60g unsalted butter, cut into small cubes and softened, plus a little extra for greasing
For the blackcurrant fondant
  70g blackcurrant (or other) jam
  180g icing sugar, sifted
2 tsp lemon juice
1 tiny pinch fine sea salt
  1-2 tsp hot water, as needed
Pour the milk into a small saucepan and heat gently until just lukewarm. Measure 140ml into the bowl of a stand mixer, stir in the yeast and leave until bubbly.
Meanwhile, whisk the remaining milk in the pan with 25g of the flour, then cook, whisking constantly, on a medium heat for about five minutes, until it thickens into a smooth paste. Set aside to cool until just warm.
Whisk the milk and yeast mix, then add the remaining 375g flour, the sugar, egg, salt, vanilla and the cooled milk/flour mix. Attach the dough hook and mix on low speed for about three minutes, until it turns into a rough dough. Turn up the speed to medium, add the butter a few cubes at a time and mix for eight to 10 minutes in total, scraping the base and sides of the bowl occasionally, until the dough is smooth and elastic. The dough should start to pull away from the sides of the bowl while still feeling soft and slightly tacky. Transfer the dough to a large, lightly greased bowl, cover and leave in a warm place for one to two hours, until doubled in size.
Line a large baking tray with baking paper. Turn out the dough on to a lightly floured work surface and weigh it. Divide the total by 12, then cut the dough into 12 equal 60g pieces. Shape each one into a tight ball by pulling the edges into the centre and pinching to seal underneath. Put the balls seam-side down on your worktop and, using lightly cupped hands, roll until smooth. Gently roll each ball back and forth to form neat, 12cm-long logs; if you like, taper the ends slightly.
Arrange the buns on the lined tray, leaving about 3cm between them (they’ll expand and just meet as they bake, which helps keep the sides soft). Cover loosely and leave to prove for an hour, until risen and puffy.
Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5, then bake the buns for 15 minutes, rotating the tray once halfway, until lightly golden. Transfer to a rack to cool completely.
Meanwhile, make the fondant. Warm the jam gently until loosened, then pass it through a fine sieve – you should have about 50g. Whisk in the sifted icing sugar, lemon juice and salt, until smooth, then add just enough water to make a thick, spreadable fondant. Transfer to a shallow bowl wide enough to dip the buns into.
Dip the top of each cooled bun into the fondant, allowing any excess to drip back into the bowl, then put on a rack for the icing to set before serving.

‘A map is never neutral’: meet the cartographers who took on centuries of western bias
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:10 UTC
14:00:10 KST

Three cartographers have spoken of their astonishment at the UN’s near-universal adoption of a map they created to more accurately show the sizes of Africa and Europe, even though they have received a few complaints from some disgruntled diplomats.
The creators of the Equal Earth projection aimed to provide an alternative to the dominant 16th-century Mercator display, which critics have long faulted for giving the impression that northern hemisphere nations are larger than they are – and therefore subtly reinforcing perceptions of where global strength lies.
“It has been a very busy week for me,” said Tom Patterson, a renowned US national parks cartographer who has had to virtually come out of retirement after being inundated with questions from governments on details of the new projection.
The UN general assembly voted this month to adopt the new map, which more accurately represents the sizes of all continents, particularly Africa. It is hoped the projection will gradually replace Mercator on school walls and government websites.
Put forward by Togo, the proposal was hugely successful, with 164 countries voting in favour. The only “no” vote came from the US, whose UN representative, Yaryna Ferencevych, said resolutions such as the “correct the map” effort were “barnacles on our work here”. The US is one of the countries that appears smaller on the new projection. It also makes Greenland – a territorial prize Donald Trump has openly coveted as a “big beautiful piece of ice” – seem significantly less dominant.
Six other nations abstained from the vote, and Patterson said he had been contacted by diplomats from government embassies in Washington DC looking for clarification.
Japan asked for a revision because it said the map made the disputed Kuril Islands appear to belong to Russia by putting them in the same shade of yellow. Ukraine also abstained, as Russian-occupied Crimea was a different colour to the rest of the country. Ukraine’s representatives at the UN said this opened a “Pandora’s box” and violated international law.
The cartographers see these objections as stemming from something of a misunderstanding. The map voted on at the UN is simply a mathematical projection of the land and sea, without human-made borders or shading. The confusion arose due to a website run by Patterson that offers free Equal Earth projections. He had annotated these with geopolitical lines and the names of countries, and has been rushing this week to update them, including switching colours and changing spellings, such as Turkey to Türkiye.
“I view the Equal Earth maps as living documents and am grateful for the many helpful suggestions that I have received,” he said.
Patterson developed the new projection in 2018 with a California-based software engineer, Bojan Šavrič, the “maths wizard” of the trio, and Bernhard Jenny, an associate professor at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia.
Jenny said people generally believed maps were accurate representations of the Earth, but that logic breaks down because we live on a curved surface. This creates a problem, as a sphere cannot easily be transformed into a flat rectangle.
“It’s like the orange peel analogy,” said Jenny. “You have to tear it and stretch it, and it’s not possible to flatten it out … so you have to make compromises.”
One global map, called the Goode homolosine projection, looks strikingly like a ripped-up orange peel. Its main problems are that it is not very pleasing to the human eye and not very easy to use for navigation – something the flawed Mercator excels at, because north is always up.
For Jenny, cartography is about aesthetics as well as science. “We cartographers say cartography is the art and science of making maps. So it’s kind of the combination of the two.”
Equal Earth is not the first attempt to address Mercator’s shortcomings. Several other projections were developed in the past century, including the Gall-Peters model, which shows the true relative sizes of land masses, but which often appears oddly elongated, almost like the continents are drooping. Jenny said: “There was a lot of backlash from cartographers who said: ‘Well, it looks like clothes are hung up to dry.’”
There are always compromises when making maps. Spend any amount of time with a cartographer and what might seem like fundamental truths quickly break down. “Which way is up?” or “Where is the centre” are not simple questions for cartographers – ancient Islamic maps had a south-up orientation, which put the holy city of Mecca in the eyeline. A London-centric worldview has long dominated how world maps are presented, with Greenwich in the centre.
“You have to make compromises,” said Jenny. The Equal Earth map, for example, would not be useful for getting around, as countries on the edges are squeezed. In fact, if any country had a claim to be upset, it could be New Zealand, which is stretched and distorted, and on the edge of the map.
“A map is never neutral,” said Jenny. “So you cannot please everyone.”
Šavrič, who worked on the mathematical formula, said he never imagined eight years ago that the trio’s research would be discussed at the highest levels.
“What pleases me more is that this creates a valuable opportunity to strengthen map literacy and raise awareness that there is no single map projection capable of providing a completely ‘true’ representation of the world,” he said. “Every map projection involves trade-offs. I particularly appreciate that the [UN] resolution does not completely ban the Mercator projection or mandate a single replacement for all maps.”
Jenny was also thrilled, watching on from Australia. “It’s kind of a cartographer’s dream, right?” he said. “The fact that the UN is debating map projections for an entire hour is already totally thrilling for cartographers, and then it was our map projection. I mean, what else can you ask for?”
He does, however, have a hunch that another factor helped the Equal Earth map: the power of a good name. “I think, definitely, that you know what it is immediately,” said Jenny. If they had called it the “Šavrič-Patterson-Jenny projection”, he joked, maybe it would not have done so well.

‘Run! Get away!’: witnesses recount Israeli ‘double tap’ strike that killed child and medic in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:10 UTC
14:00:10 KST

Mohammad Abdul Zinati was walking home from school through the rubble of Salah Khalaf Street, in northern Gaza City, when he stopped at a supermarket where a group of classmates and friends had gathered.
Shortly before 3:30pm, an explosion tore through the air. Along with several others, Mohammad rushed into the street to see what had happened.
When the smoke and dust cleared, they saw a man lying bleeding on the dusty road. He was badly wounded, but still alive. The man was calling for help, and Mohammad ran towards him.
He did not hear the shouts of his cousin, who had spotted an approaching Israeli drone. Within seconds, the drone released a glide bomb, designed to allow operators to identify and strike targets with a high degree of accuracy.
The munition plunged towards the street, detonating just metres from the teenager. Mohammad did not have time to react before a second blast killed him.
The Guardian verified footage of the attack, and spoke to witnesses and weapons experts in an effort to shed light on the latest Israeli strike to kill a child in Gaza.
“We heard a loud explosion and tried to make our way to the scene to find out what had happened,” said Tamer Lubbad, a witness who filmed the attack. “We found a man lying on the ground. He was still alive and calling for help.”
The man injured in the initial strike was later identified by Gaza’s civil defense as the paramedic Sharif Shadi Labad. The Israeli military said that Labad was targeted because he was a Hamas militant.
Several other civilians approached Labad, as he lay injured in the street. Among them was Mohammad Zinati’s cousin, Mohammed Rajeh Zinati, 26.
“I ran from the house towards the street to find out what had happened,” he said.
“On my way, I saw my cousin coming out of the supermarket. He was running towards the site of the strike. I started shouting at him: ‘Mohammad, stop!’ but he didn’t hear me and kept going. Then I saw a drone in the sky.
“I started shouting: ‘Run! Get away!’ At that moment, Mohammad had reached the injured man. As soon as he got there, the drone struck him.”
“Mohammad was hit directly in the chest and abdomen and was killed almost instantly. I couldn’t do anything to rescue him,” said Zinati.
Video filmed later showed Mohammad’s body lying under a white shroud outside al-Shifa hospital after the attack, as his father bid him an emotional farewell, reciting verses from the Qur’an.
People who knew Mohammad said he was a much-loved figure in the neighbourhood.
“He was a kind, helpful, polite and respectful boy,” his cousin said. ‘‘He would help elderly to collect water from the water trucks. When he was killed, people from the neighbourhood came out into the street, crying for him.”
The IDF has repeatedly rejected allegations that it deliberately targets civilians, saying it assesses and takes into account the risk of civilian harm when carrying out strikes.
However, weapons experts who reviewed the video said the teenager’s death may have been avoidable.
‘‘The bomb that is visible before impact is a Mikholit, which is deployed by Israeli unmanned vehicles (UAVs) or drones, said Trevor Ball, a conflict researcher and trainer at Bellingcat and drone expert. ‘‘These UAVs have high-quality cameras that would have been able to see the teenager and the man approaching the body. Some variants of the Mikholit at least are capable of being redirected to a different target/point while in flight.’’
The strike that killed the teenager and the paramedic appears to fit the pattern commonly described as a “double-tap” attack: an initial strike followed by a second on the same location after rescuers or bystanders have arrived to help the wounded.
In a statement to the Guardian, the Israeli military said Sharif Shadi Ibrahim Labad was a Hamas terrorist who belonged to the elite Nukhba forces. The IDF stated that Labad had participated in the 7 October attacks in 2023 at the Erez border crossing and was targeted because he was planning new operations.
Asked why the second attack went ahead when its target was visibly a minor, the military did not respond, but said it ‘‘is aware of reports indicating that an uninvolved individual was harmed as a result of the strike targeting the terrorist, regrets any harm to uninvolved individuals and makes every effort to minimise such harm”.
The Israeli military said the incident was under review.
On Tuesday, medical sources in Gaza reported an Israeli strike on al-Bureij refugee camp that killed an adult and a five-year-old child, identified as Udai al-Muridi.
A pregnant Palestinian woman died on Saturday from injuries sustained after being shot in the head by Israeli forces south of Khan Younis, according to her family and medical workers.
The woman, named as Iman Shalouf, 27, who was nearly eight months pregnant, was sitting inside her family’s tent in the Mawasi area when Israeli gunfire struck her, according to paramedics and witnesses.
The Israeli military said it had no information about the killing of the pregnant woman.
According to Unicef, several other children have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza in recent days, including two sisters aged six and 12, who were killed with their parents in an airstrike on Beit Lahia while they slept, and three other girls aged, three, eight and nine, who were killed by gunfire.
According to the territory’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025. Since Israel’s war in Gaza began on 7 October 2023, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to health officials.

Improved air quality linked to better mental development in toddlers, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:10 UTC
14:00:10 KST

Improvements in air pollution are leading to brighter, smarter toddlers, according to a new study from Columbia University in New York.
For more than two decades, Prof Frederica Perera and a team from the Columbia Center for Children’s Environmental Health measured the air pollution exposure of pregnant women and the development of their children in the disadvantaged communities of northern Manhattan and the South Bronx. More than 1,100 children were assessed when they were one, two and three years old.
Perera said: “We tested cognitive processing including memory and sensory perception, problem-solving such as matching shapes, stacking blocks and communication, both speech and language comprehension. In the early years of the study, we reported significant associations between prenatal exposure to air pollution and neurodevelopment effects in the children. That was bad news.”
Over the course of the study, air pollution in central New York improved massively. Clean-air legislation reduced some pollutants from the city’s yellow taxis by as much as 80%. Heavy fuel oils are being phased out for heating the city’s buildings and cleaner fuels are being used in the city’s buses. Fine particle pollution and levels of nitrogen dioxide halved between 1998 and 2016.
Perera continued: “Would we see an association between improved air quality and improved mental development scores in the toddlers over time?”
The good news is that the toddlers’ scores improved as the air pollution improved. This was especially clear when the children were two and three years old, and during times of sharper falls in air pollution. The researchers were also able to take into account the effects of other factors that may have affected the children’s development. These included rapid declines in the proportion of children who lived with a tobacco smoker, which fell from 34% to 18%, and increases in maternal education, with a nine percentage-point increase in the proportion of mothers who had successfully graduated from high school.
The New York study adds to the growing evidence that air pollution is a fixable problem and that health improves when air pollution is reduced.
In the UK, the introduction of London’s ultra-low emission zone was accompanied by an improvement in children’s lung health and fewer children with clinically impaired lung function. For adults in central London, there was a 3% reduction in annual trends for emergency admissions, including an 8% reduction for heart problems and a 6% reduction for breathing problems. A reduction of about 25% in GP visits for heart and breathing problems followed the implementation of a clean-air zone in Bradford, West Yorkshire.
Despite the improvements in New York, Perera emphasised: “We cannot conclude that contemporary levels of air pollution are safe for the neurodevelopment of all children.”
Action on air pollution requires bold political leadership. It is often controversial and can be made into a divisive political issue, but it can work. Perera said: “We need more studies such as ours to increase public awareness of the value of clean air and climate policies and motivate policymakers.”
A recent report by the UN Environment programme found that integrated action on air pollution and climate change emissions makes economic sense too, with an average return of $15 in economic benefits for every $1 invested.

MPs urge ministers to break off Thames Water talks with US hedge funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:09 UTC
14:00:09 KST

Andy Burnham is under further pressure to take control of ailing Thames Water from a cross-party group of MPs who are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds who are effectively running the company.
Adding their voices to demands that the prime minister takes public control of the company, which has debts of £20bn and is being controlled by a group of 100 hedge funds and distressed-debt investors, the MPs said in a report that ministers should consider emergency legislation to take control of its financial affairs to stabilise the company.
Alistair Carmichael, the chair of the environment, food and rural affairs committee (Efra), said it was unbelievable that the special administration regime (SAR) for insolvent or failing water companies could not be triggered for Thames Water on performance grounds alone.
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has suggested that an SAR – effectively temporary public control – cannot be triggered under the current law because of the way the US hedge funds that bought Thames Water’s debt have kept it running while seeking a deal to renegotiate its liabilities.
The report said Ofwat and the government should withdraw from negotiating with the consortium of distressed-debt specialists who lacked the proper expertise to turn around a vital public service.
Carmichael said the creditors were operating in an opaque way, seeking relief from environmental penalties and dragging out negotiations while reaping millions of pounds in debt interest.
“Thames Water’s 16 million customers have largely lost faith in it,” he said. “They are sick of seeing their waterways polluted, their bills going up, and drinking water gush through broken pavements while supplies run low. We believe Thames Water can be turned around, but not by giving the keys back to the people who have been joy-riding in the family car.
“The government should reject offers from the company’s creditors in return for relief from fines for pollution and poor service. We do not believe this opaque consortium of 100 hedge funds and others has the interests of the public, the company or the environment at heart.”
The report said ministers should explore all potential alternative options, including an SAR or using fresh legislation to draw a line under the debacle and restore stability to the sector by putting Thames Water on a sound footing for new buyers.
Carmichael said putting the company into special administration once its money ran out could be the only way to reset its fortunes. “Liabilities that the government will face in the short term may be offset by a future sale of Thames Water once a new buyer can be found,” he said.
The intervention comes after 64 MPs debated a 200,000-strong petition, set up by the campaigner Ash Smith of Windrush Against Sewage Pollution, to hold a referendum on putting the privatised water industry back into public ownership.
MPs on the Efra committee said they were concerned that not enough regulatory due diligence had been carried out on the US-led consortium that bought Thames Water’s debt.
Elliott Investment Management is one of the leading creditors in the group that includes Silver Point Capital, BlackRock and M&G. Elliott’s founder and co-chief executive is Paul Singer, a Trump donor whom Bloomberg has described as “the most feared investor in the world”.
The consortium of hedge funds – known as London & Valley Water – is attempting to take over Thames in a multibillion-pound restructuring. It is seeking relief from environmental fines which could be worth up to £1bn, requesting leniency on environmental measures including pollution, leakage and other performance targets imposed a year ago.
MPs said: “Their demands demonstrate that they will not prioritise the swift turnaround in performance that Thames Water so desperately needs.
“Whilst keeping the company in limbo by drawing out negotiations, these creditors are simultaneously reaping millions in debt interest and fees. We have grave concerns … L&VW is an opaque consortium which is failing to live up to the transparency the public expects of the water sector.”
The committee said it was difficult to see why SAR had not already been instigated for Thames Water. “Thames Water is at the end of the road. The company’s performance and the behaviour of its creditors are unacceptable. Their investment strategies are based on extracting value through debt rather than ensuring long-term success.”
A spokesperson for the London & Valley Water consortium said: “Our enhanced proposal will address all feedback from Ofwat and ministers and is the fastest route to fix Thames Water’s complex problems.
“The plan will write off billions of pounds of debt to achieve an investment grade rating and provide £10bn of new capital from experienced investors to improve and upgrade Thames Water’s infrastructure and clean up local rivers.
“All fines Thames Water faces will be paid, all profits will be reinvested, and no dividends will be taken until the company is turned around and returned to the public markets. There will be no cost to the government or taxpayers, and customers will be protected from the costs of Thames Water’s restructuring.
 “A new board with specialist expertise will oversee Thames Water’s transformation and work tirelessly to drive the turnaround and rebuild trust. We are committed to ensuring Thames Water provides the service that customers and local communities deserve. This group of investors has never been in control of the company and has never received a dividend from Thames Water. They have stepped in to fund a significant revenue shortfall to ensure Thames Water’s record capital investment programme can continue without disruption.”
A Defra spokesperson said: “Thames has been failing the public for a long time, and this government has been clear that nothing’s off the table when it comes to a solution that delivers for customers and the environment.”

Children and mature adults we know about, but why is society so clueless about young people in between? | Gaby Hinsliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:09 UTC
14:00:09 KST

When did you realise you had finally grown up? It’s a trick question, obviously: maturity is just realising that life is full of things you don’t feel old enough for but somehow manage anyway, while getting better at pretending to know what you’re doing. But the question is worth asking nonetheless, because for gen Z the goalposts of grownup life are clearly shifting.
It’s a truism that adulting now comes later than it did to generations who still don’t consider adulting a verb, with 43% of 25-year-olds still living at home and plenty more jobless university graduates boomeranging back there this summer, thanks to a grim labour market. Since they’ll probably be working longer into what were once retirement years, perhaps it’s only natural that they’re taking longer to get started. But there’s a fine line between choosing to grow up more slowly and becoming trapped into a kind of limbo between childhood and adulthood, with nobody to pull you out of the morass beyond parents who aren’t sure how to handle this new life stage either.
If your unemployed 22-year-old is getting rejection after rejection, should you rewrite their job applications for them, or let them figure it out for themselves? What do you do with an 18-year-old too depressed to leave their bedroom, now they’re old enough to make their own GP appointments but not mature enough to know they need one? Kidulthood can be a minefield.
The idea that the state should recognise the years roughly between 18 and 25 as a phase distinct from either childhood or full adulthood, which needs its own tailored policies, is catching on around Westminster. The Nuffield Foundation thinktank, which has spent two years researching changing journeys to adulthood, held a seminar this week drawing together threads from academia to Alan Milburn’s genuinely thoughtful review of what is causing so many young people to be Neet (not in education, employment or training). As Milburn put it to the Nuffield Foundation’s Carey Oppenheim, councils have to ensure that teenagers are studying or training up to 18, but what happens after that is not their problem. Yet in the Netherlands, the state’s responsibilities extend up to 24 or, in some cases, 27. Guess which country has fewer Neets.
More broadly, he suggested, the British state may be too quick to shrug off responsibility for young people struggling with the transition to adulthood. “We haven’t aligned now with the reality of the transitions that young people are going through in their lives,” he said.
In Australia, Oppenheim points out, the equivalent of Britain’s children and adolescent mental health services runs from age 12 right up to age 25, recognising a growing argument within medicine that adolescence doesn’t end neatly at 19. But in Britain, teenagers still hit a cliff edge, tumbling abruptly out of children’s mental health services into adult ones where the threshold for intervention can be far higher. Even the new social media ban for under-16s assumes teenagers are mature enough at 17 to handle what they couldn’t the day before.
Meanwhile the IPPR thinktank’s State of A Generation project, another deep dive into the coming of age process, warns of a society where “transitions to adulthood are blocked” and young people are increasingly nihilistic about their future.
There’s much we still don’t understand about this evolving life stage, including how far to accept it and how far to push back. If a quarter of 18- to 34-year-olds living with their parents say they’re genuinely happy at home or not ready to leave, rather than feeling stuck, does that imply a worrying failure to launch? Or, as the demographer Prof Ann Berrington argues, a new form of “privileged dependence”, where some young people enjoy a financial and emotional security that ultimately boosts them into adult life, and it’s the young people who can’t go home in a crisis we should worry about?
There’s an obvious danger here of over-babying young people, potentially making them even more anxious in the process, or of the state intruding too far into the lives of twentysomethings who are coping fine. As the parent of a 19-year-old, I’m well aware that gen Z are often far more resilient and competent than they get credit for.
But a significant minority do seem to be falling into a gap between childhood and adulthood, and in a chilly economic climate they look increasingly exposed. Maybe the real mark of having finally grown up is feeling ready to help someone else do the same.
- 
  Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Is the tie dead? Fashion connoisseurs hope not as House of Lords relaxes rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:08 UTC
14:00:08 KST

The House of Lords has long been derided as a stuffy relic of the past. But now its benches, usually filled with haughtily dressed men, could soon resemble something more akin to “dress-down Friday”.
One of the nation’s most storied chambers of power has enacted a rule change: men are no longer required to wear a tie in the House of Lords. Instead, they should opt for “business attire”.
Ties have long been a knotty item of neckwear. For some, they are a nuisance: too tight and they are uncomfortable, too loose and they look a bit shabby. For others, such as Stephen Fry, who professed his love for ties in a 256-page book, they can add a touch of undeniable class.
Peter York, a writer and style commentator, is firmly on the traditional side of the debate, saying the dumbed-down dress code will “end in tears”.
“Lords are not famous for being well-dressed at the best of times. If they can go without ties, they can also wear plimsolls and stuff like that. They will look silly,” said York, who owns hundreds of ties.
He called them “little works of art”, and decried those who shunned them while dressing formally. “It looks as if you’re not completely dressed, or you’ve forgotten something,” he said.
On Savile Row, views on ties were mixed. “I don’t think ties are completely dead, they’re just having a down moment,” said Guy Hills, 58, a fashion photographer and owner of Dashing Tweed, who was sauntering down the street in a green tweed suit. Something else was also green: his moustache.
He said his dyed facial hair might be allowed in the House of Lords, and is in support of the relaxed dress code, believing that members have a responsibility to keep up with fashion trends.
“They used to be the driving force of fashion, especially around Savile Row. They would go to their tailors and try to outdo each other. When you stop all that, and it becomes like a living museum, then the whole menswear fashion world stops,” he said.
Hills usually has something around his neck. “I can’t go out without a scarf because it looks too slovenly,” he said. But Thursday afternoon was, unluckily, one of the rare occasions he was without a silk scarf or cravat.
While ties aren’t totally “in”, Hills thinks they could make a comeback. “The younger generation is now getting more interested in sustainability and proper clothing. A tie really finishes a whole outfit off,” he said.
Among the few wearing a tie on Savile Row was Chaand Singh. The 25-year-old, who works in marketing, had decided to wear a navy tie from Next because of an important work meeting. “Dressing up and adding a tie elevates the look,” he said – so much so that he had received compliments from people. “Someone said that I look a bit more sharp today.”
Ties were no longer an office must, said Singh – but he thinks they still have their place. “I’ve got some from the 80s with cool patterns. They’re usually wider and designed when fashion was a bit more experimental,” he said. “I would wear them at work for the right scenario, but casually as well. Some girls even wear ties as belts.”
What do tailors on the Row think? “The House of Lords should be a mirror of society. What better way of doing it than reflecting current trends?” said James Sleater, 45, the owner of Norton & Sons. “Women don’t have to wear ties, and if men have the option, it’s OK by me.”
Sleater said that in the “post-Covid era, there has been a huge decline in neckwear and the number of people wearing ties to the office”, adding that the “relaxation of dress codes is symptomatic of people working several days a week at home”.
Norton & Sons sees people from all walks of life. “Yesterday we had an ex-prime minister and today we’ve got a Hollywood star having a fitting. We also see people wanting a suit for their first job and people celebrating a wedding,” he says. Have these customers shunned ties and other neckwear in droves? Actually, no. “We’re seeing the reversal of this trend,” says Sleater. “We’re selling more neckwear this year than we did in previous years.
“If you’re no longer forced to do something, it almost becomes a pleasure to it,” he adds. “To wear a suit to work when you don’t have to is a joy. When you’re told to do it, you’re almost feeling rebellious and you don’t want to do it.”
People have opted for “more characterful textures rather than just plain silks or bright brash colours”, though Slater sees a limit to a potential neckwear revival. “I don’t see cravats or bow ties coming back,” he said.
As for Lords who can keep their ties at home, some are in favour of the new rules. “In truth, the only people now wearing ties for business purposes are estate agents and funeral directors,” Lord Davies of Brixton, a Labour peer, told the Telegraph. “The tie is disappearing.”
It remains to be seen if Davies’ fellow Lords will heed the message.

France selects THUNDART for long-range land strike
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:00:00 BST
14:00:00 KST

France has selected the THUNDART system from MBDA and Safran Electronics & Defense to provide the French Army with a new sovereign long-range land strike capability and replace the existing Unitary Rocket Launcher, according to the companies.
The French Defence Procurement Agency, the DGA, has notified the programme following an initial development phase which included a successful demonstration firing in April 2026. THUNDART is intended to provide precision strike at long range in high-intensity and heavily contested environments, with the system designed, developed and produced in France.
MBDA and Safran say the programme is also intended to give the French Armed Forces full autonomy of use by 2030, reducing reliance on foreign-controlled technologies for a capability regarded as increasingly important in European land warfare. The two companies will establish a 50/50 joint venture in the Paris region to take the programme forward. It will oversee development, production and in-service support, as well as future upgrades and potential adaptation of the system for other environments and export customers.
Safran’s contribution includes navigation and optronics technology intended to allow the weapon to retain accuracy where access to satellite navigation is disrupted or denied.
Alexandre Ziegler, Head of the Defense Global Business Unit at Safran Electronics & Defense, said: “This selection reflects the complementarity of our expertise with MBDA. Faced with the critical challenges of interference and denial of access to GNSS signals, Safran Electronics & Defense provides its proven leadership in inertial navigation and optronics technologies to ensure accuracy in all circumstances.”
He added: “I would like to thank the DGA for their renewed confidence. THUNDART will provide our armed forces with a decisive and sovereign tactical advantage.”
The programme is intended to replace France’s LRU, or Lance-Roquettes Unitaire, as the Army moves to restore and expand its ability to conduct tactical deep strikes from land.
MBDA said the project would draw on mature subsystems while industrial preparations were already being put in place ahead of production.
Stéphane Reb, Executive Vice President Programmes and Managing Director of MBDA France, said: “The notification of the THUNDART programme marks a decisive step for French sovereignty in terms of long-range land strikes.”
He added: “By leveraging mature subsystems and an industrial ramp-up that is already underway, we are able to respond with agility to the Army’s most specific needs. The close partnership with Safran Electronics & Defense, embodied in the creation of a joint venture, allows us to mobilise all the skills of our teams and our production capabilities to deliver a complete solution within optimised deadlines.”

LRT English Newsletter: Drones and pigs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

LRT English Newsletter – September 18, 2026
What a week it has been! On Sunday afternoon, people in and around Vilnius received air alert warnings about a possible drone sighting. Well, that turned out to be just a flock of birds. However, it turned out that an actual drone had flown across southern Lithuania a little earlier. No alert was issued in that case (the military said the drone posed no immediate danger – and perhaps the sighting occurring at the ungodly hour of 4 AM made them conclude the alert would not be appreciated), which gave the defence minister occasion to voice concerns about public safety and security alert protocols. He later said he was satisfied with the military’s reasoning for not sending out the alert.
But then came Tuesday and, right after midnight, another drone was spotted flying from Belarus westwards. NATO fighter jets were scrambled from the air base near Šiauliai to shoot it down just south-east of Kaunas, the first such case in Lithuania (it happened in Latvia this summer). No one was hurt and no property was damaged, although nearby residents reported being seriously frightened.
What was the drone and what was its target? Russia hawks issued the predictable “we will not be intimidated” statements and calls to up the ante, while the defence minister cautioned that it might take some time before investigators can give reliable answers. Still, the president came forward after a State Defence Council meeting to say it was probably a Russian Gerbera launched towards Ukraine but knocked off course by Ukrainian electronic warfare.
As if that was not enough dronefare, Vilnius Airport suspended traffic for half an hour on Tuesday over a suspicious airborne object and foresters discovered a crashed drone in the woods of northern Lithuania. This one, however, appeared to have been used by smugglers and fallen down several months ago.
ANTI-MUSLIM ACTION
Last Friday, several biker groups decided to show Lithuania’s Muslims – many of them recent migrants – that they are not welcome. They disturbed prayers at a mosque in Kaunas with loud music, revving their bikes, chanting nationalist slogans – and even displaying a pig’s head.
The incident brought to the fore developments that have been brewing for quite some time. Besides the usual anti-migrant sentiment, there have been tensions within Lithuania’s Muslim community: the country’s indigenous Muslims, mostly of Tatar descent, have been feeling outnumbered and overwhelmed by the newcomers (this has been used by some right-wing politicians to present their positions as defence of historic Muslims rather than Islamophobia). Moreover, residents around the Kaunas mosque have complained about traffic problems during prayers – a point that has also been invoked in discussions about the bikers’ action.
Relatively few political leaders have censured the incident as hate speech, although on Wednesday, around sixty public figures and former politicians published a letter condemning it. Reportedly, police officers were present during the action but refrained from interfering. Under some public pressure, the police have opened an investigation into possible incitement of hatred – having initially treated it as simply an unsanctioned rally.
KAUNAS PRIDE
So it’s been an eventful week for Kaunas. On Saturday, it held its second-ever Pride March (the first one happened in 2021), attracting around 500 participants who demanded legal regulation of same-sex partnerships, trans-inclusive healthcare, and LGBTQ+ representation in school curricula. Moreover, Palestinian flags featured prominently at Kaunas Pride, with many participants chanting “no pride in genocide”. This has led to accusations, even from within the LGBTQ+ community, that the organisers veered too far from the traditional focus of pride events and might have alienated parts of the community.
ANOTHER BELARUS DEAL
This week, US President Donald Trump’s special envoy for Belarus John Coale made another trip to Minsk – with a stop in Vilnius – brokering a deal exchanging political prisoners for sanctions relief. This time, 25 prisoners were brought to Lithuania on Wednesday, while the US lifted sanctions on two Belarusian companies. This is a significantly smaller batch than before – in March, a similar deal saw the release of ten times as many political prisoners – but Coale said he hoped another one will be concluded soon.
Lithuanian leaders, who are notoriously sceptical about any sanctions relief for Belarus, nevertheless thanked Coale for his efforts – while making clear they still didn’t like Lukashenko.
CORRUPTION WITH EU MONEY
This week, Lithuania’s anti-fraud agency carried out several high-profile searches at the National Paying Agency, the main body that disburses the EU’s generous agricultural subsidies. According to reports, the investigation extents to the agency’s director and his deputy, the latter already facing charges of directing EU funds towards his relations.
EDITOR’S PICKS
– A Cuban dance teacher allegedly helped organise a terrorist attack in Lithuania on the orders of Russia’s military intelligence agency. LRT Investigation Team reports.
– Art unites, art divides. This time, it’s two gilded skulls representing a sixteenth-century love story between the King of Poland and his Lithuanian wife.
– The UK’s University of Cambridge is considering establishing a professorship in Lithuanian studies.
– Is Lithuania losing its grip on the national sport, basketball?
– Kaunas may beat Vilnius to (re)introducing a new mode of public transit, the tram.

and it may appear in our Letters section.
France's Auchan, which is known for its supermarkets across Europe, put its Russian subsidiary under local management in 2023, considering itself an essential civilian service and refusing to leave.
Meanwhile, Russia has damaged the property of international businesses operating in Ukraine with missile and drone attacks.
On Aug. 29, a Russian attack damaged a PepsiCo production facility in southern Ukraine's Mykolaiv Oblast, the company said.
In another attack on Aug. 23, Russia struck a factory belonging to U.S. multinational food company Mondelez International in Sumy Oblast, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
Two Russian drones hit the facility located in the city of Trostianets, damaging the site and injuring several employees, according to Sybiha.

‘Once-in-a-century’ crater discovered on Moon (PHOTOS)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:53:06 UTC
13:53:06 KST

‘Once-in-a-century’ crater discovered on Moon (PHOTOS)
The largest newly formed crater ever discovered in the solar system has been found on the Moon, in what scientists have described as a once-in-a-century impact event.
The crater, measuring 222 meters (728 feet) across and 43 meters deep, was identified using images from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC), according to a study published in Science Advances on Wednesday.
Researcher Robert Wagner first spotted the feature during a routine check of images taken by LROC’s Wide-Angle Camera in October 2025. Scientists then used higher-resolution observations over the following months to measure the crater and examine the surrounding terrain.
According to NASA, the crater formed between April 11 and May 22, 2024, when a comet or asteroid roughly the size of a three- to six-story building slammed into the lunar surface.
The Moon’s got a big new crater! 🕳️
Spotted by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, the McGetchin crater formed when a rock as big as a six-story building crashed into the Moon. It’s 141 feet deep and wider than the length of two football fields.🪨💥🌕https://t.co/I2fX7bPts1pic.twitter.com/Zft4mKUv1Z
The collision hurled debris across the surrounding terrain and created a “cold spot” about seven kilometers (four miles) wide, where nighttime temperatures are up to nine degrees Celsius (16 degrees Fahrenheit) lower than in nearby areas.
Researchers believe the impact loosened, or “fluffed up,” the regolith – the layer of loose rock and dust covering the Moon – making it less dense and therefore less able to retain heat.
Officially named McGetchin after pioneering lunar scientist Tom McGetchin, the crater dwarfs previously detected recent impacts. Before its discovery, the largest contemporary impact crater identified on the Moon measured about 70 meters across.
The discovery comes as the Moon becomes an increasingly important focus of international space exploration.
The US is “very much in a space race” with China, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told CBS News in July. NASA’s Artemis program is targeting 2028 for its first crewed lunar landing since the Apollo era, with the longer-term goal of establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.
Russia and China, meanwhile, announced plans in 2021 to jointly develop the International Lunar Research Station.
As part of the project, Russia plans to deploy a power station on the Moon within the next decade. During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Moscow last May, Russia and China signed an agreement on building a nuclear power plant on the Moon to provide energy for the planned research station, which is expected to become operational in the mid-2030s.
