NATO 3.0 marches into Copenhagen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:51:26 UTC
13:51:26 KST

NATO 3.0 marches into Copenhagen
At NATO’s first high-level summit since Ankara, the bloc’s new, Europe-centric incarnation is taking shape. But it’s ordinary Europeans who stand to lose their future, and potentially their lives.
NATO’s Military Committee is meeting in Copenhagen on Friday and Saturday. Chaired by Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, the Military Committee, which is NATO’s highest military authority, is tasked with turning the bloc’s strategic goals into executable plans. When NATO orders a battlegroup to Lithuania, for example, the Military Committee ensures its tanks will be able to get there across multiple countries’ rail networks, its troops will be supplied and housed, and the deployment will not leave another sector of the bloc’s so-called ‘eastern flank’ unmanned.
Accordingly, NATO is keeping the meeting’s agenda under wraps. The organization’s website simply states that the defense chiefs will take part in a “Session 1” and “Session 2” of talks, followed by a press conference, a photo opportunity, and then a “Session 3” of discussions.
Looking at the political decisions made since the bloc’s headline summit in Ankara in July, the broad aim of the conference becomes clearer: flesh out NATO’s plan to militarize Europe and prepare the continent for war with Russia, all while insulating the US from the consequences of the conflict.
What is NATO 3.0?
Coined by US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby, ‘NATO 3.0’ is an America-first reworking of the Cold War pact. In a speech to NATO defense ministers in February, Colby explained that the US will, going forward, focus on preparing for a potential clash with China in the Indo-Pacific, leaving NATO’s European members to “assume primary responsibility for the conventional defense of Europe.”
Under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth’s visionary leadership, we are driving toward a NATO 3.0 in which Europe takes primary responsibility for its conventional defense. Many said that it could not be done – that Europe couldn’t or wouldn’t step up. That is being disproved… https://t.co/svqGBLPIdE
— Under Secretary of War Elbridge Colby (@USWPColby) July 2, 2026
Europe will increase its military spending to NATO’s current target of 5% of GDP and shift to wartime levels of defense production, Colby explained, all while the US retains control over the bloc’s nuclear weapons. The Europeans will also be expected, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth stated in June, to guarantee “access, basing and overflight” for American forces.
At Ankara in July, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte sold this one-sided deal as a win for Europe. “We are rebalancing our security for the better, that is what NATO 3.0 is all about,” he said.
We’re rebalancing our Alliance: a stronger #NATO with Europe & Canada spending more, producing more and doing more for their security
Building for our future
This is NATO 3.0 pic.twitter.com/pgmvA4CcAW
In light of US President Donald Trump’s threats to withdraw US forces from Germany and annex Greenland, a more Europe-centric NATO was an easy sell for Rutte at the time. Trump’s threats toward Greenland were likely a key factor in the choice of Copenhagen for this weekend’s meeting. However, in the months since Ankara, Rutte and NATO’s European leaders have revealed what the shift actually means for the continent.
Europe steps up and pays
NATO 3.0 means the death of the European welfare state. In the UK, where living standards have already suffered their worst decline since the Second World War, meeting the bloc’s pre-Ankara 3.5% spending target will involve “eye-watering” cuts to education, transport, and justice budgets, George Robertson, who co-wrote the country’s defense strategy, warned in June. Even before the spending target was hiked to 5%, Robertson claimed that the British public was “too comfortable,” and must accept the “pain and great difficulty” of “preparing for war.”
In Germany, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s plan to rebuild the Bundeswehr as “the strongest conventional army in Europe” has already precipitated social security cuts and a planned three-year hike in the retirement age. “The welfare state that we have today can no longer be financed,” Merz announced last August, before increasing Germany’s defense budget by almost 40% in a single year and telling Germans to “work harder.”
The Netherlands and Sweden have introduced emergency taxes to fund rearmament, with the Dutch levy branded as the “freedom contribution.” Estonia has increased income tax, Belgium and Finland have cut social spending, and 18 of NATO’s EU members have borrowed money from Brussels to build out their militaries since last May.
“On average, European countries easily spend up to a quarter of their national income on pensions, health, and social security systems, and we need only a small fraction of that money to make defense much stronger,” Rutte told the European Parliament last year. The “small fraction” demanded by Rutte has since almost doubled.
Serving American interests
In return, the Europeans are not getting the strategic autonomy that some, such as France, want. NATO’s “interoperability” standards mean weapons manufactured in Europe are built to American standards, and the AI and cloud computing technology that guides them is provided almost solely by American companies.
The Ankara Summit Declaration states that “we are developing an interoperable transatlantic warfighting cloud and adopting powerful AI models.” With the EU relying on the US for 80% of its digital infrastructure, American companies such as Palantir, Anduril, and SpaceX will be the beneficiaries of this development.
Furthermore, while the US handed control of three operational commands – Norfolk in the UK, Naples in Italy, and Brunssum in the Netherlands – to European commanders earlier this year, Washington took over management of NATO’s highest Land, Air, and Maritime commands in exchange, and maintains the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) post.
Although NATO 3.0 envisions Europe alone deterring Russia, the bloc’s European members are still expected to go along with American wars far beyond their borders. Speaking in the UK this week, Rutte called it “essential” that Britain’s “armed forces continue to provide the hard power NATO needs” to tackle “Russia and its war against Ukraine, terrorism, Iran and the tectonic shifts of global geopolitical competition.”
NATO was not formed to counter Iran, but the US still punished its European members who refused to aid the US-Israeli war on Iran earlier this year, threatening a complete trade embargo on Spain after Madrid denied overflight and basing to American aircraft taking part in the war, and pulling troops from other countries seen as insufficiently supportive of the war.
Bleeding for NATO
In addition to handing over their money and autonomy, Europeans risk handing over their lives, if NATO’s proxy war in Ukraine degenerates into open conflict with Russia. Having dangled the prospect of NATO membership in front of Ukraine since 2008, fomented the pro-Western Maidan coup in 2014, and juiced Ukraine with weapons and training over the next decade, the US has finally succeeded in dumping the resulting conflict on Europe’s lap, with the eager participation of the continent’s Atlantacist leaders.
NATO 3.0 makes it explicit that Europe now owns this conflict, and it is the possibility of escalation that will likely occupy the bloc’s Military Committee in Copenhagen this weekend. Managing the grim minutiae of war – predicting casualty rates in an open confrontation with Russia and preparing hospitals and morgues, for example – is the committee’s remit, and NATO’s European members are already thinking in this direction.
Germany is currently assessing whether its civilian hospitals could handle an influx of 1,000 wounded soldiers per day, and considering reopening a massive subterranean medical bunker in the city of Ulm. The German military practiced moving casualties from field hospitals in Lithuania to operating theaters in Germany during its largest-ever medical exercises in March.
Norway has trained its surgeons in treating combat injuries and ordered that 7,000 hospital beds be made available for wartime casualties. France is preparing for what Paris calls a “major engagement scenario” by equipping civilian hospitals to absorb military casualties. Sweden and Lithuania have begun stockpiling blood.
A short war
NATO’s Military Committee planned for these eventualities throughout the Cold War. However, the bloc’s European members understood that if the war went hot, only US intervention would save them. Charles de Gaulle was famously skeptical of this promise, asking John F. Kennedy whether the Americans would be willing to “trade New York for Paris” in a nuclear war with the Soviets. With NATO 3.0, the US has openly told Europe that Washington’s contribution to its security will be more “limited and focused,” in Colby’s words.
Nevertheless, NATO’s European leaders, from Rutte down to the generals and admirals on the Military Committee, continue to march toward war with Russia, against all logic and self-interest. These preparations have a momentum of their own, which can be accelerated by miscalculation and political commitments; Europe’s leaders learned this lesson the hard way in the opening months of the First World War.
This time around, the potential consequences are even greater. Russia possesses the world’s largest nuclear arsenal, and in a stark warning on Wednesday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov declared that “if Europe, which talks daily about preparing for war against Russia, attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short.”

AI-related products accounted for 20% of revenue in the second quarter, up about 70% from the previous quarter. Aces expects the proportion to rise to 27% in the third quarter and 30% in the fourth quarter.

Aces expects shipments to increase significantly in the second half of the year. The Bloom Energy-related business is expected to generate about NT$1 billion in revenue this year and potentially reach NT$3 billion in 2027.
Aces has also entered the supply chains for AI servers using chips developed by Amazon Web Services and Meta. It supplies high-speed connectors for both mainboards and smaller circuit boards.
Aces shipped about 12 million high-speed connectors in the first half of the year. Shipments are expected to reach about 21 million in the second half and 33 million for the full year, with the company targeting more than 50 million units next year.

125 years of Ivan Tabakov - the forgotten classic of Bulgarian painting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:36:10 UTC
13:36:10 KST

Author
Diana Tsankova
News
125 years of Ivan Tabakov - the forgotten classic of Bulgarian painting
“The artist had a remarkable gift for rendering light, bringing greater vitality to his subjects,” says Hristo Bozhkov, curator at the Vratsa Art Gallery
Friday 18 September 2026 07:05
Friday, 18 September 2026, 07:05
Ivan Tabakov (self-portrait)
PHOTO artzona.bg
Font size
September 18, 1901, is the birthdate of Ivan Tabakov, one of Bulgaria’s major painters. His refined sensibility and distinctive ability to recreate the visible world were nurtured from an early age in an atmosphere steeped in classical art. This combination of artistic sensitivity and musical culture would go on to shape his perception of colour, light and the human figure.
PHOTO galleryloran.com
Born in Sofia, from an early age Ivan Tabakov showed an interest in the violin, while his sister, Tsvetana Tabakova, would later become one of Bulgaria’s celebrated opera singers. Despite the musical milieu in which he grew up, he gradually discovered his true vocation in painting. At the Sofia Academy of Art, he studied under the distinguished artists Professors Nikola Danushev and Nikola Marinov before leaving for Paris.
Hristo Bozhkov, curator at the Ivan Funev Art Gallery in Vratsa
PHOTO Regional History Museum in Vratsa
“He remained in the French capital until 1932, where he continued his artistic training and exhibited actively,” says Hristo Bozhkov, curator at the Ivan Funev Art Gallery in Vratsa.
“With his well-known portraits of women from 1930 and 1931, he took part in the Salon d’Automne, and a year later he exhibited his paintings at the Salon des Indépendants. After returning to Bulgaria, he began painting seascapes, probably influenced by his friendship with the celebrated Bulgarian marine painters Alexander Mutafov and Mario Zhekov.
In 1933, he held his first solo exhibition in Bulgaria, presenting mainly works from his Paris period, alongside portraits and paintings depicting scenes of rural life. In addition to drawing inspiration from countless subjects encountered in his native land, the artist travelled extensively throughout the world, and his work was well received. At the 1942 Venice Biennale, he exhibited a portrait of the writer Georgi Raichev, attracting the attention of the Italian press. The Milan Academy of Fine Arts subsequently named him an honorary member.”
Paris on the Seine, 1960s
PHOTO galleryloran.com
The Vratsa Art Gallery holds 12 works by Ivan Tabakov. Among them are Morning on the Seine, with its radiant light playing across the river, and Boats for Repair, inspired by the Bulgarian marine painting tradition, as well as his depictions of the cathedrals of Saint-Séverin and Sainte-Geneviève, the large portrait of opera singer Tsvetana Tabakova and My Wife, along with Autumn, a landscape rendered in an impressionistic manner.
Tsvetana Tabakova, 1930s
PHOTO galleryloran.com
“Ivan Tabakov left a lasting mark primarily as a portraitist and landscape painter, although art historians also place him among the artists strongly influenced by Impressionism,” the gallery curator adds. “At the Académie Julian in Paris, his professors Albert Besnard and Marcel Baschet encouraged him to engage with the high academic tradition of European art, where he rediscovered his interest in portraiture, landscape and still life. Baschet was one of the leading portraitists of his time, while Besnard was a passionate adherent of Impressionism.
“Ivan Tabakov had a remarkable ability to render light, which gives his figures greater vitality, and in this respect he clearly absorbed something of Albert Besnard. This makes him a particularly interesting artist, trained at prestigious European academies as well as at the Bulgarian Academy, which laid the foundations of his academic education.”
1960s
PHOTO galleryloran.com
“Unfortunately, even during his lifetime he remained undeservedly in the shadow of the more prominent names of his generation, and after his death his name gradually fell into oblivion,” art historian Lyudmil Veselinov notes. In recent years, several galleries have sought to bring back into the light one of the forgotten classics of Bulgarian painting.
"Vasil Levski creates a secret revolutionary committee", 1973
PHOTO galleryloran.com

Hungarian chess great Judit Polgar: Make your own moves
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:35:49 CST
13:35:49 KST

Hungarian chess legend Judit Polgar speaks during a press conference for the 12th Judit Polgar Global Chess Festival in Budapest, capital of Hungary, Sept. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Hu Zhixuan)
by sportswriters Zhou Xin, Chen Hao
BUDAPEST, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- For Judit Polgar, one of the greatest female chess players in history, the game has always been about making decisions and taking responsibility for them.
Across more than two decades at the highest level, the Hungarian grandmaster studied opponents, prepared with computers and faced some of the strongest players of her generation. But once she sat down at the board, nobody else could make the move for her.
"In chess, you are responsible for every move," Polgar told Xinhua on Thursday at a press conference for the 12th Judit Polgar Global Chess Festival in Budapest. "You make mistakes, but you also learn that mistakes can be corrected."
The youngest of the famous Polgar sisters, she helped Hungary win the Women's Chess Olympiad at 12 and became a grandmaster at 15 years and four months, breaking Bobby Fischer's then-record as the youngest titleholder.
She later reached the world's top 10 and built her career largely in open competition, defeating a number of leading male players, including world champions.
For Polgar, elite chess demanded far more than calculation. "What does my opponent want to do? What do I want to do? If I make this move, how will my opponent react?" she said.
A wrong move cannot be taken back. The player must accept the new position, reassess the situation and decide what comes next.
That experience also shaped her attitude toward technology. Polgar was part of a generation of top players that saw computer analysis become an important part of professional preparation. She used engines to study positions and review games, but also learned not to rely on them blindly.
"There was a period when I trusted it, and then I trusted it too much," she said. "I paid a price for that, and even lost games."
The lesson remains relevant today: technology can help, but it cannot replace human judgment.
That idea was also reflected at Thursday's press conference, where a magician used a card trick to introduce a discussion about artificial intelligence.
"Magic is a carefully constructed illusion, and sometimes AI can feel like that too," Polgar said.
An answer may look convincing, she added, but people still need to question, verify and understand how it was reached.
Since retiring from competitive chess in 2014, Polgar has devoted more time to education and promoting the game among young people. She believes chess can help develop concentration, problem-solving skills, emotional control and the ability to take responsibility for decisions.
"The process of finding the solution and eventually reaching the answer is the most important thing," she said.
The 12th Judit Polgar Global Chess Festival will be held on Sept. 26 at the Hungarian National Gallery in Budapest, with "critical thinking in the age of artificial intelligence" among its main themes.
For Polgar, the link between chess and the AI era goes back to what she learned as a competitor: players may prepare with coaches, databases and powerful engines, but when the clock is running and the position is on the board, responsibility lies with the player.
"Technology may offer more answers than ever before, but you still have to make your own moves," Polgar said. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China beat Oman 2-0 in the opening match of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games men's hockey competition on Friday, with Gao Jiesheng and Du Shihao both scoring from penalty corners at Gifu Prefectural Green Stadium.
Gao broke the deadlock in the second quarter to give China a 1-0 halftime lead. Du doubled the advantage in the third quarter, and China held on to secure the victory.
Gao said China had put some of its training-ground work into practice but had yet to reach its best, with fatigue affecting the team in the latter stages and some details still needing improvement.
"We'll review the problems from today's match and prepare for the next one," he said.
Competing at his second Asian Games, Gao said he hoped to stay composed, give his all in every match and gain experience while pursuing a medal.
"Our goal is definitely to finish in the top three. We also want to fully demonstrate what we're capable of in training," he said.
Du said China gradually picked up the tempo by implementing the coach's tactical instructions.
"We need to fight for every game and every opportunity, taking it one step at a time," he said.
China coach Chi Gang praised the players for responding positively to difficulties and maintaining their composure in a challenging opening match.
"Even with the win, we need to review our performance carefully, pay greater attention to detail and raise our level for the matches ahead," Chi said.
China will next face Thailand in its second group match at the same venue on Sept. 22. ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: Geotourism gains ground as travelers seek more than scenery
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:35:43 CST
13:35:43 KST

LANZHOU, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- At the Zhangye Colorful Danxia Scenic Spot in northwest China, middle school student Xu Yan held up an English textbook and watched as the image on its cover aligned almost perfectly with the colorful, layered hills before him.
"Seeing it in person gave me a much deeper understanding of this kind of Danxia landform," said Xu, who had traveled from south China's Guangdong Province.
He was one of many visitors who arrived at the scenic spot in Gansu Province during the summer vacation with the same textbook in hand. Matching the textbook's cover image with real-life landmarks has become popular on Chinese social media, but at geological sites, the exercise is also taking on an educational dimension.
Across China, dramatic landforms are increasingly being treated as places to explore and understand, rather than simply photograph. Hiking, field study, camping and science courses are being added to conventional sightseeing, giving rise to a form of travel that asks visitors to "read" the landscape.
The scale is considerable. China has 51 UNESCO Global Geoparks, the largest number in the world. A national report on tourist attractions counted 2,047 A-rated scenic areas centered on geological and geomorphological resources, or 13 percent of all such attractions in the country.
Travel data point to the same trend. Online travel platform Trip.com Group's 2026 summer travel report found growing interest in experiential study tours, while nature exploration ranked among the leading choices for family trips.
At Zhangye, this change can be seen in the form of guided tours that take small groups closer to geological formations, where visitors examine tilted strata and the layers that give the hills their distinctive appearance.
Children on study tours go a step further. Equipped with geological hammers and guided by instructors, they learn how minerals containing iron and manganese contribute to different colors in the landscape. In 2025, Zhangye UNESCO Global Geopark, where the Zhangye Colorful Danxia Scenic Spot is located, received 216 study-tour groups involving 170,000 student visits.
"Visitors are no longer satisfied with conventional sightseeing," said Li Junling, deputy head of the general management department of the scenic spot.
Elsewhere in China, geological attractions are bringing more science into the visitor experience.
At Danxia Mountain in Guangdong, from which the Danxia landform takes its name, geological field routes have been combined with science interpretation. The scenic area works with universities and research institutions to train guides and science-education volunteers, while courses on landform evolution and environmental protection take schoolchildren into the field.
In Chishui, southwest China's Guizhou Province, meanwhile, geological education is paired with hiking and immersive experiences. Visitors can explore red Danxia cliffs, waterfalls and forests, while light-and-sound installations illustrate how the landform evolved over hundreds of millions of years.
Gao Hongshan, a professor at the College of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Lanzhou University, in Gansu, said the significance of such experiences lies in changing how knowledge is acquired.
Allowing visitors to use geological compasses, microscopes and other tools turns abstract concepts into something they can observe and test themselves, he said. Virtual and augmented reality can also be applied to make geological processes easier to grasp.
For geological destinations, however, richer visitor experiences must be balanced with the protection of sensitive geological heritage.
At Danxia Mountain, key field-study routes are confined to controlled areas and separated from sensitive geological formations, while Zhangye limits access to some core areas through small-group tours with designated vehicles and guides.
This is where science education can become part of conservation itself.
Cheng Hongyi, an associate professor at Lanzhou University, said that when visitors understand the scientific value and fragility of geological heritage, conservation can become a voluntary act, rather than a mandate imposed on them, and that is a key value of geological tourism. "Science communication is the soul of geological tourism."
Local people are increasingly benefiting from the geological tourism. Nantai Village, about a 10-minute drive from the Zhangye Colorful Danxia Scenic Spot, now has 128 households engaged in tourism-related businesses. Their per capita annual income stands at approximately 27,400 yuan (roughly 4,054 U.S. dollars), and around 80 percent of that comes from tourism. ■

Istanbul to host 2027 Spanish Supercopa across three stadiums
China

MADRID, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- The Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) on Thursday presented this season's Supercopa at an event in Istanbul.
The four-team tournament will see La Liga champion FC Barcelona face Atletico Madrid in the first semifinal on Feb. 2, while Copa del Rey winner Real Sociedad meets Real Madrid the following day. The final will be played on Feb. 6.
Unlike recent editions, the Supercopa will be staged across three venues in Istanbul: Barcelona against Atletico at Fenerbahce's Sukru Saracoglu Stadium, the second semifinal at Besiktas's Vodafone Park and the final at Galatasaray's Ali Sami Yen Stadium.
"There will be three great matches in three great stadiums capable of hosting a total of over 150,000 spectators," said RFEF President Rafael Louzan. "Istanbul has hosted the Champions League finals in 2005 and 2023, as well as the 2026 Europa League final."
"It boasts the necessary infrastructure, stadiums, and a passionate fan base. We are certain that Istanbul will fully embrace the Supercup."
The RFEF said Istanbul was chosen from seven candidate cities. Saudi Arabia, which had hosted the Supercopa since 2020 except for 2021, was unavailable this year as it will stage the AFC Asian Cup in early 2027.
Louzan said the event would be "an extraordinary occasion that will also boost the city's tourism and international profile." ■

Japan's central bank lifts policy rate to 31-year high of 1.25 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:35:28 CST
13:35:28 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The Bank of Japan (BOJ) on Friday raised its policy interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to 1.25 percent, the highest in about 31 years, following a two-day board meeting.
The central bank lifted the rate again after increasing it to 1.0 percent at its June policy meeting, the shortest interval between increases since the BOJ began the current rate hike cycle in March 2024.
The decision came amid mounting concerns that Japan's inflation could overshoot the BOJ's expectations, as the yen's slide to its lowest level in decades against the U.S. dollar has driven up import costs, while the prolonged Middle East conflict and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have sent crude oil prices surging.
Two of the BOJ's nine policymakers voted against the rate hike.
Rising interest rates would push up borrowing costs for both businesses and households, potentially weighing on economic activity and posing a challenge for the BOJ's efforts to contain inflation without hampering growth. ■

====================================================================================================

Markets bet 95pc chance of September rate hike after latest RBA comments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:31:51 UTC
13:31:51 KST

RBA leaders warn that interest rates are just back to 'sensible level'
In short:
RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser said, "We're probably rather closer now to a more sensible level of long-term global real interest rates than we were a year or two ago."
More economists have joined financial markets in tipping a September rate hike, with the possibility of another in November.
What's next?
The RBA's Monetary Policy Board will meet on September 28-29 to determine the next move in the cash rate target.
Economists believe that the Reserve Bank's senior officials have decided that interest rates need to be hiked in September, and they expect the RBA's board to rubber stamp an increase in the cash rate to 4.6 per cent.
This view was already developing following public appearances by deputy governor Andrew Hauser on the ABC's 7.30 program last week and the bank's chief economist Sarah Hunter at two conferences over the past fortnight.
"We think tactically November's a better choice but certainly the internal members of the board are making noises that they want to go," former RBA assistant governor and current Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis told ABC News yesterday.
"You can see that they're trying to signal to the market that they want to raise rates. So September is a genuine possibility as well."
However, an appearance in front of the federal parliament today by RBA governor Michele Bullock, deputy governor Andrew Hauser, and assistant governors Sarah Hunter and Brad Jones has many economists firmly convinced the bank will hike at the end of its next two-day meeting on September 29.
RBC's head of economics and rates strategy Robert Thompson was previously expecting a rate rise in November, but is now forecasting one at the September meeting as well which, if correct, would take the cash rate to a peak of 4.85 per cent — the highest level since before rates plunged in the wake of the 2008 global financial crisis.
"September now seems all but a lock, with November becoming the more contentious decision-point. On the other side of the cycle, we keep a first cut in November 2027," he wrote in a note this afternoon.
"RBA communication has tipped us over.
"The barrage of recent RBA communication (capped off by a lengthy House Economics Committee appearance today) has left us with little doubt that bank insiders have already made up their minds — a hike in September is the necessary course of action."
Marcel Thieliant from Capital Economics agrees that a September rate hike "now looks like a done deal".
However, he thinks that will be the RBA's last move higher.
"Monetary policy is already quite restrictive and we think the bank will be wary of causing a sharp rise in the unemployment rate," he argued.
"Accordingly, we don't expect any further tightening after September."
Financial markets are now pricing in a 95 per cent chance of a rate rise in September, according to LSEG data, with a 37 per cent chance of a follow-up hike in November.
What did the RBA officials say about interest rates?
The clearest indication that interest rates are likely to move even higher, and potentially stay there, came from RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser.
He backed a view that had been recently expressed by leading US economist Kenneth Rogoff that the decline in long-term interest rates between the GFC (2007-2009) and COVID-19 (2020) was an anomaly, rather than the norm, and that we're now returning to a more normal period in which long-term interest rates will be higher.
"Interest rates were never going to be zero or near zero for a long while," Mr Hauser observed.
"We all thought maybe they normalised a year ago.
"I think my personal view — as a personal view — is that we're probably rather closer now to a more sensible level of long-term global real interest rates than we were a year or two ago."
He wondered aloud whether the angst about current levels of interest rates might be related to people coming to terms with that.
"I think the interesting question is, have borrowers adjusted to that new reality?"
RBA governor Michele Bullock gave indications that the bank's ability to "look through" higher oil and fuel prices might be wearing thin, noting they have been elevated for much longer than people were originally anticipating.
"I think there's much more of an inclination [from businesses] to think that we need to pass through these cost increases because it's going to be much more persistent," she said.
"So they're the sorts of things that are shaping our views, I think, and shaping the views of overseas central banks."
While the bank has repeatedly and recently reiterated its desire to protect as many of the employment gains post-COVID as it can, Ms Bullock said that is also becoming more difficult.
"And the other point I would make is that these supply shocks, the Middle East in particular, it has worsened the trade-off between inflation and employment," she told the committee.
"And a typical textbook response people say is, 'Well, it's a transitory shock. You look through it, and then it will come back.'
"But … it's much harder to look through when there are persistent shocks, because of the risk that will flow through to inflation expectations.
"I think we have to acknowledge that the trade-off has got worse, that this particular Middle East shock has made us poorer, and we can't respond to that by letting inflation get out of control."
Both Ms Bullock and Mr Hauser get a vote on the nine-person Monetary Policy Board that will meet on September 28-29 to determine the cash rate.
RBA still sanguine about housing downturn
While the RBA governor acknowledged that "conditions in the housing market have softened, and a larger-than expected easing could be a downside risk to economic activity," she also played down the degree of the decline.
"These falls follow a period of strong growth — housing prices are still around 50 per cent higher than they were in early 2020," Ms Bullock observed.
Brad Jones, the RBA's assistant governor (financial system), who is in charge of safeguarding financial stability, said the surge in Australian house prices were far larger than in other comparable countries.
"If your starting point for that comparison is prior to COVID, the run-up in Australian housing prices exceeds that of large advanced economies, also smaller open economies," he commented.
"It's been a very material run-up, and so we've seen 5 per cent to 6 per cent declines in Sydney and Melbourne, 1 per cent to 2 per cent in the other states."
He said, in that context, the property price declines in Australia this year have "not been overly material".

====================================================================================================

Country diary: Dinner time for the buzzard family is not a dignified affair | Kate Blincoe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:30:07 UTC
13:30:07 KST

I’m out on the farm most days, but I miss so much. It took a few days to notice a mother mallard with her late brood of 12 ducklings until they were all dabbling in a yard puddle. Dad sees more than me. He told me of the lazy adult buzzard that waited in a tree, then dive-bombed a peregrine that had caught a pigeon. The peregrine dropped its prey, which the buzzard then delivered to a hay bale already strewn with feathers. A pair of juvenile buzzards swiftly followed, ready for a meal.
Later, Dad placed the trail camera at the bale. The young buzzards were soon back in position with yet another dead pigeon. The footage tells a story that many parents will recognise after the long summer holidays.
One young buzzard claims the pigeon, turns its back on the other and opens its wings around the food. Known as “mantling”, it creates a share-proof barrier. The other bird looks disgruntled, shifting around, head down, trying to work out a plan. It sticks a leg out under its sibling’s defensive wings and is told off with a shrill screech.
Opting instead for being persistently annoying, it eventually provokes the pigeon-possessor to rise in attack. There’s a funny moment when both birds overbalance and plummet off the side of the bale. Another high-pitch squeak arises, off-camera. I shouldn’t anthropomorphise, but the expressions of the birds throughout this little drama do seem very familiar.
There are three pairs of buzzards that nest on the farm, each wood has its couple. Usually seen soaring on thermals above the farm, or loafing around in the woodland canopy, they are in turn majestic and clumsy. Despite centuries of persecution, followed by the myxomatosis outbreak in the 1950s that reduced their favourite rabbit prey, buzzards somehow persisted, and more recently increased in numbers.
The bales have now been cleared from the fields and this next generation of buzzards must fend for themselves.
Meanwhile, back in the yard, each night there is a diminishing of ducklings. We’re down to eight now. Still an impressive amount in the numbers game of reproduction, but they have a long way to go until they too are independent.

Denmark plans fivefold increase in fines for repeated violations of residency rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:28:39 UTC
13:28:39 KST

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.

Controversial politician loses Copenhagen seat after residency case

“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.

Questions about Anthropic and Queensland data centre answered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:25:04 UTC
13:25:04 KST

Anthropic is set to run Claude out of a Queensland data centre, here's what you need to know
It's set to be the largest data centre project in Australia, but the Western Downs Digital Park (WDDP) has left many Australians with unanswered questions.
Artificial intelligence behemoth Anthropic has signed a long-term lease to run its Claude AI system out of the yet-to-be-built data centre in Queensland's Western Downs.
Zerra DC, a developer based in Singapore, has forked out $30 billion to build the data centre, and it is expected to take four to six years to build the facility.
Despite that, Anthropic plans to start using Building One at the centre in 2027.
It's important to note that Anthropic's lease is subject to Foreign Investment Review Board approval.
Queensland Premier David Crisafulli says this data centre investment will drive down energy costs for consumers and bring jobs to the community.
But as Queensland opens the door to artificial intelligence, here's some things you should know about the proposed centre in Western Downs.
Where is the Western Downs data centre?
The site will be located on Dalby Kogan Road in the western Queensland suburb of Kogan.
The 725.5-hectare plot is 37km north-west of Dalby and approximately 250 kilometres north-west of Brisbane.
How much water is it going to use?
The developers claim the data centre will be 100 per cent air cooled. That would, in theory, result in far less water consumption than other data centres.
Zerra DC said the first building, or Phase 1 of the project, will require 21,000 litres of water a day once fully operational.
Per year, that amounts to 7.7 million litres of water required for the first building.
"That's nothing," Ian Wright, associate professor in environment science at Western Sydney University said.
"That's absolutely tiny."
He said that would be similar to the water consumption of a small shopping mall.
"I would say that was a fraction of what I was expecting. I expected it would need more like 21,000 litres in a matter of minutes."
For the entire campus of four buildings, Zerra DC estimates a total of 25.5 million litres of water would be required per year once fully operational.
Zerra DC says the data centre will also meet 40 per cent of its daily water demands through "on-site water recycling" which it claims will bring the actual outside water requirement down to around 13,000 litres a day.
It says that will be met by rainwater harvesting and the facility will not use groundwater for operations.
However, it will be able to draw on groundwater as a last-resort contingency, according to the developer.
How does air cooling help?
The air-cooling set-up for this facility will use a heat-rejection system that uses closed-loop water circulation within the data centre, but heat is rejected to the outside air rather than through evaporation.
Mr Wright said if the system works, it would be "brilliant", but he had concerns.
"That would be a game changer and that goes against my knowledge of what happens around the world," he said.
"I suppose there's a dubious edge to my voice here — it just sounds too good to be true."
This system has been successfully used in other data centres, however usually on a much smaller scale as they have been known to struggle with high-density server racks, which are common in AI workloads.
"It looks like they've done their homework," Mr Wright said.
"It could be pretty much water neutral. I reckon the world will be watching to see if you could build something this big air cooled."
What are the ongoing jobs at a data centre?
According to Zerra DC, the data centre is expected to provide around 1,400 jobs directly at the facility once fully operational.
It says those ongoing roles will lie in mechanical, electrical, controls, security and ICT information, as well as communications technology which covers computing, telecommunications, networks, software and related digital systems.
A report from the UK government found that while data centres require a lot of staff to build, the number of daily jobs created for operations is "relatively modest" and is likely only ever a few hundred.
The Virginia state government in the US found that a 23,226 square metres (sqm) data centre "may have approximately 50 full-time workers".
The facility in Western Downs will utilise approximately 195,000sqm of total floor space once fully built and the sheer size is one reason for the greater need for staff, the developers said.
While the facility is being built, the developer says a further 1,500 on-site construction workers will be required, with indirect jobs also expected to arise both during construction and ongoing at the facility.
What about power concerns?
In the proposal for the development, Zerra DC said the digital park will "connect directly to the high-voltage transmission network at the existing Braemar substation".
The infrastructure required for the connection and the connection process itself would be provided and organised by the tenants of each building, Zerra DC said.
For Building One, that is Anthropic. The AI giant plans to go to market for long-term power purchase agreements with renewable energy suppliers.
The data centre would have a peak electrical capacity of 2.16 GW.
Electro-mechanical engineer Dr Andreas Helwig said that is extremely large by Australian standards.
"If fully built out and operating at typical hyperscale utilisation, it would draw around 43–47 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy per day," he said.
He added that is roughly 25–30 per cent of Queensland’s entire average daily electricity consumption.
According to Energex, the entire network for south-east Queensland delivers roughly 61 GWh per day across the entire regional grid.
Dr Helwig said that households in the local area near the site should not be impacted, but the facility will pointed to the size of the continuous load once more.
The GWh capacity of 2.16 is equivalent to "more than three Darling Downs gas stations running at full output", Dr Helwig said.

New tiger cat species identified in Bolivia, first in over a century
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:16:28 UTC
13:16:28 KST

New tiger cat species identified in Bolivia, first in over a century
Leopardus tilcayo is the first new living cat species named and described in more than a century.
A tiny wild cat that lives in Bolivia’s lush cloud forests has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time in more than a century that a new living feline species has been formally named and described.
Called “tilcayo” by local communities, the cat is part of a group called tiger cats, which are found across much of South America.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2Trump administration moves to end rule protecting swaths of forest land
- list 2 of 2Singapore’s plans to clear forest for homes lead to rare public protests
It was discovered in the Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to the researchers.
Given the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, the cat measures 46cm (18 inches) long and weighs about 1.4kg (3 pounds), making it smaller than an average domestic cat.
“Its fur is light brown … with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body,” according to Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic Explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.
Little is known about the cat’s biology and lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be more active at night, Nogales-Ascarrunz said.
Tiger cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp in Belgium said.
Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because “its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats”, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This made us wonder, what tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?”
The team analysed DNA from 38 cats sampled across several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.
“We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” Lescroart said.
Genetic analysis suggested that the tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4 million years ago.
The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru’s Yungas, naming it Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo, after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca Empire that included the area it inhabits.

Indonesia gets its first aircraft carrier amid debate over cost and military ambitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:04:57 UTC
13:04:57 KST

Indonesia has received its first aircraft carrier, a former Italian warship that the government says will strengthen the archipelagic nation’s maritime security and disaster response capabilities.
The 41-year-old former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, with capacity for short takeoff and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters, arrived Friday morning at a naval base in North Jakarta’s Tanjung Priok port, where it was welcomed with a military ceremony.
Italy in March agreed to give the carrier, which was retired in 2024, to Indonesia in a move aimed at boosting Italy’s broader defence engagement with the south-east Asian country. Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship.
The transfer would make Indonesia only the second country in south-east Asia with a carrier in its fleet. The first was Thailand’s HTMS Chakri Naruebet, which was commissioned in 1997 after being procured from Spain along with carrier-capable AV-8S Matador jump-jets.
The carrier will be formally commissioned into the Indonesian Navy next week as the KRI Gajah Mada, named after the famed 14th-century Majapahit-era military leader, whose campaigns and vision of a unified archipelago have made him one of Indonesia’s most celebrated historical figures.
Defence development was one of the top priorities for president Prabowo Subianto’s administration, as he has advocated an expansion of the military through the purchase of submarines, frigates, fighter jets, missiles and pushed for more defence cooperation with various countries.
But the Garibaldi acquisition has sparked a fierce debate among defence analysts, economists and opposition politicians who question whether Indonesia needs an aircraft carrier at all and whether the government should be spending millions of dollars to refurbish and operate an ageing warship while facing mounting fiscal pressures at home.
Indonesia’s finance ministry approved $450m in financing for the aircraft carrier program in 2025. However, some lawmakers have warned the overall bill could be far higher. TB Hasanuddin, a member of parliament’s Commission I, said the cost of retrofitting the carrier alone could reach 16tn rupiah (about $900m).
Unlike major naval powers that use aircraft carriers to launch fighter jets far from home shores, Indonesia views the vessel as a mobile command centre and support hub for helicopters, drones and maritime operations across its thousands of islands.
Speaking during a disaster management meeting early this month, Prabowo said the vessel would help authorities combat forest and peatland fires that regularly blanket parts of south-east Asia with hazardous haze.
Prabowo said the carrier could accommodate up to 10 medium-sized helicopters, including aircraft with capabilities comparable to the Black Hawk and Mi-17, and could carry large quantities of water and be deployed to areas with large numbers of fire hotspots.
He also outlined plans to operate drones from the ship and use it as a mobile platform that could be rapidly deployed to help in the event of natural disasters, which are common in Indonesia, a nation that sits in the Pacific “Ring of Fire.”
Operating a carrier is extremely costly, however, and experts have questioned whether Indonesia’s leadership has thought through whether one is necessary for the country’s defence or disaster-relief needs.
The acquisition comes as Indonesia’s economy faces growing fiscal pressures. Prabowo’s government has been funding a free nutritious meals program – which has been tainted by multiple food poisoning incidents – and other costly initiatives while economists have warned about slowing growth, weaker state revenues and widening budget constraints, prompting closer scrutiny of major government spending projects.
“The plan to acquire the Garibaldi must be based on genuine operational needs and our ability to operate it, rather than being driven by pride or other considerations,” said Muhammad Fauzan Malufti, of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
He said policymakers must weigh not only the vessel’s acquisition and modernisation costs, but also the Navy’s ability to sustain its operations, including personnel, maintenance, fuel, weapons systems and supporting infrastructure.
Fauzan said the government should be transparent about those considerations, particularly given the vessel’s age. He cited Thailand’s carrier as a cautionary example, saying it has spent much of its service life in port because of operational and budget constraints.
“The bottom line is that this should not be forced. Otherwise, the benefits could be outweighed by the costs,” Fauzan said. “The money might be better spent on other priorities, such as increasing the number of frigates in the fleet.”
Military analyst Khairul Fahmi of the Institute for Security and Strategic Studies said aircraft carriers are not a priority for Indonesia, which is focused on preventing adversaries from operating freely in the country’s territorial waters.
“Indonesia has a greater need for submarines, frigates and asymmetric weapons systems to protect its maritime sovereignty,” he said.
But he added that if Indonesia is seeking to position itself as a major maritime nation, “an aircraft carrier can be both a symbol of national power and a multifunctional platform capable of supporting a wide range of military and non-military missions.”

Northrop expands NATO missile defence partnerships
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:56 BST
13:00:56 KST

Northrop Grumman has signed new agreements with companies in Estonia and expanded cooperation with Polish industry as it pushes its air and missile defence, weapons and surveillance systems further into Central and Eastern Europe, according to the company.
The agreements were announced during the MSPO defence exhibition in Kielce, Poland, and cover work ranging from Integrated Battle Command System integration and sustainment to medium-calibre weapons production and airborne surveillance.
In Estonia, Northrop Grumman has signed memorandums of understanding with Go Craft and DefSecIntel. Go Craft will work on defence system integration, while DefSecIntel will support specialised mast fabrication and production linked to systems including the Integrated Battle Command System, or IBCS.
IBCS is already operational with the US Army and Poland and is being positioned by Northrop Grumman as a wider European command-and-control solution for integrated air and missile defence. The system is designed to combine information from different sensors and connect them with available weapons through a common battle-management architecture, allowing commanders to select what Northrop Grumman describes as the “best shooter” for a particular threat rather than tying individual sensors to individual interceptors.
Ben Davies, corporate vice president and president of Defence Systems at Northrop Grumman, said: “Central and Eastern Europe is at the forefront of efforts to strengthen NATO’s collective defence posture. By deepening our collaboration with local industry and aligning our advanced, modernised capabilities with the needs of regional allies, we are helping to build a more integrated, resilient and effective defence architecture across domains.”
The company is also expanding cooperation in Poland around its Bushmaster family of Chain Guns.
Northrop Grumman said it was deepening work with Polish vehicle manufacturer Huta Stalowa Wola on technology transfer, service and support for Bushmaster cannons, which are already fitted to Polish Rosomak and Borsuk armoured vehicles.
The aim is to increase European support and production capacity for the weapons as demand for medium-calibre firepower grows across NATO.

The spectre of ‘remigration’ is haunting Europe. Slovenia in 1992 gives us a blueprint for this state terror | Miha Mazzini
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:00:09 UTC
13:00:09 KST

So much of your daily life – your job, your health, your home – hinges on the fact that your name is in a government database. Are you a legal citizen of your country, with everything that entails? You are, until an anonymous bureaucrat hits a key one night and strips it all away, turning you into an illegal immigrant. It happened in Slovenia in 1992.
“I took my son to register for secondary school. The clerk rifled through the papers, then stared at me as if refusing to see the boy standing right next to me. Finally, she said: ‘But you don’t have a son. He doesn’t exist.’” I can’t forget the look on the face of the woman who was telling me this story. It was a mixture of deep hurt and bewilderment, with a pause after every sentence, as if she were walking through a minefield. During the research for my book Erased, I compiled countless stories like this: stories I once would have thought impossible.
On 26 February 1992, the Slovenian government quietly deleted 1.3% of its citizenry overnight. The criterion was frighteningly simple: anyone born in another part of the former Yugoslavia who was a permanent resident of Slovenia (regardless of whether they considered themselves naturalised) suddenly lost their citizenship, their right to reside, their healthcare, their pension: everything. They were transformed into illegal immigrants overnight, without prior notification, and with no right to appeal. The goal was to cleanse Slovenia of a Balkan “fifth column” and pivot closer to Europe.
I have long felt this dark piece of Slovenian history to be an ugly stain on the conscience of my nation; but its spirit is spreading across Europe and beyond. The horrors of migrant deaths in the Mediterranean and the English Channel are regularly witnessed and documented, the victims dying at the very gates of “fortress Europe”. But even if you are already inside the fortress, even if you consider yourself fully naturalised, you are perhaps no longer safe. In an age of constant video surveillance, there is nothing fantastical about an official refusing to renew a permit, or unearthing a minor “offence” committed decades earlier, to strip away your citizenship.
The spectre of “remigration” is haunting Europe, and its shadow looms ever larger. What Slovenia did in 1992 has become a blueprint for a quiet, bureaucratic form of state terror.
The woman who told me about her son lived in a village equidistant between two towns. During her pregnancy, she had to choose between two maternity hospitals. After the collapse of Yugoslavia, the town she had picked was across the new border in Croatia, while her village remained in Slovenia. And so, on that fateful day in 1992, her son ceased to exist. His story had a happy ending: Slovenia is a very small country, and if you have a wide enough network, you’ll eventually find someone who knows someone. So the boy emerged from the ranks of the disappeared and was able to attend school. But for those without friends in high places, things rarely ended happily.
One man was rushing to work, speeding, when he was pulled over by the police. Unable to find him in the registry, they took him to an asylum centre. He had been born in Serbia, but Slovenia’s only border with the former Yugoslavia is with Croatia. So they deported him there instead. Croatia was at war with Serbia at the time, and the man was treated as a prisoner of war. He was lucky: had he been born in Croatia, he would have been conscripted and sent straight to the frontlines.
For six years, 1.3% of the population hid and survived however they could. They worked illegally for subsistence wages, at the mercy of bosses and landlords. One man locked himself in his flat, eating old canned food, refusing to open the door to anyone. It was a wise strategy. There were cases of the erased returning home to find their locks changed: someone had simply claimed and occupied their flat, realising the victim would have no recourse to call the police.
There were also stories of profound kindness: a citizen who officially contracted every disease imaginable because he kept lending his healthcare card to the erased; a waitress who walked out of her shift with a first aid kit to treat an injured, erased man who had just been thrown out of the hospital. Relying on the kindness of strangers, however, is a lottery I wouldn’t wish on anyone.
In 1998, the Slovenian constitutional court ruled the erasure unconstitutional, and the immediate threat subsided. But the long road to restoring rights and securing measly compensation for the victims turned into a gruelling odyssey that, for some, continues to this day.
A monument has since been erected for the erased in Ljubljana, and a park named after them. But it is always easier to build a monument than to issue an apology, let alone settle dues. The UK has its own unresolved equivalent in the Windrush generation – and their monument is standing, too.
Many of the erased never doubted their status because they considered themselves Slovenians. Overnight, they were expected to deport themselves to countries they had no meaningful connection to. I was reminded of their fate when reading about the US administration’s “operation second look”, which entails ICE agents scavenging decades-old files for minor administrative discrepancies in the hope of stripping people of their citizenship.
As it so often does, Europe follows America’s lead. Gregory Bovino, the former US Border Patrol “commander-at-large”, was recently in Europe and treated like a rock star. At a rightwing gathering in Portugal he noted that he and the Austrian ethnonationalist Martin Sellner are “on the same sheet of music”. Perhaps the original Slovenian experiment in “remigration” was indeed exactly what it was claimed to be back then: a step closer to Europe, but a meaner and more sinister version of Europe.
- 
  Miha Mazzini is a writer, film-maker and anthropologist

EU warns Turkey to clean up waste treatment or face trade ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

BRUSSELS — The European Commission will consider banning the export of plastic waste to Turkey if the country fails to address pollution and environmental concerns, a Commission official told POLITICO.
The warning comes after a Commission assessment found evidence of environmental damage linked to Turkey’s treatment of plastic waste that could breach EU rules.
“If there is no adequate answer or measure taken by the authorities, the Commission might launch the procedure to suspend the export of plastic waste to Türkiye,” the Commission official said. The assessment itself recommended continuing shipments to Turkey despite the findings.
Advertisement
While a suspension would be in line with EU rules on the shipment of waste, it would also jeopardize the bloc’s most important market for trash. Last year, Turkey received a third of the EU’s exported plastic waste.
The Commission assessment, dated Sept. 1 and obtained by POLITICO, reported a long list of concerns over Turkey’s treatment of EU waste, including the fact that only around 10% of plastic waste is recycled in the country, while the majority goes to landfills, is mismanaged or leaks into the environment.
The Commission official said the report pointed to “several instances” of plastic waste mismanagement, generating “serious pollution problems.”
Despite evidence of practices that could breach EU rules, the report said the Commission would hold off on suspending exports and instead engage with the Turkish authorities on these concerns.
The bloc’s Waste Shipment Regulation — which restricts exports of certain types of EU waste to third countries to curb pollution — says the EU can stop the export of waste to OECD countries that fail to show the waste is managed in an “environmentally sound manner.”
The law specifically requires the Commission to assess whether OECD countries importing large volumes of plastic waste are managing it without causing significant environmental or health damage.
Advertisement
The assessment focused on Turkey because it’s the biggest importer of European waste by far. Last year the country imported 510,000 tonnes of EU plastic waste, the equivalent of about 25 billion 500ml soft drink bottles. This represented 70% of plastic waste exported to OECD countries and 36% of all exported plastic waste.
Under the rules, exports of plastic waste to non-OECD countries will generally be banned from Nov. 21.
That might reroute plastic waste to OECD countries like Turkey, the Commission official said, so it’s important to understand the situation and “strengthen” cooperation with the country to prevent problems arising from this.
Non-OECD countries that show they can manage waste in a sustainable manner can request to be exempted under the law to continue receiving waste.
The list of countries seeking an exemption is expected to be published in the coming days. The Commission is required to adopt the list by November.

China aims to cement its place at forefront of biomedical innovation with new 5-year plan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:46:11 CST
12:46:11 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China on Friday released a five-year plan for its pharmaceutical industry, outlining targets such as keeping biomedical research, development, and application at the global forefront by 2030. This move signals the country's resolve to turn drug innovation into a strategic strength.
The plan, jointly issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and nine other authorities, calls for a major leap in the core competitiveness and international influence of China's pharmaceutical industry from 2026 to 2030. It is hoped that core technologies in key fields will see systematic breakthroughs during this period.
Specifically, first-in-class drugs developed in China should account for no less than 25 percent of the global total, with the number of innovative drugs approved for market ranking among the world leaders. The innovative drug sector is expected to grow at an average annual rate of at least 20 percent, according to the plan.
China also expects the biomedical sector to take shape as a national pillar industry at an accelerated pace.
The combined revenue of pharmaceutical enterprises above a designated scale threshold -- an annual main business revenue of 20 million yuan (about 2.96 million U.S. dollars) -- should reach at least 3.5 trillion yuan by 2030, the plan says.
The number of companies with an annual revenue exceeding 10 billion yuan should grow to 50. At least five Chinese drugs should achieve global annual sales exceeding 1 billion U.S. dollars, according to the plan.
The plan arrives at a pivotal moment as China's pharmaceutical industry is shifting rapidly from its traditional identity as a supplier of active pharmaceutical ingredients and a large consumption market, toward a new phase defined by the export of innovative drugs.
In the first half of this year, 38 innovative drugs were approved in China, of which 31, or more than 80 percent, were domestically developed. As of the end of 2025, China had 4,751 innovative drugs in the pipeline, accounting for one third of the global total and placing it first in the world for drugs under development.
The broader industry also showed great vitality. Value-added output of China's pharmaceutical enterprises above the 20-million-yuan revenue threshold grew 6.4 percent year on year in the first half of this year.
Moreover, China's innovative drugs have gained wider global reach. The total value of overseas licensing deals for innovative Chinese drugs has surpassed 120 billion U.S. dollars this year, up 36 percent year on year. ■

New Zealand police to get power to issue move-on orders
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:46:00 CST
12:46:00 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand police will soon be able to issue move-on orders to people displaying disorderly behavior in public places after legislation passed its final reading in parliament on Friday.
The orders are intended to give police an additional tool to deal with public disorder and will not criminalize homelessness, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said in a statement.
"Only people who refuse those orders will face prosecution," Goldsmith said, adding that a move-on order itself is not a criminal charge.
Under the legislation, police can issue orders to people whose begging unreasonably interferes with the use or enjoyment of a public place, people sleeping rough, or those displaying disorderly, disruptive, threatening or intimidating behavior.
Orders can also be issued to people obstructing or impeding someone from entering a business, breaching the peace, or behaving in a way that indicates an intent to inhabit a public place.
The orders will apply to people aged 18 or older and require them to leave a specified area for up to 24 hours. People ordered to move on for begging or rough sleeping can return to the area if they do not engage in prohibited behavior, according to the bill.
Goldsmith said the government is committed to "fixing the basics in law and order" and making central cities safe for residents, workers and visitors. ■

CANBERRA, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has made Australians poorer and is driving upside risks to inflation, the head of the nation's central bank said on Friday.
Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Governor Michele Bullock told a parliamentary hearing in Canberra that upside risks to inflation appear to be materializing, with a spike in oil prices due to the conflict in the Middle East expected to add directly to inflation.
These supply shocks, the Middle East in particular, have worsened the trade-off between inflation and employment, she said.
"I think we have to acknowledge that the trade-off has got worse, that this particular Middle East shock has made us poorer, and we can't respond to that by letting inflation get out of control."
The RBA's Monetary Policy Board, which Bullock chairs, will next meet to consider interest rates at the end of September.
The board increased the cash rate target by 0.25 percentage points three times in the first six months of 2026, but kept the key interest rate on hold at 4.35 percent at its most recent meetings in June and August.
Bullock said the meeting at the end of September would consider whether the current rate will be sufficient to bring inflation back within the RBA's 2-3 percent target band within a reasonable time.
"It's more important than ever that we bring inflation back to target," she said.
The most recent data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed that annual inflation fell from 3.8 percent in June to 3.5 percent in July, which was the lowest figure since November 2025. ■

S. Korea's producer prices rebound in August on scorching heat, energy costs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:45:42 CST
12:45:42 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Prices for goods and services among South Korean suppliers rebounded last month on the back of scorching heat and higher energy costs, central bank data showed Friday.
The producer price index (PPI) edged up 0.2 percent in August from a month earlier, reversing from a brief downturn in the previous month, according to the Bank of Korea.
It was driven by a surge in prices for agricultural, livestock and fisheries products, which jumped 3.8 percent in the cited month.
Agricultural product prices soared 4.9 percent as a severe heatwave led to poor crop yields, while livestock product prices advanced 2.8 percent due to higher pork prices caused by heat deaths.
Prices for electricity, gas, water and waste among suppliers gained 0.9 percent month-on-month in August, propelled by an 11.0 percent spike in industrial city gas rates.
Producer prices for industrial products, including oil products, remained flat as higher prices for coal and petroleum products were offset by lower prices for electrical equipment.
Services prices were also unchanged as a rise in costs for food and accommodation services was counterbalanced by a fall in expenses for financial and insurance services. ■

Trump hails ‘major progress’ on setting up US Army base in Poland
The US has made major progress in negotiations to establish a military base in Poland, President Donald Trump has announced.
His remarks came as Russia warned that it would retaliate if the territory of Poland or the Baltic states were used for a NATO attack against the country.
Poland, which borders the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad to the northeast, is a key logistics hub for delivering Western military aid to Ukraine and is one of Kiev’s main supporters in Europe.
“GREAT NEWS! Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday.
“If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance.”
Nawrocki responded by promising to find “the best possible location” for the base. “We are ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defense cooperation: seriously, responsibly, and always together,” he wrote on X.
The US already maintains a permanent Army garrison and command headquarters in Poland, although most of the 10,000 US troops stationed in the country serve on a rotational basis. During Trump’s first term in 2018, Poland offered to host a permanent base tentatively named ‘Fort Trump’.
Under Trump’s successor, President Joe Biden, the US established a garrison headquartered at Camp Kosciuszko in Poznan and permanently stationed the V Corps Forward Headquarters in the city.
Tensions between Russia and NATO have flared in recent months as eastern members of the US-led military bloc have accused Russia of launching drone incursions. Moscow has dismissed the allegations as unfounded.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said during a trip to Kiev over the weekend that “if Russia attacked us and we took our gloves off, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly.”
Russian presidential aide and former security chief Nikolay Patrushev responded to Sikorski by warning that “Polish statehood would cease to exist within two or three days” if a conflict breaks out.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reiterated this week that the country has no intention of attacking NATO members, but said that if the bloc attacks Russia, the war would be “very short.”

Breaking: SA government commits $109m to help struggling wine industry
