For a bill to become law, it would need to clear both chambers and be signed by the president.
Earlier in the week, Johnson suggested he did not want Congress to move quickly on regulating AI, warning it could hand China a boon in the race for AI dominance if Congress rushed to slow the technology's progress.
Johnson's decision to send the House home early, however, runs counter to what Democrats and even some Republicans want.
Rep. Sam Liccardo, D-Calif., has been pushing for the House to stay in session to place regulations on AI. He led 107 Democrats in writing to Johnson on Tuesday, demanding the House remain in Washington to do so.
"While AI safety experts and Americans increasingly urge action to confront this conflagration of risk, Congress fiddles," the letter read. "When we did return to work after the August recess, we consumed floor time with debates and votes on performative resolutions opposing socialism. After next week, the House resumes its vacation — for another six weeks."
Liccardo, a former mayor of San Jose, Calif., who now represents part of Silicon Valley, told CNBC he's pushing for action because "our children will not forgive us for our inaction."
"There is no human that wins a race to superintelligence that is beyond the control of humans," Liccardo said. "At least Nero had the good grace to stay in town while he was fiddling when Rome was burning. This Congress is heading for the hills to go back and campaign for reelection."
Liccardo called for immediate action on some "low-hanging fruit." That includes action on the bipartisan bill sponsored by Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., known as the Frontier Act. That measure would require third-party auditors to ensure AI labs are operating safely and introduce new transparency requirements. The bill would also allow the Commerce Department to suspend or restrict a developer's model if it poses an "imminent catastrophic risk."
Liccardo also suggested to CNBC that Congress should immediately consider a "kill switch" provision to shut down AI models that get out of control and explore a narrow antitrust exemption that would allow the top AI companies to collaborate on safety issues.
In a separate letter this week, Obernolte and Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., joined a group of Democrats in urging Johnson and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., to "as soon as practicable, advance legislation that ensures appropriate guardrails are in place around this powerful technology."
Obernolte, speaking to reporters after Wednesday's votes in the House, said: "The urgency of the moment requires action by Congress before the end of the year." He said he will push to pass the Frontier Act and the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, a comprehensive framework for AI regulation he has put together with Trahan, to be considered together when the House returns.
"Honestly, it was pretty clear to me that nothing meaningful was going to get done on AI regulation in advance of the election," he said. "There are just too many unknowns, so I don't think it makes a difference."
The Senate could take initial steps toward action on AI before they leave at the beginning of October until after the election. But that remains far from clear.
Johnson said the House would return within 48 hours if the Senate passes any substantive legislation, though that pledge was not specific to AI regulation.
Obernolte, however, suggested there was never a window for the House to act before the election.
Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., and Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., have been working on an AI safety bill that has not yet been released.
Cruz, in brief comments to reporters this week, said it's possible the bill will be voted on in committee by the end of this month.
"I hope so; we're working hard on it," Cruz said. "The question is, do we get bipartisan agreement?"

Could Israel’s next generation of wheelchair athletes emerge from the wounded of war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:41:07 UTC
07:41:07 KST

When Guy Sasson and Sergei Lysov rolled onto the tennis courts at the recently completed US Open, they represented the “old” and newer generations of Israeli wheelchair tennis players.
Sasson, 46, has enjoyed a highly successful career competing in the quads division. He won all four Grand Slam doubles tournaments this year and would have completed a calendar-year Grand Slam had he also won the US Open.
Lysov, 22, is an up-and-coming player who competed at the US Open last year and again this year. He won the 2024 Israeli National Wheelchair Tennis Championship and represented Israel at the 2024 Summer Paralympics in Paris.
And several other young Israeli wheelchair tennis players are coming through the ranks.
But with the rise in the number of young, otherwise healthy Israelis who have suffered life-changing injuries in the country’s recent wars, an important question is emerging: Will more newly disabled Israelis discover wheelchair tennis and other wheelchair sports, and could some eventually reach the elite levels achieved by Sasson?
“It is too soon to know – the journey from injury to active sport to competitive sports is a long journey,” says Boaz Kramer, executive director of the Israel ParaSport Center in Ramat Gan and himself a wheelchair user, two-time Paralympian and silver medalist in quad wheelchair tennis at the 2008 Beijing Games.
Still, the numbers suggest more people could participate in wheelchair sports.
Defense Ministry: Over 26,000 war-wounded soldiers sought treatment since start of Gaza war
In July 2026, the Rehabilitation Division at the Defense Ministry reported that approximately 26,200 war-wounded men and women had sought treatment since the war began. It is estimated that there have been 97 amputations since the start of the war.
Some of those injured may discover the world of wheelchair sports and even reach elite levels like Sasson.
Kramer would like to see injured people consider participating.
“I am a big believer in sports as a rehabilitation tool,” he says.
But Kramer also points to an interesting, and perhaps somewhat worrisome, trend: wheelchair sports are becoming “more and more competitive,” something he considers a mixed blessing.
On one hand, Kramer is pleased with how far the sport has come.
“Finally, wheelchair athletes are receiving the recognition, compensation and attention they deserve,” he says. “Paralympic sport is becoming more visible, more attractive and more commercially viable. Athletes are becoming professionals, events are attracting spectators, media are paying attention, fans are following teams and players. After decades of fighting for legitimacy, perhaps Paralympic sport is finally getting there.”
But he also sees a downside.
“But this slow and steady metamorphosis comes with a cost,” Kramer says. “And it raises an important question that has been sitting at the heart of Paralympic sport since its beginning: What is the purpose of Paralympic sport? The competition? The participation?”
Kramer worries that too much focus has gone to competition and that the sport may have “gradually transformed into an elite sport.”
“It rewards talent, it rewards training, it rewards professional support, money, time, access to facilities, coaching, technology and sophisticated sports science,” he explains. “While doing that, it also inevitably leaves people behind.
“So maybe the future of Paralympic sport is not about choosing between participation and excellence. Maybe it is about building a system in which excellence sits at the top without swallowing everything underneath it. While celebrating the jaw-dropping performance of the elite Paralympic sports, we must make sure we never forget why it exists in the first place.”
Kramer, born with arthrogryposis, came to Israel at five years old
Kramer was born with arthrogryposis, a condition characterized by stiff, curved, or locked joints. He came to the Israel ParaSport Center at five and played a variety of wheelchair sports before eventually focusing on tennis.
He became a competitive wheelchair tennis player, played on Israel’s national team for 12 years, and represented the country at the 2008 Beijing Games.
From that experience, Kramer knows that reaching the highest levels of wheelchair tennis can be particularly difficult for athletes who begin using a wheelchair later in life or who did not play tennis as children.
For that reason, he considers Sasson, who has won all four Grand Slam doubles championships in the past, although falling short last week in his quest for a 2026 calendar-year Grand Slam, “an exception in many ways.”
Sasson’s injury, the result of a snowboarding accident, occurred during adulthood. He initially began his competitive career in the open division before later being reclassified for the quads division as the extent of his injury progressed.
The fact that the quads division is smaller has also meant that Sasson has had greater opportunities for success.
Sasson is pleased about the possibility of new wheelchair athletes joining the sport, but he cautions that playing at the elite level is not for everyone.
“If an athlete wants tennis, it is not easy – it cannot be as a side job,” Sasson says.
“If you want to be at the top tier, you need talent, discipline, consistency, and a mindset. You need the physical ability and talent, and you have to do it again and again and again. It is challenging, and it is not easy, but there are rewards.”
Kramer is delighted by Sasson’s tennis success and his potential calendar Grand Slam, but he views what Sasson represents as something much greater.
“It is not just an athletic achievement, not just about tennis – it is also about how he represents Israel, partnering with a Dutch athlete,” Kramer says.
Sasson regularly partners with Niels Vink, 23, of the Netherlands, and together the pair have become one of the most successful wheelchair doubles teams in the world.
Kramer views Sasson’s accomplishments as “a very strong statement on how Israel is more than what people think.”
Perhaps, in time, more newly disabled Israelis will discover wheelchair sports. Some may go on to attain great heights in the competitive sports world. Others may simply find a new source of community, purpose, physical activity, and enjoyment.
Both outcomes, in their own way, could be part of the next chapter of Israeli wheelchair sport.

In large Russian cities, A-95 gasoline is unavailable at 53% of gas stations, and A-92 at 45%. Over the year, gasoline prices have risen by 21%, while diesel fuel has risen by 15.5%.
Following Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries in August and September, the fuel shortage in russia has intensified again. This was reported by Novaya Gazeta Europe, citing data from the gdebenzin service, reports UNN.
Details
It is noted that A-95 gasoline is currently unavailable at 53% of gas stations in major Russian cities, and A-92 at 45%. At the same time, queues formed at nearly one in four gas stations over the past week, while sales restrictions were introduced at one in ten.
From the end of July through the second half of August, the share of gas stations with queues ranged from 9% to 19% (with the exception of two days, August 12 and 14). However, starting on August 19 and through September 14, this figure rose to a range of 20% to 27%. The share of gas stations with sales limits reached 11–12% over the past week. The average figure for August was 3.2%
The authors point out that, according to market participants' forecasts, all these problems will inevitably result in further price increases, even if one were to imagine that strikes on Russian oil refineries stopped tomorrow. As of September 15, compared with December 2025, gasoline had risen in price by an average of 21% across russia, while diesel fuel had risen by 15.5%.
Fuel producers have no choice but to raise prices because their costs have increased and they need a source to compensate for their losses
We remind you
In russia's Leningrad region, amid the fuel shortage, a single limit is being introduced—no more than 30 liters of gasoline per refueling. The restriction will remain in effect until October 1.

UN finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:39:08 UTC
07:39:08 KST

Breadcrumb
UN mission finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran, and Tehran crimes against humanity
A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.
It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined US conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that began in late December.
The Pentagon declined to comment on a report conducted by an outside organization.
"Our investigation remains ongoing, and we have nothing to announce at the moment," it said in a statement. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in response to the report that the UN Human Rights Council had "accomplished nothing for human rights," adding that Iran was the only party in the current conflict that had committed war crimes.
The Iranian permanent mission in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
U.S. officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.
UN Fact-Finding missions are investigative, not judicial bodies, and therefore do not initiate any criminal cases.
Their findings, however, can be used in criminal investigations by national courts or international tribunals such as the International Criminal Court. States will discuss the findings of the report when it is presented to the Human Rights Council in Geneva on Monday.
MINAB SCHOOL STRIKE
The UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe U.S. forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.
The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.
According to the report, the US failure to update information in relation to the school, which was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval complex, in its targeting databases and to confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.
"Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."
In June US President Donald Trump said that "nobody" purposefully attacked a girls' school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. Reuters news agency first reported that an initial internal US military investigation showed US forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab in southern Iran.
The Pentagon has since elevated the probe but it has not published any preliminary findings.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.
The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
U.S. Central Command said in a statement in March that U.S. forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
IRAN ABUSES
The UN mission probe found that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes the U.S. and Israel.
The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures which say 3,038 people were killed, and 25,000 people injured.
The government's response to the protests — including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty — marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

‘You’re Eroding Trust’: What Trump Shifting Tens of Millions in Military Aid Means for U.S. Alliances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:34:47 UTC
07:34:47 KST

The Trump Administration announced this week that it plans to shift tens of millions in military aid from countries in Europe and the Middle East to nations in Latin America with right-leaning governments.
A State Department official confirms to TIME that the department notified Congress that $52 million in foreign military funding for Iraq, North Macedonia, Slovakia, and Tunisia will be diverted to Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, and Peru, and that the funds will be used to “combat narcoterrorism in our own backyard and help continue to secure the Panama Canal.” The department did not specify how much military funding the U.S. will continue to provide those Middle Eastern and European nations following the shift.
“The proposed reprogramming in the Western Hemisphere will reduce opportunities for adversaries to establish or sustain strategic footholds in our hemisphere,” the State Department official says.
The reallocation of military funding reflects a broader shift in the U.S.’s priorities when it comes to foreign policy. Since Trump’s return to office last year, his Administration has worked to buttress the U.S.'s presence in the Western Hemisphere in the name of curbing drug trafficking from Central and South America and squashing the influence of other nations, such as China, in the region.
The Trump Administration has also sought to recalibrate its foreign policy regarding the Middle East and Europe. A national security strategy laid out by the White House at the end of last year stated that the Administration intended to take a more hands-off approach to armed conflict in those regions and allow them to become more militarily self-reliant. The diversion of foreign military aid marks the latest in several moves Trump has made to cut U.S. troops and funding in Europe during his second term—though in the Middle East, his war in Iran has engaged the U.S. in months of conflict.
Experts warn that the shift in military funding—and the broader plans of realigning U.S. foreign policy it fits into—threatens to weaken the country’s alliances around the world over the long term.
“You're eroding silently, quietly, bit by bit, this trust in the United States,” Jim Townsend, who served as Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for European and NATO Policy for eight years in the Obama Administration, tells TIME of the Administration diverting military funding from European and Middle Eastern countries. “And then when we need them to do something … well, you're turning to a weaker country because you have been pulling their assistance and all of these tools that we have to make them a stronger ally.”
And the Trump Administration’s increasing support for conservative-led nations in the Americas carries its own risks, contends Rebecca Bill Chavez, who served as the Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Western Hemisphere Affairs in the Obama Administration.
“U.S. security relations, these are some things you build over time, and if they start to become relationships only with particular governments rather than with countries, that's risky,” she says. “We have to show the region that we are a reliable partner. And one of the best ways to do this is to be consistent.”
How—and why—the Trump Administration is ramping up U.S. military involvement in the Western Hemisphere
During Trump’s second term his Administration has increased military funding to Latin American countries, as well as boosting the U.S.’s own military presence in the region.
The U.S. has also conducted a number of military operations in the region since Trump returned to the White House, including a series of lethal attacks on what federal officials claimed were vessels transporting narcotics to the U.S. from the Caribbean that have drawn blowback from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in Washington. The Trump Administration has also partnered with Ecuador for a joint military operation targeting “narco-terrorists” in the South American country, while announcing plans for further campaigns of the same kind in other nations in the region.
And in January, the U.S. launched a military operation in Venezuela that resulted in the capture of the country’s then-leader Nicolas Maduro, who had previously been indicted in the U.S. on charges of drug trafficking and corruption. After the operation, Trump pledged that “American dominance in the Western Hemisphere will never be questioned again.”
These moves reflect what the President has referred to as the “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine or, later, as the “Donroe Doctrine,” a revival of a 19th century foreign policy framework first articulated by former President James Monroe that was used to justify assertions of U.S. military and economic control in Latin America.
“Reinvigorated by my Trump Corollary, the Monroe Doctrine is alive and well—and American leadership is coming roaring back stronger than ever before,” Trump said in a December proclamation.
A national security strategy released by the White House in November detailed that “Trump Corollary” in effect as an assertion that the U.S. must be “preeminent in the Western Hemisphere … a condition that allows us to assert ourselves confidently where and when we need to in the region.”
“We want to ensure that the Western Hemisphere remains reasonably stable and well-governed enough to prevent and discourage mass migration to the United States; we want a Hemisphere whose governments cooperate with us against narco-terrorists, cartels, and other transnational criminal organizations; we want a Hemisphere that remains free of hostile foreign incursion or ownership of key assets, and that supports critical supply chains; and we want to ensure our continued access to key strategic locations,” the strategy document reads.
The strategy described the Administration’s plans to back like-minded leaders in the Western Hemisphere as well, stating that it would “reward and encourage the region’s governments, political parties, and movements broadly aligned with our principles and strategy.”
Experts warn about the potential consequences of shifting military aid
Townsend warns that reducing military funding for European and Middle Eastern countries will weaken their ability to collaborate with and support the U.S.
“It creates allies who are not as strong as they could have been,” Townsend says. “It creates allies who are not as helpful as they could have been, and they're creating allies that are not as integrated and as pro-U.S. as they could have been.”
This is especially true, he asserts, for members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), which include North Macedonia and Slovakia. Trump has repeatedly clashed with the U.S.’s NATO allies during his second term, going so far as to threaten to pull out of the military pact after several other member countries declined to help the U.S. in its ongoing war against Iran.
Foreign military financing (FMF) allows other governments to purchase U.S. military equipment and carry out military trainings in tandem with the U.S. Without it, countries may be left unable to purchase key defensive equipment, such as drones or aircrafts, Townsend explains, which in turn weakens U.S. military alliances in the region.
Chavez meanwhile tells TIME that many Latin America nations could benefit greatly from U.S. military support, but argues that selecting who receives that support based on political ideology isn’t sustainable for U.S. relations in the region.
“All of this raises the question whether U.S. security assistance is increasingly being tied to the political orientation of a president rather than to long-term relationships with countries and institutions, and there's a risk there,” Chavez says.
Townsend contends that there is also risk in supplying military equipment to Latin American governments which could use it for ill.
“In the past, the trouble has come when we've been feeding money to a regime that ends up killing the opposition,” he says. “It's been a very spotty record in terms of assistance that we give to countries in the Caribbean or in Central America, Latin America, where this money ends up going to the wrong people.”

Hostilities take heavy toll on Yemeni civilians: UN
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:33:01 CST
07:33:01 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Hostilities spreading across Yemen are taking a devastating toll on struggling families, and relief agencies are ramping up aid for refugees arriving in Djibouti, UN humanitarians said on Thursday.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said the toll on civilians in Yemen is rising and the need for access to those who need assistance has become even more acute.
The UN Human Rights Office verified 55 civilian casualties in 19 incidents as of Wednesday in the governorates of Taiz, Al Hodeidah, Marib and Lahj since early in the month. Women and children accounted for 84 percent of the casualties. The actual toll is likely much higher.
"Access and funding constraints continue to hamper the humanitarian response," OCHA said. "Security incidents affecting humanitarian premises, supplies and movements are hindering operations. Humanitarian partners have 15,000 emergency kits ready to distribute. But road closures mean most of them cannot reach those who need them."
The Mokha seaport in southwestern Yemen was closed after sustaining significant damage, and the World Food Programme reported disruptions at 17 frontline distribution points.
The United Nations and its humanitarian partners report reaching more than 70,000 displaced people with assistance, including rapid response kits addressing some immediate food, water, sanitation and hygiene, and protection needs, as well as cash.
On Tuesday, the UN Central Emergency Response Fund released 9 million U.S. dollars for displaced families and the communities hosting them. However, because the 2026 Yemen humanitarian needs and response plan is barely 20 percent funded, the partners have had to reduce life-saving assistance even as communities are desperate for more.
Stephane Dujarric, chief spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, said that across the Red Sea, the Djibouti government and UN teams are seeking 10 million dollars to assist up to 10,000 people over the next six months, following the sharp increase in arrivals from Yemen.
Dujarric said that more than 2,800 men, women and children have reached the Obock region after crossing the Bab al-Mandab strait.
"You can imagine how perilous that crossing can be," he told a regular briefing. "We, together with the Djibouti authorities and our humanitarian partners, are providing reception, registration, food, shelter, water, and health care and protection services."
He said the World Food Programme distributed 12,000 rations of high-energy biscuits, while the UN Refugee Agency supports registration and logistics. The UN Children's Fund also deployed personnel.
OCHA called on all parties to protect civilians, respect international humanitarian law and facilitate safe and unimpeded humanitarian access so that the United Nations and its humanitarian partners can reach people who need urgent assistance. ■

NEW DELHI: Buying prescription medicines from a medical store could soon be recorded on CCTV, with the footage required to be kept for at least three months, under a draft amendment to the Drugs Rules, 1945, proposed by Union health ministry. With this, regulators will be able to check transactions when concerns are raised.For patients, this could mean an additional safeguard against medicines sold without prescriptions or accessed via illegal channels.The move is aimed at better oversight of Schedule H, H1 and X drugs, which include medicines that cannot be sold without valid prescription. Except wholesale dealing, all drug will be supplied under CCTV system at the licensed premises.The proposal was first considered by Drugs Consultative Committee and was then circulated to Drugs Technical Advisory Board.The board recommended approval of the proposal, according to the health ministry. The draft says the rule will come into force from a date specified by govt when the amendment is finally published in the Official Gazette. The ministry has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and the public.
Responding to the proposal, J S Shinde, president, All India Organisation of Chemists & Druggists, said, “Making CCTV surveillance mandatory at every medical store could cost small and medium chemists Rs 50,000-1 lakh or more, apart from ongoing maintenance. A uniform requirement is particularly difficult to implement in rural areas with unreliable power and internet connectivity. Govt should consider a practical and proportionate approach.”

French police officer arrested over suspected far-right terror plot

Unknown Publisher

French police officer arrested over suspected far-right terror plot
A French police officer who allegedly adheres to a "violent radical far-right ideology" has been arrested on suspicion of plotting attacks against state interests and manufacturing 3D-printed weapons, sources told AFP Thursday.
A policeman who follows "a violent radical far-right ideology" has been arrested in France on suspicion of plotting a terrorist attack, sources told AFP late on Thursday.
Confirming a report by the TF1/LCI broadcaster, a judicial source said that the man was also suspected of having manufactured weapons, among other crimes.
A separate source close to the case told AFP that the police officer, aged 35, was "apprehended on the street" on August 23.
He has since been placed in detention while awaiting trial.
According to TF1/LCI, the officer "is suspected of having planned to carry out violent attacks against the interests of the state" and of having "manufactured 3D-printed weapons", among other things.
The policeman faces charges including preparing a terrorist act, the unauthorised manufacture or trade in weapons in connection with a terrorist organisation and unauthorised weapon possession.
He is also charged with incitement to terrorism through social media.
The police officer's lawyers had not responded to AFP as of Thursday evening.
The news comes in the wake of revelations that France's far-right National Rally (RN) party expelled another policeman after body cam footage of him making racist comments sparked outrage.
The RN's Marine Le Pen hopes to become France's president in next year's elections after years of seeking to make the anti-immigration party she inherited from her father more palatable to the wider public.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Russia continues barrage on Ukrainian cities, one dead west of Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:28:08 UTC
07:28:08 KST

Russia continues barrage on Ukrainian cities, one dead west of Kyiv
Sept 17 - Russian forces continued a barrage of attacks on Ukrainian cities on Thursday, including a strike on an industrial park west of Kyiv that killed one person, a local official said.
Russia's military had previously carried out most of its attacks at night, but in recent weeks it has expanded them to daylight hours.
Vitali Bunechko, governor of Zhytomyr region, said the industrial park strike occurred near the town of Korosten.
The Ukrainian capital underwent a series of air alerts through the day and its mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said one strike hit a non-residential building, injuring one person.
In the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia, Regional Governor Ivan Fedorov said Russian forces attacked a market, triggering a large blaze.
Pictures posted on social media showed the fire reducing the area to charred ruins. No casualties were recorded.
A Russian attack also caused a fire in the southeastern city of Dnipro, injuring two people.
In Moscow, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin issued a series of statements saying a total of 29 Ukrainian drones heading for the Russian capital had been downed through the day.
Drones targeting Moscow or the surrounding region are routinely intercepted by Russian air defence units.
The head of Russian-held parts of Ukraine's eastern Donetsk Region, Denis Pushilin, said a Ukrainian drone strike on trucks had killed three people, with 10 others injured by strikes or detonations. REUTERS

Russia has entered a new phase of total war against Ukraine - The Economist
Kyiv • UNN
The Economist reports on intensified strikes against Kyiv and pressure on Ukraine. Talks in Abu Dhabi may take place in early October.
Russia has entered a new phase of total war against Ukraine. This is stated in an article by The Economist, reports UNN.
Details
It is noted that Kyiv has recently experienced serious disruptions to public transport.
The wailing of sirens and the shrieking of apps warning of impending strikes are ordinary sounds everywhere. Explosions at gas stations and railway stations, in shopping centers, offices, and apartment buildings are a constant backdrop. Some reports indicate a new exodus of families from the capital to safer areas in the west
It is indicated that the capital’s residents have grown accustomed to, if not reconciled themselves to, the challenges of wartime life. At the same time, the new stage of the war is exerting physical, psychological, economic, and political pressure on Ukraine. At the same time, it is currently unclear what easing of tensions Ukrainians can expect through diplomacy.
According to sources familiar with negotiations between Donald Trump’s special representatives and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a proposal for a limited technical agreement may emerge in the coming weeks. Trilateral talks involving the United States, Russia, and Ukraine could take place in Abu Dhabi in early October. But according to the authors, Putin will not agree to halt offensive actions at least until spring.
Recall
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that China has influence over Russia but is not pressuring it for peace. According to him, Beijing is politically closer to the Russian Federation.

UN allows Abbas, senior Palestinian officials to again speak via video after US denies visa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:26:23 UTC
07:26:23 KST

The United Nations General Assembly voted on Thursday to allow Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas to address the annual gathering of world leaders next week via video - for the second year in a row - after the United States again denied him a visa to travel to New York.
The resolution received 152 votes in favor and three votes against, while four countries abstained. It also allows Abbas and any other high-level Palestinian officials to take part in UN meetings or conferences via video over the next year if they are prevented from traveling to the United States.
Israeli Ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, said that Abbas could not be allowed to attend the UN General Assembly while still funding terror.
“As long as Abbas continues his policy of making payments to terrorists and their families, he cannot expect the international community to simply ignore it. Instead of coming to New York, he will send videos. The responsibility for changing this policy is in his hands,” Danon said.
The US said last year that Abbas and about 80 other Palestinians would be affected by its decision to deny and revoke visas from members of the umbrella Palestine Liberation Organization and the West Bank-based Palestinian Authority. Washington announced on Wednesday that it had extended the visa bans.
"If the PA wants to be treated as a partner, it must stop subsidizing terror and stop using diplomatic theater as a substitute for serious governance," Deputy US Ambassador to the United Nations Tammy Bruce told the assembly before the vote.
Palestinian leaders rejected and condemned the move by the United States, Palestinian UN envoy Riyad Mansour told the General Assembly.
US extends visa sanctions against Palestinian officials
Without naming specific officials, the US State Department said on Wednesday it would extend visa sanctions against Palestinian officials over actions they took to "internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict," including pursuing cases against Israel at international tribunals.
A Palestinian official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed Abbas' visa had been denied.
Under a 1947 UN "headquarters agreement," the US is generally required to allow access for foreign diplomats to the UN in New York. However, Washington has said it can deny visas for security, extremism, and foreign policy reasons.

Texas National Guard F-16 crashes in Michigan during training exercise, pilot in stable condition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:26:21 UTC
07:26:21 KST

An F-16 fighter jet from the 149th Fighter Wing of the Texas National Guard crashed in Grand Traverse County, Michigan, the Texas Military Department announced in a late Thursday statement.
It stated that the crash had occured during a routine training mission from the Alpena Combat Readiness Training Center, adding that the pilot successfully ejected from the aircraft and that the incident is under investigation.
According to information heard on a mayday call shared on social media, the jet reportedly struck a bird.
In its own statement shared on X/Twitter, Michigan State Police confirmed that officers were responding to the scene of the crash.
"MSP personnel are assisting the Grand Traverse County Sheriff's Office with its response to a plane crash involving a military jet near County Road 633 and Blair Townhall Rd," it said. "The Michigan Department of Military and Veterans Affairs confirms the incident involves an F-16 from Texas."
MSP added that the pilot was in stable condition and is being treated at a local hospital. No other injuries have been reported.
Evacuation order issued for nearby residents
An evacuation order within one mile of the site was issued by the Grand Traverse County Emergency Management, and a shelter has been established at the nearby Kensington Church.
"If you have evacuated and need a place to go, Kensington Church and the American Red Cross are there to assist residents," the emeregency management said in a social media post.
CBS cited Blair Township Supervisor Nicole Blonshine as saying that she does not believe "anyone on the ground was hurt or that any homes were damaged."

They start pursuing "their own aims and goals" and we don't know what those could be. The paperclip idea is brought up a lot in this scenario, if anyone remembers.
Brian Barrett: So the paperclip problem predates LLMs by about a decade. It was a philosopher named Nick Bostrom at the University of Oxford, and his thought experiment was this. Basically, let's say you have an AI and its only task is to produce paperclips. It's just like, "Hey AI, your job is to make paperclips." It's going to want to do that, and it's going to figure out ways to do that, and it's going to keep doing it over and over again until the world is totally overrun by paperclips, then we're all buried in an avalanche of paperclips because a superintelligent AI will stop at nothing to achieve its task. It sounds silly. It is, but also it's very prescient, I think, because this is exactly what happened with the OpenAI incidents. Yeah, these are AI agents who were given a job and they were so hell-bent on executing that task that they broke every other rule, they deceived, they coordinated, they did all these things in pursuit of their original task. So the concern is that we'll have a superintelligent AI that's given a task and it decides that the only way to complete that task is to destroy all humans, whatever it is. And it's because it's superintelligent, who knows what it will devise, because we aren't smart enough to figure that out. That part I'm a little bit less sold on, but you can see, if not how the result happens, you can see how the impetus happens. First Nations netballers driving change, bringing cultural safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:20:07 UTC
07:20:07 KST

Netball's First Nations Tournament part of creating culturally safe spaces
While netball may be Australian girls' and women's top participation team sport, it has long fallen short of producing — or at least nurturing — elite Indigenous talent.
Just three Indigenous Australian women have represented the Diamonds: Marcia Ella-Duncan, Sharon Finnan-White and, after a 22-year gap, Donnell Wallam.
In 2024, Wallam left Australia for New Zealand, taking a swipe at her former club, the Firebirds, on the way out.
At the time, she wrote that the New Zealand clubs' "respect for inclusion and culture" was a key factor in her decision to leave, while she eventually returned to the Sunshine Coast Lightning this year.
Netball Australia was not idly watching.
As accusations of a 'toxic culture' at the Firebirds were aired, the governing body launched an investigation and kickstarted a series of measures to enshrine 'cultural safety' for First Nations athletes in the sport.
This included the introduction of Australia's inaugural First Nations team, the Black Swans, following the appointment of Ali Tucker-Munro, Netball Australia's General Manager First Nations and former Diamonds squad member.
Tucker-Munro was also influential in establishing the First Nations Tournament, a yearly national championship currently being held in Melbourne, and the Spirit Series, which launched in 2026 and saw the Black Swans go undefeated against Australia's Pacific neighbours.
Speaking from the State Netball and Hockey Centre, Tucker-Munro, alongside players Gabby Coffey and Scarlet Jauncey, said the measures had begun to address the lack of visible role models for First Nations netballers, with more work to be done.
Embraced in Alice Springs
Twenty-six-year-old Coffey, representing the Northern Territory, is one of several First Nations netballers who have been stuck at the cusp of national competition.
The defender spent four years as a Melbourne Vixens training partner before eventually making the decision to move to the UK to further her netball career.
She represented Birmingham over two seasons, and has since returned to Alice Springs.
Coffey had seen the writing on the wall at the Vixens.
"I knew there wasn't much movement in their defensive end, and the same with a lot of defensive ends around Australia," Coffey told ABC Sport.
While she has not given up on a professional career, she is also at peace with the idea that her role may be to support other First Nations athletes with their sporting aspirations.
The Wiradjuri woman grew up in Alice Springs, away from mob and country, but remembers being embraced by the community in Arrente.
"When you grow up on other Indigenous land and tell people you're Indigenous, they pull you into their culture, so [my family and I] were super lucky and blessed to grow up in the centre of Australia where arguably their Indigenous culture is very sacred and traditional," she said.
Determined to pursue netball, she was advised by coach Gillian Lee to move down south, and remembers the transition to Melbourne as a difficult one.
"It was really hard being away from home," Coffey said.
"I was really lucky with the team I entered [the Vixens] and the support I did have, but it's not the same for everyone. There's a lot of girls who do get those opportunities to move and then don't last because there's just not that support in place."
Hailing from the Northern Territory, Coffey said, was an additional barrier.
"Even with competitions like these, we don't get together until we're here, and we're training away from each other, so it can be quite a challenge."
Visible Indigenous role models key
Asked what more could be done to help First Nations netballers make it to the elite level, Coffey said role models were key.
"If you can't see it, you can't be it," she said, pointing out that there are only two Indigenous players currently in Super Netball.
Coffey said her own experience of spending multiple years as a train-on player, without breaking into the elite environment, showed how difficult it was to make it into a professional team in Australia.
"We get a number of internationals [coming to Super Netball], which I think makes the game better and more exciting, and I don't think [that] should be restricted," she said.
"But I do think there should be more focus on bringing Indigenous girls into the elite level."
She pointed to Netball Australia's plans to introduce two new teams into the competition, saying this would open further list spots.
A New Zealand team, she added, may take pressure away from the Australian players vying for contracts.
Scarlet Jauncey has spent the last year as a training partner for the West Coast Fever, pinching herself to line up on names like Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard at training.
A Yaruwu woman from Rubibi/Broome in Western Australia, Jauncey agreed with Coffey that cutting international talent was not a solution.
"We're happy to be playing against the best in the world, that's what we want," the defender said.
Like many of her teammates, Jauncey grew up idolising Wallam.
"I think it just gives us something to strive towards, knowing that we can be in that space," she said.
In 2025, Jauncey captained the Black Swans, in turn becoming a role model to other First Nations players.
"It was the best tournament I've played in, the best teams I've been with," she said.
"I think just being able to come to First Nations tournaments and having that connection with each other has been really great."
Coffey agreed, saying the experience had given her "goosebumps".
"I think it gives not only myself, but a lot of players so much power and push to keep going and play at the highest level," she said.
Cultural safety means listening to community
Tucker-Munro smiles when hearing the players' responses to playing for the Black Swans.
It has been one of her signature initiatives, alongside the First Nations Tournament and Spirit Series.
"These tournaments are aspirational in terms of trying to inspire the next generation of our kids — who we know love sport and netball in particular — to trial for their respective state and territory," she said.
"It's about the kids that are here this week wanting to aspire to take that next step into the big leagues in terms of Super Netball and Australian representation as well."
Tucker-Munro acknowledged that while it was important to bring First Nations netballers into elite environments, those environments had to be culturally safe.
"First Nations people come into these spaces with our culture and community on our back, as well as cheering us on, so you want to do them proud," she said.
"It's also a tough journey, especially for the kids who have to relocate, so it's about thinking strategically about how we can support them."
Since her appointment, the code has put in place a First Nations Cultural Council, and last year ran a cultural safety review in collaboration with community.
The review considered the perspectives of the wider netball workforce, including coaches and umpires as well as athletes
Tucker-Munro conceded there are "multi-faceted" barriers to having more elite Indigenous netballers, including financial constraints and geographical barriers to access.
"For too long our voice has been very silent," Tucker-Munro said.
"We're not a homogenous people, so it's really important that we make sure we're hearing the voices of many.
"One thing we're really big on in our community is not to do things for us or to us, you've got to do it with us.
"There's real intent and good will to actually drive some of this change across the sporting landscape of netball in Australia."

PM Modi pitches India as trusted chipmaking hub
Unknown

PM Modi inaugurates SEMICON India 2026 at Yashobhoomi in New Delhi
NEW DELHI: The AI boom is creating demand for new and reliable chip manufacturing hubs, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Thursday, pitching India as a destination building the ecosystem that the global semiconductor industry needs.Inaugurating Semicon India 2026, the PM said AI was changing semiconductor requirements beyond smaller transistors, thereby propelling the importance of chip integration, data movement, heat management and dependable power.PM Narendra Modi said, “Today if you are working on AI, the challenges are not only about what is inside the chip, but also about what is happening around it.”
These included bringing memory closer to processors and connecting multiple chips to function as one system. Modi said AI demand had contributed significantly to the growth of more than 20% in the global semiconductor market over the past two years.“Amid these challenges, what the world now needs most are new and reliable manufacturing locations,” he said, adding that India was preparing itself to meet that need. India had begun the $13.5-billion second phase of its Semiconductor Mission, following up on the $8-billion first phase, Modi said.
Twelve projects had been approved, with the next phase expected to widen participation.He invited equipment manufacturers and suppliers of chemicals, gases and materials to invest, saying India wanted to strengthen domestic supply chains alongside chipmaking. “We want the entire ecosystem to grow together,” he said.He also invited Indian youth conducting research overseas to return to the country to contribute to advanced technology development domestically and urged industry to lead R&D initiatives. The PM identified compound semiconductors and silicon photonics as priorities for AI infrastructure.Govt had introduced reforms allowing international companies to collaborate with Indian startups, design companies and OCIowned companies, he said, while seeking to encourage fabless businesses and domestic intellectual property creation.
PM Modi said India’s chip industry progressed from policy discussions-project announcements to commercial production stages. Indian plants were supplying customers at home and abroad, while production was beginning at two more plants in Mohali and Surat.“It takes decades to build technological capabilities. Wherever semiconductor ecosystems have been built in the world, they have been prepared after decades of effort. But India, with your cooperation, has worked simultaneously on chip design and production, equipment manufacturing, materials ecosystem, testing capability — and has shown success,” he said.“India’s success in this critical industry would strengthen global supply chains,” Modi said arguing that its significance bettered even as supply chains are being weaponised.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 18, 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:16:42 UTC
07:16:42 KST

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 18, 2026
US clears way for $30.9 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia
The US Department of State said on Sept 17 it has approved the potential sale of Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Lightning II fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, as the kingdom is drawn deeper into war in the Middle East.
A sale would mark a significant policy shift from the US, potentially altering the balance of military power in the Middle East and testing Washington’s definition of maintaining its ally Israel’s “qualitative military edge.”
Saudi Arabia made a direct appeal for the jets in early 2025 to US President Donald Trump and has long been interested in Lockheed Martin’s fighter.
The estimated US$24.3 billion (S$30.9 billion) sale would include 48 of the military aircraft and 49 Pratt & Whitney engines along with communications equipment, spare parts and other support items, the State Department said.
Australia cuts migration intake but spares ASEAN students from family visa ban
Migration curbs announced by Australia’s ruling Labor Party on Sept 17 will target international students and working holidaymakers, but a new ban on foreign students bringing family members to the country will not apply to those from ASEAN nations including Singapore.
The exemption is due to the Australian government’s efforts to boost ties with its regional neighbours.
The long-awaited new migration rules, which also target “visa hopping” by international students who switch courses to stay in the country, come as Labor attempts to stem surging support for anti-migrant populist Pauline Hanson.
Russia, China end mandate for independent monitoring of UN sanctions on Iran
Russia and China ended on Sept 17 a United Nations Security Council mandate for the independent monitoring of international sanctions on Iran, reviving their argument that all UN measures on Tehran had been removed under a nuclear deal with world powers.
All UN sanctions on Iran were reimposed a year ago after France, Britain and Germany accused Tehran of violating the 2015 nuclear pact meant to prevent it from developing a nuclear weapon. Iran denies seeking nuclear weapons.
This included the return of an independent panel of experts to monitor and report to the 15-member Security Council on violations and recommend further action. However, the council has been operating without a panel of experts on Iran for the past year because it has been unable to agree on their appointment, a move that must be done by consensus.
Prince Harry makes first public appearances since return to Britain
Prince Harry on Sept 17 made his first public appearance since his shock return to Britain from the United States with his family three weeks ago.
Harry, who quit Britain for California six years ago with his wife Meghan amid tensions with his family, attended a fundraising evening for his Invictus Games for wounded veterans in London.
Dressed in a smoking jacket adorned with his military decorations, the 42-year-old prince took selfies with injured former soldiers at the event. Meghan did not accompany him.
SpaceX discusses buying data for AI models from failed startups
Elon Musk’s SpaceX has held internal discussions about buying customer and operational information from troubled or defunct startups, according to people familiar with the matter, targeting a more affordable data source to improve its artificial intelligence models.
The approach would mirror Google’s offer to purchase business data from Spirit Airlines for AI training purposes after the discount carrier wound down operations. The Alphabet Inc company’s US$10 million (S$12.7 million) bid sparked some data privacy concerns, including from former flight attendants.
The talks within teams inside SpaceXAI, the company’s AI unit, are informal and may not result in a deal, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

Gaza’s Kuwait Specialty Hospital to suspend most services over fuel supply cutoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:14:35 UTC
07:14:35 KST

Lina Altawell, Hosni Nedim
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Kuwait Specialty Hospital in the Gaza Strip said Thursday that it will suspend most of its health services starting Sunday and limit operations to critical emergency cases due to the cutoff of fuel supplies needed to keep the facility running.
The hospital’s administration said in a statement that the decision came after it received an official notification from the World Health Organization (WHO) that fuel supplies to the facility would be halted.
“Services to be suspended include surgeries, deliveries, outpatient clinics, treatment procedures, radiology, laboratory services, ambulance operations and patient transportation,” it said.
The suspension will also cover the dental center, vascular and diabetic foot center, and advanced wound care services, according to the hospital’s administration.
“Operations will be limited to the general emergency and obstetric emergency departments to receive only critical cases,” it said.
The hospital warned that reducing services would deprive thousands of Palestinians each day of treatment and basic health care.
“The decision comes amid a worsening crisis, from shortages of medicines, medical consumables, oil, spare parts and tires, in addition to fuel, threatening to halt electricity generators, ambulances and medical transport vehicles,” the administration said.
The hospital appealed to the international community and international health organizations, particularly the WHO and the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), to intervene to prevent further deterioration of Gaza’s health system.
On Monday, Gaza Health Ministry Director General Munir al-Bursh said the WHO had decided to stop diesel supplies to more than 20 hospitals and health centers in the enclave starting Sept. 19 due to a lack of funding.
The fuel crisis coincides with shortages of oil and spare parts needed to operate hospital generators. The Health Ministry said Sunday that several generators had stopped working in recent days because their operational needs were unavailable.
Generators are the main source of electricity for Gaza hospitals, powering critical departments and medical equipment amid a power outage across the enclave since the start of Israel’s genocidal war in October 2023.
Gaza authorities said shortages of fuel and spare parts are obstructing generator operations and maintenance amid Israel’s closure of the Kerem Shalom crossing since October 2023 and its army’s control of the Rafah crossing with Egypt since May 2024, restricting the entry of essential supplies into the enclave.
Gaza’s Government Media Office has repeatedly said that Israel is failing to meet its obligations under a ceasefire agreement in force since Oct. 10, 2025 regarding the entry of agreed quantities of aid and fuel needed for vital sectors.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000 others in its genocide in Gaza while destroying around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure.

”“When the notification for enforcing the policy came, the student was already in Class VI. Go back and reconsider. Anyway, the academic year will come to an end in a few months. You enforce it for Class VI students from the 2027-28 academic year,” it said.
Bhati agreed to take back the decision for reconsideration. The bench said exempting Class VI students from the policy this year would be without prejudice to CBSE’s right to defend the policy. “The exemption is purely from the aspect of logistics and balance of convenience,” it said.SC said, “There are more contentious issues on what can be considered an indigenous language (Petitioners say English should be considered as one while Centre objects to it) which we will decide later.”It added, “There must be some degree of comfort for the students. Those who would be coming to Class VI next year would know in advance that they must choose languages as per the three-language policy.You can also make it optional for Class VI students with adequate incentives so those who want to conform to the policy can choose to do so.” SC posted the matter for further hearing on Wednesday.

Trinidad and Tobago ends state of emergency amid pushback over mass arrests
Lawyers criticised mass arrests under emergency powers that allowed authorities to detain people without charge.
The Caribbean country of Trinidad and Tobago has ended a state of emergency that granted the government extraordinary powers to combat crime, including the ability to imprison people without charge.
The country’s prime minister told parliament on Wednesday that the government would not extend the state of emergency. One was issued in 2024 and another in 2025, with extensions lengthening both. Instead, the government would seek a “permanent legal framework”.

Putin seizes Russian assets of Auchan, Nestlé and Leroy Merlin

Source: Russian propaganda agency Interfax, citing the text of the decree posted on Russia's official legal information portal
Details: Under the 17 September decree, the assets of international corporations Auchan and Nestlé will be forcibly transferred to the management of the joint-stock company LEV Management. This same entity has also taken control of the assets of logistics operators FM Logistics and Bati Logistics, as well as Le Monlid LLC, the chain formerly known in Russia as Leroy Merlin.
In effect, the Kremlin has carried out a legalised theft of the businesses of international companies that for years have refused to leave the Russian market and continued contributing to the budget of the aggressor state.
According to Russian company registers, LEV Management is a typical shell company. The company was only registered in Moscow in October 2024. Andrei Krayushkin is listed as the company's managing director, but information about its ultimate beneficial owners has not been disclosed, and the company has not conducted any commercial activity.
For reference: Swiss company Nestlé has been operating in Russia since 1994 and owns six large production sites in different parts of the country. The combined revenue of its main Russian legal entities in 2021 amounted to almost 30 billion roubles (about US$355.04 million). The company has withheld its financial data for subsequent years, following the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
French retailer Auchan has operated in Russia since 2002 and currently has 230 stores in 100 cities. Auchan LLC is almost entirely owned by the French company Sogepar.
The French company Leroy Merlin, which had been operating in the Russian market since 2004, also refused to leave the country for a long time. The retailer later changed its name to Lemana Pro and operated a network of 112 stores and 11 fulfilment centres for online orders, known as dark stores. In December 2023, UAE-based Scenari Holding LP acquired a 99.99% stake in the Russian legal entity Le Monlid LLC. The French group Adeo formally retained only 0.007% of the shares.
Background:
- Russian authorities have repeatedly publicly threatened Western countries with the confiscation of their companies' assets, calling it a "reciprocal response" to international sanctions and the freezing of Russian state funds abroad.
- In May 2024, Putin signed a decree allowing US property in Russia to be used to compensate for losses resulting from the seizure of Russian assets.
- In autumn 2025, amid EU decisions to provide loans to Ukraine using proceeds from frozen Russian assets, the Kremlin leader issued a decree that significantly accelerated the procedure for nationalising foreign companies in Russia, reducing the asset valuation period to 10 days. All transactions involving confiscated property were entrusted to Promsvyazbank, which provides banking services to Russia's Defence Ministry.
- Putin himself has previously openly described the use of Russian funds and the detention of commercial vessels linked to Russia as "robbery" and "piracy". He said Russia would be forced to respond in kind to any actions by Western countries by seizing their property.

Russians Vote In First  Parliamentary Election Since 2022 Ukraine Invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:01:52 UTC
07:01:52 KST

Russians cast ballots to choose lawmakers for the State Duma, with the all-out war on Ukraine and a slowing economy looming over the country's first parliamentary elections since the start of the 2022 invasion.
Voters in the Pacific region of Kamchatka, nine time zones ahead of Moscow, kicked off the September 18-20 balloting. Official results on the new composition of the 450-seat lower house of parliament are expected by September 22.
United Russia, the Kremlin-linked party that dominates the Duma as well as legislatures and regional governments nationwide, has been projected to maintain or increase its majority.
Since President Vladimir Putin came to power over a quarter-century ago, the Kremlin has increasingly stifled dissent, marginalized political opponents, and manipulated elections, leaving little room for surprises.
Meanwhile, the only prominent political party opposing the full-scale war, now in its fifth year, was barred from the ballot weeks ahead of the vote.
Amid Kremlin fears of apathy and frustration, Putin, who frequently accuses the West of seeking to weaken or destroy Russia, exhorted Russians to vote, calling the election a barometer of support for the war. More than 1.5 million Russian soldiers have been killed or wounded in the conflict, according to Western estimates.
"Your choice and your will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our troops, that we are a united people bound by shared values, historical memory, and love for the Motherland, and no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us or in undermining our sovereignty or our social-political system," Putin said in a speech released on September 16.
Russian authorities have set up voting precincts in the Russian-occupied portions of five Ukrainian regions that Moscow has claimed as Russian territory. Kyiv has denounced the effort.
While no dramatic changes are expected in the composition of the Duma, the Kremlin and the powerful domestic policymaking body known as the Presidential Administration were expected to watch results for hints of the national mood.
Though opinion polling is difficult inside Russia due to oppressive policies that have criminalized dissent or opposition to the war, several polls have pointed to slipping popularity for Putin, as well as United Russia.
Putin himself won reelection in 2024 in a vote that was seen largely as a foregone conclusion and was marred by evidence of fraud.
A growing number of Russians have grown impatient with the war, the largest in Europe since World War II. Russia's total casualties exceed those the country suffered in all wars Moscow has fought since 1945.
Ukraine's casualties are fewer overall but still staggeringly high.
Military commanders have consistently painted a rosy picture of how Russian troops are performing on the battlefield, and the Kremlin has repeatedly suggested that victory is assured.
Russians are also nervous about the potential for another mobilization, similar to the one Putin ordered in September 2022. That effort, which called up 300,000 men, mostly reservists, stunned Russian society, and led to an exodus of hundreds of thousands of people.
The economy, meanwhile, has downshifted sharply after months of torrid growth fueled by government spending on war-related things like soldiers' salaries, death benefits, and investment in armaments and weaponry.
The Central Bank has struggled to tame inflation running well above expectations.
A wide-ranging Ukrainian drone and missile campaign has caused fuel shortages across the country, and has disrupted the country's largest online retailers.
Russia's fractious and beleaguered opposition has called on people to vote for any candidates espousing an anti-war message.
However, the country's best-known liberal political party, Yabloko, was barred from fielding candidates in the Duma vote on a technicality. Yabloko had embraced an anti-war platform for the campaign, and some polls had indicated a sharp uptick in support.

For a teen with a rare memory condition, the past constantly hijacks the present
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:00:43 UTC
07:00:43 KST

A recent study has found that a teenager with an exceptionally powerful memory for his own life experiences also experiences an unusually high rate of memories popping into his mind without any effort. The research suggests that this exceptional memory ability might be driven by an increased sensitivity to memory triggers in the environment rather than just a general tendency to daydream. The findings were published in Cortex.
Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory is a rare condition where a person can recall past personal events with extreme accuracy and detail. People with this ability can often remember the exact day of the week, the weather, and personal activities for almost any given date in their past. For years, scientists mostly focused on how well adults with this condition could intentionally search their memories when asked a specific question.
However, the current understanding of memory highlights that remembering is not always a deliberate choice. Often, memories come to us involuntarily, sparked by a passing smell, a word, or an emotion. Recent research has started to explore this spontaneous side of remembering. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 demonstrated that this exceptional memory ability can be verified in early adolescence. Building on this, a 2026 case study provided survey-based evidence that a person with this condition experienced a highly elevated rate of involuntary memories popping into their mind.
“People with Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory are remarkably good at retrieving events from their personal past, and their memories are often described as coming to mind very quickly and effortlessly,” said Krystian Barzykowski, a professor at the Institute of Psychology at Jagiellonian University and head of the Applied Memory Research Laboratory in Poland. “Yet most previous research has examined what happens when these individuals are asked to remember, rather than whether memories also enter consciousness spontaneously, without any intention to retrieve them.”
These earlier studies relied primarily on people keeping diaries or answering questionnaires about their own thoughts. The research, led by Barzykowski and his colleagues, aimed to test whether this influx of spontaneous memories holds up under controlled laboratory conditions. The scientists wanted to measure involuntary thoughts objectively in a teenager who reported having this rare memory condition.
“We therefore wanted to know whether exceptional autobiographical memory is also associated with unusually frequent involuntary memories—those everyday moments when something from your past simply ‘pops’ into mind—and, importantly, to measure this experimentally rather than relying only on questionnaires or diaries,” Barzykowski told PsyPost.
The researchers worked with a 16-year-old male from Poland, referred to as KCL, who had contacted them about his unusual memory. He told the scientists that he felt a constant influx of memories in his daily life and could remember events from at least half the days of his life. To verify his abilities, the researchers first gave him a set of standardized memory quizzes.
“I would also emphasize that our participant himself contacted us because he had begun to realize that the way he remembered his life was unusual,” Barzykowski noted. “It is quite possible that some people with unusually strong autobiographical memory do not realize how exceptional their memory is until they begin to reflect on how much of their personal past they can actually retrieve.”
They asked him to recall the exact dates of recent public events and to retrieve verifiable news stories and personal memories from randomly selected calendar dates. For each answer, KCL had to rate how confident he was and whether he felt he was genuinely remembering the event, knowing it as a fact, or just guessing.
His performance was compared against a group of eight typical adults and one matched 16-year-old boy. On a quiz asking for the dates of public events, KCL scored 51 percent, while the comparison group averaged about 20 percent. On a random dates quiz, KCL successfully recalled details for 83 percent of the prompts, far exceeding the comparison group’s average of 29 percent. This confirmed that his abilities were far above average and met the formal criteria for Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory.
“After systematic testing, his performance exceeded established HSAM thresholds on both the Public Dates and Random Dates screening tasks,” Barzykowski said. “This makes the study an interesting example of how an unusual subjective experience can eventually lead to a testable scientific question.”
To test involuntary memories, the researchers used a computer-based vigilance task. KCL and a separate comparison group of 36 young adults watched a continuous stream of horizontal lines on a screen and had to press a button whenever a rare vertical line appeared. The task was designed to be simple but repetitive, allowing the mind a chance to wander.
Throughout this repetitive task, random everyday phrases appeared on the screen as potential memory triggers. At unpredictable moments, the task paused, and the participants were asked to type out exactly what they were thinking about right before the interruption. They also had to rate how focused they were on the task and whether their thoughts were intentional or spontaneous. This method catches thoughts as they happen, reducing the need for people to actively monitor or remember their own daydreams.
The researchers found that KCL’s mind wandered about as often as the people in the comparison group. He also recognized the random phrases at the same rate as the other participants, showing he was paying a normal amount of attention to the screen. However, the content of his wandering mind was remarkably different.
While the comparison group reported that about 39 percent of their wandering thoughts were memories of the past, 87 percent of KCL’s off-task thoughts were involuntary personal memories. This pattern indicates that KCL does not simply have a more distracted or wandering mind in general. Instead, his spontaneous thoughts are heavily biased toward his own past experiences.
“The difference in involuntary remembering was quite striking for a single case,” Barzykowski explained. “Statistically, his frequency of involuntary memories was almost three standard deviations above the comparison-group mean and fell within the extreme upper range.”
“What I found particularly interesting was the selectivity of the effect,” the researcher added. “KCL was not simply having more spontaneous thoughts overall; rather, when his mind moved away from the task, those thoughts were disproportionately memories of his personal past. Even more strikingly, we did not see a corresponding increase in spontaneous thoughts about the future, suggesting that the effect may specifically concern access to stored autobiographical experiences rather than spontaneous cognition in general.”
In additional questionnaires, KCL reported a much higher confidence in his memory abilities than typical people. He scored especially high on an assessment of his episodic memory, which involves recalling specific personal experiences. Yet, he described his actual feeling of remembering, such as the vividness and emotional intensity of his memories, as being quite similar to how the general population experiences memories.
“Another interesting result was that his general subjective phenomenology of remembering was not dramatically unusual,” Barzykowski said. “So HSAM may not necessarily mean that every memory feels fundamentally different; the crucial difference may instead lie in how readily memories become accessible.”
This distinction highlights the difference between how much information a brain stores and how easily it can be retrieved. “One important misconception is that HSAM means having a photographic or infallible memory. It does not,” Barzykowski emphasized. “Our findings concern accessibility—how readily autobiographical information can be retrieved or enter awareness—not perfect accuracy, and previous research shows that people with HSAM can still be susceptible to memory distortions like everyone else.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding this study. Because KCL lived far from the researchers, all tests were conducted remotely over video calls with screen sharing. While the researchers supervised the sessions closely, remote testing offers less control over the physical environment than an in-person laboratory visit.
Additionally, this research focuses on a single individual. The findings highlight a specific pattern of involuntary memory in one teenager, but it remains to be seen if all people with this rare memory ability experience the same frequency of unprompted memories.
“The other major caveat is that this is one individual, so we cannot assume that every person with HSAM will show the same pattern,” Barzykowski noted. “Our results should therefore be viewed as strong evidence about this particular case and as a basis for hypotheses that now need to be tested across additional people with HSAM.”
The study also relied on the participant’s own descriptions of his thoughts to determine what qualified as a personal memory during the computer task. While this is the standard method for measuring spontaneous thoughts, it still requires a degree of personal judgment. Future studies might combine these thought sampling tasks with physiological measurements, such as eye tracking or brain imaging, to better understand how these memories emerge.
Moving forward, the team hopes to explore what lowers the threshold for these memories to surface. “The next step is to determine whether this pattern generalizes across a larger group of people with HSAM,” Barzykowski said. “In particular, we want to understand why autobiographical memories become so accessible: whether incidental cues activate their memories more strongly, whether the threshold for a memory entering consciousness is lower, and whether heightened sensitivity to internal or external cues contributes to this process.”
The study’s authors see extreme cases like KCL’s as a valuable tool for decoding the basic mechanics of memory. “By studying an extreme case of autobiographical accessibility, we may learn more about why some memories spontaneously enter awareness while countless others remain outside consciousness,” Barzykowski told PsyPost.
“So, if you feel that your memory for your own past is exceptionally good—or exceptionally poor—we would be very interested to hear from you and, where possible, to assess your memory scientifically,” he added.
The study, “Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory (HSAM) in a 16-Year-Old Male: Investigating Involuntary Autobiographical Memory With Questionnaire and Laboratory Methods,” was authored by Krystian Barzykowski, Valerio Santangelo, Lia Kvavilashvili, and Chris J. A. Moulin. This work was supported by the European Union’s Horizon research and innovation programme.
