Royal Navy gives no dates for key Hybrid Navy design stages
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
23:00:40 BST
07:00:40 KST

The development timelines for its Type 91 uncrewed missile vessel, Type 94 uncrewed radar platform and new Common Combat Vessel remain unknown, despite all three forming the core of the future system intended to replace the Type 45 destroyers.
Three separate parliamentary questions from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty asked when the Type 91 and Type 94 concept phases would begin and end, and when the initial design stage of the Common Combat Vessel would be completed.
In each case, Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard gave the same answer: “Work on the Type 91-94 and Common Combat Vessel continues. Further detail will be released as appropriate as these programmes develop.”
The answers leave the detailed development schedule unclear, although broader milestones for the Royal Navy’s Hybrid Navy programme have previously been set out.
Current planning assumptions envisage Hybrid Navy capabilities being introduced progressively from the early 2030s, while the Navy has previously said it wants the Common Combat Vessel and wider maritime air defence system to arrive in step with the retirement of the Type 45 fleet from the mid-2030s onwards.
The Government has committed to procuring at least six Common Combat Vessels, which will act as the crewed command and control element of the future distributed air defence force. The ships will work with Type 91 uncrewed missile platforms and Type 94 uncrewed sensor vessels, separating functions currently concentrated aboard a Type 45 destroyer across a network of crewed and autonomous ships.
The Type 91 is intended to contribute missile capacity to the future maritime Integrated Air and Missile Defence system, while the Type 94 will provide distributed sensing. Defence has said the intention is for the Type 91 and Type 94 platforms to operate without crews rather than as lean-crewed or optionally crewed vessels. The Common Combat Vessel would sit at the centre of that network, coordinating the autonomous elements while also carrying personnel responsible for support and maintenance.
There is already an ambition to have a prototype uncrewed missile platform in service by 2030 as part of the first large autonomous vessels entering the fleet. That does not amount to a confirmed service-entry date for the operational Type 91 fleet, with ministers subsequently saying detailed requirements and delivery timelines remain subject to concept and assessment work.
The Common Combat Vessel itself remains at an early stage. In July, Pollard said it was still in the initial stages of design and that different hull forms were being explored.
The programme is intended to replace the earlier plan for a conventional Type 83 destroyer with a more distributed approach to maritime air defence. Rather than putting sensors, weapons and command systems aboard a small number of large warships, the Navy plans to distribute them across a larger mix of crewed and uncrewed vessels.
Further uncertainty also remains over where the Common Combat Vessels will be built. Asked separately this month whether a lead shipyard had been identified, Pollard again said: “Work on the Type 91-94 and Common Combat Vessel continues. Further detail will be released as appropriate as these programmes develop.”

Discovery of mikveh reveals unknown ancient Jewish settlement in southern Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:59:06 UTC
06:59:06 KST

There you are, all set to build a new neighborhood in southern Israel, but a 2,000-year-old ritual bath gets in the way. You don't want to damage a precious artifact, but you do want to expand the gritty city of Kiryat Gat. What to do?
Dig the mivkeh up and move it intact was the solution at the Israel Antiquities Authority, not because mikvehs from the Second Temple period are rare. But this one and other sundry finds are the first indication that there was once a Jewish settlement in what is now Kiryat Gat's Carmei Gat neighborhood, the antiquities authority said Thursday.
The mikveh was found during a salvage excavation by the authority, and it wasn't small. It was 4 meters (13 feet) wide and weighed 25 tons. Removing it was a trial by engineering. It took four IAA conservation experts two weeks to completely expose the buried bath.
"Then, close-knit drilling was carried out underneath it through which steel beams were inserted. This infrastructure strengthened the ancient pool and enabled it to be detached from the ground," the authority says.
To protect the ancient plaster coating the walls, to waterproof them, the conservators applied gauze and adhesives to the ancient stones. The trauma of being lifted out and hauled away could easily damage the plaster, the experts note. Then the entire structure was wrapped in a foam material to help it withstand the jolting.
Ultimately the hero of the day was a 300-ton crane operated under the auspices of the conservators.
Once placed on a wide-load truck, the mikveh was transported in style to the National Treasures Department at nearby Beit Guvrin, next to Beit Guvrin-Maresha National Park. The plan is to put the bath complete with its original plaster back once the new neighborhood has been built, the antiquities authority says. Maybe not exactly, but at least nearby.
The discoveries were a surprise because during the Second Temple/Roman period, Jewish settlements were known to have thronged the Judean Lowlands, but not this stretch. The archaeologists also found measuring vessels made of stone, which are a hallmark of Late Second Temple-era Jewish life.
Under Jewish law, kitchenware and other vessels made of cloth, wood and leather must be ritually cleansed after exposure to contaminants such as swine or human cadavers. And corrupted clay vessels must be destroyed, on the rationale that unglazed clay is porous (which it is) and the filth has penetrated the very matrix of the plate, cup, bowl or platter.
The Jewish sources don't mention stone as a material for household utensils, and evidently they were unaware that limestone is porous too (with porosity of 1 percent to 40 percent, meaning up to 40 percent of the stone can be cavities capable of being filled by fluids). Thus an assumption developed that this material couldn't become ritually impure. Stone dishes therefore became widely used among Jews from about 40 B.C.E. for about 150 years, the archaeologist Shimon Gibson revealed. Stoneware only went out of use after the debacle of the failed Bar Kochba Revolt in 135 C.E.
Now stone vessels have been found in this area of Kiryat Gat, where we didn't know Jews had lived during the Roman period. But clearly they did.
"The Jewish settlement we discovered here is the first and the only known one in this area," the heads of the excavation for the antiquities authority, Elena Kogan-Zahavi, Maayan Margulis and Shira Lifshitz, said in a statement. "In the seam between the Judean Lowlands and the northern Negev, no Jewish settlement was known until now."
The Bar Kochba Revolt ended more than the penchant for stoneware. It also ended this settlement in the northern Negev in the south, the archaeologists deduce. The place would only be resettled about 500 years later when the Negev's more habitable areas became the home of farming communities in the Byzantine period, most likely because the more hospitable areas had become densely populated.
Note that this isn't the first time an ancient mikveh has been moved so it could be preserved. In 2020, a mikveh at Kibbutz Hanaton in the Galilee was also dug out and moved – to save it from becoming the foundation of a new intersection. There was never a plan to return it to its home, now the middle of a road. It's nearby at the kibbutz.

Trump hails 'major progress' in setting up US base in Poland
September 17, 2026
US President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that significant progress had been made toward establishing a US military base in Poland.
"Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
In August, Warsaw revealed that it was in talks with Washington regarding a permanent US military presence in Poland.
"If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance," Trump added in a social media post.
His announcement comes despite his administration's launch of a formal review of its military presence in Europe. This has raised fears among allies that the US could reduce its military presence there.
How did Warsaw react?
Nawrocki, who is a conservative ally of the US president, thanked Trump on X, saying Poland was "ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defense cooperation."
He added, "I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base."
Meanwhile, Zbigniew Bogucki, the head of the Polish president's chancellery, called Trump's announcement "great news for Poland." He also noted that it came on the 87th anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Poland.
In August, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said his country was discussing with the United States the possibility of establishing a permanent US base on its territory.
"We have already completed the initial stage of the process, not to mention the political will, which was expressed long ago," Zalewski told the public broadcaster TVP.
Poland secures NATO's eastern flank
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been pushing for a larger allied presence on NATO's eastern flank.
Nearly 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in Poland, a member of both NATO and the EU. However, they are there almost exclusively on a rotational basis.
Poland's proximity to Ukraine and Russia is a key factor in its security strategy. The country allocates approximately 5% of its gross domestic product to defense spending and has been working to increase the United States' military presence.
In the meantime, Washington heavily criticized several European countries for refusing to allow US forces to use NATO bases in its war with Iran.

Thousands are starving in occupied Oleshky. People have no food, no way out, and Russian forces bomb incoming aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:54:12 UTC
06:54:12 KST

Oleshky, a Ukrainian city under Russian occupation in Kherson Oblast, is facing a severe humanitarian crisis, with more than 6,000 people, including around 200 children, potentially trapped there, according to Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets.
Civilians are going without food, drinking water, medicine, and other basic necessities while facing daily shelling and drone attacks, Lubinets said.
The crisis has become so desperate that some residents are trying to escape on their own without waiting for an organized evacuation, crossing mined fields because they see no other way out. They risk being killed by mines or Russian drones, but are attempting to leave because staying in Oleshky has become even more dangerous.
“People need to be saved,” Lubinets said, describing the city as a “death trap.”
Thousands remain trapped
Lubinets said his office has received 176 appeals concerning the humanitarian situation in the temporarily occupied territories of Kherson Oblast and has verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to safely leave the area.
He stressed that these are only people his office has managed to identify. Based on the population of Oleshky and the surrounding area, more than 6,000 people may still remain there, including around 200 children, he said.
The civilians remaining in the city are effectively in a “gray zone,” according to Lubinets. They face daily shelling and drone attacks while lacking food, drinking water, medicine, and other essential assistance.
“The stories make your blood run cold. And so there is only one task — to get our people out of this deadly danger,” Lubinets said.
“There is real hunger there”
Other reporting indicates that the shortages have persisted for months. According to Kherson Regional Military Administration head Oleksandr Prokudin, food deliveries to Oleshky have almost completely stopped, while Russian forces prevent residents from evacuating.
Natalia Soboleva, an Odesa volunteer who tracks the situation in Oleshky, told Espreso that residents are gathering grass and searching through destroyed basements for food.
“There is hunger there, real hunger,” she said.
The blockade has also affected humanitarian efforts. Soboleva said Russian forces attacked humanitarian vehicles attempting to bring food and water into the city. During the latest reported attempt on 1 September, Russian troops shelled four volunteer vehicles.
The crisis in Oleshky has been independently documented by international organizations and media. The UN, Human Rights Watch and the OSCE have all reported severe shortages of food and medical care, dangerous conditions for civilians, and restrictions on humanitarian aid and evacuation.
International monitors confirm Russia’s blockade of occupied Oleshky, where the living starve and the dead go unburied
Russia has not confirmed evacuation, so civilians risk mines to escape
The ombudsman said some people are now trying to leave independently. They are crossing mined areas despite the risk of being killed by a mine or targeted by a drone because they do not see another way to escape.
This desperation has also been documented by Human Rights Watch, which said there is no organized evacuation route from Oleshky and that people attempting to leave face Russian military checkpoints and a dangerous journey through occupied territory.
Lubinets said Ukraine has been pressing for an organized humanitarian evacuation.
Ukraine and Russia had previously reached agreements and established clear procedures for such a mission, he said. Lubinets also secured the International Committee of the Red Cross’ readiness to participate within its mandate.
Ukraine prepared a list of people for evacuation and coordinated with its Security and Defense Forces to establish a ceasefire during the humanitarian mission.
But Russia has not confirmed its readiness to carry out the evacuation, according to Lubinets.
Mined in, starved out, hunted from above—life in the towns Russia demands at the peace table
Months ago, he said, he informed international organizations, including the United Nations and the ICRC headquarters in Geneva, about the critical situation and called for assistance to prevent mass deaths.
Lubinets said his office continues to collect and verify information and coordinate with the ICRC, international organizations and Ukrainian authorities. It is also continuing to press Russia for an urgent evacuation of civilians remaining in Oleshky.
The situation is difficult to independently verify because Oleshky is under Russian occupation and access to the city is severely restricted. But reports of the humanitarian crisis have been corroborated by the UN, Human Rights Watch, the OSCE and other international organizations, as well as Ukrainian and international media.

====================================================================================================

Experts warn of growing threats as England's salmon stocks hit record low
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:46:59 CST
06:46:59 KST

LONDON, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Atlantic salmon in England are facing growing pressures both in rivers and at sea, British scientists warned on Thursday, as stocks fall to their lowest level on record amid deteriorating freshwater habitats and increasingly hazardous marine conditions.
The latest Atlantic Salmon Stock Assessment shows that 95 percent of England's principal salmon rivers are now below the level needed to sustain their populations, the highest proportion on record.
The assessment was produced by the Environment Agency (EA), the Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science and Natural Resources Wales.
The scale of the decline is particularly evident in the number of salmon returning from the sea. According to the EA, 15 to 20 out of every 100 young salmon that migrated to sea would once return as adults. Now, only one or two do.
The agency said salmon face pressures throughout their life cycle, ranging from pollution, migration barriers and water scarcity in freshwater habitats to aquaculture and bycatch at sea, with climate change intensifying many of these threats.
In rivers, the EA identified water quantity, water quality and damaged habitat as key pressures.
Charles Tyler, professor of environmental biology and toxicology at the University of Exeter, told Xinhua that it was extremely difficult to attribute the decline to any single factor, but said pollution was likely to be an important contributor because salmon depend heavily on clean water to survive and reproduce.
"This is the very sad face of where we are in the UK with most of our salmon rivers," Tyler said.
He said even where pollution was not directly toxic to returning salmon, it could disrupt their sense of smell, which they rely on heavily to return to their natal spawning grounds. Pollution such as eutrophication could also damage spawning beds.
The decline, however, is not confined to rivers. The EA said similar trends are being seen across the North Atlantic, with much of the pressure occurring at sea and beyond the control of any single country.
"Life on the high seas during salmon migrations has always been very risky, but those risks have multiplied over time as the sea has become more overcrowded, overexploited and polluted," Callum Roberts, professor of marine conservation at the University of Exeter, told Xinhua.
Tyler also pointed to pressures on wild fish stocks at sea. He said he suspected that too many salmon were being harvested at sea, citing the scale and technology of modern fishing vessels.
"These figures are stark," EA Chief Executive Philip Duffy said. "Recovery requires collective action."
The EA said it is tackling pollution and illegal water abstraction, restoring rivers and wetlands, and removing barriers that prevent salmon from reaching spawning grounds.
Under commitments running to 2032, the agency also plans to restore peatland, remove barriers to salmon migration and restore habitats along principal salmon rivers. ■

4 obstacles threaten return of displaced Syrians: UN official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:46:49 CST
06:46:49 KST

UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs Tom Fletcher (C) speaks at a Security Council meeting at the UN headquarters in New York, Sept. 17, 2026. Tom Fletcher said Thursday that continued displacement, localized insecurity, regional escalation and landmines are threatening the return of displaced Syrians. (Manuel Elias/UN Photo/Handout via Xinhua)
UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs Tom Fletcher said Thursday that continued displacement, localized insecurity, regional escalation and landmines are threatening the return of displaced Syrians.
More than 2 million internally displaced Syrians and 1.8 million refugees have returned home voluntarily since December 2024. This historic wave of return, the highest in Syria in decades, is a profound sign of hope, Fletcher told the Security Council.
However, 5.5 million people inside Syria have not yet returned, nearly 800,000 of them still in camps. And currently only 18 percent of Syrians outside the country say that they plan to return home in the coming year, he said.
"Without homes, schools or clean water, today's returnees risk becoming tomorrow's displaced," said Fletcher.
A second challenge is localized insecurity.
Attacks by the Islamic State in eastern and northeastern Syria, along with sporadic violence, rebuilding challenges and bureaucratic hurdles, threaten lasting peace. True stability is not possible until every community, most crucially Syria's women, is fully integrated in the nation's political and economic fabric, he said.
The escalation of tension across the region means maritime choke points, disrupted supply chains, reduced humanitarian access and even greater economic pressure on Syrian families, he said.
With disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz, and now to Bab al-Mandab, higher fuel and transport costs will increase the prices of food, medicines and other essential goods for families already struggling, he warned.
Landmines are making recovery efforts a lethal gamble, said Fletcher.
Since December 2024, explosive ordnance has killed 880 people, including 269 children, and maimed 1,616 more, nearly 40 percent of them children. Mines block the fields, orchards and grazing lands that families need to feed themselves, he said. "You cannot build an economy over a minefield."
Fletcher said there is a need to invest in the transition out of humanitarian need and toward reconstruction and growth, to remove the obstacles standing between recovery and development, and to invest the political capital needed to keep Syria out of regional conflict.
"Syrians have endured enough. They are making progress that has defied many who predicted or wished it impossible. Let us also meet this moment," said Fletcher. ■

(Manuel Elias/UN Photo/Handout via Xinhua)

Fighting has raged fiercely since Wednesday across the Kahbub mountain area and surrounding heights in the southern province of Lahj, where Houthi fighters launched a renewed push against government defensive positions, a Yemeni government military official told Xinhua.

At least 25 Houthi fighters were killed and several others wounded, he said, adding that repeated strikes had made it increasingly difficult to evacuate casualties from the mountainous battlefield.
The battle remained fluid on Thursday, with several commanding heights changing hands during repeated attacks and counterattacks. Neither side had secured a decisive breakthrough, according to the two officials.
Both sides have sent additional fighters, weapons and military vehicles into the area, raising the prospect of further heavy fighting for control of positions overlooking approaches to Bab al-Mandab.
The latest fighting follows major Houthi gains along Yemen's southwestern Red Sea coast earlier this month. Wildfire impact in Greece goes beyond burned area: expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:46:40 CST
06:46:40 KST

ATHENS, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- As Greece enters the latter part of its wildfire season, Elias Tziritis, wildfires actions coordinator at WWF Greece, said a growing challenge is not only how much land burns, but which areas are affected and whether they are hit repeatedly.
"The ecological footprint should no longer be measured solely by how many hectares are burned," Tziritis told Xinhua on Wednesday, "We also need to consider which areas are being burned and whether they are being affected repeatedly. In such cases, the ecological footprint is greater."
According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), about 33,524 hectares had burned in Greece by Sept. 9. Greek Minister of State Akis Skertsos said the figure was 30.1 percent below the average of the previous 20 years.
Tziritis said the figure alone could not capture the ecological impact of wildfires, adding that repeated fires can leave Mediterranean ecosystems with too little time to regenerate naturally.
"When an area burns repeatedly within a very short period of time, Mediterranean vegetation does not have the opportunity to naturally regenerate," he said. "This raises concerns about the restoration and recovery of the forest."
He pointed to Porto Germeno, a seaside resort about 60 km west of Athens, as one example. Around 11,300 hectares were burned there this summer, including about 3,500 hectares that had already burned in recent years.
Repeatedly burned areas may require particular protection compared with forested areas that have not yet been affected by fire, said Tziritis.
The expert also said wildfires have increasingly affected large mountain ecosystems in northern Greece, adding that similar challenges are being observed in other Mediterranean countries, including Spain.
"We are seeing that wildfires are becoming increasingly intense," he said, adding that although the absolute number of wildfires may be declining, their intensity is increasing.
Previous assessments have also highlighted the impact of repeated fires. A review by WWF Greece and the FLAME Fire Meteorology Group released last November found that more than 13,000 hectares in Greece had burned twice within less than 20 years.
Greece's official wildfire prevention season runs from May 1 to Oct. 31. With the season still underway, Tziritis said burned area remains an important measure, but the condition of affected ecosystems and their ability to recover also need to be taken into account. ■

In July, U.S. share prices edged lower following strong gains earlier in the year, while long-term U.S. interest rates ticked up and the U.S. dollar depreciated against the Canadian dollar, Statistics Canada said. (1 Canadian dollar = 0.71 U.S. dollar) ■

UN Tourism lowers 2026 global international arrivals growth forecast to 1-2 pct

06:46:17 KST

MADRID, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- UN Tourism on Thursday lowered its forecast for growth in global international tourist arrivals in 2026 to between 1 percent and 2 percent, from the 3-4 percent projected in January, as conflict in the Middle East and rising travel costs weigh on momentum.
The latest edition of the World Tourism Barometer showed that international tourist arrivals rose by just 0.4 percent year-on-year in the first half of 2026. Around 690 million tourists travelled internationally during the period, about 3 million more than a year earlier.
International arrivals increased by 2 percent in the first quarter, but fell by 1 percent in the second quarter. In June alone, arrivals declined by 3 percent year-on-year.
Africa recorded a 4-percent increase in international arrivals in the first six months of the year, followed by Europe with 3 percent and the Americas with 2 percent. Arrivals in Asia and the Pacific rose by 1 percent, but remained 11 percent below 2019 levels.
The Middle East saw international arrivals decline by 22 percent as conflict directly affected the region, according to the report.
UN Tourism Secretary-General Shaikha Al Nuwais said: "The latest data shows a sector absorbing real pressure and finding a way forward. Tourism has not stopped growing, but that growth is fragile. The Middle East situation has touched destinations far beyond the region itself and serves as a clear reminder that, in such a connected world, resilience needs to be built everywhere and not just when a crisis begins."
UN Tourism said its revised outlook would depend on the duration of the conflict and its impact on oil prices and overall inflation.
High prices and uncertainty are expected to keep travellers focused on value for money, with many likely to choose destinations closer to home or opt for domestic travel, the report said. ■

Finland's economy to grow 1.7 pct in 2026 due to exports, investment: institutes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:46:11 CST
06:46:11 KST

HELSINKI, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Finland's economy is expected to grow 1.7 percent this year, two Finnish economic research institutes said Thursday, as stronger exports and investment support the recovery, while high unemployment and rising public debt remain major challenges.
The Research Institute of the Finnish Economy (Etla) forecast gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 1.7 percent in 2026, accelerating to 1.9 percent next year before slowing to 1.4 percent in 2028.
Labore, another Finnish economic research institute, also raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.7 percent, up 0.8 percentage points from its spring estimate. It expects growth of 1.6 percent in 2027 and 1.5 percent in 2028.
Both institutes identified exports and investment as key growth drivers.
Etla expects Finnish exports to grow by 3.7 percent this year and 3 percent next year, supported by strong industrial order books, improved cost competitiveness and shipbuilding deliveries. Labore forecasts export growth of 4.7 percent this year.
Etla expects investment to rise by 5.4 percent this year and by more than 9 percent in 2027. Public investment is providing much of the boost this year, particularly through fighter jet procurement, while private investment is expected to take the lead next year, partly driven by major data center projects announced by Google earlier.
Private consumption is also recovering. Etla expects it to grow by 1.3 percent this year, although higher interest rates, living costs and continued household saving are limiting the rebound.
The labor market is expected to recover more slowly. Etla forecasts the unemployment rate at 10.5 percent this year before a gradual decline, while Labore puts it at 10.4 percent. Both expect employment conditions to improve as growth continues.
External risks remain significant. Etla Chief Economist Jenni Paakkonen said the Middle East conflicts have pushed up prices and costs and prompted a monetary policy response from the European Central Bank. Etla's forecast assumes that traffic through the Strait of Hormuz will return closer to pre-war levels in the coming years.
Etla warned that a faster-than-expected rise in interest rates, an escalation of geopolitical crises or the outbreak of new ones could weaken growth below its forecast.
Despite the improved growth outlook, both institutes warned that Finland's public finances remain under heavy pressure.
Labore expects public debt to reach 94.5 percent of GDP by 2028. Etla said the debt-to-GDP ratio will exceed 90 percent this year and shows no sign of stabilizing.
Etla Managing Director Aki Kangasharju called for measures to strengthen public finances, while stressing the need to invest in productivity and long-term growth. ■

Uganda breaks ground for 320-million-liter petroleum storage terminal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:46:10 CST
06:46:10 KST

KAMPALA, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Uganda on Thursday started construction of a 320-million-liter petroleum storage terminal in the central district of Mpigi, as the country seeks to strengthen fuel security and supplies to domestic and regional markets.
Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni presided over the groundbreaking ceremony for the over-300-mln-USD Kampala Storage Terminal, which is being developed by the Uganda National Oil Company (UNOC), the state-owned company responsible for the country's petroleum supply.
The terminal will more than double Uganda's current estimated petroleum storage capacity of 160 million liters, which includes both public and private facilities, according to a statement issued by State House.
Museveni said adequate storage infrastructure was critical as Uganda develops its petroleum sector and works to improve the security and efficiency of fuel supplies.
He said government intervention had helped reduce the cost of petroleum products, adding that the country must now plan for adequate strategic reserves.
"Now that we are moving well on developing our resources, we must plan for storage," he said.
The president said the new terminal should not be considered the final solution to Uganda's storage requirements, stressing the need for larger facilities to meet future demand.
Minister of Energy and Mineral Development Monica Musenero said the terminal would serve as a strategic storage hub and strengthen Uganda's petroleum supply chain.
"We welcome the commitment by UNOC to complete the project within 24 months, and the ministry will support the successful implementation of this project," Musenero said.
She called for improved road connectivity to the terminal, particularly its link to the Mpigi Expressway, as well as the development of railway infrastructure to facilitate the transportation of petroleum products. ■

The Kennedy Center closed on Wednesday and will remain closed for at least seven days to assess what its executive director Matt Floca called “acute risks to public safety” from structural deterioration. The legal dispute follows Judge Cooper’s earlier rulings that blocked efforts to add Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center without congressional approval.

US set to approve 10 Patriot interceptors for Ukraine from Germany, records show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:38:56 UTC
06:38:56 KST

The United States is poised to approve the transfer to 10 Patriot interceptor missiles from Germany to Ukraine, according to U.S. congressional records dated Sept. 15.
The news comes as Ukraine faces a critical shortage of Patriot air defense munitions, the only weapons reliably capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles.
Germany will soon transfer to Ukraine 10 MIM–104E GEM–T Patriot interceptor missiles valued at $29.6 million, the U.S. State Department said in its notification to Congress.
While the supplies will come from Germany, the U.S. Arms Export Control Act requires Congress to review transfers of American weapons to third countries if the initial cost of the materiel exceeds $14 million.
As long as Congress does not pass a joint resolution banning the re-export of the weapons, the transfer will automatically be authorized.
"This transfer is consistent with U.S. security assistance objectives," the State Department said in the notification. "The United States government is prepared to authorize this transfer, having taken into account political, military, economic, human rights, and arms control considerations."
read also
Earlier in September, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said that Berlin was prepared to to provide Ukraine with additional supplies of PAC-2 interceptors for Patriot systems, as well as other air defense munitions.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said at the time that Germany's decision would "bring peace closer."
The GEM-T Patriot missile represents an upgrade of the PAC-2, equipping the interceptorwith a new fuse and systems that improve its radar sensitivity. It is most effective against drones and cruise missiles, while the more modern PAC-3 interceptor — designed with "hit-to-kill" precision targeting technology — remain the best defense against ballistic missiles.
Ukraine relies on the U.S.-made Patriot air defense system to repel Russia's increasingly frequent and deadly mass combined attacks against major cities.
Under U.S. President Donald Trump, Washington ended large-scale defense funding and delivery of U.S. military aid to Ukraine, leaving Kyiv to rely on support from other partners to obtain key weapons systems.
Patriot interceptors have been even harder to come by as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has diverted supplies to the Middle East.

Trump administration approves sale of F-35 jets to Saudi Arabia

Trump administration approves sale of F-35 jets to Saudi Arabia
The deal, which still needs approval from Congress, comes as Riyadh seeks Washington’s help in its war with Yemen’s Houthis.
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has asked lawmakers to clear the sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia for an estimated $24.3bn.
“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a major non-NATO ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region,” the State Department said in a statement on Thursday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

- list 2 of 3Saudi Arabia promises to respond to Houthi attacks ‘firmly’
- list 3 of 3Five killed as Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis trade attacks
The administration said the sale of the jets, the most advanced fighter aircraft the US has, would “not alter the military balance in the region” in keeping with longstanding US policy that Israel must have a military edge over potential regional adversaries.
The announcement comes after the Houthis in Yemen claimed on Wednesday they shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over Marib, a key city in their battle against Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces. The group released video of fighters in the city standing before burning wreckage of what appeared to be a US-made F-15 fighter jet with Saudi Arabian markings.
The Houthis claim the aircraft was shot down with a “locally made” surface-to-air missile, which would mark a dramatic change in the group’s ability to wage war in the area. Until now, Saudi Arabia’s military has enjoyed relative air superiority in Yemen, and has relied heavily on its ability to carry out air strikes in the neighbouring country.
Intensifying fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis reportedly killed at least five people, including three children, on Thursday.
Saudi Arabia has unsuccessfully sought to have Washington play a more direct role in the kingdom’s conflict with Houthi forces. The US has said it will not directly intervene in the conflict between the Iran-backed Houthis, Saudi Arabia, and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
Chinese concerns
Washington also has concerns about potential Chinese espionage related to the jets.
The New York Times reported this week that US intelligence analysts have raised the possibility that Beijing could acquire F-35 technology through its partnerships with Riyadh.
US congressional Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democratic member of the House Intelligence Committee, expressed opposition to the sale on those grounds.
The deal should not go ahead “when our own intelligence community is warning that it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party,” Krishnamoorthi said in a statement.
Saudi Arabia signed a mutual defense agreement, dubbed the Mecca Agreement, with Pakistan and Turkiye last month, a sign the countries are seeking ways to provide for mutual defence that relies less on Washington.
Saudi Arabia has long sought to buy F-35s, but officials from Israel – the only country in the region with the fighter jets – have voiced concern about their sale to Riyadh despite a push for the kingdom to normalise relations. Turkiye, a NATO member that took part in a multi-country development of the F-35 jets, has been barred from receiving the aircraft since 2019 after it purchased anti-aircraft missiles from Russia.

China’s Djibouti base upgrades should boost its monitoring reach, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:38:14 UTC
06:38:14 KST

China’s Djibouti base upgrades should boost its monitoring reach, report says
- China has upgraded its military base in Djibouti with new antennas and satellite equipment to enhance monitoring of military activity across the Middle East and Africa.
- The base improvements enable better communication between Chinese forces in the region and headquarters in China, strengthening intelligence and command capabilities.
- The Djibouti base, opened in 2017 near a vital maritime chokepoint, supports China’s expanding naval presence and offers potential insights into other countries’ military operations nearby.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – China has made upgrades to its military base at Djibouti that should significantly enhance its ability to monitor military activity across the Middle East and Africa, a report by an American think-tank released on Sept 17 said.
Washington’s Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) said commercial satellite imagery showed that China’s military had installed new antennas, satellite communications equipment and other assets at its only formally acknowledged overseas military base.
Conflicts involving the Houthis, Iran, the United States and Israel have brought substantial military activity into the region, increasing the potential value of intelligence collection from the base, the report said.
CSIS said two new communications compounds that had appeared at the base since mid-2024 likely form part of a broader intelligence and military command architecture, and would strengthen communications between Chinese forces operating in the Middle East and Africa and military headquarters in China.
“The type and orientation of the base’s new equipment is varied, enabling transmission and detection across a wide range of signals and frequencies,” the report said.
The facilities would provide China with “a much more robust picture of the operating environment in the region”, the report said.
China’s Washington embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.
The report said the base in Djibouti opened in 2017 and serves as a key hub for Chinese naval operations in the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea. The facility sits near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important choke points for maritime trade.
“The base’s capabilities have continued to evolve over time to enable increasingly sophisticated operations, helping the PLAN establish a growing foothold in the region,” the report said, referring to China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy.
It said the facilities would likely enable the Chinese military to monitor the activities of other militaries operating nearby, although it was not possible to determine whether they were actively intercepting communications.
The report said the US, France, Italy and Japan all operate bases less than 16km from China’s.
It said China could potentially derive useful information even from encrypted military communications and “draw valuable insights into US and other militaries’ operations by observing the direction, origin, frequency, and pace of their signals”.
It said the facility could support Chinese efforts to expand its footprint in Africa, where Beijing has steadily increased both economic and security engagement. REUTERS

Netanyahu to take UN podium while Palestinian leader again denied visa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:31:00 UTC
06:31:00 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over war crimes committed in Gaza, is set to take the podium at the U.N. General Assembly next week, while the U.S. again denied Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas a visa to travel to New York.
As last year, Abbas, a regular at the U.N. General Assembly, will address the body of global leadership by video. The U.N. General Assembly voted Thursday overwhelmingly, 152 votes to three, for the Palestinian leader to be able to appear virtually once again this year.
Palestinian leaders rejected and condemned the move by the United States, Palestinian U.N. envoy Riyad Mansour told the General Assembly.
Under a 1947 U.N. "headquarters agreement," the U.S. is required to allow access for foreign diplomats to the U.N. in New York. However, the U.S. has prevented Abbas and his delegation from traveling for two consecutive years.
As it did during the era of Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) leader Yasser Arafat, Washington has used its status as the U.N. host country to exert political pressure, imposing severe restrictions on visas, transit permits and the size of Palestinian delegations.
In 1988, the U.S. denied a visa to then-Palestinian leader Arafat when he sought to address the U.N. General Assembly.
While a leader accused by the ICC of "using starvation as a method of warfare and deliberately targeting civilians" is given a place at the U.N. podium, the host country is denying the same opportunity to the legitimate Palestinian leader whose people are being killed.
The U.S. decision comes as violence by Israeli occupiers and by forces against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has escalated in recent months.
Israel, which has occupied the West Bank since 1967, has stepped up illegal land seizures of Palestinian land, while violence has intensified since October 2023.
Netanyahu to address U.N. General Assembly
The ICC issued arrest warrants in late November 2024 for Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.
Israel's genocidal campaign has killed more than 73,820 people in the Palestinian enclave since October 2023.
The warrants, issued following an application by the ICC prosecutor's office, constitute a binding obligation for more than 120 countries that are parties to the Rome Statute.
The U.S., which hosts U.N. headquarters, however, is not a party to the Rome Statute and is hosting in New York a suspect wanted by the international court.
Netanyahu is therefore set to address the U.N. General Assembly this year, as he did last year.
Dozens of diplomats walked out of the U.N. General Assembly hall as Netanyahu took the podium during the September 2025 session, leaving much of the chamber empty during his speech.
Outside, demonstrators opposed attacks on Gaza gathered in Times Square to protest Netanyahu and Israel.
This year, diplomats from several countries are again expected to stage a diplomatic boycott by walking out during Netanyahu's speech, while mass protests are also expected across New York.
The contrasting treatment in New York has also raised questions about the Western world's frequently invoked concept of a "rules-based international order."
Western governments, including the U.S., have faced criticism for refusing to recognize ICC decisions involving Netanyahu, despite having previously used mechanisms ranging from intelligence sharing to pressure on third countries to support efforts to enforce the ICC warrant against Russian President Vladimir Putin over the Ukraine war.
Civil society organizations including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have repeatedly called for Netanyahu, who is subject to an ICC warrant, to be arrested.
Alongside the ICC proceedings, Türkiye has also sought to activate international mechanisms against those responsible for crimes in Gaza, taking concrete steps toward having an Interpol Red Notice issued for Netanyahu and other officials.
A Red Notice potentially exposes a wanted individual to arrest across Interpol's 196 member countries, restricting Netanyahu's freedom of movement and leaving him with only a limited number of routes where he has specific diplomatic assurances.
The ICC warrants, however, have not been enforced in practice, with critics attributing what they describe as double standards among Western countries that are parties to the Rome Statute.
During his trips to the U.S., Netanyahu has flown through the airspace of Rome Statute parties France, Italy and Greece despite the court's warrant, with those countries failing to fulfill their obligations toward the ICC.
Netanyahu's visit to Hungary in April 2025 also took place with a special guarantee from the government of then-Prime Minister Viktor Orban that he would not be arrested.
Netanyahu's aircraft is reportedly set to land at Newark Airport in New Jersey rather than at an airport in New York.
Asked whether the ICC arrest warrant would be enforced if Netanyahu came to New York for the U.N. General Assembly meetings in September, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said: "Whatever the law allows me to do in New York City, that's what we will do, but we won't be writing our own laws to that end."
"I believe that Prime Minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague. He's a war criminal who has been charged by the International Criminal Court," Mamdani said.

What the China-Nepal floods teach us about crisis communication

Opinion
What the China-Nepal floods teach us about crisis communication
In an unfolding disaster, families need quick, practical updates and journalists need access the moment safety allows
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Bernard Chan, born in 1965, is a Hong Kong businessman. 
The Himalayan disaster that tore through the China-Nepal border last month was a human calamity before it became a media story. A torrent of ice, rock, mud and debris swept through valleys, destroying key infrastructure, severing roads and communications, and leaving families desperate for news.
In Gyirong county in the Tibet autonomous region, the disaster hit a major border crossing and created a rescue environment as physically difficult as any imaginable. The human toll extends beyond the confirmed dead. With people unaccounted for and recovery work continuing, families on both sides of the border are still waiting for answers.
In terrain like this, uncertainty is unavoidable. Rescue operations were hampered by unstable slopes, damaged roads and difficult conditions in a narrow gorge, delaying the arrival of heavy machinery. Those constraints also restricted the flow of information from the area in the first few days.

No timeframe for more possible rate rises in Japan
The Governor of the Bank of Japan Ueda Kazuo is addressing the media in Japan about the decision to lift interest rates to 1.25%, a new 31-year high.
He has faced multiple questions from the press about whether more rate hikes are coming, and said there isn't a "specific timeframe".
Today's rise follows an increase in June, marking the fastest pace of rate hikes since 1990.
But while it was widely anticipated, the decision to raise wasn't unanimous, with two board members voting to keep the policy unchanged, which has raised some concern in the market.
The yen slid despite the rate increase.
Mr Ueda said they would decide on the future pace of rate hikes "while considering developments in the Middle East, the expansion of AI, and exchange rates".
"With inflation now approaching 2%, we will maintain that level to ensure sustained stability," he told reporters.
" We do not have a specific timeframe, such as three months, in mind for the future pace of rate hikes."
He said the bank would work to anchor inflation at 2% and based on that "discuss and decide" the pace of any rises at each meeting.
He was also asked about decisions by other central banks around the world to also raise rates, and said he hadn't spoken to them, but would be interested in their reasoning.
The press conference is continuing.
Bathla collapse points to a ‘flight to quality’, Built Living CEO says
The collapse of property developer Bathla highlights the risks of developments operating too close to the financial edge, according to Built Living chief executive Dale Connor.
Asked what the Bathla collapse showed about the industry, Connor said developers and builders needed strong financial backing to withstand movements in construction costs.
"You still need quality builders. You still need quality developers that are financially sound and backed by, backed by strong investment, getting onto the very edge of delivery, quality funding and, and and investment that, that that always provides the risk of if there's movement in cost, then the whole thing can, can fall apart.
"So I think that there is a flight to quality that comes out of it."
Connor said the collapse also fed into the case for moving more construction into controlled factory environments.
"I I think it also lends to this conversation around being able to do more off site modern methods of construction designed for manufacturing assembly where the quality is sort of almost guaranteed.
"Indeed it's in a factory environment as opposed to loose in the field."

Rapid house price growth
The feedback from the Senate Standing Committee hearing with RBA is truely enlightening. How any country’s house prices could rise 50%+ in a 6 yr period, off what I would consider an already inflated base, suggests monetary and fiscal policy were fundamentally flawed. External shocks acknowledged (COVID/Middle East), it seems we always wait until there is a crisis before governments act. Migration settings, taxation, interest rates etc.
- Peter
Thanks Peter,
It's easy to forget, but at the start of 2020, before the COVID pandemic hit Australia, the cash rate target was already sitting at just 0.75%.
At the time, the Herald's economics editor Ross Gittins wrote an article with this headline: RBA should stop pretending there is any more it can usefully do.
A cash rate of 0.75% is exceptionally low, but at the time, inflation was still struggling to rise above 2%.
But then COVID hit in early 2020, and the RBA slashed the cash rate target to just 0.1%, and Philip Lowe suggested that it could stay at 0.1% for years if that's what it was going to take to get wages growing again. And that set a fire under house prices. We're still living with the fallout from that period.
It would be fascinating to see what the RBA would do if it had that time again. Maybe it would behave exactly the same. Maybe it would do things differently. Who knows?
At any rate, Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis (formerly RBA assistant governor) recently made the point that Australian house prices actually started to rise much faster than household incomes decades ago, in the late 1990s, after the banking system had been deregulated and once inflation, and interest rates, both started to decline after the early 90s recession.
"A lot of the increase in house prices to household income has been a multi-decade consequence of lower inflation and financial deregulation that happened some decades ago," she said.

Trump officials move to dismantle key protection for US endangered species
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:28:15 UTC
06:28:15 KST

More than 1,600 critically imperiled species protected under the US Endangered Species Act (ESA) face losing further federal protections following a new reinterpretation of the 1973 law by the Donald Trump administration.
A September 14 memo distributed to Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) field offices by FWS director Brian Nesvik calls for a reinterpretation of what it means to “take” an endangered species. Under the ESA, “take” is defined as “to harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or to attempt to engage in any such conduct”.
The memo, obtained and shared by the Center for Biological Diversity, reinterprets the law to mean that harming or killing an endangered animal would no longer be considered illegal unless the action was specifically intended to cause harm or death.
“A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it, because the vessel’s course was not set against the whale,” the memo said, adding: “Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them.”
The reinterpretation effectively excludes economic activities such as logging, mining and industrial development from the ESA’s prohibition on “take” when those activities foreseeably kill or injure wildlife without intentionally targeting them.
The memo follows the Trump administration’s repeal in July of the ESA’s definition of prohibited “harm,” which was defined as “an act which actually kills or injures wildlife,” including acts that “may include significant habitat modification or degradation”.
Interior secretary Doug Burgum justified the repeal in July by saying: “For years, federal agencies abused the ESA to obstruct lawful land use and burden American families and businesses.”
Earlier this month, 20 states and Washington DC sued the Trump administration over its decision to redefine “harm,” including removing “modification or degradation” of habitat from conduct that can constitute a prohibited take.
In a statement on Thursday to the Guardian about the administration’s reinterpretation of “take,” the interior department, which oversees the FWS, said: “As outlined in the final rule, the department determined that the previous regulatory definition of ‘harm’ expanded the Endangered Species Act’s prohibition on ‘take’ beyond the text Congress enacted. The final rule restores that interpretation while maintaining the ESA’s core protections for listed species.”
The memo has drawn swift backlash from environmental advocacy organizations. The Center for Biological Diversity pointed to the supreme court’s 1995 6-3 decision in Babbitt v Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon, in which the majority rejected the argument that “take” is limited to actions deliberately directed against endangered species.
“If you chop down a tree full of endangered birds or race a huge ship through a pod of endangered whales, you should be held accountable for your destructive acts,” Brett Hartl, the Center for Biological Diversity’s government affairs director, said.
“But this administration wants to give wildlife killers a get out of jail free card. Imposing new limitations on the entire definition of take is a flagrant and illegal attempt to rewrite the Endangered Species Act via unilateral fiat. This would drive imperiled species over the cliff to extinction,” he added.
Similarly, the environmental law nonprofit Earthjustice told the Guardian: “The government’s new legal position is a prescription for extinction. It says that as long as you claim you didn’t mean to kill an endangered species, the law can’t and won’t stop you. That’s ridiculous.
“The supreme court decided this issue in the Sweet Home case and its ruling still represents the best reading of the Endangered Species Act. We’ll see the Trump administration in court about this.”
The Trump administration’s reinterpretation of the ESA is the latest in a series of environmental rollbacks. Since returning to office last January, Trump has moved to weaken federal protections for old-growth forests, potentially jeopardizing habitat for 400 endangered species across the US; scrapped drilling restrictions near a world heritage site in New Mexico; and directed his administration to consider the delisting of gray wolves from the ESA.
During the signing ceremony for the latter, Trump asked: “You can shoot them as of today?” Agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins replied that Burgum “has to do a little magic, but yes”.

US approves visas for top Iranian leaders to attend UN General Assembly

US approves visas for top Iranian leaders to attend UN General Assembly
Iran’s delegation to UNGA will be smaller this year, with travel restrictions and limits on luxury goods purchases.
The United States is allowing an Iranian delegation to attend the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City next week, a Department of State spokesman said, in spite of the protracted war that is raging into its seventh month.
A source familiar with the matter confirmed the delegation would cover Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and their essential staff to attend the High-Level Week in person.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3UN fact-finding mission says US committed possible war crimes in Iran
- list 2 of 3Macron and Aoun discuss efforts to back Lebanon’s army, end Israeli attacks
- list 3 of 3Russia, China veto UN mandate to monitor Iran sanctions
“Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week,” the State Department spokesman said.
The US official added that only a scaled-down delegation will be permitted, and that they will confront tighter travel curbs and luxury import prohibitions “per our policy”.
The 81st UNGA will unfold against the backdrop of a grinding military impasse between the two countries, with no clear path towards reopening the Strait of Hormuz or reviving Washington-Tehran talks of ending the war.
The disruption of the vital chokepoint — which handles roughly 20 percent of global seaborne energy transit — has sent global oil prices soaring.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly said that the conflict with Iran is nearing its end, and recently claimed his administration has held direct talks with officials in Tehran, even as fighting flares in Yemen between Houthi forces and the Saudi-led coalition over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, where Houthi forces have seized control.
Washington recently barred Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and dozens of Palestinian Authority (PA) officials from entering the US for the UNGA for the second consecutive year. The visa denial by the Trump administration last year relegated the usually present Palestinian leader to address the global body virtually. The Palestinians will still be represented at next week’s high-level meeting of the UNGA by their diplomats who are already accredited to the UN.
Without explicitly naming President Abbas, the State Department announced a broader visa ban targeting officials from the PA and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), due to “their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace,” the statement said.
“Punitive measures and restrictions imposed on Palestinian officials do not contribute to advancing peace or combating violence,” the authority’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates said in a statement in response. “Rather, they weaken the Palestinian partner committed to a political solution and encourage forces working to undermine the two-state solution and impose the reality of occupation, settlement and annexation by force.”
The UNGA will be meeting under the heavy strain of continued geopolitical crises, such as Russia’s war on Ukraine, escalating Middle East volatility and deepening economic disturbances that have triggered widespread inflation and affordability crises across the globe.

AI exposes Pentagon’s aging networks to growing cyber threats: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:17:50 UTC
06:17:50 KST

Diyar Guldogan
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Artificial intelligence is increasing the cybersecurity risks facing the Pentagon’s aging computer networks, as increasingly capable tools allow adversaries to identifnd combine weaknesses in US defense systems more quickly, according to a Washington Post report.
Lt. Gen. Paul Stanton, the Pentagon’s top cyber defense official and head of the army’s cyber defense command, said the Defense Department has experienced a “tenfold” increase in cybersecurity vulnerabilities amid the rise of AI.
“We have postponed and deferred the sustainment and maintenance of our systems to our potential peril,” Stanton said last week at a Washington conference, said the report. “No more.”
The comments came amid an intensifying debate in Washington about the risks of artificial intelligence, following the resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who warned that the technology could “kill us all by the end of the next decade.”
Cybersecurity experts said the Pentagon’s exposure to AI-enabled cyberattacks poses an immediate national security concern, as adversaries gain more sophisticated tools to exploit weaknesses in US military networks, according to the Washington Post.
They warned that years of deferred maintenance and outdated infrastructure could make the Defense Department’s systems increasingly vulnerable, while upgrading the networks could take years as AI capabilities continue to advance rapidly.
“This has become a pretty urgent priority,” Michael C. Horowitz, director of the defense and national security program at the Council on Foreign Relations, was quoted by the newspaper. “The risk is that adversaries gain a greater ability to disrupt U.S. information networks to get access to American military data and thus compromise national security.”
