Customer Data Permanently Lost in Iran Strikes on Amazon Data Centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:15:00 UTC
04:15:00 KST

Half a year after Iranian drone strikes knocked out multiple Amazon data centers, the US tech company has acknowledged the permanent loss of some customer data that was hosted in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates.
Amazon Web Services was “unable to restore access to the resources and data” hosted in some of the war-damaged data centers, according to an AWS dashboard update posted on September 15. The development was first reported by Reuters and suggests that the Iranian strikes inflicted catastrophic damage on the data centers.
Customer data was irretrievably lost in one of three AWS availability zones in the United Arab Emirates region, specifically the mec1-az2 availability zone. Each availability zone is serviced by one or more Amazon data centers.
The company is still working on “recovering regional resources” and restoring resources hosted in the other two availability zones in the United Arab Emirates. The AWS update described ongoing work to replace “affected infrastructure” and promised to update customers on a restoration of services in the coming months.
But the destruction was apparently even more widespread for the data centers in the Bahrain region, because Amazon said it was unable to restore access to resources and data across all three availability zones there.
“The damage to our infrastructure spanned multiple availability zones and exceeded what our regional and multi-AZ services are designed to withstand,” the AWS update said.
The company had already suspended customer billing in the affected AWS regions in Bahrain and the UAE and has spent the past six months attempting to restore normal operations.
The Iranian drones first struck the Amazon data centers on March 1 in the opening days of the ongoing war that began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28.
AWS immediately urged customers to migrate resources to other cloud regions and use remote backups to restore any “inaccessible resources.” The cloud service also reportedly issued $150 million in customer credits following the initial Iranian strikes in March.
A follow-up Iranian strike focused on Amazon’s data centers in Bahrain on April 1. The latest AWS update acknowledged this “disruption” of a second availability zone in the Bahrain region in April but described most affected customers as having already followed the company’s recommendations to migrate their cloud computing workloads elsewhere.
On July 24, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched yet another strike using missiles that specifically targeted a remaining Amazon data center structure in Bahrain. That damage was independently confirmed by satellite imagery.
“We remain committed to supporting our customers in Bahrain in the long term and will share a further update in early 2027,” the latest AWS update said.
Meanwhile, the US-Israeli war with Iran has since spiraled into a broader regional conflict and growing global energy crisis because of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. One of the few silver linings has been the surging interest worldwide in renewable power generation, such as solar rooftop panels.
This story originally appeared on Ars Technica.

“What Ukraine needs right now”: Poland to provide Ukraine with scarce F-16 missiles to shoot down jet-powered drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:11:13 UTC
04:11:13 KST

Poland will provide another aid package to Ukraine, which will include, among other things, “what Ukraine needs right now,” Deputy Minister of National Defense Stanisław Wziątek said, reports Polskie Radio. He said the package would include missiles for F-16 fighter jets, which the Ukrainian military uses to shoot down Russian drones.
Ukraine is critically short of missiles for F-16 fighter jets, which shoot down Russian UAVs. Recently, it was reported that pilots sometimes took off without missiles, using only the aircraft’s built-in M61A1 Vulcan cannon, which is dangerous for civilians. Poland’s newly promised aid will include these missiles for Ukraine.
Among other things, Poland will provide aviation equipment, the report said. Media reports added that the aid package may be worth around €50 million.
Ammunition for F-16s and possible aviation equipment
“Our aid is in the process of being prepared. Everything will happen in a moment. I cannot say what it contains, I can only say that it is what Ukraine needs right now. This includes basic ammunition. These are the ones mounted on F-16s to shoot down Russian drones,” Wziątek said.
AIM-9 and AIM-120 are air-to-air missiles that the Ukrainian Armed Forces use with F-16s to fight Russian aviation, Militarnyi says. The outlet adds that last year Ukrainian F-16s were spotted with APKWS II missiles, which are effective against drones. As for the aforementioned aviation equipment, Poland may provide decommissioned MiG-29 fighter jets or drones, the media outlet suggests.
The MiG-29 does not use the same scarce stocks of AIM-9 and AIM-120 missiles.
Missile shortage is not new
In July 2025, America abruptly suspended arms supplies to Ukraine, affecting some types of weapons. Among them were more than 90 US-made AIM air-to-air missiles that were in Poland and on their way to Ukraine, but were withdrawn by the US, according to a Wall Street Journal article. Since then, Ukraine has received Western aid for air defense systems, but missiles have remained among the items in short supply.
Ukraine faced a severe shortage of F-16 missiles from late November to mid-December, according to Reuters. One source said Ukraine had "nothing to put on its jets for almost a month."
While F-16s likely rank first by number in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, the Soviet-made MiG-29 ranks second, Euromaidan Press. Ukraine had enough R-73 missiles for this fighter, but when the Ukrainian Armed Forces also began using them for ground-based launchers after 9M33 missiles for Soviet Osa air defense systems ran out, the rate of consumption increased sharply.
Ukrainian forces were observed resuming the use of older missiles that had been considered obsolete. There is an alternative: using the fighter’s cannon. However, this practice is dangerous.

‘I don’t work for Netanyahu': Ofer Winter can be Israel's next kingmaker - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:08:44 UTC
04:08:44 KST

The demand for political renewal after the October 7 massacre was central to Ofer Winter’s election pitch: Give new people enough power, and they could change Israel’s Right, even under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Hamas’s massacre prompted expectations that a new generation of leaders would emerge, yet familiar figures continued to dominate. Former ministers Yoaz Hendel and Chili Tropper formed a joint party, then split. Tropper joined former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar slate.
Brig.-Gen. (res.) Winter, who had never served in the Knesset, offered another route. His Amcha Yisrael, or People of Israel, party made recruiting parliamentary newcomers part of its appeal, including immigrants, advocates for Israel abroad, and people whose families had been affected by the war.
Israelis vote for party lists. Governments normally depend on alliances commanding at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, allowing a small party whose support is essential to bargain for ministries and policy changes. Winter wants the Defense Ministry. First, he has to win enough votes to enter the Knesset.
He spoke with The Jerusalem Post from his temporary office in an old Jerusalem building, where he hosted activities for different parts of Israeli society. On the stairs, people approached him one by one: a haredi (ultra-Orthodox) man, a settler, a man without a kippah, and others.
Each person who approached expressed support for Winter
They expressed support. One asked why he had not joined forces with a small new haredi party advocating military conscription. Winter stopped for everyone, shaking hands, hugging people, and answering questions. His directness appeared to resonate.
“I don’t work for Netanyahu,” he said. “I don’t work for anyone.”
His candidates had other options, he said. “If we had been looking for a seat, we could have found a seat,” he added, meaning he was offered seats on different slates but declined immediately.
Winter acknowledged that supporting Netanyahu had cost him potential voters. He said he was choosing among available alternatives and seeking enough strength to change policy within government.
Calls to send all 120 MKs home were an impractical slogan, Winter said, adding that change would take time.
He refused pressure to merge with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party, and he resisted Netanyahu’s efforts to consolidate smaller parties. Parties that fall below the electoral threshold receive no seats.
Winter challenged the assumption that his voters would otherwise support existing right-wing parties. He also objected to the hostility toward him from that camp.
“I’m not Hamas,” he said. “Don’t confuse a friend with an enemy.”
“There are people who cannot bring themselves to vote for the current Right, for the existing government,” he added, citing younger voters and reservists as his core constituency.
Asked what distinguished him from Smotrich, Winter replied: “Look at my list.”
He described it as closer to what the Likud, Netanyahu’s party, should have been: “Religious, nonreligious, Jews, Arabs, Druze.”
No. 2 on his list, Yoseph Haddad, is an Arab Christian advocate for Israel who volunteered for military service and was wounded in the Golani infantry brigade. Winter wants him to become public diplomacy minister and defend Israel’s positions abroad.
Former television journalist Netali Shem Tov’s family was displaced from Metula, near the Lebanese border.
Sigal Kraunik-Atia lost her husband, Kibbutz Be’eri’s security coordinator, in the October 7 massacre.
Winter repeatedly highlights new immigrants to Israel
Winter repeatedly highlighted the olim (new immigrants).
Former Jerusalem deputy mayor Fleur Hassan-Nahoum immigrated from Gibraltar and became prominent in international advocacy.
Lali Deri arrived alone from France at age 14 and a half and became an activist and commentator. Her son, Saadia Yaakov, was killed fighting in Gaza.
Their experience connected his slate to Jewish communities abroad.
Winter also described a roots trip with his immigrant parents that reinforced his appreciation of having a Jewish state.
The diversity came with clear ideological boundaries. He opposed a Palestinian state and wanted Israel’s Jewish character preserved. He also opposed religious coercion and welcomed non-Jewish citizens who identify with Israel into its leadership.
Winter commanded Givati during the 2014 Gaza war, Operation Protective Edge, and later led the 98th Division. His religiously worded letter to soldiers before the 2014 fighting provoked controversy. He left the military in 2024 after being passed over for promotion to major-general.
“I lived with a sense of mission,” Winter said. “Otherwise, I would not have been able to do it, nor would my family.”
His wife raised eight children while working as a school principal, he said. He insisted he had left the army without anger.
As defense minister, Winter said he wants to change military doctrine “from containment to decisive victory.” He acknowledged wartime achievements but expressed disbelief that Hamas remained standing after years of fighting.
“Reservists are not supposed to serve in the IDF for three years,” he said. “Reservists need to be at home.”
They need to work, educate children, develop the economy, and help absorb immigrants, he added.
Winter described Eisenkot as an architect of the prewar security approach he opposed. Eisenkot could, nevertheless, join a broad government.
“But I don’t think he can be defense minister,” he said.
Winter also welcomed former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman into such a coalition “as ministers.”
Regarding Netanyahu’s responsibility, he was unequivocal.
“Netanyahu is responsible,” he said. “Whether he says it or doesn’t say it, he is responsible. He was prime minister. There wasn’t somebody else here.”
Winter distinguished the immediate failures of the military and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), Israel’s domestic security service, from political leaders’ responsibility for accepting assessments and approving policy. The failure had developed over at least a decade, he said.
“Nobody can take the responsibility away from Netanyahu,” he added.
Winter has publicly made military-service legislation a condition for joining the government.
His plan combines greater benefits for those serving, Defense Ministry oversight of yeshivas, and military units accommodating haredi religious requirements.
“The more you serve, the more you receive,” he said. Combat and reserve service should bring greater benefits, he added, and those failing to report would lose access to dealings with the state. He did not elaborate.
Drawing on his experience establishing a haredi company in Givati, Winter said recruitment required the army to honor its promises to religious soldiers.
“Don’t reeducate them,” he said.
Winter said there was room for women combat soldiers alongside religious accommodations, supported continued Torah study for exceptional scholars, and wanted other haredim to have routes into service, education, and work.
Regarding Gaza, he advocated what he calls voluntary emigration.
“Let them choose where they want to go,” he said.
Winter said the government had considered him to lead its emigration initiative, but then backed away after hearing his intentions. He did not identify the officials involved.
Winter’s account of his proposed wartime strategy included moving the population, besieging those who remained, and allowing emigration. He also advocated separating civilians from Hamas and striking the organization with full force.
The interview left unanswered how voluntary departure would operate alongside that pressure and what conditions civilians choosing to remain would face.
“Our soldiers come before enemy civilians,” he said, regarding his wartime instructions.
Winter hopes for a double-digit seat tally, drawing support from the Likud, other right-wing parties, the center, and first-time voters. That remained his assessment of the party’s potential.
Whether he could reshape a Netanyahu government depended on voters giving him enough influence to enforce his demands, he said.
“We will act from within, but we will not compromise on certain things,” Winter said.

Ferguson Marine to build tugboats for commercial sale
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:05:04 BST
04:05:04 KST

Ferguson Marine is to begin building a small number of tugboats for sale on the commercial market, with the Scottish Government providing working capital to keep shipbuilding activity moving at Port Glasgow after delays on a proposed package of four further vessels.
Economy and Transport Secretary Stephen Flynn told Holyrood that he had agreed Ferguson Marine’s proposal for financial backing, describing it as a way of retaining productive work and critical skills during a gap in the yard’s order book.
He said: “I have agreed that this proposal should be taken forward because I agree with the board that it represents a sensible, commercial approach to maintaining productive activity within the yard.”
The tugboats are expected to be built for subsequent sale rather than against an existing customer order, with the state-owned yard then seeking buyers on the commercial market.
Ferguson Marine is expected to work with an established shipbuilder on a pre-packaged design, potentially Dutch shipbuilder Damen, allowing construction to begin relatively quickly. Flynn said the arrangement was intended to provide greater certainty while the Government continues work on plans announced earlier this year for four new vessels to be built at Ferguson Marine, including two CalMac ferries.
He said: “Providing working capital to the yard has the potential to retain critical shipbuilding capability and workforce skills during an important period for the business.”
Flynn added: “I have therefore asked officials to work with the company to progress the necessary commercial, financial and governance arrangements as quickly as possible.”
The proposed four-vessel package has not yet reached contract award, with Flynn telling MSPs that “robust due diligence” was still being carried out before the contracts could be placed. He said the working capital was intended to provide “certainty for the yard during the gap between the delivery of the Glen Rosa and the award of these new contracts by making sure we have a commercial alternative in place with tugboats.”
Ferguson Marine is currently completing MV Glen Rosa, the second of the two large CalMac ferries built at Port Glasgow. Delivery is expected before the end of 2026, after which the yard currently has no contracted shipbuilding work scheduled for 2027. The lack of confirmed follow-on work has increased pressure on the yard. Ferguson Marine announced in August that it was seeking voluntary redundancies, with up to 70 positions potentially affected.
The Scottish Government had previously pledged to award work for four smaller vessels directly to Ferguson Marine, including two ferries, but the necessary due diligence on those contracts is still under way.
The delay drew criticism from opposition parties. Scottish Liberal Democrat transport spokesperson Willie Rennie MSP accused the Government of failing to carry out the necessary legal work before announcing its intention to award contracts directly to Ferguson Marine.
Rennie said: “It’s now clear the government failed to carry out appropriate legal checks before it told parliament earlier this year that it would make a direct award of a ferry contract to the Ferguson yard.”
He added: “The consequences are being felt by the third of the workforce who have lost their jobs as a result of the government’s negligence.”
Rennie also called on Flynn to set out when a decision would be made on the contracts, saying: “The workers deserve not to wait another minute.”
The tugboat plan is intended to bridge the period between completion of Glen Rosa and any future vessel awards, while giving Ferguson Marine a product it can offer into the wider commercial market.
Flynn said the Government, which brought Ferguson Marine into public ownership in 2019, continued to believe the yard “can have a strong future as a modern and competitive shipyard.”

Third person dies from malaria in cluster near Germany’s Frankfurt Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:04:53 UTC
04:04:53 KST

Third person dies from malaria in cluster near Germany’s Frankfurt Airport
Frankfurt grapples with a rare malaria outbreak tied to air travel, marking three deaths in recent months.
A third person has died from malaria after a recent cluster of cases linked to Frankfurt Airport, in what German officials have described as an extremely rare air-traffic-related outbreak of the tropical disease.
In a statement on Thursday, city administration said the person died at Frankfurt hospital and was one of two infected residents living in the Schwanheim district, in the immediate vicinity of the airport.
Recommended Stories
list of 1 itemend of list
The two new malaria cases in the neighbourhood had been reported on Tuesday.
“Both individuals had become infected with the malaria-causing parasite Plasmodium falciparum, even though they had not travelled to a malaria-endemic region and had not worked at the airport,” the statement said.
According to the city’s public health department, the two newly infected people contracted the disease from a mosquito flown into Germany on an aircraft or in luggage.
Six Frankfurt airport workers had contracted malaria tropica, the most dangerous form of the disease, in July, authorities said. Two later died.
Malaria is a potentially life-threatening mosquito-borne disease that is extremely rare in Germany.
The malaria parasite is spread between humans by some types of mosquitoes, but not through direct human-to-human contact.
Frankfurt Airport operator Fraport said it set up traps to catch mosquitoes and sent the insects to a laboratory in Antwerp in Belgium in July and August, but results were not available yet.
Health authorities have warned doctors near the airport to consider malaria in patients who come in with a fever.
Airport workers and residents have been urged to seek medical advice in case they display symptoms including fever, chills, headaches, confusion, seizures and breathing difficulties.
An airport spokesperson said local public health authorities had the power in principle to order airlines to disinfect aircraft.

He pointed to an emergency declaration by 44 nations outside the council chamber that condemned a high-level visit by Israeli leadership to Mount Hermon as an unlawful act and a "blatant violation" of international law.
He emphasised that while Damascus approached US-sponsored security talks in good faith, Israel "responded to dialogue with airstrikes, incursions, and violations and attacks." 
He underscored that pursuing a diplomatic arrangement does not mean Damascus will "accept occupation or relinquish the rights of our people," while defending bilateral cooperation with regional partners as an exercise of sovereign state consent.
Rejecting Israeli claims on communal divisions, Olabi asserted that Syrian Kurds have integrated into state institutions, Syrian Jews are "back renovating their synagogues" and Druze figures who "rejected foreign support" are now in the parliament.
Moreover, relaying a message from the UN chief, UN Deputy Special Envoy for Syria Claudio Cordone said “violations of Syrian sovereignty and territorial integrity must cease” and the 1974 Disengagement Agreement must be respected.
Cordone said Israel’s military presence in southern Syria directly breached the agreement through “near daily incursions, temporary checkpoints, searches of homes and artillery fire”, particularly in Quneitra and western Daraa.
He said security concerns could not be addressed sustainably through unilateral military action or an open-ended military presence. His remarks followed a September 9 visit by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to Israeli forces deployed on Mount Hermon.
Cordone also said tensions in Suwayda should be resolved by Syrians “without disruptive foreign interference” under the September 2025 roadmap.
Israel has occupied Syria’s Golan Heights since 1967 and unilaterally annexed the territory in 1981, a move not recognised internationally.
Following the fall of Bashar al Assad’s government on December 8, 2024, Israel expanded its occupation of Syrian territory and took control of the buffer zone and positions on the Syrian side of Mount Hermon.
Fuel prices, displacement add pressure
UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs Tom Fletcher warned that shipping disruptions across the Bab al Mandeb Strait and Strait of Hormuz were driving up freight and insurance costs and lengthening supply times into Syria.
A 40 percent rise in diesel prices this week threatened bakeries, water pumping and winter heating, Fletcher said. The minimum expenditure basket has also risen 33 percent since June 2025, forcing aid agencies to halve food rations for the most vulnerable families as food and education programmes remain only 26 percent funded.
More than 2 million internally displaced people and 1.8 million refugees have voluntarily returned since December 2024.
Still, 5.5 million people remain displaced across Syria, including nearly 800,000 living in camps where women and children make up more than 75 percent of residents.
Explosive ordnance remains a major obstacle to recovery, killing 880 people, including 269 children, and injuring 1,616 since late 2024. Fletcher said contamination was also blocking access to agricultural land.
“You cannot build an economy over a minefield,” he said.
He also urged international donors to convene a dedicated reconstruction conference and help address private-sector banking over compliance.

Ukraine plans record defence spending in 2027
KYIV - The Ukrainian government plans to spend a record two thirds of its budget on defence IN 2027 as costs mount in its war with Russia, government documents showed.
Russia’s four-and-a-half-year offensive has battered Ukraine’s economy, causing billions of dollars in destruction and punching a huge hole in its neighbour’s finances.
The war-torn country initially used its own revenues to pay for defence spending but has increasingly relied on foreign backers for these outlays.
The Ukrainian government will seek an additional US$53 billion (S$67 billion) in foreign aid in 2027, including from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, it said.
“The draft budget for 2027 was formed at a time when Russian aggression was continuing, and security and defence needs remained crucial,” Ukraine’s finance minister Sergiy Marchenko said in a press release published on Sept 15.
“This is unquestionably the government’s number one priority. All possible internal resources of the state are being channelled towards ensuring Ukraine can effectively resist the aggressor,” he added.
Ukraine plans to spend a record 4.9 trillion hryvnia (S$140 billion) on defence and security in 2027, around 44 per cent of its GDP and a record since Russia invaded in 2022, according to the release.
About a third of this will go towards wages for soldiers, while the remainder will largely go towards weapons and equipment, the release said.
In comparison, Russia planned to spend around 13.6 trillion rubles ($205 billion) on defence in 2027, or around 30 per cent of its budget.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sept 15 warned that Parliament would have to pass “unpleasant and unpopular” measures to attract foreign financing, among them a tax on foreign parcels.
“Right now, without these things, it is impossible to ensure the full needs of our defence and the resilience of Ukraine,” he said.
The Ekonomichna Pravda newspaper reported on Sept 17 that the finance ministry had postponed spending on preparing the energy system for winter until December owing to a lack of funds.
Ukraine has received around US$200 billion in financing from its foreign partners since Russia invaded in 2022, as well as billions of dollars in military aid. AFP

Shirt brand owner shares fix to get thousands of Temu dupes taken down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:00:02 UTC
04:00:02 KST

Lonely Kids Club fashion brand owner shares fix to get thousands of Temu dupes taken down
In short:
Warwick Levy, owner of Lonely Kids Club, found thousands of copies of his T-shirts on Temu.
He struggled to use Temu's violation reporting form before discovering a workaround.
What's next?
Mr Levy has shared his solution to help other designers who find copies of their work on Temu.
When Warwick Levy learned copies of his T-shirts were being sold on Temu, he did not know how to handle it.
The Sydney-based owner of Lonely Kids Club, a genderless graphic tee company, hoped the problem would go away.
It did not.
"It got to a point where our entire website was scraped, and we have thousands of designs … so all our designs were on Temu," Mr Levy said.
"Our top-selling designs were on there like 10, 20, 30, 40 times from different sellers, all with lots of sales attributed."
The copies hurt sales. The bestselling "get in the van" shirt, featuring a drawing of the Healthy Harold giraffe, suddenly became significantly less popular.
"At the time we thought maybe it's just gone stale. But then once it got removed [from Temu], it picked back up almost immediately," Mr Levy said.
Like many other small designers in Australia who have found their work copied by overseas giants, Mr Levy did not have the time or money to take the fight to court, and was unsure what government bodies would be able to support him.
"I'm a very small self-funded business without any sort of capital or investors. That sort of thing just didn't feel feasible," he said.
He reached out to Temu, which is an online marketplace that sells goods and ultra-fast fashion, and was directed to its Intellectual Property (IP) Violation form, but the problems did not stop there.
"I spent like half an hour, 40 minutes going through and putting in data and then, right before the end where you then click to submit, it just disappeared. The whole window vanished, and then I lost all my work," he said.
"I tried it again, spent another 40 minutes and then, again, it disappeared.
"I really stressed out because I was like, 'I've lost my work twice. I feel very helpless in this situation, and I don't know what's going on.'"
Mr Levy launched his business in 2011, working out of his bedroom. He now has a studio-warehouse in Artarmon where he collaborates with artists and has a focus on ethical, local production.
"It felt like I let [the artists] down because the work was stolen from my website and so that was my responsibility to remove it," he said.
Once Temu began selling copies, Mr Levy got complaints from customers about receiving low-quality garments, not realising they had purchased duplicates.
"We actually had one person not that long ago sort of say like, 'Why would I buy this design from you when everyone's selling it?'" Mr Levy said.
"I say, 'Well, first of all, it's our design. No-one else is meant to be selling it. Everyone else has stolen it.'"
The workaround
After struggling to successfully navigate Temu's IP violation portal on different browsers, he found a workaround to complete the form.
Mr Levy said he started by having the information needed for the report prepared in a separate document. Then he opened the IP form in an incognito window, signed in and never closed the tab.
By acting fast, he was able to get the form through to the final stage. After that, he said it took days before he received a confirmation.
Mr Levy realised complaining about trademark violation sped up the process, and he said the copies were eventually removed, something that took just over a week.
A Temu spokesperson said it promptly removed the listings in question after the Lonely Kids Club's reports were received.
"Sellers are required to comply with applicable laws and platform policies, and those found to violate our IP policies are subject to enforcement actions, including listing removal, account suspensions, or permanent bans," the spokesperson said.
In the hope of helping other designers, Mr Levy has shared detailed instructions about how to get violating Temu listings taken down on the Lonely Kids Club website, and has since added software to his website to help prevent design theft.
Support from fans
Mr Levy said while he still found copies of his work online, it was not at the same scale as Temu.
Throughout the process, the small business owner received great support from his fans, releasing a "How shit is Temu" tee that became very popular.
"People did come out saying, 'I would never buy it from Temu again. Thanks for telling us and we'll make sure that we report it wherever we can as well,'" Mr Levy said.
"It was really sweet."
He said he would like to see a hub created to support Australian designers impacted by IP violation.
"I think Temu's more just created a culture with their marketplace that the sellers know they can scrape and steal and no-one's going to stop them until it gets noticed,"

These tiny crocodiles may be at risk, but they can't be listed as 'threatened'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Australia's pygmy crocodiles aren't a new species, but they still need protection, experts argue
In short:
NT's pygmy crocodiles aren't genetically different enough to be a separate species from freshwater crocodiles or even a subspecies, a new study suggests.
Some scientists say this "unique ecological form" of crocodile may still need targeted conservation.
What's next?
Further research into a second pygmy crocodile site at Bullo River is needed, as well as ecosystem studies and movement patterns from both populations.
The Northern Territory is synonymous with big open skies and humungous crocodiles.
But high in Arnhem Land's remote sandstone escarpments you will also find Australia's smallest snapping handbags.
It's here, more than 100 kilometres up the Liverpool River, that freshwater crocodiles only grow half as long as their downstream neighbours.
Since this population of "pygmy crocodiles" was first reported in Western science in the 1980s, there has been debate over whether the isolated reptiles were a different species.
"Species status can have major conservation implications," wildlife geneticist Jaime Góngora of the University of Sydney said.
"If these crocodiles were a separate species, they would likely require their own conservation assessment and management plan."
But a new study published in Ecology and Evolution by Professor Góngora and colleagues that compared the genetics of different populations of freshwater crocodiles concluded they were one species.
Professor Góngora said the genetic differences in the small Liverpool River crocodiles was no greater than that found between freshwater crocodiles (Crocodylus johnstoni) that lived in other river systems.
"They are a unique population, but we did not find strong evidence that they are a separate species," he said.
While not a new species, Professor Góngora said pygmy crocodiles represented an ecological form of freshwater crocodile adapted to isolated escarpments.
He said this could warrant more protection for the Liverpool River crocodiles and a second population of small crocodiles in the Bullo River.
"Those adaptations are valuable and worth conserving," Professor Góngora said.
Why are they so small?
The small size of pygmy crocodiles compared to other freshwater populations is thought to be an example of "phenotypic plasticity", a phenomenon whereby a species develops different characteristics based on where it lives.
"A simple example is that identical plants can grow tall and lush in good soil but remain small and stunted in poor soil," Professor Góngora said.
"They are still the same species, but they respond differently to different conditions."
Centre for Crocodile Research managing director Sally Isberg, who was not involved with the study, said their small size came from adapting to smaller water pools on the escarpment, where less prey was available compared to down river.
"They've been able to mature at a smaller size because obviously the end goal is to pass on your genes,"
The original survey that described the Liverpool River's pygmy crocodiles found them in the upper reaches of the river past natural barriers, like waterfalls, where there weren't any large fish species.
The surveyors found the largest mature female pygmy crocodiles were between 1.07 metres and 1.12m long, and a male was 1.18m.
Elsewhere in the NT, female freshwater crocodiles mature at about 1.5m and grow up to 2m in length. While males mature at 1.6m to 2m and reach 2.5m.
Professor Góngora said freshwater crocodiles were known to grow larger in habitats with more permanent water and more abundant food.
For example, in the catfish-filled Lake Argyle in Western Australia, freshwater crocodiles have been recorded reaching lengths of about 3m.
Do pygmy crocodiles need more conservation effort?
Dr Isberg said there was a point of alarm a few years ago for Bullo River pygmy crocodiles when cane toads, which can kill predators when ingested, moved through the region.
The exact state of the two pygmy crocodile populations is unclear, with no current population estimates.
Professor Góngora said there were high levels of inbreeding in the Liverpool River population compared to other crocodiles in the genetic study.
"That is not surprising given how isolated these crocodiles are," he said.
"Inbreeding can reduce genetic diversity, which may make populations less resilient to environmental change and other threats."
Professor Góngora said more research was needed to understand the extent of inbreeding and whether it was affecting their long-term health, survival and ability to adapt to future challenges.
He said future research directions included more genetic sampling of the Bullo River crocodiles, studies on movement patterns and connectivity of the two populations between river systems, and ecological research into food availability, habitat quality and how the pygmy crocs responded to environmental pressures.
"Together, that would help us better understand how isolation and evolutionary processes are shaping these crocodile populations," Professor Góngora said.
In the meantime, he said conservation agencies could identify pygmy crocodiles as "unique management units" and prioritise them for monitoring, threat mitigation and recovery actions.
A spokesperson for the flora and fauna division of the NT Department of Lands, Planning and Environment told the ABC in a written statement the concept of an "ecological" species was interesting, "but would likely apply to isolated populations of many species".
The spokesperson said the new study confirmed pygmy crocodiles were not genetically distinct enough to be a subspecies or separate species of freshwater crocodile.
"This means that they could not legally be listed as a threatened species," they said.
The spokesperson said the remote pygmy populations were naturally protected from many threats.
But they also noted the spread of cane toads was a problem for all freshwater crocodiles.
"There are currently no effective measures to reduce the impacts of cane toads at a landscape scale, although there is some very promising research in the development of 'Peter Pan' tadpoles."

04:00:00 KST

The U.S. Department of State said Thursday it had approved the potential sale of Lockheed Martin's F-35 Lightning II fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, as the kingdom is drawn deeper into war in the Middle East.
A sale would mark a significant policy shift from the U.S., potentially altering the balance of military power in the Middle East and testing Washington's definition of maintaining its ally Israel's "qualitative military edge."
Saudi Arabia made a direct appeal for the jets in early 2025 to U.S. President Donald Trump and has long been interested in Lockheed Martin's fighter. But Israel, the only country in the region to operate the jets, has objected to the sale.
The estimated $24.3 billion sale would include 48 of the military aircraft and 49 Pratt & Whitney engines along with communications equipment, spare parts and other support items, the State Department said in a statement.
The F-35, built with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection, is considered the world's most advanced fighter jet.
"The proposed sale will improve Saudi Arabia's capability to deter current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defense, and improving interoperability with US forces," the State Department said.
It "will also augment Saudi Arabia's operational aircraft and enhance its air-to-air, and air-to-ground self-defense capability," it added.
Saudi Arabia, the largest customer for U.S. arms, has sought the fighter for years as it looks to modernize its air force and counter regional threats, particularly from Iran. The kingdom's renewed push for what would constitute two squadrons comes as the Trump administration has signaled openness to deepening defense cooperation with Riyadh.
The Saudi Air Force flies a mix of fighter aircraft, including Boeing F-15s, European Tornados and Typhoons.
The F-35 issue has also been intertwined with broader diplomatic efforts. The administration of former U.S. President Joe Biden previously explored providing F-35s to Saudi Arabia as part of a comprehensive deal that would have included Riyadh normalizing relations with Israel, though those efforts ultimately stalled.
Trump has made arms sales to Saudi Arabia a priority since returning to office. In 2025, the United States agreed to sell the kingdom an arms package worth nearly $142 billion, which the White House called "the largest defense cooperation agreement" Washington has ever done.
The State Department has notified Congress about the proposed sale, which would require the approval of U.S. lawmakers.
Saudi Arabia is pursuing ambitious economic and military modernization plans under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030 agenda. The kingdom has sought to diversify its defense partnerships in recent years while maintaining its decades-long security relationship with Washington.

AI king Jensen Huang pushes ‘responsible optimism’ at King Charles III’s gathering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:57:54 UTC
03:57:54 KST

AYRSHIRE, Scotland — King Charles relied on all his pulling power to bring together some of the most powerful people in the world of AI to a rural corner of Scotland.
Preparations for Thursday's event at the 18th century estate of Dumfries House, first reported by POLITICO, had been in the works for months in close communication with the U.K. government.
But the significance of the event intensified in recent weeks after a series of alarming incidents of AI agents escaping their testing environments to hack other firms, and warnings from those in the industry that humanity’s very existence could be under threat.
Advertisement
For the first time since worries about AI eradicating humanity sparked a wave of calls for immediate regulation, the companies were all under one roof. Charles addressed the dire warnings in his remarks to his guests.
“There seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands and being used in potentially catastrophic ways,” he said. “Surely, then, we need sufficient means of control before it is all too late.”
But after weeks of fervent debate about the need to increase oversight and slow the pace of development, tech leaders at the event were eager to change the mood music back to something sunnier.
Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, whose chips are the engines for almost every player in the AI race, said “we have to build this technology safely and securely and responsibly” — but also with what he termed “responsible optimism.”
And while “every government should be involved,” Huang argued against sweeping new laws, saying the onus was primarily on the industry to ensure its products are safe.
“Those of us building AI must test systems rigorously, protect privacy, anticipate misuse, and secure the infrastructure society will depend on. When a product is not safe enough, we should hold it back and keep engineering,” he said — a thinly veiled rebuke to leading AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic whose agents sparked the most recent panic, and whose representatives were in the room.
Advertisement
Even Demis Hassabis, the co-founder of Google DeepMind who has cautioned about the risks of humans losing control over increasingly powerful AI systems and has advocated for the creation of a new international standards body, struck a hopeful tone.
“The chance of something bad accidentally happening if we get things wrong is definitely non-zero,” Hassabis said.
But Hassabis said he was “very confident and optimistic that we can collectively address these risks and find solutions to these technical problems.”
Royal prerogative
Behind closed doors, roughly 60 attendees invited to the exclusive gathering were asked by King Charles to address two “simple questions,” as outlined in the monarch’s speech.
First, “how can we harness the benefits of AI with safety at his heart,” and second, “how can we build international cooperation and consensus to achieve this, so no nation is left behind, but the human race is left in place?”
The answers to those questions will, the palace hopes, become written principles to guide the development of AI in a way that centers humanity and nature — though they are not expected to be finalized for several months.
Advertisement
Three years since the U.K. hosted the inaugural AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park, it once again lent on its history and global standing at a pivotal moment to convene senior figures from across the world — including, notably, China — and spanning industry, finance, philanthropy and academia.
“Only His Majesty has that sort of convening authority,” said George Williamson, CEO of the Alan Turing Institute, the U.K.’s national AI body, who attended the event. Williamson said it showed the importance of hearing from a range of voices, “not just the technologists and scientists who usually dominate the airwaves.”
For the U.K. ministers and government officials in the room, it could prove an opportunity to showcase the country’s influence and ingenuity, British strengths that received plaudits from Huang.
In separate statements, both Anthropic and OpenAI said they were “grateful” for the king convening the meeting at a crucial moment for the sector.
While “AI has extraordinary potential,” its “growing capabilities rightly raise important questions about safety and how we ensure it always serves people,” OpenAI’s Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar said. “We need to address those questions together.”
Whether a closed-door meeting of the tech elite will do anything to quell public fears around AI is less certain: Hours before attendees arrived at Dumfries House, OpenAI announced it had found six more instances of its AI models exhibiting “concerning behavior.”

Former Maduro Ally Pleads Guilty in US to $195M Money Laundering Scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:56:00 UTC
03:56:00 KST

Reported by
A Miami federal court brought a decade of investigative reporting to a close on Wednesday as Colombian-born businessman Alex Saab pleaded guilty to money laundering—years after Venezuelan news outlet Armando.info first began uncovering his state corruption schemes.
Saab, a top financial ally of ousted Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro, admitted to using the U.S. financial system to launder bribes connected to Venezuela’s Local Committees for Supply and Production (CLAP)—a state program meant to distribute food to impoverished communities. He faces up to 20 years in federal prison and has agreed to forfeit $195 million, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.
The guilty plea serves as a vindication for Armando.info, a local investigative news outlet and OCCRP member center. More than nine years ago, the outlet pioneered reporting that brought Saab out of the shadows, exposing his ties to multimillion-dollar state contracts and the delivery of low-quality food to vulnerable populations.
At the time, Saab and the Maduro government vehemently denied the links. Saab sued the Armando.info team in Venezuela, arguing he had no connection to the CLAP program.
"The lawsuit was an attempt to censor us, to silence us… He knew everything we said was true," Roberto Deniz, a journalist and editor at Armando.info, told OCCRP. Calling Wednesday's plea the end of a public narrative built to protect the businessman, Deniz added: "It is the end of a charade, a farce… Now he told the truth."
Saab’s legal entanglements in the U.S. originally stemmed from a separate 2019 indictment. Federal prosecutors charged Saab alongside his business partner, Álvaro Pulido Vargas, with laundering over $350 million diverted from a Venezuelan state contract to build low-income housing. Following his 2020 arrest in Cape Verde and subsequent extradition to Miami in 2021, Caracas mounted an aggressive diplomatic campaign—granting Saab diplomatic status, labeling his detention a "kidnapping," and claiming he was securing goods to bypass U.S. sanctions.
In December 2023, President Joe Biden granted Saab a pardon amidst diplomatic negotiations to secure the release of seven Americans imprisoned in Venezuela. Among the freed U.S. citizens were Joseph Cristella, Eyvin Hernandez, Jerrel Kenemore, and Savoi Wright.
In addition to the Americans, Venezuela also released fugitive Leonard Glenn Francis, also known as “Fat Leonard,” who was implicated in the U.S. Navy’s largest corruption scandal in history. Francis had bribed officers in exchange for ship-servicing contracts, overbilling the Navy by more than $35 million.
Upon his return to Caracas, Saab was greeted personally by Maduro, who publicly hailed him on social media as a "brave and patriotic man who resisted with dignity a 1,280-day kidnapping." Saab was welcomed with honors and appointed Minister of Industry and National Production.
However, his fortunes reversed again following the collapse of the Maduro regime this past January. Venezuela's interim government, led by Delcy Rodríguez, deported Saab back to the United States, alleging he had committed fraud involving his identity documents.

Serbia opens factory to assemble Israeli-made drones

Serbia has opened a factory to assemble advanced Israeli-made drones, which will supply the Serbian military and armed forces in other countries.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated the facility jointly operated with an unnamed Israeli company on Thursday.
“Our plans are huge,” Vucic said in a social media post showing a video of him touring the facility with Israeli Ambassador Avivit Bar-Ilan, adding that at least three more factories will be opened across Serbia with Israeli partners.

Serbia is one of the few countries in the Western Balkans that is not a NATO member, and it has invested heavily in its military to “preserve neutrality”.
It has faced scrutiny over arms exports to Israel, which BIRN and Haaretz said rose from 1.4 million euros ($1.6 million) in 2023 to 42.3 million euros ($48.5 million) in 2024.

GM Defense delivered its first batch of PAC-3 MSE missile-housing components to Lockheed Martin on Sept. 16, just 22 days after the two companies signed a formal production contract, Lockheed Martin said in a post on X.
“The message is clear: we’re moving at the speed of relevance,” Lockheed Martin said. “The future of defense is being written now, and we’re setting a new standard for speed and agility in the industry.”
The delivery follows a memorandum of understanding GM Defense and Lockheed Martin signed in June 2026 to combine Lockheed’s missile production expertise with General Motors’ high-rate commercial manufacturing capacity, part of a broader push to widen the industrial base that builds the PAC-3 MSE interceptor. Neither company has said what portion of the missile the housing components cover or how many units GM Defense will supply under the contract.
The PAC-3 MSE, a hit-to-kill interceptor built to shoot down ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and aircraft, has seen a sharp jump in demand over the past year. The U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin a $9.8 billion contract in September 2025 for 1,970 interceptors, the largest deal in the history of Lockheed’s missiles and fire control business. In January 2026, Lockheed Martin signed a framework agreement with the Department of War to triple annual PAC-3 MSE production capacity from roughly 600 to 2,000 interceptors over seven years, and the government followed in April with a $4.7 billion contract to help fund that faster production pace.
That surge in demand traces in part to the missile’s use in combat. Lockheed Martin has said the PAC-3 MSE helped defend forces and infrastructure during Operation Epic Fury, the U.S. military campaign against Iran earlier this year. Seventeen partner nations, including the United States, Germany, Poland, Japan and Romania, have signed agreements to field the interceptor, and the Navy is separately working with Lockheed Martin to integrate the PAC-3 MSE into its Aegis Combat System for the first time.
GM Defense’s role adds to a supply chain Lockheed Martin has been expanding on multiple fronts. British manufacturer GKN Aerospace has built PAC-3 MSE launch tubes for decades and has also produced the interceptor’s mid-section and seeker housing components under a separate agreement dating to 2021. Lockheed Martin signed a similar memorandum of understanding with Germany’s Diehl Defence in October 2025 to explore expanding PAC-3 MSE production in Europe.

US clears way for $24.3 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:53:17 UTC
03:53:17 KST

US clears way for $30.9 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia
WASHINGTON - The US Department of State said on Sept 17 it has approved the potential sale of Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Lightning II fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, as the kingdom is drawn deeper into war in the Middle East.
A sale would mark a significant policy shift from the US, potentially altering the balance of military power in the Middle East and testing Washington’s definition of maintaining its ally Israel’s “qualitative military edge.”
Saudi Arabia made a direct appeal for the jets in early 2025 to US President Donald Trump and has long been interested in Lockheed Martin’s fighter.
The estimated US$24.3 billion (S$30.9 billion) sale would include 48 of the military aircraft and 49 Pratt & Whitney engines along with communications equipment, spare parts and other support items, the State Department said.
Washington weighs weapons sales to the Middle East in a way that ensures Israel maintains a “qualitative military edge”, effectively guaranteeing that Israel gets more advanced US weapons than regional Arab states.
The Saudi embassy in Washington welcomed the proposed sale, describing it as a further step in defence cooperation between the two countries.
“The proposed F-35 sale reflects the strength and enduring nature of the Saudi-US strategic partnership and the continued advancement of our defence cooperation,” the embassy said on X.
The F-35, built with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection, is considered the world’s most advanced fighter jet.
Israel has operated the aircraft for a decade, building multiple squadrons, and remains the only Middle Eastern country to possess the weapons system.
Saudi Arabia, the largest customer for US arms, has sought the fighter for years as it looks to modernise its air force and counter regional threats, particularly from Iran.
The kingdom’s renewed push for what would constitute two squadrons comes as the Trump administration has signalled openness to deepening defence cooperation with Riyadh.
The Saudi Air Force flies a mix of fighter aircraft including Boeing F-15s, European Tornados and Typhoons.
The F-35 issue has also been intertwined with broader diplomatic efforts.
The administration of former US President Joe Biden previously explored providing F-35s to Saudi Arabia as part of a comprehensive deal that would have included Riyadh normalising relations with Israel, though those efforts ultimately stalled.
Trump has made arms sales to Saudi Arabia a priority since returning to office.
In 2025, the United States agreed to sell the kingdom an arms package worth nearly US$142 billion, which the White House called “the largest defence cooperation agreement” Washington has ever done.
Congressional scrutiny could pose challenges to any F-35 sale.
Lawmakers previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh following the 2018 murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, and some members of Congress remain wary of deepening military cooperation with the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia is pursuing ambitious economic and military modernisation plans under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 agenda.
The kingdom has sought to diversify its defence partnerships in recent years while maintaining its decades-long security relationship with Washington. REUTERS

Poll tracks Zelensky's trust rating amid corruption investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:52:23 UTC
03:52:23 KST

A poll conducted immediately after recent investigations by Ukraine's independent anti-corruption agencies found that President Volodymyr Zelensky's trust rating stands at 54%, the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) reported on Sept. 17.
The survey was taken between Aug. 21 and Sept. 10, during an investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO). The large-scale corruption scandal implicated senior officials from the Presidential Office, including former deputy head Iryna Mudra.
According to the KIIS poll, 54% of Ukrainians said they trusted Zelensky, while 41% said they did not trust him. Among respondents who trusted the president, 18% said they trusted him "fully," while the other 36% reported trusting him "somewhat."
Of those who said they did not trust Zelensky, 25% reported that they did not trust him at all while 16% said they "tend not to trust him."
Zelensky's trust rating was generally higher among women, young adults, military personnel, students, and people from Ukraine's central, northern, eastern, and southern regions.
Trust in the president was generally lower among men, people aged 45-59, western Ukrainians, and residents of Kyiv.
read also
The ratings show virtually no change from the previous month's poll results (55% trust, 40% do not trust), before the latest corruption scandal was brought to light.
KIIS Executive Director Anton Hrushetskyi, however, noted that "the cumulative negative impact" on Zelensky's trust ratings from multiple major corruption investigations involving figures linked to the president "could ultimately prove irreversible."
Trust in Zelensky has skyrocketed during certain moments of national unity, but those ratings fall over time and ongoing anti-corruption probes "are only cementing a critical attitude" toward Zelensky's office, Hrushetskyi said.
"(W)hile Ukrainians maintain their trust in the President as the nation's leader during this brutal war, they also expect appropriate decisions and actions — particularly regarding the fight against corruption and the making of sound personnel appointments," Hrushetskyi said.
KIIS also noted that while about have of the survey was conducted after the recent investigation into former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, the results do not take into account the events of Sept. 14, when the disgraced official attempted to launched a retaliatory attack on NABU and SAPO.

US approves visas for Iranian leaders to attend UN summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:52:00 UTC
03:52:00 KST

The Trump administration has granted visas to senior Iranian officials, including the country's president and foreign minister, to attend next week's U.N. General Assembly high-level meetings in New York despite the ongoing war between Washington and Tehran.
The State Department said Thursday that it had approved visas for Iran's "core delegation," along with essential staffers to participate in the U.N. meetings. The core delegation includes President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, according to U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to visa privacy laws.
"Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend U.N. General Assembly High Level week. The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year," the statement said.
The move is unusual due to the more than six-month-long conflict between Iran and the United States and no sign that agreements to reopen the Strait of Hormuz or return to talks on Iran's nuclear program are close. It also comes as Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have stepped up attacks on Saudi infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea, another major maritime route in the region where impediments have helped drive a surge in global oil prices.
In addition, Iran remains the world's leading state sponsor of terrorism, according to the United States, which has imposed significant sanctions against the country and launched a new campaign in recent weeks aimed at severing "critical financial lifelines."
As the host country for the United Nations headquarters, the U.S. is generally limited in what it can do to prevent foreign leaders from coming to the General Assembly. However, it has in the past denied visas to - or discouraged applications from - leaders involved in active conflicts with the United States.
For last year's U.N. meetings of world leaders - which took place before the Iran war began on Feb. 28 but after the U.S. and Israel launched air strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025 - the State Department also approved a limited number of visas for Iranian diplomats but also imposed rigid restrictions on the delegation's movements.
Those included severe limitations on how far Iranian officials could travel in New York City from their U.N. mission and barred them from shopping at wholesale membership stores, such as Costco and Sam's Club.
The decision on the Iranian visas was announced just a day after the State Department denied visas to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and his delegation to come to the General Assembly.
"Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level week," the State Department said. "The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year."
The department accused the Palestinian Authority - which administers parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank - of trying to "internationalize" the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza by bringing cases to the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court as well as continuing to pay stipends to prisoners jailed in Israel for attacks on Israelis.
The Palestinian Authority condemned the move and called Israel's actions "the real threat to the two-state solution and prospects for peace." It also said it remained committed to long-stalled negotiations but defended its efforts to gain Palestinian recognition through international bodies and courts.
"Punitive measures and restrictions imposed on Palestinian officials do not contribute to advancing peace or combating violence," the authority's foreign ministry said in a statement. "Rather, they weaken the Palestinian partner committed to a political solution and encourage forces working to undermine the two-state solution and impose the reality of occupation, settlement and annexation by force."
The U.S. does not recognize the Palestinian Authority as a full member of the United Nations, although the General Assembly and certain U.N. agencies and bodies have done so.

Labor pounces on migration problems, but leaves massive wedge for critics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:48:00 UTC
03:48:00 KST

analysis
Tony Burke delivers overdue migration policy, but is it sturdy enough to withstand critics?
Tony Burke was late to the National Press Club to announce the government's migration policy on Thursday.
Six weeks late, to be precise.
After the embarrassment of having to abort his earlier press club appearance, followed by senior ministers faffing around over the details, and unsuccessful negotiations between government and opposition, Burke produced a package that, on his own admission, did not include everything he'd wanted.
It attacks some problems. But the government will be wedged between those who think the changes don't go far enough and critics who believe they're draconian.
The government will stop the entry of most overseas students' families, which will make life harder for some and, presumably, discourage others from coming at all. Universities will be concerned.
Working holiday-makers wanting to stay two or three years will face the luck of the draw, under a new ballot system.
Only 5,000 will get a third year, compared to 31,000 last year. Some farmers and businesses in regional areas looking for labour will be worried.
A proposed "No Further Stay" condition for visitor visas is a blunt instrument, but it aims to address a major loophole being exploited.
Burke candidly anticipated he'll come under attack for toughening compliance measures, with greater use of detention as the government tries to deport overstayers.
But again, a substantial challenge remains in a system where enforcement has become too loose.
Delicate balance on numbers
The measures won't satisfy those who desire a much smaller migration program.
They are about achieving the budget target of 225,000 Net Overseas Migration (NOM) by 2027–28, not going lower.
Voters wanting a substantially bigger squeeze on total intake will still look to One Nation, or wait for the Coalition, which is still wrestling with its own alternative.
In terms of numbers, it's a delicate balance. As Burke told parliament: "If you make cuts too deep, too hard in the immigration system, you trash the Australian economy."
The government's changes to prioritise skilled workers in vital areas such as health care and construction will be well received. This should have been done years ago.
Equally, the crackdown on "rogue" migration agents is long overdue.
Burke would have liked to act against those he called "disingenuous protection claims" — people who, coming to the end of their visa hopping, launch a protection claim that might give them "up to nine years working in Australia" while their appeals drag on.
"To give a sense of the gravity of this, if we took the people who apply from countries where more than 85 per cent of the applications fail, that constitutes 80 per cent of our caseload. This is an issue I'd like to be able to deal with."
But that needs legislation, and no agreement was reached in two recent meetings between Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor.
With One Nation effectively "owning" the immigration issue on the right these days, the opposition would like to move on from it, but eventually felt it could not afford to give too much ground to Labor.
One wonders, however, if the government should not have just included the measure to deal with bogus claims, to see whether the opposition might give in under parliamentary pressure.
Loading
Untidy handling from Burke
Burke's belated appearance came days after One Nation did its pre-emption act, with its own policy launched on Monday — albeit a plan that has been blasted by opponents, stakeholders and many experts.
Inside and outside Labor, Burke's untidy handling of what is a central issue has had some people scratching their heads.
When he was installed in the home affairs portfolio, replacing Clare O'Neil, who'd struggled in the job, Burke was widely seen as both competent and the classic "safe pair of hands".
After all, he's one of the elite group competing to lead Labor eventually.
Burke's mistake was getting ahead of his colleagues by lining up the press club before the policy process had been finalised.
When the draft went to senior ministers, they had issues.
Burke was reluctant to cancel his speech, which made the last-minute pull-out look worse.
Reports of a big split between Burke and Treasurer Jim Chalmers over the policy were overblown; indeed, Chalmers tried to facilitate Burke's attempt to meet his initial timetable.
But Chalmers's general stance on immigration is very forward-leaning, putting him close to that of South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas, who recently warned about "the prospect of mainstream politics entering a political race to the bottom for who can cut migration numbers the most".
The migration policy changes proposed by the various parties will have big fallouts for stakeholders and the economy. But many discontented voters may just make their judgements on the bottom line numbers.
It doesn't take the ubiquitous opinion polls to tell us the electorate is in a very bad mood, with angst about immigration just one strand in this.
Within Labor they talk about the mid-term blues. They've been in this territory before, of course — remember, quite close to the last election, the government's very future appeared at possible risk. Now it has a huge majority to protect it.
On the other hand, in previous difficult times, One Nation hadn't become the mini-monster now confronting both conservative and Labor parties.
On Monday the government will release the latest Intergenerational Report, which charts the economic and budgetary challenges for the coming four decades.
These are formidable, especially for a country with fundamental problems, notably a seeming inability to boost productivity and the pressures of an aging population.
The challenges of the future 40 years will seem theoretical to many people, given how quickly things change.
Forty years ago, the power of social media and AI, which obsess us now, was well over the horizon.
What won't pass people by is another rise in interest rates, at present considered a high prospect when the Reserve Bank meets at the end of this month.
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.
