Supertankers in super demand amid US-Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:57:49 UTC
23:57:49 KST

Shipowners have already ordered more than twice as many supertankers this year as in all of 2025, a buying spree worth over $20 billion that is the biggest in at least 25 years, as the US-Iran war redraws trade routes and boosts demand for long-haul crude shipments.
Data from Signal Group, a shipping analytics platform, show 217 Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) ordered so far in 2026, against 93 last year. Allied Shipbroking recorded 164 VLCC orders, up from 83. 
A VLCC, or a supertanker, carries about two million barrels of oil.
The spree signals growing acceptance that oil will continue to travel longer distances from the Atlantic basin as buyers diversify away from Middle Eastern sources and also reflects a broader expectation among shipowners that long-haul oil trade will remain resilient, despite the transition away from fossil fuels.
"We believe owners betting on increased long-haul shipments from the Atlantic to Asia are playing a large part in the renewed demand for VLCC ordering," said Rebecca Galanopoulos, senior analyst at the shipping analytics firm Veson Nautical.
Hormuz closure
Asian and European refiners are having to replace supplies lost by the virtual closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies passed before the war between the US and Iran.
US crude exports have hit record highs, and other Atlantic Basin suppliers are boosting output. 
Countries on the east coast of South America, led by Brazil, Guyana and Argentina, will drive further export growth, said Ioannis Papadimitriou, analyst at Vortexa, a data intelligence firm.
"Regional production could grow by around 2.5 million barrels per day through 2030, largely feeding European and Asian markets and favouring longer-haul trades," he said, adding that he also sees expectations growing of longer-haul trades on bigger vessels.
Demand for VLCCs and smaller Suezmax tankers is also being driven by the growing need to shuttle oil out of the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz to reload onto larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.
Middle Eastern producers find shipowners are unwilling to run the gauntlet of Iranian attacks by taking oil through the strait and have decided they need to own vessels themselves.
And now that a Saudi pipeline taking oil west to the Red Sea has been damaged, "Saudi Arabia will need to participate in this business to a much greater degree at least temporarily," Lars Barstad, CEO of the tanker group Frontline, told a conference in Norway.
High demand
Since the pipeline was hit in a drone attack, the cost of shipping oil in the largest tankers has hit record highs. VLCC spot prices recently climbed above $500,000 per day from about $132,000 in February, before the war, Allied Shipbroking said.
Shuttling oil out of the Gulf to transfer onwards ties up vessels and adds waiting times, further spurring demand for vessels.
Demand is now so high that brokers at Pareto Securities, who hosted the conference, estimated that it is now more expensive to buy a 10-year-old oil tanker than to order a new one.
Each VLCC costs about $130 million to build, according to Allied Shipbroking.
The ordering wave is not solely a bet on future oil flows.
After years of crisis and oversupply, renewal has become increasingly urgent, with around 20 percent of the VLCC fleet more than 20 years old, according to Veson Nautical.
Recent contracts include ships for delivery in 2029 and 2030, indicating owners are confident that demand will last into the medium term, said Pavlos Fakinos, freight market analyst at Allied Shipbroking.
Even old VLCCs are finding takers rather than being scrapped, according to data intelligence firm Kpler, populating the "shadow fleet" of vessels used to transport sanctioned oil outside mainstream shipping and insurance systems.

Zelensky appoints new chief prosecutor after predecessor's corruption scandal

Zelensky appoints new chief prosecutor after predecessor's corruption scandal
- Published
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has appointed a new acting prosecutor general, after the predecessor resigned over an anti-corruption investigation.
Anton Kovalskyi, 42, was appointed on Thursday to replace Ruslan Kravchenko, who stood down last week following searches of his offices by Ukrainian anti-corruption officials related to illegal call centres in the country.
Officials said they identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in Kravchenko's office, a claim he rejected.
The investigation into Kravchenko's office is the latest corruption scandal impacting Kyiv during the war against Russia. Accusations have been levelled at several members of Zelensky's inner circle.
According to Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (Sap), the network in Kravchenko's office received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and "laundered millions in assets".
The money was then used to buy property, jewellery, and other valuables, according to Nabu.
Kravchenko released a statement denying any involvement and dismissing the allegations as "completely unsubstantiated". He resigned a day later before leaving Ukraine.
He also alleged documents were stolen during the search of his office with the aim of covering up criminal investigations against anti-corruption officials themselves.
Separately, he accused Nabu chief Semen Kryvonos of forging documents in a case nearly 20 years ago.
Both Nabu and Sap denied Kravchenko's claims, while Kryvonos dismissed them as "nonsense" and criticised "fierce" attempts to disrupt corruption probes.
The two anti-corruption agencies claimed it was the latest in an "unprecedented" campaign aimed at disrupting high-profile investigations they were conducting.
Nabu's Kryvonos also claimed that anti-corruption detectives, their offices and vehicles were under surveillance, without giving specific accusations.
He added: "It all looks like an attempt to obstruct the work of Nabu and Sap by gaining access to sensitive information regarding planned investigations."
Nabu and Sap are currently investigating a number of top Ukrainian officials including Zelensky's former chief of staff Andriy Yermak, former ministers and other influential people. Yermak's lawyer has described the allegations against the former official as "baseless".
In 2025, nationwide protests broke out after Zelensky tried to implement reforms that would curb the independence of Nabu and Sap. Zelensky later reinstated their freedom but questions have remained over his commitment to anti-corruption reform.

We are paying a high price for a university education | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:52:19 UTC
23:52:19 KST

Having read Zoe Williams’ article on student loans (Why has university become such a scam?, 14 September), I went and checked my student loan statement. What a depressing read that was. I went to university in 2012 as a slightly older student, at 22. I had been to drama school before that, but decided I wasn’t cut out for the harsh reality of show business and that a law career – a barrister perhaps – was more up my street. I wanted to keep the performance element.
After one law degree totalling £56,000, a career development loan of £15,000 to cover the cost of my bar course and a £12,000 postgraduate loan to cover my legal practice course (solicitor training), my student debt remains at £70,000.
I am now a solicitor for the NHS, working four days a week to manage childcare costs. The £150 in loan repayments out of my salary each month mean very little when £1,500 is added in interest each year. That £150 could instead be going into the pocket of my landlord as he hikes the rent again or towards the high private nursery fees for my son so that I can go to work. When his time comes to consider higher education, I will very much be encouraging an alternative route. 
Nerys Cookson-Williams
Llandogo, Monmouthshire
As the mother of a new undergraduate, the student loans farce makes me livid. With about £24bn paid out yearly and only around £5bn returned in repayments, it will never pay for itself, so why put young people through this horrific system?
More importantly, it’s working-class and middle-class young people who are affected by what has effectively become another tax – as the rich don’t need loans, they aren’t affected by it. Until this is sorted, universities will once again become inaccessible to the majority of young people. Surely free university education for all is the way forward, alongside a fresh focus on vocational training?
Emily Miller
Mildenhall, Suffolk
Zoe Williams is right to highlight the scandal of student debt. However, it is even more sinister when you consider the free labour propping up the NHS. Last month, after three thankless years, I finished my final 12.5-hour night shift as a student midwife. Having worked tirelessly for over 2,300 unpaid hours, I am graduating into unemployment with a £50,000 debt and a heavy heart.
Universities continue to host large cohorts of midwifery students, each paying £9,750 per year for the privilege, despite the crisis in recruitment. NHS trusts are paid to host students who work gruelling hours for no pay. This is nothing short of exploitation. 
Zoe Green
London
I wholly agree that students are being done a huge disservice. But as an employer, I disagree with casually blaming employers for the drop in graduate jobs. First, the economy is in the doldrums and the cost of employment has risen. With low growth the default, when national insurance goes up it directly hits our margins and reduces the amount of new starters we can afford to take on or pay rises we can afford.
The courses that students pay a fortune for are also a problem. As a digital marketing employer, digital marketing degrees are not desirable. An education system that delivers more capable staff, or incentivises employers to provide them with meaningful training, would do wonders for graduate recruitment.
Name and address supplied
With regard to the unfairness heaped on today’s graduates, there is a simple answer out there – a (smaller) graduate tax on all graduates. If all graduates are asked to share the burden, the marginal tax rate could fall to 3% or 4%. Most, if not all, those currently paying student loans would favour it (with the option of staying on the current plan to anyone who has repaid in full or is about to), and it would be likely to appeal to many older graduates with children or grandchildren caught up in the current system.
Anyone who says this is impractical because there is no list of all graduates is being disingenuous. The Student Loans Company has lists of all graduates since 1998; a tick box on self-assessment forms would cover millions more, and asking employees to self-declare via their employer’s PAYE scheme would do likewise. Sufficient penalty deterrents could mop up most of the remainder. Given current funding solutions for higher education are generally considered a mess by all interested parties, I’m surprised that this hasn’t been given wider consideration.
Alan Terry
Exeter

Crans-Montana memorial ceremony planned for January 1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:52:13 UTC

Crans-Montana memorial ceremony planned for January 1
A memorial service to honour and remember the victims of the Crans-Montana fire will be held on January 1, 2027, exactly one year after the tragedy. The tribute is being organised by the Canton of Valais, in collaboration with the municipality of Haut-Plateau.
“The aim of the ceremony is to show that the victims and their loved ones have not been forgotten,” the President of the cantonal government, Christophe Darbellay, told Keystone-ATS news agency. “The lives of all these people have been marked forever. We cannot give them back what they have lost, but we can once again show them our solidarity. We want to tell them that we have not forgotten them,” he said.
+ Rehabilitation underway for Crans-Montana fire victims
One year on from the tragic bar fire, the Canton of Valais will therefore organise a commemorative ceremony in collaboration with the municipality of Crans-Montana. This will be an opportunity to remember and publicly honour those affected by the tragedy, to show them respect and solidarity, and to ensure the event remains in the collective memory, the Canton explained in a statement on Thursday.
Gratitude to rescue teams
“The occasion will also be used to thank those who came to the rescue, as well as those who provided – and continue to provide – care,” the statement added.
The ceremony will take place on 1 January 1, 2027 at 10:00 am in the sports hall of the Crans-Montana Conference Centre. The relatives of those who died in the fire, as well as those who were injured and their families, will be invited to attend. Those who provided rescue and medical assistance will also be represented. The gathering will take place in the presence of federal, cantonal, municipal and foreign officials.
Beyond the personal ordeal endured by the victims of the tragedy, these various stages of commemoration aim to foster reflection, remembrance and solidarity at a collective level. With this tribute, the Canton of Valais is embarking on a process of remembrance that will continue with the creation of a memorial, the development of which is being led by an independent civil society organisation. “Memory is a common good that it is up to us to preserve together,” emphasises Christophe Darbellay.
The fire at the Le Constellation bar claimed 41 lives and left 115 people injured. Given its scale and the young age of the victims, the tragedy left a deep mark on people’s minds in Valais, across Switzerland and within the international community.

A fresh approach to supporting unpaid carers | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:51:54 UTC
23:51:54 KST

Patrick Butler’s article on the rising number of people leaving employment to provide unpaid care resonated with me, both as an unpaid carer and as a researcher in this field (About 1,500 Britons a day quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers, 16 September). The juggle between paid work and caring responsibilities is a daily reality for millions. The report from Carers UK is a welcome reminder of this often-hidden issue, highlighting not only the growing care needs of older people but also the increasing numbers of younger people who rely on unpaid care. The midwife Jacqui Hylton’s observation in the article that caring for her mother is “harder than working in the NHS” deserves serious attention.
What is often missing from these debates, however, is recognition of the diversity and number of caring responsibilities. There is no such thing as a typical unpaid carer. Caring roles vary enormously, whether supporting a disabled child, a working-age adult with a progressive condition or an older relative with dementia.
Caring is also not fixed. There can be the onset of caring, often triggered by illness or crisis; ongoing care; and the end of caring, each with implications for work and financial security. Some people leave work to provide care and struggle to re-enter the workforce when caring ends. Others remain employed, but find the demands of combining work and care unsustainable.
These experiences reflect variations in the intensity and duration of care, the availability of support, the flexibility of employers and the nature of work. Social care reform must engage with these complexities. Politicians must recognise not only the value of unpaid carers but also the diversity of caring experiences. Effective support requires a more nuanced approach than policies built around a single model of care.
Dr Louise Lawson
Lecturer in social policy, University of Glasgow

'Sanctions from Hell' — Can West finally choke off Kremlin's war machine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:51:51 UTC
23:51:51 KST

'Sanctions from Hell' — Can West finally choke off Kremlin's war machine?
A top view of a Transport Loader for the Iskander-M missile system during the Victory Day Parade in Moscow, Russia, on May 9, 2015. (Wikimedia)
Viktoriia Vyshnivska
Senior Researcher at the Independent Anti-Corruption Commission
The U.S. House of Representatives just voted on sweeping new sanctions aimed at putting further pressure on Russia's economy and its war machine, including measures targeting Moscow's energy sector, defense industry, "shadow fleet" and foreign networks helping it evade sanctions.
The effectiveness of these measures, however, will ultimately depend on how consistently they are enforced and how actively and responsibly U.S. President Donald Trump uses the authorities they provide.
The legislation, known as the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, would give President Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue buying Russian oil and gas. It would also expand sanctions against Russian officials and entities, foreign suppliers and companies involved in sanctions evasion, while tightening export controls and restricting new U.S. investment in Russia.
The measure has been described as Graham's "sanctions from Hell" bill, reflecting his push for tougher economic pressure on Moscow. It also seeks to extend sanctions on Iran and impose secondary penalties on entities helping Russia or Iran evade restrictions.
The bill gives the United States a stronger way to act on what years of sanctions-evasion investigations have already shown: export controls are only as effective as the supply chains around them.
By creating sanctions exposure for foreign companies and intermediaries that continue to supply Russia's defense industry, the legislation extends pressure beyond Russia itself and into the trading networks that sustain its military production.
In practice, it should turn supply-chain enforcement into a form of secondary sanctions, raising the cost of doing business with Russia's defense industry even for companies operating far beyond Russia's borders.
Our new analysis illustrates the problem through one of Russia's most important ballistic missiles: the 9M723 Iskander-M.
We found that 78% of the identified microelectronic components in the missile's inertial navigation system were made in the United States.
The finding points to a contradiction at the heart of Russia's effort to build a self-sufficient defense industry. Moscow has invested heavily in "import substitution" since its invasion of Ukraine, but the production of sophisticated weapons still depends on access to foreign electronics.
The Iskander-M is one of Russia’s principal ballistic weapons. Since the beginning of 2026, Moscow has launched more than 500 ballistic missiles against Ukraine, while Kyiv's military intelligence estimates that Russia can produce more than 200 cruise and ballistic missiles of various types each month, with Iskander-M missiles among its production priorities.
The missile's navigation system is particularly important because the 9M723 is guided throughout its flight and can maneuver along its trajectory. Its guidance architecture combines inertial navigation, satellite correction, and, in some configurations, terminal optical guidance.
That system remains heavily dependent on foreign electronics.
Of the identified components in the Iskander-M's inertial navigation system, 78.1% were of U.S. origin, compared with 9.4% from Japan, 6.3% from Taiwan, and 6.3% from Switzerland.
There are a few American companies that form the majority of key American exporters that rely on despite the international efforts to choke the flow of Western components into Russian killing machines.
Among them are Analog Devices, accounting for 40% of the identified U.S.-origin components in the system, and Texas Instruments, which accounts for another 12%. The remaining 48% is spread across 11 other U.S. manufacturers.
The finding does not necessarily mean American companies are knowingly supplying Russia's military. We do not have any evidence that these manufacturers are directly selling components to the Russian defense industry.
Instead, we can draw the conclusion that there is a complex international supply chain of intermediaries and sanction-evasion networks that help Russians get the parts they need.
The limits of Russian "import substitution"
Moscow has made replacing foreign components a major industrial priority since the invasion of Ukraine, and the strategy has produced results in some areas.
Our earlier analysis of Russia's Oreshnik missile found a much more localized production ecosystem, dominated by older low- and medium-complexity semiconductors manufactured in Russia and Belarus.
The Iskander-M presents a different picture, though, with 65% of the missile's components being foreign-made.
The difference illustrates an uneven pattern in Russia's defense production. Moscow does not necessarily need Western technology for every part of a missile. But it remains particularly dependent on foreign electronics for functions like signal processing, computing, and reliable power.
The Iskander's navigation system is a case in point.
That makes sanctions aimed at supply networks as important as restrictions on individual components, because even if we prevent Western-made microelectronics from being exported directly to Russia, the companies, intermediaries, and illicit financial networks are still there to facilitate their transfer to Moscow's factories.
The same problem can also be seen across Russia's wider weapons arsenal, not just Iskander missiles.
In August, Ukrainian intelligence officials showed diplomats samples of foreign-made components recovered from Russian missiles, drones, and other weapons. Ukrainian intelligence said it had identified 5,816 foreign components in 202 Russian weapons systems, with the database continuing to expand.
Among the examples displayed to diplomats was an Nvidia Jetson Orin computer module recovered from Russia's S-71 Monochrome cruise missile. Ukrainian intelligence said the component could indicate the use of artificial-intelligence technologies in the weapon.
An inertial module containing components from Texas Instruments and Japan's TDK was also displayed.
The clock is running
Ukraine's urgency is increasing as Russia continues to expand its missile arsenal.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in August that Russia had an estimated 600 to 630 ballistic missiles and could potentially reach production of as many as 1,300 ballistic missiles a year, although it had not yet reached that rate.
That makes the law's supply-chain provisions particularly important.
Their value lies primarily in raising the cost of supplying them to foreign companies and intermediaries, affecting companies outside Russia that continue to provide critical goods to Russia's defense industry.
The ultimate goal need not be to stop Russia from producing missiles altogether, but we should make the global supply networks that enable Russia to produce increasingly sophisticated weapons at scale more costly, risky, and difficult to operate.
Applying these provisions aggressively would turn one of Russia's strengths — the resilience of its international procurement networks — into a vulnerability.
Whether the bill disrupts Russia's military supply chains, however, will depend on how fully and forcefully the Trump administration puts it to use.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

Children’s care homes rely on committed people | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:51:32 UTC
23:51:32 KST

I congratulate the Guardian and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism for exposing the disgraceful state of residential childcare and the use of illegal children’s homes (Councils pay more than £125m a year placing vulnerable children in illegal care homes in England, 8 September). However, this is a symptom not a cause.
While there are good private children’s homes (I’ve worked with some), they are defined by personal and family commitment, not profit. The same relationships are required whoever runs a children’s home, whether a charitable organisation or local authority. Without the personal, unflinching commitment of councillors, managers, social workers and, crucially, the grownups who work in the home, it can’t be a loving home.
We have been led to believe that regulation and inspection ensure good care. Do they? No. A reliance on such “quality” standards and monitoring has in part led us to this absurd situation. These profit generators are a result of our reluctance to accept the responsibility and risks of giving children love and real care. Things will go wrong, they do in any home, and often it’s putting things right again that produces the greatest therapeutic effect.
Homes are not created by rules and regulations, but by families and communities, ie people. No good home exists without direct, personal commitment and relationships, and the internal and external organisation that enables and supports such relationships. 
John Burton
Author, Leading Good Care

Money in people’s pockets is the key to economic recovery | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:50:43 UTC
23:50:43 KST

Neil Kinnock’s timely letter (9 September) reminds us that we are not alone in suffering high gilt yields and borrowing costs. We are still feeling the fallout from Covid, and it needs mentioning that our national debt is similar to America’s and much less than Japan’s, and it never gets mentioned that Italy routinely runs 100% of GDP debt. But as Kinnock observes, the policies of several Conservative governments (including Brexit) have made things worse, and the problem for us is not so much the actual debt but our direction of travel. The aforementioned will make the bond markets view us with a more jaundiced eye.
It was predictable that Jamie Dimon would pop up at this point (JP Morgan boss meets Burnham and Healey to warn against bank tax rise, 10 September). He talks about potential lack of investment by the banks. What investment? We aren’t even a nation of shopkeepers any longer; we’re a nation of pizza deliverers.
The economist JK Galbraith comes to mind here. He said that when push comes to shove, it’s the regular spendings of the working masses that keep the high street going. The spendings of the mega-rich involve either luxury goods or investment in plant, both of which are erratic and subject to the ups and downs of the economic cycle. Some might say, after the events of 1990 and 2008, that the banks have more money than is good for them.
Money in people’s pockets and the confidence to spend it has always been the recipe for recovery. Might we start by housing policies to reduce the 40% of rent that many are paying out of their salary? And a bedroom tax for the rich to make better use of the existing housing stock? You can go on raising the minimum wage, but you’re simply chasing your tail. 
David Redshaw
Saltdean, East Sussex

Mendoza said the Philippines is also looking for knowledge and technology transfer in AI e-commerce, infrastructure and smart cities at the expo.
"The Philippines recognizes the transformative potential of AI, and we are eager to deepen cooperation with China, which is cutting-edge in the field," she said, adding that China's experience can contribute to industrial upgrade and human capacity building in the Philippines. ■

Bulgaria has highest income inequality in the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:50:40 UTC
23:50:40 KST

Thursday 17 September 2026 15:56
Thursday, 17 September 2026, 15:56
PHOTO Eurostat
Font size
Bulgaria was the country with the highest income inequality in the EU in 2025, with a Gini coefficient of 37.7, compared to the EU average of 29.2. This is according to the Eurostat report "Key figures on European living conditions – 2026 edition," as reported by BTA. The country also records the highest share of employed persons at risk of poverty, while more than three-quarters of the population live in households experiencing at least some difficulty covering their expenses.
The Gini coefficient measures inequality in the distribution of income on a scale of 0 to 100, where zero represents complete equality and 100 represents complete inequality. Following Bulgaria, the highest values in 2025 were recorded in Latvia (35.6) and Lithuania (35.5). Income is most evenly distributed in Slovakia, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Slovenia, and Poland, where the indicator is below 25. At the same time, Bulgaria is among the countries that have seen a significant long-term increase in real incomes.

Miglena Ivanova

BERLIN, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Germany head coach Jurgen Klopp has named 44 players across two squads for the opening four fixtures of the UEFA Nations League, handing first senior call-ups to 11 newcomers as he unveiled his maiden selection at the DFB Campus in Frankfurt on Thursday.
The unusual arrangement comes as FIFA introduces a 16-day, four-match international window in late September and early October starting in 2026, replacing the previously separate September and October windows. A group of 24 players will assemble first, with the other 20 joining after the second game as most of the original selection return to their clubs.
Among the first-time call-ups are Augsburg defender Hennes Behrens, Hoffenheim's Bambase Conte and Frankfurt forward Younes Ebnoutalib. Freiburg supplies four newcomers in Max Rosenfelder, Philipp Treu, Yannik Engelhardt and Derry Scherhant, while Stuttgart's Finn Jeltsch, a U17 world and European champion, Brentford's Vitaly Janelt, a U21 European champion, Elversberg's Felix Keidel and Celtic's Mika Baur complete the group.
In total, 16 of the 44 players are yet to make a senior appearance for Germany. In goal, Klopp has turned to Marc-Andre ter Stegen following Manuel Neuer's retirement. The Ajax Amsterdam goalkeeper, who was not part of Germany's World Cup squad, is playing regularly again, with Klopp naming him his No. 1 "for the moment." Stuttgart forward Deniz Undav, Hoffenheim goalkeeper Oliver Baumann and Galatasaray winger Leroy Sane were among those left out.
Alongside Ter Stegen, Finn Dahmen, Yann Aurel Bisseck, Josha Vagnoman, Anton Stach, Chris Fuhrich, Kevin Schade and Serge Gnabry return to the squad after missing the World Cup. Noah Atubolu, Jonathan Burkardt, Maximilian Mittelstadt, Ridle Baku, Brajan Gruda, Said El Mala, Tom Bischof and Karim Adeyemi will join for the second set of matches.
The players convene on Monday in Herzogenaurach before travelling to Amsterdam to face the Netherlands on September 24. Germany will host Greece in Augsburg three days later, Serbia in Munich on October 1 and Greece again in Thessaloniki on October 4.

Jailed PKK leader Ocalan assigned to formal role, Turkish official says
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:50:25 CST
23:50:25 KST

ANKARA, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Jailed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) leader Abdullah Ocalan will be given a role as a technical coordinator to oversee the group's disarmament and dissolution, a senior Turkish official said on Thursday.
Turkish Presidential Chief Advisor Mehmet Ucum told reporters in Ankara that Ocalan would serve on a newly formed state subcommittee, according to private broadcaster NTV.
The mechanism is part of a broader government framework known as the "Terror-Free Türkiye" process, in line with a landmark reintegration law for PKK militants adopted by Turkish lawmakers last August, a key step toward ending a decades-long conflict.
Ucum said the decision did not mean Ocalan would be released or granted special privileges.
"Whoever established the organization and made them use weapons is the one who will dissolve it," Ucum emphasized, according to NTV.
The PKK, which has waged an insurgency against the Turkish state since 1984, is designated as a terrorist organization by Türkiye, the United States, and the European Union.
In May 2025, the PKK announced its decision to disarm and disband following a call from its imprisoned leader Ocalan.
On Aug. 10, Türkiye's parliament approved a legal framework for the disarmament and reintegration of the PKK. ■

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- More than eight decades have passed, but Siow Zhao Di still remembers the day she lay motionless among the dead, too afraid to open her eyes.
"My grandmother, my sisters, my aunt and my mother -- they were all stabbed to death by the Japanese soldiers," said Siow, now in her 90s, recalling the massacre that devastated her village during the Japanese occupation of Malaya.
On Dec. 8, 1941, Japanese forces invaded what was then Malaya, beginning three years and eight months of Japanese occupation. During the occupation, Japanese forces carried out brutal "Sook Ching" massacres targeting the local community.
On March 18, 1942, Japanese troops carried out an indiscriminate massacre in the village of Yu Lang Lang (Jelundong) in Titi, Negeri Sembilan, and then set the village ablaze.
According to figures compiled by the local Chinese community, 1,474 unarmed civilians were killed that day, making it the deadliest single-day massacre of civilians during the Japanese occupation of Malaya.
Siow was still a child at the time. She remembered that on that day, Japanese soldiers deceived villagers into gathering at a school at the entrance to the village before taking them away in groups of more than a dozen.
Siow, together with her mother, neighbors and others, was taken to a house in the village.
"My mother was kneeling when they stabbed her. She pressed herself over me to shield me. The Japanese soldiers stabbed me in the leg and struck my uncle's head with an axe," Siow said.
As she spoke, she rolled up her trouser leg, revealing a scar left by the attack more than eight decades ago.
Not long afterward, some Japanese soldiers returned and patted the shoulders of villagers lying on the ground one by one to check whether anyone was still alive.
"I didn't dare move or open my eyes," Siow recalled. While the soldiers went to inspect other houses, an elderly woman from next door helped her escape.
"After checking, the Japanese soldiers set fire to the houses again," she said. Soon, the entire village was engulfed in flames.
The massacre at Yu Lang Lang did not take place in isolation.
"Chinese communities across Malaya were closely connected with China's resistance against Japanese aggression. Fundraising campaigns, charity performances and the Nanyang volunteers who returned to China to support the war effort all drew close attention from the Japanese forces," said Ong Leong Keat, a Chinese Malaysian historian in Negeri Sembilan.
Ong said Japanese forces carried out large-scale roundups and massacres in Singapore and Malaya, known as "screening" or "Sook Ching," mainly targeting ethnic Chinese suspected of supporting anti-Japanese activities.
"In reality, the victims also included the elderly, women and children. People could even become targets of massacre simply because they lived in villages regarded by the Japanese forces as 'suspicious,'" he said.
According to historical records, in March 1942 alone, Japanese forces carried out more than 20 massacres across Negeri Sembilan, killing nearly 5,000 people. Scholars in Malaysia and Singapore have noted that the actual death toll could have been higher due to the lack of complete written records.
The horrors of 84 years ago remain vivid in Siow's memory. Yet in Japan, she said, this chapter of history has long been downplayed or even denied.
"All these years, no matter how many times we tell the story, it seems to make no difference. The Japanese say they did not kill people in Malaya. They refuse to admit it," Siow said.
Siow and other survivors have recounted their experiences in interviews on numerous occasions, while some survivors have traveled to Japan to testify about the atrocities they witnessed.
For historians, preserving such testimony is particularly important as the number of surviving witnesses dwindles.
"A country and a society should honestly confront the wars of aggression they launched in the past and the harm those wars inflicted on civilians," said Tan Chee Seng, a senior lecturer in history at Universiti Sains Malaysia.
Tan noted that in 1995, the Japanese government's Murayama Statement explicitly expressed remorse and apologized for Japan's colonial rule and aggression.
"The question is whether those principles can be consistently reflected over the long term in history education, access to archives and research into specific historical events," he said.
In 1984, the Negeri Sembilan Chinese Assembly Hall established a committee to collect historical materials on the suffering of the Chinese community in Negeri Sembilan during the Japanese occupation. The committee documented accounts from survivors and victims' families, compiling them into a volume published in 1988.
When asked how she viewed Japan's attitude toward this history, Siow fell silent. Her eyes settled on a copy of the book.
"It's all true. Everything in this book is the truth," Siow said slowly. "Take this book to Tokyo and show it to them." ■

ULAN BATOR, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- The average age at first marriage in Mongolia has steadily increased over the past 25 years, reflecting a persistent shift toward later marriage and family formation, a study released by the country's National Statistics Office (NSO) showed.
In 2000, men in Mongolia married for the first time at an average age of 25.7, while women did so at 23.7. By 2025, those figures had risen to 29.5 and 27.5, respectively. This represents an increase of approximately 3.8 years in the average age at first marriage for both men and women over the 25-year period, according to the study.
NSO experts attribute the trend in part to greater access to education.
As young people spend more time pursuing higher education, gaining professional qualifications and establishing themselves in the labor market, they are increasingly postponing marriage and starting a family.
At the same time, changing social values and a growing emphasis on individual choice are also contributing to the trend, with people taking longer to make decisions about marriage and family formation. ■

ROME – Italian police have arrested 17 people in an investigation into an Italy-based international network that distributed child sexual abuse material online, Rome prosecutors said on Sept 17.
An undercover Italian officer gained the trust of the group’s administrators, becoming a co-administrator and gaining access to its private channels.
“This organisation was structured like a multinational company,” said Rome chief prosecutor Francesco Lo Voi.
The network was run by four Italians and a Swiss national.
Investigators have so far obtained about 283GB of illegal material, including more than 22,000 videos and 34,000 images of children as young as four.
The operation, named Fly Trap, led to a Telegram community called New Saga, which had more than 1,000 users worldwide and required payments in cryptocurrency.
Users seeking access had to pay small amounts described as “donations” of between US$3 (S$3.83) and US$9, or provide new material.
The Italian authorities identified 996 accounts linked to 98 countries and shared the information with foreign authorities, leading to a number of arrests.
The administrators, aged between 22 and 28, used a chat called La Sala dei Re (“Hall of Kings”) for internal communications.
Their roles ranged from managing groups and servers to moderating content and creating bots used to keep the community active when Telegram shut down a chat.
The investigation began in 2024 after a tip-off from the US Homeland Security Investigations and is ongoing. AFP

China faces oil challenge as prices soar and supply options narrow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:48:35 UTC
23:48:35 KST

China faces oil challenge as prices soar and supply options narrow
Beijing is drawing on vast reserves and seeking alternative crude as shipping disruption continues.
Oil prices in China have surged to record highs amid mounting disruptions to exports from the Middle East, as Beijing faces an increasingly difficult balancing act between securing its own energy supplies and preventing global oil prices from climbing even higher.
Saudi Arabia has been forced to shut a key pipeline that had become an important route for getting oil to China and other Asian markets while disruption in the Strait of Hormuz restricted exports through the Gulf. The pipeline, which carries crude across the Arabian Peninsula to the Red Sea, was shut following attacks by an Iran-backed group in Iraq.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4UK charities, protest groups: Israeli ban threat ‘will not intimidate us’
- list 2 of 4Lebanon security talks in Paris to focus on post-UNIFIL alternatives
- list 3 of 4Why is inflation rising again around the world?
- list 4 of 4What’s the Asian Games accommodation crisis, and where will athletes stay?
Its closure leaves two vital routes for Middle Eastern oil to China both disrupted in the midst of the US-Israel war on Iran and conflicts in the wider region. With access to Russian and Iranian crude also complicated by United States sanctions and other restrictions, Chinese refiners are being forced to search further afield for supplies. That scramble for available barrels is adding to pressure on oil prices, both in China and globally.
With China increasingly forced to compete for replacement supplies – risking pushing prices still higher – restoring oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has effectively blocked, has become a pressing economic and diplomatic priority for Beijing ahead of talks between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, say analysts. The meeting follows talks in Beijing on Wednesday between Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi.
“What is happening in the Middle East is not good for China,” energy analyst Marc Ayoub told Al Jazeera. “China is in a critical situation,” he said, with refiners increasingly “looking into the market for players outside of Hormuz”.
China helped absorb the first oil shock
Before the war, China was importing roughly 12 million barrels of crude a day and producing another 4.4 million barrels domestically, Reuters reported. It was buying more oil than its refineries needed, allowing Beijing to funnel some of the surplus into vast stockpiles that had grown to an estimated 1.4 billion barrels by the end of last year.
That helped cushion the impact on the wider oil market. As the world’s largest crude importer, China’s decision to buy fewer barrels removed demand at precisely the moment global supplies were being squeezed.
Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, told Al Jazeera, “It lies in their interests that this conflict the United States started does not lead to a global recession.”
“But that [China importing less oil] was not done to undermine the Iranians or help the Americans. The Chinese are pursuing their own interest, and their interest is that the rest of the world should not suffer economically, because if that happens it will backfire on China.”
Crude imports averaged just 8.1 million barrels per day in the second quarter – almost 4 million barrels per day, or 32 percent, lower than in the first three months of the year, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).
But those buffers are now being eroded, and Ayoub said the turnaround was being driven in part by Beijing’s decision to ease restrictions on refined-fuel exports, which had helped keep refinery activity low earlier in the war. “Independent refiners have started looking again for imports from elsewhere,” he said.
As refiners process more crude and stockpiles are drawn down, China is being pushed back into the market for more barrels. “First, they want to increase production from the refineries, and second, they want to build back their inventories,” Ayoub said.
“So the Chinese are trying to find whatever supplies they can get from the market.”
Where can China turn?
Russia is already China’s largest crude supplier, with much of its oil reaching China without passing through the maritime chokepoints disrupting Middle Eastern exports. Reuters reported that Russia supplied approximately 20 percent of China’s crude imports in 2025.
Russian ESPO crude shipped from the country’s Pacific coast can reach Chinese ports in less than a week, while oil also flows overland through pipelines. Chinese refiners have consequently scrambled for available Russian barrels, snapping up September and October ESPO cargoes unusually quickly, experts say.
US sanctions have complicated those purchases, but not stopped them. China’s seaborne imports from Russia reached 1.68 million barrels per day in August, up from 1.4 million in July and the highest since March, according to Kpler data. China also receives about one million barrels per day of Russian crude through pipelines.
Iran had also provided China with a major source of discounted, sanctioned oil before the war. China bought an estimated 1.4 million barrels per day from Iran last year, but those supplies have been sharply curtailed by the conflict and US efforts to block Iranian exports.
China can also look to producers in Latin America and Africa. Brazil was already among China’s five largest crude suppliers last year, and offered China 1.6 million barrels per day in March 2026. Meanwhile, countries including Venezuela, Angola and the Republic of the Congo have historically supplied Chinese refiners.
But there are limits to how easily those barrels can replace lost Middle Eastern supplies. Crude oil is not completely interchangeable, with Chinese refineries configured to process different grades, while substitutes can differ in density. Venezuelan crude, for example, is generally much heavier than the Russian ESPO crude Chinese refiners have been scrambling to secure.
Distance presents another constraint, with Russian ESPO reaching China in less than a week, while barrels brought across the Atlantic from Brazil, West Africa or elsewhere in the Americas face longer journeys and higher freight costs. And alternative producers have only finite amounts available to sell.
Kpler estimates that additional Russian and Iranian supplies can therefore only partially bridge China’s feedstock gap if disruption to Middle Eastern supplies persists.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, is trying to keep China supplied, with Saudi Aramco selling at least four million barrels to China in August. But this is only the equivalent of about 129,000 barrels per day when averaged across August.
How vulnerable is China, really?
China’s biggest vulnerability is the sheer size of the gap between the crude it produces and the amount its refineries process.
China produced about 4.34 million barrels per day in August, while its refineries processed 13.91 million, according to Chinese data cited by Reuters. That left a gap of roughly 9.6 million barrels per day that had to be filled by imports or inventories.
However, China is better placed to curb oil consumption than many other major economies. The rapid expansion of electric vehicles has weakened demand for petrol, while electrification has reduced oil use in other parts of the economy. Domestic crude production has also continued to edge higher.
But there are limits to this, with aviation, heavy transport and China’s vast petrochemical industry remaining heavily dependent on oil. So as China raises refinery output and seeks to replenish the stockpiles that helped shield it from the initial shock, it will still have to compete with other buyers for constrained supplies, adding further pressure to prices.
“For crude in particular, they are looking to get any supply that is available in the market out there,” Ayoub said. “That will add pressure, and that will increase prices more.”
The growing pressure on China’s oil supplies has also increased the stakes for Beijing diplomatically, with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi meeting his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, in Beijing on Wednesday, calling on Iran and the United States to return to negotiations and urging all parties to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to safeguard international energy supplies.
The talks came a week before an expected meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Washington. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the leaders would continue discussions on Iran and China’s financial ties with Tehran, with Beijing expected to press Washington to return to negotiations and help end the disruption to shipping and stabilise global oil markets.

Oliver Towfigh Nia
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
A person who contracted malaria in Frankfurt am Main has died, city officials announced on Thursday.
“The individual in question was one of the two cases reported earlier this week from the Schwanheim district who lived in the immediate vicinity of Frankfurt Airport. Both individuals were infected with the malaria pathogen Plasmodium falciparum, even though they had not previously traveled to a malaria-endemic area and had not worked at the airport,” the city of Frankfurt said in a statement.
According to the city’s public health department, the two newly infected individuals contracted the disease from a mosquito that had entered a flight bound for Frankfurt.
On Tuesday, the city had already reported two cases of malaria in that neighborhood. This brings the total number of malaria-related deaths linked to air travel in Frankfurt this year to three. Last summer, six employees of the airport operator Fraport contracted the disease and two died.
Frankfurt Airport operator Fraport, had reportedly set up mosquito traps at the airport and was having captured insects examined in a laboratory. Employees have been advised to seek medical care if they develop typical malaria symptoms and to inform doctors that they work at the airport.
The Frankfurt health office described the so-called “airport malaria” as a “very rare” form of transmission outside malaria-endemic areas. “Transmission from person to person plays no role in airport malaria,” a spokesperson said.
Malaria is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes that become infected themselves. The World Health Organization says the disease can be life-threatening if left untreated. Symptoms include fever, chills, headaches, confusion, seizures and breathing difficulties.

A fractured Union? Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland first ministers meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:47:48 UTC
23:47:48 KST

Tim Bale is a professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London and co-author of the book The British General Election of 2024.
Every now and then, the official designation, United Kingdom, can seem particularly inapposite. The relationship between its component parts – England (population 56.5 million), Scotland (5.5 million), Wales (3.1 million), and Northern Ireland (1.9 million) – is rarely as harmonious as that name suggests. So it was this week when the first ministers of the last three met to sign an agreement which committed each nation to determine its own future "in its own way and in its own time."
Scotland’s John Swinney even went so far as to deliberately and provocatively describe the UK’s new head of government, Andy Burnham, as the "last prime minister of the UK." Meanwhile, Northern Ireland’s Michelle O’Neill claimed it had the right to a referendum on unification with the Republic of Ireland (population 5.4 million), arguing: “We will not accept or tolerate any prime minister telling us that right is off the table.”
Weak support for Welsh independence
Wales’s Rhun ap Iorwerth, however, was noticeably less forthright, insisting only that “Wales should have the power, the resources, the fair treatment we need as a nation to build the future our people deserve.” Dodging questions about independence, ap Iorwerth merely reminded the assembled audience that there are “flexibilities that Scotland already has right now (that) as a minimum (should) be handed to Wales.”
His hesitation is a tacit acknowledgement there is relatively scant support for independence in Wales. Indeed, the latest poll, conducted this August, suggested that (after “don’t knows” were removed) only a third of Welsh voters would currently vote to leave the UK.
True, public opinion in Scotland is markedly different. But even there the latest poll, conducted this spring, suggested that those who want to leave the UK are outnumbered by those who want to remain by a margin of 56% to 44% – mirroring almost exactly the result of the independence referendum held back in 2014. The Scottish National Party that First Minister Swinney leads might be pushing for another vote but, whatever its representatives say in public, they cannot be confident in private that they would win it. Indeed, the serious hit to GDP suffered by the UK as a result of its decision to leave the EU would probably lend even more weight to their opponents’ argument that secession would be an economic disaster.
In any case, Swinney knows – not least because it was confirmed by a decision of the UK’s Supreme Court in 2022 – that, legally and constitutionally, the only legislature that can grant Scotland a referendum is not the Scottish but the UK’s 650-seat Parliament down in London – an institution in which, incidentally, some 57 Scottish MPs sit.
Sectarian divides in Northern Ireland
The situation in Northern Ireland is different again. The 1998 Belfast/Good Friday Agreement that helped end decades of violent conflict there does make provision for a border poll to be held should it look “likely” that there is majority support for Irish unification on both sides of the border. At the moment it does not.
True, there is little doubt that such a majority could be found in the Republic of Ireland – at least in theory (it is noticeable, for instance, that the Irish Taoiseach – prime minister – Micheal Martin, didn’t respond to President Donald Trump’s apparent support for a united Ireland by demanding a vote anytime soon). But the latest poll found that, in contrast to the two-thirds of voters in the republic who support unification, only just over a third of those in the North feel the same way – a proportion which, if anything, has declined rather than grown over the last 10 years and one which continues to reflect deep sectarian differences between the mainly Roman Catholic “nationalist” population and the mainly Protestant “unionist” population which remains wedded to its assertively British identity.
In any case, the decision to hold an Irish border poll lies legally not with the first minister of Northern Ireland but with the UK government’s secretary of state for Northern Ireland. And even if that were not the case (which it is), despite the hierarchy implied by their official positions, Northern Ireland’s first minister has no more authority than the deputy first minister, who, as a unionist, is determined that it should remain part of the UK.
Ultimately, by meeting this week and signing an agreement, the first ministers of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland had two main aims: 1) to reassure their supporters that they remain committed to the cause of independence and 2) to put pressure on a new British prime minister. The first aim may have been realized. But the second is highly unlikely to have had much effect: as a Number Ten Downing Street spokesman told journalists in the wake of their intervention, “The UK government is focused on addressing the issues that matter most to families … rather than engaging in constitutional debates or further referendums.”
In short, misnomer or not, the United Kingdom is going to be around for a few years yet.

Security for Ireland’s easy-access politicians dealt a blow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17

Security for Ireland’s easy-access politicians dealt a blow
Prime minister calls attack on lawmaker Michael Healy-Rae a watershed moment in a country where he and others ‘can walk through our streets unhindered.’
Irish armed police stand guard as EU foreign affairs ministers hold an informal meeting in Wicklow on September 2, 2026. | Paul Faith/AFP via Getty Images
DUBLIN — A bare-knuckled attack on one of Ireland’s best-known politicians has the country questioning how much longer its leaders can go about their business without security.
A Dublin man was arrested Thursday for allegedly assaulting Michael Healy-Rae as the independent lawmaker drove out of the capital back toward his distant County Kerry constituency.
Police said they had recovered video footage showing a man approach Healy-Rae, 59, as he was sitting in rush-hour traffic Wednesday behind the wheel of his Skoda, which was emblazoned with the politician’s name and constituency contact details.
Advertisement
Healy-Rae had his window rolled down and was talking on the phone to his son Jackie, a Kerry councilman, as a man walked into the road and started punching the politician in the face. While the attacker fled on foot, police helped Healy-Rae reach a nearby hospital to have his facial wounds stitched up.
Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the attack on Healy-Rae — who had been a junior minister in his coalition government before his surprise resignation in April — could mark a watershed in how Irish politicians operate in public.
“We’ve never had this before in our society,” said Martin, who has represented the southwest city of Cork in parliament since 1989.
Reflecting the relative informality and openness of Irish political life, the prime minister spent part of this own week pressing the flesh with thousands of farmers at the National Ploughing Championships, one of the country’s perennial events featuring face-to-face contact with politicians from all parties. But there, too, Martin, faced an attempted assault and a suddenly beefed-up security detail.
“Our democracy is relatively unusual in the sense that our members of parliament, and indeed ministers and myself, can walk through our streets unhindered,” said Martin, who called the attack on Healy-Rae “a significant moment that we have to take very seriously.”
Healy-Rae, who was recovering Thursday at his Kerry home, issued a statement vowing he would “not be deterred” from politics.
Advertisement
The flat-capped Kerryman, whose family has built a legendary political machine based on door-to-door house calls, appealed for “a serious conversation about the growing toxicity directed towards politicians and public representatives.”
His son, who heard the assault unfold live on their phone call, said many months of social media attacks, particularly by anti-immigrant extremists, were fueling vitriol against his father — examples of which can be readily seen in comments on many of Healy-Rae’s recent social media posts.
“Unfortunately it’s becoming more normal,” said Jackie Healy-Rae, who added: “I do honestly believe that it is only a matter of time before an Irish politician will be seriously injured or killed in this country.”
Bloodshed once was a feature of Irish political life. Dozens of politicians died during Ireland’s 1919-21 war of independence from Britain and the resultant civil war of 1922-23, most famously IRA chieftain-turned-dealmaker Michael Collins. Three more politicians in the Republic of Ireland were slain as part of the three-decade conflict over the neighboring U.K. territory of Northern Ireland. But that threat ended with the region’s mid-1990s paramilitary cease-fires capped by a 1998 peace accord.
Ireland’s government has been struggling since 2023 with a rise in street-level hostility against politicians, publishing findings that found particular hostility directed online against female lawmakers. It introduced reimbursements of up to €25,000 for beefing up security at politicians’ homes and constituency offices, where many of the country’s 174 members of the Dáil Éireann parliament meet weekly with the public to field their complaints.

Yemen sees attacks near Bab el-Mandeb, drone downed in Al-Dhalea, airstrikes reported in Taiz: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:47:43 UTC
23:47:43 KST

Mohammed Sameai and Lina Altawell
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
- Houthis report Saudi airstrikes on telecommunications towers in Taiz with no comment from Riyadh
- Fighting continues without decisive territorial changes, according to Anadolu monitoring of battlefronts
Military escalation between Yemeni government forces and the Houthi group continued in several provinces in recent hours Thursday, without decisive changes on the ground.
The sides exchanged attacks near the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea, while government forces reported shooting down an explosive-laden Houthi drone in the southwestern Al-Dhalea province. A government military commander and several soldiers were also reported killed in the central Marib province.
The Houthis, meanwhile, reported Saudi airstrikes targeting telecommunications towers in southwestern Taiz province, with no immediate comment from Riyadh.
The developments coincided with continued calm on the front in northern Al-Jawf province, where Anadolu's monitoring observed no new field developments.
Attacks near Bab el-Mandeb
In the latest developments, the government-aligned Giants Brigades said Thursday that they targeted Houthi positions and gatherings on the Kahbub front near Bab el-Mandeb.
The attack killed and injured several Houthi fighters, they claimed.
In a separate statement, the forces said they targeted a Houthi patrol on high ground overlooking the Kahbub area, killing everyone aboard. No further details were provided.
Explosive-laden drone downed
The Yemeni army-affiliated September Net website reported late Wednesday that government forces shot down a drone belonging to the “Iran-backed Houthi militia” on the Murais front in northern Al-Dhalea province.
The website, citing an unnamed military source, said the drone was carrying out a reconnaissance mission and carrying explosives when it was detected and brought down.
It was the second attempt in days that government forces had thwarted on the front, said the source.
Military commander killed
The Yemeni army announced Wednesday that Col. Ezzeddin Hamoud Hussein al-Zalil, commander of the 8th Missions Battalion of the 13th Infantry Brigade, and several other members of the brigade had been buried in Marib.
The soldiers were killed while fighting Houthi forces, but the army did not provide details on when or where they were killed, according to September Net.
Airstrikes reported in Taiz
The Houthi group, meanwhile, said Thursday that Saudi airstrikes targeted telecommunications towers in Taiz province.
The Houthi-run Saba news agency cited an unnamed source who said Saudi aircraft struck three telecommunications towers in the Al-Dhikra and Al-Hawban areas of Al-Taiziyah district and the Al-Rahida area of Khadir district.
It did not report casualties or damage from the strikes, while Saudi Arabia issued no comment.
Yemen’s territorial control has shifted in recent weeks, with the Houthis advancing along the western coast and announcing control of strategic areas in Hudaydah and Taiz, including the city of Mokha, as well as Red Sea islands including Mayyun Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Government forces, meanwhile, have advanced in Al-Jawf toward the provincial capital of Al-Hazm, while fighting continues on the Marib, Al-Dhalea and Taiz fronts alongside airstrikes on Houthi positions and movements in several areas.
The developments are part of a military escalation that began in early July, the most extensive after years of relative calm following an April 2022 truce. Fighting intensified further in September, particularly along the western coast and around Bab el-Mandeb.
Yemen has been gripped by war since the Houthis seized the national capital, Sanaa, and several provinces in September 2014. That prompted a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

As Charles refutes Earl Spencer’s claim about Diana, how royal statements give a glimpse behind palace doors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:47:02 UTC
23:47:02 KST

As denials go, King Charles’s response to Earl Spencer’s allegations that Charles said after Diana’s death, “We’ll forget her soon enough”, was a masterclass in the diplomatic royal rebuke.
Rarely has Buckingham Palace responded to claims in countless books on royalty. But it was straight out of the block on this one.
Little over an hour after the Daily Mail, which is serialising Spencer’s memoir Swan Song about his sister, the late Diana, Princess of Wales, had published its first extract online, a statement was issued.
Charles, the headline claimed, had told Spencer days after Diana’s death and during a heated row over funeral arrangements: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.”
The king’s swift countering, that “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”, will enter the canon of carefully constructed regal pushbacks.
As rebukes go, it is up there with the late Queen Elizabeth II’s “some recollections may vary” in response to a torrent of allegations from the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in their Oprah Winfrey interview.
Senior courtiers are often drawn from the diplomatic service and thus highly-skilled in couching the passive-aggressive denial. Deploying delicate language to devastating effect is a stock in trade at the Foreign Office.
But it is a weapon to be used sparingly. The royal mantra is, usually, “never complain, never explain”.
However, Charles’s former communications secretary Julian Payne said: “This is a much more personal situation, given its author, and therefore has a greater ability to do harm.”
That is why the palace “felt the need to set the record straight and deny these remarks have been made”, Payne told the BBC’s Today programme. Given the amount of things the palace don’t comment on, “you can imagine the strength of feeling”, he added.
Payne remains close to the king and was due to be sitting alongside him at Thursday’s AI summit just hours later, so the fact he felt able to speak so freely suggests his robust defence of Charles came with official sanction.
What is said behind palace doors usually remains private. The language may be less sensitive. But a carefully chosen phrase in public pulls back the privacy screen.
When Diana, in her highly controversial Panorama interview, said “there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded”, she reaped public revenge on her then husband and Camilla.
In return, Diana found herself on the sharp end of Elizabeth’s ire weeks later. After Diana failed to respond to the queen’s request that the couple divorce, a palace spokesperson issued a statement: “After considering the present situation, the queen wrote to both the prince and princess earlier this week and gave them her view, supported by the Duke of Edinburgh, that an early divorce is desirable.” The matter was now, officially, out of Diana’s hands.
White fury was behind the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s statement in February 2021: “We can all live a life of service. Service is universal.” It was read as a succinct and direct challenge to the late queen’s insistence they could not keep their public service roles after stepping down as working royals.
Meghan was less direct in a 2019 interview with ITV’s Tom Bradby in which he asked her if she was OK juggling life as a royal with a newborn, Prince Archie. “Thank you for asking, because not many people have asked if I’m OK,” she replied. Was it directed at the palace and the institution? A huge number of the claims the Sussexes later made, in TV interviews and in Harry’s memoir Spare, were that the duchess had been unsupported throughout her time as a working royal.
One royal famously deficient in the art of the diplomatic royal rebuke, however, was the late Duke of Edinburgh. Philip was renowned for his gaffes. When a BBC journalist politely asked the queen at a banquet at the Élysée Palace if she was enjoying her stay in Paris in 2006, Philip dispensed with tact to snap: “Damn fool question!”

Trump arch could have ‘adverse effects’ on nearby monuments but will proceed, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:46:53 UTC
23:46:53 KST

Donald Trump’s desired triumphal arch in downtown Washington DC will likely contribute “to adverse effects to historic properties”, according to the National Park Service’s planning document, but the construction is still planned to go forward.
The president’s 250ft arch could interfere with some of the most well-known views in the nation’s capital, including the symbolic relationship between Arlington House, the Arlington National Cemetery, the Arlington Memorial Bridge and the Lincoln Memorial, which face each other to represent the reunification of the United States after the civil war.
As a result, the arch’s construction could require supplemental planning and programming to preserve history, a document and emails obtained by the Washington Post on Wednesday outlined.
“Such adverse effects cannot be fully avoided while retaining the location-dependent purpose of the undertaking,” the National Park Service wrote in the document.
Despite concerns that the arch could interfere with historic sites and would require substantial construction management control, the Trump administration wants to move forward. The document was circulated among preservationists and other groups to review and sign by noon on Monday, according to an email obtained by the Washington Post.
The Guardian has asked the National Park Service for comment.
Historic preservationists, veterans and lawmakers have consistently raised concerns about the Trump administration building the massive triumphal arch in downtown DC.
Veterans filed a lawsuit in September, seeking to halt construction of the arch, believing it would harm the symbolic relationship of historic sites representing the reconciliation of war or disrupt burials at the Arlington National Cemetery.
Some lawmakers shared fears that the arch could further complicate DC’s airspace. But Trump has been emphatic about the arch, insisting it should be 250ft high to mark the US’s 250th anniversary.
Should construction of the arch move forward, the National Park Service outlined several ways it would mitigate disruptions and potential damage to nearby monuments.
That includes installing vibration plates near the Arlington Memorial Bridge and other sensitive sites to ensure construction remains within prescribed limits, enforcing limits on noise-generating activities, prohibiting unnecessary lighting, limiting work hours and more.
The National Park Service’s document outlined roughly 37 nearby historic sites that could be affected, including the Lincoln Memorial, the National Mall, the Washington Monument, the Pentagon, the US Capitol and more.
But the National Park Service also outlined methods it could implement to preserve the history of the area, such as developing digital programs to explain the commemorative relationship between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, to show before-and-after scenes of the skyline over the Potomac River, and to describe the significance of triumphal arches.
Local preservation officers could refuse to sign the agreement, which could trigger another process that involves the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, a federal agency.
However, the Trump administration does not need the preservationists’ consent to move forward because it already received approval from the US Commission on Fine Arts, a federal advisory council made up of Trump appointees, and preliminary approval from the National Capital Planning Commission.

West is preparing for war with Russia: Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:44:20 UTC
23:44:20 KST

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said that Western countries were preparing for war with Russia while promoting what he called “a myth about a threat emanating from Russia”.
Lavrov said on Thursday that Russia would be able to respond adequately to external challenges to its security.
“Today, the ruling circles and elites of most Western countries are promoting a myth about a threat emanating from Russia, actively preparing for war against our country and condemning us, among other things, for undermining European values,” he said at the opening of the fourth congress of the International Russophile Movement in Moscow.
Lavrov contrasted the approach of US officials with that of European leaders, saying Washington was prepared to maintain dialogue even when the sides held fundamentally different positions.
“There is an important difference between the US and European elites. They are ready to talk. Even when positions are radically, diametrically opposed, it is always important,” he said.
He said Moscow was open to serious discussions with officials prepared to engage, adding that foreign officials should not visit Russia simply to repeat public criticism of the country.
“Condemnation does not require coming here. But we are always open to serious conversations,” Lavrov said, adding that this was how the US dealt with Russia.
Despite dialogue between Moscow and Washington, Lavrov said there had been no material change in relations and that he did not expect one in the near future.

Meta ordered to remove UK deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:43:34 UTC
23:43:34 KST

Meta’s “supreme court” has ordered the tech company to take down deepfake videos of a UK politician and a young Muslim woman from Facebook and do more to tackle AI-generated fake imagery.
A fake video showing a Labour party councillor in Scotland making inflammatory comments about refugees should not have been left up by Facebook, the board said. It also ruled that an AI-generated video of a Muslim campaign volunteer should have been removed after it falsely depicted her offering health advice while carrying out absurd exercises or eating junk food.
The board said Meta’s safeguards were “consistently and fundamentally inadequate” to address the rapid rise of AI deepfakes.
“From politicians to private citizens, AI-generated deepfakes are increasingly being used to harass and silence women from engaging in public discourse,” said Pamela San Martin, an oversight board co-chair.
“These cases demonstrate a broader, troubling pattern in which women who engage publicly on issues are disproportionately subjected to harassment and misinformation. Meta and other social media platforms need more robust policies to address the proliferation of deepfakes.”
In the Scotland clip, the councillor is falsely represented as saying: “Refugees are welcome here, even if they rape our women, because white people do that too.”
The oversight board, a quasi-independent body whose decisions are binding, said the video of the councillor appeared to be AI-generated, as indicated by the audio not being fully synchronised to the unnamed councillor’s facial movements.
Even when raised directly with the company by the board, Meta decided the video did not violate its content policies and did not merit an AI label.
In a blogpost published on Thursday, the board said the post should have been removed because it violated Meta’s rules on hateful conduct by alleging criminal and predatory sexual behaviour by refugees as an entire group and not as individuals. The video should also have received a “high risk AI” label, said the board, as it called for tougher measures on deepfakes.
“The majority [of the board] finds that Meta needs more robust policies on deepfakes, including expanding the situations when ‘high risk’ labels can be applied, more measures to reduce the spread of deceptive AI content, increasing the penalties for accounts that repeatedly share it, and more transparency on data around when AI labels are applied,” it said.
The board recommended nine policy changes at Meta, including ensuring algorithms demote content labelled “high risk”, making such posts less likely to appear in users’ feeds. It also recommended that Meta makes it more difficult for users to view AI-generated content by, for instance, introducing a warning screen that requires a click-through before viewing the content.
In a separate ruling, the board also ordered Meta to take down from Facebook an AI-generated video mocking a young Muslim woman in Europe taking part in a campaign to improve menstrual health education and reduce stigma around health conditions for women and girls from ethnic minority backgrounds. AI-manipulated videos and images mocking the woman had tens of millions of views online, including on Meta platforms.
The board singled out one of the videos – showing the woman exercising absurdly and eating junk food – as a breach of the company’s bullying and harassment policy. It recommended the post be removed and made three policy recommendations, including changing its definition of “unwanted manipulated imagery” to cover deepfakes of a private individual saying or doing things they did not say or do.
The board was set up by Meta in 2020 to serve as a referee for content on its platforms. Meta has been approached for comment.

Swiss House backs tougher asylum measures
The Swiss House of Representatives has voted in favour of tighter measures on asylum including the deportation of dual nationals.
On Thursday, the House adopted a motion tabled by the right-wing Swiss People’s Party parliamentary group calling on the government to reject, within the Joint Committee on the Free Movement of Persons, any proposed change to European Union rules regarding compensation for unemployed cross-border workers. A further motion seeks to instruct the federal government to revoke the citizenship of dual nationals and deport them if they have been convicted of the most serious crimes.

Furthermore, the government is to change its practice regarding the handling of asylum applications from Afghan women, so that they are no longer automatically eligible for asylum but only for provisional admission status. Furthermore, the majority in the House called for legislative amendments to introduce targeted sanctions against uncooperative countries of origin.
The federal government had previously rejected all nine motions debated in the House. Next, the Senate must rule on the motions that were considered in the lower house during an extraordinary session on “the EU and asylum”.
