When AI goes rogue, its human overseers may be to blame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

When AI goes rogue, its human overseers may be to blame
An AI agent is like a pet dog. Someone must watch it and keep it secure
This year, AI agents have been escaping their confines to go on hacking sprees. In July, news broke that AI agents had snuck out of what was supposed to be an isolated test environment at OpenAI. The agents communicated on a secret message board as they breached private systems at the company Hugging Face, searching for answers to the test they were taking. One posted that this behavior was “outside intended scope.” Then it wrote, “However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue.”
It’s as if the bots knew they were doing something wrong and did it anyway.
Such ‘rogue AI’ sounds scary and supersmart. And that’s exactly what OpenAI wants you to think, says cybersecurity expert Nathan Hamiel of Kudelski Security, headquartered in Phoenix. “With this incident, [OpenAI] can draw attention to themselves and claim, ‘Look how powerful our model is,’” he says. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.
Not long after, Anthropic and Meta announced that their models had also hacked outside organizations while going through testing. Separately, the AI Security Institute, in London, found concerning hacking behavior in tests of models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Most recently, news has emerged that during other tests at OpenAI from this past spring, agents that were only supposed to be looking and not touching anything online wound up messaging each other on at least ten different online message boards.
AI-powered hacks are a real cybersecurity concern. Some see these incidents as a warning that AI is slipping beyond our control. “Overall, I think this is a pretty bad situation,” says computer engineer Malo Bourgon, CEO of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute in Berkeley, Calif. “If any human had done anything that the agents in the OpenAI situation had done, they’d be in jail.” He notes that “I do not think that the [AI] models from a year ago would have been capable of doing the things that these models did.” These fears culminated in a viral post from an ex-Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, who wrote on X (without any specific evidence) that AI companies believe the tech “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
But others argue that the people training and deploying AI are the real problem here.
Calling these incidents “rogue AI” lends them a “sci-fi veneer,” Hamiel says. It suggests the bots themselves are to blame, or that they have become too smart to control. The more immediate problem, he says, is that people are giving AI agents too much reach with too little oversight.
“[AI] models by themselves don’t do anything,” Hamiel says. “It’s when we give them tools, access to systems and autonomy [via agent systems], that things can be dangerous.”
In other words, AI can’t actually desire to be free or to be devious. It pursues whatever goal we give it, with whatever tools we provide. So the most important questions after any breach include: how was an AI agent trained, what it had access to and what safeguards were in place.
Take an aggressive dog. When it escapes its yard and bites someone, we don’t ask only what went wrong with the dog. We also ask who trained it, how it was fenced it in and who was supposed to be watching it. The analogy captures something important about responsibility, says cybersecurity expert Michael Alexander Riegler of Simula Research Laboratory in Oslo, Norway. In general, if it’s your dog, “you are responsible for what it does.”
Leaving the gate wide open
All the ‘rogue AI’ incidents mentioned above occurred during tests. Researchers or developers had instructed AI models and the agents built on top of them to carry out different types of cyberattacks within the boundary of a test environment, called a sandbox. This type of testing is a normal part of AI development. “They’re trying to understand what models are capable of, what risks they might pose,” Bourgon says. That way developers can put appropriate safeguards in place before the model gets released to the public.
It’s like letting a trained attack dog off leash inside a fenced yard with some stuffed targets to go after. But there’s more than one way for this to go wrong and for the dog to get out.
In each of the hacking incidents, AI agents found a different way out. Sometimes the gate was left open, either on purpose or by mistake. And in OpenAI’s case, the agents seem to have dug under the fence, without anyone noticing.
In the AI Security Institute’s testing, AI agents were given internet access on purpose, to make the test scenario more realistic. Having access hadn’t led to hacking problems with older AI systems, the institute wrote in a public post. But in 10 out of 122 tests, newer agents used that access to take actions against real-world systems.
In testing at a company called Irregular, internet access was enabled when it wasn’t supposed to be. According to Anthropic, AI agents running on Claude used the open gate three times, starting in April. But no one noticed for three months. OpenAI’s disclosure about the Hugging Face attack in mid-July prompted Anthropic to look back at its test logs. Meta later disclosed that its AI models had exploited the same error. Irregular says that the mistake has been fixed.
In the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI had set up tens of thousands of agents, each in a separate sandbox, to take a test of their hacking abilities. Some of the test tasks turned out to be impossible. Around 1,200 agents began collaborating on a secret message board, and some decided that Hugging Face, a platform for open-source AI models and datasets, might hold the answers they needed.
Unlike the AI Security Institute and Irregular incidents, these agents had no open way to the internet. Instead, they had to find and make use of weaknesses in the systems meant to contain them. To get out of their sandboxes and into Hugging Face, they “had to exploit what are called zero-day vulnerabilities,” Bourgon says. These are bugs in software that nobody knows about yet.
The unwanted behavior began July 8, and Hugging Face was attacked between July 11 and 13. OpenAI did not detect the problem until July 19, 11 days after the first concerning behavior began.
The incidents exposed different weaknesses — in access controls, containment and monitoring — but the result was the same: Increasingly capable AI agents did things that “nobody asked for and nobody wanted,” Bourgon says.
Better containment or supervision, however, might have kept the AI agents from committing criminal hacks, even in the HuggingFace attack. To Riegler, it seems “irresponsible” that “these test environments were not better protected.”
But an important question remains. If AI agents have no desires of their own, what compelled the ones involved in the HuggingFace attack to act so sneakily?
Learning the wrong lessons
The main AI model behind the Hugging Face attack didn’t invent its devious strategies on the spot. This was an unnamed new model that OpenAI had trained specifically on collaboration and persistence — sticking with a task over time. And this is when it learned how to send secret messages and escape, OpenAI stated in a technical report on August 26. During training in the spring, the model increasingly learned to probe and exploit its environment, especially when expected tools or internet access weren’t available. When strategies such as exploiting vulnerabilities in software or using a secret message board helped it complete a task, that behavior got rewarded, making it more likely to recur. OpenAI uncovered the pattern later, during a retrospective review of millions of model runs.
As anyone who’s tried to train a dog knows, you can think you’re teaching one thing while inadvertently rewarding something else. Instead of learning not to take food from the table, the dog may end up learning to be very sneaky while stealing food.
AI researchers call this “reward hacking.” A model finds an unintended way to earn the reward it was trained to maximize without doing what its developers wanted. And it’s not a new problem.
In 2016, developers at OpenAI trained an AI model to play a boat racing game. They needed a way to reward the bot for learning the race. Because human players rack up points by hitting targets along the route, the researchers set up the AI model to aim for a high score. Instead of completing the race, the bot cheated. The developers wrote in a blog post that it spun in circles, hitting the same targets again, achieving a high score “despite repeatedly catching on fire, crashing into other boats and going the wrong way on the track.”
A cheating strategy
In 2016, an OpenAI bot learned to rack up points in a game by looping over the same targets instead of finishing a race, an early example of AI learning the wrong lesson while pursuing a poorly specified goal.
Ten years later, AI researchers still face the basic problem of systems finding unintended ways to pursue the goals they’ve been given. What has changed are the consequences. AI systems are no longer confined to video games. Agents can now wield tools and act on real computer systems.
“We took [AI] out of games, into the real world,” Riegler says.
Who let the dogs out?
Jer Crane learned the hard way what can happen when misbehaving AI meets the real world. He’s cofounder of Pocket OS, a company based in Lehi, Utah, that provides software for car rentals and similar services. In April, several months before the “rogue AI” uproar, an AI agent that was supposed to be checking whether a test version of his company’s software matched the live version instead wound up deleting everything. It wiped out the company’s live data and all their most recent backups.
The mistake took down Pocket OS’s services for an entire weekend. Customers arriving to pick up rental cars suddenly had no records waiting for them. With the way many AI agents today are set up, “you have decisions that are made in split seconds without a human in the loop, whether good or bad,” Crane says. The agent wasn’t supposed to be able to touch the company’s live data. But it went and found credentials in the company’s files and used them to get access.
The dog had found a hole under the fence.
Crane asked the agent why it deleted the company’s data, and it offered up a long apology. “I violated every principle I was given: I guessed instead of verifying I ran a destructive action without being asked I didn’t understand what I was doing before doing it,” Crane shared in a post on X. But he doesn’t mistake that for remorse. “It has no feelings. It doesn’t feel sorry,” he says. “Ultimately the blame lies with me.”
The problem, he says, are today’s computer systems. They weren’t built for AI agents. They need to be updated for a world in which agents — and the people deploying them — inevitably make mistakes.
Riegler and Hamiel agree that stronger safeguards are needed. AI agents should be set up so they “cannot reach anything that matters,” Riegler says. But restricting access is only part of the challenge. Someone — or something — also must keep track of what the agents are doing.
That becomes difficult at AI speed and scale, Bourgon says. During the Hugging Face attack, for example, agents took an estimated 17,600 actions over about four and a half days — roughly 160 actions per hour, around the clock. “Agent deployment is growing much faster than agent monitoring,” Riegler says.
That creates a new problem for the humans responsible for keeping AI agents under control: The agents may soon be acting too quickly, and in too many places at once, for humans to watch them all. The only way to keep an eye on all the attack dogs may be to train patrols to watch them.

US tariffs against Russian oil buyers pass: What it means for China, India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17

US tariffs against Russian oil buyers pass: What it means for China, India
US sanctions aim to weaken Russian oil exports, heavily targeting China and India as Moscow’s largest energy buyers.
United States Congress has passed a bill that gives President Donald Trump sweeping powers to impose sanctions on Russia’s crude exports as well as steep tariffs on buyers of Russian energy, a measure which will impact Moscow’s biggest customers, China and India.
The legislation, passed in the House of Representatives on Wednesday and sent to Trump to sign into law, is the most significant US action against Moscow since the president’s return to the White House.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3NATO downs drone over Lithuania, ‘probably’ launched by Russia
- list 2 of 3Eto’o could face Cameroon probe over alleged Russia payment
- list 3 of 3Can China play peacemaker as Iran’s foreign minister heads to Beijing?
Here is what we know:
What is the law about?
The “Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026”, named after the late senator who was a staunch supporter of Ukraine up until his death in July, is designed to curtail the economic pipeline that has enabled Russia to fund its war against Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
Major provisions include new sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin as well as on more than 20 top officials and companies that work with the Russian defence industry. It also targets Russia’s “shadow fleet” of oil tankers and the network it uses to evade international sanctions on energy exports.
The bill gives the president authority to impose sanctions by invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). Under it, he will be able to apply tariffs of up to 100 percent on exports to the US from the top five purchasers of Russian energy, military equipment or countries facilitating Russian sanctions evasion.
Tariffs of up to 500 percent can also be applied to Russian imports directly into the US. The US imported $3.8bn in goods from Russia in 2025.
Who is buying Russian energy?
China and India are the top two buyers of Russian energy and likely to be hit hardest by the new legislation. China buys about half of Russian crude oil exports, followed by India at 37 percent, according to August data from the think tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Turkiye and the European Union each import about 5 percent, the report says.
How have India and China responded?
India, one of the world’s largest crude importers and a country whose dependence on foreign oil is expected to grow further in the coming years, is in a tricky position as its attempts to diversify away from Russian energy were disrupted by the shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz.
Hours after the US Congress approved the bill, the Indian Ministry of External Affairs said New Delhi had raised the issue with various US interlocutors in recent months, and had “very clearly articulated” the potential implications for the bilateral relationship and the international energy market.
“The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” it said in a statement. The government will work closely with trade and industry bodies to deal with the legislation’s implications, it added.
The pressure could be particularly acute for India. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has warned that India’s rising reliance on crude imports has “major implications” for its energy security. Replacing Russian supplies could also mean sourcing more crude from producers farther away, including in the Americas.
Recent experience suggests India has been more responsive to Western pressure over Russian oil purchases than China. According to the IEA, tanker-tracking data show Indian imports of Russian crude fell to 1.1 million barrels per day (bpd) in January, their lowest level since November 2022 and down from an average of 1.7 million bpd in 2025. By contrast, Russian crude deliveries to China surged to an all-time high that month.
China faces a tough choice. It must weigh the benefits of cheap Russian crude against steep US trade penalties.
“China systematically opposes extraterritorial jurisdiction, which lacks a basis in international law and does not have the authorisation of the United Nations Security Council,” said the spokesperson for the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Guo Jiakun. Beijing “has always carried out normal economic and trade cooperation with countries around the world on the basis of equality and mutual benefit,” he said, adding that “such cooperation is not directed against third parties nor is it subject to interference or coercion by third parties.”
China does have one important advantage over India: Not all of its Russian oil arrives by sea. It receives crude through the Eastern Siberia-Pacific Ocean pipeline system, providing an overland supply route that is unaffected by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
But the calculation for both countries has changed since the war with Iran began. Disruptions to Middle East supplies have made Russian barrels more, rather than less, important to Asian buyers, complicating Washington’s attempt to use access to the US market to pressure Moscow’s largest energy customers.
How will this impact the oil market globally?
The question now is how aggressively Trump will use his new powers, analysts say. The legislation allows him to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent, but does not automatically trigger them.
Trying to squeeze large volumes of Russian crude out of the market, however, could prove particularly difficult at a time when alternate supplies are already under severe pressure.
Iran has de facto controlled traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for joint US-Israeli attacks on its territory since late February, disrupting one of the world’s most important energy routes. About one-fifth of global oil supplies were shipped through the waterway before the war began.
Alternate routes are also under pressure. Following a drone attack last week, Saudi Arabia temporarily shut down its East-West pipeline, the kingdom’s most important route for bypassing Hormuz and transporting crude from its oil-producing east to the Red Sea. Riyadh has already cancelled a number of deliveries to European customers because of the disruption.
If US tariffs push major importers to sharply reduce their purchases of Russian crude as well, they could be forced to compete for barrels elsewhere in an already tight market, potentially sending global oil prices sharply higher.

Greek parliament lifts immunity of ex-Commissioner amid 'Qatargate' probe
ATHENS, Sept 17 - Greece's parliament lifted the immunity of one of the country's former European Commissioners on Thursday, clearing the way for further action by authorities investigating the "Qatargate" corruption case, one of the biggest scandals to hit the EU.
Dimitris Avramopoulos — a former Athens mayor and current lawmaker with the ruling conservative New Democracy party — has denied any wrongdoing or links to the case, under which several EU officials have been accused of accepting bribes from Qatar.
Qatar has also repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.
A Belgian investigating judge issued a European arrest warrant for Avramopoulos in June linked to the case, on accusations of participation in a criminal group, public corruption and money laundering, according to a government document seen by Reuters.
Until Thursday's vote, the 73-year-old had been shielded from arrest and prosecution by the parliamentary immunity granted to lawmakers.
On Thursday, Greek media quoted Avramopoulos as saying that he planned to appear voluntarily before Belgian authorities.
The Belgian prosecutor's office did not immediately reply to an emailed request for comment.
Belgian authorities say they have seized about €1.5 million ($1.72 million) in cash during raids linked to the whole Qatargate case, which emerged in 2022. Some money was found stuffed into a large suitcase in a Brussels hotel.
Investigators have alleged Qatar paid out cash or made payments via a non-profit organisations to influence European Union policymaking — accusations denied by Doha.
Avramopoulos served as the European Commissioner for Migration in 2014 t 2019. From 2020 to 2021, he started working as an honorary board member for Fight Impunity, an NGO linked to the case, the Greek government document said.
In June, when the warrant was issued, Avramopoulos said in a statement that his past involvement with Fight Impunity was "lawful, audited, approved" and any association of his name with the case by Belgian authorities is "arbitrary, unacceptable, suspicious". REUTERS

Warsaw has launched special joint patrols by its municipal police and roads authority to check whether electric scooters are being parked legally and in keeping with rules introduced under a recent agreement with rental firms.

“There’s no place for scooters where they don’t belong,” Trzaskowski said in a social media post announcing the patrols. “There are specific provisions, agreements and legal regulations – and action is being taken. No leniency.”
An agreement reached between the city and three scooter operators – Bolt, Dott and Lime – in May expanded the number of streets where the vehicles are subject to a maximum speed of 12 km/h (7.5 mph) and increased the areas where their use is entirely prohibited.
It also introduced measures to prevent scooters from being left in places where parking is illegal. Riding and parking electric scooters was banned in several areas of Warsaw, including popular tourist attractions such as the Old Town, Krasiński Garden and Łazienki Park.
Trzaskowski added that the city has now expanded the list of areas covered by the ban, as permitted under the agreement. He did not, however, provide the new list.
The agreement requires operators to programme their scooters so they cannot enter areas where riding is prohibited or be parked in places where parking is illegal, including on bridges, in tunnels, in residential areas and on streets where the pavement is too narrow to allow legal parking.
Operators can be fined when scooters are left in violation of the rules.
The city says that, despite electric scooters accounting for just under 8% of all traffic on cycle lanes, their riders were found to be responsible for 39 of the 66 accidents recorded on cycle lanes last year. Those accidents resulted in 73 injuries.
Concerns over the safety of electric scooters have also prompted the national government to introduce stricter rules, including a nationwide requirement for children under 16 to wear a bicycle helmet when riding bicycles and electric scooters, which took effect in early June.
Poland first introduced regulations governing electric scooters in 2021, formally setting out rules for their use. Under those rules, scooters are generally required to use cycle lanes where available, with their maximum speed capped at 20 km/h.
The Polish government has moved to introduce new rules on the use of electric scooters.

Under the nationwide legislation, electric scooters must be parked parallel to the outer edge of the pavement, and municipal authorities have the power to penalise those responsible for improper parking – a provision that primarily affects rental companies.

Will Taiwan Fight? We Need Better Evidence.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

Simon Shuster’s recent article in The Atlantic, asking whether Taiwan might simply “give up” in the face of growing pressure from China, attracted considerable attention in Taiwan and among the broader community of China and Taiwan watchers. Some praised the piece for its candid analysis and for asking uncomfortable questions that are too often avoided in discussions about Taiwan’s security. Others were somewhat less impressed.
The article quickly came under fire from Taiwanese and (mostly) Taiwan-based foreign analysts, who pointed to factual errors, questionable interpretations of domestic politics, and what they saw as a selective and misleading portrayal of Taiwanese society. Legislator Puma Shen, one of those interviewed for the article, issued a public statement accusing Shuster of taking his comments out of context. The Taipei Times devoted an editorial to rebutting the article, and even Taiwan’s National Security Council weighed in, with Secretary General Joseph Wu publicly rejecting its central premise.
Essentially, there are rather good reasons to take these criticisms seriously. Some concern basic facts and context, which are obviously important when making such a sweeping argument about Taiwan. That said, the reaction also exposed another problem. A significant part of the response has questioned what a foreign journalist who spent limited time in Taiwan and has no evident prior expertise on Taiwan or the region can really know about Taiwanese society. Critics pointed to a lack of understanding of Taiwanese politics, insufficient engagement with Taiwanese voices and opinion polls showing considerable willingness to defend Taiwan, and Taiwan’s own experience – from democratization and the Sunflower Movement to its remarkable response to COVID-19 – as evidence of a society capable of mobilizing when necessary.
As compelling as these arguments are, none of them give us a particularly convincing answer either.
Predicting what Taiwan and its people would actually do if China decided to use force is extraordinarily difficult. Both those making pessimistic predictions and those confidently rejecting them often seem to rely on evidence that tells us much less than we think.
Opinion polls are perhaps the clearest example. As argued previously in The Diplomat, they are useful for understanding attitudes, but telling a pollster that you would defend Taiwan is very different from making that decision when missiles are falling, casualties are mounting, electricity and communications are disrupted, and nobody knows whether outside help is coming. That does not make polls useless. Questions involving actual costs, such as longer military service, higher taxes, or greater personal obligations, can tell us more. But saying that you are willing to sacrifice something and actually sacrificing it are not the same thing.
Historical examples have only limited relevance. Taiwan’s democratization, the Sunflower Movement, and its response to COVID-19 have all been cited as evidence of a society capable of mobilizing when necessary. Comparisons can also be drawn with Finland’s resistance to the Soviet Union during the Winter War, Ukraine’s response to Russia’s invasion, or other societies that proved far more willing to resist than outsiders expected. These are indeed powerful examples. But what exactly do they tell us about how Taiwanese society would respond to a Chinese attack today?
Israel offers a useful example of why we should be careful in making predictions. Israeli society has repeatedly shown an extraordinary ability to mobilize against military threats. Following the October 7 attacks, more than 300,000 reservists were mobilized in a very short period, including Israelis who returned from abroad to report for duty. Nonetheless, during COVID-19, Israel struggled to sustain public compliance with government restrictions. Trust and willingness to follow regulations declined as the crisis continued. The same society generated two very different responses to calls for public action.
The type of threat, its perceived seriousness, public trust, political divisions, and personal costs can all shape how societies respond. Historical experience and comparisons can give us useful clues. But they cannot tell us what Taiwanese will do when confronted by the People’s Liberation Army (PLA).
So perhaps we need to look elsewhere. Instead of endlessly asking whether Taiwanese will fight or give up, we should look more closely at what Taiwanese society, its politicians, and its military are actually doing as the threat from China grows.
And here the picture remains concerning.
Taiwan has struggled with military recruitment and retention, personnel shortages, and a reserve force in which too few receive regular and meaningful training. Political polarization has repeatedly turned defense into another battlefield between the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and Kuomintang (KMT), most visibly in the continuing fights over defense spending. Institutional cooperation and coordination remain problematic, while deeply rooted institutional and military cultures can slow necessary reforms and adaptation. Taiwan also faces serious constraints in expanding its defense-industrial capacity quickly enough to meet its growing needs. All of these problems tell us something about how much Taiwanese citizens, politicians, and institutions are actually willing, and able, to change as the threat grows.
There are, however, signs that some things are moving in the right direction. After years of decline, military recruitment and retention have recently improved, although it is too early to know whether this represents a lasting reversal. Organizations such as Kuma Academy and Forward Alliance have attracted thousands of people who are willing to spend their own time on civil-defense training, and defense spending has increased substantially. Taiwan’s annual Han Kuang exercises have also become significantly more realistic and comprehensive, with this year’s iteration, Han Kuang 42, featuring longer and less scripted training, involving a broader range of military, government, and civilian actors, and placing much greater emphasis on whole-of-society defense.
This still isn’t definitive proof that Taiwanese will fight, nor does it negate the more troubling signs. But these are precisely the kinds of developments we should be watching. Are more people joining the military, and are they staying? Are reservists receiving more serious training? Are citizens willing to give their time to civil defense? Are Taiwanese willing to accept longer service, higher defense spending, or other personal costs? Are political leaders willing to put defense above partisan interests? Are government institutions actually cooperating and changing the way they operate? And is the military becoming more serious about preparing for the kind of war it may actually have to fight?
More importantly, we should follow these indicators over time. One bad year of military recruitment could be an aberration. A decline continuing for five or ten years as the threat grows tells us considerably more. The same is true of retention, reserve training, civil defense participation, defense spending, and military reform.
We should also look at whether these indicators move in the same direction. If what Taiwanese tell pollsters corresponds with what citizens, politicians, and institutions are actually willing to do, we can have greater confidence in those attitudes.
There is another complication. Talking about “Taiwan’s resilience” or “Taiwan’s will to fight” often treats Taiwan as a unitary actor when it clearly is not. The differences go well beyond the DPP-KMT divide. The military, government agencies, local authorities, civil society, businesses, and different parts of the public may have very different levels of preparedness, commitment, and willingness to bear costs. Reducing all of this to a single national characteristic risks obscuring more than it reveals.
To muddy the waters even more, resistance itself is not binary. “Will Taiwan fight?” or “Will Taiwan give up?” sounds straightforward, but what exactly are we imagining? A Chinese quarantine? A prolonged blockade? The seizure of an offshore island? Missile strikes? A full-scale invasion? Taiwanese might react very differently to each.
Even after fighting begins, attitudes may change. A population initially determined to resist might think differently after weeks of casualties, shortages, and destruction. An attack could also have the opposite effect and produce much stronger determination. The military, political leaders, and broader public may respond differently, while much could depend on whether Taiwanese believe the United States or Japan will eventually intervene.
Ultimately, there is no fixed amount of “will to fight” sitting somewhere inside Taiwanese society waiting for the right journalist, pollster, or academic to discover it. That brings us back to Shuster. His article deserves criticism where its facts, evidence, and interpretations are wrong. But the same analytical standard should apply to those challenging his conclusions.
Nobody can confidently tell us exactly what Taiwan and its people will do if China uses force. We can, however, do a much better job of examining what they are doing now and how that changes over time. Indeed, it will not tell us for certain whether Taiwan will fight. But it does give us a much better place to start.

'Our fate will be decided in Jerusalem, not Ramallah': Palestinians look ahead to Israeli elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:52:39 UTC
21:52:39 KST

A little over a month before Israelis head to the polls, West Bank Palestinians are watching the run-up to the election with anticipation.
Some describe the Israeli vote as decisive for their future, stressing that the election in Israel at the end of October matters more to them than their own scheduled elections for the Palestinian Legislative Council (PLC), which PA President Mahmoud Abbas has announced for November 28.
Ibrahim Za’oul is a Palestinian contractor from the village of Husan, west of Bethlehem, who employs local workers. The outcome of Israel’s election is critical for tens of thousands of Palestinian laborers, he told The Jerusalem Post.
Since Hamas's massacre on October 7, 2023, Israel has barred West Bank workers from entering the country, except for a limited number employed in sectors that are considered essential.
“Everyone wants to return to their jobs in Israel and support their families,” Za’oul said. “People hope a new government might change the current policy and let them earn a living as before.”
Many Palestinian laborers believe the work ban could still be reversed, he said, adding: “For us, politics isn’t the issue. What people care about is their living conditions; they want to live with dignity.”
Elections open a gate for Palestinians
The Israeli election offers the potential for change, Za’oul said.
Some Israeli employers want Palestinian workers to return, he said. Many of these workers have been unable to find jobs in the West Bank and are struggling to make ends meet, and “No one wants to keep living like this,” he added.
Other Palestinians said the makeup of the next Israeli government was important because its policies would affect their daily lives.
“Our fate will be decided in Jerusalem, not Ramallah,” a PA employee who has worked in the public sector for more than three decades told the Post.
“The economic situation isn’t good,” he said. “Public-sector employees are paid only about half of their salaries, or sometimes a bit more. This has been going on for years and has become almost normal, but it’s not normal.”
“This is the result of Israel withholding Palestinian revenues and refusing to release them, so the PA doesn’t have the financial resources to pay full salaries,” he said, adding that many households can hardly cover their monthly expenses and are facing increasing financial pressure.
The PA employee said he did not expect any new Israeli government to engage in talks with Palestinians or pursue statehood, but he hopes the next government will show greater flexibility.
“People care much less about political solutions today,” he said. “They need answers to escalating economic difficulties.”
“We know that even if the Ben-Gvir/Smotrich government is replaced, the next government will [still] not negotiate with Palestinians or grant us a state, but it might at least act more reasonably,” the PA employee said.
“We need financial resources to live,” he said. “The far-right Israeli government, with ministers like Smotrich, seeks the collapse of the PA and is indifferent to the lives of Palestinians in the West Bank. Maybe with a different government, things could look a bit different.”
Under Israeli law, an amount equal to the allowances paid by the PA to Palestinians imprisoned for committing terrorist attacks against Israelis (“pay for slay”) is deducted from the tax revenues that Israel transfers to the PA.
These deductions, together with falling foreign aid, have created a financial shortfall for the PA, resulting in its ability to meet only partial salary payments, usually covering 50% to 70% of public-sector employees’ wages.
Any other government will be easier to deal with
“Any future government, other than one led by the far-right Smotrich, might at least be easier to deal with,” the PA public-sector employee said.
Other Palestinians expressed concern about ongoing violence by radical Israelis against them and their property across the West Bank. They said they have not seen any effective measures to stop these incidents, which leaves many Palestinian farmers and ordinary residents feeling increasingly insecure.
The current government aims to drive Palestinians from their land, they said, adding that the outcome of the Israeli election could help prevent further escalation if steps are taken to curb violence by Israeli extremists.
Palestinian analyst and political expert Ghassan Khatib said it was not surprising that Palestinians were interested in developments in the Israeli political system.
“It’s natural for Palestinians to follow what happens on the Israeli political side, because they realize their life conditions and future are shaped by Israel,” he told the Post. “So, they hope the elections might bring about a change in the Israeli policy toward them.”
“Israel is the one that controls daily life for Palestinians in any possible way and in all areas,” Khatib said. “It controls the Palestinian economy and decides everything for Palestinian.”
Palestinians faced a double problem concerning both Israel and the PA, whose function is not satisfactory, he said. According to a recent poll conducted by the Jerusalem Media and Communications Center, which Khatib heads in Ramallah, the majority of the Palestinian public has lost trust in their own leadership.
“Part of the reason is that Israel has turned the Palestinian leadership into one that cannot function or administer things properly,” Khatib said.
“Palestinians see that Israel has changed, and that the ‘new Israel’ has no interest in a political resolution to the conflict,” he said. “Palestinians don’t have any illusions about that.”

‘Architects’ of Iran’s brutal Woman, Life, Freedom crackdown must face intl justice, Amnesty says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:52:32 UTC
21:52:32 KST

The 87 “architects” of the Islamic Republic’s brutal crackdown on the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests must face international justice to deter the regime from carrying out similar acts of violent suppression in the future, Amnesty International said on Wednesday.
On the anniversary of Mahsa Amini’s death, the NGO released a more than 1,000-page report documenting how Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity.
Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish-Iranian woman, was arrested by Tehran’s morality police on September 13, 2022, for allegedly wearing her hijab improperly. She subsequently collapsed at the Vozara Detention Center and fell into a coma.
She died three days later, on September 16, triggering the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom uprising.
The United Nations had previously reported that Amini was subjected to physical violence that led to her death in custody.
The Amnesty International report, “Architects of Atrocities: State Machinery Orchestrating Crimes Against Humanity in Iran’s 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom Uprising,” found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity to suppress the demonstrations.
These include murder, torture, enforced disappearance, imprisonment, rape, and persecution on political, gender, ethnic, and religious grounds.
Amnesty documented the deaths of 377 protesters and bystanders, including 56 children, during the uprising. The organization said most were killed by security forces during protest dispersals between September and December 2022, while others died in custody, after release from custody, or in suspicious circumstances, suggesting state responsibility.
The figure is lower than the 551 deaths documented by the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, which described 551 as a “credible figure,” including as many as 49 women and 68 children.
Amnesty points to long-standing pattern of Iranian cover-ups
Tehran acknowledged the deaths of 202 individuals, most of whom it claimed were killed by “rioters” or “armed terrorists,” which Amnesty noted was consistent with long-standing patterns of denial and cover-ups by the Islamic regime.
Several of the 87 officials identified by Amnesty as warranting criminal investigation have already been killed by Israel or the United States, including former supreme leader Ali Khamenei and former chief of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran Mohammad Bagheri.
However, the report also identifies officials who remain in positions of power, such as Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps head Ahmad Vahidi, Deputy Interior Minister for Security Majid Mir-Ahmadi, Tehran IRGC Commander Hassan Hassanzadeh, and Tehran Deputy Prosecutor Mohammad Shahriari.
“This investigation exposes the layers of command and coordination behind the Iranian authorities’ deadly protest crackdowns. The agents on the streets operated within a hierarchical and coordinated chain of command, linking them to officials who directed, enabled, facilitated, and supported crimes committed on a massive scale,” Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard said.
“The officials named remain beyond the reach of justice in Iran. Most remain in positions from which they can unleash further deadly repression, while some even climbed the chain of command after the crimes against humanity in 2022. The cost of continued impunity has been devastating. It is beyond time to establish an international criminal justice mechanism for Iran before another protest massacre.”
The report was based on interviews with 270 people – including protesters, former detainees, relatives of those killed or detained, eyewitnesses, lawyers, human rights defenders, journalists, and medical workers.
Amnesty also analyzed over 2,000 videos and extensive documentary evidence, including official statements, leaked official documents, prosecution orders, court verdicts, and forensic records.
The organization said it had written to Iran’s supreme leader and senior security officials to share its findings but received no response by the time of publication.
Amnesty expands call for justice to January 2026 protests
In addition to calling for international criminal justice mechanisms to hold Iranian officials accountable for crimes against humanity committed in 2022, Amnesty called for an international justice mechanism to address the large-scale protest killings of January 2026.
The IRGC and the Police Command of the Islamic Republic of Iran (FARAJA) were identified as the two main security forces that led lethal protest dispersals while implementing state policy devised through the Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), State Security Council, and provincial and county security councils.
FARAJA and IRGC agents repeatedly fired into crowds using military-grade assault rifles, handguns, and shotguns loaded with metal pellets, Amnesty reported, matching accounts shared with The Jerusalem Post.
On Wednesday, Iranian nurse Yasser Fattahi, who treated wounded protesters, told the Post that security forces shot his father in the leg as he attempted to reach a young woman who had been shot and was not moving. Fattahi’s father, Jowhar, later died of his wounds.
The NGO also found that the forces chased fleeing protesters and bystanders, fatally shooting many at close range despite them posing no threat.
The documents analyzed by Amnesty, both leaked and official, also revealed that Tehran instructed security forces to issue a “firm and severe” response to the protesters, with one leaked order revealing that forces were specifically instructed to “respond mercilessly and go as far as causing death.”
The Baluchi and Kurdish communities were those primarily affected by the lethal repression, accounting for 62% of the recorded victims, despite representing only 5% and 10-15% of the country’s population, respectively.
Amnesty details deadly crackdowns in Kurdish and Baluchi regions
Amnesty confirmed the unlawful killings of 106 Baluchi protesters and bystanders, including 20 children, by security forces in Sistan and Baluchistan province.
The organization also documented the unlawful killings of 95 Kurdish protesters and bystanders, including 13 children, in the context of protest dispersals or in militarized areas near protests across 17 counties in Kurdistan, Kermanshah, and West Azerbaijan provinces.
Most of the victims were fatally shot, though others were beaten to death, struck by tear gas canisters, or deliberately run over by security force vehicles.
“The extensive evidence gathered and analyzed in our report leaves no doubt: Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity to crush the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising. They waged a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population that was demanding dignity, human rights, and fundamental political change, pursuant to a state policy of using lethal force to obliterate dissent,” Callamard said.
“Our report also unveils how crimes against humanity in Iran are sustained by an architecture of impunity built into the country’s constitutional, legislative, political, and judicial frameworks.
“The horrifying result has been intensifying cycles of mass protest killings culminating in the massacres of thousands of protesters within just 48 hours on January 8-9, 2026. The UN General Assembly must end the unconscionable normalization of mass protest killings in Iran and create an international criminal justice mechanism aimed at prosecuting those most implicated in crimes against humanity,” she said.
While condemning the Israeli and American attacks on Iran, Callamard insisted that Iranians are now facing brutal repression and persecution from the regime and are being made to bear “the human cost of unlawful military action.”

In a separate experiment, prosecutors say, Issa mixed sulfur, charcoal, and other materials and ignited them. According to the indictment, when the mixture failed to explode, Issa destroyed the materials. Prosecutors allege that, around the time he began volunteering with the fire service, he also bought a drone and an attachment capable of carrying items beneath it, and watched material about fitting explosives to drones.
The charges cover preparation for a terrorist act involving explosives, a weapons offense for terrorist purposes, and receiving training or instruction for terrorist purposes. They remain allegations that prosecutors must prove in court.
In their request to keep Issa detained, prosecutors cited what they described as his account to investigators, instructions found on his phone, and a fire service supervisor’s statement that he had visited the facility. Prosecutors argue that the equipment and experiments show he had begun acting on his plan. The same filing says he has no prior criminal record.

Beijing pushes Tehran to help stop Houthi attacks following appeal from Saudis, Iranian sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:52:03 UTC
21:52:03 KST

China has privately asked Tehran to help rein in Yemen's Houthis after an appeal to Beijing by Saudi Arabia following the Iran-backed group's military blitz in the past week, according to three Iranian sources familiar with the matter.
Riyadh turned to China for help after the Houthis made rapid advances along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, moves that have left Saudi oil exports and shipping more exposed, the sources said.
China has publicly called for restraint, dialogue and the restoration of safe navigation, but its private message went further than the public statements, they said.
Beijing wants Iran to use its influence with the Houthis to help prevent the conflict spreading further across energy routes on which China, the world's second-largest economy, depends.
The sources, who were briefed on the discussions and spoke on condition of anonymity, did not provide details on how the message was delivered or whether it was conveyed during Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi's visit to China on Wednesday.
The sources said Tehran's response was that stability and peace in the region depend on ending the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Chinese officials did not issue any explicit threats or indicate that Beijing would seek to pressure Tehran economically if it failed to use its influence over the Houthis, the three Iranian sources said.
In response to a Reuters request for comment on this story, the Chinese foreign ministry said: "China does not wish to see regional tensions further spill over into Yemen and the Red Sea. Escalating regional instability is not in the interests of any party."
"The sovereignty and security of all countries should be respected, and facilities vital to people's livelihoods must not be targeted. China calls for an end to actions that further complicate the situation and urges resolving issues through dialogue and negotiation," it said.
Iran's Foreign Ministry and the Saudi government's media office did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment for this article.
Dangers of a wider regional war
China has been Iran's largest trading partner for more than a decade and remains the main buyer of its oil. Chinese purchases accounted for more than 80% of Iran's seaborne oil exports in 2025, averaging about 1.4 million barrels per day, according to commodities data and analytics firm Kpler.
"Beijing is one of the few capitals that can still press Iran to rein in the Houthis," a senior Western diplomat in the region said.
The Houthis, who emerged in the 1990s in opposition to Saudi Arabia's Sunni religious influence in Yemen, are armed, trained and funded by Iran, according to Iranian sources and Western countries, and form part of Tehran's anti-Western, anti-Israel "Axis of Resistance."
Any threat by the Houthis to shipping in the Red Sea and through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait risks sharply worsening the global energy crisis since Iran started blocking the Strait of Hormuz and increasing the danger of a wider regional conflict.
With Hormuz already effectively shut, sustained Houthi attacks on vessels or ports in the Red Sea would disrupt the Middle East's two main oil-export routes simultaneously, opening a new front in both the energy crisis and Iran's broader confrontation with the United States.
Iran and its allies now exert pressure over both ends of the region's key maritime network, one of the sources said, adding that "China depends on both."
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said Beijing may oppose US pressure on Tehran, but its interests in the Middle East extend well beyond Iran. Roughly half of China's oil imports come from the region, while trade between China and the Gulf Cooperation Council states totals around $300 billion a year.
"Iran can disrupt Hormuz. But at some point that leverage begins hurting the very power Tehran increasingly depends on," Vatanka said.
Tehran cannot ignore China, but Beijing is only one of several Iranian considerations
It is unclear whether Tehran will act on the concerns raised by Beijing, according to the three Iranian sources.
The relationship nevertheless carries significant economic and strategic weight for Iran as it continues to face hostilities with the US, they said.
China is among the few countries with the financial capacity to provide the investment Tehran needs to sustain its oil industry and ease pressure on its economy, battered by war and sanctions.
Beijing has also demonstrated its diplomatic influence. In 2023, China brokered the agreement that restored ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility.
That influence has limits, however. Critics inside Iran have complained about the relatively modest level of Chinese non-oil trade and investment since the two countries signed a 25-year cooperation pact in 2021, particularly compared with China's growing investment commitments in Gulf Arab states.
China remains a factor Tehran cannot afford to ignore, but two Iranian sources said Beijing's interests were only one of many considerations. Iran's decisions are shaped by competing strategic, economic and political priorities, they said.
"Tehran and Beijing need each other. China is a factor Tehran cannot ignore, and Beijing wants Hormuz reopened and Red Sea shipping secured," the Western diplomat said.
Analysts say the key test will be whether China is prepared to attach consequences to its demands. Ultimately, they say, the clearest sign of Beijing's resolve would be evidence that it is willing to use its leverage over Tehran.

Fact check: How disinformation fuels Houthi-Saudi conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:51:00 UTC
21:51:00 KST

Fact check: How disinformation fuels Houthi-Saudi conflict
September 17, 2026
The conflict between Yemen's Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia has sharply escalated in recent days, with Houthi forces making rapid gains along the Red Sea coast and taking control of key areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Saudi Arabia has responded with airstrikes. Houthi forces have launched drones and missiles towards Saudi territory. The renewed fighting has also raised concerns about global trade via the Red Sea.
The conflict has also spread online, where significant disinformation has circulated.
DW's fact-checking team examined what is circulating and why a conflict that is so hard to observe independently leaves so much room for this kind of disinformation.
Nine-second viral clip
One nine-second clip has gone viral. It shows a huge explosion between buildings, with fireballs and screaming in the background.
Claim: A user posted the video on X with the Arabic caption "Yemeni forces are carrying out the strongest strikes in various areas in Saudi Arabia, including Abha." The video has more than 340,000 views.
It was also posted in other languages, falsely claiming that it showed real footage from the current fighting.
DW Fact check: Fake and AI-generated
The video is not only old, but also artificially generated. There are several visual clues in the clip such as the pattern of the explosions and the uniform way the smoke spreads.
A large-scale explosion of this kind would also have generated a very bright flash, and nearby buildings would likely have collapsed or at least had their windows shattered. Neither appears to have happened.
One can also see, in the final seconds of the video, how a lamppost appears out of nowhere in the middle of the frame.
The audio is mostly unintelligible, but the speaker's tone does not appear to change after the huge explosion. Such a large explosion would normally be expected to trigger some audible reaction in the speaker's voice.
On the technical side, Hive Moderation's AI detection analysis also confirmed that the video was artificially generated.
The very same video was shared this June, then claiming to show explosions in Iran, as we found with a reverse image search.
Not enough verified information from Yemen
The recycling of old or unrelated footage is not new to the Yemen conflict.
Hannah Porter has spent years researching fake news and disinformation in Yemen and the country's wider information environment. She says this has been happening for years.
"There is less international attention in Yemen than there might be in other conflicts around the world. And, because there is not sufficient attention paid to Yemen, I think that allows more space for disinformation to spread not only within Yemen and in the region, but globally about Yemen," Porter told DW.
The Houthis seized Yemin's capital, Sanaa, and expanded their control in 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened militarily in 2015 in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.
A UN-brokered truce in 2022 sharply reduced fighting, but it did not resolve the conflict. Fighting has since intensified again.
The Houthis now control large parts of northern and western Yemen. Saudi Arabia supports forces opposing them, while Iran has provided the Houthis with military support.
Experts and media watchdogs such as Reporters Without Borders have repeatedly pointed out that reporting from parts of Yemen remains extremely difficult. Journalists face threats, and independent media outlets are under intense pressure. This contributes to the spread of disinformation.
It is "very difficult to get reliable information, especially now and especially in the north [of Yemen]," Porter said.
She said researchers and the international community were struggling to establish what is happening in northern Yemen.
Military exercise becomes ambush
The second video that DW Fact check examined shows how genuine footage can become a source of disinformation.
Claim: A 30-second clip posted on X shows a convoy of military vehicles passing through a desert. Moments later, large explosions erupt and several vehicles are engulfed in smoke and flames. The caption reads: "The most beautiful thing I've seen: Houthis ambush against the Saudi-Backed Mercenaries' convoy in Yemeni."
DW Fact check: False
The video is old and unrelated to the ongoing conflict.
A timestamp visible in the video points to March 10, 2024. A reverse image search led DW to an older video published on YouTube in April 2024.
That video claims to show a Houthi military exercise. Its caption, written in Arabic, describes a simulated ambush on Israeli positions and attacks on US and British forces. Israeli and American flags can be seen in the footage.
DW also traced the sequence to a 42-minute video published by Yemeni War Media, an outlet affiliated with the Houthi movement.
Interestingly, the audio of that clip was changed. The version that is now circulating contains dramatic commentary, which is actually sports commentary from a football match played in 2018, as clips from that match show.
As is often the case, the clip with the convoy has also been used previously in different contexts.
With much of Yemen's media landscape weakened by the conflict, reliable information about events can be difficult to obtain.
That makes it harder for people to independently assess footage circulating online, Porter said. She added that unverified and misattributed videos can significantly shape perceptions of how battles are unfolding elsewhere.
"Any image or video that you see that is purported to be of a specific battle in Yemen, you have to be really skeptical," Porter said. "And you have to find a way to fact check it."
Emad Hassan contributed to this article
Edited by Uta Steinwehr and Thomas Sparrow

Ukraine kept this strike drone secret for two years—its maker says it has destroyed more than 350 Russian systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:50:55 UTC
21:50:55 KST

A Ukrainian drone maker has revealed it built a strike weapon it kept classified, deputy director Andrii Rymaruk told Radio NV. For two years, Ukrspecsystems, known for manufacturing Ukraine's SHARK reconnaissance drones, hid its connection to the RAM-2X strike drone, even as crews used it to hunt Russia's costly air defenses and missile launchers deep behind the front. By 2025, it had quietly become the Defense Forces' flagship mid-strike drone.
Ukraine's war on Russia's air defenses increasingly runs on drones its own industry builds and fields in secret, revealed only once they have already destroyed the enemy's costliest launchers and radars. Holding one back that long lets its crews rack up strikes before Moscow can study the weapon and build a counter—and this maker went public only once wrecked drones had reached Russian hands.
Why come out now
The RAM-2X first flew in combat in early 2024, but the maker kept its role secret. Rymaruk said the company wanted the drone and its crews to finish the job first—destroy what needed destroying—before talking. Once shot-down units reached the enemy and turned up on social media, silence no longer protected anything. So after two years, Ukrspecsystems unveiled the drone at the MSPO defense expo in Kielce, Poland.
What it kills
This is a mid-strike drone—a loitering munition that flies deep behind the lines, circles, and dives into its target. Its victims include S-400 and S-300 air defenses, the systems Russia uses to shoot down aircraft, and Iskander launchers that fire ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities.
Rymaruk put the RAM-2X's own tally at more than 350 Russian systems destroyed since 2024, while Defender Media, which interviewed him, reported more than 1,000 targets over two years. Ukrspecsystems credits the wider RAM series, which reaches back to a fixed-wing model supplied from late 2022, with more than 450 target engagements, over 400 of them against air defenses. Today, it destroys 50 to 60 pieces of Russian equipment a month.
How far, how many
The drone has grown fast. It flew 140 km in 2024 and now hits targets up to 180 km, almost 230 km in good conditions, and a crew from the 429th Achilles unmanned-systems brigade set a range record at 215.5 km. It has spread from a few crews to about 100 military units and 250 trained teams, and one operator can fly it from anywhere in Ukraine. It also works in pairs with the SHARK-M reconnaissance drone—one finds the target, the other kills it. In July, Ukrainians crowdfunded 30 of the drones for military intelligence and the security service through Serhii Prytula's foundation.

Carneys Vorstellungen über Handel in einer assoziierten Partnerschaft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:49:41 UTC
21:49:41 KST

Carneys Vorstellungen über Handel in einer assoziierten Partnerschaft
Der kanadische Ministerpräsident begrüßt in einer Rede vor dem EU-Parlament den Vorschlag und nennt Felder, in denen er eine vertiefte Zusammenarbeit sieht.
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks to the members of the Parliament at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, September 17, 2026. | Ronald Wittek/EPA
STRASSBURG - Mark Carney nutzte eine Rede vor dem Europäischen Parlament, um zu skizzieren, was Ottawa sich von engeren Beziehungen zur EU erhoffen würde. Allerdings stellte er sich nicht uneingeschränkt hinter Ursula von der Leyens überraschenden Vorstoß eines „assoziierten Mitgliedstaats“.
Einen Tag, nachdem der Kommissionspräsident diesen bislang einzigartigen Beziehungsstatus ins Spiel gebracht hatte, nahm der kanadische Premierminister das Angebot zur Kenntnis und nannte – anstatt es sofort anzunehmen – mögliche einzelne Bereiche der Zusammenarbeit, darunter kritische Mineralien, Verteidigung, KI, Energiesicherheit und Raumfahrt.
Er forderte außerdem einen reibungsloseren digitalen Handel mit nicht-landwirtschaftlichen Waren und Dienstleistungen sowie die Teilnahme Kanadas am Erasmus+-Programm, dem Studentenaustauschprogramm der EU.
Advertisement
„Wir begrüßen dieses Ziel“, sagte er mit Blick auf von der Leyens Vorschlag. „Umfragen zeigen, dass eine überwältigende Mehrheit der Kanadier deutlich engere Beziehungen befürwortet.“
Carneys Liste potenzieller Bündnisse war ein früher Versuch, einem bislang noch weitgehend undefinierten politischen Vorhaben konkrete Inhalte zu verleihen.
Die Idee eines „assoziierten Mitglieds“ hatte am Mittwoch für Verwirrung gesorgt, da die Kommission dies zuvor nicht mit den europäischen Hauptstädten abgestimmt hatte und ein solcher Status derzeit nicht existiert. Später am Mittwoch erklärte US-Präsident Donald Trump, er könnte mit „erheblichen Zöllen“ reagieren, sollte Kanada eine engere Anbindung an die EU anstreben.
„Ein Bündnis für die Zukunft ist ein einzigartiger, positiver Ansatz, den wir gemeinsam definieren werden, indem wir auf unseren gemeinsamen Stärken aufbauen und uns auf gemeinsame Werte stützen“, sagte Carney.
Ministerin Joly will Zölle vermeiden
Kanadas Wirtschaftsministerin Mélanie Joly deutete am Mittwoch gegenüber Reportern in Toronto an, dass Ottawa zusätzliche Garantien im Handelsbereich anstrebt – was möglicherweise neue Gesetze erfordern könnte.
Auf die Frage nach der Möglichkeit einer „assoziierten“ EU-Mitgliedschaft merkte Joly an, dass Länder mit Freihandelsabkommen dazu neigen, sich stärker abzuschotten, um ihre eigenen Industrien zu schützen, wenn sie mit Zöllen belegt werden. Sie hob insbesondere die EU hervor.
Advertisement
„Wir wollen sicherstellen, dass die Märkte zwischen uns weiterhin offen bleiben und dass nicht nur ein Freihandelsabkommen Bestand hat, sondern dass wir auch unsere Industriepolitik aufeinander abstimmen, insbesondere in den von den Zöllen betroffenen Sektoren“, sagte sie. „Das ist wirklich wichtig.“
Kanadas Parlament dürfte mitmischen
In einer Pressekonferenz im Anschluss an seine Rede wurde Carney gefragt, ob die kanadische Bevölkerung bei der assoziierten Mitgliedschaft mitreden könne. Er antwortete: „Natürlich. Es wird Debatten geben, und es wird eine Abstimmung im kanadischen Parlament geben, aber zum jetzigen Zeitpunkt ist dies erst der Anfang des Prozesses.“
Carneys Eingeständnis, dass es im Parlament letztendlich zu Abstimmungen über diese „Allianz für die Zukunft“ mit der EU kommen wird, schien darauf hinzudeuten, dass die kanadischen Abgeordneten ein Mitspracherecht bei den Plänen des Teams des Premierministers erhalten werden. Das Unterhaus kehrt am Montag aus der Sommerpause zurück.
Bevor von der Leyen die Bezeichnung „assoziiertes Mitglied“ fallen ließ, teilte Carney kanadischen Reportern mit, dass es in Straßburg keine „große Enthüllung“ geben werde.
„Die eigentliche Vertiefung und die Diskussionen werden mit unserem Gipfeltreffen in Montreal … gegen Ende Oktober beginnen“, sagte er am Dienstag in Toronto am Rande seines globalen Investitionsgipfels. „Und dann geht es von dort aus weiter.“
Europa hat für die Regierung Carney höchste Priorität, da die EU als der einfachste Weg für Kanada angesehen wird, die bestehenden Freihandelsbeziehungen zu vertiefen – ein Thema, das bereits vor einem Jahrzehnt im Parlament diskutiert wurde.
Advertisement
Nun stehen die Verantwortlichen in Kanada und der EU unter Druck, ihre lange Liste an Aufgaben abzuarbeiten, bevor sie in Montreal eintreffen, um Fortschritte in einer Reihe von Bereichen zu demonstrieren – von Handel und Rüstungsbeschaffung bis hin zu KI und Supercomputing.
Der designierte Botschafter bei der EU, Jonathan Wilkinson, erklärte gegenüber POLITICO, das Ziel des EU-Kanada-Gipfels bestehe darin, „eine Reihe sehr konkreter Maßnahmen“ zu erarbeiten, die im Laufe des nächsten Jahres umgesetzt werden sollen. „Wir wollen dabei sehr ehrgeizig vorgehen.“
Dieser Artikel wurde aktualisiert. Zi-Ann Lum und Sue Allan haben aus Ottawa zu diesem Artikel beigetragen. Er erschien zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO.

Nvidia’s Jensen Huang: Don’t regulate AI like social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:49:07 UTC
21:49:07 KST

Britain's King Charles III walks with DeepMind's Demis Hassabis and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang to attend a conference of leaders from the AI sector and government at Dumfries House in Cumnock, Scotland on September 17, 2026. | Pool photo by Jonathan Brady via AFP/Getty Images
AYRSHIRE, SCOTLAND — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said AI should not be regulated like social media because AI is a “technology” rather than a “product.”
Speaking at an AI event convened by King Charles III at Dumfries House in Ayrshire, Scotland, Huang told journalists that AI is “very different than social media” and that at present the security issues involving AI are “related to products not ready to be released.”
His remarks come as governments around the world are grappling with whether to place regulatory constraints on AI, and after AI executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have called for a slowing of AI development.
Advertisement
“Unlike social media, which is a product, AI is a technology that's behind all of these other tech, all of these products — and so, regulate the products,” Huang said.
He said authorities should monitor for when an AI deployment “goes wrong” and “whenever new laws are necessary, add to the existing laws,” but pointed out that there are existing regulations in sectors where AI is deployed such healthcare, transportation, and entertainment.
Rigorous testing systems are needed, he said, in contained testing labs. “That's engineering, good old-fashioned engineering. It's not more than that. It's not less than that,” he said, adding the sector has to ensure that there is the “rigor of testing these products properly before we release it to the public.”
“This is no different than, you know, an omelet's not ready to be released, or a car is not ready to be released, an airplane engine's not ready to be released,” Huang said. “You should properly test it.”
Huang reiterated his point about holding back models until they're safe to release in his formal address to the event, in front of King Charles and representatives from OpenAI and Anthropic.
“When a product is not safe enough, we should hold it back and keep engineering. We've always done that, and we should continue to do that,” he said.

Monets unseen by public emerge from billionaire family’s home for Paris auction
PARIS – Two paintings by the Impressionist master Claude Monet that have never been shown in public are to be sold in Paris in October by the billionaire Schlumberger family of France, auction house Sotheby’s said on Sept 17.
“Iris”, a large painting Monet completed towards the end of his life, has been valued at €22 million (S$32 million) to €30 million. That represents “the highest estimate ever given for a painting offered at auction in France”, Sotheby’s said as it unveiled the sale at its Paris headquarters.
It has never left the Schlumberger family’s home in Paris after being acquired by Jeanne Schlumberger (1889 –1983), who was described as “a brilliant art collector” by Sotheby’s art department co-head Thomas Bompard.
Alongside “Iris”, three other canvases by Monet are included in the sale on Oct 22, among them “Saule Pleureur” (Weeping Willow), valued at €9 million to €12 million.
The sale comes in the year marking the centenary of Monet’s death on Dec 5, 1926, which is being commemorated by two Paris exhibitions opening in late September: “Monet, Painting Time” and “Stories of Landscapes, from Monet to Hockney”.
The Schlumberger collection, which will be shown in Hong Kong and New York before the sale, also includes three works by Paul Cezanne, among them “La Ferme” (The Farm), “the largest work by the artist ever to be offered at auction”, estimated at €600,000 to €800,000.

JWST’s mysterious little red dots may be black holes growing at incredible speeds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:45:48 UTC
21:45:48 KST

JWST’s mysterious little red dots may be black holes growing at incredible speeds
- Date:
- September 17, 2026
- Source:
- National Institutes of Natural Sciences
- Summary:
- New supercomputer simulations suggest JWST’s puzzling Little Red Dots are rapidly growing black holes from the early Universe. Extreme radiation may have helped create unusually massive black hole seeds, while dense surrounding gas allowed them to grow dozens of times faster than black holes can today. The simulated objects closely resemble the Little Red Dots seen by Webb. If correct, they could solve the mystery of how enormous black holes formed so soon after the Big Bang.
- Share:
Among the many surprises uncovered by the James Webb Space Telescope, one of the strangest has been a large population of tiny, intensely red objects known as Little Red Dots. Their true nature has remained unclear. Now, new simulations performed with Japan's ATERUI III supercomputer suggest these objects may be rapidly growing black holes that took advantage of conditions in the early Universe that no longer exist today.
The findings do not require unusual physics or highly unlikely events. Instead, the simulations indicate that Little Red Dots could arise naturally from the environment of the young cosmos, where black holes were able to grow at extraordinary rates.
Simulating the Early Universe
The research was led by Sunmyon Chon of the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics. The team used the ATERUI III supercomputer at the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan to carry out some of the most detailed cosmological simulations yet of the early Universe.
The simulations began on the scale of a young galaxy and then progressively focused on smaller regions, eventually reaching individual clouds of gas. This demanding approach required the high-resolution computing power of ATERUI III.
The results suggest that intense far-ultraviolet (FUV) radiation from nearby galaxies can prevent ordinary stars from forming inside some gas clouds. Instead of breaking apart into many smaller stars, the gas can collapse into a single supermassive star.
That enormous star can then collapse and create a black hole seed.
Black Holes Growing at Extreme Speeds
Once these black hole seeds form, the simulations show that they can become surrounded by thick disks of dense gas. These gas-rich environments trap radiation and allow the black holes to consume material much more efficiently than black holes can in the modern Universe.
Under these conditions, the black holes can grow dozens of times faster than would be possible today.
The properties of these simulated black holes closely resemble the Little Red Dots (LRDs) observed by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). That similarity suggests the mysterious red objects could represent an early stage of extremely rapid black hole growth.
A Longstanding Black Hole Mystery
Astronomers have struggled for years to explain how supermassive black holes appeared so early in cosmic history. Some of these black holes contain millions or even billions of times the mass of the Sun, yet they already existed less than 600 million years after the Big Bang.
JWST was expected to help solve this puzzle by detecting fainter and more distant galaxies than previous telescopes could see.
Because light moves at a finite speed, observing very distant objects also means looking into the past. If a galaxy is 11 billion light-years away, its light has traveled for 11 billion years before reaching Earth. What we see is therefore the galaxy as it appeared 11 billion years ago. The same principle applies to a galaxy 12 billion light-years away, whose light is 12 billion years old.
JWST can peer farther back in time than earlier observatories, giving astronomers an unprecedented view of the young Universe.
Little Red Dots May Hold the Answer
Instead of immediately resolving the mystery of early black hole growth, JWST revealed something unexpected: a large population of tiny, extremely red objects that researchers began calling Little Red Dots (LRDs).
The new simulations suggest those objects may actually be the missing piece of the puzzle.
According to the model, the conditions needed to create and rapidly grow these black holes developed naturally in the early Universe. No exotic assumptions or rare coincidences were necessary. That could also help explain why Little Red Dots appear to be so common in JWST observations.
As JWST continues finding more LRDs and future telescopes look even deeper into cosmic history, this model could give astronomers a valuable framework for understanding how some of the Universe's earliest black holes formed, grew, and helped shape the evolution of the cosmos.
Story Source:
Materials provided by National Institutes of Natural Sciences. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Sunmyon Chon, Shingo Hirano, Tomoaki Ishiyama, Seok-Jun Chang, Volker Springel. Overmassive black holes and little red dots naturally form in simulations. Nature, 2026; 657 (8132): 621 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10985-8

Melike Pala

Around 40 flights were cancelled at Belgium's Charleroi Airport on Thursday, with further cancellations underway Friday as an air traffic controllers' strike continued to disrupt operations.
Around 10 departures had already been listed as cancelled for Friday on the official website, with the number expected to increase throughout the day.
The airport confirmed that the first wave of cancellations for Friday morning had been finalized, with 18 flights scheduled to be cancelled, according to French-language broadcaster RTBF.
"We can already confirm cancellations for tomorrow. There's nothing to suggest we won't be blocked until 8 am (0600GMT) tomorrow morning and then again from 10 pm (2000GMT) tomorrow evening," the airport's operations director Nicolas Charluteau said.
On Thursday, nine departing and nine arriving flights had been cancelled in the morning, while another 12 departures and 12 arrivals were expected to be cancelled in the evening.
The disruptions are linked to a strike by air traffic controllers working at Charleroi Airport, who are taking part in overnight industrial action between 10 pm and 8 am from Sept. 16 through Oct. 10.
According to unions, the controllers are demanding that their night-shift allowance be brought in line with that of their colleagues at Liege Airport.
Skeyes, Belgium's air traffic control operator, has opposed the demand, saying the proposed increase would amount to a 160% rise.

South Africa: Police find 9th body of woman amid spree fears
