Oschadbank, EBRR sign second EUR 50 mln ESSF guarantee tranche
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:05:31 EEST
21:05:31 KST

Oschadbank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) signed an agreement on a second EUR 50 million tranche under the guarantee instrument of the Energy Security and Stability Facility (ESSF), the state-owned bank's press service said.
The document was signed on September 15 in London during the EBRD's annual meeting with its partner banks in Ukraine.
The program provides for partial EBRD coverage of risks associated with Oschadbank's investment loans to finance projects in power generation and energy efficiency. The guarantee coverage amounts to 50% of the respective loan.
"Demand for this instrument is confirmed by the first tranche that has already been implemented. The new EUR50 million will make it possible to continue financing projects that help businesses, communities and other clients strengthen their energy resilience," Oschadbank Chairman of the Management Board Yuriy Katsion said.
According to him, such financing is particularly important ahead of the fall and winter period because of risks to energy supplies resulting from continuing Russian attacks on energy infrastructure.
The ESSF is aimed at small and medium-sized enterprises, medium-sized corporate clients, municipalities, small state-owned enterprises, private households and condominiums associations. Financing is directed toward distributed generation, renewable energy sources, energy storage systems and improvements in the energy efficiency of residential, commercial and municipal buildings.
The total financing volume of the ESSF program is EUR 2 billion. In addition to Oschadbank, seven other Ukrainian banks participate in the program: state-owned PrivatBank, Ukreximbank and Ukrgasbank, as well as UkrSibbank, ProCredit Bank, Credit Agricole Bank and Raiffeisen Bank.
The program is implemented with financial support from the European Union (EU), France and the Netherlands.
As reported, on February 12, 2025, the EBRD and Oschadbank signed an agreement on the bank's participation in the ESSF, providing for a portfolio risk-sharing instrument without pre-financing for subloans totaling up to EUR 100 million.
Grant support for borrowers under the program may cover 10-30% of investment costs. Increased grant amounts are provided, in particular, for war-affected enterprises and households, as well as borrowers contributing to the reintegration of veterans, people with disabilities and internally displaced persons.
At least 70% of subloans must be directed to projects meeting the criteria of the Green Economy Transition (GET), while up to 20% of total financing may be allocated to long-term capital investments by SMEs to modernize technology and equipment in accordance with EU standards.
According to National Bank data, as of August 1, 2026, Oschadbank ranked second among Ukraine's 59 banks by total assets, at UAH 514.21 billion.

EU Commission proposes under-13s social media ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:03:54 UTC
21:03:54 KST

EU Commission proposes under-13s social media ban
STRASBOURG, France, Sept 17 - European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen set out a sweeping plan to keep children safe from online dangers on Thursday, proposing to ban under-13s from social media and require online services to design safe children's accounts.
The move follows similar initiatives in Australia, Britain, China, India, Turkey and several European Union countries over concerns about the impact Meta's Facebook and Instagram, TikTok, Google's YouTube and ChatGPT have on children's mental health and safety.
Australia's challenges in enforcing its world-first social media ban for children under 16 could see Europe facing an uphill battle as well.
"Today, our children are engaging with some of the most sophisticated technology ever created, and it was not created with children's well-being and development in mind," von der Leyen told a press conference.
She said the proposed EU Kids Act "will set clear boundaries in the digital world just as we do it on a daily basis in the real world".
PARENTAL CONTROL
Under the proposal, which must be negotiated with EU countries and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law, accounts for children aged between 13 and 15 will be under parental control.
Social media and video-sharing services, online video games, AI companions and chatbots for children below 18 will be subject to a list of dos and don'ts.
These include a ban on addictive features, profiling-based recommender feeds, infinite scroll, reward tricks and unsolicited contact from strangers. AI companions and chatbots must be turned off by default.
Online platforms must design algorithms safe for children and provide easy-to-use parental controls and tools to block and mute users.
The companies, which must verify users' age when they open an account via age assurance tools, risk fines as much as 6% of their global annual sales for non-compliance. They will also have to pay a supervisory fee to fund regulators' supervision.
Tech lobbying group CCIA Europe, whose members include Google and Meta, warned of the privacy risks arising from the proposal and conflicting requirements under other EU laws.
"Collecting age information, identity credentials, and data linking children with parents or guardians at this scale would undoubtedly create an attractive target for cybercriminals," CCIA head Daniel Friedlaender said.
"The Kids Act creates legal overlap and duplication that ultimately weaken protections for children and consumers," he said. REUTERS

Saudi Arabia explores uranium for energy diversification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:03:25 UTC
21:03:25 KST

Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia plans energy diversification via Jabal Sayid uranium deposit
Saudi Arabia's announcement on 14 September of the discovery of huge geological resources estimated at 114 million tonnes of ore containing concentrations of uranium and rare earth elements at the Jabal Sayid deposit in the Medina region has highlighted a move towards developing an integrated national nuclear fuel cycle and local value chain, starting with ore extraction and extending to yellowcake production.
The strategic shift aims to accelerate Saudi Arabia's peaceful nuclear programme and diversify its electricity mix, alongside building advanced industrial partnerships with US and European companies to strengthen global critical mineral supply chains.
The technical and historical characteristics of the Jabal Sayid deposit, located about 350 kilometres northeast of Jeddah, reflect complex geological significance.
The site hosts active underground copper mining operations, while recent surveys by the Sedimentary Cover Initiative have revealed deep rock layers containing both radioactive ores and heavy rare earth elements.
The development comes amid Riyadh's desire to move beyond the export of unprocessed raw materials and become an industrial partner capable of producing high-purity oxides and critical inputs needed for future industries and clean defence technologies, according to a report published by Mining, a platform specialising in mining news and international metals markets, on 14 September.
There is currently technical and investment uncertainty, given that the geological data released so far have not disclosed the net quantities of uranium that can actually be extracted from the total mass of rock deposits, according to economist Munir Rashid.
Rashid told The New Arab that developing uranium deposits, processing and refining the ore, and enriching its content to make it directly and safely usable for electricity generation requires heavy financial investment, advanced techniques and high-level technology.
Rashid said the crucial issue in this process is calculating the cost of producing and refining uranium domestically.
He pointed out that if the cost of producing and processing the ore locally is higher than the prices of imports available on global markets, it would be better for the national economy to rely directly on imported material rather than bear operational costs that are not commercially viable.
Processing and refining nuclear ores requires complex technical procedures, including the establishment of advanced chemical and industrial complexes for acid leaching and selective precipitation to isolate radioactive compounds from accompanying metallic elements with high recovery rates.
This would pave the way for processing ores from the Medina deposit and converting them into yellowcake concentrates according to the strict international industrial standards required to operate civilian reactors and nuclear power plants, according to a report published by ChemAnalyst, which specialises in chemical and industrial materials analysis and supply chains, on 15 September.
Reducing dependence on crude oil remains the main economic gain and ultimate benefit for the kingdom from developing nuclear energy, as it would provide additional quantities of oil for export to international markets and generate higher foreign-currency revenues.
It would also directly reduce environmental pollution and carbon emissions associated with power generation, Rashid said.
He added that the discovery of uranium ores alongside other minerals in a single deposit was positive from a mining perspective, but that it was still far too early to determine the kingdom's net benefit before completing field studies, assessing separation and refining costs, and comparing them with available alternatives.
These field steps are complemented by an active diplomatic and regulatory track in Vienna on 14 September, where the Saudi side held talks with officials from the International Atomic Energy Agency and international partners to frame peaceful nuclear cooperation agreements and establish joint safeguards for technology transfers and securing the civilian fuel cycle.
This comes amid ongoing strategic discussions with the United States on nuclear agreements and strict regulatory frameworks for transferring technical knowledge and securing peaceful enrichment cycles in line with international non-proliferation standards, according to a report published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace on 9 September.
The announcement of the discovery of uranium resources, alongside rare earth elements in the Jabal Sayid area, is a promising indicator for Saudi Arabia that strengthens opportunities for economic diversification and provides new sources of state revenue, according to economist Hossam Ayesh.
Ayesh told TNA that the discovery represents a strategic addition to the Saudi peaceful nuclear programme.
He explained that it expands the potential domestic resource base for uranium, particularly as the kingdom is pursuing another parallel route to extract uranium associated with phosphoric acid production in the phosphate fertiliser industry.
Saudi Arabia aims not to rely on a single source but is building a multi-source base to strengthen national energy security over the long term.
The Jabal Sayid deposit occupy a prominent position on the strategic resources map because they contain promising concentrations of heavy rare earth elements, such as dysprosium and terbium, which are crucial for manufacturing defence technologies, electric motors and advanced computing systems.
This places the project among the leading mining projects capable of balancing global supply chains for critical materials and diversifying their extraction centres, according to a report published by Mining.com.au, which specialises in resource exploration and global mining supply chains, on 15 September.
But the discovery does not mean immediate nuclear fuel self-sufficiency, as moving from natural ore to yellowcake and then to ready-to-use nuclear fuel requires advanced technologies and additional processing stages, Ayesh said.
However, he also noted it provides an important foundation for building part of the value chain locally.
Nuclear energy also plays a vital complementary role alongside solar, wind and gas by providing stable electricity around the clock as a permanent baseload, reducing the need to burn large quantities of oil and gas domestically to generate electricity and desalinate water.
This would allow larger quantities of hydrocarbons to be directed towards export markets and provide the feedstock needed to support and expand higher-value domestic petrochemical industries.
The announced industrial partnerships with US and European companies in critical mineral supply chains are significant beyond the traditional investment aspect, as they coincide with Western efforts to reduce dependence on China for securing vital metals, according to Ayesh's analysis of the geopolitical and competitive dimensions.
He noted that Saudi Arabia has an advantage in this context by combining mining resources, abundant energy supplies, advanced infrastructure, a strategic geographical location and investment capital, while Western partners provide advanced technology and accumulated expertise in extraction, separation and refining processes.
Uranium and rare earth elements thus become part of a single strategy aimed at securing energy sustainability, maximising the value of mineral wealth, localising technology industries and strengthening Saudi Arabia's position in global supply chains for energy, technology and artificial intelligence.
This would move the kingdom, according to Ayesh, from being solely a hydrocarbon exporter to becoming a major and reliable player in the clean energy economy.

Can art offer a blueprint for healing? That’s the argument Dana Awartani, 39, makes in her work. The Saudi Arabian artist creates immersive installations of silk panels by ripping and “darning” (or repairing) the fabric. She also works with experts in ancient craft traditions to build installations that double as memorials to places destroyed by conflict. At this year’s Venice Biennale, she covered the floor of Saudi Arabia’s pavilion with 29,000 clay bricks, handmade by 32 master artisans, which referenced 23 damaged sites across the Levant. Entering the installation felt like being transported into an archaeological dig. Laid without binding agents, the floor was designed to crack over the course of the show’s run—an acknowledgement of the fragility of cultural heritage and the violence of erasure. Awartani, who trained in Islamic art traditions, will open solo shows at Lisson Gallery in London in November and Norway’s Stavanger Art Museum next year.

Ken Griffin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:01:33 UTC
21:01:33 KST

“My first love in art was the proverbial one that got away,” says Ken Griffin, the CEO of the hedge fund Citadel. In 1999, he lost out on a sculpture of a dancer by the French Impressionist Edgar Degas. He has rarely let it happen again. Over the past two decades, Griffin has emerged as one of the world’s most dogged, deep-pocketed collectors. His treasures include Abstract Expressionist paintings worth nine figures, rare historical documents, and a Madonna and Child attributed to Leonardo da Vinci.
While Griffin previously lent many of his most valuable works to museums anonymously, he has expanded and become more public about his activities over the past year, a shift he says is designed to facilitate scholarship and education as well as satisfy public curiosity. He loaned the da Vinci to the Met this spring, doubling the number of paintings by the Renaissance master on view in the U.S.
The billionaire has also expanded his support of Florida museums since his much-publicized relocation to Miami from Chicago in 2022. Over the summer, an exhibition of 10 works by Jean-Michel Basquiat from his collection went on view at the Pérez Art Museum in Griffin’s new hometown. In 2027, he will place a Richard Serra sculpture he bought earlier this year on public display in a park next to the museum. “It’s monumental, it's thought-provoking, and, bluntly, it's just fun,” Griffin says of the work. “An institution has a different criteria to collect than I do as a private individual. I place a huge importance on the aesthetic appeal of a work. Does this work visually make me happy?”

Olugbile Holloway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:01:32 UTC
21:01:32 KST

In 1897, British troops sacked Benin City in modern-day Nigeria, and stole about 5,000 artifacts collectively known as the Benin Bronzes. Despite decades of calls for repatriation, many of these looted objects remained in museums in Europe and the U.S. until 2021, when some governments and institutions finally began to return them. Last June, Olugbile Holloway, the director-general of Nigeria’s National Commission for Museums and Monuments, facilitated one of the largest single repatriations of the looted Benin Bronzes to date: 119 objects from the Netherlands. In February, he oversaw the return of over 100 artifacts from the University of Cambridge to Nigeria.
According to Chika Okeke-Agulu, an expert in African diaspora art history, the historic agreement stems from Holloway’s ability to quell confusion both within Nigeria and abroad about the rightful owner of the bronzes. Holloway—whose background is in corporate advertising—says he and the Benin Oba, or monarch, adopted a 20-page agreement outlining shared commitments to the artifacts’ future. Because of that agreement, Holloway says, the Nigerian government presented a unified front in its request for the return of bronzes from the Netherlands. The director-general has now set his sights on negotiating the future of Nigerian antiquities at the British Museum, which is prohibited by law from deaccessioning its collection of bronzes.

Dayanita Singh creates images that pulse with life. The Indian photographer is known for unfiltered shots of local shopkeepers, strangers, and friends and family. Wolfgang Tillmans has relentlessly pushed the boundaries of photography. A decade before camera phones, he recognized the power of capturing unguarded portraits of LGTBQIA+ people and their communities, helping to destigmatize queer life during the AIDS crisis. The German artist also pioneered a style of colorful abstract chemical prints that have become among the most sought-after contemporary photographs, with auction prices surpassing $750,000.

In May, he won the $185,000 Roswitha Haftmann Prize, Europe’s largest monetary art award, affirming his status as one of today’s most potent photographers.

Yale School of Art Dean Kymberly Pinder wants her Master’s of Fine Arts students to graduate debt-free. Carmelo Anthony
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:01:31 UTC
21:01:31 KST

Athletes often draw comparisons to artists, and basketball Hall of Famer Carmelo Anthony—who danced around defenses, innovated angles, and showed a delicate touch around the basket en route to scoring 28,289 points in his 19-year NBA career—counts as a master craftsman. So it’s only fitting that Anthony, like other professional athletes, is starting to make his mark as an art collector. Anthony—who owns works from the likes of Ernie Barnes, the former pro football player who went on to become a noted painter; South African portraitist Nelson Makamo; and the urban contemporary artist Cryptik—moved out of his New York City apartment into a suburban house in 2022 to give his vast collection more breathing space.
How many pieces does he own? “I’ve stopped counting,” Anthony tells TIME. “I’m not one that goes out there to try to look for the trends, or to see what everybody else is doing. I’ve gotten more intentional on quality over quantity.”
Anthony’s love for art came early, his taste shaped by the street graffiti and Earth, Wind & Fire album covers he noticed growing up in Brooklyn and Baltimore. By the time he was drafted into the NBA in 2003, he was already familiar with Barnes, whose seminal 1976 work “The Sugar Shack,” depicting a joyous dance hall in the segregated South, had appeared on a Marvin Gaye album cover and in the credits of the 1970s hit sitcom Good Times. “How his artwork was implemented into the Black culture,” says Anthony, “was special to see.”
After Anthony joined the New York Knicks in 2011, his passion grew. He listened to former players reminisce about traversing the SoHo art scene and collecting works by the likes of Jean-Michel Basquiat and Andy Warhol. Anthony started popping into art galleries on the road, and by the time he stopped playing in 2022, he’d amassed many of the works that now fill his home.
In a busy post-NBA career (he’s also invested in wine, cannabis, apparel, and production companies), Anthony isn’t slowing down. “Everybody is looking at you crazy,” he says. “‘Melo, what are you doing?’” With art, Anthony sees endless possibilities. He may attempt, at some point, to learn painting himself. “The next step is to actually start to try to visualize stories and try it.”
One day, he’d like to bring his collection to the public. The dream location for such an opening? Baltimore, where he moved when he was 8 years old. “A lot of the art that I have comes from being emotionally attached to the city, and all things that I've been through,” says Anthony. “To be able to start it there would mean a lot.”
The collector has advice for other athletes—or anyone, really—looking to take the art plunge. “Art can be intimidating,” he says. “But just don't be in a rush. Take your time. If you don't understand it right there, leave it and come back to it. If it brings you back, then you know that's the piece. That’s when you know it's genuine.”

Loïc Gouzer has made a career out of shaking up the once staid and stuffy auction business. While hundreds of objects might be sold in a single afternoon at Christie’s or Sotheby’s, Gouzer’s app, Fair Warning, allows a select group of collectors to bid on one carefully-chosen work at a time. Sales on the app have set world auction records for contemporary artists including Elizabeth Peyton and Steven Shearer. In November, Fair Warning sold a 1974 Andy Warhol portrait of French film icon Brigitte Bardot for $16.7 million, the highest auction price recorded for the artist that year. Gouzer earned his reputation as the enfant terrible of the art market at Christie’s, where he was instrumental in coordinating the sale of Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi in 2017, generating $450.3 million. Nearly a decade later, it remains the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction. Gouzer’s flair for showmanship continued in May with Fair Warning’s sale of Banksy’s Girl and Balloon on Found Landscape at Tiffany’s Fifth Avenue flagship in New York City, where it fetched $18 million.

Alicia Keys and Swizz Beatz Are on the 2026 TIME100 Art List
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:01:30 UTC
21:01:30 KST

When Alicia Keys and Kaseem “Swizz Beatz” Dean first started collecting art together well over a decade ago, they were mostly just doing it for the love of the game. “We started collecting without a mission, to be honest,” Dean says. “We were collecting because we love art. We were collecting because it was something amazing to do together.”
Now, more than 130 pieces from the married couple’s personal trove—which they refer to as the Dean Collection—are being shown in museums across the U.S. in a traveling exhibition called “Giants.” As the name suggests, the featured works loom large, both literally and figuratively: a hulking tire wrapped in chains by Arthur Jafa, a painted diptych of BMX bike riders popping wheelies by Amy Sherald, vibrant photography from the streets of New York City shot by Jamel Shabazz. The selected works make up only a small fraction of the thousand-plus holdings the couple has acquired over time.
Since opening at the Brooklyn Museum in 2024, “Giants” has made stops in four other American cities, with still more planned across the globe through 2031. The show broke attendance records at the Museum of Contemporary Art San Diego in August by attracting more than 25,000 people in the almost four months it was there.
Keys, 45, and Dean, 48, are towering figures themselves. She is a 17-time Grammy-winning singer-songwriter; he is a DJ, rapper, and producer with a Grammy of his own. All things considered, it’s not much of a surprise that the pair has become so deeply immersed in the art world. As Dean says, “Art and music are brothers and sisters.”
It was the connection between these two creative universes that allowed the couple to zero in on a mission for the Dean Collection: they would use it to celebrate and uplift living visual artists, especially those who are Black, by creating a collection that felt like a family. Keys and Dean began to develop deeper relationships with the artists whose work they were collecting. They visited studios and brought their five children along; they answered late-night phone calls; they offered advice when they could.
“What got us a lot of love and credibility was being human and not transactional,” says Dean. Throughout the time they have been collecting, Keys says, “We’ve been able to develop a relationship with the artist that’s really from a pure place, and there’s really a friendship there. There’s a mutual respect.”
“We’ve always been in a different state of mind just because we are also artists,” she adds. “So the way we relate to artists is going to naturally be different than anybody else.”
Their shared music knowledge has also allowed Keys and Dean to bring fresh perspectives to the business side of art. Visual artists do not typically receive royalties, at least in the U.S., when their work is resold through an auction house, gallery, or private sale. If a collector buys a painting for $10,000 and sells it for $1 million one year later, the artist never sees a penny of the windfall.
“We never could understand that,” Dean says. Musicians typically receive royalties anytime their work is reproduced or used commercially. “Why should the rules apply for us and not for the visual artists?”
On Sept. 9, the couple announced Deans’ Choice—a groundbreaking elective program through Bonhams auction house that allows U.S.-based sellers to direct a percentage of proceeds to the living artist behind a sold work. Even if only a handful of sellers choose to participate, “we already won,” Dean says. “This is the beginning of something amazing, and we feel that a lot of people will do the right thing.”
Deans’ Choice was a dream that took seven years to become reality, the couple says, but their desire to do right by the artists they patronize has only grown stronger in that time. “We can’t come in and just break the rules,” Dean says. “But we could start to change things that we don’t like.”
“The ideal industry for any creative person should be a place where they are completely empowered,” Keys says. “The Dean Collection is by the artist, for the artist, with the people.”

Anne Kraybill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:01:30 UTC
21:01:30 KST

Does art really exist if nobody ever sees it? This question drives Anne Kraybill, the CEO of Art Bridges, a kind of art-sharing enterprise that helps extract works from viewer-free storage rooms so they can be displayed at museums (often rural, often under-resourced) around the U.S. The concept is more complicated than it sounds because of insurance, shipping costs, and issues around preservation—as well as the general tendency for art institutions to operate in silos. Art Bridges, with funds provided by Walmart heiress Alice Walton, helps clear obstacles to the free exchange of art, with training, logistical help, and of course, funding. Currently, for example, it’s supporting the Heckscher Museum in Huntington, N.Y., as it lends an exhibition of Emma Stebbins sculpture to the Driehaus in Chicago starting in October. One bugbear of Kraybill’s, for example, is the strict humidity standard that many galleries impose on other institutions before lending out works—standards that old, rural buildings often cannot meet. Art Bridges has found and funded research and conferences to clarify what kind of climate control is necessary to protect artworks, and what is merely optimal. Art Bridges is now working with 253 museums. “Collectively,” says Kraybill, “there's more than enough art to bring these new experiences to the public across the country.”

Charles Stewart

When telecom tycoon Patrick Drahi acquired Sotheby’s in 2019, he raised eyebrows by naming Charles Stewart the now 282-year-old auction house’s chief executive. Stewart, 56, had a long career in banking and corporate leadership but had never worked in the art world. Fast forward to 2026, and he is the longest-tenured current head of a major auction house. He’s also managed some growth within a challenging market.
Under Stewart, Sotheby’s has opened a new Hong Kong flagship featuring a retail boutique and, in November, relocated its New York headquarters to a landmarked Madison Avenue building whose past tenants include the Whitney, the Met, and the Frick Collection. He has expanded Sotheby’s ties to the Gulf, securing around $1 billion of investment from Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth fund in late 2024 and launching live sales in Saudi Arabia in 2025—a first for a Western auction house. The firm’s offerings have diversified, too, expanding further into collectibles and even taking a controlling stake in collectible cars specialist RM Auctions. It seems the CEO’s outsider thinking has paid off: altogether, Sotheby’s sold nearly $50 billion of art and luxury collectibles in Stewart’s first seven years.

If old-fashioned-seeming genres like history painting and portraiture have begun to feel fresh again, you can thank Kerry James Marshall. ====================================================================================================

Apple Watch Series 12 Review: Finally, a Readiness Score (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:01:00 UTC
21:01:00 KST

After wearing it day and night for a week, I found that better health tracking, faster charging, and a simpler interface make Apple’s latest smartwatch noticeably easier to live with.
New Health Sensing System increases frequency and breadth of health metrics. New Readiness score. Audio Intelligence. Faster charging. Cleaner watchOS 27 interface. Beautiful bronze finish, and ceramic is back.
TIRED
Still only 24 hours of battery life. Privacy concerns around Siri Recap and Live Rewind.
On the surface, the Apple Watch Series 12 doesn’t appear to be a major upgrade over last year’s release and, in many ways, it isn’t. But after a week of wearing it day and night, I noticed that the Series 12 feels more intuitive, putting fewer steps between me and the information I need from my everyday smartwatch.
Health tracking is more thorough, thanks to a new Health Sensing System and faster S11 chip. The watchOS 27 update, first announced at WWDC in June and finally available to consumers, gives the Apple Watch a cleaner, streamlined interface that positions Siri AI at the center of the user experience. The most notable addition is perhaps Audio Intelligence, a suite of listening tools powered by Apple Intelligence. Plus, in a fun return, the Series 12 also comes in ceramic, a premium finish Apple discontinued in 2020.
Not everyone needs the upgrade, though. If you’re coming from the Series 8 or older, the Series 12 is a generational leap, with a better display, longer battery life, and newer health features, including sleep apnea and hypertension notifications. Owners of the Series 9 or 10 have fewer reasons to swap, but the battery improvements alone (18 hours to 24 hours) may be compelling. If you already have the Series 11, Audio Intelligence probably isn’t going to be enough to justify replacing a watch that’s already capable of most of the same functions.
Polished, Inside and Out
Visually, Apple isn’t fixing what isn’t broken, and I’m not mad about it. The Series 12 looks nearly identical to its predecessors, but Apple highlights it as its thinnest Apple Watch yet. The aluminum and titanium models measure 9.7 millimeters thick, and the ceramic option is 9.85 millimeters thick. I didn’t notice a difference during everyday wear, but the Apple Watch Series remains one of the most comfortable smartwatches I’ve tested. Aside from the new Hermès collection, there aren’t any new band designs this year, but Apple has added new colors to the existing lineup.
Photograph: Boutayna Chokrane
The new finishes are exciting, particularly the return of ceramic. Apple first offered a ceramic option with the Series 2 in 2016, and it was discontinued in 2020. Today, it’s available in pearl white and night blue, both of which give the Series 12 a softer finish that looks more like an accessory. The ceramic feels more like a fashionable move rather than a functional one, but Apple is following a trend seen across brands like Oura.
I’m testing the aluminum model in the new dark bronze finish, which has become my favorite. It complements most of my wardrobe and gives the watch a more cosmopolitan look than some of Apple’s sportier colorways. Aluminum models are also available in the standard light gold, black, and space gray; titanium comes in natural and a new radiant gold. The aluminum models are now coated with Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is 60 percent tougher than the previous Ion-X glass. I haven’t had enough time with the watch to meaningfully test that durability claim, but for someone who tends to knock their smartwatch on doors and countertops, it’s an improvement I’ll happily accept.
Battery life remains rated at 24 hours, which is slightly disappointing when competitors can go longer between charges. The saving grace is faster charging. Fifteen minutes of charging now provides up to 12 hours of battery life, and five minutes gets you up to 10 hours of sleep tracking. This has been the most useful upgrade for me. I can set the watch to charge while I’m getting ready for bed and put it back on for sleep tracking.
Photograph: Boutayna Chokrane
The Series 12 ships with watchOS 27, but most of the software changes will also arrive on compatible older Apple Watches. I particularly love the revamped app layout. Instead of having to hunt through a sea of icons or scroll through an exhaustive list, Apple now surfaces five Siri AI-suggested apps, the Siri app, and a shortcut to the full app grid. The apps I need most are immediately available without cluttering the display.
Apple is also making the watch easier to navigate with one hand, adding a single-tap gesture to Apple’s existing double-tap and wrist-flick controls. Tap your index finger and thumb together to select widgets in Smart Stack; double-tap lets you scroll through them. A wrist flick can return you to the watch face, silence timers, or dismiss notifications. These gestures are particularly handy (ha) when you’re multitasking or if you want to use your watch discreetly.
Better at Reading You
The new S11 chip brings the standard round of faster CPU and GPU performance, along with a more efficient Neural Engine. S11 also powers a remodeled pedometer to improve step counts and distance measurements, particularly during indoor walks and runs. Compared to Series 11, I didn’t notice much difference in numbers. I do, though, appreciate the new Steps complication, which puts my real-time step count on the watch face, so I can check my progress without opening the Activity app.
Video: Boutayna Chokrane
The bigger hardware upgrade is Apple’s new Health Sensing System. The Series 12 has 32 electrodes for improved skin contact during ECG readings, compared with two on the Series 11. The photodiodes have been rearranged in a ring configuration for improved optical sensing, and larger green LEDs have been added for more accurate heart rate readings.
The result, and one of the watch’s biggest selling points, is that it takes more frequent readings. The Series 12 measures heart rate every five seconds, even while you’re moving, whereas the Series 11 takes readings every five minutes when you’re relatively stationary. The Series 12 can also measure heart rate variability (HRV) as often as every five minutes, compared with every two hours on the Series 11, and it measures two variants: recovery HRV and overall HRV. For health-conscious people, the higher sampling frequency gives you a more continuous picture of how your body responds to stressors throughout the day instead of a handful of isolated snapshots. You can see those readings in the Heart Rate app or through the new live heart rate complications.
Video: Boutayna Chokrane
Readiness has at last arrived for anyone who has been anticipating a unified recovery score from Apple. The new Readiness app pulls together activity, sleep, and other health data to estimate how prepared you are for the day ahead. It takes seven days of sleep data before the score becomes available, which is standard for wearables to determine a baseline.
I like having the score as a quick shorthand instead of attempting to contextualize the individual metrics myself, but I stay skeptical of any recovery score that simplifies complicated physiological states using a proprietary algorithm. That said, Readiness is useful as a prompt to pay attention to your body, and I’m glad Apple finally has one.
Apple is also planning a redesigned Health app later this year, including a new Longevity tab and metrics such as Health Age, which compares your health data with that of your demographic. I haven’t been able to test those features yet, but I have a feeling my Health Age will either be oddly gratifying or immediately anxiety-inducing.
A Little Too Attentive
Audio Intelligence may be Apple’s most controversial addition. The suite brings four audio-focused features, including accelerated Shazam and Sound Recognition, the latter of which has been available on the iPhone since 2020. The more intriguing additions are Siri Recap and Live Rewind, which push the Apple Watch into murky waters by using its microphone to capture and process audio. I haven’t been able to test either feature yet; both are slated to arrive later this year.
Siri Recap is Apple’s answer to the AI notetaking boom. When enabled, it can transcribe conversations and generate summaries using Apple Intelligence. I can see the appeal for meetings and classes. During a briefing, I saw Siri Recap turn a PTA meeting into a detailed set of notes and reminders that seemed genuinely useful.
Live Rewind is harder to wrap my head around. The feature maintains a rolling buffer of recent audio so you can ask the watch for a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Double-press the Digital Crown and, in theory, you can recover something you just missed without asking the other person to repeat themselves.
The privacy concerns are justified, and you can read more about them here. Apple says the audio is processed in a protected memory area called the Secure Enclave. The S11 chip has an isolated buffer for sensor data, and Apple says raw audio isn’t accessible to the operating system, apps, the user, or Apple. The company also says these features don’t create or store audio recordings.
That’s somewhat reassuring, but it doesn’t eliminate the always-listening worries. Live Rewind supposedly plays an audible chime when activated to alert people nearby. Whether a beep is sufficient consent is a personal judgment call. I will test these features myself once they roll out and will report back.
Apple has refined the everyday experience, added health metrics people actually want, and resisted the temptation to bury the watch under a pile of new features. It’s a thoughtful update, and that makes the Series 12 the best Apple Watch yet.

Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public office and buildings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:00:50 UTC
21:00:50 KST

The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading” ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.
The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.
The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.
“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.
“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”
Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.
Schools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.
A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could be classified as potential harassment.
The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.
Courts in England and Wales in the UK and New York state in the US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedly classified them as body-worn cameras and barred them from the “federal workspace”.
A local council in Sydney on Tuesday became the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.
In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.
The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.
Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisions and said she would consult businesses on their approach.
“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.
“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”
Vision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.
Gallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.
“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.
Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.
The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.
Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.
Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.
“Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said.
Additional reporting from Caitlin Cassidy

Welcome to the age of the grown-up soft drink

I have written recently about several families of nonalcoholic drinks that are having a moment: tonic water, flavoured sparkling water and wine substitutes. It stands to reason that soft drinks are enjoying their time in the sun. Quite literally, too: the heat of 2026 has demanded some serious refreshments and UK booze consumption is at a record low. But it has dawned on me that there is a broader trend in alcohol-free beverages beyond individual categories, namely that we are living in the age of the grown-up soft drink.
By that I mean those with less sugar and more complexity than post-mix drinks, or “soda pop” (as my daughter now calls them, thanks to the KPop Demon Hunters song of the same name), which are clearly aimed at adults. One example is the tribe of “functional” drinks that have hit the market in the past year or so and that have supposed health benefits or performance-enhancing qualities, such as improving focus or helping you to slow down. Sonic Tonics’ CBD-infused 0% drink, for example, promises to shift your mood, and it certainly quenches thirst with a really original flavour profile of bitter hemp root with sweet and floral fig and violet. And while usually sceptical of celebrity-backed products with wellness claims, Gillian Anderson’s G Spot drinks are genuinely delicious. The passion fruit and habanero chilli is my favourite; I can’t support its aphrodisiac claims (allegedly due to its ingredients including butterfly pea and L-arginine, both of which are said to increase blood flow to the sexual organs), but, at £6.50 for four from Ocado, it’s cheaper than trying Gwyneth Paltrow’s sex oil.
There are also several low-sugar “premium” soft drinks that are worth writing home about, such as deli favourite Something & Nothing, which contains no sweeteners and only natural sugars; the yuzu and the mango and Thai basil flavours are both perfect. Rapscallion Soda was developed to make satisfying soft drinks without a sugar crash; raw fruit is extracted and mixed with citrus, spices and carbonated water: think burnt lemon with cracked black pepper and dry lime with makrut lime leaves.
Then there are drinks designed to be consumed on occasions when you might otherwise drink alcohol. Botivo has created a sparkling, premixed version of its nonalcoholic botanical aperitivo – if you don’t like shrubs or drinking vinegars, it may not be for you, but I find it a wonderful alternative to amaro-based cocktails such as the negroni. Fever-Tree, meanwhile, has launched its own “non-alcoholic spritz”, which is sweeter and not very bitter. Perhaps my favourite discovery of the week, however, is Non, an Australian wine alternative that blends verjus (unripe grape juice) with the likes of raspberry, chamomile and salt. That’s my kind of soda pop.
Five new drinks to tickle your tastebuds
Rapscallion Burnt Lemon £3.60 (250ml) Gail’s. The edgiest, tartest lemon meringue pie of your life – in liquid form.
Botivo £3.50 (250ml) Waitrose. The bittersweet botanical aperitivo can now be enjoyed on the hoof – cheers!
G Spot Awaken £6.50 (4 x 250ml) Ocado. This “may improve libido”, but it will definitely titillate your taste buds with its chilli kick.
Non 1 £19.99 (750ml) Sous Chef. A blend of tart verjus, chamomile and salted raspberry that’s super for sipping or supper.
Sonic Tonics Hemp Root Fig & Violet £36 (6 x 240ml) Sonic Tonics. A really unique, florally bitter soft drink with CBD – buzz without fuzz.

The UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050, Andy Burnham has argued in his strongest comments yet on the issue, saying it is no longer possible for Britons to believe they are not already affected by a changing climate.
Writing for the Guardian about new plans for a mass of community-led local green energy projects, the prime minister said the UK must “believe in itself”, and set out his determination to reach net zero targets, which have been rejected by the Conservatives and Reform UK.
The tone marks a contrast to the summer, when Burnham faced criticism for a seemingly muted response to the heatwaves, droughts and wildfires that affected the UK, with his main initiative being a ban on portable barbecues.
“I am determined that we meet the commitment on which Labour was elected and reach net zero by 2050,” Burnham said. “I want Britain to believe in itself again.”
Saying he wanted to connect local communities to green power projects – to reach net zero targets and make energy more affordable – Burnham said: “I am acutely aware that our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged from our hottest summer on record.”
He went on: “Punishing heatwaves left nurses collapsing on hospital wards and bus drivers working in 40C cabs. Wildfires destroyed homes, leaving families with nothing. And more extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead.
“The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is here and with us now. The British people are no longer insulated from the consequences, and they do not want to be excluded from the solutions. They are looking for ways to do their bit. Community energy gives them that chance.”
The issue is still a tricky one for Burnham, who is facing significant pressure from both sides over whether to approve the Jackdaw gasfield and Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea.
A number of Labour MPs believe approving the projects would send a negative signal on climate efforts, and would provide a boost to the Greens, who argue that Labour is insufficiently serious in tackling the climate emergency.
A seemingly imminent decision to approve Jackdaw has been delayed until later this autumn, prompting the Greens to accuse Labour of wanting to bury the issue before the high-profile Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, is challenging for the seat vacated by Keir Starmer.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, had been poised to give her recommendation to approve the field off the coast of Aberdeen, but it has been put off. Consultations on Jackdaw and Rosebank closed last month, with Fahnbulleh since considering her response.
Approving either or both projects would place renewed pressure on Burnham over his commitment to net zero.
No 10 officials point out that Burnham discussed the climate emergency in his first Commons statement as prime minister at the start of the month, and when he visited Stourbridge in the West Midlands in August after fires there. But in August, a series of climate organisations accused him of being silent about the subject during the heatwave.
In his Guardian article, Burnham tied net zero plans to devolution, setting out funding for so-called people’s power projects, where communities will have a stake in local green energy projects, such as solar panels, windfarms and hydro schemes.
He wrote: “Across Britain, people are taking back control of the things that matter to them: their pubs, their libraries, their leisure centres. Some have already done the same with energy. There are fine examples in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland of community energy schemes, which keep the lights on, the local economy moving and the benefits close to home.
“These projects work and we want to take them nationwide … The climate crisis presents us with an enormous challenge and possibility. In the coming years, we need to change the way we travel, the way we build homes and the way we produce energy. I have long seen the green transition as the best chance we will ever have to reindustrialise Britain.”

British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it | Andy Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:00:48 UTC
21:00:48 KST

On the day I became prime minister, I pledged to bring power to every postcode. Today, we begin to make good on that promise in the most literal sense. With nearly £30m of funding for People’s Power projects, communities across every nation of the UK will soon have the chance to build and control their own clean energy supply.
This investment means villages, towns and cities can harness the natural resources around them with solar panels on libraries, publicly owned windfarms, hydro schemes in their rivers, or whatever else works for them. The purpose is to put money back in people’s pockets while giving them a direct role in tackling the climate crisis.
Every council and community group awarded funding will have at least part-ownership in its renewable energy projects. That means, in the years ahead, more and more communities in Britain will do more than simply host solar panels and wind turbines. They will own a stake in them and retain a share of the wealth they create.
Today’s announcement is part of this government’s sustained effort to make energy more affordable. In my first week in office, I said I would remove VAT from household electricity bills. From the beginning of October, that policy kicks in, giving families some much-needed breathing room. But the only lasting way to bring down bills is to produce more of our own clean, renewable energy at home, which People’s Power will achieve.
I am acutely aware that our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged from our hottest summer on record. Punishing heatwaves left nurses collapsing on hospital wards and bus drivers working in 40C cabs. Wildfires destroyed homes, leaving families with nothing. And more extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is here and with us now. The British people are no longer insulated from the consequences, and they do not want to be excluded from the solutions. They are looking for ways to do their bit. Community energy gives them that chance.
Across Britain, people are taking back control of the things that matter to them: their pubs, their libraries, their leisure centres. Some have already done the same with energy. There are fine examples across the UK of community energy schemes that keep the lights on, the local economy moving and the benefits close to home.
These projects work and we want to take them nationwide. Today’s investment is the first down payment on a £1bn Great British Energy programme, the biggest investment in community energy ever, which will eventually fund more than 1,000 People’s Power projects.
The climate crisis presents us with an enormous challenge and possibility. In the coming years, we need to change the way we travel, build homes and produce energy. I have long seen the green transition as the best chance we will ever have to reindustrialise Britain.
With this in mind, I believe there are two routes we can follow. There’s the traditional Whitehall way: make people pay for the change with more regulation and higher costs, and allow private companies to reap the rewards. Or we can pursue a different route: help people make the change by creating jobs, lowering bills and bringing power back to them.
That is the approach I took as mayor of Greater Manchester. When we brought the buses back under public control, we capped fares and made the fleet cleaner. The result was a transport system designed around the needs of the people who pay for it and rely on it. We are applying the same principle to community energy.
I am determined that we meet the commitment on which Labour was elected and reach net zero by 2050. I want Britain to believe in itself again. That will not happen by asking people to stand still while the world spins around them. Everyone should have a say and a stake in their future. That is what No 10 North is all about. It is what today is about – it is community power in every sense. Power owned by local people, power generated by local projects and power returned to every postcode.

  Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

Ukraine brought back the bodies of 252 Ukrainians from Russia, the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said in a statement on Sept. 17.
Citing Russian authorities, the headquarters said the bodies "belong to Ukrainian citizens, including military personnel."
"Law enforcement investigators, together with expert institutions of the Interior Ministry, will conduct all necessary examinations and identify the repatriated bodies," the headquarters said.
The repatriation was carried out through the joint efforts of Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, the Joint Center under the Security Service of Ukraine, the Armed Forces, the Interior Ministry, the Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights, the Secretariat of the Commissioner for Persons Missing in Special Circumstances, the State Emergency Service and other security and defense agencies, according to the statement.
Despite suffering heavier losses in the war, Russia is likely to hand over more Ukrainian bodies than Ukraine hands over Russian bodies because Russian forces have captured more Ukrainian bodies during offensive operations, according to the Kyiv-based independent analytical platform VoxUkraine.
The return of fallen Ukrainian soldiers has accelerated since peace talks resumed in early 2025. Repatriation operations have become one of the few areas of continued humanitarian cooperation between Ukraine and Russia.
In its Telegram post, the Coordination Headquarters thanked the International Committee of the Red Cross for assisting with the latest repatriation, as well as Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel involved in transporting the returned bodies.
The latest repatriation follows a previous operation on Aug. 13, when Ukraine brought home the bodies of 261 deceased individuals that Russia said could belong to Ukrainian service members.
While Ukraine regularly reports the number of repatriated bodies it receives from Russia, it does not publish data on the remains of Russian soldiers returned to Moscow. The figures are not publicly available.

Couples bonding over bad habits may age faster at the cellular level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:00:23 UTC
21:00:23 KST

A happy marriage usually promotes a longer life, but a new study shows this benefit depends heavily on a couple’s shared daily habits. When partners bond over poor diets and bad sleep, their relationship satisfaction might actually accelerate their biological aging. The findings were published in the journal Brain, Behavior, and Immunity.
Researchers wanted to understand why the health benefits of marital satisfaction vary so wildly from one couple to the next. Stephanie J. Wilson, a psychology researcher at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, led a team of scientists to investigate a concept called symptom-system fit theory. This theory suggests that indulging in unhealthy behaviors together can actually boost a couple’s sense of connection. For example, staying up late to watch television or overeating junk food might make partners feel in sync and satisfied with their relationship.
Over time, however, these shared unhealthy routines could erode physical health. The research team suspected that health behaviors might dictate whether a happy marriage protects against aging or accelerates it. To test this idea, they examined the biological aging of 107 married or cohabiting couples ranging in age from 40 to 87.
The researchers measured marital quality through detailed surveys and by observing the couples in a laboratory setting. During the lab visit, couples engaged in three distinct conversations. They discussed a recent positive event, talked through a personal problem, and tried to resolve a long-standing relationship conflict. Trained coders watched the recorded interactions to evaluate how positively or negatively the partners treated each other.
Participants also provided information about their health behaviors. They answered questions about their physical activity, sleep quality, and adherence to a healthy Mediterranean-style diet. Researchers combined the data from both partners to create average health behavior scores for each couple.
To measure biological aging, the team collected blood samples from the participants at the start of the study and again two years later. They analyzed the blood for three different markers of cellular aging. The first marker was telomere length, which refers to the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes. These caps wear down every time a cell divides, and critically short telomeres cause cells to malfunction.
The second marker involved DNA methylation, which consists of chemical tags on genes that control how they function. Scientists can read these patterns like an internal clock to estimate a person’s biological age. The third marker was a protein called p16INK4a. This protein accumulates when cells enter a state called senescence, meaning they stop dividing but refuse to die, instead releasing harmful inflammatory chemicals into the body.
Looking at the initial data from the first lab visit, the researchers found a link between happy relationships and slower aging. People who reported higher marital satisfaction generally showed lower levels of the senescence protein p16INK4a. However, this youthful cellular profile only appeared among couples who maintained regular physical activity.
A similar pattern emerged during the observed conversations. Couples who showed active, positive support for each other during discussions exhibited slower aging in their DNA and lower levels of the senescence protein. Yet this protective effect was isolated to couples who reported good sleep quality and a healthy diet. When researchers applied strict statistical tests to rule out chance associations, some of these initial healthy patterns were not statistically significant.
The most striking results appeared when the researchers tracked changes over the two-year study period. Couples who started out highly satisfied with their marriages experienced slower increases in the senescence protein over time. But a completely different pattern emerged for the protective telomere caps on their chromosomes.
High marital satisfaction predicted faster shrinking of these telomeres among couples who reported poor sleep and unhealthy diets. In other words, relationship happiness seemed to accelerate cellular aging when paired with bad habits. Similarly, couples who acted highly positive toward each other during the initial lab tests showed accelerated aging in their DNA clocks over the next two years if they shared a poor diet.
These longitudinal results align with the symptom-system fit theory. The data suggest that relationship happiness can become a health risk when it is reinforced by shared negative habits. A happy marriage cannot completely compensate for a lack of sleep, limited exercise, or a diet filled with processed foods.
The participating couples were predominantly white, highly educated, and healthier than average adults. Future research will need to test these ideas in more diverse groups to see if the patterns hold across different socioeconomic backgrounds.
Additionally, while the two-year timeframe shows how habits precede biological changes, the observational design cannot definitively prove that relationship satisfaction directly causes faster or slower aging. The researchers measured an association that they plan to test further with longer-term studies. Identifying how toxic and supportive marital patterns interact with daily health routines will help clarify the physical impacts of a romantic partnership.
The study, “Is a happy marriage a double-edged sword for biological aging? Preliminary evidence for the moderating role of couples’ health behaviors,” was authored by Stephanie J. Wilson, Annelise A. Madison, M. Rosie Shrout, Lisa M. Christian, Elissa S. Epel, Christin E. Burd, Jue Lin, Samuel H. Molli, Rebecca Andridge, Harry T. Reis, and Janice K. Kiecolt-Glaser.

Labor considers smart glasses restrictions, new national AI standards
In short:
The federal government is considering a ban on smart glasses in Commonwealth workplaces while advancing a broader suite of AI policies.
New standards for data centres and frontier AI training are out for consultation as ministers focus on workplace protections, investment and online safety.
What's next?
Anthony Albanese travels to the US on Friday, where he will hold talks with tech companies and world leaders.
A ban on smart glasses capable of covertly recording people is being considered for Commonwealth buildings amid concerns about the technology's privacy and security risks.
Restricting the use of wearable devices is among a wide range of technology issues on the federal government's agenda, with ministers progressing plans for Australia's uptake of artificial intelligence and related workplace protections, data centres, investment and online safety.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will travel to the US on Friday for high-level talks with tech executives and world leaders while major employers gather in Canberra for a round table and separate consultation begins on national AI standards for data centres and frontier model training.
AI will also feature in the upcoming 2026 Intergenerational Report due to be released next week, with Treasurer Jim Chalmers revealing he met with an Anthropic official to discuss the technology's economic opportunities and potential risks.
Mr Albanese said AI and online safety would be a major theme of his visit to Apple's headquarters in California and attendance at the United Nations General Assembly in New York next week.
"We want Australia to be a country that helps shape the AI age rather than simply responding to it," he said.
Labor mulls smart glasses ban
With growing community backlash over the increased availability of more affordable smart glasses capable of secretly recording people, the government has made its first move to rein in the technology.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has asked the Australian Public Service Commission for advice on the use of smart glasses across Commonwealth workplaces, including whether the technology should be "prohibited" and what exemptions might be appropriate.
Senator Gallagher said the Australian Public Service should always set the standard as a "model employer".
"Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information, and we need clear and consistent guidance for public servants," she said.
The government has already asked the nation's Privacy Commissioner to give the use of smart glasses "priority consideration" amid widespread community concerns about their potential impact.
National standards for data centres and training frontier AI
The government has also opened consultation on national AI standards covering large data centres and the training of frontier AI models in Australia.
The proposed rules would set mandatory requirements for data centres covering power supply, energy costs, water use, location, community engagement and skills.
They would also impose safety, security, transparency and local investment conditions on frontier AI training.
Consultation will remain open until October 9 with the government planning to legislate the standards early in the new year.
Industry Minister Tim Ayres said the standards were about ensuring Australia captured the technology's "enormous opportunities" while maintaining the trust and confidence of the community.
"By setting high standards now, Australia can shape the future of this technology rather than simply adopting standards made overseas," he said.
Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton said the government had been "clear" about welcoming AI investment, provided it was on "Australia's terms".
AI will be 'defining influence' on Australia's economy
AI will also feature prominently in next week's 2026 Intergenerational Report, which will examine what the technological shift could mean for productivity, jobs and investment in decades to come.
An excerpt of the report described AI as a "defining influence" on the economy over the next 40 years.
Mr Chalmers said Australia had a "big opportunity" to lift productivity, investment and living standards, but must not be "complacent" about potential downsides.
"The global AI boom is worth hundreds of billions of dollars and we are positioning Australia to capture more of that supply chain," he said.
This week Mr Chalmers met with Anthropic special envoy Jeff Bleich, which the treasurer said was a "really valuable opportunity" to discuss both the economic opportunities of AI and importance of safeguards.
Mr Bleich said Anthropic was committed to realising the "enormous potential" of AI in a "safe, responsible way".
"Working with like-minded countries such as Australia is an important part of that," he said.
Mr Bleich said Australia brought a skilled workforce, strong institutions and a "clear-eyed approach" to new technology.
"We want to invest in those strengths and to keep working with the government so that Australians share in the gains from AI," he said.
Major employers gather to talk AI
Meanwhile, Microsoft, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and the Commonwealth Bank of Australia are among the major employers who will be attending an AI round table hosted by Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth on Friday.
The meeting is one of five consultations being held this month with unions, employers, small business and academics to help develop Australia's first best practice guidance for AI in the workplace.
Discussions will focus on the lessons from businesses already adopting AI, how to build trust and confidence in the technology and ensuring any benefits reach workers as well as employers.
Ms Rishworth said the consultations would ensure the guide reflected the "realities of modern workplaces".
"Labor believes workers should have confidence that the adoption of AI will improve the way we work, not simply train their replacement," she said.

US likely committed war crimes against Iranian civilians: Independent experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

UN fact-finding mission on Iran focuses on plight of civilians
The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran confirmed that civilians in the country suffered serious human rights violations and “crimes against humanity committed by their government,” while finding "reasonable grounds" to believe that the United States committed “war crimes” in the context of its ongoing conflict with the Islamic Republic.
In a report released Monday, the mission concluded that killings by security forces “occurred on a massive scale in all provinces” of Iran, during the Government's “violent crackdown” on mass protests that stretched from last year into this year.
The mission also reported that at least 221 children – some as young as two years old – were killed and that security forces attacked health care facilities, “beating and arresting wounded protesters and arresting some health care workers, discouraging victims from seeking life-saving care.”
The mission added that tens of thousands of people were subjected to arbitrary detention, where they faced "torture, solitary confinement and denial of legal advice, while families were left without any information about the whereabouts of their loved ones, amid circumstances that raise concerns about enforced disappearances."
The mission noted the execution of at least 29 men in connection with the protests following summary trials - five of whom were publicly executed - and warned that more than 70 people, including five women and three boys, still face imminent risk of execution.
The report concluded that “many of these grave violations amount to crimes against humanity – including murder, imprisonment, torture and other inhumane acts committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians.”
‘Reasonable grounds’
Following the attacks launched by the United States and Israel on Iran in February, the mission found "reasonable grounds to believe that the United States committed a war crime by launching indiscriminate attacks that killed or injured civilians or damaged civilian objects."
These attacks included Tomahawk missile strikes targeting the clearly identifiable Tree of Tayyiba Elementary School in Minab, killing more than 150 people, including about 120 children, as well as another air strike in which precision missiles launched clouds of tungsten pellets over a clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area in Lamard, killing 22 civilians.
The mission urged both Iran and the United States to immediately cease "all violations and crimes," provide full compensation to the victims, and ensure that such acts are not repeated.
Calls for peace, justice
The independent experts – who are not UN staff and do not represent any organization – reiterated the UN’s call to all combatants to immediately cease hostilities and work towards a permanent peace.
“They should also ensure that allegations of violations of international human rights law and international humanitarian law by all parties are independently investigated and those responsible held to account,” the report reads.

World News in Brief: Winter aid for Gaza, West Bank; Haiti food production; migrant deaths at sea; human rights funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

World News in Brief: Winter aid for Gaza, West Bank; Haiti food production; migrant deaths at sea; human rights funding
The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) is seeking to raise $97.5 million to protect 540,000 children and their families in Gaza and the West Bank from harsh winter conditions in the coming months.
Nearly 84 per cent of Gaza’s population – more than 1.76 million people – live in overcrowded displacement sites or damaged shelters, leaving families vulnerable to freezing temperatures, heavy rain and flooding.
At least 11 children, including infants, in the Gaza Strip were reported to have died from hypothermia last winter.
In the West Bank, violence, displacement, movement restrictions and a deepening financial crisis are further limiting vulnerable families’ ability to cope with winter shocks, UNICEF wrote in a press release.
The funding would allow UNICEF to provide more warm clothing, thermal blankets, digital cash assistance, emergency shelter reinforcements and tents. The agency will also work with partners to reduce flood and disease risks.
UNICEF is urging donors to provide flexible, timely funding so it can pre-position supplies before winter arrives.
Meanwhile, UN Humanitarian Coordinator for the Occupied Palestinian Territory Ramiz Alakbarov announced on Thursday that the UN’s aid agency (OCHA) will allocate $2 million to power health facilities in Gaza for four months.
FAO plants seeds of hope in Haiti
In the hills and plains of Haiti’s hardest-hit regions, families who have gone months eating whatever they could find are once again planting their own fields.
Emergency support from the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) is reaching 13,000 vulnerable households – roughly 65,000 people – across 10 municipalities in Artibonite, Centre and Ouest, helping them restore local food production amid one of the world’s most severe hunger crises.
More than half of Haiti’s population faces acute food insecurity, driven by violence, economic collapse, broken supply chains and repeated climate shocks, according to FAO.
For many rural families, the FAO programme – funded with more than $16 million through a UN-managed pooled funding mechanism – is arriving at a critical moment. FAO said it will deliver more than 205 tonnes of crop and vegetable seeds and more than 160,000 small livestock to 326,000 vulnerable people.
“In humanitarian crises, emergency food production is a life-saving intervention that empowers vulnerable households to quickly produce food and reduce reliance on importations and repeated humanitarian assistance,” FAO Representative in Haiti Pierre Vauthier said.
Built by Haitians, for Haitians
Local communities are shaping the response by helping FAO identify those most in need and decide what support will help most.
“This emergency food production campaign demonstrates that investing in local capacities is one of the most effective ways to respond to the food crisis,” Mr. Vauthier said. “Implemented by Haitians for Haitians, it enables vulnerable households to rapidly produce their own nutritious food.”
A second phase will bring ducks, poultry, guinea fowls, rabbits and goats to more than 29,394 households, offering families a source of protein and a measure of self-sufficiency at the same time.
Mediterranean migrant deaths rise this year
Arrivals to Europe by sea have fallen sharply this year, but deaths and disappearances along Mediterranean migration routes have increased, according to new data from the UN’s International Organization for Migration (IOM).
Nearly 60,000 migrants and refugees have reached Europe by sea so far in 2026, a 39 per cent decline from the same period last year. But at least 2,292 people have died or gone missing attempting the journey, up from 1,999 by the same time last year.
Arrivals in Italy from the Central Mediterranean route fell 55 per cent from 48,231 to 21,393, while deaths rose from 844 to 996.
Increasingly desperate
On the Eastern Mediterranean route, arrivals in Greece fell by about 5,000, while deaths increased by 133. Spain also recorded fewer arrivals but maintained a similar number of deaths.
IOM Director General Amy Pope said the figures show migrants are taking increasingly dangerous journeys and called for greater international cooperation, including expanded safe and regular pathways.
The figures cover verified incidents through 15 September. IOM warned the true death toll is likely higher.
‘Entire’ human rights monitoring system risks crumbling: Türk
The protection of human rights is a core founding principle of the UN, but a key part of this mission is on the verge of collapse because of funding cuts, High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk told the Human Rights Council on Thursday.
“Today, I am very concerned that the entire human rights treaty body system is at risk of crumbling,” Mr. Türk said.
He cited funding cuts necessitating staff reductions, which has increased delays in processing requests for help, as well as the declining participation of Member States in reporting alleged violations.
Ten treaty body committees are based in Geneva, made up of independent experts who assess countries’ progress in implementing international accords or conventions, including on the elimination of racial discrimination and the promotion of children’s rights.
This is not the first time the High Commissioner has warned about a serious lack of funding for human rights work.
His appeal to Member States to fulfill their international obligations comes ahead of the publication of a report on the treaty body system by UN Secretary-General António Guterres next week during the UN General Assembly’s high-level week.
