New UN system platform puts millions of data points at users’ fingertips, says Guterres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

New UN system platform puts millions of data points at users’ fingertips, says Guterres
How do you make sense of a world facing interconnected crises, from poverty and hunger to climate change, if the facts are scattered across dozens of different places?
The United Nations system is hoping to make that task much easier with the launch of the UN System Data Commons, a new online platform that brings together data and statistics from across the Organization into a single gateway.
Speaking at UN Headquarters in New York on Thursday, Secretary-General António Guterres unveiled the new platform, which allows users to search, explore and access trusted publicly available data from 26 UN entities in one website.
“Behind every statistic is a human story,” the UN chief said, pointing to children whose futures depend on education, families struggling with rising food prices and communities facing growing climate risks.
“To serve them, we must understand their challenges – and know whether we are making a difference,” he said.
One place for trusted information
The platform, available through data.un.org, allows users to search nearly 44 million data points using everyday language rather than navigating multiple websites and databases.
Users can explore trends, compare information across different topics and countries, and trace data back to its original source.
“Access to the knowledge of the United Nations system should never depend on knowing how to navigate its organigramme,” Mr. Guterres said.
The Secretary-General noted that a policymaker often had to look across many different platforms to build a complete picture.
A result of the UN80 Initiative, the new portal removes those barriers by bringing together publicly available data and statistics from the entire UN system in one place.
A tool for the AI age
The launch comes as artificial intelligence is increasingly changing how people find and use information.
Mr. Guterres warned that although people have more information available than ever before, there is often less certainty about what can be trusted.
"If trusted facts are hard to find, unreliable data and misinformation will fill the void," he said.
He stressed that AI-generated answers are only as reliable as the information behind them and said the new platform is designed to help ensure trusted UN system data can be easily found and linked back to its source – by people and digital systems alike.
The website also allows researchers, developers and organizations to connect UN system data directly to their own applications and analytical tools through direct interfaces.
Turning evidence into action
The initiative, known as the UN System Data Commons, brings together public data from 26 UN system entities but does not replace their existing platforms.
Instead, it connects them through a shared gateway, making information easier to discover and access, in accordance with their respective terms of use.
“The UN system produces some of the world's most trusted public data,” said Guy Ryder, Under-Secretary-General for Policy, who added:
“Yet, when that information is dispersed across multiple platforms, its full value is not always realized. The UN System Data Commons now brings this public good into one place, helping people everywhere turn authoritative data into better-informed decisions.”
According to the Secretary-General, the project also demonstrates the goals of the UN80 initiative. It is shared infrastructure – built faster and more efficiently than if each UN organization acts alone.
Calling it “reform people can use,” Mr. Guterres said in his remarks Thursday evening that the value of the new platform would be measured by whether it leads to better support for countries, better-informed decisions and stronger results for people around the world.
“Trusted evidence should not sit behind institutional walls,” he said. “Let us bring it within reach of everyone working for a more peaceful, sustainable and just world.”

Guterres calls for action as hate speech spreads across new platforms online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:00:00 UTC

Guterres calls for action as hate speech spreads across new platforms online
The UN Secretary-General has called for concerted action by governments, technology companies and civil society to stamp out hate speech, emphasizing that “its toxic message is spreading fast and striking deep”.
António Guterres was speaking at the opening of a global conference on promoting interreligious and cultural dialogue held at UN Headquarters in New York on Thursday.
“In its worst forms, hate speech incites violence, drives conflict, and contributes to the perpetration of atrocity crimes – including genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and ethnic cleansing,” he said.
“We have seen it happen before and we see it happening now. And we cannot let it continue.”
‘Weaponising new technology’
The Secretary-General quoted from the UN Charter which commits the world’s people to “practice tolerance and live together in peace with one another as good neighbours”.
Although the Organization has pushed hard to fulfill that pledge, “hate speech has always worked against this vision,” he told participants.
“And today, its toxic message is spreading fast and striking deep,” he said.
"Taking on new forms. Finding new pathways. And weaponising new technologies, from digital platforms and algorithms to Artificial Intelligence.”
Common humanity tested
He warned that the growing reach of hate speech “is testing our shared humanity” by eroding trust, dividing communities and dehumanizing entire groups. It is also attacking and weakening “our capacity for acceptance, empathy, understanding, and respect for diversity.”
The Secretary-General said racism, misogyny, and xenophobia are being celebrated. At the same time, antisemitism, anti-Muslim hatred, discrimination against minority Christian communities, and hatred of other religious and ethnic groups are being normalised.
Step up action now
“We must raise our collective voice and reject hatred. And we must redouble our efforts to tackle hate speech, online and offline,” he said.
He stressed the need to address the root causes, drivers and consequences by strengthening inclusive dialogue among nations, cultures and religions that is grounded in respect and equity.
He was also clear that “reining in hate speech does not mean extinguishing freedom of expression, but freedom of expression must never be an excuse for causing or compounding harm.”
‘A shared responsibility’
The Secretary-General said the international community already knows how to stop the damage caused by hate speech and pointed to two UN initiatives in this regard, namely the Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech and the Plan of Action to Safeguard Religious Sites.
“But we cannot conquer hate speech on our own,” he said.
“Governments, regional and multilateral organizations, the private sector, and civil society – including faith communities, academia, and the media – have a shared responsibility to help build peaceful, just, and inclusive societies.”
Insisting that “we all have a role to play,” the Secretary-General ended his remarks by delivering an urgent message to the international community.
“We must work together to foster mutual understanding,” he said. “To end the tragic cycles of fear, hatred, and violence. And to build the cohesive and stable societies envisioned in the Charter.”

Gender equality woefully off track, new UN report reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Gender equality woefully off track, new UN report reveals
At the current rate of progress, gender equality would take 171 years to achieve, a new UN report finds as institutions built to advance gains are being defunded and demobilised.
Strikingly, not a single indicator on the Sustainable Development Goal for gender equality (SDG 5) is on track to be met by 2030, the initial deadline, according to Gender Snapshot 2026.
These targets include ending discrimination, gender-based violence and such harmful practices as forced marriage and female genital mutilation alongside ensuring women’s full participation in leadership and securing economic and property rights.
Read the full report here.
Who holds the power?
Women continue to face systemic barriers to entering political life.
The UN report highlights the persistent concentration of political power among men, finding that six in seven countries are currently led by men.
Indeed, the cost of running for office can exceed 100 times a country’s average per capita income, excluding many women before the race even begins. In some countries, up to eight in 10 women running for office also face violence in public life.
Even when women do enter government, they are disproportionately steered away from the portfolios that hold the highest security and economic power. Close to nine in 10 defence ministers and more than eight in 10 finance ministers are men.
Beyond government, women make up only six per cent of CEOs globally and lead fewer than 20 per cent of the highest courts, leaving the decisions shaping business, law, employment, and the global economy overwhelmingly in the hands of men.
This imbalance seriously undermines democracy as a country cannot fully uphold human rights or democratic principles while half its population lacks an equal voice in leadership and decision-making, the report stresses.
Violence and discrimination
Millions of women also continue to endure some extremely severe forms of violence and discrimination across the globe.
Nearly one in five girls is married before the age of 18, and an estimated 230 million women and girls worldwide are survivors of female genital mutilation.
Nearly one in three women globally have survived partner or sexual violence in their lifetime, and in the past 12 months alone, 316 million women experienced physical or sexual violence by an intimate partner.
Importantly, the report finds that not a single country has achieved full legal equality, and 51 per cent of the 131 countries studied still have significant legal gaps.
Nearly two thirds of countries provide no or little legal protection for women’s land rights, creating significant barriers to land ownership and secure tenure. Fewer than 30 per cent of nations studied ensure joint land registration or women’s participation in land governance.
No longer a priority
Solving these issues has also been removed from priority agendas.
Amid broadening cuts to funding for development aid, programmes addressing gender inequality are amongst the hardest hit, with such funding falling to its lowest level since 2021.
One in four institutional mechanisms for gender equality have seen their operating budgets cut over the past two years, and one in three have had their institutional power eroded over the same period.
Meanwhile, amid funding cuts, 42 per cent of UN entities report a weakening of their gender equality efforts.
“What the Gender Snapshot 2026 shows is that this is not inevitable,” said Li Junhua, UN Under-Secretary-General for Economic and Social Affairs.
“It is the result of choices, made visible through data. Investing in gender equality, institutions, and the statistical systems that hold them to account is not a cost. It is the fastest route back to the 2030 Agenda’s promise of equal power for all.”

Romanian shelter offers an alternative to stray dog culls

Romanian shelter offers an alternative to stray dog culls
CATEASCA, Romania, Sept 17 - Every day at dawn, eight veterinary vans pull out of the Smeura animal shelter, deep in a forest in central Romania, and fan out to villages where they sterilize dogs for free.
The pilot programme run by German animal welfare association Tierhilfe Hoffnung has one main aim — to show there is a better alternative to the country's policy of culling unwanted animals.
Romania authorised the capture and euthanasia of strays in 2013 after a child was killed in an attack. Thirteen years on, animal groups say the country still has one of Europe's largest populations of roaming dogs, estimated at 500,000.
The shelter itself has been taking in strays, and sent more than 2,200 of them out for adoption last year alone. But as each one leaves, another arrives.
"The dogs keep coming," Tierhilfe Hoffnung manager Matthias Schmidt said. "If we want to solve the problem, we have to sterilize intensively and en masse in order to achieve this result."
Calls to end euthanasia have increased since an investigation by international animal welfare organization Four Paws earlier this year found evidence of systemic neglect, overcrowding and abuse in publicly funded animal shelters.
"In the next five years we want to solve the problem ... by identifying (dogs), vaccinating against rabies, registering them in a national program, and sterilizing them," Schmidt said.
So far this year, Smeura has carried out nearly 40,000 sterilisations, of both strays and pets, at the mobile units and the unsubsidised shelter, one of the largest in the world, sprawling on the site of a former fox farm.
This week in the village of Cateasca, a steady stream of owners brought their pets to be treated.
The procedure was good for the animals and public safety, said Iulian Stoica, who had come with three dogs. "I think it's better not to over-populate the streets with abandoned puppies," he said. REUTERS

Bern museum returns cultural artefacts to Namibia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:54:55 UTC
20:54:55 KST

Bern museum returns cultural artefacts to Namibia
After 120 years in Bern, a collection of cultural artefacts is returning to Namibia. The Bern Historical Museum has transferred ownership to the town of Usakos, where the objects were originally acquired under colonial rule. An exhibition in Bern explores the theme of repatriation.
The exhibition Destination: Usakos will run from September 18, 2026 to July 4, 2027, as the Bern Historical Museum (BHM) announced on Thursday. It features objects which the museum has already transferred to the Namibian town of Usakos.
The collection was assembled in the early 20th century in what was then “German South-West Africa”. In 1906, the Swiss engineer Victor Solioz and his wife Marie acquired around 286 everyday objects, jewellery and weapons from Namibian railway workers. At the time, Solioz was working as chief engineer on a German railway project. The exact circumstances of the acquisition remain unclear to this day. The couple brought the collection to Bern, where the museum purchased it in 1928.
A years-long process of restitution
In June 2026, the BHM transferred ownership of the entire collection to the Usakos Town Museum. Twenty-eight of the artefacts are already in Namibia. The majority are now on loan and on display in Bern, before the objects are also repatriated at the end of 2027.
+ Swiss colonial exploitation highlighted by National Museum
The repatriation was preceded by a process lasting several years. Since 2018, the museum has been strengthening its ties with partners such as the Museums Association of Namibia and the Usakos Town Council. From 2023, a collaborative project was launched in which new knowledge about the objects was gathered in cooperation with the descendants of the railway workers.
Coming to terms with the past and responsibility
“Cultural heritage should be used where it holds significance for people as a source of knowledge and identity,” museum director Thomas Pauli-Gabi was quoted as saying in the press release. The exhibition curator, Samuel Bachmann, added that a collection linked to Namibia’s greatest national trauma could not be retained against the wishes of the descendants. A study from 2024 showed that museums in German-speaking countries hold around 19,000 artefacts from Namibia, while the National Museum of Namibia itself possesses only around 1,600 objects.
A future in Usakos
For the Usakos Town Museum, this is its first collection of its own. The town’s deputy mayor, Kleophas Johannes, expressed the hope that the artefacts would remain at the Usakos Museum for the next 120 years. They must not be locked away again, but must be accessible to the community.
The development of Usakos is closely intertwined with the construction of the Otavi Railway and German colonial history. At the beginning of the 20th century, in what was then German South-West Africa, the railway served as the logistical backbone of the colonial power, Germany. The railway linked the Atlantic port of Swakopmund with lucrative copper mines.
Local labour was exploited for the construction of the railway and the extraction of minerals from the mines. Land and natural resources were seized from the indigenous population without compensation. To this day, the construction of the Otavi Railway is regarded as an example of the interplay between economic exploitation, military oppression and the establishment of colonial structures.

Good luck to Andy Burnham convincing voters he is giving them “breathing space”, if the Bank of England ratchets up interest rates in the coming months.
That was the prospect opened up by Thursday’s minutes of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) meeting, which left rates unchanged at 3.75% – for now – but suggested policymakers may be unlikely to hold out much longer.
“If the conflict in the Middle East persists for an extended period, as appears to be the case,” the Bank governor, Andrew Bailey said. “It is likely that policy may have to tighten.”
With classic Bank understatement, Bailey said that since hostilities heated up again, there had been, “a seeming loss of urgency to find solutions”.
When Burnham arrived in Downing Street in July, the war had abated, and the UK economy was puttering along nicely.
Since then, the resumption of the Iran conflict has pushed global oil prices back above $100 a barrel, with painful knock-on effects across Europe and Asia.
In the UK, inflation hit 3.1% in August, driven by rising fuel prices. And even without a interest rate rise from the Bank, mortgage rates have already jumped, as markets contemplate a period of higher inflation. The MPC now expects inflation to be above 4% in the first quarter of 2027.
The minutes of its meeting suggested a marked reluctance to raise rates for now. While energy prices have shot up, the jobs market remains weak, helping to contain the risks of the “second-round effects” that allow inflation to become embedded.
And the six-to-three vote for a hold was the same as at their last meeting in July, suggesting no rush to jump immediately. Yet there was also a growing sense of concern about the impact of soaring energy costs.
The widely expected hold decision leaves the Bank an outlier among leading central banks.
Kevin Warsh, the chair of the Federal Reserve, defied Donald Trump’s urgent calls for rate cuts on Wednesday by increasing US borrowing costs for the first time since 2023 – a move that went down well in financial markets, but predictably infuriated the president. The European Central Bank raised its rates last week; the Bank of Japan is expected to follow on Friday.
Burnham kicked off his premiership with modest but tangible cost of living measures, such as capping bus fares and slashing VAT on electricity bills.
But he now faces a double whammy. Higher inflation and energy prices threaten to overwhelm the benefits of such handouts; but higher interest rates on government borrowing has increased the costs of future measures to protect consumers.
All this at a time when – as the MPC acknowledges – weather shocks are likely to push up food prices, and bond markets remain fragile.
The new prime minister has made clear he expects to focus more on domestic affairs and less on striding the global stage than his beleaguered predecessor Keir Starmer.
But if – as currently seems likely – the Iran war goes on and on, the costs of geopolitics will be felt at home regardless.

Former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit, who authorized the investigations of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and later decided to indict him, could take the witness stand in Netanyahu’s criminal trial weeks before elections.
Netanyahu’s defense asked the Jerusalem District Court on Thursday to summon him.
The defense requested seven days of testimony, beginning on October 11 and continuing on October 12 and October 18-22. The first proposed date falls four days after the third anniversary of October 7, and just over two weeks before the October 27 election.
It would be Mandelblit’s first appearance as a witness in the trial. Israeli law requires the attorney-general’s consent to open a criminal investigation against a sitting prime minister. Mandelblit gave that consent and, in 2019, decided to charge Netanyahu in Cases 1000, 2000, and 4000.
His testimony is likely to focus on what he authorized investigators to examine, when he authorized it, and whether police went beyond those limits. The defense has argued that some investigative steps lacked the required approval and has challenged evidence obtained through them.
Prosecutors say Mandelblit approved the investigations and dispute the defense’s account of what his consent covered.
Wiretap on Netanyahu associate stopped due to lack of proper approval
That disagreement has surfaced again in recent testimony. Former investigator Shmuel Sharvit said a court-authorized wiretap on Netanyahu associate Natan Eshel was stopped after less than a month because it had not received the necessary approval from Mandelblit.
A former police legal adviser, Alon Tsarfati, testified that the attorney-general’s consent was required to open an investigation, but not for every step taken within one.
At a hearing this week, Eran Kamin, a former senior Lahav 433 officer, said he had met journalist Ben Caspit at a café to check the reliability of information about gifts to the Netanyahu family; the defense questioned him about an alleged transcript discussing private investigators and airport cameras, whose accuracy Kamin disputed.
The prosecution has pointed to Mandelblit’s approval of inquiries into gifts to Netanyahu. The defense has questioned whether that approval extended to particular lines of inquiry. Mandelblit could now be asked to address the competing accounts directly.
Mandelblit announced his decision to indict Netanyahu in November 2019, and the indictment was filed in January 2020. The trial began that May. Netanyahu took the witness stand in December 2024 and finished testifying in June of this year. The defense has since called other witnesses, including former investigators.

"Today, our societies are being rocked by new storms: the upheavals linked to climate change, the erosion of democratic norms, and the use of trade as a weapon."

Argentina's Milei submits bill to strengthen sanctions on Falklands activities
Sept 17 - Argentina's government has presented a bill to crack down on companies operating in the Falkland Islands, potentially escalating tensions with the United Kingdom over the territory that is controlled by Britain but claimed by Argentina.
The proposal introduced on Thursday toughens sanctions on companies and people who unlawfully participate in activities in the Falklands and in Argentina's maritime spaces and continental shelf in "any type of activity aimed at the utilization of renewable or non-renewable natural resources" without authorization from Argentine authorities.
It also creates a National Security Council, led by Argentina's president, to oversee national security policy and safeguard critical infrastructure and national sovereignty.
Its seven members will include the president's cabinet chief, foreign minister, defence minister, economy minister, secretary of national intelligence and the president's legal secretary.
The bill seeks to "punish those who exploit our natural resources illegally, create incentives for them to cease such conduct, and provide the national government with tools to protect itself against external threats," the president's office said in a statement on Thursday.
The new bill aims to revamp 2011 legislation with a tougher regime and stronger sanctions aimed at companies and their shareholders and suppliers, the statement added.
The Argentine government said last week it had opened sanctions proceedings against at least 60 companies and individuals linked to offshore oil exploration around the islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas.
Argentina, which invaded the islands in 1982 and fought a 10-week war over them before surrendering to Britain, has accelerated efforts to crack down on companies involved in the Sea Lion oil project since earlier this month U.S. President Donald Trump suggested Washington could reconsider its traditionally neutral position on the Falklands dispute.
Trump's comments came amid his frustration at what he saw as Britain's limited support for U.S.-led military operations in the Middle East.
Centre and left-wing opponents have long accused Milei of not doing enough to defend Argentina's claim over the Malvinas and now say he is acting for political reasons ahead of a likely 2027 re-election bid.
The owners of the Sea Lion offshore project, Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, had said the oilfield project holds valid licenses from the Falkland Islands government and have indicated they do not expect Milei's actions to derail development. REUTERS

Haredi parties plan to remain outside government coalition until draft law is resolved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:53:10 UTC
20:53:10 KST

The haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties are preparing for the possibility of a dramatic shift in their political strategy after the elections, initially refraining from recommending a candidate for prime minister and remaining outside the coalition that is formed, while the new government is forced to deal with the crisis surrounding the draft law, haredi sources involved in internal political discussions told Maariv on Thursday.
Once the issue that has shaken the haredi political establishment is resolved, the haredi parties could then consider joining the sitting government.
Haredi sources familiar with the internal discussions said the emerging direction is currently not to recommend either Benjamin Netanyahu or Gadi Eisenkot to the president, based on the assumption that the haredi parties would sit in the opposition during the initial period following the elections.
"The feeling right now is that we won't recommend anyone," a haredi source said. "The haredim are coming in with the intention of sitting in the opposition for the first year."
This is not a formal decision adopted by Shas or United Torah Judaism, nor is it a plan agreed upon by the party leaders. Haredi sources stressed that, at this stage, it reflects a prevailing mood and a commonly expressed view in discussions within the haredi political establishment.
"This still isn't something that people sat down and wrote in a document and had approved by the rabbis," one source said, "but it is a widely held view."
Sources familiar with the haredi discussions said the position has also come up in conversations with senior officials in the haredi parties.
Government will struggle to get past draft law deadlock
At the center of the issue is the deadlock surrounding the draft law. Haredi sources believe that under the current circumstances, it would be extremely difficult for a government dependent on the haredi parties to pass legislation that both meets their demands and survives political and legal obstacles.
That has led to the possibility now being considered: The next government would be required to deal with the issue while the haredi parties are not part of it.
Under the scenario being discussed, the haredi parties would sit in the opposition, oppose the draft law advanced by the government, and even attack it, but they would neither be signatories to the legislation nor bear responsibility for the compromise language.
"Some kind of draft law will pass, we won't be tied to it, and we'll be able to attack it from the opposition," a haredi source explained. "After the law passes, that obstacle will already be behind us."
Even supporting a Netanyahu government from outside the coalition is not necessarily seen as a solution. Some within the haredi political establishment believe the latest term demonstrated the cost of being fully identified with Netanyahu at a time when the haredi community was at the center of the public battle over conscription.
"They realized that being on the grill isn't good," a haredi source said.
In his view, outside support could leave the haredi parties in essentially the same position: They would continue paying the public price associated with being identified with the government, while the problem that led them to remain outside it would still be unresolved.
Once a draft law is passed, another possibility that currently appears more distant could also open up for the haredi parties: joining a government headed by Eisenkot.
Haredis will not rule out joining centrist coalition
Haredi sources estimate that the conscription issue is currently the main obstacle to such a move. If the law were already behind them, they would not rule out joining a centrist coalition that is not based on the Netanyahu bloc.
"After a year, the haredim could enter any government," a haredi source said. "Every government wants to expand and become more stable. The haredim know how to be good coalition partners. Once the draft law is no longer on the table, there is no reason they couldn't be brought in."
That assessment is based on the political experience of the haredi parties and the assumption that a government that has already been formed and weathered the conscription crisis could seek to broaden its coalition and strengthen its stability.
If the government formed after the elections does not want to bring them in after a year, sources in the haredi political establishment said that continuing to sit in the opposition would also be a scenario they could live with.
A draft law passed by a government that is not dependent on the haredi parties would present them with a complicated equation.
Haredi sources estimate that the content of such a law would be tougher for the haredi public and further removed from the parties' demands. At the same time, they believe that a law passed without coalition pressure from the haredi parties could enjoy broader public and political legitimacy.
In their assessment, that could also affect the government's ability to defend the legislation before the High Court of Justice.
The positions Eisenkot himself has presented add further context to the scenario.
In recent months, Eisenkot has made clear that he does not intend to compromise on the principle of service, and has said that if the choice is between forming a government and compromising on the draft law, he would prefer another election.
The framework he has presented is based on mandatory military, national, or civilian service, an end to the blanket exemption, sanctions on those who do not serve, and the possibility of allowing up to 3% of each annual cohort to defer service for one year for Torah study.
Haredi sources assume that a law passed under a government headed by Eisenkot would be far removed from their demands. From the opposition, they could oppose the law without bearing responsibility for passing the legislation, and after its enactment they could reassess their relationship with the government.
Eisenkot's public position fits into that picture. He has made mandatory service one of his fundamental conditions for forming a government.
This could create a situation in which, at least initially, both sides are interested in the same separation: Eisenkot makes mandatory service a basic condition, while some in the haredi political establishment believe they would be better off sitting in the opposition while the legislation is passed.
After the law is enacted, the calculations of both sides could change.
Haredi sources deny having secret deal with Eisenkot
According to the haredi sources, there is no secret deal with Eisenkot behind the scenario.
"There are no talks with Eisenkot," a haredi source said, meaning that, according to the source, there are currently no negotiations or political coordination regarding the future scenario.
Eisenkot has publicly rejected the claim that he is "flirting" with the haredi parties and said he has not held talks with Shas MKs over the past year.
The possibility of eventually sitting in a government headed by Eisenkot is therefore not being presented within the haredi political establishment as the result of any advance agreement with him.
From the perspective of the haredi sources, it could become a practical option if the draft law has already become a fait accompli and the main obstacle from their perspective has been removed.
The major question will be Shas.
At the same time, the party is fighting to win back voters who have shifted toward Itamar Ben-Gvir and Otzma Yehudit, and it is therefore expected to continue presenting a clearly right-wing line during the election campaign.
Nevertheless, haredi sources find it difficult to envision a scenario in which, on the day after the elections, Shas alone joins a government while United Torah Judaism remains outside it.
"When the moment of truth comes," a haredi source assessed, "Shas won't do something different from United Torah Judaism."
Haredi parties enter 2026 elections in weak position
Also in the background is what sources in the sector describe as the relatively weak position in which the haredi parties are entering the elections.
"The haredim are coming into these elections very weak," one source said.
Shas is concerned, among other things, about voters moving to Otzma Yehudit, while the haredi political establishment as a whole is bearing the cost of the ongoing conscription crisis.
That backdrop is also contributing to the view that this time it may be better not to enter the government immediately and once again find themselves at the center of the confrontation over the law.
Once the conscription issue is resolved, the traditional priorities of the haredi parties are expected to return to the center of coalition negotiations: funding for yeshivas and institutions, and arrangements addressing the needs of the haredi public.
Sources in the political establishment estimate the main budgetary cost would be about NIS 1.2 billion to NIS 1.4 billion, and in any case no more than roughly NIS 1.5 billion.
From their perspective, that sum would not constitute a significant obstacle in the context of a state budget worth hundreds of billions of shekels, and a government seeking to broaden its support base could find a way to provide it.
If the move materializes, it could also affect the long-standing relationship between the haredi parties and the Netanyahu bloc.
There is no discussion within the haredi political establishment of severing ties with Netanyahu, but sitting in the opposition during the initial period could restore political room for maneuver that has nearly disappeared in recent years.
From the perspective of the haredi sources, the decision over coalition partnership can wait. First, they want to see how the conscription issue is resolved. Only afterward do they want to examine which government, if any, it would be right for them to join.

“This lawsuit holds Jeffrey Epstein’s estate accountable for a crime that has never been fully addressed on its own terms,” said Hillary Nappi, a lawyer with AWK Survivor Advocate Attorneys.
The lawsuit alleges that Epstein and his associates were involved in the possession, production and distribution of child sexual abuse material beginning in the early 1990s and continuing until his death in 2019.
Epstein estate defendants named
The lawsuit names Epstein’s estate co-executors, lawyer Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Khan, as defendants.
Their lawyer, Daniel Weiner, declined to comment, according to NBC News.
Epstein was arrested in 2019 and charged with federal sex trafficking offenses involving minors.
He died by suicide in a New York jail that August while awaiting trial.
No federal child pornography charges were filed against Epstein.

A fifth of Russian refining sits idle, and the sector’s earnings still grew
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:46:55 UTC
20:46:55 KST

Russian oil refineries earned more in the first half of this year than in the same period a year earlier, even as Ukrainian drone strikes kept a fifth of the country's refining capacity out of action, The Moscow Times reported. Record wholesale prices and fast-growing payments from the federal budget have more than covered what the attacks and the repairs cost. Russian consumers are covering the rest at the pump.
Where the profits come from
Russian refineries earned 938 billion rubles ($11.1 billion) in the first half of 2026, 16.2% more than a year earlier, according to the state statistics service Rosstat. Ukrainian drone strikes have put a fifth of the country's refining capacity out of action.
Two things produced that result, according to Promsvyazbank analyst Yekaterina Krylova: high wholesale prices on the SPIMEX commodity exchange, and a sharp increase in state fuel subsidies.
Wholesale prices took off in March, after the war in the Middle East began: light petroleum products have risen 37% since late February and diesel by a third, with July bringing record exchange prices of 82,600 rubles ($982) per tonne of AI-95 gasoline. Crude got cheaper for the refiners over the same stretch, as the ruble price of Urals oil peaked in spring and fell through the summer while the products made from it kept getting dearer.
Ukraine says drones hit Russia’s gas heartland over 3,000 km from its border—a wartime record
The budget pays the difference, the country pays the bill
Russia's damper mechanism compensates oil companies for selling fuel cheaply at home rather than exporting it, and the payments grow as the gap between domestic and world prices widens.
The Finance Ministry paid out close to 350 billion rubles ($4.2 billion) a month in the second quarter, and 500 billion rubles ($5.9 billion) for July and August together. Krylova expects the subsidies and the prices together to widen net margins by 45% in the third quarter, to 35,000 rubles ($416) per tonne of gasoline.
Russia's retail prices tell the other half of the story. Gasoline has risen 21.2% since January and diesel 18.4%, well above Russian inflation. Budget money lets the majors, which own both the refineries and the filling-station chains, hold their own forecourt prices near inflation. Independent chains have no such cushion: they buy at the higher wholesale prices and sell dearer, which is how Russia has been squeezing them out of the market. For drivers, the crisis has been physical as well as financial, with rationing and dry pumps spreading across dozens of regions.
Kazakh refinery deal could ease Russia’s front-line fuel pressure—but it covers just 0.3% of demand
What the strikes have cost
Ukrainian drones have been hitting Russian refineries since 2024, and the campaign escalated sharply from August 2025, when strikes deep inside Russia became systematic. Russian refineries disclose none of their losses from it.
Ukraine's General Staff estimated the total damage to the Russian oil industry since August 2025 at $13.5 billion, in a count published in early July. The insurance broker Mains put direct losses to the oil and gas sector from drone strikes last year at more than 100 billion rubles ($1.2 billion), and above a trillion rubles once lost profit and indirect damage are counted.

Likud revives 'Arabs are flocking to the polls' campaign - this time targeting opposition voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:45:41 UTC
20:45:41 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel Elections
- Likud revives 'Arabs are flocking to the polls' campaign- this time targeting opposition voters
Likud revives 'Arabs are flocking to the polls' campaign- this time targeting opposition voters
Likud plans to take advantage of a precedent-setting decision by the Elections Committee under which voter-turnout figures will be published for individual polling stations during election day
The Likud party is preparing to revive its controversial “Arabs are flocking to the polls” campaign, this time with a focus on voter turnout among opposition supporters.
Likud plans to take advantage of a precedent-setting decision by Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg, under which voter-turnout figures will be published for individual polling stations during election day.
The party intends to use the data to mobilize its supporters by highlighting high turnout in opposition strongholds and Arab communities. Likud officials reportedly expect particularly strong turnout among opposition voters and hope that real-time updates will encourage the party’s own supporters to cast their ballots.
Sohlberg’s decision was originally presented as a compromise after Likud was barred from using the Elector voter-management system. The latest developments, however, could allow the party to benefit from both polling-station turnout data and real-time reports from its representatives about who has voted.
Following a lengthy and contentious debate on Sunday, the Central Elections Committee voted 19–11 to allow party representatives to continue reporting in real time which registered voters have cast their ballots and which have not.
Sohlberg had initially prohibited the practice. The High Court of Justice subsequently ruled that the matter fell outside his authority and returned it to the Central Elections Committee for a decision.
The controversy began last month, when Sohlberg ruled that polling-station committee members and party observers could not report voters’ identities to their parties during election day. He determined that sharing information about whether, when and under what circumstances a person voted—including the type of polling station used, such as one in a hospital or one adapted for people with limited mobility—could violate the individual’s privacy under the Privacy Protection Law.
Sohlberg also found that election law does not explicitly authorize party representatives to transfer such information for political activity and that, without clear legal authorization, the practice should be prohibited.
Likud challenged the ruling before the High Court. The court concluded last week that Sohlberg did not have the authority to decide the issue on his own and referred the matter back to the Central Elections Committee.

Black Sea attacks push commercial ships into Marmara anchorages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:44:00 UTC
20:44:00 KST

(İHA Photo)
Hundreds of commercial vessels are crowding anchorages in the Marmara Sea as shipowners increasingly avoid the Black Sea amid a surge in attacks on civilian ships linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.
More than 200 commercial vessels bound for the Black Sea have been struck by unmanned aerial vehicles or missiles over the past four months, including Turkish-flagged ships.
The attacks have turned the Marmara Sea into a vast parking area, with hundreds of vessels dropping anchor rather than proceeding into the Black Sea.
Speaking to Turkish media, business representatives called for navigational safety to be restored in the Black Sea.
Yusuf Yalçın Çapoğlu, vice president of the Turkish Shipowners’ and Operators’ Association (KOSDER), said attacks brought commercial activity in the Black Sea to the brink of collapse.
“The number of vessels entering and leaving through the straits has fallen below 30. Under normal circumstances, that figure was above 200,” Çapoğlu said.
“Ukraine is doing everything it can to prevent vessels engaged in trade with Russia from going there. Russia is retaliating. Ships are being hit by missiles and drones. Recently, a vessel bound for Georgia was struck on its way there. The shipowner changed his mind and turned back. It was hit again on the way back,” he added.
Even when the vessels are not operating, shipowners continue to incur substantial costs for every day they remain at anchor.
“Whether you operate the vessel or not, you have to pay these expenses. They start at around $2,500 a day and can rise to $5,000, $6,000 or even $7,000,” Çapoğlu said.
He also warned that if there was no end in sight to the situation, shipowners could take the drastic step of unloading their vessels rather than continuing to operate under such conditions.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Sept. 15 said that to the growing number of attacks targeting civilian vessels in the Black Sea is unacceptable in remarks made in Azerbaijan.
Fidan said Türkiye had issued the necessary warnings to the parties, adding that he believed common ground could be found if the required political will was demonstrated and the two sides acted in good faith.

“We emphasize once again that attempts to create a de facto situation in violation of the demilitarized status of Meis Island, which is located extremely close to the Turkish coast, are incompatible with international obligations and will not be accepted by our country,” the ministry said.
Türkiye’s objective is to develop good unneighborly relations with Greece based on dialogue and turn the Aegean Sea and Mediterranean into a basin of peace and stability, it added.
However, the ministry reiterated that Türkiye will not tolerate any actions that undermine its regional rights or attempt to create a fait accompli.
“We call upon Greece to comply with its obligations arising from international treaties and to refrain from violating the demilitarized status of the islands,” the ministry said.
On a question about the relocation of the 51st Commando Unit to Söke district of Aydın province in the Aegean region from eastern Anatolian city of Tunceli, ministry officials said the decision was taken in June and in line with military needs.

Klopp wants Germany football team to 'reclaim the flag'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:41:00 UTC
20:41:00 KST

Klopp wants Germany football team to 'reclaim the flag'
September 17, 2026
Jürgen Klopp used his first squad announcement as Germany's new head coach to deliver a stirring speech in favor of what he described as "positive patriotism."
"I'd like to reclaim the flag for myself — or for us," Klopp said.
"I want us to always wave it in a way that makes no one think: 'What's wrong with you?'" he said. "But, rather, that people simply get the feeling that you're happy and understand how lucky you are to have been born, raised or moved to this wonderful country."
This was an apparent reference to the recent state election in Saxony-Anhalt, which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won in a landslide victory.
Klopp said of the election "that some people probably thought it was OK, while many others thought: 'Good heavens, what's going on there?"
The former Borussia Dortmund and Liverpool head coach was quick to say he is not a political expert and that he doesn't want to talk about politics at every press conference, but that he doesn't want to "leave national pride to the wrong people."
Rather than leaving that up to misinterpretation, something Klopp said was possible, he turned toward the concept of "positive patriotism."
"I can be proud to be German and still be open-minded, diverse, kind and friendly," he said. "I actually think we're a wonderful country."
The 59-year-old added that, just as he had selected the current squad by looking at what the country had to offer in terms of football talent rather than what it was lacking, it might help to do the same when looking at the country as a whole.
This echoed a similar sentiment of former Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann, who spoke emotionally after Germany's Euro 2024 exit.
"Being together must become more important again. We must not be consumed with envy, always paint everything in a negative light and not begrudge our neighbors anything," Nagelsmann said.
"I believe that if everyone starts within their own small circle — on their street, helping their neighbors when something comes up [...] [we can] support one another, integrate everyone, welcome them, and help them feel at home, and bring people together to work with us toward a better future."
Klopp highlights power of football
Klopp was quick to turn to the power of football, while also recognizing its place in wider society.
"It's more important that we have doctors. It's more important that we have nurses. It's more important that we have a great, great many people in a wide variety of professions," he said, before adding that football can "foster a sense of community that lets us truly feel the power of sports."
Klopp cited the recent successes of Alexander Zverev, the world champion field hockey team, the home World Cup in women's basketball and the success of athletes at this summer's European Athletics Championships as further positive examples of the power of sport.
"That's our mission. We have to create the right atmosphere — I know that. But to do that, we need people who are willing to embrace it," he said.
Master class in communication
Klopp's delivery was a textbook example of how to create alignment across his messaging. His squad, made up of 44 players including 11 new faces, is a reflection of the diverse society that Klopp proudly referenced.
His engagement with the media was also strategically smart. After laying down clear boundaries in his first press conference that included him saying he would quit if coverage strayed into the personal, Klopp this time opted to seek to include the media as part of the process while also subtly reminding them of what he sees as their role.
When explaining his choice to name such a large squad with so many new and young players, Klopp said he wasn't going to tell members of the media how to do their job when it comes to assessing players, but said that he knew how he would do it. In between the lines, this was an indirect appeal to the media to choose coverage that would foster the development of this new era of players rather than hinder it by being overly critical or negative.
On top of that, Klopp did all of this while wearing a baseball cap with the words "one of 83 million" written on the front. This is in reference to a Germany's approximate population and an expression about how everyone has an opinion on the Germany team and so is therefore a "Bundestrainer" (national team coach). It also came across as an attempt to assign a shared responsibility for the team's success.
Germany's Euro 2024 campaign briefly instilled some pride over the flag again, as did Germany's women in the Euro 2022 final. The most impactful though, was the 2006 World Cup in Germany, which provided the biggest positive cultural shift in the general German attitude toward national pride since World War II.
Now, through the vehicle of football, Germany's new head coach has declared a desire to restore that pride. Klopp said his whole career had brought him to this moment.
After these words, it felt like all the disappointments the Germany team — and their fans — have endured over the last few years may also have brought them to the right leader.

German court holds Meta liable for 'fraudulent' ads on Facebook, Instagram
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:38:14 UTC
20:38:14 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
A German court has ruled that US technology company Meta can be held legally liable for "fraudulent" advertisements published by third parties on Facebook and Instagram.
The Frankfurt Regional Court said Thursday that Meta must stop the publication and distribution of fake advertisements that unlawfully used the logo of a financial information portal and the name and images of its well-known founder.
The case was brought by a company operating an online portal offering comparison calculators, product reviews and consumer guidance on financial products, as well as its founder and managing director.
The portal has more than 600,000 followers on Instagram and around 29,000 on Facebook.
According to the court, unidentified users used the company’s registered logo and images of its founder to promote purported financial investments, directing users to external links in what appeared to be fraudulent schemes.
Several affected users subsequently contacted the plaintiffs.
The company reported nearly 260 violations to Meta in August 2024 alone, but identical or substantially similar advertisements continued to appear. Meta took up to 62 days to remove some of the content.
The court found that the advertisements seriously infringed the company’s corporate personality rights and the founder’s personal rights.
Meta exercises control through algorithms
The court rejected Meta’s argument that it could avoid liability under the EU’s Digital Services Act because it had no prior knowledge of the fraudulent content.
Referring to a recent ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union, the judges said liability protections do not apply in the same way when a service provider exercises control over displayed content.
Meta determines the ranking and timing of advertisements through an automated auction process and controls the distribution of content in users’ feeds through algorithms, the court said.
Unlike platforms that offer purely chronological feeds, Meta therefore exercises control over the advertising content shown to users, it added.
The court ordered Meta to compensate the plaintiffs for future damages arising from the distribution of identical or similar fraudulent advertisements.
The company must also provide information about the advertisements and disclose the revenue it generated from them.

Who are among the attendees at the Ophir Awards?

The Lebanese Parliament gave a vote of confidence in Prime Minister Nawaf Salam’s government on Wednesday, 68-12, with two abstentions.
Hezbollah lawmakers left the session without taking part in the vote, signaling their opposition to the government without voting against it. According to official statements and recordings of the session and two-day debate, there were heated exchanges involving other members of the Shi'ite bloc.
Lebanese journalist Youssef Diab said he believed Hezbollah had chosen not to vote against the government and instead withdrew from the session “to save face.”
In previous years, no democratic process or government plan could proceed without Hezbollah’s approval, he told Saudi Arabia’s Al Hadath news channel. Hezbollah’s inability to overturn the government would expose the extent to which it had been weakened, and therefore, withdrawing was preferable, he added.
Indicating division in the Shi’ite bloc, MPs from the Amal Movement voted for Salam’s government. Some of them acknowledged that their vote had not reflected their personal views.
Amal official Qablan Qablan said he was voting to give Salam’s government a vote of confidence “with regret.”
MP: Hezbollah losses, refusal to transfer land to LAF 'brings Israeli occupation'
Although Salam opened and closed the session by discussing his government’s commitment to financial and economic reform, asserting a state monopoly on weapons, the 2027 budget, reconstruction in southern Lebanon, and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the country, only the latter seemed to prompt heated outbursts and personal insults on the floor.
Independent Lebanese MP Michael Moawad told Hezbollah lawmakers their losing of wars is what “brings Israeli occupation.” Hezbollah’s refusal to hand Ali Taher Ridge over to the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) meant that he could be “handed over to the Israelis,” he said.
“Has the south been destroyed because Nawaf Salam is the head of government, or because Hezbollah has dragged us into war?” Moawad asked, drawing numerous objections from both Amal and Hezbollah lawmakers. “Hezbollah decides on the war, and the government pays the price. Its losing wars have led to occupation. Hezbollah’s refusal to disarm weakens the state in the face of Israel.”
MP Ziad Hawat also accused Hezbollah of bringing the IDF back into the country, an accusation that was interrupted by Hezbollah MP Hussein Jachi, who shouted, “Some of our colleagues think Israel is not an enemy.”
Hezbollah continued to receive criticism from other lawmakers throughout the session. Hours after the initial confrontation, Tripoli-born Sunni MP Achraf Rifi and Hezbollah lawmakers argued over the position of Syrian refugees in Lebanon and Hezbollah’s involvement in the civil war.
Hezbollah refuses to disarm, cede land to government forces
Independent Beirut MP Paula Yakoubian also questioned why Hezbollah had not handed over areas of southern Lebanon without an Israeli presence to the LAF.
“Why doesn’t Hezbollah hand over a map of its weapons to Lebanese negotiators so that they can secure an Israeli withdrawal and the return of displaced people?” she asked.
Independent Beirut MP Ibrahim Mneimné said: “We hear criticism of Hezbollah, but after everything that has happened, they must acknowledge their responsibility.”
Lt.-Col. (res.) Sarit Zehavi, founder and president of the Alma Research and Education Center, told The Jerusalem Post the developments and widespread condemnations of Hezbollah in the Lebanese Parliament were not a surprise, especially given the widening rift between the pro- and anti-Hezbollah camps in Lebanon.
While the recent vote and comments made during the session were important demonstrations of the attitudes held in Beirut, they did not change the fact that the Lebanese government had failed to take meaningful action to disarm Hezbollah and establish a monopoly over its weapons, she said.

Both Ofer Winter’s party and the Hendel-Zelekha list crossed the electoral threshold with four seats each.
The balance between the blocs remained inconclusive, with 52 seats on each side, leaving neither with a majority to form a government.
Channel 13 poll: Likud hits low, but Netanyahu bloc strengthens

Despite this, the Netanyahu bloc strengthened to 54 seats, compared with 52 for the change bloc.

Channel 12 poll: Change bloc weakens, Likud and Otzma Yehudit lose three seats
Yashar continued to lead in the Channel 12 poll with 23 seats, down two from the previous survey.
Netanyahu’s Likud also weakened, losing one seat to reach 20.
The biggest shift was in the balance between the blocs. The bloc opposed to Netanyahu fell by two seats to 66, including 54 seats for Zionist parties and 12 for Arab parties.
At the same time, the coalition also weakened by two seats to 50.
Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha shifted the situation, with their list crossing the electoral threshold and winning four seats. As a result, it effectively sits in a “third bloc,” outside the two main camps.
Within the anti-Netanyahu bloc, the Joint List also strengthened at the expense of some of the bloc’s Zionist parties.
Channel 14 poll shows opposite picture: Right at 64 seats, Likud still first

Likud remained the largest party with 30 seats, down one, while Eisenkot’s Yashar also lost one seat to stand at 21.
Bennett’s B’Yachad rose from seven to eight seats, as did United Torah Judaism. Yisrael Beytenu fell from seven to six.
There was also movement within the Arab parties: Hadash-Ta’al-Balad rose to seven seats, while Ra’am fell to five, leaving their combined strength unchanged at 12 seats.
Channel 16 poll: Winter and Hendel-Zelicha clear electoral threshold
The biggest surprise in the Channel 16 poll came from the parties hovering around the electoral threshold.
Ofer Winter’s People of Israel and the joint list of Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha each crossed the threshold with four seats, altering the balance between the blocs.
The Netanyahu bloc stood at 52 seats, compared with 53 for the opposition.
Eisenkot’s Yashar led the poll with 21 seats. Netanyahu’s Likud came second with just 18 seats, while Bennett’s Beyahad strengthened to 16.
Three parties tied for fourth place with nine seats each: the Democrats, Otzma Yehudit, and Shas.

'Yemen was already suffering', NGOs tell TNA as crisis deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:36:21 UTC
20:36:21 KST

Breadcrumb
'Yemen has already been suffering': aid groups tell TNA renewed war will deepen crisis
Yemen's renewed fighting is deepening an already desperate humanitarian crisis, aid groups have warned The New Arab, as clashes across the country displace tens of thousands of people and international funding cuts leave relief organisations struggling to respond.
Heavy fighting broke out across Yemen on 3 September after Ansar Allah, commonly known as the Houthis, launched an offensive to seize the country's Red Sea coast from the UN-recognised government, triggering battles around Taiz and Marib.
Khanzad Shah, Islamic Relief's acting country director for Yemen, told The New Arab that the organisation was "extremely worried that this new escalation will now make the humanitarian crisis here even worse, and make it even harder for families to get food and healthcare".
"The crisis in Yemen has largely been forgotten by the world, and this is a wake-up call that the people of Yemen are still suffering," he added.
Aid groups have been forced to navigate shifting frontlines and a precarious security situation while responding to a crisis already strained by deep cuts to international assistance.
Frontlines reignite: The Fall of Mokha
On 3 September, Yemen's frontlines, dormant for four years, reignited after the Houthis launched an offensive in Taiz governorate aimed at capturing the Red Sea port city of Mokha.
After around a week of back-and-forth fighting, the Houthis made a rapid advance along the coast on 10 September, capturing Mokha and later reaching the outskirts of Lahj province.
As the fighting raged, civilians fled south, Shah told The New Arab.
"People are moving from around Taiz to Lahj and then onto Aden to try and find safety and support," he said.
"Many of these families don't have enough food or water as they had to flee with whatever they could carry. In some areas, whole villages have reportedly emptied."
According to the UN refugee agency UNHCR, around 100,000 people have been displaced by the fighting across the country, with 2,400 crossing the Red Sea to Djibouti.
The agency told The New Arab that 63% of all newly displaced households originate from Taiz, while refugees displaced to Djibouti are being registered in Markazi refugee camp.
The fall of Mokha shocked the UN-recognised government because of the speed with which the city and surrounding coastline were captured. Fighting is expected to continue after the government declared a "kill box" in the area and, backed by the Saudi Air Force, launched strikes on Houthi targets.
The capture of the coast has also raised international concern over the potential impact on global shipping and energy markets following major disruption around the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Iran war and previous Houthi attacks on shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb since the start of Israel's war on Gaza.
For MSF, however, the fall of Mokha has prompted more immediate concerns over the city's civilians and the safety of its team operating at Mokha General Hospital.
In a statement released on Friday, MSF's Yemen country coordinator, Lou Cormack, said the Houthi takeover of the city "has had a major impact on both medical activities and the needs of the population in recent days".
"The rapid advance of Ansar Allah [Houthi] forces has fundamentally changed the situation," she said, forcing MSF to alter plans to reopen a former field hospital in Mokha, provide water to displaced people and establish cholera isolation and treatment units in Mokha and Khawkah to the north.
Instead, MSF has focused on keeping Mokha General Hospital operating after Yemeni healthcare workers fled alongside civilians. Only 30 healthcare workers remain at the hospital, providing minimum services.
"Almost all other healthcare facilities in the city have stopped functioning, largely because their staff had left," Cormack said, adding that bombardments were continuing and that MSF would remain to provide healthcare to civilians amid uncertainty over what comes next.
Mobilising a response despite fighting and funding cuts
Alongside the fighting on the coast, the International Rescue Committee told The New Arab that the conflict had rapidly spread across the country.
"Frontlines have reopened across five governorates in a matter of days, key roads have been cut, and many families are once again being displaced into areas with little capacity to receive them," Carol Sekyewa, the IRC's Yemen country director, said.
Sekyewa said 18 million people across Yemen were already facing acute hunger before the latest escalation and warned that disruptions to essential supplies or restrictions on access could have catastrophic consequences.
"The IRC is continuing to provide vital, life-saving health and protection services, but every road that closes makes it harder for people to reach treatment and for humanitarian organisations to deliver assistance."
Fighting is also raging around the hills and peaks surrounding the partially besieged city of Taiz, the capital of the governorate where Mokha is located. The Norwegian Refugee Council is mobilising there to assist newly displaced people.
"Several families who were already in displacement and were residing [in] displacement sites that are in frontline areas in Taiz have fled to new locations," Alison Bottomley, an advocacy adviser with the NRC based in Yemen, told The New Arab.
"NRC is responding to the emergency needs of these displaced families in their new locations," she added, noting that people need shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene, with many having fled in the middle of the night.
"We met families who told us they had to leave home at three o'clock in the morning before walking 15 kilometres to find safety."
Bottomley said that despite the four-year ceasefire that paused much of the fighting, Yemen remained in the grip of a humanitarian crisis, particularly after deep cuts to international aid programmes at the beginning of US President Donald Trump's second term.
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development estimates that aid spending from Development Assistance Committee countries fell 23.1% in 2025 from 2024 levels, with a further 5.8% decline projected for 2026.
The funding cuts have affected the NRC's ability to respond. Bottomley told The New Arab that "the number of stock and emergency resources is limited, with overall humanitarian response deeply underfunded".
This includes Houthi-controlled northern Yemen, which accounts for 70% of the population, where funding reductions have led to cuts in food, nutrition and health services.
"It is critical that there is a commitment to support vulnerable people in Yemen," Bottomley added.
The UNHCR told The New Arab that alongside limited stockpiles, the fighting is "raising broader concerns over humanitarian logistics" as potential closure of the Bab al-Mandeb could affect humanitarian and commercial shipping serving Yemen, Sudan, and other operations in the region.
Oxfam has also had to scale back operations around Taiz. Fatma Jaffar, the organisation's advocacy media manager in Aden, told The New Arab that it had been forced to shut down one intervention in the area, where it helped run a community centre with a local partner.
Jaffar said Oxfam was continuing to provide services in other parts of Taiz, "but still we're in a kind of emergency, like we're anticipating something to happen, and of course taking into consideration our staff and operations and the safety of them".
"Until now, we're not seeing massive access issues," she said, adding that the organisation was coordinating with authorities in both the north and south. However, "the security situation is what's stopping us from intervening in certain areas when we're trying to gather content, when we're trying to gather data around impacts".
"It's very sad as a Yemeni to see all of these people fighting, and unfortunately the victims are the civilians in the middle of the chaos."
Oxfam, which has operated in Yemen since 1982 when the country was still divided between north and south, has increasingly shifted from civil society and governance projects towards humanitarian and resilience work since the civil war erupted in 2014.
The breakdown of the relative calm brought by the four-year ceasefire has again disrupted the organisation's humanitarian work, with Oxfam now focusing on supporting internally displaced people across the country. Jaffar said there were two million displaced people around Marib alone, where Oxfam has an office, as well as in Taiz.
"For us right now, the priority is to respond to the IDPs that we're seeing in the districts that we're intervening in and trying our best to mobilise sufficient resources," Jaffar said, adding that the organisation was struggling with funding but stepping up advocacy efforts to secure more.
"Yemen has already been suffering a decade-long conflict, so being dragged further into this conflict only puts us at risk," she said.
"My only hope is that it doesn't escalate further, and we see all of the conflict parties reaching an agreement."

Possible U.S. war crimes in Iran cited by U.N.-backed experts

U.N.-backed experts allege U.S. war crimes in Iran
Geneva — Human rights experts commissioned by the United Nation's top human rights body say they have found "reasonable grounds" to believe the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including on a school in the southern city of Minab.
The international fact-finding mission on Iran says the findings center on a pair of airstrikes that killed scores of civilians, including women and children.
A preliminary U.S. assessment suggested that the United States was "likely" responsible for the deadly February attack on the school but did not intentionally target it and may have hit it in error, possibly due to the use of dated intelligence that wrongly identified the area as still part of an Iranian military installation, a person briefed on the preliminary intelligence told CBS News.
The Trump administration has not directly accepted responsibility or released findings of a Pentagon investigation into the attack on the school on the war's first day, using Tomahawk missiles.
Iranian health officials and state media said about 170 people were killed, most of them schoolgirls between the ages of 7 and 12.
"Following the United States and Israeli attacks on 28 February, the mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects," the fact-finding team said in a statement. It said the school in Minab was "clearly identifiable."
The U.N.-backed team also alleged the U.S. had committed war crimes in relation to a missile strike that dispersed tungsten pellets over a "clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area" in the southern city of Lamerd, also on Feb. 28.
The U.N.-backed team said 22 civilian men and women were killed. U.S. Central Command has denied responsibility for the strike on Lamerd.
The team also said Iran's state security forces had committed killings on a "staggering scale," referring to a January crackdown on nationwide anti-government protests, and alleged that their actions amounted to "crimes against humanity."
It said civilians were caught between "gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's deadly conflict with the United States and Israel."
The fact-finding mission on Iran, chaired by jurist Sara Hossain of Bangladesh, is made up of independent experts and was created in 2022 by the Human Rights Council, the U.N.'s top human rights body.

Evangelical Christian group Proclaiming Justice to the Nations said Wednesday that the Texas State Board of Education had accepted several of its curriculum recommendations, following testimony in which its president, Laurie Cardoza-Moore, challenged the participation of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.
The organization, known as PJTN, said its proposals addressed civics, history, social studies and Holocaust education, with an emphasis on the influence of Judeo-Christian traditions on the United States. Its September 16 statement did not identify which recommendations had been incorporated into the adopted standards.
The Republican-controlled board approved revised high school social studies standards on September 4 by an 8-4 vote. The changes, scheduled for implementation in 2030, included teaching Christianity’s influence on American history and identifying 1948 as the year Israel was established “in the ancestral homeland of the Jews,” the Houston Chronicle reported.
“For decades I have fought to keep anti-American and anti-Semitic content out of our classrooms,” Cardoza-Moore said in remarks released by PJTN. “How can we let terrorists decide our children’s curriculum?”
CAIR representatives addressed board, despite terror designation
During her testimony, according to the transcript provided by the organization, she questioned why CAIR representatives had been allowed to address the board, citing Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s designation of the group as a foreign terrorist organization.
Abbott issued that designation in November 2025. It was a state action, distinct from designation under the federal government’s foreign terrorist organization process.
Cardoza-Moore also cited CAIR’s inclusion as an unindicted co-conspirator in the Holy Land Foundation terrorism-financing case. CAIR was never indicted in that case and denied the allegations. The group filed a federal lawsuit challenging Abbott’s designation as unconstitutional and defamatory.
CAIR has rejected allegations that it is affiliated with Hamas or the Muslim Brotherhood. In its published response to such accusations, the organization described itself as independent of foreign movements and said it condemned terrorism, including attacks carried out by Hamas.
Cardoza-Moore argued that understanding America’s religious and intellectual foundations should be central to the revised standards, formally known as the Texas Essential Knowledge and Skills, or TEKS.
“I am here to advocate for the incorporation of Judeo-Christian history and values within our standards,” she told the board. “It was upon Judeo-Christian values that this great nation was built.”
The curriculum overhaul drew opposition from Muslim advocates. In a separate statement Wednesday, CAIR’s Austin office called for the board to reconsider the standards, arguing that their treatment of Islam would encourage prejudice against Muslim students.
PJTN projected that the Texas changes could eventually influence instruction for as many as 25 million students nationwide, citing the state’s influence on educational materials. The statement provided no calculation or supporting evidence for that estimate.
Cardoza-Moore traced her textbook advocacy to 2012, when she challenged a passage in a Pearson human geography textbook used in Tennessee that she said legitimized the 2001 Hamas suicide bombing at Jerusalem’s Sbarro restaurant. PJTN said the disputed reference was subsequently removed.
“Students cannot fully understand America if they do not know and understand the laws, history, ideas, and traditions which shaped America,” she told the Texas board.
