Dozens of members of the European Parliament from Patriots for Europe, the European Parliament's third-largest group, signed a charter adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) principles on combating antisemitism and commemorating the Holocaust at a special conference in Strasbourg on Wednesday.
During the conference, participants expressed support for Israel and settlement in the West Bank, while opposing sanctions and boycotts imposed on them.
The conference was held against the backdrop of measures and sanctions promoted in recent years by several European countries against parties associated with settlement in the West Bank. Participants included members of the European Parliament and senior officials from right-wing and conservative parties across the continent, alongside Likud MK Ariel Kallner. Samaria Regional Council head Yossi Dagan and president of the Likud Court, attorney Michael Kleiner, addressed the conference in recorded messages.
Patriots for Europe brings together representatives of right-wing and nationalist parties from several European countries. Its members include representatives of the Czech ANO party, Hungary's Fidesz, the Freedom Party of Austria, the Dutch Party for Freedom, and France's National Rally.
The signing of the charter adopting IHRA principles was central the the conference. According to the charter, certain expressions directed against the State of Israel may, depending on the context, constitute expressions of antisemitism. It also emphasizes combating Holocaust denial and distortion of the memory of the Holocaust.
Palestinian workers will pay price for European West Bank sanctions, Kleiner says
Kleiner focused his remarks on the potential economic consequences of sanctions on the West Bank, arguing that those who could ultimately pay the price are Palestinian workers employed by Israeli businesses and factories.
"The sanctions imposed by 12 countries, led by Britain, on Judea and Samaria are a double-edged sword," Kleiner said. "Those who will suffer from them most are tens of thousands of Palestinians who make a living working for Jews in Israel and Judea and Samaria."
Kleiner pointed to SodaStream as an example of what he said could happen if Israeli factories in the area were boycotted.
"The example is the attempted boycott of SodaStream: The factory moved to the Arava and was not harmed, but 500 Arab workers lost their livelihoods and were forced to work in the Palestinian Authority for much lower wages," he said. "The factories will not close, but the sanctions could severely harm the workers' livelihoods."
According to Kleiner, this illustrates a paradox in the sanctions policy: Measures intended, according to their proponents, to help Palestinians could in practice harm the livelihoods of Palestinians employed by Israelis in the West Bank.
Kallner, chairman of the Knesset committee for cooperation with the European Parliament, also criticized the sanctions and linked them to the fight against antisemitism.
"When sanctions are imposed against the Jewish state and against the people of the Bible who returned to the land of the Bible, this is a double standard, this is hypocrisy, and this is modern antisemitism," he said.
European antisemitism threatens more than Jews, Kallner warns
Kallner added that antisemitism in Europe was not a threat to Jews alone.
"Antisemitism begins with the Jews, but it never ends with the Jews," he said.
According to Kallner, Israel stands "on the front line of the struggle between civilization and barbarism," and European countries should stand alongside it.
Dagan welcomed conference participants in a recorded message and presented cooperation with Europe's right-wing parties as part of a shared struggle against terrorism and efforts to delegitimize Israel.
"We are fighting to defend Europe. We are fighting to defend Israel. We are fighting to defend the future of Western civilization as a whole," Dagan said. "We stand together against barbaric terrorist attacks. We stand together against the new war, the war of delegitimization campaigns and the war of lies."
The conference and signing of the charter are part of efforts by Israeli figures and representatives of the settlement movement to deepen ties with right-wing and conservative parties in Europe, at a time when pressure and measures against parties associated with settlement in the West Bank are increasing in several European countries.

====================================================================================================

India’s BRICS balancing act is keeping the bloc from becoming an anti-Western alliance - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:23:55 UTC
19:23:55 KST

BRICS has finally found consensus, but the terms of that consensus reveal how divided the grouping remains.
On Saturday, leaders meeting in New Delhi unanimously adopted a 140-paragraph declaration after months of disagreement over the Iran war. The agreement calls for maximum restraint in the Middle East, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and diplomacy as the route to resolving conflicts.
Crucially, it avoids naming the United States, Israel, or Iran.
For India, which holds the BRICS chairmanship, getting all 11 members to sign the declaration is a diplomatic achievement. But it also illustrates the limits of BRICS as a geopolitical bloc.
The challenge was particularly acute because Iran and the UAE, both BRICS members, have been caught on opposing sides of the regional conflict. Iran has attacked targets in the Gulf, while the UAE maintains close security ties with Washington. Their foreign ministers had already failed to produce a consensual BRICS statement earlier this year.
India nevertheless helped bring the two sides into the same diplomatic room, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian meeting Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan on the summit’s sidelines.
That is the kind of BRICS India wants: influential enough to give emerging powers a larger voice, but flexible enough to accommodate countries whose strategic interests sharply diverge.
The same calculation is visible in the economic agenda.
Reducing dependence on the US dollar
China and Russia have pushed to reduce dependence on the dollar and develop alternative financial mechanisms. India has resisted the idea of a common BRICS currency, favoring more practical arrangements such as greater use of national currencies and improved cross-border payment systems. The New Delhi declaration did not endorse a single BRICS currency.
This matters because India has little interest in replacing American financial dominance with a China-centered alternative. New Delhi wants room to trade with Russia, maintain energy ties with Iran and the Gulf, and participate in BRICS while retaining access to American markets, Western capital, and technology.
That is strategic autonomy, not an anti-American strategy.
The Ukraine issue provides another revealing example. Unlike previous BRICS declarations, the New Delhi statement made no specific reference to the Russia-Ukraine war, a clear indication of how difficult it remains for the expanded grouping to reach common language on a conflict involving one of its founding members.
The contrast with Gaza is striking. The declaration devoted substantial attention to the Palestinian issue, reaffirmed support for Palestinian statehood and the two-state solution, and called for humanitarian access and an end to practices that could alter Gaza’s demographic or geographic character.
This is where the New Delhi summit matters for Israel.
Israel should not dismiss BRICS as an irrelevant talking shop. Nor should it assume that an expanded BRICS automatically constitutes a coherent anti-Israel alliance.
The summit demonstrates the opposite: the group contains countries with competing interests, and India in particular is resisting efforts to turn BRICS into a unified anti-Western geopolitical vehicle.
At the same time, Israel should recognize that BRICS diplomacy will increasingly create political pressure on Jerusalem.
The declaration’s treatment of Gaza, its emphasis on Palestinian statehood, and its criticism of actions affecting the occupied Palestinian territories demonstrate that Israel faces a growing diplomatic constituency outside the traditional Western framework.
India’s role is therefore especially important. New Delhi maintains close ties with Israel while also maintaining strategic relationships with Iran, the Gulf states, Russia, China and the United States. Its BRICS policy reflects the same multi-alignment that increasingly defines Indian foreign policy.
India is not trying to make BRICS a Western alliance. It is also resisting efforts to make it an anti-Western alliance.
The New Delhi declaration is consequently best understood as an Indian diplomatic success with clear limitations. BRICS can still produce consensus, but only through carefully calibrated language that avoids forcing members to choose sides on their most divisive geopolitical disputes.
For Israel and the US, that distinction matters. A stronger BRICS may challenge parts of the existing international order, but the New Delhi summit does not show the emergence of a unified alternative bloc.
It shows something more complicated: India is trying to ensure that BRICS becomes a powerful negotiating forum without allowing China, Russia, or any other member to turn it into a geopolitical instrument.
The writer is an India-based lawyer specializing in cross-border trade and investments, and a senior fellow with the South Asia Democratic Forum in Brussels.

Chile weighs ethanol-gasoline blend as government seeks cheaper fuels amid fiscal strains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:23:26 UTC
19:23:26 KST

Chile weighs ethanol-gasoline blend as government seeks cheaper fuels amid fiscal strains
Sept 17 - Chile, one of Latin America's largest oil importers, has started to consider adopting ethanol-blended gasoline as spiking oil prices this year have strained the economy and government finances, according to documents seen by Reuters.
The energy ministry has drafted a proposal to shift to E10 ethanol blending — mixing 10% ethanol with gasoline — that could reduce government fuel supply costs by approximately $107 million annually, according to a memo prepared by ministry officials.
Data from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, or OPEC, showed that Chile imported 181,000 barrels per day of crude oil in 2025. Oil prices have soared during the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Brent, the global benchmark for crude oil, traded at over $105 a barrel on Wednesday, up from about $73 a barrel before the war began.
Ethanol-gasoline blends are widely used across Latin America. In Brazil, the $20 billion ethanol industry is second only to the U.S. Brazil has long been known for its fleet of "flex-fuel" passenger cars that can run on a blend of ethanol, now topping 30%, mixed into gasoline.
Chile has no ethanol-blending mandate, and is one of the few countries in the region still relying on MTBE, an octane-boosting gasoline additive.
The government has held off on adopting ethanol blends because Chile lacks significant domestic production, lacking sufficient land to grow enough crops to support a domestic ethanol industry, according to a U.S. Grains Council briefing reviewed by Reuters.
Yet without the ethanol option, Chile remains exposed to global price swings. In March, as U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran ramped up, the government of the mining-dependent nation stopped fully cushioning the shock at the pump due to oil price volatility, with its MEPCO fuel stabilization mechanism straining public finances.
Switching to an ethanol-gasoline blend would help phase out MTBE and ease pressure on President Jose Antonio Kast's administration following the oil supply disruptions, which have stoked public discontent.
"The government is out of money," Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz said in March.
According to the grains council briefing, the switch to E10 would be relatively simple and affordable for Chile. State oil company ENAP would need to invest about $10.8 million to adapt refining, terminal and storage infrastructure, the ministry said in its internal memo. It said the transition could be introduced gradually and partly offset by lower carbon-tax payments.
A shift to a 10% blend, and even a 15% blend, could be achieved by 2030 in Chile, the grains council said.
In May, the ministry released a roadmap to diversify fuel sources and lower carbon emissions by 2030, including through fuel blends.
The ministry did not respond to requests for comment on the memo, including on the timing of any transition to ethanol-blend gasoline and why Chile had not pursued it sooner.
Chile already depends on the U.S. for 85% of its gasoline supply, according to the grains council briefing. A switch to ethanol could benefit corn growers, the council said, since the grain is used to make the fuel.
Such a move "replaces one import dependency with another," the ministry conceded in its memo. Chile's ethanol imports currently come mostly from Argentina, followed by Bolivia.
Production in neighboring Brazil has risen sharply under the government mandate to use more ethanol in gasoline. REUTERS

The shooting comes less than three months after a deadly attack at a high school in Tacloban City, where at least three students were killed and about 20 others wounded in June.

Malaysia confronts complexities of schizophrenia after school killing ruling

4-MIN READ4-MIN

When Cindi suffered her first severe psychotic episode a decade ago, she could no longer tell where reality ended and her imagination began.
“My reality and fantasy [were] all distorted. I had no idea what was real, what was not,” the 38-year-old, who asked to be identified only by her first name, told This Week in Asia.

Kim’s sister says only ‘idiots’ think N Korea to give up nukes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:20:28 UTC
19:20:28 KST

People sit near a television screen showing a news broadcast with file footage of a North Korean missile test, at a train station in Seoul on September 12, 2026. (AFP Photo)
The powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un said on Sept. 17 that the country’s nuclear-armed status was “absolute,” calling those hoping for its denuclearization “idiots.”
North Korea has legally enshrined its status as a nuclear weapons state, with its leadership declaring the country’s atomic arsenal permanent and irreversible.
U.S. President Donald Trump said in August that Pyongyang possesses 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons, with Seoul putting the figure at between 80 and 120.
“The DPRK’s position as a nuclear weapons state is absolute which cannot reverse with anything,” Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, said in a statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
Pyongyang’s nuclear arsenal “makes a significant contribution to deterring the outrageous acts of international rogues,” she said.
Kim’s statement came during the General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in Vienna, where she said the “familiar silly talk” of efforts to denuclearize the North was expected.
“If they believe that it is really possible, they will only hear the word of idiots,” she said.
“No matter how rhetorically the hostile forces may deny, the reality in which the nuclear position of the DPRK has been permanently settled physically and legally cannot change even a bit,” she added, using the acronym for North Korea’s full name.

Lebanon security talks in Paris to focus on post-UNIFIL alternatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:20:20 UTC
19:20:20 KST

Lebanon security talks in Paris to focus on post-UNIFIL alternatives
The security talks come as Israeli forces continue to carry out attacks across southern Lebanon despite a “ceasefire”.
European and Arab military chiefs are meeting in Paris to assess the Lebanese Armed Forces’ needs and discuss the looming end of the United Nations peacekeeping mission UNIFIL, amid fears of a renewed Israeli military campaign in southern Lebanon.
Thursday’s talks will initially be chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron alongside Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Jordan’s King Abdullah II.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Israel says it destroyed Hezbollah base in Lebanon’s Ali al-Taher ridge
- list 2 of 4Lebanon’s students head to classes that double up as shelters for displaced
- list 3 of 4Israel-Lebanon talks postponed as explosions rock southern Lebanon
- list 4 of 4How Israel’s destruction of south Lebanon is making displacement permanent
The United States will be represented by a senior military official involved in Middle East security issues, the Reuters news agency reported.
The meetings come after Israel and Lebanon held several rounds of US-brokered talks aimed at easing tensions along their border.
A US-mediated framework deal was agreed between Israel and Lebanon in June, but the agreement did not force Israel to withdraw from the large area of southern Lebanon it occupies, and Israel has continued its attacks on the country.
On Wednesday night, Israeli forces carried out a series of attacks across southern Lebanon, according to the country’s National News Agency.
Meanwhile, Israeli air attacks killed at least 13 people, including six children, in a town in southern Lebanon last week, according to Lebanon’s Ministry of Public Health, in one of the deadliest days of Israeli bombardment in recent weeks.
UN mission to end
The most immediate concern of the meeting in Paris will be the security vacuum that could be left when the almost 50-year mission of UNIFIL, which has about 7,500 personnel, leaves in January.
Despite Lebanon and France both favouring an extension of the UN mandate, neither the US nor Israel has signalled support for prolonging the mission.
The officials in Paris will discuss options for a new international mission, backed by France and Italy, operating outside a UN mandate, as well as a possible European Union-led mission.
Both concepts would reportedly focus on training, equipment, intelligence sharing, and mentoring support for the Lebanese Armed Forces.
Paris said it wanted the “operational context, parameters and modalities” of the deployment to be clarified at Thursday’s discussions, as a prerequisite for what it hopes will be “robust” international support for the Lebanese forces.
Fears of a renewed Israeli military campaign are growing in Lebanon after escalating attacks, despite a “ceasefire” that was intended to halt Israeli aggression and allow the thousands of displaced people in Lebanon to return home.
Disarming the Lebanese armed group Hezbollah remains a key condition for Israel’s withdrawal from southern Lebanon, according to the deal signed, with Aoun reiterating his determination to disarm the group, but “without confrontation”.

UK charities, protest groups condemn Israeli ban threat after sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:19:24 UTC
19:19:24 KST

UK charities, protest groups condemn Israeli ban threat after sanctions
Having warned London of ‘consequences’ for sanctions, Israel targets UK charities, campaign groups and Palestine Action.
London, United Kingdom – British charities, Palestinian advocacy organisations and the proscribed Palestine Action group have condemned an official Israeli letter maligning their representatives and activists and recommending they be barred from entering Israel.
The document, seen by Al Jazeera, was issued by Israel’s Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism. It recommends border authorities bar employees and activists associated with aid organisations including Oxfam, Islamic Relief Worldwide, Save the Children, Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) and the Norwegian Refugee Council, which receives UK funding, as well as campaign groups including the Palestine Solidarity Campaign and Friends of Al-Aqsa.
The letter, dated September 8, the day the UK banned imports from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, was previously reported by the BBC and Jerusalem Post.
Ismail Patel, founder of Friends of Al-Aqsa, which openly advocates for the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, is accused in the letter of joining anti-Israel demonstrations in London and making “harsh statements against Israel” in public appearances and interviews.
“To hear Israel is planning to ban Friends of Al-Aqsa for our BDS campaign clearly shows BDS is working and impacting Israel,” Patel told Al Jazeera. “Israeli restrictions will not intimidate us.”
Israel’s Diaspora Affairs Ministry did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Israel follows through on threat of ‘consequences’
Israel had warned the UK against the new sanctions, with its Ministry of Foreign Affairs raising the prospect of “consequences” for what it called “hostile moves”.
Shortly after the trade ban was announced, Israel, which controls access to Gaza and the occupied West Bank, barred 11 British MPs and a lawyer from entering and ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem. It also announced the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center located in Kiryat Gat, southern Israel. And it has ended British training of Palestinian Authority forces in the occupied West Bank.
“In light of this [the trade ban], attention should be directed to the ongoing and subversive activities of various British organisations promoting boycotts, sanctions, and economic and political measures against the State of Israel,” the leaked letter reads.
It makes further accusations against 11 groups in total. The claims against them range from advocating for engagement with Hamas for humanitarian access; demanding an arms embargo against Israel; having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood or working with “terrorist” organisations.
Save the Children is accused of describing Israel’s actions as “deliberate starvation” and “genocide”.
A spokesperson told Al Jazeera that, alongside other NGOs, it is already unable to secure visas for staff needing to cross Israeli-controlled borders into Gaza or the West Bank, “at a time when needs have never been greater”.
Israel has intensified restrictions on international aid groups since the genocidal war in Gaza began, including measures affecting the entry of food, medicine, foreign volunteer doctors and humanitarian workers.
MAP said the letter forms part of Israeli authorities’ “wider restrictions on international charities operating in the occupied Palestinian territory”. It noted that two MAP individuals named in the letter had received the humanitarian medals awarded by King Charles.
The letter describes Palestine Action, which has carried out raids against Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems, as a “network of radical branches promoting direct action intended to damage the Israeli defence industry”.
“This letter is further proof that we were not banned because of anything to do with ‘terrorism’,” Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori told Al Jazeera. “As the letter admits, our activity was always focused on damaging the Israeli defence industry.”
In a related development, UK Lawyers for Israel has called on the government to consider proscribing Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, as a terrorist organisation, The Telegraph reported. The lobby group alleged, in line with Israeli accusations, that MSF had employed people with links to Palestinian armed groups.
MSF said it had been the target of a “disinformation campaign” for months. It said staff accused by Israel of having “ties to terrorism” were only reported to the organisation after they had been killed, and that Israeli authorities had not shared evidence of military involvement before their deaths.

Two Britons among three people killed in plane crash in Switzerland
ZURICH, Sept 17 - Two Britons were among the three people who died when a small plane crashed into a Swiss mountainside this week, the British Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said on Thursday.
Swiss police said the Cirrus SR22T light aircraft crashed in the Fluhalp area near the spa town of Leukerbad in the southwestern canton of Valais on Tuesday afternoon.
Valais police said the plane departed from the city of Lugano and made a stopover at Sion airport before setting off again towards Buochs airfield in Canton Nidwalden.
However, the plane crashed into a mountainside at about 4 pm (1400 GMT) for reasons that are still unclear. Emergency services and rescue specialists rushed to the scene but all three occupants of the plane were found dead, police said.
"We are providing support to the families of two British nationals who died in Switzerland and in contact with the local authorities," the office said, without providing more details.
The victims are still being identified, said police who gave no information on the third person. REUTERS

As Canadian tariffs bite, Republicans search for a winning message
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:18:37 UTC
19:18:37 KST

As Canadian tariffs bite, Republicans search for a winning message
NEW YORK, Sept 17 - High gas prices and the rising cost of living had already made affordability a defining issue in this year’s midterm elections. Then President Donald Trump escalated his trade war with Canada.
Now, Republican candidates in northern border states most affected by the tariffs are trying to strike a balance between appealing to Trump’s loyal base and reaching independent voters that polls show have soured on his handling of the economy and his fight with Canada.
The economies of Michigan and Maine have long been intertwined with Canada’s, covering everything from auto parts to lumber to fruit-picking equipment. That has raised the stakes in two states that Republicans will likely need to win in the November 3 elections if they are to hold the US Senate - and their respective candidates have taken notably different approaches with voters, each with its own political risks.
The Senate races in both Michigan and Maine are considered toss-ups by the Cook Political Report.
U.S. Senator Susan Collins of Maine is breaking with Trump, criticizing the tit-for-tat exchange of tariffs and seeking carveouts for affected industries. Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers, by contrast, has criticized Canada and made the case that his close relationship with the president will help blunt the impact of the trade war.
Because the Canadian tariffs emerged so recently, candidates have largely been left to devise their own responses mid-campaign, said David Hopkins, a political scientist at Boston College.
And both will “need to move beyond the Republican coalition” to win their races, he said. “When something unpopular happens at the behest of your own party leader, it puts you in that very awkward place.”
The National Republican Senatorial Committee, which supports Senate candidates, has not taken a public stance on the Canadian tariffs and did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
‘POLITICAL PRESSURE’
The United States imposed 50% tariffs on some $20 billion of Canadian goods last month, accusing its northern neighbor of unfair trade practices. Canada's own retaliatory tariffs – ranging from 15% to 50% on $20 billion of U.S. goods – took effect on September 8.
Canadian officials have made no secret of the fact that their levies were designed with politics in mind.
“We're being wise and strategic to put political pressure,” Canada’s Minister of Industry Melanie Joly said in August.
Americans are about four times as likely to blame the current trade dispute on Washington rather than Ottawa, according to a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll conducted late last month. Only 20% of respondents supported higher tariffs on Canadian goods.
Such figures have cleared the way for Collins to declare Trump's trade war with Canada a "mistake." A moderate Republican representing a state that prides itself on political independence, Collins has a history of challenging party orthodoxy on issues including healthcare, abortion and gun control.
Now locked in a close race against Democrat Troy Jackson, she is again trying to distance herself from a president whose popularity has sunk to record lows.
Canada is Maine’s biggest trading partner, accounting for 69% of imports and 41% of exports in 2025, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. More than 80% of the state’s heating oil and gasoline is imported from Canada, and its three most iconic products – wild blueberries, lobsters and lumber – all depend heavily on cross-border trade.
Collins has voted four times to oppose Trump’s tariffs, and on August 28 wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer outlining the economic impact on her state.
In her letter, she focused on road salt and cement – products that the administration subsequently exempted from the tariffs.
Jackson responded with sarcasm. “I mean, yeah, thank you for the road salt,” he told reporters at a recent campaign event. “What has she done to stand up, to get Trump to back off of parts coming in from Canada, fertilizer coming in from Canada for farmers?”
TARIFF DAMAGE
In Michigan, which exports more than almost any other state to Canada, analysts say the tariffs could be especially damaging to the struggling wood products sector, particularly kitchen cabinet makers.
Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has said Trump “is right to put America First - and tariffs are necessary, but are not a one-size-fits-all solution.”
He has also presented his closeness with the president as a strength rather than a liability.
“You can send somebody back [to Washington] who gets up every day and tries to gouge the president’s eyes out or you can send somebody back who’s going to walk in and say, ‘Hey, can we work on this part of the trade deal,’” he said.
Rogers’ Democratic rival, Abdul El-Sayed, has tried to make light of his political predicament.
“He’s caught between knowing full well that these tariffs are bad for Michiganders and having to appeal to Daddy Trump every single time he opens his mouth,” El-Sayed told CNN.
Spokespeople for Collins and Rogers declined to comment for this story.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Kush Desai said “President Trump will never waver from putting Americans and America First, whether in trade negotiations or through an economic agenda of tax cuts and deregulation.”
Even though presidents have limited control over economic growth, Hopkins said, tariffs give people who are dissatisfied with their financial situation another reason to blame Trump and his fellow Republicans.
"It's sort of easy to tell a story of what it is that Trump has done to make things less affordable," he said. REUTERS

US Congress passes sweeping Russia sanctions bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:15:26 UTC
19:15:26 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin delivers a televised address in Moscow on September 16, 2026 (AFP Photo)
U.S. lawmakers approved broad new sanctions on Sept. 16 designed to squeeze Russia over its war in Ukraine, sending the legislation to President Donald Trump after months of delay.
The Republican-led House of Representatives passed the package by 262-159, giving a final congressional green light to the most substantial U.S. legislative effort against Moscow since Trump returned to office.
Trump has said he will sign the measure, which sailed through the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month.
The legislation targets Russia’s energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions.
It also gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, including potentially China and India, in an effort to choke off revenue financing Moscow’s war.
But its sweeping tariff powers produced an unusual split among Democrats, who overwhelmingly support Ukraine but have resisted handing Trump greater authority over trade.
Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called the bill “deeply flawed.”
“White House lawyers drafted the current text to maximize President Trump’s authority to impose new import taxes on the American people, and to minimize any obligation to actually impose new sanctions on Russia or its enablers,” he said.
Dozens of Democrats nevertheless backed the measure, offsetting opposition from a handful of Republicans who objected to sanctions on free-market or non-interventionist grounds.
Supporters argue that tougher economic pressure is needed, with Russia’s full-scale invasion grinding through its fifth year and no peace settlement in sight.

Canada's Mark Carney welcomes 'ambition' of becoming associate EU member during his speech to the European Parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

Canada's Carney welcomes associate status idea in EU speech
September 17, 2026
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has said he welcomes the "ambition" of a European Union proposal to make the country the bloc's first associate member.
Carney made the remarks while addressing the European Parliament on Thursday, in a speech that focused on Canada's and the EU's shared security and economic interests.
In an address in which Carney spoke in English, French and German, the Canadian prime minister lauded European culture and values of democracy, freedom and human rights, which he said Canada shares.
"We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defense of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication," the Canadian leader told the chamber, to applause.
Europe and Canada are 'stronger together', Carney tells EU Parliament
"We hold common values for which we have always fought and in whose defense we must always remain vigilant," he said.
"Europe and Canada are each strong," he said. But he added that "Europe and Canada are even stronger together."
"I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival — only with better manners," he said. "We do not seek power to dominate others," he added, in a thinly veiled reference to the US.
"The objective is not self-sufficiency, it's collective resilience," Carney said.
His speech to European lawmakers comes as the EU and Canada look to strengthen their ties amid a growing rift between Canada and its southern neighbor and main trading partner, the US.
Ties between Canada and the US have hit a historic low in recent months, with the North American neighbors locked in an escalating trade war since Carney and US President Donald Trump failed to agree on a deal this summer.
EU defends Canada alliance plan after Trump tariffs threat
On Wednesday, the European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU was willing to make Canada its first-ever "associate member," days after the Wall Street Journal reported that Carney was exploring an "associate membership" with the bloc — a position that does not currently exist. Carney has acknowledged that "associate membership" still needs to be defined.
During her State of the EU address, von der Leyen said the bloc needed to adapt to an "openly hostile world" marked by aggressive power politics and "frayed relationships," the latter a clear nod to the turbulent ties between Brussels and Washington since Trump returned to the White House.
Prior to his visit this week, Carney had confirmed that he wanted to establish a "unique alliance" between Canada and the EU.
"We share the same values, we have the same priorities and we have very complementary strengths," the prime minister said.
Trump on Wednesday slammed the EU's plans to make Canada an associate member.
"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina. The US president also described the prospect of Canada joining the EU as "laughable."
How did the US-Canada relationship come to this?
Ties between Canada and the US have plummeted since Trump began his second term in January 2025. He has targeted Canada with tariffs and suggested that the US could annex Canada as its 51st state.
Trump has also referred to Carney, as well as his predecessor as prime minister, Justin Trudeau, as the "governor" of Canada.
The growing rift has also seen Trump sign an executive order renaming Lake Ontario, a Great Lake between the US and Canada, to "Lake America."
Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

EXPLAINER - AfD’s rise in eastern Germany: What the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern vote means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:14:52 UTC
19:14:52 KST

Voters in the eastern German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern will elect a new state parliament Sunday, with the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) leading in polls.
The vote comes two weeks after the anti-immigration party won 43.8% of the vote in neighboring Saxony-Anhalt. That result was the AfD’s strongest showing yet in a German state.
Sunday’s ballot is being watched far beyond the Baltic coast.
Many want to know if the AfD’s rise in the east is still growing -- and how badly Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) will do after its historic defeat in Saxony-Anhalt.
A new Insa poll published Wednesday put the AfD at 37% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, more than double its 16.7% in 2021.
The center-left Social Democrats (SPD) have closed the gap to 35%.
Chancellor Merz’s conservative CDU was polling at 7% -- its weakest result in the state since German reunification. In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state elections in 1990 and 1994, the CDU had finished first, winning 38.3% and 37.7% of the vote, respectively.
Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is a thinly populated state on the Baltic Sea, with Schwerin as its capital. The SPD has governed there since 1998 with changing partners.
Popular Social Democrat Manuela Schwesig has been premier since 2017. In the 2021 election her party won 39.6% and formed a coalition with the Left Party.
Her popularity extends beyond the party’s grassroots base, and a recent survey by public broadcaster ZDF found that nearly 60% of voters said they would back her if the premier were elected by direct vote.
Schwesig has made preventing an AfD majority the centerpiece of her campaign.
She has repeatedly said that either the SPD will perform strongly in this election and form a democratic coalition, or the state risks an AfD victory that would bring “extremists to power.”
The AfD’s candidate for premier, Leif-Erik Holm, has been a member of the federal parliament since 2017 and served as the party’s economic spokesperson.
His campaign has focused on the social and economic problems and often accused the SPD-led government of having a “disastrous record.”
He said 28 years of SPD rule are enough and that the state needs change under an AfD government.
Support for the AfD has grown in eastern Germany over anger about migration, living costs and distrust of the parties that have long run the country from Berlin.
According to a recent survey for public broadcaster NDR, voters’ top concerns were schools and education, the economy and immigration, followed by unemployment and the labor market. Those issues also feature prominently in the parties’ platforms.
The AfD program for the state is titled “Ready for the Blue Turn,” a reference to the party’s signature blue color. It promises economic and family relief, while setting out a harder line on migration.
It calls for an “admission stop” and for the “remigration” of Syrian refugees living in the state – a contested term used on the far right for large-scale returns of migrants.
The party also wants the state's own border and deportation police, more state detention facilities for people awaiting removal, and a “task force against foreign offenders.”
It would ease gun laws and drop some police paperwork for checks carried out without suspicion.
On energy it advocates a return to nuclear power, and abolish Germany’s carbon tax.
In German state parliaments, a party does not need 50% of the vote to govern alone.
It needs at least half the seats won by parties that clear the 5% threshold. Votes for parties below 5% are discarded.
Polls suggest that the Left Party (10%) and the CDU (7%) will also win seats in the Schwerin Landtag, alongside the AfD and its main rival, the SPD.
The Greens are hovering around the 5% threshold. The left-populist BSW is below it in the latest Insa survey. That uncertainty shapes several possible paths.
If the Greens clear 5%, a coalition of the SPD, the Left Party and the Greens could still reach a majority. The current SPD-Left Party alliance alone would not have a majority on the latest numbers.
If the AfD finishes first but short of a majority, it would need a coalition partner or outside support to take power. The SPD, the CDU, the Greens and the Left Party are all holding to a “firewall” policy — a political rule that they will not form a coalition with the AfD.
The BSW says it is open to talks but insists on an independent, non-party premier — a formula that remains untested after similar debates in Saxony-Anhalt.
The Mecklenburg-Vorpommern vote is not just about who governs one eastern state.
It is also being read in Berlin as a measure of the country’s overall political mood.
The AfD’s rise and the CDU’s losses are widely linked to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s unpopularity, fueling pressure inside his party for him to step aside.
In the Feb. 23, 2025, national election, Merz’s CDU/CSU won 28.5% and the AfD 20.8%. Several polls since have shown that gap narrowing or reversing.
A GMS survey published on Monday put the AfD at a record 30% nationwide, 10 points ahead of the CDU/CSU at 20%.
Meanwhile, the tension is palpable.
Merz has cancelled a planned trip to New York next week for the UN General Debate to focus on the state votes.
Senior CDU leaders will meet internally on Monday, with CDU and Bavarian sister party CSU lawmakers due to meet two days later.
Speculation about a leadership challenge has been building for weeks.
On Wednesday, however, all eight CDU state premiers issued a joint statement backing Merz ahead of Sunday’s elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and in Berlin.
Political observers, however, say a big AfD win coupled with another historic CDU defeat on Sunday could still trigger a leadership fight next week.
The city state of Berlin is voting the same day, raising the prospect that the CDU could also lose power in the capital.
A bid to change the CDU’s leadership would not automatically dissolve the federal parliament or trigger a snap election.
If party pressure forces Merz out, lawmakers could elect a new chancellor without a nationwide vote.

From Syria to France, how soaring fuel costs inflame protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:14:18 UTC
19:14:18 KST

Breadcrumb
From Syria to France, how soaring fuel costs are inflaming protests
Protests over soaring fuel prices and rising energy costs have recently erupted across several continents as regional conflicts push up oil prices and put greater pressure on households and businesses.
Oil prices climbed back above $100 a barrel last week after new US strikes on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf, while renewed fighting in Yemen has raised fresh concerns over shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
In the US, rising fuel costs have also prompted warnings that households reliant on heating oil could face price increases of as much as 40% this winter.
The impact is being felt well beyond the cost of filling up a car. More expensive diesel and petrol feed into transport, food deliveries, manufacturing, construction, agriculture and electricity generation, meaning a shock at the pump can quickly become a wider cost-of-living crisis.
Here are some of the countries where fuel and energy costs have triggered protests, strikes or growing public anger.
Syria
A sharp increase in fuel prices over the weekend sparked protests across Syria, marking the largest demonstrations the country has seen since the fall of Bashar al-Assad two years ago.
The government temporarily raised the price of a litre of diesel to 175 Syrian pounds ($1.43), an increase of around 40%, while petrol prices rose by more than 25%, according to the state-run SANA news agency. The Energy Ministry blamed the increases on the global rise in fuel prices and ongoing maintenance at the Baniyas refinery, the country's largest refinery, which has increased Syria's reliance on imports.
Most demonstrations were peaceful, but protesters on Sunday blocked the highway linking Hasakah and Deir Ezzor, burned tyres and stopped oil trucks, according to conflict-monitoring organisation ACLED.
Diesel is particularly important in Syria because it is used for far more than transport. It is also widely relied on for heating and power generation, meaning higher diesel prices can affect households both on the road and at home as winter approaches.
The same is true across neighbouring Lebanon, where diesel is widely used by private generators as well as for heating. A rise in the cost of diesel can therefore hit households through electricity and heating bills as well as transport and other everyday costs.
Iran
Iran is facing a different but closely related fuel crisis, with long queues at petrol stations and strikes by truck drivers adding to growing economic pressure.
The government has been struggling to maintain fuel subsidies, while cuts to subsidised fuel allocations have angered drivers. Taxi drivers in particular have been affected by reductions in their subsidised fuel allocation, according to the Union of Truckers and Drivers.
The economic fallout from the Israel-US war and an American blockade has added to problems already facing ordinary Iranians, including a plunging currency, worsening joblessness and rising prices for everyday goods.
Portugal
In the coastal Portuguese city of Espinho, around 80 people protested on Saturday over rising fuel and living costs.
The demonstration was organised by local business leaders and workers seeking government action. Protesters marched towards the home of Prime Minister Luís Montenegro in the city, according to Portuguese news agency Lusa.
The Portuguese Association of Firefighters has also warned that rising fuel prices are placing a heavy burden on fire services, particularly volunteer organisations. The government announced a package of measures on Monday aimed at easing the impact on freight companies, taxi drivers, firefighters and social-sector organisations.
France
In southern France, around 50 fishermen blocked a major fuel depot in the coastal town of Fos-sur-Mer on Tuesday in protest at rising prices.
The blockade lasted several hours and included brief clashes between protesters and police, according to local broadcaster BFMTV.
The mayor of Fos-sur-Mer, Philippe Maurizot, described the fishing sector as facing a "deep crisis" requiring an urgent state response. He also warned that rising costs, higher fuel prices, restrictions, insufficient incomes and a lack of future prospects had left some workers in an "unbearable" situation.
Guatemala
Truck drivers and other protesters blocked highways in several parts of Guatemala last week in response to rising fuel prices, causing disruption in different areas, according to the Associated Press.
Peaceful demonstrations were also held in the capital, with protesters demanding immediate government action.
Guatemala's Congress is considering legislation that would cap fuel prices until the end of the year. Under the proposed measure, the government would provide support to fuel importers if international prices rise above the ceiling.
Philippines
Transport workers from the Manibela group went on strike on Monday over rising fuel prices, calling for government support and the abolition of taxes on fuel.
The strike coincided with another round of price increases that took effect on Tuesday, raising the price of petrol by 5.68 pesos, alongside further increases in diesel and kerosene prices, according to the Philippine News Agency.
Bus and other public transport drivers have been dealing with higher operating costs for months, with prices having risen sharply in March and remaining above levels seen before the war.
In Manila, protests also took place near the presidential palace during the peak of the earlier price shock, as transport workers and others voiced anger over the rising cost of energy.
Sudan
Sudan illustrates how fuel shortages can become catastrophic even when the immediate trigger is not global oil prices.
In Khartoum, the price of a gallon of fuel has climbed to around 55,000 Sudanese pounds (US$92) on the black market, while shortages have left hundreds of vehicles queuing at petrol stations.
But the roots of Sudan's crisis lie primarily in the country's internal war, which began in April 2023, and its consequences, including the collapse in the value of the Sudanese pound and the disruption of domestic supply and distribution networks.
The situation shows that energy security depends not only on global prices or oil production, but also on whether countries can transport, distribute and sell fuel reliably inside their own borders.
Why fuel prices trigger wider crises
Fuel costs affect far more than transport. Higher diesel and petrol prices raise the cost of food, goods, manufacturing, construction and agriculture. In countries such as Lebanon and Iraq, expensive diesel can also drive up electricity costs because of reliance on private generators.
The impact is particularly severe where people already face weak currencies, unemployment, unreliable electricity and high food prices.
The latest protests across the Middle East, Europe, Latin America and Asia show how quickly an energy shock can spread through economies. With regional conflicts threatening shipping through Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb and winter approaching, further price rises could increase pressure on households and governments.

Hong Kong will lack 130,000 workers by 2028, fewer than projected due to talent policies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:14:08 UTC
19:14:08 KST

Hong Kong will lack 130,000 workers by 2028, fewer than projected due to talent policies
Shortage mitigated by AI development and talent import policies, labour chief says, as top talent visa renewal to be relaxed for tech founders
Hong Kong will be short of 130,000 workers by 2028, about a third less than originally projected, a reduction the city’s labour chief attributed to the development of artificial intelligence (AI) and government policies to import labour and top talent.
A day after the release of the city’s first five-year plan and annual policy address, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said on Thursday that authorities would exempt start-up founders approved under the Top Talent Pass Scheme from needing to provide proof of company income when renewing their visas to better support these entrepreneurs.
“Our previous manpower projection found that we will be short of 180,000 workers by 2028, but in the latest study, to be announced in detail next week, the shortfall will be reduced to 130,000,” he said.

In Silicon Valley, AI data center boom meets local resistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:13:22 UTC
19:13:22 KST

In Silicon Valley, AI data centre boom meets local resistance
- Silicon Valley's San Jose is promoting AI data centre growth for economic benefits but faces local resistance over concerns about energy, water use, and pollution impacts.
- Residents and groups demand stricter reviews, transparency, and environmental studies before approving new data centre projects, while city officials advocate responsible development.
- California lawmakers propose bills to ensure large energy users pay fair costs and increase transparency, with industry warning of potential negative effects on investment and jobs.
AI generated
SAN JOSE, California – In Silicon Valley’s biggest city, residents and environmental groups are organising against a wave of proposed data centre projects that officials have courted in a bid to position the city as a hub for AI infrastructure.
The clash highlights a challenge confronting policymakers nationwide: how to support an industry viewed by government and business leaders as critical to economic competitiveness while responding to growing public concerns about the electricity, water and pollution impacts of the infrastructure required to power it.
In California, that debate is particularly fraught because the state is home to many of the companies driving the AI boom, including Google, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic.
San Jose, a city of nearly one million and California’s third-largest, has embraced the industry’s growth. In 2025, city leaders announced an agreement with utility PG&E to speed delivery of power to large energy users such as data centres.
The city estimates each new facility could generate between US$3 million (S$3.8 million) and US$6 million in tax income annually for services such as police, fire protection, libraries, roads and parks.
Despite Silicon Valley’s wealth, however, many residents remain unconvinced that the benefits of the wave of tech-driven growth tied to AI-focused facilities will be broadly shared.
“The companies have to prove to us why they deserve our resources and how they’re going to give back to the community,” said Ellina Yin, a leader of the grassroots I Love San Jose coalition.
Yin and others are pushing for stricter public review, more transparency around energy and water use and studies of health and environmental impacts before more projects are approved.
Mayor Matt Mahan says the answer is not to halt data centre development but to ensure it is done responsibly.
“People are right to question, ‘Is this pushing up my energy costs? Is it using our clean water supplies? Will it degrade quality of life in my city?’” Mahan told Reuters. “These are very fair questions.”
The fight comes as California Governor Gavin Newsom weighs a package of Bills intended to protect state residents from the costs of powering data centres and increase transparency around their energy and water use.
PG&E said new large customers can help spread fixed grid costs across a broader customer base and help lower bills.
Air quality is a particular concern. In April, a coalition led by the Center for Biological Diversity petitioned the Bay Area Air Quality Management District to strengthen oversight of diesel backup generators used at data centres, arguing that existing regulations predate the recent expansion of AI-related facilities.
The district said it is exploring whether stronger protections are warranted.
New legislation pending
The concerns raised in San Jose have increasingly made their way to Sacramento, California’s capital.
Lawmakers recently gave final approval in both the state Senate and Assembly to several Bills addressing data centres, including measures intended to ensure large electricity users pay their share of grid-related costs and requirements aimed at increasing transparency around energy and water consumption.
State Senator Steve Padilla, who authored several of the measures, said California has an obligation to lead because it is home to many of the world’s largest technology companies.
The Data Center Coalition, an industry trade group whose members include Google, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic, said it supports responsible growth but argued the Bills unfairly single out data centres rather than other large industrial and commercial electricity users. The group warned the measures could discourage investment and push jobs, tax revenue and projects to other states.
Newsom has until the end of September to either sign or veto the legislation. His office declined to comment because the Bills are pending before the governor. REUTERS

Russia says new US sanctions, if signed by Trump, would make  Ukraine peace deal harder

Russia says new US sanctions, if signed by Trump, would make Ukraine peace deal harder
MOSCOW, Sept 17 - The Kremlin said on Thursday that further U.S. sanctions against Russia would make it harder to reach a peace deal in Ukraine.
On Wednesday, the U.S. House of Representatives passed a sweeping sanctions package intended to increase economic pressure on Russia over its war in Ukraine, sending the bill to President Donald Trump to sign into law.
"We are, of course, monitoring the progress of this document. It falls under the category of unfriendly actions, and of course the imposition of any additional sanctions by the U.S. would certainly complicate efforts to find a peace settlement in Ukraine," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
U.S.-mediated efforts to end the 4-1/2-year Ukraine war have been stalled for months, but President Donald Trump sent two envoys to Moscow and Kyiv earlier this month in an effort to get the process moving again.
The U.S. sanctions bill targets Russia's energy and defence industries, as well as its "shadow fleet" of tankers that evade existing sanctions, in order to deprive Moscow of revenues to finance the war with Ukraine.
It also authorises Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on China, India and other countries to reduce their dependence on Russian oil and gas.
India has warned Washington that new measures to levy tariffs over the purchase of Russian oil could impact bilateral ties. REUTERS

France can provide defense aid to Ukraine but should scale back financial support, Le Pen says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:11:02 UTC
19:11:02 KST

France can provide defense aid to Ukraine but should scale back financial support, Le Pen says
France cannot continue supporting Ukraine at the current level due to its own financial constraints, the co-leader of the French far-right National Rally (RN) party, Marine Le Pen, said on Sept. 16.
"This is not an act of hostility towards Ukraine. We can continue to train their soldiers, their armies; we can continue to provide them with equipment so they can defend themselves," Le Pen told the French media.
However, France "cannot continue" providing the same financial aid "given the considerable amount we have done so far," the Euroskeptic leader added.
The comments come less than a year before the French presidential election, with surveys putting Le Pen far ahead of any other candidate at 33-34%, making her the most likely successor to pro-European President Emmanuel Macron.
Le Pen argued that France cannot keep spending money abroad while "there isn't a single euro... to index pensions."
Her views echo those of her party's co-leader, Jordan Bardella, who said earlier in September that France should not "abandon" Ukraine completely but cannot continue financing the war-torn country indefinitely and without any guarantees.
The RN has come under criticism from other French parties over its Ukraine policy after Louis Aliot, the RN's vice-president, suggested "turning off the tap" on support for Kyiv.
France has been one of Kyiv's most strategically important allies amid Russia's full-scale war, spearheading pro-Ukrainian initiatives and providing the country with jets, long-range missiles, intelligence support, and other aid.
Macron has also been one of the leading voices in the Coalition of the Willing, a group of over 30 nations coordinating assistance for Ukraine and preparing post-war security guarantees, including a potential deployment of a European-led peacekeeping force.
However, the Kiel Institute's Ukraine Support Tracker says that France lags behind in support provided to Kyiv relative to its economic strength, especially compared to Germany, the Nordics, or the Baltic countries.
As of June 2026, Paris devoted a little over 1% of its GDP to bilateral and EU support for Ukraine, while much less populous countries like Denmark, Estonia, and Lithuania contributed over 3%, Kiel Institute researchers say.
Before Russia's all-out invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Le Pen openly expressed her admiration for Russian President Vladimir Putin, said she did not believe Russia's annexation of Crimea was illegal, and her party took a 9-billion-euro loan from a Russian bank in 2014 despite sanctions.
Le Pen and her party sought to cast away their pro-Kremlin rhetoric after 2022, denouncing Russian aggression and praising Ukrainian defenders. At the same time, Le Pen has opposed more decisive support for Kyiv, such as the deployment of French peacekeepers on the ground.
The nationalist leader has made three unsuccessful runs for the French presidency and was thought to have lost the chance for a fourth attempt when she was convicted of embezzling EU funds and banned from running for public office last March.
However, a Paris appeals court in June 2026 shortened the ban, clearing her path for the presidential run.

'I'm not a doomer': US Senator Mark Warner makes the case for acting fast on AI guardrails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:08:54 UTC
19:08:54 KST

'I'm not a doomer': US Senator Mark Warner makes the case for acting fast on AI guardrails
WASHINGTON, Sept 17 - The U.S. Congress should pass legislation by the year-end setting AI safety standards, as an immediate first step toward broad guardrails for an industry whose rapid development has alarmed tech CEOs and the public alike, U.S. Senator Mark Warner told Reuters in an interview.
Warner, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and a leading congressional voice on technology and national security, dismissed much of the doomsday talk surrounding AI but said the time is ripe politically for legislative action, with worries over AI "now at tipping point for Americans."
"I'm not a doomer," the Virginia Democrat said in the interview on Wednesday. "This talk about human extinction is over the top."
He warned, however, of possible trouble ahead, raising "the idea that these swarms of AI agents might jump the fence and take over a banking system or take over a water system or, God forbid, take over a hospital."
A sudden groundswell has risen in favor of federal intervention after OpenAI said in July that an autonomous AI agent went rogue during a security test and hacked into another company, subverting human control.
Warner, who invested in startup companies in wireless telecommunications and other tech sectors before entering politics, said there is an opening for acting before a new Congress is sworn in next January.
"In the short term, I think the only thing we can actually ... get done is a set of safety protocols," he said, adding that UK protocols could be a template for the United States, as could programs that other nations, including China, are pursuing.
TRUMP, REPUBLICANS WARY OVER AI REGULATION
Even that short-term goal, though, is likely to be a heavy lift.
Many Republicans, following the lead of President Donald Trump, are hesitant to thrust the federal government into the AI industry, which is powering U.S. investment and stock market gains.
"I think we need to be careful that we don't get too much government drama," Republican Representative Roger Williams of Texas said in a sidewalk interview near the Capitol on Tuesday. "I think you start out by letting the private sector see how they can compete and make it grow," Williams added.
Republican Representative Ralph Norman of South Carolina, a member of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus, said that while voters want guardrails, "that's going to take a lot of time to work through that." He added: "I'm for limited government."
A bipartisan bill, whose backers range from Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota to Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, is being refined and Warner said he is reviewing it.
But he stopped short of backing that bill as a first step.
"I think it's well-intentioned, but a lot of it's focused on after-action report, or incident disclosure after action," he said, adding: "We can't wait to have an incident and then look back and see how do we fix it."
TRUMP-XI MEETING PUTS FOCUS ON GLOBAL COLLABORATION
While Trump has taken a hands-off stance toward AI regulation, Washington will be watching closely whether he maintains that position when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House on September 24.
U.S. opponents of domestic regulation of AI say any government restrictions would simply give China the upper hand in the AI revolution.
But for many Democrats, including Warner, the U.S. must work together with China, France, the UAE and other nations that are developing AI industries, as the world tries to thwart bad actors.
"This is really one where we have to go back to a level of international collaboration," Warner said, at a time when Trump has been pulling away from such cooperation.
Doing so would benefit U.S. industry, he said.
"It would be in their best interest to have an outside, independent, international veteran in this room."
FEDERAL ROLE FOR AI SAFETY
Warner said eventual legislation could include the creation of a new federal agency overseeing AI.
"Nobody would climb on an airplane or drive a car without some level of outside safety reviews. And the industry would need something like potentially even an antitrust exemption to talk to each other."
With the 100 senators pushing for varying provisions, it could make for a prolonged battle — one that Warner said the country cannot risk.
"I don't think whether we call it a pause or pacing means that we're going to stop innovation" in the AI industry, he said.
One relatively easy provision to legislate, Warner said, would be to impose safety standards as a prerequisite for corporate tax breaks, such as the bonus depreciation.
For the economy, he said there were downsides to AI advancements, such as rising unemployment in some sectors that he said the industry has not addressed while the economy transitions.
But "there will be enormous growth" around blue-collar jobs, such as electricians and welders and healthcare advances. "Everyday Americans and not just a bunch of tech guys out in San Francisco" will benefit, he said.
As he campaigns for a fourth Senate term in this November's midterm election, Warner, 71, warned that Congress often waits for a disaster before addressing problems.
Asked to predict the likelihood of AI safety legislation happening in 2026, Warner said he is not good at making predictions, but made one exception.
"If we don't do something and something happens, there's a 95%-plus probability that Americans are going to be even more pissed off at Congress than at President Trump." REUTERS

Is NATO ready to fight? The Ukraine war is raising doubts among military analysts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:08:43 UTC
19:08:43 KST

Is NATO ready to fight? The Ukraine war is raising doubts among military analysts
KYIV, Sept 17 - Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of people. It has also served as a proving ground for new weapons systems and raised an uncomfortable question for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization: Is the alliance prepared for the next war it might have to fight?
Five Ukrainian and Western defense officials told Reuters that developments on the battlefield are moving so quickly that some NATO weapons and tactics risk becoming outdated. While Ukraine – which is not an alliance member – adapts in weeks, NATO buys and develops systems over years, sometimes decades.
The Ukraine war and U.S. President Donald Trump’s haranguing of European allies have prompted many NATO members to dramatically increase their defense spending. The Pentagon is currently reviewing its military presence in European countries, which Trump has accused of sponging off U.S. protection and refusing to help prosecute his unpopular war against Iran.
Denys Shtilerman, the co-owner and chief designer of Fire Point, a leading Ukrainian missile and drone builder, told Reuters that tanks are now “worthless” because a drone costing about $5,000 can destroy one. Yet Europe still spends heavily on tanks – which, say many military analysts, still have a key role to play in future battles.
Cheap drones have also transformed warfare in other ways. Troops gathering in groups or large vehicle convoys all become far easier targets.
“They are good at storming positions,” Oleksandr Pivnenko, Commander of the National Guard of Ukraine, said of the international troops his units trained with last year. “But if there’s a drone overhead and you don’t even look up, what do you think will happen to your squad?”
In June, Reuters attended a NATO military exercise near Paldiski in Estonia – a small Baltic country now fortifying its 210-mile border with Russia – in which American and European troops treated dozens of simulated casualties at wartime field hospitals. But the exercise took place with the assumption that NATO would command the airspace above the hospitals – no longer a given in the age of cheap, stealthy, long-distance drones.
Rather than simply receiving NATO training and assistance, Ukrainian officials described a growing role for Ukraine in teaching the alliance lessons drawn from the war with Russia. Yet they also said NATO’s military bureaucracy struggles to absorb those lessons. A Ukrainian officer who underwent NATO psychological operations training in Romania told Reuters that some alliance training materials still relied on case studies from World War Two. NATO didn’t respond to questions about the officials’ criticism of its training and bureaucracy.
The Ukraine war has also exposed a vulnerability that NATO officials say is far harder to solve: air and missile defense. Russia’s relentless barrages against Ukrainian cities have highlighted Europe's dependence on sophisticated U.S. anti-missile systems such as the Patriot, first used in the 1991 Gulf War. Ukraine has a critical shortage of Patriot interceptors – the missiles fired to destroy incoming threats.
Fearing that its reliance on Patriots might become a strategic vulnerability, Europe is building non-U.S. alternatives. Ukraine is awaiting delivery of the new French-Italian SAMP/T-NG air-defense system, designed to intercept ballistic missiles. France has promised to accelerate its deployment to Ukraine, and European diplomats previously told Reuters it was expected to arrive by next spring.
In a statement, the Ukrainian defense ministry said its soldiers and NATO’s had much to learn from each other, hailing Ukraine’s use of drones and radioelectronic warfare as “globally unmatched" and praising European efforts to help tackle Russia’s drone and missile bombardments.
In July, Ukraine and nine European allies launched an air-defense coalition that includes plans to jointly develop a new anti-ballistic missile system. Known as Freyja, the project is a consortium of about a dozen companies with Fire Point as the lead private-sector partner. The goal is to build a system that is cheaper and faster to produce than the Patriot, while ensuring that Europe, not the U.S., controls its manufacture.
“If you spend $20 billion on your air defense system, you must be independent in your security,” said Fire Point’s Shtilerman. REUTERS

Nigeria sends state police amendment bill to state assemblies for ratification
ABUJA, Sept 17 - Nigeria's parliament has sent a constitutional amendment bill that would establish state police forces to the country's 36 state assemblies for ratification, advancing a key security overhaul by President Bola Tinubu as he faces mounting pressure over worsening insecurity ahead of January elections.
• National Assembly clerk Kamoru Ogunlana said the Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, which contains provisions for state police, has been cleared by federal lawmakers and sent to Nigeria's 36 state assemblies for consideration.
• Ogunlana said the National Assembly had asked states to return their resolutions within 30 days, but added that the timeframe was administrative and not constitutionally binding.
• The bill must be approved by at least two-thirds of state assemblies, or 24 of the 36 states, before it can become law.
• Supporters say state police would improve responses to local security threats by decentralising policing powers from the federal government.
• Other constitutional amendment proposals still awaiting final approval include local government autonomy, independent candidacy, reserved legislative seats for women and citizenship by investment.
• If ratified by the required number of state assemblies, it would be one of the most sweeping changes to Nigeria's security and governance framework since the country returned to civilian rule in 1999. REUTERS

The missile and drone strikes targeted Ukraine’s capital Kyiv as well as the Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions.
Ukrainian officials say at least 19 people have been injured in Russian missile and drone strikes targeting Kyiv and surrounding areas.
Ukraine’s Air Force said on Thursday that it destroyed or suppressed 131 Russian aerial targets during the overnight attacks, adding that the main areas targeted were the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions.

Strikes were recorded at 36 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at five sites.

Three bulk carriers and a ferry used to carry supplies for the Ukrainian military were hit in the port of Chornomorsk, added the ministry.

“We have a situation where just a few days ago, [US President] Donald Trump announced that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy targets,” as Trump has blamed the Russia-Ukraine war for the rising cost of diesel around the world, said Challands.
However, “neither Russia nor Ukraine have agreed to this and they are continuing to hit each other’s energy targets”, said Challands, with Russia promising to increase its “mass attacks on the Ukrainian energy grid going into the winter months”.
Russian attacks “almost collapsed the Ukrainian energy grid” last winter, with Ukraine’s energy providers now saying that they are “expecting another very tough winter” but hoping that it will be better than the previous one, said Challands.
A Ukrainian drone attack hit an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl, northeast of Moscow, said President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The resulting fire from the attack had been extinguished, announced regional governor Mikhail Yevrayev.
Zelenskyy also reported damage to Russian warplanes and helicopters in a strike on a military base in the southern city of Rostov.
“There have also been good results in the Black Sea,” the president said on social media, without giving further details.
Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine exchanged the bodies of their war dead, with Moscow handing over the remains of 252 people and receiving 23 bodies in the swap at the Belarusian-Ukrainian border, Belarusian state news agency BELTA reported.

The EU Wants to Break Up Kids and Their Chatbots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:06:50 UTC
19:06:50 KST

The EU plans to ban chatbots from simulating emotions or interpersonal relationships in interactions with anyone under the age of 18 as the bloc tries to stop children from developing emotional dependencies on the technology.
The rules will be part of the EU Kids Act, proposed on Thursday, which includes similar restrictions on minors’ access to social media and video-sharing platforms. Children under 13 will be banned from accessing chatbots without their guardians’ supervision, and digital platforms will have to build child-safety protections into their products or face fines of up to 6 percent of total worldwide turnover, according to a draft of the legislation seen by WIRED.
Chatbots operating in the EU will also not be allowed to retain memory of interactions between separate conversations under the new rules, since the Commission worries this could lead to systems accumulating sensitive data of minors over time and potentially reinforcing harmful interaction patterns.
Providers of online social networking sites, video-sharing platforms, and games should not automatically activate or encourage the use of AI chatbots on their services, the proposed law will also stipulate. That includes not pinning AI companions and general conversational chatbots at the top of a minor’s contacts list, it says—as had been done by Snapchat.
The proposal is limited to AI companions and general conversational chatbots seen by the Commission to pose serious risks to minors’ health, safety, and well-being. Simeon de Brouwer, a policy adviser at the Brussels-based advocacy group European Digital Rights, welcomes the chatbot measures, but tells WIRED it doesn’t make sense to restrict them to young people only. “Don’t we all deserve to be protected from AIs designed to be addictive, from AIs which create emotional dependencies, or from AI features which are activated and pushed by default onto users?” The EU says its Digital Fairness Act, due to be unveiled later this year, is expected to propose clampdowns on addictive design more widely.
In documents seen by WIRED, the European Commission says it is worried that dependency on chatbots may negatively impact a child’s development and its relationships with other humans. It’s also concerned by chatbots giving minors dangerous advice, including on their mental health and personal development, which it said can shape and encourage risky behavior.
“Platforms have been playing fast and loose with children’s mental health,” President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press conference on Thursday. Around half of Europeans aged 11 to 25 have discussed intimate or personal matters with AI chatbots, according to an Ipsos BVA survey across France, Germany, Sweden, and Ireland. Australia and the UK are both attempting to restrict minors’ access to chatbots through their social media bans.
It also highlighted the harms of deepfakes generated by chatbots, which von der Leyen nodded at in Wednesday’s State of the Union speech: “We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images … Europe has the power to act.” While the EU AI Act has required synthetic content to be labeled as AI-generated since August, the rules currently only apply to deepfakes generated for commercial use.
The Commission also blames digital distraction for a decline in basic skills in young people. Children who say they use AI chatbots for schoolwork get lower test scores than those who don’t, according to research spanning 91 countries by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. Concerns about cognitive impacts and deskilling “expose the absence of children’s rights from the design of GenAI’s tools,” researchers from the independent network EU Kids Online wrote in a report.
