S. Korea's knowledge services deficit widens in H1 on demand for overseas AI, streaming services
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:53:14 CST
17:53:14 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's knowledge services deficit widened in the first half amid surging demand for overseas artificial intelligence (AI) software and streaming services, central bank data showed Thursday.
The country posted a deficit of 6.44 billion U.S. dollars in knowledge-intensive services trade during the January-June period, up from a deficit of 5.44 billion dollars in the second half of last year, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
It marked the second-largest half-yearly deficit in the country's history, trailing only the deficit of 7.0 billion dollars tallied in the second half of 2010.
The widening deficit was fueled by intellectual property royalties, which saw their shortfall expand from 4.00 billion dollars in the second half of 2025 to 4.90 billion dollars in the first half of 2026.
Notably, the computer and mobile software copyright sector, which includes fees for global AI services, registered a record-high deficit of 2.84 billion dollars in the first half, up from 2.31 billion dollars in the previous half.
Trade in multimedia copyrights, which includes subscriptions to global online video streaming platforms, swung from a surplus of 290 million dollars to a deficit of 40 million dollars in the cited period.
Cultural and leisure services provided a buffer, with its surplus advancing to 720 million dollars in the first half from 530 million dollars in the previous half.
Surplus in the information and communication services slightly shrank from 2.87 billion dollars to 2.42 billion dollars, while the deficit in professional business services moderately narrowed from 4.84 billion dollars to 4.67 billion dollars. ■

S. Koreans face "deficit-surplus-deficit" financial lifecycle, with surplus peaking at 45
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:52:57 CST
17:52:57 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- South Koreans faced a "deficit-surplus-deficit" financial lifecycle, with their lifetime surplus peaking at age 45, statistical ministry data showed Thursday.
The Ministry of Data and Statistics released the 2024 National Transfer Accounts to analyze the relationship between consumption and labor income across different age groups.
From birth to age 27, individuals spent more than they earned, resulting in a deficit.
The deficit peaked at age 16 and reached 46.04 million won (about 33,330 U.S. dollars), driven by private educational costs for college entrance preparation.
South Koreans transitioned into a financial surplus at age 28, with their labor income outpacing consumption until age 60.
The surplus reached its peak of 19.32 million won at age 45 as per-capita labor income hit a lifetime high of 46.51 million won at that age.
Labor income shrank from age 61, when people entered their retirement years, shifting them back into a deficit.
It was fueled by rising medical and healthcare expenditures in the older generation. ■

To safeguard the LMC region's development, he stressed the need for stronger collective action within the LMC framework.

====================================================================================================

Across China: The "cabbage revolution" -- How China is using science to feed 1.4 billion people
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:52:51 CST
17:52:51 KST

WUHAN, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- There is nothing remarkable about the tiny cabbage seedlings growing in the fields of Jiayu County in central China.
They are barely more than rows of green tufts against the soil, too young to look anything like the firm heads that will eventually find their way onto dinner tables across the country.
Yet these modest plants tell the story of a decades-long scientific effort to develop better seeds, breed tougher varieties and make one of China's most ordinary vegetables more productive and reliable.
Known as China's "cabbage UN" for its vast collection of varieties, Jiayu in Hubei Province has become a major hub for cabbage breeding, testing and production.
The effort goes back to the 1980s, when China still relied on cabbage seeds imported from countries including Japan and the Netherlands.
"We were determined to build our own capacity and take food production into our own hands," said Qiu Zhengming, chief scientist with the Hubei Academy of Agricultural Sciences, who works at a vegetable science and technology demonstration park in Jiayu.
Led by pioneers, including Fang Zhiyuan of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, generations of researchers set out to find a way to ensure that people in China could have fresh, high-quality cabbage throughout the year.
They started with the seed.
Scientists developed China's first cabbage hybrid, followed by disease-resistant varieties and strains suited to different growing seasons. For winter harvests, they bred varieties that could withstand the cold while producing sweeter heads.
The results have accumulated over decades. Today, more than 70 percent of winter cabbage grown in China's major winter-cabbage producing areas comes from domestic varieties, according to researchers.
"Using science and technology to improve production is important," Qiu said. "Once you have that foundation, farmers' incomes become more stable."
At Jiayu's 460-mu (about 31-hectare) vegetable science and technology demonstration park, researchers test more than 2,000 cabbage varieties each year, continually introducing and screening new ones to find those best suited to local conditions.
The experiments go beyond cabbage. Researchers are also developing new varieties of vegetables that are staples on Chinese dinner tables, including winter melon, pumpkin and Chinese cabbage.
Modern breeding techniques, including hybrid breeding and genetic technologies, are being used to improve resistance to cold and disease and to increase levels of fiber, vitamins and minerals. A nearly 100-mu area has also been established for fully mechanized cabbage production trials.
The fields themselves have become part of the experiment.
At the demonstration park, a network of digital sensors monitors weather, temperature, soil conditions, pests and diseases, as well as water and fertilizer levels.
When something goes wrong, an alert can be sent directly to a farmer's smartphone. Drones fly over the fields to monitor crop health.
The shift is giving farmers more control over their fields. Instead of relying on unpredictable weather, they can make decisions based on data.
Farmers can also order seeds directly from a researcher-managed seed bank, saving them the time and uncertainty of breeding their own varieties and helping them avoid losses caused by bad weather.
Jiayu's vegetables now reach markets across the country, including Hong Kong, Shanghai and Guangzhou. About 75,000 local farmers are involved in vegetable cultivation and their incomes have increased.
For farmer Liu Lianhong, the benefits are measured in more familiar terms. Her household income comes mainly from land-transfer payments and annual dividends from a vegetable farming company, while she also works there. These days, she is busy transplanting cabbage seedlings and clearing weeds.
What is happening in Jiayu is part of a much larger effort in China to use agricultural science to strengthen domestic food supplies.
Perhaps the best-known example is hybrid rice, pioneered by Yuan Longping. The breakthrough dramatically increased rice yields and helped China meet much of its own demand for rice.
Hubei, a major grain-producing province, is now developing high-yield, high-protein corn as an alternative that could help reduce reliance on imported soybeans. Researchers are also breeding fish with improved meat quality.
In neighboring Henan Province, scientists have developed rice varieties less prone to lodging. In Shaanxi Province, researchers have developed drought-tolerant, high-yield wheat.
Some of these agricultural technologies and varieties have also traveled beyond China, helping farmers in Central Asia and Africa increase production and incomes.
These efforts are about more than seeds, technology and yields. They are ultimately about people's lives.
"Of all the things that matter, the well-being of people matters most," Qiu said. ■

UN accuses US military of committing war crimes, Iranian regime of crimes against humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:50:36 UTC
17:50:36 KST

A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.
It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined the US's conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that began in late December.
The Iranian and US permanent missions in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
US officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.
Minab School strike
The UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe US forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.
The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.
According to the report, the US relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike. Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.
"Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."
In June, US President Donald Trump said that "nobody" purposefully attacked a girls' school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. Reuters first reported that an initial internal US military investigation showed US forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab in southern Iran.
The Pentagon has since elevated the probe, but it has not published any preliminary findings.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.
The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports center in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
US Central Command said in a statement in March that US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
Iran abuses also recalled
The UN mission probe found that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes, the US and Israel.
The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures, which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people injured.
The government's response to the protests - including violence and killings, cutting off the internet, and the use of the death penalty- marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

Diaspora Ministry launches site collating United Nations bias against Israel in war against Hamas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:49:56 UTC
17:49:56 KST

The Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Ministry on Wednesday launched its first comprehensive international campaign aimed at exposing what it says is the United Nation's mechanism of bias against Israel ahead of the UN General Assembly's general debate, which is set to begin in New York on September 22.
The information presented on the website addresses alleged bias and manipulation, reports of famine in Gaza, UNRWA, accusations of genocide, and publications in which the ministry says the UN amplifies such claims.
The ministry's digital campaign, produced through the Government Advertising Agency, will focus on the United States and target journalists, diplomats, and decision-makers, aiming the direct them to the sources presented on the website.
The campaign will be accompanied by a new website the ministry launched after extensive research and data collection. The website brings together, in an accessible format, the ministry's work examining UN publications and the conduct of UN bodies since the October 7 attack.
According to the ministry, the website presents a broad picture of what it describes as a mechanism of bias against Israel and a system of falsehoods: information presented without sufficient context, claims that gain an authoritative status once they appear in UN publications, and the UN's subsequent amplification of those publications, which the ministry says strengthens misleading narratives.
The website compiles a large volume of information and enables journalists, diplomats, researchers, and decision-makers to follow six interconnected areas and examine the sources behind the findings.
Its launch will be accompanied by a campaign timed to coincide with international attention focused on the UN General Assembly in New York. The campaign videos will present issues examined on the website and direct viewers to the publications and sources cited there.
Site details UN information manipulation, toxic culture, manufactured narratives
The website is divided into six main sections.
The first, "Information manipulation by UN actors," details what the ministry describes as the adoption and dissemination of claims by UN officials, statistical distortions, and the omission of context considered essential to understanding the data. The website alleges that professional definitions were changed and statistical indicators manipulated in order to reach predetermined conclusions before they had been factually examined on the ground, particularly regarding claims of "starvation" and "genocide."
The second section, "Toxic institutional culture," focuses on what the ministry describes as language, statements, and patterns of conduct within the UN that allow one-sided positions against Israel to become embedded in the organization.
A third section, titled "The famine that wasn't," examines the data, forecasts, and messaging through which claims of famine in Gaza received institutional legitimacy and global attention. The ministry claims that this section demonstrates that the UN's presentation of the data is far removed from conditions on the ground.
The fourth section, "UNRWA compromised," compiles findings and allegations concerning Hamas infiltration of the agency and the conduct of UNRWA's leadership following related disclosures. It presents what the ministry describes as intelligence evidence indicating extensive infiltration of UNRWA by Hamas operatives, which it says involves at least 12% of the agency's employees in the Gaza Strip, alongside the discovery of terrorist infrastructure beneath UNRWA headquarters and facilities.
A fifth section, "Manufacturing a genocide narrative," examines how some of the gravest accusations against Israel were formulated and disseminated, as well as what the ministry describes as the false basis presented in support of them.
The final section, "Self-reinforcing ecosystem," tracks the way a claim passes between different actors and publications before returning to international discourse carrying an additional stamp of authority, even when its original source has not been independently verified again.
The website also seeks to expose what it calls a process of "propaganda laundering," described as a three-stage mechanism in which unsubstantiated data originating from Hamas is cited by UN agencies, such as OCHA, stripped of reference to its original source, and then disseminated to the public and international legal bodies as "verified UN facts."
The main findings highlighted in the campaign include allegations of internal silencing and persecution. The ministry says it documented pressure and harassment directed at individuals who sought to maintain what they considered factual accuracy, while those who adopted anti-Israel narratives were allegedly rewarded and promoted.
"For far too long, the world has treated the UN's stamp as a substitute for fact-checking. This website exposes how the poison machine against Israel works: A narrative enters the system, receives institutional authority, is quoted again and again, and influences the positions of governments, media outlets, and the public. Since October 7, the cost of this bias has been particularly high. Anyone can examine what lies behind the headlines," Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Minister Amichai Chikli said.
UN officials claim they were pressured to condemn Israel
Testimony and quotations from senior officials and experts who worked within UN mechanisms are presented as evidence of what the campaign describes as a culture of silencing, pressure, and data manipulation.
World Health Organization representative Dr. Michel Thieren is quoted as saying: "The terms 'genocide' and 'famine' were thrown around from the very beginning. The crimes were defined in advance, and then the organizations tried to prove them. For me, this is completely abnormal."
Alice Wairimu Nderitu, the UN's former special adviser on the prevention of genocide, is quoted as saying: "I was bullied and harassed every day... This never happened in any other war. Not in Ukraine, not in Sudan, not in Myanmar. The focus was always on Israel... By taking one side and condemning it every day, you completely lose the purpose for which the UN was established."
The campaign states that Nderitu refused to define the fighting as "genocide" without an authoritative legal determination, and that her UN contract was subsequently not renewed.
UN Special Rapporteur on Torture Dr. Alice Edwards is quoted as describing heavy pressure from UN colleagues aimed at preventing her from publishing an official letter documenting Hamas's crimes on October 7.
"There was a campaign to prevent the letter from being published. It was weeks of bullying and intimidation," she said.
Former UN sanctions coordinator Edmund Fitton-Brown is quoted as saying: "The reverence for the UN allows weak evidence, activists' assumptions, and ideological leanings to launder themselves and become mainstream and accepted opinion."
'The UN rewrites the truth'
The campaign's video series visually depicts what the ministry describes as the manipulation of information and systematic falsification. In the videos, hands working inside what is portrayed as UN headquarters cut up and reassemble headlines from major newspapers. Headlines such as "Humanitarian aid stolen by Hamas," "Stop Hamas terror," and "Hamas harms civilians" are physically altered so that the word "Hamas" is replaced with "Israel."
The campaign concludes with the message: "The UN rewrites the truth."
"The website is an information source that brings everything together, unlike individual publications that do not create the same effect. When you examine where the information came from and how it passes between the different actors, you understand the mechanism," Hadas Maimon, head of the Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Ministry's senior public diplomacy division, said.

How to move an ancient mikvah? Inside the IAA's operation to conserve a Second Temple ritual bath
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:49:54 UTC
17:49:54 KST

The Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) recently undertook a complex engineering operation to conserve a Second Temple-era mikvah found during archaeological excavations in the Carmei Gat neighborhood of Kiryat Gat.
Financed by the Israel Lands Authority, the excavations were completed ahead of construction and development works slated to happen in Carmei Gat to preemptively protect the 2,000-year-old structure from harm.
Discovering the mikvah, as well as stone measuring vessels, provides direct evidence of the existence of a Jewish settlement in the area at the time. Stone vessels, which according to Jewish law do not become ritually impure, were widely used among Jews during the Second Temple period.
“The Jewish settlement we discovered here is the first and the only known one in this area,” explained IAA excavation directors Elena Kogan-Zahavi, Maayan Margulis and Shira Lifshitz. “In the Judean Lowlands, many Jewish settlements from the Roman period are known, but in the seam between the Judean Lowlands and the northern Negev, no Jewish settlement was known until now.”
Findings from the site indicate that the ancient settlement was likely abandoned by its Jewish inhabitants during the Bar Kokhba Revolt in the second century CE. The site was revived some 500 years later during the Byzantine period by an entirely different population.
Preparing the mikveh to be moved
As development work progressed, the IAA’s Conservation Administration was faced with a new, even more daunting task: how to temporarily transfer the mikveh, weighing 25 tons, from its current location to the Israel’s National Treasures Department.
Four members of the administration worked for two weeks straight to expose the mikveh in its entirety.
First, they dug around it to expose it on all sides. Then, careful drilling was carried out underneath the structure, and steel beams were then slid through to support the mikveh and allow it to be pulled from the ground.
The ancient plaster on the mikveh’s walls also required special treatment.
The IAA’s team gently covered it in gauze and adhesives to prevent vibrations from the ancient pool’s transportation from causing the plaster to peel off. The entire structure was reinforced with foam to allow it to safely withstand the lifting and the jolts along the journey.
But even after the mikveh was detached from the ground, the challenge was far from over.
Due to the distance between the crane's base and the mikveh, a crane with a lifting capacity of 300 tons was required to lift the 25-ton structure. The mikveh's unusual width, about 4 meters, also required the use of a wide-load transport vehicle.
Transporting the mikveh
Transporting the mikveh to the nearby Beit Guvrin storehouse became an operation in itself.
In order to transport the large, highly sensitive cargo, the road was closed to traffic, and escort vehicles drove in front of and behind the truck.
“Once you lift up a structure like this, there is no going back,” said Eyal Kaho, a senior conservator at the IAA who led the operation. “If it falls apart, we've lost the mikveh.”
“Therefore, every detail must be considered in advance. The day before an operation like this, you don't sleep. You're under pressure, because the responsibility is yours and there’s simply no price that can compensate for mistakes. Even after 36 years at the Israel Antiquities Authority, every time, the adrenaline rises anew.”
Once construction in Carmei Gat is completed, the mikveh will be returned to the site where it was found. It will be integrated into an open public space at the heart of the new neighborhood.
Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu (Otzma Yehudit) noted that the discovery of the mikveh in Kiryat Gat adds an “important dimension to our understanding of Jewish settlement in the Land of Israel during the Second Temple period.”
He explained that the IAA’s operation reflects Israel’s national commitment to preserving its heritage amid its rapid development.
“Its future incorporation into the neighborhood’s public space will enable residents and visitors to encounter tangible evidence of Jewish life from 2,000 years ago as part of their daily lives.”

The defense believes that since the suspicion against Kryvonos was recognized as invalid due to procedural violations, an identical approach must be applied to Poroshenko's suspicion in the coal case. A corresponding motion has been submitted to a panel of judges at Shevchenkivsky District Court of Kyiv.

ETH researcher among favourites for Nobel Prize in physics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:48:50 UTC
17:48:50 KST

ETH researcher among favourites for Nobel Prize in physics
In just over two weeks’ time, the 2026 Nobel Prizes will be announced in Stockholm. The identities of the winners remain a closely guarded secret right up until the last moment. Nevertheless, there is already a flurry of speculation. A Swiss-British researcher is also being tipped as a possible laureate.
Nicola Spaldin, a professor at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology ETH Zurich, features on the list of researchers of Nobel Prize calibre published on Thursday by the British-American data firm Clarivate.
The names of those nominated for a Nobel Prize are, as a rule, kept secret for 50 years. No information about the committees’ deliberations are made public. The laureates are only informed immediately before the official announcements. It is therefore difficult to predict who might win a prize.
+ British researcher wins top Swiss science award
The list of Nobel Prize contenders compiled annually by Clarivate is based on the impact their work has had within the scientific community – in other words, on how often their academic articles have been cited by other scientists.
Novel materials
Clarivate considers ETH researcher Spaldin to be a potential Nobel Prize candidate in the field of physics. This is due to her theoretical work on so-called magnetoelectric multiferroics.
These are materials that can be influenced by both magnetic and electric fields. This makes them of interest for applications such as energy-efficient data storage or high-precision magnetic field sensors. Spaldin laid the theoretical foundations for this class of materials.
In total, Clarivate has included 22 researchers on its list this year. Alongside Spaldin, those named come from the US, Canada, Denmark, Israel, Japan and China.
Success rate
Since 2002, Clarivate has honoured a total of 487 researchers as so-called “Citation Laureates”. Some 89 of them went on to win a Nobel Prize. This corresponds to a success rate of around 18%. Often, several years elapsed between inclusion on the list and the award of the Nobel Prize.
Clarivate, for example, predicted the Nobel Prize for the Swiss physicists Didier Queloz and Michel Mayor – albeit six years before they received it.
More
The Basel researcher whose work triggered a longevity revolution
Other researchers working at Swiss universities who have not yet received a Nobel Prize were also honoured as Citation Laureates in previous years. These include the chemist Michele Parrinello (Università della Svizzera italiana and ETH Zurich), the biochemist Michael N. Hall (University of Basel), the chemist Michael Grätzel (Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne – EPFL), the economist Ernst Fehr (University of Zurich), the physicist Daniel Loss (University of Basel) and the immunologist Andrea Ablasser (EPFL).
The Nobel Prizes in the sciences will kick off on October 5 with the Nobel Prize in Medicine. This will be followed on October 6 by the announcement of the Nobel laureates in Physics, and on October 7 by those in Chemistry.

‘Poor bear the impact’: Sugar prices soar in India, souring festive season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:46:11 UTC
17:46:11 KST

‘Poor bear the impact’: Sugar prices soar in India, souring festive season
India is one of the world’s largest sugar consumers, but usually produces even more. A crisis has flipped that equation — hitting sugarcane farmers and low-income consumers alike.
Jai Krishan, a 43-year-old labourer from Bihar in northern India, has saved 15,000 rupees ($160) to travel home from Indian-administered Kashmir, where he works, to celebrate Diwali with his family in November.
Each year, he buys boxes of sweets — laddu, barfi and kaju katli — to take home as gifts for his family and friends. He spends about $35 just on sweets for Diwali, he says, as he prepares afternoon tea for himself and his roommates in their rented accommodation in the Hawal area of Srinagar, Indian-administered Kashmir’s largest city.
“For someone from a lower-middle-class family, this is a lot of money. But Diwali is one of the most important festivals for Hindus and you cannot skip celebrating it,” he says.
This year, though, Krishan fears he may have to cut back on other purchases — such as toys and clothes — to keep his limited budget under control. The price of sugar has risen sharply in recent months, with retail prices reaching as high as 75 rupees ($0.79) per kilogramme (2.2 pounds) — up from 40 rupees in September 2025 — in some markets, raising concerns that the cost of sweets could also increase.
“I can reduce my spending on clothes or other things, but I cannot return home without bringing sweets for my family,” Krishan said.
The price rise comes as India enters its festival season. Celebrations begin in late August with festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi and Onam, before gathering pace in October and November with Navratri, Durga Puja, Dussehra and Diwali, popularly known as the festival of lights.
India’s sweets sector is worth more than $1.1bn, with peak festive sales accounting for more than 40 percent of annual revenue. Traditional sweets can contain 30 to 60 percent sugar by weight, making sugar a major ingredient. India is the world’s largest consumer and second-largest producer of sugar.
The country consumes between 29 million and 32 million metric tonnes of sugar each year, roughly 15 percent of global consumption. But it produces about 20 percent of the world’s sugar, second only to Brazil — an amount that means that the country usually has enough supplies of sugar for its needs, with some to spare for exports.
Not this year.
A rare sugar shortage
Sugar production, according to government data, is expected to be about 30.6 million tonnes in the current season, which runs from October 2025 to September 2026. This is 11 percent lower than the government’s earlier estimate of 34.3 million tonnes.
The government attributes the lower production mainly to a decline in sugarcane cultivation and lower rainfall during the El Nino weather pattern. It has also accused hoarders of storing extra sugar once the effects of El Nino became clear, to further tighten supplies in a bid to earn extra profits.
But Mukesh Chandra, a sugarcane farmer from Punjab, says several other factors have contributed to the fall in production and the rise in sugar prices.
He points to a shift by some farmers from sugarcane to other crops, high labour costs coupled with low returns from sugarcane farming, and the diversion of sugarcane to ethanol production as among those reasons.
“These factors have led to a decline in the amount of sugarcane available for processing, putting pressure on sugar supplies and pushing up prices,” Chandra told Al Jazeera. “Why would a farmer cultivate a product that is going to give him less returns?”
The Indian government, however, has rejected the claim that diverting sugarcane to ethanol production under its ethanol blending programme has contributed to the surge in sugar prices. It pointed to figures showing that the share of sugar diverted to ethanol has fallen from about 12 percent in 2022-23 to about 9 percent in 2025-26, with nearly three-quarters of India’s ethanol now made from grains such as maize.
India introduced ethanol blending to reduce its dependence on expensive crude oil imports, strengthen energy security and increase farmers’ incomes by creating a market for surplus crops. The initiative is also intended to reduce vehicle emissions and support the country’s broader decarbonisation goals.
Moving away from sugarcane
Regardless of the Indian government’s assertions, Chandra argues that the economic logic of sugarcane farming works against cultivators.
He estimates that producing 100kg of sugar costs about 470 rupees ($4.90), including expenses for labour, irrigation, cultivation and transportation, as well as the extraction of sugarcane juice and its processing into sugar. But the return is only about 416 rupees, leaving farmers with a loss of approximately 54 rupees per 100kg. He said sugarcane farmers also do not receive the same level of support available to farmers growing crops such as paddy — particularly with fertilisers, diesel and electricity.
The United States-Israeli war on Iran has also complicated economic equations for farmers, with fuel prices — and so, electricity costs — rising. The inflation due to the war “has added a further burden on our shoulders,” Chandra said. “The rise in fuel prices has increased the cost of running water pumps used to irrigate sugarcane fields, adding to farmers’ expenses at a time when their margins are already low.”
Suresh Pal, another sugarcane farmer from the state of Uttar Pradesh, agrees that sugarcane production is declining. He attributes the current shortage and price rise to a combination of agricultural and climate-related challenges faced by farmers in the state.
Farmers in Uttar Pradesh remain heavily dependent on the Co-0238 variety of sugarcane, which, Pal said, has become increasingly vulnerable to diseases such as red rot fungus and pest attacks. He added that continuous cultivation and the heavy use of chemicals have also contributed to soil degradation, while the crop’s high water requirements have put further pressure on the state’s groundwater resources.
“We are facing problems from many sides. The varieties we depend on are becoming vulnerable to diseases, the soil is losing its strength and water is becoming harder to manage,” Pal told Al Jazeera. “And at the same time, the cost of farming is increasing. Fertiliser, pesticides, labour and irrigation are all becoming expensive,” he added.
For small farmers, Pal believes, the financial strain is made worse by delayed payments from sugar mills, leaving them with little money to invest in better seeds, modern farming methods and new technologies. “When the mills delay our payments, how can a small farmer invest more in his fields?” Pal said. “Our costs keep rising, but the money we earn from farming is not increasing at the same pace. This is making it difficult for people like me to continue cultivating sugarcane.”
A Diwali that’s less sweet
To manage domestic supply, the government has authorised the duty-free import of one million tonnes of raw sugar, with a cap on rates, until October 31, 2026. The move is aimed at easing supply pressures ahead of the festival season.
“The measure is best understood as a price ceiling rather than a price cut,” said Sanjay Kumar, professor of economics at Delhi University. The government waived heavy import duties to allow the import of sugar at about $0.55 per kg. “That price now limits how high domestic sugar can go, because once imported sugar is cheaper, no mill can hold its own price above the landed cost for long,” Kumar added.
But so far, that strategy doesn’t seem to be working.
That, Kumar said, is because the imports are of raw sugar; the domestic Indian market demand is primarily for refined sugar.
Aman Jaswal, a resident of Patna in Bihar, said sweets were costing 15 to 20 percent more this year. “Sweets are closely tied to happiness in Indian culture. Whether it is Diwali, a wedding or a religious occasion, we rarely celebrate without them,” Jaswal said. “Even prasad [the sweets offered during religious rituals] is shared among people. Gifting sweets is a way of sharing happiness and it has become part of our celebrations and relationships.”
Back in Srinagar, Krishan, the labourer, has already started thinking about what he can sacrifice this year to be able to afford sweets for his family back home.
He has taken to walking to work, instead of taking public transport.
“My workplace is about eight kilometres from my room but I walk to save 50 rupees ($0.52) a day for the happiness of my family,” he said. “What difference does it make to the rich? They will celebrate the festival with great pomp and show anyway. It is poor people like me who will bear the impact.”

Trade between India and Russia reached a record $68.7 billion last year.

One dead after torrential rain and flash floods hit Barcelona region
- Published
North-eastern Spain has been hit by torrential rain and flash floods, leaving one person dead and causing widespread disruption across the region.
Spain's national weather agency AEMET issued warnings for heavy rain across eastern regions on Wednesday, including a red alert for Barcelona's coastline.
Rescuers recovered the body of a man on Thursday in Olivella, around 40km (25 miles) west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away by a stream, authorities said.
The deluge has disrupted travel across Catalonia and Valencia, with flights cancelled and roads submerged. Authorities have advised against unnecessary travel, while Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez warned of "very complicated situations".
Emergency services in Catalonia said they received more than 850 calls related to the downpours and catalogued over 500 incidents.
Catalan firefighters said on X on Thursday that they had recovered the "lifeless body of a man" in Olivella, correcting earlier reports that had identified the missing person as a woman.
Videos shared on social media showed partially submerged cars and rescue workers attempting to reach a vehicle trapped in a heavily flooded underpass.
In Barcelona, some metro stations were closed and buses diverted, while regional trains were disrupted and flights delayed or cancelled at El Prat airport.
Neighbouring Valencia had more than 70mm (2.76in) of rain fall in just half an hour in several municipalities, according to AVAMET.
"Rarely have we seen such rainfall accumulations in 30 minutes," the meteorological association said on X.
Emergency services reported 478 incidents in the Valencia province, mostly involving property damage, leaks and traffic disruption.
In the regional capital, all metro lines were suspended and the city's airport shuttered for several hours, causing flights to be diverted.
The downpour comes as Spain emerges from its hottest summer on record and an exceptionally warm start to September.
Scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the Mediterranean storms that typically hit eastern Spain in autumn.
The Mediterranean Sea absorbs heat during summer, increasing evaporation and contributing to heavier rainfall when storms develop.
The flooding comes less than two years after devastating flooding in Valencia killed more than 230 people.

Zelenskyy: Ukraine, Slovenia working on preparing Drone Deal
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:39:13 EEST
17:39:13 KST

Ukraine and Slovenia are currently working on preparing a Drone Deal, President Volodymyr Zelensky has reported following a meeting with Slovenian Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Tone Kajzer and Minister of Defense Valentin Hajdinjak, who are visiting Kyiv.
"Today in Kyiv, a government delegation from Slovenia together with representatives of leading companies. Met with Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Tone Kajzer together with Minister of Defense Valentin Hajdinjak. Our countries are working on preparing a Drone Deal, and we discussed the initial results and joint defense projects that we can implement," Zelensky wrote on his Telegram channel on Thursday.
According to him, during the meeting they discussed at length Ukraine's future in a united Europe, regional security, and constant Russian attacks.
"I thanked for Slovenia's contribution to PURL of $50 million and all support. And we are very grateful for such respect for all our people and for our soldiers who gave their lives defending Ukraine and all of Europe. Today we together honored their memory with a minute of silence," Zelensky wrote.
The Drone Deal is a multi-year international cooperation program initiated by Ukraine, aimed at comprehensive interaction in the security and defense sphere. It unites Ukrainian combat expertise, supply chains, and defense-industrial cooperation.
The Drone Deal can include a range of projects depending on specific partner requests, such as air defense development, scaling of drone technologies, training programs, and defense-industrial production. The entire system is built on Ukrainian combat experience.
The 10-year format of agreements allows for building a more flexible yet stable partnership. These arrangements are designed for a long-term period and create the basis for stable financing of cooperation.
The program is aimed at large-scale export of Ukrainian defense technologies, attracting foreign investment, and joint production of unmanned and anti-drone systems tested in real combat conditions. The National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (NSDC) serves as the coordinator of this program.
Prior to the full-scale war, Ukraine prohibited the export of its own weapons, but the Drone Deal format officially opened this possibility during martial law. The main idea is that Ukraine offers Western partners and other states its unique combat experience and technologies, receiving in exchange financing and access to foreign production capacities. Each agreement is adapted to the specific needs of the partner country.

Pakistan army chief urges Iran to persuade Houthis not to target Saudi energy facilities: Sources

17:38:46 KST

Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir has urged Iran to persuade Yemen's Houthi group not to target Saudi Arabia's energy facilities, Pakistani government sources told Anadolu on Thursday.
In Islamabad's latest attempt to bring a negotiated settlement to the raging Middle East conflict, Munir spoke to Iran's top diplomat Abbas Araghchi over the phone, urging Tehran to "use its influence" on Houthis to halt their strikes on Saudi oil and economic infrastructure, the sources added.
The two spoke during Araghchi's visit to China on Wednesday, Iranian state media confirmed.
"The army chief discussed the overall regional situation, with special focus on Houthis' attacks and revival of stalled direct talks between the US and Iran," a source familiar with the developments said.
Islamabad has already warned that the recent escalations would further complicate the already complex regional scenario.
Describing Araghchi's response as "hopeful," the sources did not provide further details.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei recently stated that Tehran does not interfere in Yemeni affairs and described the Houthis as independent actors "pursuing their own interests."
The latest conversation comes a day after a Houthi drone was intercepted near the holy city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia, which invited ire from the international community, including Muslim countries. Houthis denied they launched the drone.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia last year inked a bilateral defense pact, which subsequently led to the signing of a trilateral Mecca defense agreement last month involving Türkiye.
Yemen has been gripped by war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.
The group has been engaged in renewed fighting with government forces since July, when it declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh, and has recently claimed advances along the Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis have also targeted the oil infrastructure of Saudi Arabia, which has further raised oil prices in the international market.
 
Committed to defense pacts, says Islamabad
Pakistan's Foreign Ministry Thursday reiterated its committment to “implementing” its bilateral defense agreement, as well as the trilateral Mecca pact.
“However, when, how, where and what force will be used against what objectives, in which modes and matters ... — operational confidentiality requires us to be discreet at this stage,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Sajjad Haider Khan told reporters in Islamabad.
He was responding to a question on whether “any mechanism had been devised as to how Pakistan will ensure that recent Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia are thwarted."
"Pakistan has for a long time ... shared the perspective that we would like to have peace and stability because this is not only in the interest of Pakistan and Iran, but also the entire region and beyond," said Khan, according to Dawn newspaper.
The situation in Bab al-Mandeb, he said, is “exceptionally serious," urging Houthis to “stop their activities.”
“In this regard, our discussions basically revolve around bringing peace and stability through dialogue and diplomacy and not through coercive measures,” he added.
 
Revival of stalled talks
Sources said that the Pakistani army chief and Iran's top diplomat also discussed ways to revive stalled direct talks with the US to end their months-long war.
Aragchi, for his part, said Iran is ready to return to negotiations as the US halts hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz and "abides by the Islamabad memorandum," the sources further said.
China is also assisting Pakistan's efforts to revive the US-Iran talks and stop the conflict from spilling over, they added.
"Beijing is equally worried about the raging hostilities because it's getting its oil bill heavier," a source said, without offering further details about China's assistance.
In his meeting with Araghchi in Beijing on Wednesday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi encouraged Iran and the US to remain rational, exercise restraint, return to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, and "engage in substantive consultations."
China "does not want to see regional tensions to spill over further into Yemen and the Red Sea," Wang added.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to meet his US counterpart Donald Trump in Washington, DC, next week, where the two sides are likely to discuss ways to resolve the lingering Middle East conflict, in addition to other pending issues between the world's two largest economies.
Pakistan has remained the main mediator between Iran and the US throughout the war that began on Feb. 28, and has maintained close contact with both sides.
The US and Iran signed the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding on June 17 and launched negotiations toward a final agreement. However, the talks later stalled over disagreements on security guarantees and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategic routes for global energy supplies and trade.
Between July 8 and July 24, the US and Iran exchanged military strikes, with Washington launching attacks on targets inside Iran, and Tehran responding by striking US military facilities and equipment in several Arab countries, including Jordan, Bahrain, and Kuwait.
After securing a ceasefire on April 8, Pakistan hosted the highest-level direct talks between the US and Iran since they broke diplomatic ties in 1979. The talks, held in Islamabad on April 11-12, ended inconclusively.
Since the war began on Feb. 28, more than 3,500 people, both civilians and soldiers, have been killed in Iran.
Tehran has hit US bases and assets in the Middle East, and the Pentagon has confirmed over a dozen fatalities, besides dozens of injuries to its personnel.

‘We left everything behind’: 125,000 people displaced as war reignites in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:37:15 UTC
17:37:15 KST

Abandoning their homes and cramming into cars, Yemeni families have fled in their thousands from a lightning advance along the Red Sea coastal plains and up the rugged hills towards the mountaintop city of Taiz as the war returned in dramatic form this month.
“We fled a large, comfortable home, and here we are struggling to find a plastic sheet and wooden poles,” said one of the displaced, Asma Taleb, a woman in her 50s who fled her home last week with her two sons and five grandchildren.
“This war doesn’t differentiate between people. Rich or poor, high class or low class, we all fled our homes on the same day and are all struggling now to find shelter.”
The family fled the Maqbanah district in the wide Taiz region and headed toward Al-Shimayateen District, arriving at a camp for displaced families where she has relatives. More than 100,000 people have fled their homes in the last month.
“The fighting was fierce in our village, and some of our civilian neighbours were killed or injured, so we fled home and left everything behind,” she told the Guardian. “Amid the fierce battles you forget everything. We left our home belongings, and one neighbour even left his livestock behind.”
As soon as Taleb arrived in the camp, she found three or four families living in every tent because newly displaced people were constantly arriving. Left with no other option, she moved in with a relative’s family and three others.
“On the first day, we were happy just to reach safety, but then we felt the suffering the next day. Displaced families kept arriving, and there was no space in the camp and not enough tents,” she added.
Some humanitarian organisations intervened, providing displaced families with canned food and hygiene kits.
Taleb said she had never left her village in her life except for brief emergencies, always returning in a day or two. This is the first time she has been forced to flee long-term, and she feels returning will be difficult.
“I dream of returning to my village today, before tomorrow, but it isn’t in my hands. The fighting is still ongoing, and more families are arriving every day.”
Renewed fighting in Yemen has displaced at least 125,000 people (about 18,000 households) since the start of September 2026, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha).
The International Organization for Migration said more than 2,000 people fleeing the hostilities have reached Djibouti’s northern shores so far, landing at scattered points along the coast near Obock.
Hatem Qasem, a farmer in his 40s from Al-Wazeyah district west of Taiz city, grew up in a village where residents rely on farming and raising livestock. He stated that when battles approached their village, they thought of nothing but their safety.
“We are farmers and rarely leave our village except for emergencies, but three days ago, the shelling and clashes were all around us, and we found ourselves in a position where we had to flee,” Qasem told the Guardian.
He explained that they sold their livestock at low prices simply to cover the cost of fleeing, as they could not take the livestock with them to an unknown destination.
“We took the children and left – around five families in one car. We couldn’t believe we managed to escape the fighting, but praise be to God, we made it,” he added.
They arrived in Al-Shimayateen district in Taiz. Although they do not have shelter there, it is a safe area where many displaced families have sought refuge.
“I am happy that we are safe now and that no one in the family was killed or injured, but we have started to realise that it will be difficult to stay here for long. We have no work here and no one to help us,” Qasem said.
According to Save the Children, at least 19 children were killed and a further 49 injured between 1 August and 9 September, bringing the total number of civilians killed in the escalating violence in Yemen to 117 and of those injured to 206. At least 175 were killed or injured in a single week (3-9 September), including 43 children, the highest weekly child casualty toll in the past 12 months.
With fierce fighting ongoing in Qasem’s village, returning home is not an option. To remain displaced, however, he needs a source of income to provide for his family.
“We will wait this month out here and see. If the fighting moves away from our village, we will return; if it continues, we will look for another solution.”
Qasem’s family of eight lives with three other displaced families in the same house – each family occupying a single room to share the cost of rent.
In Al-Safia makeshift camp, displaced people have no work and depend entirely on humanitarian organisations for their basic needs.
In 2026, an estimated 22.3 million people in Yemen – more than half the population – require humanitarian assistance and protection services, including 5.2 million displaced people, according to Ocha.
Ali Qaid, manager of the executive unit for Internationally Displaced People Camps Management in Taiz governorate, confirmed that some humanitarian organisations have begun providing aid to newly displaced families arriving in areas like Al-Shimayateen. However, he noted that many civilians remain trapped in active combat zones.
“Displacement from the western districts of Taiz governorate is still ongoing, and many people are trapped in the middle of the fighting, preventing humanitarian organisations from reaching them with assistance,” he told the Guardian.

Australia to restrict student, backpacker visas in migration clampdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:35:00 UTC
17:35:00 KST

Australia to cut student, backpacker visas in migration curb
September 17, 2026
Australia will cut migration by toughening visa rules for foreign students, backpackers and working holidaymakers, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Thursday.
Under the new rules, foreign students will no longer be allowed to bring partners and children to join them while they study in Australia, and people who overstay their working holiday visas will face tougher enforcement.
The government is also cracking down on so-called "visa hopping," where foreign migrants who are already in Australia move from one type of temporary visa to another to extend their stay.
"If you want to come on a temporary basis to Australia, apply for a temporary visa. If you want to come to Australia permanently, apply for a permanent visa. And if you no longer have a valid visa, you should leave Australia," Burke said.
What else did the Home Affairs Minister say about the migration reforms?
In remarks to the National Press Club in Canberra on Thursday, Burke insisted that immigration remains "fundamentally a strength" for Australia, but acknowledged that rules needed adjusting to ease pressure on housing.
"We need immigration to soften enough that housing has a chance to catch up," he said, while stressing the housing shortage was not caused by migrants.
Burke said it was "simply demonstrably wrong" that his ruling center-left Labor party was beefing up its visa rules as a response to a surge in the polls by the far-right One Nation.
This year, the group has become one of the country's most popular parties, campaigning on pledges to slash migration to the country as part of its "Australia First" approach, which has drawn similarities to US President Donald Trump.
The hard-right party said this week that it would cut the number of temporary migrants by 750,000 over the next three years to give Australians "breathing space."
The cost of living and immigration have ranked as some of voters' most pressing concerns in recent polls.
What is the migration situation in Australia?
The changes are set to see net annual migration fall from the current 300,000 to around 225,000 by 2028. That would see numbers return to the levels before the Covid-19 pandemic.
Annual migration surged to its highest level of 538,000 in 2022, after borders reopened.
Data on Thursday showed that migration numbers had declined to 292,100 in the year to March, 47% below the peak following the pandemic, Burke said.
Students make up the biggest immigrant group: some 753,000 foreign students live in Australia, most of whom come from China and India.
The reforms will see Australia return to its policy of a decade earlier when those who overstayed were given two weeks to leave the country or face detention and deportation, the minister said.
People seeking to extend their working holiday visas in rural areas will enter a ballot for a second or third year.
Applicants with skills in construction and housing will be prioritized for visas, Burke said.
Relatives of visa holders wanting to visit the country will have "no further stay" conditions applied to their visas.

Mark Carney addressed the European Parliament a day after Ursula von der Leyen’s surprise proposal to make Canada the EU’s first “associate member” left capitals scrambling.
Questions remain on what the new status would mean, how it would differ from existing partnerships — and how it will all go down with Washington, after Donald Trump threatened “serious tariffs” on Europe if it followed through.

Türkiye expands measures to contain fund market strains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:31:43 UTC
17:31:43 KST

Türkiye has expanded measures to address payment problems in the fund market, suspending trading in funds run by seven asset managers on its electronic fund platform while the Central Bank increased liquidity support following a sharp stock market sell-off.
The Capital Markets Board (SPK) ordered a halt to purchases and sales on TEFAS, Türkiye’s electronic fund trading platform, for all funds established by Tera Portföy, Pusula Portföy, Hedef Portföy, Atlas Portföy, A1 Portföy, Pardus Portföy and Bulls Portföy that trade on the platform.
The board also ordered the liquidation of specified funds established by these companies, under procedures it would determine.
In a separate measure, the SPK allowed brokers to lower the minimum maintenance margin for securities bought on credit from 35 percent to 20 percent. Brokers may apply the lower requirement in line with their risk policies, taking client requests into account.
The temporary arrangement runs through the close of trading on Oct. 2, subject to further announcements by the board.
The measures followed a Sept. 17 meeting of the Financial Stability Committee, chaired by Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek. The committee described the fund market problems as “temporary and manageable” and pledged swift action to ease the liquidity squeeze and prevent contagion.
In a statement released by the Treasury and Finance Ministry, it attributed market volatility to credit and liquidity problems at some funds managed by a limited number of portfolio management companies.
It said there was no fundamental or structural risk to the functioning of Borsa Istanbul or the capital markets, with the difficulties concentrated in a particular segment of the fund market.
The Central Bank announced that it would increase funding through one-week repo auctions, taking liquidity conditions into account. It subsequently opened a 300 billion Turkish Lira auction on Sept. 17, up from 1 billion liras the previous day, Bloomberg HT reported.
The bank also said it would update banks’ borrowing limits in its Interbank Money Market to reflect the banking system’s current balance-sheet size. Bloomberg HT, citing sources, reported that those limits had been increased tenfold to 510 billion liras.
The Central Bank will also reduce collateral haircuts in its markets, allowing banks to borrow more against eligible assets.
The benchmark BIST 100 index fell 5.54 percent to 13,122.58 on Sept. 16. It opened 1.32 percent lower the following day but reversed those losses, trading more than 2 percent higher by 10:28 a.m., according to Bloomberg HT.
Fund disclosures had outlined the payment difficulties. Pusula Portföy announced on Sept. 15 that some funds it managed had defaulted on payments to investors seeking to redeem their holdings.
Tera Portföy subsequently reported redemption payment defaults in its lira money market fund and an equity fund. Tera Holding Chairman Emre Tezmen described the difficulties at certain funds as a temporary liquidity shortage and said group companies continued to operate.
Atlas Portföy said on Sept. 17 that redemption payments at its PSE money market fund were delayed while it worked to strengthen the fund’s liquidity.
The Financial Stability Committee said regulators would continue to act against those found to have engaged in market-disrupting activity. The Central Bank said it would monitor liquidity conditions closely and take further measures if needed.

Russia’s Su-57 skips external fuel tanks for Egypt flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:29:06 UTC
17:29:06 KST

Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation said its Su-57 stealth fighter flew to an air show in Egypt this month using fuel tanks built into its internal weapons bays instead of the external drop tanks fighters typically carry on long ferry flights.
UAC said the aircraft made the trip to the El Alamein International Airshow with one intermediate stop, and still had enough fuel for another 1,000 km (620 miles) after landing. That reserve let the jet fly a demonstration flight the following day, which UAC and Rostec, the state conglomerate that owns UAC, described as comparable in fuel use to a full air combat sortie.
External tanks are standard on most fighters for long ferry flights, but they add drag and increase an aircraft’s radar signature, working against the low-observable shaping that defines a stealth design. Using internal tanks instead lets the Su-57 stretch its range without that tradeoff.
“The ability to use insert fuel tanks inside the weapons bays instead of external suspensions fully corresponds to the fifth-generation aircraft concept,” Rostec said in a statement. “This solution preserves the aircraft’s aerodynamics and provides a significant ferry range reserve. The flight showed that among tactical aircraft, the Su-57E is unmatched in combat radius and time aloft.”
The Su-57E is the export version of Russia’s Su-57 fighter, built with low observability, high maneuverability and a wide range of compatible weapons, according to UAC. The company says deliveries to foreign customers are already underway, though it has not named which countries have received aircraft or in what numbers.
The jet has appeared at a string of international air shows over the past two years, including Zhuhai in China in November 2024, Aero India in February 2025, and the Dubai Airshow that November, where a Su-57E carrying the tail number 509 was on static display. This year’s El Alamein show, running Sept. 8-10 at El Alamein International Airport on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast, was the aircraft’s second appearance in the country after the inaugural edition in 2024.
The Russian jet shared the ramp at El Alamein with U.S. Air Force and Texas Air National Guard aircraft, including C-130J and C-130H transports, A-10 attack jets, F-16s and F-15Es, along with a Chinese contingent of fighters, tankers and airborne early warning aircraft. Organizers billed the event as trade-only, open to approved business and government visitors rather than the public, with Egypt’s Ministry of Defense, Air Force and Ministry of Civil Aviation backing the show.

Independent Journalism Is Critical For European Resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:29:00 UTC
17:29:00 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen delivered the EU’s annual state of the union address on Wednesday, calling for the robust defense of European values and warning of the dangers of cognitive warfare, foreign propaganda, and disinformation powered by viral deepfakes.
Shaped by social media algorithms and surging AI, the integrity of Europe’s information space has become a core security and economic concern as foreign adversaries and extremists seek to paralyze democracies. Von der Leyen promised to respond by toughening sanctions enforcement and putting more funds towards promoting the rule of law.
Europe is right to treat these issues as a high-stakes, generation-defining challenge. But there was a key omission in her speech: Independent journalism is a precondition for democratic resilience, and supporting it must remain a priority for the EU. Journalism exposes the inner workings of the threats facing our institutions, and populates our public spaces with reliable, factual, nuanced information. It is the most durable answer Europe has to the disinformation and foreign interference the President warned against. Only an informed public can make free choices.
While media freedom is folded into the EU’s broader Democracy Shield and rule of law frameworks, journalism lacks protection as the distinct, load-bearing pillar of democratic resilience that it is. In the face of rising attacks, Europe needs more explicit prioritization of financial support and protections for journalists.
It’s not hard to find real-world examples of why this is so important. OCCRP’s cross-border reporting often generates valuable findings for over-stretched enforcement agencies that struggle to work across borders. Our recent investigations have exposed scam networks with tens of thousands of European victims, and revealed cognitive warfare operations deployed by the Kremlin in European capitals. We have also helped identify war criminals torturing Ukrainian prisoners, and mapped the trade routes through which European materials continue to strengthen the Russian war machine. We don’t have numbers for the whole industry, but our reporting alone has triggered 477 government investigations and 842 arrests or indictments since 2009.
President von der Leyen rightly lauded the recent Hungarian elections as a sign of hope. In that contest, Hungarians reacted in part to the long record of corruption racked up by Viktor Orban and his cronies. How did they know about that? In large part thanks to the intrepid reporting of independent journalists, including OCCRP partners Direkt36 and Átlátszó. In Lithuania, investigative reporting led to a powerful demonstration of democratic accountability this year, with a prime minister stepping down amid an integrity scandal. In the EU’s neighbors, the students who mobilized nationwide protests in Serbia were also empowered by journalists’ findings, while journalists in Ukraine have held the government to account and prompted it to act on corruption allegations.
We know that the European Commission values journalism, as evidenced by initiatives like the European Media Freedom Act and enhanced anti-SLAPP rules.
But its support must outpace the rising threats in their physical, legal, digital and reputational forms. OCCRP alone faces 80+ lawsuits, and is fending off unprecedented DDoS attacks on its web infrastructure and AI-enabled takedown requests by PR firms hired by wealthy targets of our reporting. Our partners in Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan face false charges and prison terms. Within EU institutions and beyond, extremist groups are villainizing the media, leading to smear attacks and online hate. The recent verdict in the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trial in Malta is a grim reminder of the pushback journalists can face when they report on politicians, crime bosses, tech oligarchs, and other power brokers.
Funding, meanwhile, is in short supply. Last year, President von der Leyen called for stepping up where others have stepped back. The funding crisis is especially urgent for nonprofit media. OCCRP and our network of 40+ European news outlets have been badly affected by the changing landscape in media funding, including the loss of an estimated $1.7 billion in U.S. funding for freedom-of-expression programs. While the EU funds journalism through several channels, what outlets still lack is sustained support for reporting on big, complex threats to democracy.
Now is the time for the EU to take a stand: prioritize journalism as a pillar of democratic resilience; bolster multi-year support for investigative reporting; and fortify the conditions in which these journalists work.
Journalists have proven their ability to counter the leading threats to Europe’s security. Their role in achieving President von der Leyen’s “strong and independent Europe” is more than symbolic. You cannot win a battle of narratives when the infrastructure that provides citizens with reliable information is crumbling beneath your feet.

UN says US strikes in Iran were war crimes, Tehran crackdown crimes against humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:26:58 UTC
17:26:58 KST

A United Nations fact-finding mission said Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe U.S. forces were responsible for deadly strikes on a school and a sports facility in Iran in February, concluding that the attacks amounted to war crimes.
In the same report, the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their crackdown on nationwide anti-government protests that began in late December.
The mission, whose mandate includes investigating serious human rights violations in Iran and preserving evidence for potential legal proceedings, is due to present its findings to the UN Human Rights Council during its September-October session.
Deadly strike on Minab school
The investigators said they had reasonable grounds to believe U.S. forces carried out the attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab, where Iranian authorities said more than 150 people were killed, including about 120 schoolchildren.
UN investigators had opened an inquiry into the strike in March after U.S. military investigators concluded preliminarily that American forces were likely responsible, although the Pentagon had not reached a final determination.
The fact-finding mission concluded that the attack was indiscriminate, caused civilian deaths and damaged civilian infrastructure, and therefore amounted to a war crime.
According to the report, the U.S. relied on intelligence indicating that a senior Iranian military commander was at the site but failed to sufficiently verify that information before launching the strike.
Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm that the building remained a military objective went beyond simple negligence.
“Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen,” the report said.
UN experts had previously described the Minab school as a protected civilian object and called for an independent investigation, saying attacks on civilian schools can constitute war crimes unless the facilities have become military objectives.
President Donald Trump said in June that “nobody” had intentionally attacked a girls’ school in Iran, citing an investigation into the incident. The Pentagon later elevated its inquiry but has not publicly released preliminary findings.
The UN mission said it found no evidence that the school was being used for military purposes.
Second strike in Lamerd
Investigators reached a similar conclusion about a U.S. strike on a sports center in Lamerd.
According to the report, the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school, killing and wounding 22 civilians. The mission concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore also constituted a war crime.
U.S. Central Command said in March that American forces had not carried out any strikes in Lamerd that day.
The findings come as the UN mission continues to warn about civilian casualties from the ongoing conflict. Earlier this week, it called on all sides to comply with international law after additional U.S. strikes in southern Iran reportedly killed civilians, stressing that parties must distinguish between military and civilian targets and take precautions to minimize civilian harm.
Iran accused of crimes against humanity
The report also examined Tehran’s response to the mass protests that erupted in late December.
Investigators concluded that Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack on civilians involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
The mission said it could not independently establish the full number of casualties but believed the toll was substantially higher than official Iranian figures of 3,038 people killed and 25,000 injured.
Iran has blamed the unrest on “terrorists and rioters” backed by exiled opponents and foreign powers, including the United States and Israel, and has repeatedly rejected allegations of systematic human rights abuses.
The UN investigators said the crackdown represented a significant escalation from previous patterns of repression, citing the scale of violence, killings, internet restrictions and use of the death penalty.
The Human Rights Council expanded the mission’s mandate in January to urgently investigate alleged violations linked to the protests that began on Dec. 28, 2025, including for possible use in future legal proceedings.

Electric cars’ market share in Europe tops 30% in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:26:46 UTC
17:26:46 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Battery-electric vehicles accounted for more than 30% of new car registrations across key European markets in August, according to an industry report released Thursday.
A total of 202,833 new battery-electric vehicles (BEVs) were registered across 16 European markets during the month, marking an annual increase of 54.2%, according to a monthly bulletin prepared by Brussels-based E-Mobility Europe and independent transport research organization New AutoMotive.
BEVs represented 30.5% of all new car registrations in the markets covered, while their estimated share across the EU reached 31.2%.
During the January-August period, BEV registrations increased 33.1% year-on-year to 1.67 million. Their market share over the eight-month period stood at 22.5%.
Germany and France led the expansion in Europe’s electric vehicle market.
France registered 36,159 fully electric cars in August, with their market share reaching 38.3%. Registrations rose 72.2% from a year earlier.
Germany recorded 68,980 BEV registrations, giving fully electric cars a market share of 32.5%. Registrations increased 34.5% year-on-year.
BEVs accounted for 98.7% of new car registrations in Norway, 85.9% in Denmark, 52.3% in Finland and 48.9% in the Netherlands.
Belgium followed with a 46.2% share, while electric cars accounted for 36.1% of registrations in Portugal.
The report covers Belgium, Czechia, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and Switzerland.
Together, these markets represent approximately 90% of the combined EU and European Free Trade Association car market.
