EU announces plan to restrict social media access for children
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:25:26 BST
17:25:26 KST

EU announces plan to restrict social media access for under-15s
- Published
The EU has announced plans to restrict social media access for under-15s across its member states, in a bid to increase wellbeing and tackle online safety.
Under the plans, there would be a gradual approach to children using social media which would include banning under 13s from accessing platforms.
Those aged 13 to 15 would only be able to access platforms for an hour per day via "mini accounts" set up through their parent or guardian's social media account.
The European Commission said social media companies would need to prove platforms were safe by design or face fines of up to 6% of their global sales. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the move would "put parents back in the driving seat".
She added the legislation - called the EU Kids Act - would give parents "the tools to help their children navigate a safer world".
The restrictions would not just affect well-known apps such as TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat but also YouTube and other video sharing platforms as well as AI chatbots and online games.
"Too many children are being exposed too early to an online world they are not ready to navigate - an environment where bullying can follow you home, where every mistake can be recorded forever," von der Leyen said.
Under the act, only children aged 15 and over would be able to set up their own social media accounts.
But von der Leyen told the EU Parliament on Thursday that "an age limit does not mean letting tech companies off the hook for the content on the platform".
She added that under the legislation - if it is approved - companies would be required to submit detailed child safety plans.
"For every person under 18, the platforms must follow the principle of safety by design, no toxic or addictive features, no traps, etc," she said.
Some individual EU countries have already announced their own plans to restrict social media for children, including France and Spain.
The proposed EU-wide legislation would supersede those, and member states will not be able to opt out from what would be a legally binding regulation.
It is understood the Commission has warned some member states they would need to repeal any national laws passed before the EU Kids Act comes into effect.
The new plans need to be agreed by EU member states and approved by the European Parliament.
Already there are questions about how this EU-wide legislation would be enforced and the plans are likely to face opposition in the months to come.
France provides an indication of how the path ahead could be bumpy as individual member states may try to strengthen or weaken the proposals.
The Macron government drew up legislation for a ban on social media for under-15s but last month the country's top court blocked it, ruling that it infringed upon freedom of expression.
French ministers have now amended their original plans.
Some critics of social media bans for children cite privacy concerns.
They worry about teenagers being forced to submit personal information as they go through an age verification process to prove they are old enough to access platforms.
The Commission has said age would be verified using the EU's preexisting age verification app, and no personal data would be collected or shared.
Social media companies will also make their position on the restrictions clear as the act is debated in the months to come.
Von der Leyen had previously proposed a social media "delay" for children in Europe, saying in May that "the discussion about a minimum age for social media can no longer be ignored".
The policy, formally outlined on Thursday, was also trailed in the EU chief's annual address on Wednesday.
In July, the EU said Meta must change the "addictive" design of Facebook and Instagram or face a heavy fine.
In preliminary findings, the European Commission said features such as infinite scroll, autoplaying videos and personalised recommendations could encourage "compulsive use", particularly among children and teens.
A spokesperson for the tech giant told the BBC it disagreed with the findings "which don't accurately take into account the significant steps we've taken to protect teens".
In a separate case, Meta agreed in August to a $18bn (£13.3bn) settlement with US states and territories to resolve claims that Facebook and Instagram harmed children. It denied any wrongdoing as part of the settlement.
The European Commission said its proposed legislation built on findings, external from its special panel on child safety online, which recommended age-appropriate regulation for children, with different guidance for each age group.
It also cited recent EU survey data, external, which found 92% of respondents considered the need to strengthen children's protection online as a top policy priority.
Von der Leyen said the Commission had "looked at Australia" - which banned social media platforms for under-16s last year - when putting together the proposal.
The ban has been difficult for the country to enforce, with its Communications Minister Anika Wells admitting earlier this month that so far no tech firm had been fined despite research showing many under-16s were still on platforms.
A similar ban for under-16s is set to come into force in the UK in spring next year.

Update: Watchdog raises questions about new chief prosecutor's asset declarations
Editor's note: this story is being updated.
President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sept. 17 appointed Anton Kovalsky, chief prosecutor of Khmelnytsky Oblast, as acting prosecutor general.
Ukraine's previous prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, was fired by parliament on Sept. 15 amid a major corruption scandal.
Media reports suggest Kovalsky could ultimately be appointed prosecutor general, rather than merely serving in an acting capacity.
The media outlet Ukrainska Pravda reported on Sept. 15 that, according to its sources, Kovalsky was the leading candidate for prosecutor general.
Another candidate for the job is Valeriy Prykhozhanov, chief prosecutor of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
Kovalsky was born in Vinnytsia in 1984 and has served in the prosecution service since 2011.
Previously he was a deputy chief prosecutor of Vinnytsia Oblast from 2020 to 2021 and the chief prosecutor of Chernivtsi Oblast from 2021 to 2025.
Kovalsky's wife registered as a businesswoman in 2023 and earned Hr 5.2 million ($120,000) during her first year in business selling sports nutrition products, the Anti-Corruption Action Center reported on Sept. 17.
"Given the nature of the business, such a high level of income for his wife at the very start of her business career raises questions," the watchdog said.
Some Ukrainian officials' wives register businesses that serve as a front for their husbands' illicit income.
Since 2018, Kovalsky and his family have used a 79-square-meter apartment in Vinnytsia registered in his mother’s name, the Anti-Corruption Action Center said.
There are questions about where his mother, who worked at a psychiatric hospital, obtained the money to buy the apartment, the watchdog added.
Her pre-tax income amounted to Hr 51,000 in 2019, Hr 72,000 in 2020, and Hr 122,500 in 2021, and she reported no savings, according to the Anti-Corruption Action Center.
One of Kovalsky's deputies at the Khmelnytsky Oblast prosecutor's office, Maksym Kuterha, has a controversial reputation.
He failed to pass vetting and was fired from the prosecution service in 2019, later worked at the Economic Security Bureau and was appointed as a deputy of Kovalsky in 2025.
In 2024 Kuterha and his wife acquired assets worth $325,000, according to the Anti-Corruption Action Center. Kuterha’s father-in-law was charged by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU), fled to Russia, and was sentenced in absentia to eight years in prison for collaboration, according to the watchdog.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from Kovalsky and Kuterha and will publish their responses once they are received.
The personal office of Kravchenko, the previous prosecutor general, was searched by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau in early September as part of a large-scale corruption investigation into an alleged scam call center protection racket run from the Prosecutor General's Office.
Within the investigation, a top prosecutor described as a “confidant” of Kravchenko was charged. Publicly revealed evidence hints at Kravchenko being implicated, and he submitted his resignation on Sept. 7.
In a bizarre twist, Kravchenko left Ukraine early on Sept. 14, under the pretext of an official trip to a conference in Paris. But the organizers told the Kyiv Independent that they had not expected him to attend, strengthening the suspicions that the trip was a fig leaf for fleeing Ukraine to avoid potential charges.
Simultaneously with leaving Ukraine, Kravchenko approved charges against the head of the anti-corruption agency investigating him.
The charges against Semen Kryvonos, head of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau, and an unnamed “close associate” of Oleksandr Klymenko, chief of the Special Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), were seen by many as a petty vendetta rather than pursuit of justice.
The charges were canceled by the Prosecutor General's Office late on Sept. 14, and Kravchenko was dismissed by parliament the next day.

Türkiye sees over 127,000 home sales in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:18:59 UTC
17:18:59 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Türkiye recorded 127,410 home sales in August, down 14.7% from the same month last year, official data showed Thursday.
According to the Turkish Statistical Institute (TurkStat), sales of new homes declined 4.5% year-on-year to 44,378, accounting for 34.8% of total transactions.
Istanbul recorded the highest number of house sales among Türkiye’s provinces with 20,426, followed by the capital Ankara with 10,851 and the western province of Izmir with 6,532.
Sales of existing homes dropped 19.4% to 83,032, representing 65.2% of the total.
Mortgaged-financed home sales, however, rose 7.2% from a year earlier to 22,131, making up 17.4% of all sales. Other home sales fell 18.3% to 105,279.
In seasonally and calendar-adjusted terms, sales of new homes increased 3.5% and sales of existing homes rose 0.7% from July.
During the January-August period, total home sales decreased 6.8% year-on-year to 950,529.
Mortgage-financed sales increased 27.6% to 188,813 during the eight-month period, while other sales declined 12.7% to 761,716.
Sales to foreign buyers edged up 0.1% year-on-year to 1,938 in August, accounting for 1.5% of total home sales.
Russian citizens purchased the most homes with 343 transactions, followed by Ukrainians with 147 and Iranians with 140.
In January-August, house sales to foreigners fell 6.3% from a year earlier to 13,141.

Environment Minister Carsten Schneider spoke at the inauguration ceremony in Hamburg for Germany's largest offshore wind park to date on Thursday.
Windpark He Dreiht off the Germany's northern Baltic coast incorporates 64 wind turbines, which can in theory provide roughly 1.1 million households with electricity.
Schneider called the opening of the facility good news for Germany as an industial producers. He said that renewable energies were not just the most environmentally friendly, but nowadays "also the cheapest and most secure way to generate electricity."
He said the construction was "economic common sense" given the billions Germany currently pays for fossil fuel imports.
"Therefore, the quicker we make ourselves independent and generate our power from our own local energy sources, the better," he said.
The offshore wind park lies around 85 kilometers northwest of Borkum and 110 kilometers west of Helgoland in the Baltic Sea. According to its owner, power company EnBW, the park should eventually account for almost 10% of Germany's offshore wind capacity in its own right.
EnBW said that it had not required any state subsidies to raised investments of around €2.4 billion (roughly $2.75 billion) for the project. The project will take some time to reach full capacity and output, as the individual turbines are being activiated and connected to the grid one by one.

Cologne police warn of WhatsApp 'ghost pairing' scam
Cologne police have issued a warning about a particular WhatsApp hacking tactic, saying they were issuing the alert "in light of recent events."
It said its criminal investigative unit, Kripo Köln, "is currently working on cases" involving what it called "ghost pairing."
Police said that criminals might first use a hacked WhatsApp account to pose as somebody's daughter, son, friend or acquaintance.
They would ask them to click on a link or scan a QR code and subsequently to confirm connecting a device. In what police said was a real-world example, scammers falsely claimed it was a vote for a friend's daughter that would give her a chance of winning free dance lessons.
"Someone who believes they are just taking part in a seemingly harmless vote is in fact linking their own WhatsApp account to the perpetrator's smartphone," police wrote. "This person can immediately not just read or delete any messages. They can also chat with contacts in the name of the unsuspecting victim — for instance asking them to transfer money. And all this, thile WhatsApp continues to operate entirely normally on the victim's phone. This is what makes the scam so hard to detect."
The solution, police said, was to be vigilant whenever asked to click on links or scan QR codes, even by known contacts — and even more so with requests to pair of link devices.
People who suspected they might have fallen prey could check easily in their own Whatsapp settings, by going to "Profile," then to "Linked devices" and unpairing any devices they did not recognize, police said.

It said many of the cuts were achieved by not renewing expiring contracts or not hiring to fill open positions, in a bid to minimize layoffs or redundancies.
It did not say how the losses were split between the two companies.
The German arm of the RTL Group — a Luxembourg-based company that broadcasts in a string of other European countries like Germany, France, Belgium and the Netherlands — acquired Sky Deutschland in a bid to strengthen its position in the streaming and sports markets in Germany.
It was already effectively competing with Sky in broadcasting sports like Formula 1 and football.

Heat and drought set to wither Germany's 2026 potato harvest
Extreme heat and drought over the summer will lead to a weak potato harvest in northwestern Europe for 2026, according to an analysis released on Thursday by the UK-based Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU).
In Germany, France, Belgium and the Netherlands the 2026 harvest is expected to fall a combined 3.1 million tons short of the five-year average harvest
The data shows the weak harvest will hit Germany particularly hard, with the country's share of the total expected potato harvest shortage coming in at 1,13 million tons.
These figures do not yet represent a final harvest report, but are an estimate.
"As fall begins, the effects of the record-breaking summer heat and drought on food and agriculture are becoming clear," said ECIU analyst Tom Lancaster.
Potatoes are among the crops in Europe that require the most water.
The analysis also reports a significant increase in prices. In Germany, spuds served at dinner are set to cost up to €280 per metric ton, compared to around €150 last year.
The expected 2026 harvest shortfall comes after oversupply in 2025 flooded the market.

Authorities advise mosquito protection amid malaria cases near Frankfurt Airport
Health authorities in Frankfurt are advising residents to consider taking precautions against mosquitoes after several recent malaria cases in the region believed to have been caused by the insects having stowed away on aircraft.
This week, two people living in the vicinity of Frankfurt Airport were reported to have contracted malaria.
In August, two Frankfurt Airport employees died after contracting malaria in an outbreak believed to have been caused by infected mosquitoes brought into Germany on an aircraft. Four other workers were infected, but recovered without complications.
The cases are part of a rare outbreak of so-called airport malaria, with the six employees infected despite not having traveled to a malaria-risk country. Authorities have not shared details about the two cases this week.
According to Germany's Robert Koch health institute, cases of airport malaria are extremely rare.
Data cited by DPA news agency shows that between 1969 and 2024, only 145 cases of locally contracted malaria were reported in Europe. At least 105 of those cases involved mosquitoes arriving on planes.
Most of these cases were in France, with only 9 reported in Germany in this time frame, making the 2026 outbreak a statistical outlier.
Malaria is native to tropical environments, and the vast majority of cases in Europe occur in summer.

Housing costs top young Israelis’ election concerns, security trails far behind - poll

2026-09-17

17:14:16 KST

Housing costs and other economic and social issues have emerged as the leading concerns among young Israelis ahead of the elections, while the security situation ranked far lower, according to a new Israel 2050 survey published Wednesday night.
The survey presented striking findings regarding the issues of greatest concern to young people in southern Israel. Rather than security, respondents placed economic and social issues at the top of their priorities, particularly their ability to establish themselves and build a stable future.
According to the findings, 75% said they would consider voting for a party they had not previously considered if it demonstrated the ability and courage to advance long-term solutions on issues important to them. Nineteen percent said they would do so without any reservations.
Housing prices were the most important issue for 38% of respondents when considering how to vote, more than twice the share for any other issue. Young respondents also gave the state particularly poor marks for its performance in this area, rating it just 2.5 out of 10.
After the cost of living, 16% said they were concerned about the state of the education system, while only 4% said the security situation was the issue carrying the greatest weight for them. Another 13% cited the situation facing young people in Israel, while 8% named transportation.
Low satisfaction across all areas surveyed
Politically, a majority of the young respondents, around 60%, defined themselves as belonging to the Right or center-Right. Just 7% identified themselves as left-wing voters, while the remainder were divided among the center-Left and center, with 6% saying they did not know where they stood politically.
Only 21% said they believe the government's current decisions are building a strong foundation for them for the decades ahead.
Forty-two percent said that leadership placing solutions in housing, transportation, and education at the top of its priorities would inspire the greatest sense of hope and optimism.
The findings also painted a similarly bleak picture when respondents were asked to rate the state's performance. Satisfaction stood below 4 out of 10 in each of the five areas examined.
The situation facing young people in Israel received a score of 3.9, while rehabilitation and strengthening of northern Israel received 3.8. The education system and transportation each received 3.5.
Housing receives lowest score in survey
Housing prices, however, received a score of just 2.5 out of 10, the lowest rating in the survey.
In effect, respondents gave the state a failing grade on every issue that most concerns them.
The dissatisfaction reflected in the survey relates not only to current conditions, but also to the state's ability to provide young people with a long-term economic and social future.
Only 21% said they believe government decisions currently being made are laying a strong foundation for their quality of life and the needs they will have in 20 to 30 years. By contrast, 41% said current decisions are doing so only to a small or very small extent.
Israel 2050 conducted the survey among a nationally representative sample of 409 people aged 18-35 from southern Israel.

NYT deletes line saying Israelis ‘view themselves’ as Oct. 7 victims, citing 'editing error'

The New York Times removed a sentence from an article on the Israeli documentary NAZA and added an editor’s note on Wednesday after acknowledging that the wording inadvertently suggested that Israelis’ status as victims of the October 7 massacre was a matter of perception.
The sentence appeared in a Monday article by NYT correspondent Isabel Kershner examining the backlash in Israel against NAZA, a documentary by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor that focuses on Palestinian civilian deaths during the war in Gaza.
The original version stated: “But Israelis still largely view themselves as the victims of Oct. 7.”
The sentence appeared immediately after a passage saying Israelis remained divided over responsibility for the political, military, and intelligence failures preceding the Hamas-led attack. The article then noted that around 1,200 people were killed in Israel and approximately 250 were taken hostage on October 7, 2023.
Following criticism of the wording, the NYT deleted the sentence and appended an editor’s note to the article.
“Because of an editing error, an earlier version of this article included a statement that was intended to convey Israelis’ perception of the government’s military response to the Oct. 7 terror attack in relation to the attacks, but inadvertently suggested that Israelis’ experience as terror victims was a matter of perception. It has been removed from the article,” the note said.
The NYT’s communications account also published the editor’s note on social media on Wednesday.
NYT under scrutiny after study shows anti-Israel bias
The paper recently faced renewed scrutiny of the newspaper’s coverage of Israel and the Gaza war. A peer-reviewed study published this month examined 1,559 NYT articles from the months following October 7 and argued that the newspaper’s coverage disproportionately framed Palestinians as victims and Israel as the aggressor.
The study’s findings and methodology have become part of a broader debate over how international media have covered the war. The study was detailed earlier this week.
The NYT’s editor’s note did not dispute that Israelis were victims of the October 7 attack. Instead, the newspaper said the deleted wording was meant to describe Israeli perceptions of the government’s military response to the attack, but was phrased in a way that conveyed a different meaning.
The corrected article remains online with the editor’s note attached.

That is a relatively small sum compared with the project's total investment of approximately $2 billion and the roughly 600,000-square-meter complex planned for the site.

Around it, a new district will be built in central Tbilisi, including luxury hotels, branded towers, a business center, and high-end retail space.

Benish founded the company in 2006 with Ilia Tsulaia and Irakli Kapianidze. The Israeli connection to the company, one of Georgia's dominant developers, was highlighted during the ceremony.

According to her, Georgia's economy grew at an average annual rate of 9.7% from 2021 through 2025, while growth was 7.9% in the first half of 2026.
The economy reached approximately $38 billion in 2025, GDP per capita stood at about $10,300, and foreign direct investment since 2021 totaled nearly $10 billion, she said.
According to Kvrivishvili, the real estate and construction sectors account for more than 15% of the country's economy.
Ilia Tsulaia, a founding partner of Archi and chairman of its supervisory board, described Trump Tower Tbilisi as "a bridge between today's reality and tomorrow's market" and a major step forward for Georgia's real estate sector.
For years, he said, developers were told that an international project on such a scale might be appropriate for Georgia in another five or 10 years.
"We could have waited another five or 10 years, but we decided that Georgia's and Tbilisi's time is now," he said.
Tsulaia also linked the decision to proceed with the project to the performance of the local economy and rising real estate prices.
According to him, the growth of the Georgian economy and the strengthening of the property market gave the partners the confidence to undertake a project of this scale.
He specifically thanked Israeli partner Benish, as well as Eric Trump. Tsulaia said Trump's enthusiasm for and confidence in Georgia during their first meeting were among the factors that pushed the partners the decide and sign the deal.
Tsulaia said the ambition was to place Tbilisi alongside cities where the Trump name has already become part of the skyline, including New York, Chicago, Las Vegas, and Miami.
The Trump brand has operated for decades in the luxury real estate market and appears on residential, hospitality, and golf projects in the US and other countries. Tbilisi marks the brand's first entry into the Caucasus.
Eric Trump, executive vice president of the Trump Organization and the son of US President Donald Trump, had been expected to travel to Tbilisi but ultimately did not attend in person.
Security considerations were cited as the reason.
Instead, he joined the event by video and answered questions prepared in advance.
Trump said that, from the Trump Organization's perspective, the Tbilisi project was based on three central conditions: the best location, the right partners, and the right timing.
He said the timing was directly connected to Georgia's current position, its rate of growth, and Tbilisi's development.
He said the initiative began with a meeting at Mar-a-Lago in Florida, where he met the developers and discussions about the project began.
Trump family compares Trump Tower in Tbilisi to New York City's
Trump compared the project with Trump Tower on Fifth Avenue in New York, one of the properties most closely identified with the family brand, saying the goal was to create an iconic building in Tbilisi that would likewise become identified with the city.
He noted that, symbolically, both are 65-story residential towers overlooking their respective city's Central Parks.
Trump also referred to his father, saying he had spoken with him about Georgia that morning.
According to Eric Trump, the president loves Georgia and the Georgian people and values relations between the two countries.
Eric Trump said there are already about 30 Trump-branded projects around the world, a figure he presented during the event, but repeatedly emphasized a special commitment to the new project.
The company's ambition, he said, was for it to be the best not only in Georgia, but by global standards.
Eric is the son of Donald Trump and his first wife, Ivana Trump, and the brother of Donald Trump Jr. and Ivanka Trump.
The president has two other children: Tiffany Trump, his daughter from his marriage to Marla Maples, and Barron Trump, his son with First Lady Melania Trump.
Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. currently play central roles in managing the Trump Organization's real estate and development businesses.
The organization was also represented at the event by Lawrence Jay Glick, executive vice president for development.
Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze, Invia founder and CEO Levan Pkhakadze, and Gensler's Robert Jackel also attended.
"We spent a long time looking for a brand, and we secured the most prestigious brand in residential real estate. It's an incredible achievement for the company and for me personally, as someone who was born here and can now bring this partnership, which is an important achievement for Georgia," Benish told Walla Money on Tuesday.
Benish said the project's American partners also chose the work with Gensler.
From their perspective, he said, architecture and planning are inseparable from the brand's standards and from the effort to place the tower alongside international luxury developments.
Benish presented Tbilisi as a market already attracting international investors and global brands, but one that, he said, still offers significantly lower entry prices than luxury markets such as Dubai.
According to him, prices for buyers in the Trump project are around $7,000 per square meter.
At that rate, a 50-square-meter apartment would cost about $350,000, and he estimated it could rent for about $2,000 to $2,500 per month.
After management fees, maintenance, and other expenses, he estimated an investor could be left with about $2,000 net per month, for an annual return of around 7%.
This is, of course, the developer's estimate and not a guaranteed return.
Benish compared that price with approximately $22,000 to $23,000 per square meter in branded luxury developments in Dubai.
In Tel Aviv, he said, prices can reach $50,000 per square meter or more, while Israel still has no comparable branded project.
In his view, that gap is central to Tbilisi's potential for appreciation.
Few locals, many foreign buyers
The tower's target market is expected to be distinctly international.
Benish estimates that only a small proportion of buyers will be local, while a significant share of demand will come from investors in the United Arab Emirates, Poland, the US, and Israel.
He estimates that Israelis could account for about 10% to 15% of buyers in the project. Archi is already highly familiar with that market.
Benish expects investors from the UAE to be among the largest buyer groups.
He said that one of the project's first buyers, a Jewish buyer from France, has already purchased two apartments in a deal worth approximately $1.8 million.
The Trump name carries significant weight in marketing the project.
The Trump Organization provides the name, brand, and standards, while the project's developers and partners carry out the development.
Trump representatives are involved in planning, branding, and setting standards, while members of the Trump family themselves promote the group's international real estate activity.
Archi does not operate only in the luxury market or in branded developments.
The company has operated in Georgia for two decades and develops residential, commercial, and lifestyle projects throughout the country.
In Tbilisi's Didi Dighomi neighborhood, for example, the company is building large-scale residential developments, including a complex of four buildings containing approximately 1,000 apartments.
The apartments begin at around 55 square meters, and Benish said prices in projects of this kind range from approximately $1,300 to $1,400 per square meter, less than one-fifth of the price in the Trump project.
Some apartments in those developments are rented by foreigners who relocated to Tbilisi.
The gap between $1,300 to $1,400 per square meter in Didi Dighomi and approximately $7,000 in Trump Tower illustrates the two ends of Archi's business: large-scale residential construction on one side, and branded luxury products aimed at international capital on the other.
Archi founding partner Meni Benish connects Israel, Georgia
Benish's own story connects Israel and Georgia.
He was born in Georgia and immigrated to Israel at age 10. He continues to work on Georgia-Israel relations and to leverage his dual national and bilingual background.
"Where I have a comparative advantage, where my money, knowledge, and experience are worth more, that is where I want to operate," he said.
Benish stressed that Israeli entrepreneurs who come to Georgia and try to run a business exactly as they are accustomed to doing in Israel may encounter difficulties.
According to him, the local business culture is different, and the ability to work with local partners and understand the mentality is critical.
Nevertheless, he recommends that Israelis consider business activity in the country, particularly in real estate.
In his view, the combination of economic growth, property prices that remain low relative to international markets, and the continued arrival of global brands represents an opportunity.
"I invite any Israeli to come consult with me and hear from the familiarity and experience I have accumulated. I have been doing this without compensation for years," he said.
For all those involved, including Benish, Tsulaia, and Archi, Trump Tower is not simply another project.
It is a test of whether Tbilisi can be repriced in the eyes of foreign investors and elevated from an emerging real estate market into the league of international luxury cities.
They are determined to pass that test with distinction.
Despite its name, Trump Tower Tbilisi is not owned by Donald Trump or the Trump Organization.
According to the legal disclaimer on the official website, Central Park Icon LLC owns and developed the property, while DT Marks Tbilisi LLC licensed the TRUMP name to the project.
Archi and Invia are the principal developers of the Downtown Tbilisi complex, and Trump Tower is being developed in cooperation with the Trump Organization.
For the Trump Organization, the project continues a model in which it expands its international activity primarily by licensing its brand to locally developed projects.
For the Georgian developers, the value of the Trump name is clear: attracting foreign buyers and bringing Tbilisi into the market for international luxury developments.
The project is being offered to buyers with 20% paid in cash followed by 60 interest-free, non-indexed installments, with a full bank guarantee.
In Georgia, the Trump Tower Tbilisi launch was met with considerable enthusiasm by media outlets aligned with the government, which presented the project as an expression of international confidence in the local economy and a new symbol of the capital's ambitions.
Independent and critical media, however, also highlighted the political dimension of the deal and the connection it creates between Georgia's leadership and the Trump family, alongside questions about who stands to benefit from it.
Some highlighted Benish's comments that only a minority of apartment buyers are expected to be Georgian and that the development is primarily aimed at an international clientele, raising a question alongside the official celebrations over the extent to which the luxury tower is actually intended for the local public.
The writer was a guest of Archi at the event.

Autonomous AI threats leave US and China minutes to prevent nuclear crisis, experts warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:14:08 UTC
17:14:08 KST

An AI system that interferes with a nuclear command network or launches a military cyber operation could leave Washington or Beijing with minutes to decide whether the other government attacked, according to US and Chinese security experts.
The experts, part of a US-China dialogue whose work helps inform official discussions, are urging both governments to prepare for such scenarios amid rising concerns about increasingly powerful and more autonomous systems.
Their proposals include red lines around nuclear systems, human control over consequential cyberattacks, and a hotline for incidents involving autonomous AI.
The recommendations were published last week ahead of planned government-level AI talks and an expected September 24 meeting in Washington between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Authors Melanie Sisson, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution think tank, and Tianjiao Jiang, an associate professor at Fudan University, participated in the US-China AI and national security dialogue convened since 2019 by Brookings and Tsinghua University's Center for International Security and Strategy.
Red lines around nuclear systems
Their proposals show how the US-China AI rivalry is moving beyond competition over chips and advanced models into questions long associated with arms control: how to prevent accidents from being mistaken for attacks, limit machine-made military decisions and set communication protocols for nuclear-armed rivals when technology behaves unexpectedly.
China's State Security Minister Chen Yixin this week wrote in a government outlet that AI "fundamentally transforms the form of military struggle." He said it had moved from playing a supporting role on the battlefield to a key role, citing AI-directed strikes in the US-Israeli war with Iran.
Brookings Institution's Sisson argued that humans should retain sole authority to initiate AI-enabled cyberattacks against the other country's nuclear command, control and communications systems or strategically important infrastructure.
An autonomous system could malfunction, exceed its instructions, or be compromised, while the country under attack might struggle to tell whether the action was accidental or ordered by its rival.
Fudan University's Jiang proposed explicit red lines preventing AI from independently deciding to use nuclear weapons or autonomously attacking nuclear command systems, along with protections around critical infrastructure including energy, finance and healthcare.
He also urged a shared definition of "meaningful human control" to prevent both countries from using identical language to justify different levels of machine autonomy.
The idea builds on a principle endorsed by then-US president Joe Biden and Xi in November 2024 that humans should retain control over decisions to use nuclear weapons.
Lora Saalman, an associate senior fellow at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, wrote in February that this was an important point of US-China convergence even as both countries showed signs of integrating AI more deeply into nuclear and nuclear-related systems.
When machines move faster than humans
Jiang also proposed a dedicated US-China military hotline for AI incidents, warning that automated cyber exchanges could escalate too quickly for human intervention.
One country's defensive AI might automatically respond to suspicious activity, while the other side could interpret that response as an attack and retaliate before understanding what actually happened.
A hotline could allow one government to tell the other that an unusual AI operation was accidental, unauthorized or still under investigation before it was treated as deliberate state action.
However, experts including Carla Freeman at Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies have questioned the utility of the existing US-China military crisis communication hotline, citing Chinese officials' refusal to answer US counterparts' calls about the "spy balloon incident" in February 2023.
The Chinese bureaucracy's rigid top-down hierarchy also disempowers low-ranking officers from taking the initiative during engagements with US counterparts, she wrote in an article for War on the Rocks in January.
"No one in the Chinese system wants to communicate with the United States until the top leadership in consultation with relevant actors within China's party-state have decided on a response, which may take days if not longer," she said.
Views in Washington and Beijing
Neither government has publicly endorsed the Brookings-Tsinghua proposals, but China has increasingly placed AI inside its existing arms-control bureaucracy.
AI is a formal portfolio of the Foreign Ministry's Department of Arms Control, which also handles nuclear weapons, non-proliferation, missiles and other international security issues.
Shen Jian, China's ambassador for disarmament affairs, told a UN meeting in Geneva in June that military AI could affect strategic stability and raise risks of miscalculation and conflict escalation, and that weapons should remain under human control. China also argues that AI safety should not become a pretext for technological barriers.
Washington has no equivalent single arms-control home for AI, with national security policy spread across the White House National Security Council, State Department, Pentagon and other agencies.
Both governments remain wary of measures that could slow their own technological development. Trump has warned broad restraints could hand China an advantage, while Beijing views many US technology controls as attempts to preserve American dominance.

NASA discovers huge 222-meter-diameter crater on Moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:13:57 UTC
17:13:57 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
NASA has discovered a huge new crater on the Moon measuring 222 meters (728 feet) across, larger than Rome’s Colosseum and the biggest contemporary impact crater observed to have formed anywhere in the Solar System, according to a study released Wednesday in the journal Science Advances.
The crater was created when an asteroid or comet fragment, estimated to have been roughly the size of a three- to six-story building, slammed into the lunar surface between April 11 and May 22, 2024. The impact occurred on the Moon’s near side and went unnoticed by telescopes on Earth and in space at the time.
NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), which has been studying the Moon since 2009, eventually revealed the impact. Automated comparisons of the spacecraft’s wide-angle images identified the new crater in August 2025, after which higher-resolution images confirmed the discovery.
Named for lunar scientist Thomas McGetchin, the crater is about three times wider than the previous record-holder found by LRO. It is also estimated to be only about 132 years per event, making such an impact exceptionally rare.
The collision dramatically reshaped the surrounding surface. Researchers found that dust and rocks were thrown farther and at higher angles than some models predicted, with changes extending more than 1,000 crater radii.
Another study detected a 6.4-kilometer-wide (4-mile-wide) region around the crater with altered thermal properties, suggesting that the impact loosened and disturbed the Moon’s upper soil, or regolith, according to CBS News.
Scientists say the discovery provides a rare opportunity to improve models of lunar impacts and surface evolution. It could also have practical implications for future astronauts.
NASA plans to study how far material ejected by impacts can travel, information that could help engineers design and protect future lunar habitats.
The findings also suggest the Moon’s surface changes faster than previously thought, meaning historic footprints left by Apollo astronauts may eventually be buried or erased by the continual “gardening” of lunar soil.

President Donald Trump said he hoped the seven-month war with Iran was nearing an end as the conflict escalated, with Saudi aircraft striking Yemen and Houthi fighters launching drones and missiles at Saudi cities.
The Iran-backed Houthis' lightning advance in Yemen along the Red Sea, their attacks on Saudi Arabia and damage to Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline have extended Tehran's reach in the war and heightened global oil supply risks.
As the war expands into a new theater, the U.S. tightened its travel warning for Saudi Arabia, banning government employees from traveling within 30 kilometers (20 miles) of the Yemen border.
Still, just hours after reports of fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, Trump told reporters Wednesday evening: "Hopefully we are toward the end of the war."
Referring to Iran, he said: "They want to make a deal. We'll see how that works out." He also said he had heard directly from Iran, without elaborating, reiterating previous comments.
Trump has offered shifting goals and timelines for the war, which began Feb. 28 when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran and Tehran struck Israel and U.S. bases in Gulf states.
The war's extension into Yemen threatens to worsen the global energy supply shortage caused by the conflict, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The strait carried about 20% of global oil and LNG before the conflict.
Traders say a prolonged closure of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline could cut off as much as 4% of global oil supply. Saudi Arabia has not said when operations might resume.
The price of Brent crude hovered about $108 a barrel Wednesday, close to its highest levels since May. The politically sensitive average retail price of diesel fuel in the U.S. hit another record high, above $6.30 a gallon for the first time.
But oil prices fell in early Thursday trading as reports that Saudi Arabia was offering extra crude cargoes through Oman reduced fears of supply disruptions in the Middle East.
Brent crude futures dropped $1.24, or 1.2%, to $104.59 a barrel by 0049 GMT, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were down $1.14, or 1.1%, at $101.29.
The rise in oil and gas prices due to the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran has become a major issue for Trump's Republican Party in the run-up to the November midterm elections.
Axios reported late Wednesday that Trump was expected to meet Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly next Tuesday to discuss the next steps in the conflict.
Citing unidentified sources, the news outlet said Trump would meet with leaders or foreign ministers from the Gulf Cooperation Council countries: Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman. The State Department and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.
The Houthis Wednesday released battlefield video of fighters seizing armored vehicles from Saudi-backed forces. The video also showed warplanes flying overhead and huge explosions billowing into the sky from desert dunes.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said his group had launched new drone and missile strikes on the major Saudi Red Sea oil port of Yanbu and at a southern Saudi airbase at Khamis Mushait. He did not say when the strikes took place.
Saree said Saudi forces had carried out as many as 450 airstrikes on Yemen this week. Officials in the Saudi-backed government controlling southern Yemen acknowledged their forces and Saudi Arabia's forces were conducting airstrikes on Houthi positions, though Riyadh has not confirmed them.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015. The conflict had largely quieted under a cease-fire in recent years but reignited when the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in July and fired at southern areas in the kingdom.

U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened action against the EU if it moves forward with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal to make Canada the bloc's first associate member.
"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina, calling the proposal "laughable."
"If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe," he added.
The European Commission said von der Leyen's proposal – which is yet to be fleshed out and will need to be approved by EU member states to go forward – was not a hostile act.
"As our President (von der Leyen) made clear yesterday, the proposed strengthening of our partnership with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength," said Olof Gill, a European Commission spokesperson.
France's Europe Minister Benjamin Haddad said the United States has no power to veto the EU's geopolitical choices.
"It is not up to the United States – or anyone else – to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans," he told Public Senat TV.
Von der Leyen made the proposal Wednesday during her annual State of the Union speech, attended by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, as she sought to deepen ties among allies in what she called "an openly hostile world."
The EU faces the risk of war on its borders due to Russia's invasion of Ukraine, while both the bloc and Canada have grappled with trade tensions with the United States and an increasingly assertive China.
Earlier this month, Carney had said he was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU as relations between Ottawa and Washington have deteriorated since Trump's return to the White House, leading to tariffs on tens of billions of dollars in cross-border trade.
It is unclear at this stage whether von der Leyen's proposal of associate membership would be backed by EU member states or by Canada.
One EU diplomat expressed surprise Wednesday at the proposal, saying "nobody really knows what it means," adding there were concerns that the European Commission chief "is overpromising and won't be able to deliver." The EU has historically resisted such flexible alliances that have no legal status.
On Thursday, another European diplomat called it an "unfortunate proposal, which has never been discussed with Member States."
A third European diplomat said Trump's reaction said more about how he views international relations than about von der Leyen's proposal.
"If this is described as a hostile act, it suggests that partnerships are a zero-sum game where closer cooperation with one means loss of sovereign choice for another," the diplomat said. "And it also hints that the U.S. sees Canada as part of its sphere of influence rather than an independent actor."
Another European diplomat added: "It’s a good thing that we learned in the meantime to not take every statement of President Trump seriously."

Lockheed hopes to sell a new F-16 to U.S. Air Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:11:22 UTC
17:11:22 KST

Lockheed Martin is pitching the U.S. Air Force on a new version of the F-16 fighter, designated the F-16G, as a way to replace aging Fighting Falcons faster than the F-35 production line can keep up.
Multiple people familiar with the aircraft told Aviation Week that the F-16G builds on the current Block 70 F-16, Lockheed’s newest production version, and would add conformal fuel tanks, 600-gallon wing tanks, an infrared search and track pod, a Sniper targeting pod and a drag chute. Those additions would extend the jet’s range and give it added sensor capability compared with earlier F-16 models still flying in Air Force squadrons.
The idea of buying new F-16s to fill out the fighter fleet is not new. Then-Air Force Assistant Secretary for Acquisition Will Roper raised the option back in 2021, pointing to the active F-16 production line in Greenville, South Carolina, as a way to add capacity while the F-35 program worked through its own delivery pace. Lockheed builds F-16s and F-35s at separate facilities, but the F-35’s more complex production process has left the Air Force short of new airframes to replace F-16s reaching the end of their service lives.
Lockheed Martin would not confirm details about the F-16G when asked on Sept. 16. The company said only that it remains ready to support the Air Force’s mission needs and described its aircraft as central to the service’s fleet. The Air Force likewise declined to comment on the F-16G specifically, saying it is still in the early stages of reviewing options for its next Future Years Defense Program and has not yet settled on requirements.
The push comes after a 2025 Air Force study identified a need for more fighter production to close a growing capacity gap. The Congressional Research Service says the service wants to grow its fighter inventory from 1,098 aircraft in fiscal 2026 to 1,558 by fiscal 2035, a target the Air Force has described as necessary to keep risk to its operations at an acceptable level under the National Military Strategy.
Other outlets have reported similar signals in recent months. Inside Defense reported in December 2025 that the Air Force was considering a new F-16 variant as a lower-cost way to fill capability gaps than buying more F-35s, and Air and Space Forces Magazine has reported that the F-16G is expected to come up for discussion at an upcoming Corona conference, the periodic gathering of the service’s top generals.
Neither the Air Force nor Lockheed Martin has said when a decision on the F-16G might come, or how many aircraft such a program could involve.

US Congress passes broad new sanctions bill to pressure Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:11:00 UTC
17:11:00 KST

U.S. lawmakers approved sweeping new sanctions Wednesday to pressure Russia over its war in Ukraine, sending the legislation to President Donald Trump after months of delay.
The Republican-led House of Representatives passed the package 262-159, giving final congressional approval to the most substantial U.S. legislative effort against Moscow since Trump returned to office.
Trump has said he will sign the measure, which cleared the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month.
The legislation targets Russia's energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow's so-called shadow fleet of tankers circumventing Western sanctions.
It also gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, including potentially China and India, to choke off revenue for Moscow's war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed the legislation's passage as "symbolic" and thanked U.S. lawmakers.
The bill is "an extremely powerful tool that can stop this terrorist war and bring Russia to the point where it has to make peace," Zelenskyy wrote in a statement.
"Sanctions must be strong so that all efforts for peace, including our joint diplomatic efforts with the United States, Europe, and our other friends, can succeed," he added.
The bill would also target companies and foreign actors supporting Russia's military and extend sanctions involving Iran.
India said Thursday it would continue buying oil "through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics."
Moscow is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners and military suppliers.
The legislation's sweeping tariff powers produced an unusual split among Democrats, who overwhelmingly support Ukraine but have resisted handing Trump greater authority over trade.
Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called the bill "deeply flawed."
"White House lawyers drafted the current text to maximize President Trump's authority to impose new import taxes on the American people, and to minimize any obligation to impose new sanctions on Russia or its enablers," he said.
Dozens of Democrats nevertheless backed the measure, offsetting opposition from a handful of Republicans who objected to sanctions on free-market or non-interventionist grounds.
Supporters argue that tougher economic pressure is needed, with Russia's full-scale invasion now in its fifth year and no peace settlement in sight.
Pro-Ukraine activists celebrated the House vote, pointing to continuing Russian attacks, including drone strikes Wednesday on civilian transport in the south that officials in Kyiv said killed five people.
Trump has generally preferred to retain control over sanctions and tariffs rather than have Congress dictate policy, which helped delay the measure for more than a year.
Its sponsor, Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly in July, had pushed the legislation since April 2025.
Wednesday's vote came just before House lawmakers were to leave Washington to campaign ahead of November's midterm elections.
"Once the bill is quickly signed and becomes law, we hope for strong U.S. enforcement to finally end the cash flows to the Kremlin's war chest," said Svitlana Romanko, executive director of Ukrainian energy lobby group Razom We Stand.
"Every day of delay is a day we in Ukraine must bury more people."

However, Poland’s security services minister Tomasz Siemoniak met CIA director John Ratcliffe last week, just days after his much-discussed trip to Russia.
Poland’s defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz is also planning to go to the US next week for urgent talks with US defence secretary Pete Hegseth.
Make of that what you will.
Tusk and other key ministers also repeatedly quoted Polish intelligence agencies in the past, whether in response to repeated security incidents, airspace provocations near Poland, or arrests of people suspected of planning acts of sabotage on behalf of Russian intelligence services.
Poland will face 'provocations ... far more dangerous that those we have faced so far,' Tusk warns
Tusk also warned right-wing opposition parties that “inciting hostility towards the European Union, towards our allies and towards Ukrainians is simply implementing Russia’s strategy.”
“Everyone must finally understand this,” he says.
Going back to security threats, he says that while “there is nothing to suggest an invasion,” Poland will “have to pass a very serious test, because we will certainly be the target of provocations and incidents far more dangerous than those we have faced so far.”
He ends his speech with a plea to the parliament:
“So we must pass this test – all of us, both politicians and the nation as a whole.
That is why I will appeal to all of you, without exception, that wherever the issue concerns the security of our borders, the airspace over Poland, or the safety of our homes, we must speak with one voice, take joint decisions, not hesitate … The nation will truly hold us all, without exception, to account for this.”
Some politicians 'just looking for excuses' to not defend Poland, Latvia, Lithuania, Tusk warns
Tusk also talks about Poland’s absolute resolve to defence all other Nato countries.
He says “this is very important, because as. a border country … we are likely to need allied loyalty under Article 5 more than Portugal or Ireland.”
He continues:
“It is not the case that all politicians in the west, in the United States or in Europe, are thinking about how to defend Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, and that they are all eager to prove immediately that they are staunch allies and will come to our aid under Article 5.
Far from all of them. There are many politicians, as well as political forces, which are currently gaining in strength and influence in European countries, who are just looking for an excuse: we won’t die for Poland; we won’t die for Latvia or Lithuania.”
He says that’s why Poland must be very openly ready to follow through on its allied commitments.
“Article 5, loyalty within the alliance, and faithfulness to our commitments must become our hallmark,” he says.
Tusk says Russia is not prepared or willing to get involved in any serious discussions about ending its aggression against Ukraine “at least until the end of winter.”
“They are convinced that this winter will be a time of dire crisis for Ukraine,” he says.
Intelligence shows Russian 'plans for hybrid strikes ... against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,' Tusk says
Tusk says that intelligence assessments show “plans for hybrid strikes using drones and missiles against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland”.
He says the latest intelligence on this is “very consistent and convincing”.
He says that Russia is expected to pretend that any incidents are “accidental” in a bid to “paralyse or at least weaken Nato’s resolve to invoke the relevant provisions” of the Nato treaty.
“There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles could be launched into the territory of one or more Nato countries on the eastern flank, and could even cause damage, and the official narrative will be that this is an accident and that there is no reason for anyone to consider any response from Nato.
The aim … will be to weaken Nato’s integrity in general and, above all, to convince … member states that Article 5 is more theoretical than practical – that is, the assumption that no one will want to die for Latvia or Lithuania, given that we are dealing with incidents rather than a declaration of war.”
He says he expects Russia to use “recurrent” incidents to use them as “an increasingly stark illustration of Nato’s helplessness” to respond in a united manner.
Coming autumn, winter will be 'most critical moment' in Russian war against Ukraine, Tusk says
Tuskis now speaking in Polish parliament,speaking about what he believes Poland and Ukraine’s other allies should be expecting in the coming months as Russia ramps up pressure and threats against Nato.
He says he wants to outline “the most likely scenario for the next few months, as it is a scenario involving serious events and one that requires us to be focused, serious and, above all, mentally prepared to face difficult challenges.”
He says “late autumn and winter” are expected to be “the most critical moment” in the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine so far.
Tusk noted that Russia is increasing its attacks using jet-powered drones, which he believes “very few [countries] are currently prepared to effectively counter.”
“Russia’s objective today is to destroy Ukraine’s economy and logistics on as large a scale as possible. … Ukraine is expected to face constant strikes of very high frequency and intensity. This includes the six main Ukrainian cities, with the destruction of warehouses containing all types of products essential, first and foremost, for the country’s defence, as well as – as we have witnessed in recent weeks – very severe damage to the railway infrastructure.”
'If anyone dares to attack us, they will face a resolute response from us and allies,' Poland's Tusk says
Meanwhile, Polish prime minister Donald Tusk warned that “if anyone dares to attack us, they will face a resolute response from us and our allies,” as he responded to growing tensions and aggression from Russia.
In a sombre speech marking the 87th anniversary of the 1939 Soviet invasion of Poland, Tusk said he would “prefer to speak only about the heroic deeds recorded in the history books,” but “Russia’s escalating aggression is not letting me do that.”
“History, as we know, does not repeat itself, but it does rhyme, and we must interpret these rhymes of history today with due seriousness,” he said.
Responding to recent Russian incidents in and around Poland – including last year’s drone incursion into Poland, a Russian missile straying into Poland in July, and recent incidents at the Polish-Ukrainian border – Tusk insisted that Warsaw “will not be intimidated.”
“Russia does not need to cross our border. It is already waging a hybrid war against us using drones, acts of sabotage and disinformation on the internet. We know from our allies that the coming months may bring further provocations,” he said.
He said he was “neither afraid nor naive” about the dangers posed by Russia.
In a strong speech, he continued:
“I am from Gdańsk. In May 1939, a certain French politician – a future Nazi collaborator – asked in the French press why anyone should die for Gdańsk. A few months later, the whole of Europe was dying.
To those who say today that this is not our war, I would like to remind them of this lesson from history. In 1939, our alliances existed only on paper, really. We were left on our own. Today, we are members of Nato and the European Union.”
We spend almost 5% of our GDP on defence. This is almost twice as much as Germany and twice as much as France. We are building one of the strongest armies in Europe; we secured €44bn from the EU’s SAFE programme, the most from all EU countries. And Polish borders are today the best marked borders on the entire continent.
Europe, which in 1939 did not want to die for Gdańsk, today funds Polish armaments.
But we are aware that even the largest army is not enough if the nation is not ready.
Therefore, I address all those who look at the future with anxiety:
We are not seeking war, but if anyone dares to attack us, they will face a resolute response from us and our allies. Long live a free and secure Republic of Poland.”
He is also speaking in the Polish parliament now, promising to set out further details on the threats facing Poland.
Germany, US sign 'letter of intent' on close defence cooperation, despite previous clashes
Kate Connolly
Berlin correspondent
Following months during which the German government has sought to convince the public that militarily (and otherwise) Germany must stop relying on its erstwhile trustworthy partner, the United States, due to the erratic, rude and unruly behaviour of its president, the defence ministers of both countries signed a “letter of intent” this week, signaling close cooperation after all.
Germany’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, visibly surprised at the warm reception he received in Washington earlier this week, said after his first meeting with US war minister Pete Hegseth he had only heard warm words of praise for Berlin over its contribution to joint defence goals.
This was in sharp contrast to the bitter tirade Hegseth had delivered to European defence ministers just weeks ago, accusing them of abandoning the US in the Iran war, or to the message disseminated by president Trump earlier this year when he announced the withdrawal of thousands of US troops who are stationed in Germany, in what was interpreted as a clear snub to Berlin.
At a time of dwindling military stocks – the US looking at its war against Iran, Germany, focused mainly on helping to defend Ukraine - the counterparts’ intention, so the letter states, is for “enhanced bilateral cooperation in the defence sector to support transatlantic industrial production and maintenance capacities” and although using slightly wishy-washy terminology, it suggests quite a political U-turn.
From accepting that the Trump administration had mentally withdrawn itself from Nato, and Berlin should become more independent from Washington as a result, the government of Friedrich Merz has now signed up to the statement “Germany and the United States agree that the current political challenges require a robust and mutually beneficial, closely integrated defence industry base on both sides of the Atlantic,” as the declaration reads.
The powerful industries of both countries “can and should” complement each other more closely in the future in the production of “state of the art” weapons systems, components and complex munitions.
Pistorius has sought to play down accusations that this is a contradiction, painting it instead as a pragmatic and direct reaction to current tensions. (What we sometimes refer to as Realpolitik.)
Today he will take delivery of F-35 fighter jets manufactured for Germany’s armed forces in Texas, before heading home tomorrow.
Romanian EU lawmaker Siegfried Muresan proposed as Romania's next prime minister
Sweden is not the only European country working to change its prime minister.
Following a day of consultations with political leaders, Romania’s president, Nicușor Dan, has nominated EU lawmaker Siegfried Mureșan to become the next prime minister.
Romania has had a caretaker government since early May, when prime minister Ilie Bolojan lost a vote of confidence in parliament.
“Romania needs a government,” Dan said, adding that “people’s lives depend on it.”
However, he acknowledged that none of the prospective candidates can currently command a clear majority in parliament, as political parties remain cannot agree on the way forward.
Dan said he had seen “a great deal of concern amongst the parties about the elections and far less concern for national interest.”
He added that Mureșan, 44, had the necessary experience to take on the role and attempt to break the political deadlock.
The MEP has been a member of the European parliament since 2014. Born to German and Romanian parents, he is also a vice-president of the centre-right European People’s Party, the European parliament’s largest grouping.
Elsewhere, the EU and China are continuing efforts to avert a trade war after an hour long call between EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart Wang Wengtao.
The EU reiterated the need to move from “rhetoric to results” with a “credible” solution that will curb China’s growing €1bn a day surplus in trade with the bloc.
Extensive work mapping the potential safeguards including quotas and price floors and possible retaliatory measures by the Chines have already been carried out in advance of Sefcovic’s planned meeting with Wang on 8 October.
A spokesperson said the call lasted more than an hour and took stock of the work carried out by officials so far covering the management of Chinese exports to the EU, the EU’s access to the Chinese market and export controls on rare earths.
Restrictions on exports of rare earths were imposed by Beijing in April 2025 but were suspended for a year last November after Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Xingping in Korea last October.
Experts expect that suspension to continue after the Trump Xi summit next week in Washington but the EU will be pushing for a crave out for the bloc.
“While genuine engagement remains a priority, it is equally important that first concrete outcomes are delivered at the second session of the Trade and Investment Council in Beijing in Cotober which the commissioner will co-chair – a signal that we are moving from rhetoric to results,” said the EU’s deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill.
Centre party leader thanks outgoing PM, says will be 'a constructive force' to keep government 'rooted in the centre'

Speaking about what’s next, she added:
“Now Sweden is entering a new political phase. The Centre party will be a constructive force to ensure Sweden gets a functioning government with a policy rooted in the centre.”
What that will actually mean in practice, we will have to wait and see.

The current parliament speaker Andreas Norlén is also hoping to individually speak with party leaders tomorrow, SVT said, getting ahead of the formal schedule (14:10).
Right-leaning bloc 'ready to continue governing Sweden if they fail,' liberal leader says
Liberal party leader Simona Mohamsson praised Kristersson’s time in government, saying he led “Sweden’s most liberal government ever,” and hailing what she sees as its successes on education and crime.
Her Liberal party, part of the outgoing government led by Ulf Kristersson, cleared the 4% threshold into the new parliament with 5.3% of the vote last Sunday.
Mohamsson thanked Kristersson for “four important years,” and giving Sweden “a fresh start when it needed it the most.”
“Now it is up to Magdalena Andersson to show whether she can put together any government foundation from the opposition’s mixed bag of left socialists, cultural relativists, and Centre Party members. My teammates to the right and I stand ready to continue governing Sweden if they fail,” she said, echoing the sentiment expressed by Kristersson earlier (13:57).
Christian Democrat leader Ebba Busch also posted a message in a similar tone, conceding the result, but praising the outgoing government’s track record.
“At present, there is no one who commands a majority in the parliament. The red-greens have not automatically won the government power. Various parties’ red lines before election day can lead to a complicated government formation,” she said.
Similar to Kristersson earlier, she also hinted at possible alternative majorities formed along the economic policy lines.
Sweden's election winner Andersson vows to 'move Sweden forward'
Meanwhile, the leader of the left-wing bloc that won Sweden’s election, Magdalena Andersson, vowed Thursday to lead the country in a “new direction” after four years of right-wing rule backed by the far right.
“The Swedish people have voted for a new direction for our country. Voted for unity and against division. The Swedish people have voted to move Sweden forward, and I want to realise the new direction that you have voted for,” she said in a speech posted on social media.
In the address, recorded in a prime ministerial aesthetics and with a Swedish flag in the background, she said she wanted to lead Sweden “away from conflicts from the sake of conflicts, and in a direction based on unity” between key parties as political talks about the new government are set to begin.
“It is up to all political parties to put the party politics aside and put Sweden and the Swedish people first,” she said.
She also talked about priorities on climate, schools, health care, and social care as examples of areas where she wanted to change the government’s policy.
Kristersson's language suggests he still hopes left-leaning bloc will fail to form government - snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
It’s worth noting that the language used by Kristersson in his resignation letter – particularly a reference to irreconcilable differences in the various parties’ stated positions (13:57) – is not accidental.
The left-leaning bloc – led by former prime minister Magdalena Andersson and her Social Democrats - consists of four parties, and there are significant friction points between them, particularly between the Left Party and the Centre Party.
The Centre Party had previously suggested it would not accept ministers from the Left; the Left, particularly now emboldened by its strong election result, is unlikely to agree to no top jobs in a government it is expected to support.
If either party drops out of the arrangement, the bloc will struggle to form a government, as there are no viable alternatives.
But their voters generally expect them to work together.
And a leading figure from the Centre Party implied on Monday (Europe Live, Monday) that they could probably find a way of working with the Left, confirming the party would take part in exploratory talks led by the Social Democrats.
Still, the discussions are likely to be tricky and could take weeks before they agree on a path forward.
Outgoing PM Kristersson is clearly hoping those discussions fail.
His supporters repeatedly pointed out before the election that you could often see the four leaders of the four right-leaning parties in his bloc together – in fact, they also had a dinner together Monday night – and they marketed themselves a “stable” arrangement that was sort of ready to go.
But same didn’t really apply for the red bloc amid some apparent internal divisions between the leaders, leaving lots of questions mark to solve only now.
Kristersson appears to be keen to exploit some of these differences.
On election night, he suggested forming an alternative coalition against socialist economic policies – widely interpreted as an attempt to woo the Centre Party back to his side.
Even then, huge questions remain over how he could secure a majority without the far-right Sweden Democrats, an option that remains unacceptable to centrists.
Expect these talks to pick up speed now that we have the official results – and a looming vacancy at the top.
Timeline for next steps after Kristersson's resignation - snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
In terms of next steps, there is a bit of time before the formal process of electing the new prime minister will get under way.
The new Riksdag is expected to convene on 28 September and elect its speaker on the same day.
The new prime minister can be proposed the next day, 29 September. That leaves just under two weeks for informal talks between now and then, and Kristersson will stay in post until a new PM is picked.
As explained in our live blog on Sunday, Sweden has a slightly unusual system of “negative parliamentarism,” which means that “if there’s a prime minister proposed, then if there is the absence of an absolute majority in parliament against the proposal, it’s interpreted as support.”
As Nicholas AylottofSödertörn University explained it to me on Sunday:
“So a party that doesn’t really want to give full support to this proposed candidate – maybe because it’s not going to be part of the coalition, but which can just about live with it, and doesn’t have a better alternative – it can abstain from the vote, and that’s counted as passive support. This makes it much easier to form minority governments.”
Meanwhile, Swedish public broadcaster SVT reported that just before Kristersson’s statement was published online, someone brought four cakes into the Social Democrat’s HQ in central Stockholm.
Guess we now know the reasons behind the delivery.
Swedish PM Kristersson resigns after election defeat
And in the last few minute, Sweden’s prime minister Ulf Kristersson has resigned from the post after official results confirmed that his right-leaning bloc lost last Sunday’s parliamentary election.
The four left-leaning parties, with former prime minister Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats as the largest party, won by just 50,359 votes, the final count showed.
The four left-leaning bloc will have 176 seats in the new parliament to 173 for Kristersson’s three-party coalition government and the far-right Sweden Democrats who were expected to join the administration after the vote, the Tidö bloc.
In a letter posted on X, Kristersson said that following the tight election results “may have complicated the conditions for the new government to be formed” with contradicting statements from different parties on their positions.
“Constructive openness from the parties in parliament will now be needed for a prime minister to be accepted, and for a new government to be able to receive support for its state budget.”
“Discussions will need to be held with all parties to find ways around these deadlocks and to create the conditions for a stable and effective government.
“It is the speaker who will lead the next steps towards forming a new government. In order for that work to begin immediately, I hereby request to be relieved of my duties as prime minister.”

Swiss Senate rejects tax on short-haul flights

Swiss Senate rejects tax on short-haul flights
The Swiss Senate does not want a tax on short-haul flights. On Wednesday, it voted 20 to 17 against taking forward an initiative from the canton of Basel-City to that effect.
While temperatures soared this summer, the country’s airports also reported record passenger numbers in July, noted parliamentarian Maya Graf from the Green party.
She added that air traffic causes noise pollution for local residents. In the densely populated Basel metropolitan area, many people are affected on a daily basis by Basel-Mulhouse Airport. However, some of these flights bring no significant added value to the region’s economy, tourism or leisure sector. An incentive tax on airline tickets for short-haul flights would help reduce unnecessary flights.
The cantonal initiative proposed defining the routes concerned on the basis of whether destinations were reasonably accessible by rail, rather than on the basis of a fixed number of kilometres.
More
A Swiss initiative wants flyers to fund trains
Speaking on behalf of the committee, Severin Brüngger from the Radical Liberal party expressed doubts about the measure’s effectiveness. Passengers would simply be likely to switch to airports in neighbouring countries, in particular Basel-Mulhouse Airport (EuroAirport). What is needed instead are measures coordinated at the international level.
Admittedly, international coordination is needed for kerosene taxation, but using this argument to oppose Swiss measures does not hold water. France has banned short-haul flights and Belgium has introduced a tax on flights of less than 500 km. This shows that it is possible for a country to take action, countered Eva Herzog from the Social Democratic party, to no avail.
The House has yet to give its verdict.
The senators subsequently rejected a petition calling for a ban on private jets in Switzerland.

UN mission finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran, and Tehran crimes against humanity
